papers.title: Detectability of Seyfert galaxies in point-source and stacking searches with a global network of neutrino telescopes
papers.abstract: Recent evidence for high-energy neutrino emission from NGC 1068 and other nearby Seyfert galaxies suggests that active galactic nuclei (AGNs) may constitute a class of astrophysical neutrino sources. Using a physically motivated neutrino emission model based on stochastic particle acceleration in magnetized AGN coronae, we investigate the detection prospects of X-ray-bright Seyfert galaxies with a detector network comprising IceCube, Baikal-GVD, KM3NeT/ARCA, and P-ONE. We find that the Circinus Galaxy is the most promising point-source target in the Southern sky and will be detected at the 5$\sigma$ level by 2038 at the latest, provided that the Seyfert population accounts for the diffuse astrophysical neutrino flux up to 100 TeV and Circinus is at least as efficient a neutrino emitter as the average source in the population. Individual detections of other nearby Seyferts are expected to remain challenging, making stacking searches informed by X-ray observations the most promising approach for discovering them within the next decade. Our results demonstrate that joint analyses across multiple neutrino telescopes, together with future MeV gamma-ray observations, will be essential for establishing Seyfert galaxies as astrophysical neutrino sources and provide a means for testing the coronal origin of their neutrino emission.

papers.intro:
The evidence for high-energy neutrino emission from the nearby Seyfert galaxy NGC 1068 presented by the IceCube Collaboration [2] has opened a promising new direction in the search for the sources of astrophysical neutrinos. Subsequent studies have highlighted Seyfert galaxies as a potentially significant source class in the TeV energy range, and recent stacking analyses in both the Northern and Southern skies have further explored their collective contribution [3, 4]. The observations of NGC 1068 and the absence of accompanying TeV γ\gamma-ray emission, despite its neutrino signal, suggest that the neutrinos originate from a “hidden” environment where high-energy photons are efficiently absorbed. This behavior is naturally accommodated in models in which particle acceleration and hadronic interactions occur in the corona of the active galactic nucleus (AGN) close to the supermassive black hole (SMBH) [43, 39]. If confirmed as a neutrino-emitting source class, Seyfert galaxies would provide a unique probe of particle acceleration and radiation processes in the immediate vicinity of actively accreting black holes, with important implications for multi-messenger astrophysics.

The potential contribution of Seyfert galaxies to the diffuse astrophysical neutrino flux has been investigated in several different studies, using a variety of modeling assumptions and generally finding results that are broadly consistent with the latest IceCube observations [42, 12, 25, 31, 40, 59, 53, 19]. In our previous work [50] (hereafter 50), we developed a physically motivated population model for neutrino emission from Seyfert galaxies based on stochastic proton acceleration in magnetized AGN coronae, in which the neutrino luminosity is tied to the intrinsic X-ray emission of each source. Our approach consistently combined a realistic coronal emission model with population synthesis and multi-messenger constraints. By fitting the public IceCube data for NGC 1068 and comparing the associated cascaded γ\gamma-ray emission to Fermi-LAT observations, we found that the neutrino-emitting region must be compact, with a characteristic coronal radius of Rc∼ 5​RSR_{c}\,{\sim}\,5\,R_{\mathrm{S}}. Similarly compact emission regions have since been inferred by Carpio et al. [19] for several nearby Seyfert galaxies. Extending our model to the full Seyfert population, we further showed that NGC 1068 cannot be representative of the broader source population. If all Seyferts shared the best-fit parameter values inferred for NGC 1068, their cumulative neutrino emission would exceed current constraints on the diffuse flux at TeV energies by 3.8​σ3.8\sigma. These results imply that those Seyfert galaxies that start to emerge as neutrino point sources must be exceptionally powerful neutrino emitters within a broader, less efficient population. Other works have come to similar conclusions, requiring a distribution of source parameters across the population [31], suppression factors [59, 53], or an X-ray luminosity function of neutrino-emitting AGNs that deviates from that of the full AGN population [19] in order to remain consistent with the observed diffuse neutrino flux.

These findings motivate a natural next step. If Seyfert galaxies are not uniformly efficient neutrino emitters, but instead comprise a population in which only a small fraction of sources resemble NGC 1068, what are the prospects for detecting them as a class? In this work, we address this question by using the physically constrained population model of 50 to forecast the detectability of Seyfert galaxies in both point-source and stacking searches, building on previous work that has highlighted the potential of stacking analyses to accelerate the discovery of populations of neutrino sources [32, 34, 15, e.g.,]. Rather than asking whether Seyfert galaxies can explain the observed diffuse flux, we investigate under what conditions individual sources and their collective emission can be identified with current and next-generation neutrino telescopes. We further explore the potential gains from combining observatories with complementary effective areas and sky coverage, as envisioned in future coordinated analyses [51, e.g.,]. Our approach places the neutrino emission scenario for Seyfert galaxies in a predictive framework, linking population-level constraints directly to concrete observational strategies.

In Section III, we introduce the present and future neutrino telescopes considered in this work and explain how we model their properties, while in Section IV, we explore the detectability of individual nearby Seyfert galaxies and discuss the role of MeV γ\gamma-ray observations as an independent probe of the coronal emission region. papers.title: A Counterexample to Polynomial Approximation for Monotone Weights
papers.abstract: We give a counterexample to a question of Borichev on polynomial approximation with monotone weights. We construct an even continuous weight $W$, strictly increasing on $[0,\infty)$, with superpolynomial growth and finite logarithmic integral, and an entire function $F$ of zero exponential type such that $F/W$ vanishes at infinity and belongs to $L^p(\mathbb{R})$ for every $1\leq p<\infty$. Nevertheless, $F$ has positive distance from the polynomials in the weighted uniform norm and in every corresponding weighted $L^{p}$ norm.

papers.title: Camera3R: Feed-Forward 3D Reconstruction from Heterogeneous Camera Models
papers.abstract: Feed-forward 3D reconstruction (3R) from unconstrained multi-view images has recently emerged as a prominent research direction in 3D computer vision. Various foundational reconstruction models have been proposed with different architectures and reconstruction paradigms. Despite being trained on large-scale perspective datasets with substantial computational resources, these models generally struggle to generalize to non-perspective images. This limitation hinders their deployment in applications involving arbitrary, unknown, and potentially heterogeneous camera models. To build on the capabilities of existing reconstruction models with minimal retraining, we propose Camera3R, a low-rank adaptation framework that efficiently extends perspective-pretrained 3R networks to any other camera models. Extensive experiments demonstrate that, with only 0.5% additional parameters and less than a day of training, Camera3R adapts a foundational 3D reconstruction model to non-perspective cameras while fully preserving its original performance on perspective inputs. Code is available at https://github.com/android-xr/camera3r.

papers.intro:
Three-dimensional (3D) visual mapping of an environment is a fundamental component in many spatial applications, ranging from autonomous navigation to extended reality systems. Decision-making within these applications rests on the fidelity of the map, e.g., accuracy of estimated points (and position and orientation of the platform), as well as completeness, or coverage, of the environment as observed by a set of cameras. In practice, the two metrics are not independently optimizable, but are coupled through sensing trade-offs. For a fixed sensing budget, a reduction in field-of-view (FoV) increases the angular resolution, which often results in higher fidelity estimates. On the other hand, an increase in FoV naturally improves environmental coverage, but typically introduces non-trivial lens distortion and measurement noise that degrade per-point accuracy. This trade-off motivates the use of multiple cameras, e.g., combinations of perspective and fisheye or panoramic (360∘) cameras, within a mixed-camera system whose cameras provide complementary fidelity and coverage.

While mixed-camera systems offer the potential to balance map fidelity and environmental coverage in 3D reconstruction, existing feed-forward 3D reconstruction models [26, 29, 15] cannot fully exploit the non-perspective or heterogeneous camera inputs. Despite being trained on large-scale datasets comprising tens of millions of images, these models cannot generalize to images captured by wide-FoV or mixed cameras. This failure mode can be attributed to a covariate shift between the training and deployment imaging platforms: The training data used by current feed-forward reconstruction models is predominantly composed of perspective images. In contrast, images captured by different camera models exhibit varying fields of view, resolutions, and distortion profiles, leading to heterogeneous photometric and spatial sampling statistics. Consequently, these models do not directly transfer to mixed-camera streams, limiting their potential to provide high-fidelity maps with broad environmental coverage, despite their strong generalization across diverse 3D scenes.

Consequently, these models do not directly transfer to mixed-camera streams, limiting their potential to provide high-fidelity maps with broad environmental coverage, despite their strong generalization across diverse 3D scenes.

A natural response to this limitation is to train separate 3D reconstruction models tailored to each camera type or imaging configuration, and subsequently register their outputs and combine them into a single map. However, such an approach would incur substantial operational overhead, and is poorly suited to spatial applications, which are often constrained by compute, memory, and overall system complexity. A key insight is that, despite differences in photometric and spatial sampling statistics due to the image formation process, images of the same 3D scene captured by different camera models should correspond to a single consistent environmental map. In other words, the heterogeneity in camera models may alter the observations, but not the underlying 3D structures being reconstructed. This intuition motivates our central thesis of whether a single feed-forward 3D reconstruction model trained primarily on images captured by perspective cameras can be systematically extended to operate on heterogeneous camera inputs without retraining from scratch.

To this end, we introduce Camera3R, a framework that enables a single feed-forward model to ingest images captured by multiple camera types to produce a consistent map. The crux of our method lies in selective adaptation to inputs during inference time through a mixture of experts. We assume access to a pretrained feed-forward model and that images can originate from a broad categorization of perspective, fisheye, and panoramic cameras. We associate each camera model with an expert, each parameterized by a set of weights. We begin by freezing the pretrained model; as it is pretrained on large-scale datasets of perspective images, we consider it an expert in itself. We surmise that the pretrained model has already learned sufficiently expressive features to model diverse 3D scenes and that the same features can be efficiently modulated, rather than relearned, to extend the pretrained model to accommodate alternative camera types. Accordingly, we introduce low-rank adaptation (LoRA) [11] to the network layers to yield experts for fisheye and panoramic cameras. However, it remains a question as to how much capacity should be allocated to each camera type to model specific distortions and viewing statistics. To address this, we employ a rank-truncation scheme that redistributes capacity by allocating higher ranks to layer-expert pairs based on need, allowing us to leverage the existing knowledge to its full extent while adding minimal overhead in parameters to the model. The result is an efficient model unified across cameras that can be trained with an order of magnitude less data than the base model itself.

In most spatial applications, the origin of the camera data stream is known; therefore, expert selection based on camera identity is sufficient to adaptively run inference on each image. Nonetheless, to accommodate general usage, we propose to learn a camera router which determines the expert to use for modulating latent features. Hence, at test time, we do not assume access to camera metadata and can handle inputs of any single camera type, as well as a collection of images originating from a mixture of heterogeneous cameras. This design naturally enables backward compatibility, where the generalizability and performance of existing feed-forward 3D reconstruction models are preserved. At the same time, new cameras can be introduced into an existing platform to improve both map fidelity and environmental coverage, and be accommodated without disruption to established workflows. We evaluate our method on multiple 3D reconstruction datasets, spanning indoor and outdoor environments. In single-camera settings, our method achieves a significant improvement over the baseline methods and fully preserves performance on perspective images. We further demonstrate that, in mixed-camera scenarios, our approach can handle a collection of images originating from any of the cameras from a heterogeneous set without prior knowledge of their identity to yield consistent and high-fidelity reconstructions. Our method is applied to three different feed-forward 3D reconstruction models to demonstrate its generalizability.

papers.title: Exploring Synchrony for Communication in Modular Neural Networks
papers.abstract: One motivation for modular neural networks is to divide computation across components that learn distinct, reusable functions, which could then be recombined to support compositional generalisation. In practice, modular structure alone does not guarantee that such roles develop, and unrestricted communication between modules can undermine any specialisation that does emerge. This raises the question of how modular communication should be organised. The problem can be viewed as an analogue of the perceptual binding problem, where synchrony has been proposed as a mechanism for coordinating distributed representations. We introduce SyncNet, a modular architecture that separates module content from a dynamical phase state: learnt Kuramoto dynamics evolve the phases, while phase alignment determines communication through a shared channel. We evaluate SyncNet on Sort-of-CLEVR for relational reasoning and on SQOOP for systematic generalisation, where lower pair variety demands more recombination at test time. SyncNet gives the best held-out accuracy of the models compared at the three lowest pair varieties, by 5.1 percentage points at the hardest, and is competitive on Sort-of-CLEVR though below the strongest attention baselines. Test-time overrides show that performance depends on phases that evolve: fixed phases cost as much as no addressing at all, and permuting which module holds which region is nearly as damaging. A content-addressed variant trained from scratch nonetheless matches it, so the benefit appears to come from the modular decomposition rather than synchrony itself.

papers.title: Spatial-Spectral Coupling as Attention: Scaling Shape Correspondence to High-Resolution Surfaces
papers.abstract: Establishing dense correspondence between high-resolution 3D shapes remains challenging due to the spatial--spectral coupling at the core of many functional-map methods, which grows quadratically with mesh resolution. We observe that this coupling is equivalent to a scaled dot-product attention formulation, with learned descriptors serving as queries and keys and spectral basis functions as values. This connection makes efficient attention implementations directly applicable to shape matching and an effective mechanism for scaling spatial-spectral coupling. We show that optimized quadratic attention implementations can scale modern deep functional map pipelines to large mesh sizes, improving both runtime and memory consumption, while sub-quadratic methods introduce errors, particularly for non-isometric shape pairs, where an exact coupling proves most necessary. These insights motivate \textit{Geo-FlashAttention}, which restricts the exact softmax to geometry-selected surface patches and achieves near-linear empirical scaling while preserving correspondence accuracy of exact implementations. Across six standard benchmarks and three functional-map pipelines, rigorous analysis shows that efficient couplings preserve correspondence accuracy. At $60k$ vertices, these insights reduce peak training memory from 106.08 to 5.67\,GiB, with Geo-FlashAttention being $1.5\times$ faster per training step than FlashAttention. This enables end-to-end learning for correspondence problems on large meshes such as cortical surfaces, where high resolution is required to preserve disease-relevant intricacies of the surface geometry. Project page available https://spatial-spectral-attention.github.io/

papers.intro:
Large-scale 3D meshes with tens of thousands of vertices are often required to represent whole-body avatars or complex anatomical shapes such as cortical surfaces (see Fig. 1). Establishing fine-grained correspondences between such shapes is a crucial prerequisite for geometry-aware analysis and processing, enabling applications such as avatar animation [41], motion transfer [60], and shape editing [59] in computer graphics, as well as intersubject comparison of anatomical variability in biomedical imaging [29, 10, 68, 5]. In particular, accurate correspondences enable the transformation of information across shape instances, allowing local geometric and semantic attributes to be transferred, compared, and statistically analyzed despite substantial variability in shape, pose, or topology [26, 23].

papers.title: From Attack Surface to Defense Architecture: Compositional Security for Agentic Coding Harnesses
papers.abstract:
AI coding harnesses couple language models to shells, filesystems, and network sockets, turning the harness into an automated Living-off-the-Land (LotL) platform: once an adversary injects instructions into retrieved content, dual-use binaries such as bash, curl, and find become the payload. We argue that security in agentic systems is a structural property of the cognitive architecture and permission composition rather than an emergent property of individual models. Static regex blacklists miss structural evasions, whereas LLM-as-a-Judge guardrails incur high latency while over-blocking benign work.
  We present ActiveSecHarness, a neurosymbolic reference-monitor architecture built around Separation of Intelligence and Authority. It combines (1) Macaroon-inspired HMAC capability tokens across four Trust and Authority Rings, (2) a 2D product taint lattice $\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{trust}} \times \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sens}}$ and a workspace provenance ledger that prevents secret laundering across disk, (3) deterministic Ring-0 OS/tool guards, and (4) bytecode certificates, split-horizon audit logs, self-healing security test synthesis, and an adaptive UserWikiManager.
  Across $N=252$ fixtures ($120$ attack, $120$ benign, $12$ kill chains), a live local LLM judge (qwen3:4b) refuses $98.3\%$ of benign work at $142.3\,\mathrm{ms}$ latency, whereas Ring 0 achieves $\mathrm{ABR}=1.000$ and $\mathrm{FPR}=0.000$ in $12.7\,\mu\mathrm{s}$ ($11{,}200\times$ faster). In a multi-step trajectory ablation, an oracle Conseca-style stateless policy misses $4/12$ kill chains ($\mathrm{ABR}=0.667$) and coarse Boolean taint blocks $83.3\%$ of benign workflows, while our 2D product lattice achieves $\mathrm{ABR}=1.000$ and $\mathrm{FPR}=0.000$ at $\approx 20\,\mu\mathrm{s}$ per step.

papers.intro:
Coding agents are useful because they act. Systems such as SWE-agent couple a language model to an agent–computer interface that edits files, navigates repositories, and runs tests and other programs (Yang et al., 2024, p. 1). OpenHands goes further, equipping agents with “a docker-sandboxed operating system with a bash shell, a web browser, and IPython server” (Wang et al., 2025, p. 2). Cybersecurity agents make the same design choice in offensive form: Fang et al. give agents a terminal and a Python interpreter so that tools such as curl can be used against live targets (Fang et al., 2024, p. 3), and Cybench evaluates agents whose actions are bash commands executed in Kali Linux (Zhang et al., 2025, p. 3). In each case the harness deliberately reuses the host’s dual-use binaries rather than inventing a closed virtual instruction set. That is the Living-off-the-Land (LotL) duality of the coding harness: the same architectural surface that enables software engineering and red-team research also turns the agent into an automated LotL executor once its instruction stream can be manipulated.

The manipulation channel is no longer speculative. Indirect prompt injection shows that “LLM-Integrated Applications blur the line between data and instructions,” so that adversaries can “remotely (without a direct interface) exploit LLM-integrated applications by strategically injecting prompts into data likely to be retrieved” (Greshake et al., 2023, p. 1). Tool-integrated agents amplify the blast radius: InjecAgent documents how malicious instructions embedded in external content aim “to manipulate these agents into executing detrimental actions against users” (Zhan et al., 2024, p. 1), and AgentDojo notes that a successful injection “can allow an external attacker to take actions (and call tools) on behalf of the user” (Debenedetti et al., 2024, p. 1). ToolEmu’s risk analysis makes the consequence concrete: even the safest evaluated language-model agent still exhibits severe tool failures “23.9% of the time according to [their] evaluator” (Ruan et al., 2024, p. 1).

What follows is often misdiagnosed as a novel model attack. Symlink and TOCTOU races, path traversal, subprocess escape, environment and PATH injection, SSRF and DNS rebinding, credential exposure, resource exhaustion, build-hook persistence, cross-agent exfiltration through shared files, and persistent workspace poisoning are classical OS and software problems. Agentic tool chaining accelerates them by composing dual-use binaries under ambient authority; it does not invent a new physics of compromise. The central thesis of this paper is therefore not merely that coding harnesses need better individual filters, but that security in agentic systems is a structural property of the architecture and of the composition of permissions—not a behavioral property of individual agents. In our companion mathematical theory of open-ended intelligence, we show that cognitive capability is not the consequence of model scale alone, “but of a particular organizational structure,” so that “the question worth asking shifts from which model to which system” (Hegelich et al., 2026, pp. 1–2). Overcoming the failure modes of both blind statistical token predictors and brittle single-layer rules requires “designing a composite architecture that keeps these requirements structurally separate while allowing them to integrate” (Hegelich et al., 2026, p. 2). Crucially, when multiple bounded agents interact through shared external memory, “[t]he collective state is not the union of individual states but the individual states together with the relations coupling them” (Hegelich et al., 2026, p. 32). Applied to security, this theorem explains why aligning individual agents in isolation is structurally insufficient: two agents whose individual steps each appear benign can still compose across shared workspace state into an unauthorized exfiltration channel unless authority and information flow are enforced across their composition.

Two common industry responses miss that architectural point. Static string or regex blacklists can catch a handful of literal patterns, yet they fail on flag permutations, Base64 or Hex pipe-to-shell payloads, spoofed archive headers, magic-byte disguises, and Unicode bidirectional (Bidi) Trojan Source encodings that make source appear different to a compiler and to the human eye (Boucher and Anderson, 2023, p. 1). Delegating the same checks to a secondary LLM-as-a-Judge is attractive as a product feature and brittle as a protection mechanism. A judge must reason correctly about whether an action violates a rule, yet systematic evaluation of LLM logical reasoning across deductive, inductive, and abductive settings—using content-neutral problems that separate reasoning from text comprehension—traces model failures to both evidence selection and the reasoning process itself (Xu et al., 2025). Heuristic detectors “provide [no] guarantee of security and regularly fall short to new attacks in practice” (Debenedetti et al., 2025, p. 3). Saltzer and Schroeder’s principle of complete mediation requires that “[e]very access to every object must be checked for authority” (Saltzer and Schroeder, 1975, p. 1280); economy of mechanism further insists that protection designs stay “as simple and small as possible,” because “design and implementation errors that result in unwanted access paths will not be noticed during normal use” (Saltzer and Schroeder, 1975, p. 1280). Asking a probabilistic model to decide decompression ratios, canonical path containment, SSRF IP resolution, or password entropy violates both principles and pays a latency tax four orders of magnitude above a deterministic kernel.

papers.title: Frequency Comb as a Probe of Fluctuation Mechanisms in Nanomechanical Systems
papers.abstract: Frequency combs are indispensable in metrology. We show that a frequency comb also probes frequency fluctuations of the system. In our nanomechanical resonator, the comb arises from self-sustained vibrations of a resonantly driven nonlinear mode. The comb lineshapes reveal exponentially correlated (Ornstein--Uhlenbeck) frequency noise. Its correlation time agrees with the independently measured relaxation time of the vibrations. The noise leads to anomalous phase diffusion. Its mechanism is generic: like the comb itself, it stems from the strong nonlinearity of the self-sustained vibrations.

papers.title: Local electronic structure of the Co2+ ions in the disordered perovskite phase of Ba3CoNb2O9: a temperature-dependent X-ray absorption and magnetic circular dichroism study
papers.abstract: We performed temperature-dependent X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) and X-ray magnetic circular dichroism (XMCD) measurements on the disordered phase of Ba$_3$CoNb$_2$O$_9$ to determine the local electronic structure of the Co$^{2+}$ ions. We employed the line-fitting inverse partial fluorescence yield (iPFY) method to obtain reliable spectra from this insulating material. From the comparison between the experimental spectra and full multiplet cluster calculations we were able to constrain the local crystal-field environment and assess the spin-orbit-entangled nature of the Co$^{2+}$ ground state. In this chemically disordered system, the Co$^{2+}$ ions retain on average an effectively cubic crystal-field environment that supports a $J_\mathrm{eff} = 1/2$ ground state. These results further establish that Ba$_3$CoNb$_2$O$_9$ is a promising platform for investigating the effect of disorder on $J_\mathrm{eff} = 1/2$ magnetism.

papers.intro:
The emergence of unconventional magnetic states in correlated electron systems is often associated with geometric frustration, in which competing interactions suppress conventional long-range magnetic order. Triangular-lattice antiferromagnets have long served as prototypical examples, exhibiting strong quantum fluctuations and hosting a variety of nontrivial ground states [1, 2, 3, 4].

The emergence of unconventional magnetic states in correlated electron systems is often associated with geometric frustration, in which competing interactions suppress conventional long-range magnetic order. Triangular-lattice antiferromagnets have long served as prototypical examples, exhibiting strong quantum fluctuations and hosting a variety of nontrivial ground states [1, 2, 3, 4].

Disorder and dilution provide another route to unconventional magnetic behavior. In site-diluted quantum magnets, randomness can fragment the magnetic lattice into orphan moments, finite clusters, and percolating spin networks, producing a broad distribution of local exchange and correlation energy scales. When combined with spin-1/21/2 quantum fluctuations, such disorder can give rise to dynamically fluctuating, short-range-correlated states without conventional static order or spin-glass freezing [5, 6, 7].

Ba3CoNb2O9 exhibits three polymorphs: the metastable disordered cubic K1 phase, the high-temperature disordered cubic K2 phase, and the ordered hexagonal H phase [8]. The K2 phase crystallizes in the cubic Pm3¯\bar{3}m space group, as shown in Fig. 1(a). The formation of these polymorphs depends strongly on synthesis conditions: while the K1-to-H transformation is irreversible, the H-to-K2 transformation is reversible and occurs near 1500 ∘C. The K2 phase can be retained at room temperature by rapid cooling [8].

The K2 phase can be retained at room temperature by rapid cooling [8].

Recent powder X-ray and neutron diffraction studies of the disordered phase revealed random occupation of the B sites by Co and Nb ions in a 1:2 ratio [7]. Muon-spin rotation measurements found no evidence of static spin freezing down to 50 mK, while magnetic neutron diffraction refinements identified strong antiferromagnetic correlations between nearest-neighbor Co ions [7]. The magnetic response was interpreted in terms of a diluted spin-1/21/2 Heisenberg model [7]. These observations indicate that significant magnetic interactions persist despite site disorder.

A central question, however, is whether the assumed spin-1/21/2 degrees of freedom are microscopically justified in the disordered cubic phase. This point is particularly important because Co2+ is not a simple spin-only ion. In octahedral coordination, Co2+ has a spin–orbit-active d7d^{7} electronic configuration, and its low-energy states are determined by the combined effects of the cubic crystal field, intra-atomic Coulomb interactions, covalency with the surrounding oxygen ligands, and spin–orbit coupling. These interactions give rise to a spin–orbit-entangled Kramers doublet, but the precise character of this doublet can be sensitive to the local crystal-field environment.

In the present compound, the random distribution of Co and Nb ions may also generate a distribution of local CoO6 environments or weak deviations from ideal cubic symmetry. Such effects could, in principle, modify the crystal-field level scheme and the spin–orbit-entangled ground state. papers.title: Excess charge in the Engel-Dreizler model of atoms and molecules
papers.abstract: We prove an explicit excess-charge bound for the exchange-free Engel--Dreizler functional of atoms and molecules. If $\alpha\lambda\le1/1233$ and $\alpha^3Z_k^2\le1/137$ for each nucleus, every finite-mass electronic minimizer whose total energy, including nuclear repulsion, is nonpositive satisfies $N-\sum_kZ_k<(5913/1000)\lambda^{3/2}K$. For the gradient coefficient $\lambda=1/9$, this gives $N-\sum_kZ_k<0.219K$. The energy hypothesis holds automatically for atoms and for local minima of the Born--Oppenheimer energy at which the electronic infimum is attained. The proof uses no symmetry of the density, restriction on the total nuclear charge, or minimum nuclear separation. We combine molecular Sommerfeld estimates with a convex nonlinear comparison in the variable $F(p)$. The failure of the latter comparison at very high density is represented by a nonnegative Newton potential. A quartic coercivity estimate, obtained from nuclear repulsion and a signed localized Hardy inequality, controls the total mass of this source. The chemical potential is retained throughout. Exact covariance yields the invariant parameter domain, and all finite numerical inequalities are reduced to rational arithmetic.

papers.title: The Shape of a Program: Path Signatures for Trace-to-Program Induction
papers.abstract: Synthesizing programs from execution traces is a fundamental challenge in algorithmic interpretability and the reverse engineering of complex systems. We bring a rough-path-theoretic perspective to program induction, treating execution traces as high-dimensional rough paths and encoding them with the path signature transform, a tool from stochastic analysis whose expectation provably characterizes the distribution of traces a program induces. On three program-induction domains, Karel, List, and RASP, our log-signature trace encoder outperforms LSTM, Transformer, and Fourier baselines in almost every setting, with its largest margins when training data is scarce. We further observe that the trace-to-program pipeline is naturally contractive: it often produces valid programs that are shorter than the ground truth. We turn this into a bootstrapping procedure that exposes redundancy in the ground-truth supervision without any external oracle, which we demonstrate on redundancy-injected versions of our datasets. Finally, the log-signature encoder induces a markedly more interpretable latent geometry than the baselines, in which the nearest neighbors of every state lie on its own execution trace.

papers.intro:
Program synthesis, the task of automatically generating code that satisfies a given specification, stands as one of the central challenges in modern artificial intelligence. While much of the recent progress has focused on synthesizing programs from functional specifications, typically provided as input-output (I/O) pairs [8, 1, 2, 4], this represents only one facet of the problem. A distinct but equally important challenge is synthesizing programs from behavioral specifications in the form of execution traces. This task is commonly referred to as program induction. Unlike I/O pairs, which treat the program as a black box, execution traces reveal the how of the computation, offering a granular view of the algorithmic decision-making process. Mastering this form of synthesis is essential for real-world applications such as reverse-engineering legacy systems, malware analysis, and algorithmic interpretability, where the goal is not just to replicate an output, but to recover the underlying logic that produced a specific sequence of states.

This direction is essential for algorithmic interpretability, as it allows us to distill opaque agents into human-readable code [30]. By synthesizing programs that faithfully reproduce the trace of a policy rather than just its final output, we gain verifiable insights into agent behavior, revealing safety constraints and logic gaps that are otherwise hidden in high-dimensional weight matrices. Towards this end, it is compelling to find more optimal methodologies for encoding behavioral traces. Unlike static I/O pairs, behavioral traces possess intrinsic temporal and geometric structure that characterizes how a task is solved, not just what the solution is. Consequently, the success of the synthesis process hinges on the representation’s ability to capture these dynamics robustly.

To tackle this task, the dominant paradigm has been to treat execution traces as discrete sequences, processing them with standard sequence models like LSTMs [13] or Transformers [29]. In this work, we propose a fundamental shift in perspective. Rather than viewing traces merely as sequences of tokens, we conceptualize them as high-dimensional rough paths and encode them using the path signature transform, a tool from stochastic analysis and rough path theory [3] that has been of growing interest in machine learning for time-series forecasting and reinforcement learning [5, 15]. The signature transform turns that geometry into a fixed-size, length-invariant embedding with a principled algebraic structure, providing a representation that is naturally aligned with how programs structure execution.

Several properties of the signature reinforce this perspective. First, the expected signature characterizes the trace distribution a program induces [6], so aggregating signatures across executions of the same program can, in principle, identify it. Second, signatures factor under any temporal decomposition of the path: by Chen’s identity, S⁡(X∗Y)=S⁡(X)⊗S⁡(Y)S(X*Y)=S(X)\otimes S(Y), so the signature of a trace is the product of the signatures of its parts (Section 4.2). Third, the signature captures the shape of the path in a fixed-size representation regardless of path length. Fourth, its runtime is linear in the path length, making it much more practical for processing long traces than Transformers with their quadratic attention complexity (Appendix A.5). Beyond these four points, the signature is a universal nonlinearity: any continuous functional of the path can be linearly approximated from its signature, so no expressive power is sacrificed for these structural advantages. This last property notably does not hold for classical operators like the Fourier transform.

papers.title: Combinatorial optimization with bounded subdeterminants
papers.abstract:
We take a first step toward a broader study of classical combinatorial optimization problems through the maximum subdeterminants of their standard integer programming formulations, yielding new positive results for several famous (NP-hard) problems. An integer matrix is totally $\Delta$-modular if every square submatrix has determinant of absolute value at most $\Delta$. For every fixed $\Delta$, it has been known that maximum clique, maximum stable set, and minimum vertex cover can be solved in polynomial time on instances for which the coefficient matrix of the natural formulation is totally $\Delta$-modular. We extend this list by showing that the same holds for many other problems, including the weighted versions of maximum cut, the traveling salesman problem, feedback vertex set, odd cycle transversal, dominating set, max 2-sat, induced matching, and cluster vertex deletion, as well as for $k$-colorability and graph isomorphism.
  Our proofs reveal several new ways in which bounded subdeterminants impose combinatorial structure: they bound the size or maximum degree of the input graph, bound packings of cycles and other obstructions, or yield decompositions into tractable graph classes such as forests, chordal graphs, graphs of bounded treewidth, and graphs of bounded linear mim-width.

The purpose of this work is to illustrate various new ways in which subdeterminants are linked to structural graph parameters and to highlight different algorithmic approaches needed to exploit the arising structure. Specifically, we will see that total Δ\Delta-modularity can force the input graph to be small or of bounded degree, bound the size of a packing of cycles or other obstructions, and admit decompositions into tractable graph classes such as forests, chordal graphs, graphs of bounded treewidth, and graphs of bounded linear mim-width. We view the diversity of our results as evidence that, should a general polynomial-time algorithm for integer programs with bounded subdeterminants exist, it is unlikely to arise from a single black-box theorem in integer programming. Instead, it may have to bring together a wide range of combinatorial arguments and algorithmic techniques.

papers.title: Hermitian K-theory for stable $\infty$-categories IV: Karoubi-Grothendieck-Witt theory
papers.abstract:
In analogy with the passage from connective to non-connective algebraic K-theory, Schlichting put forward the Karoubi-Grothendieck-Witt spectrum as an approximation to Grothendieck-Witt theory by a functor invariant under idempotent completion. In this paper, we extend his construction to the setting of Poincar\'e $\infty$-categories and characterise the resulting functor by the expected universal property.
  Our main result places these Karoubi-Grothendieck-Witt-spectra in an exact sequence involving the ultimately decorated L-spectrum and homotopy orbits of non-connective K-theory. This confirms a conjecture of Williams which had remained open even for rings in which $2$ is invertible, and allows us to deduce universal characterisations for ultimately decorated L-theory. We obtain these results by unifying the Bass-Heller-Swan and Ranicki-Shaneson splittings into a general decomposition theorem that yields, in particular, formulas for Grothendieck-Witt groups of Laurent polynomial rings.
  Finally, we construct multiplicative structures on both versions of our Grothendieck-Witt and L-functors and refine their universal properties to multiplicative ones. Along the way, we show that the original versions are even idempotent with respect to Day convolution.

papers.title: Imaging exoplanets below the telescope stability limit
papers.abstract: Exoplanet imaging is the main method for detailed characterization of planets orbiting beyond 1 au but it requires suppressing the bright glare of the star to see the faint planet light. As well as sophisticated instrumentation, effective image processing is necessary for starlight suppression, which continues to be a substantial limitation. Standard algorithms use reference images for starlight modelling and thus they are limited by inevitable telescope instabilities that change from reference to science observation. Addressing this challenge will increase the number of planets amenable to direct imaging and will be a notable step towards imaging exo-Earths with future observatories. Here we present a new physics-based method for starlight subtraction. Our method combines a multistep optimization with a flexible physical model to produce a starlight model, allowing modelling and compensation of instrument instabilities. We use automatic differentiation (autodiff) to optimize millions of model parameters. We demonstrate our method on observations from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) Near-InfraRed Camera (NIRCam) coronagraph instrument. We achieve sensitivity 2-15 times superior to standard techniques, including the first detection of 51 Eridani b at 4.3 $\mu$m. This is the first time, to our knowledge, that such an approach has demonstrated substantially improved sensitivity on real, on-sky coronagraphic imaging. Our framework can be extended to other current and future ground-based and space-based observatories, including the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope and the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO), potentially relaxing the unprecedented stability requirements needed to make these a success.

papers.title: Identification of the C IV $\lambda\lambda$5801, 5812 Emission in the Off-Nuclear TDE 2025abcr
papers.abstract: TDE 2025abcr is a tidal disruption event (TDE) located approximately 9 kpc in projection from its host galaxy nucleus. Our spectroscopic follow-up with the Very Large Telescope (VLT) reveals C IV $\lambda\lambda5801, 5812$ emission, representing the first identification of this C IV doublet in a TDE. These transitions are uncommon in active galactic nuclei (AGN) spectra but have been observed in supernova flash spectra and Wolf-Rayet (WR) stars. We propose that the doublet arises from the combined effects of continuum fluorescence and photon trapping in the 312 \r{A} transition, analogous to the mechanism operating in nitrogen-sequence Wolf-Rayet (WN) winds. This mechanism requires intense extreme-ultraviolet (EUV) illumination and a high optical depth, providing a distinctive diagnostic of the physical conditions in optically thick TDE outflows. These requirements, together with the relatively narrow widths of the broad emission lines, the presence of Bowen fluorescence features, and the small inferred blackbody radius, favor a compact and dense envelope in TDE 2025abcr. The optical C IV doublet may have been overlooked in previous observational and theoretical studies of TDEs, motivating more detailed radiative-transfer calculations for optically thick outflows. With future TDE samples from Rubin/LSST and WFST, a larger C IV TDE sample will test if this population systematically favors a compact photosphere.

papers.intro:
A tidal disruption event (TDE) occurs when a star passes sufficiently close to a massive black hole (MBH) to be torn apart by tidal forces, producing a luminous flare as the bound debris returns and accretes onto the MBH [38]. Modern wide-field time-domain surveys have increased the number of known optical TDEs to more than 100, enabling systematic studies of their population properties [50, 21, 58]. Complementing studies of sustained accretion in active galactic nuclei (AGN), TDEs reveal otherwise quiescent MBHs in inactive galaxies [17, 52, 57] and provide laboratories for testing accretion theory across rapidly changing accretion rates [46, 51, 47, 55].

Optically selected TDEs typically exhibit diverse emission-line properties and spectral evolution. Based on the presence of transient hydrogen lines or helium lines, TDE spectra are commonly classified as TDE-H, TDE-He, TDE-H+He, or TDE-featureless [50, 21]. A subset of TDE-H+He spectra also exhibits N III λ​4640\lambda 4640 and O III λ​3760\lambda 3760 emission associated with Bowen fluorescence, revealing illumination by an extreme-ultraviolet (EUV) source [6, 28]. These Bowen TDEs tend to have smaller blackbody radii and higher temperatures [50], together with narrower emission lines than hydrogen-dominated events [9], suggesting a connection between spectral diversity and the structure of the emitting gas. More generally, TDE line widths range from several thousand to ∼104\sim 10^{4} km s-1 and often decrease as the flare fades, a behavior that can be explained by electron-scattering broadening in an evolving reprocessing layer [41]. Line strengths and ratios further probe the excitation conditions, radiative-transfer effects, and elemental abundances, although these contributions can be difficult to disentangle [40, 48].

papers.title: Enforcing Axioms for AI Alignment under Loss-Based Rules
papers.abstract: Many alignment methods, most notably reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), train reward models by minimizing a loss on pairwise comparisons of model responses. Inspired by principle-guided methods such as Constitutional AI, we treat each principle as a voter that compares responses according to that principle, for example, preferring the more helpful or less toxic response. We represent these voters as linear directions in a fixed embedding space, a simplifying assumption motivated by the Linear Representation Hypothesis. In this linear social choice model, Ge et al. (2024) showed that an optimal linear reward model can violate Pareto optimality (PO): From the principles-as-voters lens, this means a response A can be less helpful and more toxic than B, yet still receive a higher reward. We ask whether richer reward models or changes to comparison data can recover PO within loss-based training. We show that PO can still fail for polynomials of any fixed degree and one-hidden-layer ReLU multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) of any fixed width $ d\ge 2 $ with suitable finite parameter bounds. We then recover PO for loss-based training of linear rewards under suitable assumptions in an idealized setting with uniform comparison directions and equal comparison lengths. These results motivate dataset design as an approach to recovering PO in constitutional-style alignment while retaining loss-based training.
papers.intro:
Many recent alignment methods follow a common pipeline: collect pairwise (binary) preferences over model responses, fit a reward (or preference) model to these comparisons, and then optimize the base model to minimize a loss correlated with aligned behavior. In the classical human-in-the-loop setting of Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) (Christiano et al., 2017), human annotators select the preferred response between candidate responses. Rather than eliciting unguided preferences, Anthropic introduced principle-oriented feedback (Bai et al., 2022a) in which annotators judge responses against explicit principles—helpfulness, honesty, and harmlessness (HHH); this principle-guided supervision later informed Constitutional AI, which formalizes a written set of principles to guide binary comparisons of model responses (Bai et al., 2022b). We use “constitutional-style” as an umbrella term for such principle-guided supervision.

We use “constitutional-style” as an umbrella term for such principle-guided supervision.

Adopting a social-choice perspective on constitutional-style alignment, we treat principles as voters that evaluate pairs of model responses by judging which better adheres to the relevant principle. From this perspective, a minimal requirement - “axiom” - for any aggregation method is Pareto Optimality (PO) (also known as Unanimity (Arrow, 1951)): e.g., in the HHH framework, if response A is more helpful, more honest, and more harmless than B, then A should receive higher reward and thus be more likely to be generated by the model. We study a setting in which principles (such as HHH) are modeled as linear directions in a representation space. This is a simplifying assumption motivated by the Linear Representation Hypothesis (LRH) (Park et al., 2023), which posits that some high-level concepts are well-approximated by linear features in learned embeddings and which has been operationally useful in mechanistic interpretability.

PO beyond observed comparisons. Reward models evaluate responses beyond their training data, so axiomatic guarantees should also apply to unseen comparisons. papers.title: Designing Accessible and Rigorous ML Experiments: No-Code Visual Workflows and Structured Guidance for Beginners
papers.abstract: Designing machine learning (ML) experiments requires beginners to plan a methodologically sound workflow and implement it in a concrete environment. We evaluated two forms of support in two within-participant studies with 18 predominantly technically trained participants: mlguide, which provides structured, evidence- backed guidance for workflow design, and AI Sandbox, a visual no-code environment for workflow implementation. After using mlguide, participants produced better high-level workflow designs, but their scores on a quiz about specific methodological choices did not improve significantly. Compared with Google Colab, AI Sandbox received higher hedonic user experience ratings, while perceived workload and acceptance did not differ significantly. These findings suggest that different forms of interactive support help with differ- ent aspects of beginner ML experimentation. The paper contributes a reusable evaluation task with instructions, a modified dataset, and a quiz, as well as empirical evidence on structured guidance for workflow design and on the experience of implementing workflows in visual and notebook-based environments.

papers.intro:
Machine-learning (ML) experimentation has become part of everyday work in research, engineering, and applied domains well beyond specialist ML teams. Yet designing a sound ML experiment remains difficult, especially for beginners and occasional practitioners. The difficulty is not only technical. Users must decide what a sensible workflow should contain—for example, how data preparation, model training, validation, comparison, and reporting should relate to one another—and also how that workflow should be realised in a concrete tool. Recent work on ML-based science has underlined the importance of these choices: recurring problems of validity, reproducibility, and generalisability often arise not from model fitting alone, but from weaknesses in the surrounding experimental workflow and reporting practice (Kapoor et al., 2024). This makes beginner support an interactive-systems problem as much as an algorithmic one.

Yet designing a sound ML experiment remains difficult, especially for beginners and occasional practitioners. The difficulty is not only technical. Users must decide what a sensible workflow should contain—for example, how data preparation, model training, validation, comparison, and reporting should relate to one another—and also how that workflow should be realised in a concrete tool. Recent work on ML-based science has underlined the importance of these choices: recurring problems of validity, reproducibility, and generalisability often arise not from model fitting alone, but from weaknesses in the surrounding experimental workflow and reporting practice (Kapoor et al., 2024). This makes beginner support an interactive-systems problem as much as an algorithmic one.

A useful way to frame this challenge is to distinguish between two coupled layers of understanding. First, users need a conceptual model of an ML workflow: what the main stages are, how they should be ordered, and what kinds of choices each stage demands. Second, users need an implementation model: how those stages are instantiated in a programming environment, notebook, or visual workflow editor. These two layers are related, but prior work suggests that they are not interchangeable. In interactive ML, user-interface design has long been recognised as central to whether non-experts can contribute effectively, inspect system behaviour, and remain in control of the learning process (Dudley and Kristensson, 2018). However, different tool families support different layers of the problem.

Computational notebooks such as Jupyter are widely used because they combine executable code, narrative text, and outputs in a single environment (Kluyver et al., 2016). At the same time, HCI studies show that notebook work is shaped by tension between exploration and explanation, by difficulties in tracking variants over time, and by recurring pain points around structure, navigation, and reuse (Rule et al., 2018; Kery et al., 2018; Chattopadhyay et al., 2020). Visual workflow systems such as KNIME and Orange make pipeline structure more explicit by representing analysis steps as composable graphs of operations rather than free-form code (Berthold et al., 2008; Demšar et al., 2013). Educational systems such as Teachable Machine and TensorFlow Playground similarly show that direct manipulation and constrained visual interaction can lower barriers and help novices build intuition about ML concepts (Carney et al., 2020; Smilkov et al., 2017). These systems, however, typically foreground implementation and interaction style; they do not necessarily provide explicit guidance about the methodological adequacy of an experimental design.

AutoML systems reduce manual effort in model and hyperparameter selection by searching over candidate pipelines and configurations (Hutter et al., 2019; Feurer et al., 2015). Yet research on human-centred AutoML also shows that automation introduces new interaction challenges around transparency, controllability, and trust. For example, ATMSeer demonstrates that users benefit from interfaces that allow them to inspect and steer the AutoML process, rather than merely receiving opaque results (Wang et al., 2019). More broadly, guidelines for human–AI interaction emphasise the importance of exposing system capabilities and limitations, supporting user control, and calibrating expectations (Amershi et al., 2019b; Shneiderman, 2020). Recent copilot research points in the same direction: in feature-rich software, guided assistance can outperform fully automated assistance on perceived control and learnability, especially in exploratory tasks (Khurana et al., 2025a). papers.title: A Hierarchical View of Ecological Encounters
papers.abstract: Encounters between individuals, or between individuals and entities like vehicles, are central to understanding a host of topics in ecology and related fields. Problems of mate-finding, predator-prey interactions, pathogen spread, and animal interactions with infrastructure all hinge on encounters. Historically, however, encounters have been difficult to observe at scale, and the relevant theoretical frameworks---which ultimately derive from the ideal gas law---have been badly mismatched to the underlying biology. Here, we synthesize and provide ecological context for recent developments in mathematics, statistics, and physics that permit the inclusion of more biological realism into encounter-related models. We propose an encounters--interactions--outcomes hierarchical framework for organizing core concepts across a diverse range of ecological scenarios. Implemented as a hierarchical Bayesian model, our framework permits tight connections with multi-level ecological data relevant to the estimation of encounter rates and their downstream impacts on interactions and outcomes. Throughout, we emphasize how the ongoing revolution in animal biologging yields empirical datasets that can be employed to quantify otherwise inaccessible rate parameters and their dependencies. We conclude with a series of major open questions about encounters designed to spur conceptual and quantitative integration across models, data sources, and ecological levels of organization.

papers.intro:
Encounters are central to ecology, whether they pertain to a predator killing a prey, a hair-snare sampling site, an infected individual transmitting a pathogen, or conspecifics meeting to mate. They provide an essential link between research focused on individuals (e.g., physiology, health, movement, fitness) and that centered on populations, such as demographic change and species interactions (Royle et al., 2018; Słomka et al., 2023). Encounters are also integral in many applied contexts, from the statistical estimation of population sizes via camera trap networks to the management of human–wildlife interactions (Grilo et al., 2021; Mestre et al., 2025; Nisi et al., 2024).

Encounters are central to ecology, whether they pertain to a predator killing a prey, a hair-snare sampling site, an infected individual transmitting a pathogen, or conspecifics meeting to mate. They provide an essential link between research focused on individuals (e.g., physiology, health, movement, fitness) and that centered on populations, such as demographic change and species interactions (Royle et al., 2018; Słomka et al., 2023). Encounters are also integral in many applied contexts, from the statistical estimation of population sizes via camera trap networks to the management of human–wildlife interactions (Grilo et al., 2021; Mestre et al., 2025; Nisi et al., 2024).

Encounters can thus have important ecological consequences. For example, video monitoring of cougar (Puma concolor) kill sites has revealed unknown predator–predator encounters that shape species’ spatial distributions (Ruprecht et al., 2021). In disease ecology, encounters between infected and susceptible hosts, or between hosts and vectors, underlie management and intervention methods (e.g., social distancing, bednets). Encounters between animals and human infrastructure can likewise have far-reaching downstream effects, such as population declines due to roadkill mortality, plane crashes caused by birdstrikes, and the impact of plastic detritus on marine species. In these and other cases, encounter consequences cannot be fully understood unless their nature, frequency, and location are clear.

In these and other cases, encounter consequences cannot be fully understood unless their nature, frequency, and location are clear.

However, encounters are often difficult to quantify. Readily available types of information, such as population sizes or densities, do not provide a reliable path to quantify the rate, frequency, or even the possibility of encounters. Similarly, direct estimation of encounters from space use data has been possible only in special cases (e.g., when auxiliary validation data were available, Buderman et al., 2021). Even when space use densities are known (i.e., even when we know how intensely animals use different regions of space), obtaining encounter rates without data on movement rates, path characteristics, or encounter radii is possible only under specific conditions (Garcia de Figueiredo et al., 2024; Garcia de Figueiredo et al., 2026). This makes encounter data a particularly informative basis for addressing spatial problems.

This makes encounter data a particularly informative basis for addressing spatial problems.

Historically, information about most ecologically relevant encounters was hard to come by. On rare occasions, encounters could be directly witnessed, but otherwise encounters could only be inferred via the law of mass action—a model originally proposed for chemical reactions. For example, if researchers were interested in characterizing the rate of encounters between two species of animals, they would typically assume equilibrium thermodynamics (mass action), plug in the densities and movement rates of the two species, and solve for the encounter rate (Hutchinson and Waser, 2007). Though widely used in the absence of ecologically relevant alternatives, this mathematically convenient approach suffers from a series of assumptions about animal movements and the nature of encounters that are very difficult to justify (Hein and Martin, 2020).

Technological advancements have facilitated detailed tracking of animal movement, allowing for remote recording of encounter processes like pollination or foraging, and permitting analysis of encounter-relevant data synthesized across diverse sources (Falcón-Cortés et al., 2021; Ruprecht et al., 2021; Smith and Pinter-Wollman, 2021; Wilber et al., 2022). However, relevant encounter theory offering an alternative to the Ideal Gas Law has lagged behind this empirical progress (but see Hein and Martin, 2020; Giuggioli and Sarvaharman, 2022; Garcia de Figueiredo et al., 2024; Noonan et al., 2021). Most traditional models focus on space use density, from which true encounter rates cannot be reliably derived. More specifically, mainstream approaches assume that encounter rates follow from mass action principles, and these generally yield only relative encounter intensities, leaving a gap between empirical estimates of encounter rates and the precise rates needed for dynamic models (Cross et al., 2013; Hein and Martin, 2020). Addressing this mismatch will require new analytical and statistical methods, potentially including non-equilibrium descriptions.

To start closing the gap between theoretical and empirical progress, we conceptualize ecological encounters and their consequences as an encounters–interactions–outcomes hierarchy that can integrate the kinds of movement-derived empirical data that are increasingly available. In the following sections, we first introduce the dyadic framework for ecological encounters (Gurarie and Ovaskainen, 2013) as the conceptual foundation to define the relationship between encounters, interactions, and outcomes. We then discuss this framework’s limitations and use them to motivate the development of a novel extended hierarchical model.

papers.title: Molecular signatures of shocked gas and enhanced cosmic-ray ionization in supernova remnant W49B revealed by ALMA
papers.abstract: Galactic supernova remnants (SNRs) interacting with molecular clouds (MCs) provide important laboratories for investigating how supernova feedback is transferred to the interstellar medium. We performed observations of the HCO+ J=1-0, 3-2, and 4-3 lines, as well as the CO J=3-2 line, toward the eastern and western regions of SNR W49B using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) and the Atacama Pathfinder Experiment (APEX) telescope. In W49B west, we identify twelve regions with broad-line profiles in both HCO+ and CO emission, with FWHM of 25-60 km/s, providing clear evidence of SNR-MC interaction. These emissions are compact (at $\sim$5 arcsec resolution) and spatially coincident with 2.12~$\mu$m H$_2$ emission, but generally offset from the 1.64~$\mu$m [Fe~II] and radio continuum peaks. Non-LTE analyses yield shocked-gas densities of (0.5-1.6) $\times 10^5$~cm$^{-3}$ and high $N_{\rm HCO+}/N_{\rm CO}$ abundance ratios of (4.2-14.5) $\times 10^{-4}$. Reproducing such high abundance ratios in shocked MCs requires high cosmic ray ionization rates (CRIRs) of a few 10$^{-14}$-10$^{-13}$~s$^{-1}$, about 3-4 orders of magnitude above the standard Galactic level. Some regions exhibit enhanced HCO+/CO intensity ratios in their high-velocity line wings, possibly due to multiple unresolved shocks spanning a range of velocities and gas densities, spatial variations in the CRIR, or both. By contrast, the ratio remains nearly constant with velocity in other regions. For these regions, we further explore the propagation of low-energy CRs through the post-shock layer. An energy-budget analysis of a representative shocked clump indicates that the shock-associated kinetic-energy reservoir substantially exceeds cumulative CR and X-ray heating inputs, with CR heating exceeding X-ray heating.[abridged]

papers.intro:
Supernovae (SNe) are among the most energetic events in galaxies, playing a key role in regulating star formation and galaxy evolution [58]. However, observational constraints on SN feedback remain challenging, and one of the reasons is the uncertainty in the specific roles of different feedback mechanisms, including shocks, radiation, and cosmic rays (CRs), in shaping the surrounding molecular clouds (MCs) [50]. Among these feedback channels, shocks have been the most widely studied heating mechanism in supernova remnants (SNRs), with their properties depending on both the evolutionary stage of the remnant and the local ambient conditions [73], while X-ray radiation and low-energy (<<1 GeV) CRs can penetrate into MCs shielded from UV radiation and play important roles in the heating, ionization and chemistry [21, 54, 17, 80, e.g.,]. Notably, about 1/4 of Galactic SNRs are known to interact with MCs [28, 8], and tens of SNRs emit X-ray and γ\gamma-ray radiation. In such environments, MCs can efficiently slow down SNR shocks, absorb radiation, and are affected by CR propagation, leading to significant variations in their physical and chemical conditions. Thus, Galactic SNRs and their molecular environments (i.e., SNR-MC associations) are prime targets for quantifying SN feedback through multi-wavelength observations [79].

W49B (G43.3−-0.2) is the most luminous Galactic SNR in the X-ray band [27], and remarkably bright in the γ\gamma-ray band [1, 24], with the latter originating from π0\pi^{0} decay due to interactions between accelerated high-energy CRs and nearby dense materials. It is also the most luminous Galactic SNR in near-IR 2.12 μ\mum H2 emission [30, 37]. These properties indicate that W49B is still undergoing vigorous energy release into its surroundings, making it an excellent target for studying the different channels of SN feedback. With an estimated age of ∼\sim5–6 kyr, W49B is evolving in a complex and inhomogeneous environment where shocks of different velocities coexist. X-ray observations suggest a fast forward shock [82, ∼\sim 500 km s-1,] propagating through relatively diffuse gas with densities of a few to a few tens of cm-3, whereas molecular observations reveal interactions with denser gas, into which much slower shocks are driven [64, 83, e.g.,].

Based on IRAM 30 m observations, [83] reported unusually high HCO+/12CO JJ=1–0 intensity ratios (0.2–1) in the shocked gas toward the southwestern region of W49B (hereafter W49B west), and in quiescent clouds located outside the southeastern boundary of the SNR (hereafter W49B east). These ratios are 1–2 orders of magnitude larger than those found in typical MCs. Interestingly, in both regions where the HCO+/12CO JJ=1–0 ratios are enhanced, the spectral line profiles show markedly different behaviors: the HCO+ JJ=1–0 line profile in W49B east is narrow, whereas in W49B west it is significantly broadened. This may suggest that this SNR influences the surrounding molecular clouds through different mechanisms in the two regions. In addition, the complex velocity structure of molecular gas along the line of sight toward W49B has complicated the identification of the clouds physically associated with the remnant, and hence its distance [84, 64, 83, e.g.,]. In this work, we adopt a systemic local-standard-of-rest (LSR) velocity of 61–65 km s-1 and a distance of 7.9±\pm0.6 kpc for W49B [83], based on the velocity range of the shocked molecular gas and the approximately constant ∼\sim64 km s-1 velocity of the 2.12 μ\mum H2 emission across the SNR [38].

The strongly enhanced HCO+/CO ratios near W49B could be explained by additional ionization from low-energy CRs and X-ray radiation from the SNR [44, 77], which enhance the abundance of H+3{}^{+}_{3} via reaction chains with H2 molecules. HCO+ molecules are primarily formed via the gas-phase ion-neutral reaction H+3{}^{+}_{3} + CO →\to HCO+ + H2. Moreover, CRs and intense X-ray irradiation can modify the CO chemistry by promoting CO dissociation and ionization, thereby reducing the CO abundances near SNRs [3, 5, 42, e.g.,]. Therefore, variations in the HCO+/CO abundance ratio provide a useful diagnostic of SNR-driven ionization feedback, consistent with predictions from state-of-the-art astrochemical simulations [4, e.g.,].

papers.title: Effects of Laser Beam Width and Measurement Noise on Tree Diameter Estimation in Laser Scanning
papers.abstract: Laser scanning has been utilized for decades to measure tree structure and geometry. Despite continuous advances in sensor technology, uncertainties arising from scanner characteristics and measurement conditions has remained relevant sources of error. In particular, factors such as laser beam diameter can introduce both systematic and random errors in the reconstructed tree geometry. This study investigates the main sources of these errors in mobile laser scanning (MLS) and quantifies their effects on stem curve (stem diameter) estimation. We discovered through simulations and experiments that the heteroscedasticity (difference in variance in ranging and scan angle) in the measurement noise is a key factor along with the beam width of the lidar, which cause the bias of the diameter estimates to depend not only on distance, but also on the tree diameter. We demonstrated that this bias can be reliably predicted and negated for trees with a diameter at the breast height greater than 10 cm using technical specifications of the sensor without any additional calibration. In experiments, the proposed bias compensation method reduced the root-mean-square error of stem diameter estimates to sub-centimeter level on boreal forest test sites. However, for small trees with diameter below 10 cm, the diameter bias becomes sensitive to the diameter of the tree$\unicode{x2013}$an unknown factor$\unicode{x2013}$and other factors, such as different bark and out-of-roundness of the stem, limiting the precision of lidar for measuring geometry of trees and applicability of the presented method.

Airborne laser scanning (ALS) enables efficient, large-area forest inventories, including individual-tree-level inventories(Hyyppa and Inkinen, 1999; Persson et al., 2002; Ma et al., 2023; Hyyppä et al., 2024; White et al., 2025). However, due to high flight altitude required for fast collection of the data and the canopy obstructions, the tree stems get few laser hits, and thus, their geometries are not directly measurable from the point clouds. Therefore, reference data are required for the prediction of tree stem attributes from ALS data. In addition to the accuracy requirement of the reference, it needs to be quick to collect and update as trees are growing and there are also disturbances abruptly changing forest structure. Furthermore, the forest change is accelerated by the climate change (Anderson‐Teixeira et al., 2013; Thom et al., 2022; Bratu et al., 2025). One promising alternative to manual reference data collection is mobile laser scanning (MLS) (Liang et al., 2014; Pires et al., 2024; Holvoet et al., 2025; Liikonen et al., 2026). MLS utilizes a lidar and an inertial measurement unit (IMU), potentially augmented with a global navigation satellite system (GNSS) receiver, for acquiring a point cloud while moving for efficient high-coverage data collection in contrast to stationary terrestrial laser scanning (TLS). The tree geometry is typically estimated from the laser scanning point clouds through geometric modeling such as circle or cylinder fitting. Acquisition of MLS data from forest sample plots is significantly faster than measurements with calipers and clinometers. Furthermore, MLS data can be used to describe the entire stem curve, i.e., the stem diameter as a function height—as opposed to just the diameter at breast height—and can provide it with better than 10 %10\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} accuracy (Hyyppä et al., 2020; Stovall et al., 2023; Muhojoki et al., 2024). Stem curve enables direct estimation of the stem volume, and the geometric information it provides can be used for estimation of the length and volume of the sawlog and pulpwood. Similar accuracy has been achieved for diameter at breast height (DBH) measurements by (Ryding et al., 2015; Bauwens et al., 2016; Cabo et al., 2018; Kuželka et al., 2022; Hoffrén et al., 2024; Vandendaele et al., 2022). It should be noted that the accuracy of the stem attribute estimation depends on tree species (Yrttimaa et al., 2022; Holvoet et al., 2025; Tavi et al., 2026) and forest structure (Ryding et al., 2015; Bauwens et al., 2016; Cabo et al., 2018). Due to the capacity to record more structural information on individual trees, MLS can also enhance forest inventories by providing alternatives for assessing carbon storage (Coops et al., 2025) and vigor (Gerbrecht et al., 2025) of each trees as well as biodiversity indicators, such as structural complexity and the amount of dead wood from each measured sample plot (Fol et al., 2023).

papers.title: When Covariance Is Not Enough: Kernel-Based Regularization for Single-Cell Counterfactuals
papers.abstract: Counterfactual editing of single cells, predicting how an observed cell would look had one factor been different, enables in-silico screening where experiments are infeasible, but is useful only if the edit is faithful to the individual and not merely to the condition. Concept bottleneck generative models make the effects of interventions interpretable by decomposing a cell's representation into known and unknown factors. Previous work uses a linear cross-covariance penalty to disentangle known and unknown dimensions. We demonstrate that this first-order criterion does not fully separate information when non-linear interactions are present. We first demonstrate the inadequacy of linear cross-factor penalization with simulation experiments with controlled edits and known non-linear covariate effects. We then demonstrate that adding a nonlinear kernel criterion, the normalized Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion, is able to recover the true intervention effects on simulation data. Finally, we apply the non-linear concept bottleneck model to a complex single-cell RNA-seq dataset and find that it improves the ability to generate counterfactual expression profiles of cells under different tissue environments.

papers.intro:
Counterfactual modeling asks what an observation would have looked like had one of its underlying factors been different when other factors are held fixed. The dominant framework is Pearl’s abduction–action–prediction [1]: infer the latent state that explains the observation, intervene on a single factor, predict the outcome. The edit is useful only if it is at once effective, it produces the requested change, and faithful, it alters nothing else. These models are particularly valuable to observational samples in biology, where high-dimensional measurements are assumed to lie in a lower dimensional space, exhaustive sampling of potential conditions is expensive and infeasible, and a sample can usually only be measured once with a single modality. Common biological counterfactual questions include what a cell’s gene expression would be in a different environment, e.g. different tissue, or under a different context, e.g. alternative drug treatment. Single-cell RNA sequencing [2], measuring the gene expression of individual cells [3] from a sample, provides increasing resolution into disease biology at ever increasing cell numbers and resolution [4, 5]. Improved throughput and decreasing costs have enabled the production of reference atlases across tissues and diseases [6, 7, 8, 9, 10], and enabled training of latent-variable models of the cell types and states [11]. However, while modern foundation models pretrained on tens of millions of cells [12, 13] can describe cellular states, they have fallen short on valuable counterfactual prediction. Improved counterfactual models of single-cell RNA-seq data would enable the exploration of the combinatorial space of cell types, patients, treatments and doses that is infeasible at current experiment scales.

Existing models of cellular response follow two overlapping directions. The second uses interpretable representations with biologically named components [20]. Several methods combine these directions through latent-space arithmetic over disentangled factors [21, 22], latent optimization with capacity-constrained unknown-attribute embeddings [23], or causally structured concept embeddings decoded by a diffusion model [24]. All emit a profile per input cell, but their evaluations do not explicitly test whether an edit preserves donor-specific identity or matches the source donor’s response under the target condition.
