The concept bottleneck generative model scCBGM combines both approaches [25] by implementing the concept bottleneck idea [26] for a generative model of cells. The model decomposes each cell’s latent representation into a supervised block of observed concepts, such as cell type, tissue or treatment, and a set of unknown factors that account for other unrecorded variation, from donor identity to library size and batch. Counterfactual predictions for the known factors can be generated via abduction–action–prediction: encode a cell, replace one concept with its target value, and decode from the same unknown factors. Because the concepts are explicit, the edit can be checked rather than trusted, which makes it a plausible route to personalized prediction. This counterfactual, however, is only valid if the two blocks are genuinely independent, such that editing a concept does not alter another concept’s effect, e.g. a donor-specific signal that makes the prediction personal. To ensure disentanglement of the latent factors and concepts, scCBGM enforces independence with a penalty on the linear cross-covariance between the blocks, a first-order criterion blind to any dependence whose conditional means agree. Kernel criteria are the known remedy in this setting: Lopez et al. constrained a single-cell VAE with the dd-variable Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion to keep the latent independent of observed nuisance factors [27]. Here both arguments are learned, the concept head on one side and the unknown block on the other, and the question is not invariance to a nuisance but whether an edit made through the concept pathway stays faithful to the individual carried in the unknowns.

papers.title: SiPM optical readout of a PICOSEC Micromegas precise timing detector
papers.abstract: By combining a Cherenkov radiator with a semi-transparent photocathode and a two-stage Micromegas amplification element, PICOSEC Micromegas detectors have achieved <20 ps charged-particle time resolution with electronic readout of induced signals. Building upon this performance, we describe SiPM-based optical readout as a novel technique for PICOSEC Micromegas detectors. Single-channel detector prototypes based on glass Micromegas technology were read out with an array of SiPMs. To allow operation in a strongly quenched gas mixture, a solid wavelength shifter is integrated in the glass Micromegas to convert UV scintillation to the visible range and maximise scintillation light output. Timing performance of glass Micromegas in electronic and optical readout modes is compared and <150 ps time resolution is achieved by optically read out scintillation light signals. The achievable spatial resolution from centre-of-gravity reconstruction of event positions from the amplitudes of signals on multiple SiPM channels is {\sigma} = 1.25 mm. This demonstrates the possibility of dual-readout of PICOSEC glass Micromegas: electronic signals and optical signals. Finally, camera-based optical readout is presented to demonstrate imaging as another avenue for position reconstruction.

papers.intro:
Precise charged particle timing is an important tool for time-of-flight measurements, particle identification and the reconstruction of interactions in particle and nuclear physics experiments. Detectors with time resolutions of a few tens of picoseconds can improve the separation of closely spaced events and extend the capabilities of systems combining tracking and timing measurements. The PICOSEC Micromegas concept addresses these requirements by combining a Cherenkov radiator with a semi-transparent photocathode and a two-stage gaseous amplification structure [2]. Cherenkov photons produced by a traversing charged particle release photoelectrons from the photocathode, which undergo pre-amplification in a thin drift region followed by further amplification in the Micromegas amplification gap. Localising the production of the primary electrons at the photocathode reduces the timing fluctuations associated with the distribution of primary ionisation along the particle trajectory in conventional gaseous detectors. The first PICOSEC Micromegas prototype demonstrated a time resolution of 24 ps24\text{\,}\mathrm{ps} for 150 GeV150\text{\,}\mathrm{GeV} muons [2]. More recently, an improved single-channel prototype achieved a time resolution of 12.5±±0.8 ps12.5\pm\pm 0.8\text{\,}\mathrm{ps} with a CsI photocathode and a readout pad of 10 mm10\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} diameter [12]. This development highlighted the importance of detector assembly, electrical connectivity and signal integrity for obtaining the best timing performance. In addition to induced electrical signals, electron avalanches in suitable gas mixtures produce scintillation light that can be used for optical readout. Fraga et al. demonstrated CCD readout of gas electron multiplier (GEM) detectors operated in He/CF4 mixtures, including imaging of the charged particle tracks produced by thermal neutron conversion in 3He [5]. Measurements of GEM scintillation in He/CF4 and Ar/CF4 mixtures also established the dependence of light yield and spectral distribution on the gas composition [6]. The visible component of the emission in CF4-based mixtures makes these gases suitable for readout with imaging sensors. These studies provide a basis for selecting gas mixtures and photon detectors with compatible emission and sensitivity spectra. Optical readout can provide spatial information without requiring a finely segmented charge collection electrode. Its implementation in conventional Micromegas detectors is, however, restricted by the opaque substrate supporting the anode. This was addressed by integrating a Micromegas amplification structure on a glass substrate with a transparent indium tin oxide (ITO) anode [3]. Operated in an Ar/CF4 gas mixture, this detector allowed avalanche scintillation light to be recorded with cameras and demonstrated X-ray imaging [4]. The transparent substrate therefore enables optical access to the amplification region while retaining electronic readout of the anode. Combining the PICOSEC detection concept with glass Micromegas technology offers the possibility of obtaining complementary timing and position information from electronic and optical signals. Silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) placed behind the transparent anode can record the temporal response of the scintillation light, while the relative signal amplitudes across an array can be used to reconstruct the particle hit position. The gas mixture must nevertheless satisfy the requirements of both amplification and light detection. Although CF4-based mixtures can provide substantial visible scintillation, this does not directly imply sufficient visible light output from the strongly quenched Ne/CF4/C2H6 mixture used for precise PICOSEC timing. In the present detector, a solid wavelength shifter is therefore integrated on the anode to convert the avalanche-induced ultraviolet scintillation light into visible light detectable by the SiPMs. Alternatively, SiPMs with (V)UV sensitivity may be chosen in combination with a substrate and anode layer with extended UV transparency.

In the present detector, a solid wavelength shifter is therefore integrated on the anode to convert the avalanche-induced ultraviolet scintillation light into visible light detectable by the SiPMs. Alternatively, SiPMs with (V)UV sensitivity may be chosen in combination with a substrate and anode layer with extended UV transparency.

In this work, we investigate SiPM-based optical readout of single-channel PICOSEC glass Micromegas prototypes incorporating a tetraphenyl butadiene (TPB). Measurements with 150 GeV150\text{\,}\mathrm{GeV} muons at the CERN SPS are used to compare the timing response obtained from electronic and optical signals and to evaluate position reconstruction from the signal-amplitudes recorded by a 2×22\times 2 SiPM array. Additionally, camera-based imaging readout is explored as an alternative means of recording the spatial distribution of avalanche light. These measurements assess the potential of combining electronic timing measurements with optical position reconstruction in PICOSEC Micromegas detectors.

papers.title: Advancing a Global Framework for AI Safety and Governance for the Well-being of Humanity
papers.abstract: The Report "Advancing a Global Framework for AI Safety and Governance for the Well-being of Humanity" is an important outcome of the AI Safety and Governance Program of World Internet Conference Specialized Committee on Artificial Intelligence in 2025. This report provides a systematic review of current global explorations and practices in AI safety and governance, identifies key issues that need to be addressed, and draws upon multilateral governance experiences from other domains. Centered on mechanism design, it explores how to build a global AI safety and governance system that ensures safety and security, promotes inclusiveness, clarifies responsibilities and accountabilities, strengthens effective coordination, and ensures authoritative and efficient governance. Guided by the principles of multilateralism and the vision of building a community with a shared future for humankind, the report proposes institutional measures and policy recommendations to establish a United Nations-centered global AI safety and governance framework. It aims to serve as a reference for governments, international organizations, enterprises, and research institutions. The report is to contribute insights and momentum to advancing people-centered and beneficial AI governance worldwide, ensuring that AI technologies truly serve the well-being of all humanity.

papers.title: Temporal Behavior Trees for Reinforcement Learning: Specifications as Rewards, Curricula, and Diagnostics
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning from formal specifications often separates task definition, reward shaping, curriculum design, and policy diagnostics into different mathematical objects. This fragmentation requires additional conversion steps and discards structure already present in the specification, such as subtask boundaries, ordering constraints, and quantitative measures. We introduce TBTCL (Temporal Behavior Tree Centric Learning), a framework that uses Temporal Behavior Trees (TBTs) as a unified interface for specification-guided reinforcement learning. A single TBT specifies the task, induces dense robustness-based rewards, defines a curriculum, and supports better understanding of learned policies. By adapting TBT syntax and semantics for specification-guided reinforcement learning, we provide a formalism that is more expressive than popular specification languages such as LTL and inherently hierarchical. We present algorithms to automatically extract a curriculum DAG and derive dense, robustness-based rewards directly from TBT semantics. Furthermore, we utilize TBT trace segmentation to build understandable competence profiles and automatically adapt the reward toward bottlenecks. We evaluate TBTCL on six specifications across discrete and continuous domains and show that Temporal Behavior Trees can serve as a specification, a reward, a curriculum, and a diagnostic.

papers.intro:
Temporal Logics are a powerful tool in reinforcement learning, enabling the formal specification of tasks and serving as the engine of Specification-Guided Reinforcement Learning. Most standard approaches convert a logical specification into a deterministic finite automaton, which is then used to guide the learning process. While this conversion is necessary to translate standard logics such as LTL (Pnueli, 1977) into a form suitable for RL, it incurs a high cost as it loses crucial information at each step. Properties such as subtask boundaries, quantitative performance measures, hierarchical structures, and task orderings and priorities are already present in the logical specification but are discarded by most methods during intermediate conversion steps.

The core cause of these problems is that most specification languages are not designed for purposes beyond task specification. A typical pipeline represents the task specification in one object, derives a reward in another, constructs a curriculum through an additional procedure and yet another representation, and then relies on separate diagnostics and derivations to understand how a learned policy behaves, performs, and fails. As such, a potential solution would be a specification language that provides the task definition, a dense reward, a curriculum, and behavioral diagnostics, without requiring separate conversion algorithms, representations, or user inputs for each. In this paper, we argue that a single formal object can simultaneously serve as the task definition, a dense reward source, a curriculum structure, and a diagnostic model.

A TBT composes STL formulas at its leaves with tree-level operators such as sequence, parallel composition, and fallback. The STL leaves provide quantitative robustness, while the tree structure describes how behaviors compose over a trace. This hierarchical structure, which combines STL formulas at the leaves with tree-level operators, enables a concise and expressive definition of subtasks and their interconnections, which are frequently goals in reinforcement learning. This combination further enables more concise and expressive specifications than those of commonly used logics such as LTL. Furthermore, the quantitative semantics encoded by a robustness metric for TBT yields a dense reward signal and builds on previous work in the field that adapted the robustness of logics such as STL for Reinforcement Learning (Várnai and Dimarogonas, 2020). Finally, TBTs support trace decomposition, connecting policy rollouts directly to the specification expressed as a TBT without additional steps, and can be used to evaluate policy behavior and identify bottlenecks and weak points.

papers.title: Spatio-Temporal Calibration of a Vehicle-Mounted Microphone Array for Autonomous Driving
papers.abstract: Microphones let an autonomous vehicle sense into areas its cameras and LiDAR cannot see, by picking up the sound that other traffic participants emit. Locating those sources and fusing them with the visual perception requires the microphone array to be calibrated and registered relative to the vehicle's other sensors. Existing calibration methods assume small, unobstructed indoor rigs, whereas a vehicle body casts an acoustic shadow that straight-line propagation cannot represent, and to our knowledge no calibration of an array distributed around a vehicle has been reported. We propose a pipeline that uses a balloon burst as a single cross-modal target, which the LiDAR locates in metric coordinates, every microphone hears as a sharp onset and a camera times. Each observation is weighted by its own timing variance, which discounts shadowed arrivals instead of discarding them and needs no model of the vehicle. On a full-size vehicle with eight microphones over a 4.9 m aperture, the held-out range residual of 6.37 cm approaches the 6.07 cm floor set by the onset timing noise, and the calibrated array tracks a moving source to within a few degrees of the vehicle's own LiDAR. A dozen bursts spread around the vehicle suffice, and spreading them matters more than adding more.
papers.intro:
Acoustic perception remains underutilized in Autonomous Vehicles (AVs) and mobile robotics, although its physics complement those of optical sensors. Cameras and LiDAR sensors are strictly line-of-sight and easily occluded, whereas sound diffracts around obstacles. An AV can “hear” an approaching emergency siren [1] or regular traffic [2] from around a blind intersection long before the source comes into view, and a distributed microphone array provides this awareness all around the vehicle [3].

papers.title: Evidence of anomalous Hall crystals in moir\'e rhombohedral graphene
papers.abstract: An anomalous Hall crystal (AHC) is a quantum state of matter, in which spontaneous electron crystallization leads to a quantized Hall effect without a magnetic field. The state can emerge in materials with strong Coulomb interaction and large Berry curvatures, such as few-layer rhombohedral graphene. Although the idea of AHCs has been invoked to explain some of the observed Chern insulators in moir\'e rhombohedral graphene (mRG), direct experimental evidence of AHCs has been missing so far. Here, we report experimental evidence of AHCs in hole-doped mRG through combined electrical transport and noise measurements. We identify a series of distinct Chern insulators spanning a broad and continuous range of doping densities incommensurate with the underlying moir\'e lattice; the states exhibit current-induced broadband noise and memory effects as well as pronounced gate hysteresis. Systematic magnetic field, temperature and gate dependence studies further support the emergence of a spontaneously charge-ordered state that acts as a parental state for the observed Chern insulators. The absence of Chern insulators at nearby integer fillings also distinguishes the observed state from the reported reentrant or extended quantum (anomalous) Hall states. Altogether, our results establish experimental evidence of AHCs in mRG and open the door for further exploration of the collective dynamics in this new state of matter.

papers.title: Optical characterization of microcellular PET and crystallized PEN reflectors in liquid argon for LEGEND-1000
papers.abstract: Efficient collection of liquid argon (LAr) scintillation light is essential for background rejection in the LEGEND experiment. We investigate microcellular polyethylene terephthalate (PET) and crystallized polyethylene naphthalate (PEN) as candidate reflector materials for LEGEND-1000. Their optical responses to 450 nm light and 128 nm LAr scintillation are measured in LAr and complemented by room-temperature reflectance measurements in air. Under scintillation illumination, PET coupled to a PEN foil and crystallized PEN increase the detected photoelectron yield by factors of $2.36\pm0.11$ and $1.75\pm0.10$, respectively, relative to a black-metal-velvet reference. A Geant4-based optical model yields reflectivity estimates at $450~\mathrm{nm}$ in LAr of $(90\pm4)\%$ for PET and $(81\pm5)\%$ for crystallized PEN, compared with $(80\pm5)\%$ for the Tetratex reference. These results motivate further investigation of both materials for LAr instrumentation, including their radiopurity, long-term cryogenic stability, and performance under matched detector conditions.

papers.title: Performance Portability Explained: Insights from accelerating ICON microphysics
papers.abstract:
Scientific computing is under increasing pressure to adapt to HPC hardware that is shaped by AI workloads. In these modern ecosystems, extracting reasonable performance without investing major engineering effort is a central issue for domain scientists. Correctness constraints and intricate reference implementations represent further impediments to development. Instead of using a double-precision implementation as a reference, considering the underlying scientific problem directly opens more opportunities for performance improvements when updating and rewriting applications.
  We take seven different portability frameworks---covering pragma-based, DSL, and data-centric approaches---and evaluate them on a microphysics kernel of the ICON climate model. Our performance benchmarks show that each different HPC system benefits from a different combination of optimizations, so we develop the measure of framework expressivity to gauge how easily each framework can customize portable implementations in this way.

papers.intro:
It is imperative for scientific computing in the HPC context to adapt to hardware ecosystems that are increasingly shaped by AI workloads. In weather and climate modeling, this shift is occurring alongside a broader transformation in both the scientific ambition and computational organization of Earth-system simulations, as kilometer-scale models and ensemble-based workflows demand ever greater computational efficiency [1, 2]. Not only are scientific applications expected to be performance portable even on the newest exascale systems, but results must remain correct across different hard- and software environments [3]. Evaluating correctness of new implementations is difficult, regardless of whether results are within tolerance for a certain reference, or physically correct for a set of standard experiments with known solutions [4, 5, 6, 7, 8].

In general, optimizing and porting scientific applications to modern accelerator architectures does not result in a faithful re-expression of an existing implementation, especially given recent trends that change floating-point arithmetic at the hardware level. Furthermore, for many real-world problems there is no reference solution to compare against, only a reference implementation which has shown to match expectations for a set of experiments empirically. Approximating the difference between the physical solution and a given implementation is a research field of its own. Instead, performance portability requires design choices at multiple levels for the efficient implementation of computations and, in tandem, the representation of the underlying problem in terms of physics and numerics.

Here, we argue that a scientific code development cannot be defined through a sequence of discrete, independent decisions. Rather, the best approach is for scientists to jointly navigate the shared design space with a spectrum of abstraction levels covering physics, mathematics, and computer science. From the precise form of equations employed, to the applied numerical algorithms and discretization strategies, down to the order of operations chosen at the hardware level, each decision has ripple effects on the final application. papers.title: Intracycle Interference in Strong-Field Photoemission from a Tungsten Needle Tip
papers.abstract: Electrons photoemitted by strong laser fields can rescatter, generating attosecond high harmonics. Spectral peaks arise from inter- and intracycle interference of coherent electron wave packets. While intercycle interference is well known, intracycle interference of plateau electrons has not been observed. We present carrier-envelope phase-resolved photoemission spectra from a nanometric tungsten needle tip driven at 1570 nm revealing such interference, supported by quantum orbit and TDSE simulations that elucidate attosecond-scale electron dynamics.

papers.title: From Growth to Devices: Oxygen-Controlled Superconductivity in BSCCO Thin Films
papers.abstract: Realizing device-compatible high-$T_c$ superconductors requires simultaneous control of oxygen stoichiometry and tolerance to nanofabrication. Here, we investigate sputtered Bi$_2$Sr$_2$Ca$_{n-1}$Cu$_n$O$_{2n+4+\delta}$ (BSCCO) thin films and establish a direct link between annealing conditions, oxygen incorporation, and superconducting transport. By independently varying the annealing temperature and duration, we identify an optimal annealing condition of $860\,^{\circ}$C for 3\,h, which yields the highest superconducting transition temperature and the narrowest transition among the investigated samples. X-ray diffraction, electron microscopy, and X-ray photoemission spectroscopy reveal a non-monotonic evolution of lattice oxygen, which governs hole doping in the CuO$_2$ planes and produces the characteristic dome-like dependence of $T_c$ on doping concentration. We further translate these optimized films into micro-devices to assess fabrication-induced effects, via micro-bridges as well as a planar Josephson junction. We demonstrate devices fabricated via both lift-off and focused ion beam (FIB) patterning methods -- proving the fabrication compatibility of these films. Importantly, we demonstrate their air-stability for extended periods of time (2 months). The combined insights offer practical guidelines for integrating cuprate thin films into superconducting electronics and quantum device architectures.

papers.title: Probing for anisotropies at different angular scales in the arrival directions of the cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory
papers.abstract: Studies of the arrival-direction distribution of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays are crucial for revealing their origin. In this work, we investigate the distribution of the arrival directions of events detected with the Pierre Auger Observatory over different angular scales. To do this, we adopt a novel method where we use a von Mises--Fisher distribution to model the excesses with respect to isotropic expectations. This method allows us to study the distribution of arrival directions over different angular scales consistently and simultaneously. We consider the events in different energy bins above 4 EeV detected from 1$^\text{st}$ January 2004 to 31$^\text{st}$ December 2022, i.e. during the entire Phase~I of the Pierre Auger Observatory, with a total exposure of $123{,}000$ km$^2$ sr yr. The most significant excess in the bins considered is a dipolar modulation in the energy range (8--16) EeV, which is compatible with previous findings of the Pierre Auger Collaboration. A dipolar modulation appears to be present for the higher energies considered as well, and at the highest energies, i.e. above 32 EeV, we find indications of its coexistence with an overdensity of intermediate angular scale, located in the Centaurus region.

At large angular scales, a significant dipolar modulation in right ascension (R.A.) was observed above 8 EeV11 1 1​EeV=10181\,\mathrm{EeV}=10^{18} eV by the Pierre Auger Collaboration. The modulation was first reported in Aab and others (2017c), and has now reached 6.8σ\sigma significance Halim and others (2024). Its direction lies around 115∘ away from the Galactic Center, suggesting that UHECRs at these energies are mostly of extragalactic origin. Moreover, the dipole amplitude has an approximately linear growth with energy Halim and others (2024).

The scan was repeated for different energy thresholds, and notably, an excess present in the Centaurus region is observed above each energy threshold. With the approach presented here, we look instead for the most significant excess of events and provide a more comprehensive characterization thereof. As a result, we get new insight into the transition from large-scale anisotropies at lower energies to intermediate-scale excesses at higher energies.

papers.title: An Information-Theoretic Perspective on Regulatory T Cell Localization as an IL-2 Interference Filter
papers.abstract: Diffusible signals enable communication between immune cells but can also create interference between nearby activation sites. In lymph nodes, effector T cells (Teff) concentrate around antigen-presenting cells (APCs), release interleukin-2 (IL-2) following antigen recognition, and sense IL-2 through cell-surface receptors. Experiments show high-uptake regulatory T cells (Treg) clustered around IL-2-producing cells. However, it is unclear how strongly responses at neighboring activation sites are coupled through diffusible IL-2, and how this coupling is influenced by the spatial organization of Treg acting as IL-2 sinks. We interpret two neighboring sites as a molecular communication system and study the effect of clustering using a three-dimensional IL-2 field coupled to T cell population dynamics. Across a broad parameter sweep, clustering Treg produces a larger mean reduction in neighboring-site interference than adding dispersed Treg. Compared with no Treg, clustered Treg suppress interference while largely preserving the strong local response with corresponding consequences for population expansion and survival. Information-theoretic analysis shows improved discrimination between weak and strong local sources at short separation, whereas at larger separation clustering primarily reduces the remaining estimated neighboring-source information. These findings support a spatial-filtering role for Treg clustering in maintaining locally informative immune responses.

papers.intro:
Lymph nodes bring together immune cells that detect and respond to antigens. Antigen-presenting cells (APCs) display antigen-derived molecular fragments to T cells, which have the task of discriminating between host (self) and foreign (non-self) antigens. We call an APC and the surrounding responding T cells an activation site: following antigen recognition, effector T cells (Teff) at the activation site release interleukin-2 (IL-2), a diffusible cytokine that supports T cell division and survival, and sense it through cell-surface receptors [1, 2]. Neighboring activation sites therefore share a chemical medium, raising the question of how each can maintain a response that reflects its own local stimulation.

Neighboring activation sites therefore share a chemical medium, raising the question of how each can maintain a response that reflects its own local stimulation.

As with nearby wireless links sharing a frequency, signals from one activation site can influence reception at another. Shared IL-2 can coordinate T cell responses, but also promote responses in weakly stimulated cells near a stronger source [2, 1]. However, regulatory T cells (Treg) strongly consume IL-2 and act as local sinks [3, 4]. Imaging studies have identified their clustering around IL-2-producing T cells [5, 6]. This motivates the hypothesis that localized uptake suppresses “interference” and helps neighboring activation sites maintain independent local readings. In this paper, we take a molecular-communication, and particularly an information-theoretic, approach to this localization: we interpret two neighboring sites as an information transfer system and ask whether Treg clustering suppresses neighboring-site interference while preserving the local response. We study these effects using a three-dimensional (3D) IL-2 field coupled to T cell population dynamics, distinguishing information about local stimulation from neighboring-source influence.

Our work connects with an emerging body of literature, applying information-theoretic analysis to the T cell’s discrimination task. Such analysis has been recently used to quantify discrimination performance in T cells [7, 8], distinguish classes of recognizable antigens [9, 10], and to determine the role of kinetic proofreading in T cell activation [11, 12]. These works build on a rich foundational literature on the information theory of ligand-receptor systems [13, 14, 15], of which the T cell receptor is an important example. More generally, information-theoretic quantities such as mutual information give a principled and model-independent measure of biological fitness [16], motivating their use in biological studies.

papers.title: Improved Myelin Water Fraction Estimation and Uncertainty Mapping in Multicomponent T2 Relaxometry via NNLS Bootstrap Aggregation
papers.abstract: Estimating the myelin water fraction (MWF) from multicomponent T2 relaxometry requires solving an ill-conditioned inverse problem, making estimates sensitive to noise. Regularization can improve stability but may introduce bias. Conventional NNLS-based methods also provide point estimates without directly quantifying voxelwise variability. To address these limitations, we propose the non-negative least squares Bootstrap Barycenter (NNLS-BB), combining residual resampling with repeated NNLS reconstruction. We average spectra and derived parameters across bootstrap replicates and use their standard deviations to characterize sensitivity to signal perturbations. The method requires neither an explicit spectral regularization penalty nor a training dataset. NNLS-BB was evaluated on 40,000 simulated voxels with signal-to-noise ratios of 50-1000, against conventional NNLS, two regularized NNLS methods, and a model-informed machine-learning (MIML) method. Scan-rescan repeatability was assessed across 20 white-matter regions in two independent cohorts comprising 13 healthy participants. NNLS-BB achieved the lowest MWF mean absolute error and root mean squared error in all simulated noise regimes. Mean absolute error decreased by 36-41% relative to conventional NNLS, alongside lower error dispersion. Compared with Bayes-Reg-$D^{-1}$ and MIML, NNLS-BB achieved comparable dispersion but substantially lower bias, although MIML reconstructed the full spectrum more accurately. In vivo, NNLS-BB yielded the lowest regional scan-rescan dispersion and highest mean correlation in both cohorts. Bootstrap standard-deviation maps provided complementary information about parameter variability. These results support residual-bootstrap aggregation for improving MWF estimation while providing voxelwise variability maps from a single acquisition.

papers.intro:
Multicomponent T2T_{2} relaxometry probes brain tissue microstructure by separating MRI signal contributions associated with water pools exhibiting different transverse relaxation properties. In white matter, one of its main applications is myelin water imaging (MWI), where the rapidly decaying signal component, typically associated with T2T_{2} values of approximately 10–30 ms, is commonly attributed to water confined between the myelin bilayers. The relative contribution of this short-T2T_{2} component defines the myelin water fraction (MWF), a widely studied MRI marker associated with myelin content. MWF has been investigated in neurological disorders affecting white-matter microstructure (Does, 2018; Alonso-Ortiz et al., 2015; Piredda et al., 2020; Rivas-Fernández et al., 2025), as well as in normal aging (Canales-Rodríguez et al., 2021a).

A conventional approach models the measured signal as a superposition of exponential relaxation components characterized by different T2T_{2} values. Their amplitudes define a non-negative T2T_{2} spectrum, which is typically estimated on a predefined T2T_{2} grid using non-negative least squares (NNLS) (Mackay et al., 1994; Whittall et al., 1997; MacKay et al., 2006). Although conceptually simple, this inverse problem is intrinsically ill-conditioned because components with nearby T2T_{2} values generate very similar signal decays over the finite set of measured echo times. Consequently, small perturbations of the data can produce substantial changes in the recovered spectrum. Related studies of multiexponential fitting, in which both component amplitudes and relaxation times are estimated, have also shown that the identification of distinct components strongly depends on the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and temporal sampling (Bertero et al., 1982; Istratov and Vyvenko, 1999).

By introducing an additional penalty, regularization stabilizes the recovered spectrum and generally reduces the variability of the derived MWF estimates. Common penalties favor spectra with smaller norms or smoother profiles (Whittall and MacKay, 1989; Graham et al., 1996; Canales-Rodríguez et al., 2021b). papers.title: Connecting field-level and n-point function measurements of galaxy bias
papers.abstract: Precise measurements of galaxy bias parameters are essential for extracting cosmological information from galaxy surveys. Field-level analyses infer bias coefficients at a finite cutoff $\Lambda$, typically related to the lattice resolution, while $n$-point function analyses typically adopt renormalization conditions defined in the low-$k$ limit. In this work, we use the renormalization group (RG) to relate field-level measurements at different cutoffs and connect them to $n$-point function measurements. We generate mock galaxy fields with a Lagrangian perturbation theory forward model and a galaxy bias expansion, and then measure the bias parameters across a range of cutoffs. We show that the RG predictions describe the measured running and, in the limit $\Lambda\to 0$, agree with the (tree-level) $n$-point function measurements of first-order $b_\delta$ and second-order $b_{\delta^2}, b_{{G}_2}$. We also measure the running on halo catalogs based on full $N$-body simulations and show that the RG prediction describes the measurements well within the predicted systematic errors. Our results establish the RG flow as a natural formulation for relating galaxy bias measurements at different cutoffs and connecting the schemes used in field-level and $n$-point function analyses.

papers.title: Toward Foundation Detection Models via Example-Based Grounding in EM-DETR
papers.abstract: DeepLearning (DL)-based Computer-Aided Diagnostic (CAD) systems have shown great promise in supporting clinicians, but their performance heavily depends on the availability of large, well-annotated datasets. In medical lesion detection, the scarcity of comprehensive, stan dardized annotations and the heterogeneity of existing datasets limit the development of robust foundation models. In this work, we introduce a novel approach to building a multi-domain foundation model for le sion detection by integrating diverse medical image datasets annotated for both anatomical structures and abnormalities. We first propose a student-teacher training strategy to effectively combine datasets with heterogeneous label spaces, mitigating catastrophic forgetting, and im proving feature learning. In addition, building on our previously pro posed example-based EM-DETR framework, we adapt it to jointly learn from multiple domain-specific datasets, enabling fine-grained, example driven detection across modalities. Our model achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) results, with image-level AUC scores exceeding previous SOTA by 1% point on four key findings in CXRs. We achieve a leading mAP50 in CXRs and mammography, surpassing EM-DETR trained on a single dataset by 2-3% points. This approach paves the way for scalable foundation models in medical imaging that leverage heterogeneous data while maintaining robust and generalizable performance.

papers.title: CFAR Detection on Non-Coherently Integrated Angular Maps for mmWave Radio SLAM
papers.abstract: Reliable multipath detection is essential for millimeter-wave simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM), where propagation paths reflecting off the environment provide geometric constraints beyond the dominant line-of-sight component. This paper develops constant false alarm rate (CFAR)-based detectors for beam-swept bistatic integrated sensing and communications (ISAC). Starting from conventional CFAR on the I/Q datacube, we derive a modified detector for non-coherently integrated angular power maps, where the post-integration noise statistics differ from those assumed by standard cell-averaging CFAR. To improve practicality, we introduce a multi-cell cell-under-test formulation and a plus-shaped training window that reduces computational cost while accounting for sidelobe structure. The proposed methods are evaluated on experimental 60 GHz indoor measurements using a snapshot-SLAM estimator. Compared with a singular value decomposition (SVD)-based detector, the proposed CFAR approaches reduce the overall positioning RMSE from 0.30 m to 0.24-0.26 m, with the largest improvement in non-line-of-sight snapshots. The multi-cell non-coherent detector further lowers the computational complexity without degrading positioning accuracy, demonstrating its suitability for practical multipath radio-SLAM.

Future sixth generation (6G) networks are expected to support integrated sensing and communications (ISAC), extending connectivity and positioning services towards radio-based awareness of the surrounding environment [1, 2]. In the use cases studied by the 3rd generation partnership project (3GPP), the same transmissions are used to sense passive objects in the environment, which improves the situational awareness of the user equipments (UEs) [2].

Bistatic cellular simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) is one realization of this idea, in which reference signals transmitted by base stations (BSs) at known locations are used to jointly estimate the state of a UE and the locations of environmental scattering points, commonly referred to as landmarks [3]. A radio-SLAM processing chain generally consists of two stages. First, received measurements are converted into path estimates of angle of arrival (AoA), angle of departure (AoD), and time of arrival (ToA). These estimates are then processed by a SLAM algorithm to recover the UE state and landmark positions. Reliable channel parameter estimation is therefore essential to the whole system. In particular, multipath-radio SLAM exploits the non-line-of-sight (NLOS) components to provide additional geometric constraints, enabling positioning when the direct line-of-sight (LOS) path is blocked [4]. Channel estimators must detect not only the dominant path, but also weaker multipath components with sufficiently accurate angular and delay parameters.

Many channel parameter estimators have been reported in the literature [5, 6, 7]. They often require knowledge of the steering vectors, beamforming weights, or antenna beampatterns. In practical beam-sweeping systems, however, only the beam indices and their nominal pointing directions may be available, limiting the applicable channel parameter estimation methods. Detection directly on the angular power map is an alternative that does not require explicit knowledge of the antenna responses. The beam reference signal received power (BRSRP)-based method in [8] addresses this limitation by operating directly on the measured AoA/AoD power map. The rank-1 singular value decomposition (SVD)-based approach provides robustness against sidelobes and noise. However, the low-rank extraction mainly retains only dominant components, whereas multipath-radio SLAM benefits from retaining weaker geometrically informative returns.

Cell-averaging constant false alarm rate (CFAR) is well suited to detect paths on the AoA/AoD power map. Its conventional threshold assumes exponentially distributed single-look samples, so it can be applied to each positioning reference signal (PRS) resource element (RE) before integration, at the cost of one detection test per RE. Non-coherent integration avoids this cost, but the resulting power-map cells are approximately Gaussian and the conventional threshold no longer holds. To overcome this limitation, this paper develops a CFAR test for multipath detection in beam-swept angular maps that accounts for the post-integration Gaussian statistics. Because a path return occupies multiple neighbouring beam pairs, the test region is extended to a multi-cell block, so the statistic is evaluated once per block rather than once per bin. A detection is stored at the strongest cell of the cell under test (CUT) block, retaining the angular resolution of the single-cell test. In addition, a plus-shaped CFAR window is proposed, to account for the directionally structured sidelobe energy along the AoA/AoD axes. The proposed method is evaluated on experimental PRS measurements from the Campus Arena at Tampere University and compared with the SVD-based BRSRP estimator of [8], using the same downstream snapshot-SLAM backend of [9]. Multi-CUT non-coherent CFAR lowers positioning root mean squared error (RMSE) from 0.300.30 m to 0.250.25 m overall and from 0.380.38 m to 0.290.29 m on NLOS snapshots, while requiring about three orders of magnitude fewer detector statistic evaluations than per-RE CFAR with binary integration.

papers.title: XAI-Driven Confidence Estimation for OOD-Resilient Runtime Prediction
papers.abstract: Machine learning-based resource management (RM) models degrade under out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs at runtime, yet existing approaches in the literature rely on a single global error margin that is overly conservative and fails to distinguish reliablepredictions from catastrophic failures. We propose Lightweight Runtime EXplainability (LEX), the first post-hoc XAI framework for input-specific runtime confidence estimation in ML-based RM. LEX clusters the embeddings of the training input space using a Gaussian Mixture Model and associates per-cluster prediction error bounds to input samples, enabling fine-grained runtime confidence signals without retraining. Evaluated on a state-of-the-art LSTM-based IPS forecasting model on Intel Alder Lake, across 34 benchmark applications, LEX achieves ~94% containment on unseen workloads and produces ~17% tighter per-input confidence bounds than global baselines. With its negligible runtime overhead, LEX advances the field by providing explainable and reliable input-specific confidence signals of ML predictions, thereby making ML-based resource management resilient to OOD at runtime.

papers.intro:
To cope with the growing complexity of modern multi-core processors and the rising demands for higher performance and efficiency, machine learning has emerged as the dominant paradigm for system-level resource management. In fact, a large body of machine learning techniques has been proposed over the past decade, including supervised models that can predict workload behavior and guide dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (Lozano and Gerstlauer, 2022), recurrent neural networks that forecast instructions per second and instructions per Joule under resource contention (Sikal et al., 2025b), and reinforcement and imitation learning models that derive resource management policies directly from hardware interactions (Narang et al., 2023; Costero et al., 2020). Collectively, these techniques have demonstrated significant improvements over heuristic baselines (Rapp et al., 2022), establishing machine learning-based resource management as a promising research direction.

Collectively, these techniques have demonstrated significant improvements over heuristic baselines (Rapp et al., 2022), establishing machine learning-based resource management as a promising research direction.

However, while very promising, machine learning models face a major generalization challenge when deployed in real-world settings. Mainly, the shift between training and runtime data distributions exposes the model to out-of-distribution samples, leading to performance degradation, i.e., catastrophic predictions, at runtime, potentially nullifying the intended benefits of machine learning-based resource management. Therefore, a resource management technique shall be resilient to such out-of-distribution events at runtime, by accounting for model mispredictions, or even ignoring them in case of catastrophic predictions. Yet, very few machine learning-based techniques in the literature have demonstrated such awareness (Chen et al., 2023; Wächter et al., 2019; Sikal et al., 2025b; Rapp et al., 2021). These techniques have employed statistical metrics about the model performance or error, e.g., standard deviation from the mean-absolute-percentage error, 90-percentiles of mean-absolute-percentage error, etc., to adjust the model prediction at runtime by accounting for its error. However, as we show in the following motivational example, relying on such global statistical metrics hides the catastrophic performance a model can exhibit when faced with out-of-distribution data samples at runtime.

The raw periodic traces are then converted into structured multivariate time series for supervised sequence-to-one forecasting. All window sequences across all runs are combined into a single dataset containing ~219K windows, with each window capturing the phase-level characteristics of the application at a specific configuration, i.e., core type and voltage/frequency level.

Experiment 1: Random split (Fig. 1.a). In this experiment, the most common evaluation strategy in the literature is followed, which consists of splitting the dataset into random 70%/30% train/test splits. With 50 different random splits, we train the model 50 times and compute the mean mean-absolute-percentage error scores across all 50 model variants. As can be seen on Fig. 1.a, the model achieves a near-perfect mean mean-absolute-percentage error of 0.40.4% and a 90-th percentile mean-absolute-percentage error of 0.70.7% on the test dataset. papers.title: Confoundry: Spatial Causal Discovery and Dynamic Effect Mapping from Earth Observation Time Series
papers.abstract: Earth observation time series provide extensive historical observations of environmental change, but causal relationships inferred from them may vary geographically and depend heavily on local model adequacy. We introduce Confoundry, a framework for spatially resolved causal discovery and dynamic effect estimation from heterogeneous Earth observation time series. Confoundry aligns multi-source raster data, removes deterministic seasonal and long-term variation, fits separate structural VAR--LiNGAM models at individual grid cells, and propagates bootstrap estimation uncertainty into mapped dynamic responses. Model diagnostics are evaluated spatially so that mapped responses can be restricted to locations meeting predefined model checks. We demonstrate the approach using monthly MODIS NDVI and ERA5-Land hydroclimatic variables over the Iberian Peninsula from 2005--2024. Of 27,050 fitted pixel models, 14,657 passed the primary diagnostic criteria. The retained models yield geographically heterogeneous model-implied NDVI responses to precipitation, temperature, potential evaporation, and shallow and deep soil moisture. Aggregated responses vary systematically along an external aridity gradient: water-related responses become relatively stronger toward drier environments, whereas temperature responses increase toward wetter conditions. A single-pixel synthetic benchmark illustrates substantial finite-record variation in recovered causal structure and dynamic effects from 20-year monthly time series. The results demonstrate that spatial causal mapping of Earth observation data is most informative when estimated responses, uncertainty, and local model adequacy are reported together.

Earth observation (EO) data and reanalysis products provide spatially extensive records of vegetation, climate, and land-surface conditions. They support applications including drought monitoring, crop assessment, ecosystem analysis, and land-surface characterization. Many EO studies describe statistical associations or predict environmental outcomes without identifying causal mechanisms. For example, a correlation between vegetation greenness and precipitation cannot by itself distinguish whether the observed covariation is the result of a direct response, shared seasonality, an indirect soil-moisture pathway, or a common driver of both variables.

Causal inference provides a way to formulate these alternatives as directed relationships with explicit assumptions [1, 2, 3]. This can help separate direct and mediated effects and generate testable hypotheses about environmental processes. Observational causal estimates remain conditional on the variables measured and the assumptions of the model; they complement domain knowledge and process-based modeling rather than replacing them.

EO data make such analyses difficult in several ways. Products differ in grid, resolution, cadence, data availability, and physical meaning. Relationships also vary across landscapes, so a single regional graph may conceal local mechanisms. Finally, environmental systems can violate assumptions commonly used in causal discovery, including linearity, independent disturbances, stable dynamics, and adequate control of common causes. Spatial causal analysis of EO data therefore requires more than applying a causal-discovery algorithm to each grid cell: it must reconcile heterogeneous observations, represent geographic variation in causal dynamics, and identify where the fitted model itself does not support causal interpretation.

Two relevant approaches to causal research involving EO data are design-based studies and systems-oriented time-series analysis. To examine local heterogeneity in both contemporaneous and delayed dependencies, we introduce Confoundry, a pixel-wise causal-analysis framework. We fit a separate structural vector autoregressive linear non-Gaussian acyclic model (VAR–LiNGAM) at each grid cell [22, 23]. Under its structural assumptions, the non-Gaussian error model can identify a contemporaneous causal order that lag-only models cannot recover. Fitting this model locally allows contemporaneous structure, lagged relationships, effect magnitude, and response persistence to vary across the study area. papers.title: High-power X-Point Target divertor experiments on the TCV tokamak
papers.abstract: Stationary power exhaust in the X-Point Target (XPT) divertor configuration is investigated in high-power ($2.5\,\text{MW}$) TCV L-mode discharges, in which the Lengyel detachment scaling metric $P_{\text{SOL}}B_{0}/(R_{0}n_{e,\text{u}}^{2})$ lies in the range expected for reactors (SPARC, ITER, ARC). Compared with a conventional single-null (SN) divertor, the XPT improves power exhaust performance, reducing the peak outer target heat flux by 40--60\% and enabling divertor detachment with nitrogen seeding under conditions in which the SN cannot be detached. Detachment evolves asymmetrically across the multiple XPT outer strike points. The sensitivities of the peak target heat fluxes and impurity emission front positions to the X-point separation ($\text{d}R_{\text{u},X2}$) are characterized and found to decrease at higher nitrogen seeding levels. Field-reversal experiments reveal the critical role of $E\times B$ drifts inherent to the magnetic topology of the secondary X-point, which drive an unconventional redistribution of density and impurity radiation in the XPT divertor and thereby cause the asymmetries between the XPT outer strike points, largely confirming the expectations from recent SOLPS-ITER modelling. A framework for understanding the power exhaust physics of the XPT is presented, detailing the roles of SOL splitting, connection length peaking, $E\times B$ drifts, and vessel geometry. Together, these results establish an experimental physics basis for the XPT divertor as a potential power exhaust solution for tokamak reactors.

papers.intro:
Next-step, gigawatt-scale tokamak fusion power plants will require divertor power exhaust solutions that integrate core performance with plasma detachment [44, 34] under divertor heat fluxes higher than those of ITER [81, 46, 88, 62, 17]. Alternative divertor configurations [70, 74, 78] have been conceived to tackle this extreme power exhaust challenge and to mitigate the extrapolation risks of the ITER-like conventional single-null (SN) divertor [59]. Through advanced magnetic shaping of the divertor, these alternative configurations are expected to reduce the separatrix density and impurity seeding [32] required to attain detachment, and to widen the parameter window for detached divertor operation [45, 13].

The X-Point Target (XPT) divertor [39, 38] is a promising alternative divertor configuration characterized by a secondary X-point along the divertor leg. First realized experimentally in TCV Ohmic L-mode plasmas [74], the XPT has been found to greatly reduce the upstream separatrix density threshold for detachment access [41]. The impurity emission front clamps at the secondary X-point, yielding a wide detachment operational window [41] that is resilient against fast perturbations in fuelling, seeding and heating [85]. In H-mode discharges with type-I edge-localized modes (ELMs), a reduction of target heat fluxes by the XPT has been observed in the inter-ELM phase [60] and, more recently, during the ELM crash [89, 91]. The large poloidal flux expansion at the secondary X-point is thought to be responsible for these exhaust benefits [41, 45], which are related to the phenomenon of X-point radiation [3, 72, 2].

The XPT is currently being considered as an alternative divertor candidate for next-step devices (SPARC [35], ARC [17], EHL-2 [80]). In particular, the ARC fusion power plant is designed with up-down symmetric (double-null) XPT divertors in long, tightly baffled outer legs. The engineering concepts required to implement the XPT in a practical reactor are being developed [36], including the creation of additional divertor volume within the breeding blanket to accommodate long divertor legs, tight baffling for neutral compression and power dissipation via plasma-neutral interactions [76, 64], and demountable high-temperature superconducting (HTS) magnets [69] enabling the placement of divertor shaping coils within the toroidal field coil volume in reactor environments. Equilibrium design and magnet control schemes for the XPT are also being studied [79, 1, 15]. This paper investigates XPT power exhaust in a recently developed high-power TCV scenario [42] in order to explore experimentally the SOL regime in which the power exhaust challenge is maximized. The highest available ECRH power (2.5​MW2.5\,\text{MW}, fully absorbed in a ∼1​m3\sim 1\,\text{m}^{3} plasma) is applied at low upstream separatrix densities (ne,u≈1×1019​m−3n_{e,\text{u}}\approx 1\times 10^{19}\,\text{m}^{-3}). To interpret these results, a framework is introduced that describes how the XPT geometry governs power exhaust and clarifies the role of the X-point separation, pointing to pathways for its geometric optimization.

Section 2 presents a framework for interpreting the SOL and power exhaust physics arising from the geometry of the XPT, detailing the roles of SOL splitting, connection length peaking, E×BE\times B drifts around the secondary X-point, and vessel geometry. Section 7 discusses the implications for reactors, and section 8 summarizes the conclusions.

papers.title: Signatures of mass transfer in open-cluster blue straggler stars. I. Collinder 261: Evidence from rotation, binarity, and chemical abundances
papers.abstract: We present the first dedicated $v\sin i$ survey of blue straggler stars (BSS) in the old open cluster Collinder 261 ($t=6.7$ Gyr), based on VLT/FLAMES-GIRAFFE spectroscopy of 40 BSS and 42 turn-off/subgiant (TO/SGB) reference stars. Seventeen of the 39 BSS entering the statistics (44%) rotate faster than 40 km/s, whereas all TO/SGB reference stars are slow rotators; fast rotation is strongly linked to spectroscopic binarity. TESS light curves identify seven eclipsing or ellipsoidal binaries with $P_{orb}=0.5$-2.1 d, all rotating at the velocity set by tidal synchronisation, so in these systems the fast rotation is maintained by a close post-mass-transfer orbit and does not date the formation event. Differential C, O, Ba, and Fe abundances for the 22 slow rotators reveal that 62% carry the surface-pollution signature of mass transfer, in two distinct patterns separated by an empty ~1 dex gap in [Ba/Fe]: a Ba-rich group tracing AGB donors and a C/O-enhanced, Ba-normal group tracing donors below the $s$-process activation mass. The BSS iron abundance is consistent with the cluster value; the few apparent Fe excesses are partly explained by differential reddening and do not affect the abundance pattern. The correlated C-O enrichment is opposite to the depletion seen in globular-cluster BSS, indicating binaries wide enough for donors to reach the AGB. With $A^+_{r_h}=0.171\pm0.034$ and $f_{FR-BSS}=44\pm8$%, Collinder 261 extends the globular-cluster rotation-density trends into the open-cluster regime: its BSS were assembled by a continuously operating binary channel, and their chemistry records the dynamical environment of the host cluster.

papers.intro:
Blue Straggler Stars (BSS) occupy a region of the colour–magnitude diagram (CMD) that should be empty according to standard single-star evolution: they appear bluer and brighter than the MSTO, mimicking a younger stellar population in an old cluster. First identified in M3 by Sandage (1953), BSS are recognised as a universal feature of old stellar systems (Bailyn, 1995; Ferraro et al., 2023). Three formation channels have been proposed. Mass transfer (MT): the primary of a binary accretes mass from an evolved companion, gaining enough material to appear rejuvenated (McCrea, 1964). This picture is supported on a population level by Rain et al. (2024), who found a significant correlation between the number of blue stragglers and the binary fraction of the host cluster in a sample of twelve old open clusters and showed that composite evolutionary sequences from binary evolution models reproduce the observed distributions in the colour–magnitude diagram. Stellar mergers or stellar triples: close binary evolution or hierarchical-triple dynamics force two stars to coalesce (Leonard, 1989; Sills et al., 2005). Dynamical collisions: direct stellar encounters in dense environments create BSS with intermediate-to-high rotation (Hills and Day, 1976; Lombardi et al., 2002). In GCs, the relative contribution of each channel depends on the dynamical environment: denser cores favour collisions and dynamically-induced mergers, whereas MT operates across all densities (Davies et al., 2004; Knigge et al., 2009). In old open clusters, by contrast, the low stellar densities effectively suppress direct collisions; here, BSS are expected to form almost exclusively through MT in binary systems and through mergers driven by close-binary or hierarchical-triple evolution, and recent studies find that mass transfer is the main channel (Leiner and Geller, 2021; Linck and Mathieu, 2026b), making these systems particularly clean test beds for binary interaction physics. Disentangling these formation channels is important for several reasons that extend well beyond BSS themselves. First, BSS are the most accessible laboratory for studying mass transfer in intermediate-age and old stellar populations: the efficiency, stability, and angular-momentum budget of MT govern the production of a wide variety of exotic objects (Type Ia supernovae progenitors, cataclysmic variables, symbiotic stars, and subdwarf-B stars) yet these parameters remain poorly constrained observationally (Taam and Sandquist, 2000; Postnov and Yungelson, 2014). By quantifying the MT-to-merger ratio in different environments and comparing the observed fractions with predictions of binary population-synthesis codes, BSS surveys provide direct empirical constraints on the mass-transfer efficiency, the critical mass-ratio for stable Roche-lobe overflow, and the common-envelope ejection parameter αCE\alpha_{\rm CE} (Iben and Livio, 1993). Second, this isolation of MT and binary-driven mergers offers a controlled setting to test MT physics without the complicating effects of the frequent dynamical encounters that dominate GC cores. Third, the MT channel leaves imprints on the companion and on the BSS surface chemistry (C/O depletion, ss-process enhancement), providing multi-messenger constraints on AGB nucleosynthesis and common envelope evolution that are difficult to obtain by other means (Gosnell et al., 2014; Nine et al., 2024). Identifying which BSS formed through MT therefore informs our broader understanding of binary stellar evolution and its end-products across stellar populations. Stellar rotation helps to separate these channels, together with radial-velocity (RV) monitoring and chemical abundances. Both mass-transfer and merger products are expected to spin up when they form (Sills et al., 2005; Glebbeek et al., 2008). Mass-transfer products then lose angular momentum through magnetic braking or, in close orbits, are locked by tides to the orbital period, so old mass-transfer products are usually slow rotators with a companion that can be detected in RV (Carney et al., 2005; Rain et al., 2021). Merger and collision products have no companion and can stay fast for longer (Leiner et al., 2018; Leiner et al., 2019). Young mass-transfer products can also rotate fast, however: in M67 and NGC 188 several BSS with hot white-dwarf companions have projected rotational velocities (v​sin⁡iv\sin i) above 40 km​s−1\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}} (Linck and Mathieu, 2026a), and stars without a convective envelope are braked very little. The rotation of a single star therefore does not identify its formation channel. Combined with binarity and surface chemistry it does constrain it, and for a population it traces the time since formation. An advantage of v​sin⁡iv\sin i is that it can be measured from a single spectrum. This diagnostic power has so far been exploited almost exclusively in globular clusters. There, dedicated v​sin⁡iv\sin i surveys have revealed that the fraction of fast-rotating BSS is not random: it correlates with the density and the dynamical state of the host cluster (Ferraro et al., 2023; Billi et al., 2026), turning BSS rotation into a probe of the environment that made them. Whether these trends are a property of dense environments or a universal feature of BSS populations is an open question, and answering it requires the other end of the density sequence: the open clusters. Rotation measurements of open-cluster BSS have only begun to appear, and few open clusters have had their BSS populations surveyed in rotation, binarity and surface chemistry together, as done by the WIYN Open Cluster Study for NGC 188 and M67 (Linck and Mathieu, 2026b; Linck and Mathieu, 2026a). This combination is needed to tie the spin of each star to its formation channel, and it is the purpose of this paper.

papers.title: Searching for Planets around Altair with JWST/NIRcam
papers.abstract: Altair (alpha Aql) is one of the nearest stars to the Sun at 5.13 pc and its age has recently been revised to 88+/-10 Myr, making it one of the youngest stars in the Solar neighborhood. This makes Altair a compelling target for high-contrast direct imaging searches for giant planets. We present two epochs of simultaneous F444W and F200W MASK430R JWST/NIRCam coronagraphic imaging observations. After post-processing, these data achieve F444W contrast levels of 2 x 10^-6 at 1" (5.1 au), 1.5 x 10^-7 at 2" (10.3 au), and a few x 10^-8 beyond 4"(20 au). Using the Sonora Flame Skimmer models, this corresponds to sub-Jupiter mass sensitivity beyond 5 au and sub-Saturn mass sensitivity beyond 10 au. We identified several candidate point sources in the field in the first epoch data. Second epoch observations confirmed that none of the candidates were co-moving with Altair and their colors are consistent with background stars. Altair has no known companions, no detected debris disk, and is not associated with any stellar association. Despite this, its youth and proximity ensure it will remain a high-priority target for future high-contrast imaging observations. We additionally discuss Altair as a potential reference star for future observations, presenting measurements of background sources in the field and showing that Altair will remain at least a few arcsec from background stars over the next 10-20 years, making it a reliable reference target for upcoming imaging campaigns including the Roman Space Telescope Coronagraph Instrument.

papers.intro:
The bright (V=0.77V=0.77) A7V-type star Altair (α\alpha Aql, HD 187642, HIP 97649) is the second nearest (ϖ=194.95±0.57\varpi=194.95\pm 0.57 mas, d=5.130±0.015d=5.130\pm 0.015 pc) A-type star after Sirius [50, 31, 74]. Thus far, Altair has no known stellar or substellar companions. Its rapid rotation (v sin i =221 km s-1, Erspamer and North 22) and extreme brightness makes radial velocity and transit planet searches impractical, and no companion has been detected in interferometric observations [53, 13]. Coronagraphic imaging remains a promising method to discover companions at wider separations. Despite having an entry in the Washington Double Star Catalog (WDS J19508+0852A) and having a half dozen associated companions identified B through G with separations ranging from 27″ to 196″, all appear to be faint, low proper motion background stars inconsistent with Altair’s proximity or motion (see subsection V.1).

papers.title: Towards a new model of the compact triple system $\lambda$ Tauri I. Improved periods and preliminary elements of the triple system
papers.abstract: We analysed our new radial velocity measurements and photometric observations (covering a time interval of 46838~days and 39100~days, respectively) as well as those from previous studies to derive accurate ephemerides for both orbits of the compact triple system $\lambda$ Tau. In the case of the inner eclipsing subsystem, we obtained a~linear ephemeris of T min.I=HJD 2440998.86069(35)+3.952952845(81)xE, improving the accuracy of the previous solutions by more than an order of magnitude. This allowed us to reproduce well all available light curve minima, including the first one recorded in 1844. Furthermore, the period of the outer subsystem, determined from radial velocity analysis, appears to be constant over the interval of available observations, with the corresponding linear ephemeris being T periast.=HJD 2456822.5(3.6)+33.02480(28)xE. Assuming near coplanarity of the inner and outer orbits, we estimated the preliminary physical properties of the whole system. We found that the secondary of the inner subsystem is filling or nearly filling its Roche lobe. We used the long-term stability of the eclipsing subsystem period to place a strong upper limit on the rate of the proposed episodic mass transfer to its primary component. Our results constitute a preparatory step for a follow-up study that will also include an analysis of a rich collection of optical spectro-interferometric observations and use a full-fledged numerical model to describe the evolution of the orbital architecture of the system. Particular attention will be focused on determining the inner orbit forced eccentricity and understanding the absence of the apsidal advance of the outer orbit in our present solution.

papers.intro:
Compact triple systems are extremely interesting objects in stellar astrophysics, as they represent unique laboratories to test various hypotheses related to their origin, they are subject to a plethora of complicated evolutionary pathways, and they offer a possibility of revealing traces of dynamical effects of various timescales within affordable decade-long periods. The latter, if properly modelled, consequently provides a unique tool to constrain the physical parameters of the stars. Analysis of the data from Kepler and the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) space-borne surveys has provided spectacular examples of systems in this category. For example, Kostov et al. (2024) reported the discovery of the so-far most compact triply eclipsing triple system, TIC 290061484 = 2MASS J21042626+5113320, with an outer period of 24.d\aas@@fstack{d}5 only, and Borkovits et al. (2025) reported ten new compact systems with outer periods between 46.d\aas@@fstack{d}8 and 101.d\aas@@fstack{d}4. Even more recently, Rappaport et al. (2026) discovered TIC 366240660, a triply eclipsing system with an outer orbit period of 30.d\aas@@fstack{d}5 in a rigorous 13:1 mean motion resonant configuration with the inner orbit. Although these new systems are fascinating in many respects and have brought evidence of previously unseen configurations, λ\lambda Tau – with an outer orbit period of only 33 d – remains the prime and archetypal representative of a stellar compact triple hierarchy. Among other reasons, its uniqueness stems from its brightness and its long observational history. Considering the availability of numerous spectroscopic and photometric observations of λ\lambda Tau (briefly overviewed in Sect. 2) and reporting results from our own dedicated campaign, which provide a new dense series of spectroscopic and photometric observations, the goal of the present paper is to provide reliable and accurate ephemerides for both inner and outer orbits in the λ\lambda Tau system. These will serve as a starting point for a follow-up study in which we will make use of additional interferometric observations and construct a state-of-the-art dynamical model of this remarkable triple star.

papers.title: Dwarf galaxy simulations with stellar-core mass- and metallicity-dependent core-collapse supernova explosion energies
papers.abstract: Core-collapse supernovae (CCSNe) are a critical source of thermal and kinetic energy and chemically enriched material in galaxies. Leveraging recent advances in CCSN modelling, we implement a novel core-mass- and metallicity-dependent prescription for stellar explodability and CCSN explosion energies, $E_\mathrm{expl}$, in the SPHGal galaxy evolution code. It accounts for black hole (BH) formation via SN failures and via partial fallback of ejecta mass, and adopts an explosion-progenitor connection calibrated to three-dimensional CCSN simulations, such that $E_\mathrm{expl}$ varies between $<0.1$-$2\, \mathrm{B}$. We ran simulations of isolated low-metallicity galaxies with variations in the input stellar feedback models. With the new explodability prescription nearly three times more BHs form compared to the canonical CCSN-model, but the reduced number of successful CCSNe has minimal impact on galactic star formation owing to the low fraction of failed CCSNe. While BH formation contributes to removal of matter from the galactic baryon cycle, the latter remains driven by galactic outflows, and most compact remnant mass is stored in white dwarves. The most significant change is instead brought about by the new average-$E_\mathrm{expl}$ that amounts to $\sim33$\% of the $1\,\mathrm{B}=10^{51}\, \mathrm{erg}$ traditionally assumed in sub-resolution CCSN-models. This reduction results in increased and less bursty star formation, reduced outflows and mass-loading factors, increased star cluster formation efficiency, and enhanced chemical enrichment and metal-recycling in star-forming regions. These results stand in contrast with outflow-launching and baryon cycle modelling in lower-resolution galaxy simulations in which canonical (i.e., $1\, \mathrm{B}$) CCSN feedback is typically assumed to produce galaxy models that match observed scaling relations.

papers.title: Revisiting the centrifugal breakout scaling relationship for H$\alpha$ emission in light of $\rho$ Oph C, the coolest B-type star with an H$\alpha$-bright centrifugal magnetosphere
papers.abstract: The corotating magnetospheres of B-type stars are strongly affected by magnetic field strength and rotational velocity, which determine both the geometry and strength of visible and radio emission; however, H$\alpha$ emission largely disappears below a bolometric luminosity of $\log{(L / L_\odot)} \sim 2.8$. The nearby B5 V star $\rho$ Oph C (HD 147932) is the least-luminous rapidly rotating magnetic B-type star to display magnetospheric H$\alpha$ emission. While $\rho$ Oph C's radio magnetosphere has been extensively studied, its magnetic field and H$\alpha$ magnetosphere have been constrained only via snapshot observations. We present a new dataset of high-resolution ESPaDOnS spectropolarimetry covering the star's rotational period, which is revisited by combining Hipparcos, K2 and TESS photometry. We find that the star's magnetic field strength and geometry are consistent with the model inferred from radio data. As expected from the magnetic model, there is very little variability in H$\alpha$. Comparison of the light curve to both equivalent width measurements from metallic lines and magnetospheric models suggests that the star's photometric variability is dominated by surface chemical abundance spots; however, there is complex rotationally modulated variability at about the mmag level which probably originates in the magnetosphere. $\rho$ Oph C is the least luminous B-type star in which magnetospheric H$\alpha$ emission has yet been detected, and its emission is notably weaker than the predictions of the centrifugal breakout model. Its photometric eclipse depth is also much lower than predicted by the CBO model. However, its radio luminosity is consistent with CBO predictions. We speculate on this basis that $\rho$ Oph C may be a transitional object between effective temperature regimes with hydrogen-dominated and decoupled metallic winds.

papers.intro:
Circumstellar magnetospheres form when the radiatively driven wind plasma of an early-type (OBA) star is trapped by a sufficiently strong magnetic field (Babel and Montmerle, 1997; ud-Doula and Owocki, 2002; Petit et al., 2013, typically a few hundred to a few thousand gauss;). The outer extent of the magnetosphere is set by the point at which the ram pressure of the wind exceeds the magnetic pressure, which typically occurs from a few stellar radii out to tens of stellar radii (ud-Doula and Owocki, 2002; Petit et al., 2013). These magnetospheres can be detected via a variety of diagnostics, each of which probes a distinct element of the magnetosphere: incoherent gyrosynchrotron radio emission reveals the high energy radio lobes (Drake et al., 1987; Leto et al., 2021, e.g.); coherent, pulsed radio electron cyclotron maser emission (ECME) is formed within auroral circuits (Trigilio et al., 2000; Das et al., 2022b, e.g.); magnetically confined wind shocks are detectable from X-ray emission (Babel and Montmerle, 1997; Nazé et al., 2014, e.g.); ultraviolet emission and absorption probes the magnetically confined wind (Henrichs et al., 2013, e.g.); and the relatively dense, cool plasma of the circumstellar environment shows up in H Balmer, Paschen, and Brackett line emission, as well as in photometric eclipses (Landstreet and Borra, 1978; Grunhut et al., 2012; Petit et al., 2013; Oksala et al., 2015, e.g.).

Due to magnetospheric braking (ud-Doula et al., 2009), magnetic hot stars are usually much more slowly rotating than their non-magnetic counterparts, with some stars having rotational periods of decades (Martins et al., 2010; Shultz et al., 2017; Shultz et al., 2018b, e.g.). If rotation does not play an important role in the magnetosphere, the magnetically confined plasma persists within the magnetosphere over dynamical timescales: the magnetosphere is loaded by the wind, and drained by gravitational infall of the plasma back to the photosphere (ud-Doula and Owocki, 2002). Such dynamical magnetospheres (Petit et al., 2013, DMs;) require high mass-loss rates to sustain sufficient density for H line emission, conditions that typically only pertain in magnetic O-type stars (Shultz et al., 2017, the magnetic B0 star ξ1\xi^{1} CMa is the only known B-type star with a DM detectable in Hα\alpha;).

Closer to the Zero-Age Main Sequence, magnetospheric braking has not had time to slow down the star’s rotation; within this age range there are many rapidly rotating stars, with periods as short as 0.5 d and surface equatorial rotational velocities in excess of 300 km s-1 (Shultz et al., 2019a). Due to magnetically enforced corotation of the confined wind plasma with the stellar surface, the magnetospheric plasma can experience rotational velocities of thousands of km s-1, leading to significant centrifugal forces (Townsend and Owocki, 2005; ud-Doula et al., 2008). This leads to the formation of a centrifugal magnetosphere (Petit et al., 2013, CM;) in which rotational support prevents gravitational infall, allowing high densities and detectable H line emission.
