This leads to the formation of a centrifugal magnetosphere (Petit et al., 2013, CM;) in which rotational support prevents gravitational infall, allowing high densities and detectable H line emission.

Since mass loading by the wind is not counteracted by gravitational drainage within the CM, the limiting density is set by the strength of the magnetic field. When the gas pressure exceeds the magnetic pressure, the plasma ceases to be guided by the magnetic field, and instead the magnetic field moves with the plasma; the centrifugal force then causes the the magnetic field to reconnect, and plasma is flung away from the star in centrifugal breakout (CBO) events (ud-Doula et al., 2008). CBO scaling has been shown to reproduce the broad characteristics of H line emission in magnetic early B-type stars: the threshold for emission onset; the scaling of emission strength; and the shape of H line emission profiles (Shultz et al., 2020; Owocki et al., 2020). CBO has also been shown to drive radio emission, which is seen only in rapidly rotating, strongly magnetized stars (Leto et al., 2021; Shultz et al., 2022; Owocki et al., 2022). A CBO model predicts both the onset of radio emission and the scaling of radio luminosity. CBO events involve magnetic reconnection, which accelerates a small population of electrons to weakly relativistic velocities, thereby populating the radio magnetosphere; thus, while Hα\alpha emission probes and the cool, dense, pre-CBO plasma, radio emission probes the high-energy, low density, post-CBO plasma. While the original radio CBO scaling relationship was derived for gyrosynchrontron emission, there are indications that it is also the source of ECME (Das and Chandra, 2021; Das et al., 2022a, e.g.).

While CBO successfully reproduces the H line emission properties of stars that possess such emission, it cannot yet explain why emission disappears for stars with effective temperatures below about 17 kK (Shultz et al., 2020; Owocki et al., 2020, or more or less equivalently, bolometric luminosities below log⁡Lbol∼2.8\log{L_{\rm bol}}\sim 2.8;). Cooler, less luminous stars have weaker winds, but in a strict CBO model, the mass-loss rate should not factor in at all: mass-loading should continue until such a point as the CBO-limited density is reached. Indeed, no such effective temperature cutoff is observed in radio emission: both gyrosynchrotron and ECME are seen even in relatively cool magnetic A-type stars (Leto et al., 2021; Shultz et al., 2022; Das et al., 2022a). Two hypotheses have been proposed to explain the lack of H emission below the temperature cutoff. First, magnetospheres might be ‘leaky’ due to non-ideal MHD effects leading to cross-field transport: a slow leakage mechanism might only become relevant at low mass-loss rates (Owocki and Cranmer, 2018, e.g.). Second, H ions might become decoupled from metallic ions in the winds of the cooler stars (Babel, 1995, e.g.). In conventional winds, radiative driving operates via energy level transitions in ionized metals, which then drag along the ionized H. If H decouples, the magnetosphere would be populated entirely by metallic ions, a ‘metallic magnetosphere’ which cannot produce H emission (Owocki et al., 2026).

papers.title: Where do we Jam? - The Impact of Real and Virtual XR Spaces on Musical Creativity, Co-Presence, Affect, and Flow
papers.abstract: Extended Reality (XR) technologies can place musicians in virtual, mixed, or real environments during networked music performance (NMP). To examine how NMP applications in XR should be positioned on the reality-virtuality continuum, we conducted a laboratory study (N = 28) comparing a simulated NMP experience in Virtual Reality (VR) with one in Augmented Reality (AR). In both conditions, musicians saw their remote partners in real time as 3D point clouds rendered with an optimized Gaussian Splatting shader. While VR allowed participants to select and customize fully virtual 3D environments, AR showed a pass-through view of the laboratory environment. We measured creativity support, flow, involvement, co-presence, and affect, and complemented these data with qualitative interviews on participants' preferences and requirements for creative environments. Our results show that participants felt significantly more involved by the immersive XR experience in VR than in AR. Positive affect, flow, and creativity support were strongly correlated in both conditions, whereas involvement correlated with flow and creativity support only in VR. Qualitative findings showed substantial variation in participants' preferences for AR or VR and also regarding the design of creative virtual environments. Together, these findings suggest that the surrounding environment is a critical design dimension in networked Musical XR, shaping collaborative musical experiences beyond merely representing remote collaborators and mitigating communication latency. Future XR-mediated NMP systems should therefore treat the surrounding space as an integral component of the collaborative musical experience, rather than as a mere visual backdrop. At the same time, they should support experiences across a broad spectrum of the reality-virtuality continuum to accommodate highly individual user requirements.

papers.intro:
Extended Reality (XR), an umbrella term encompassing Virtual Reality (VR), Augmented Reality (AR), and Mixed Reality (MR), has rapidly evolved in recent years. In particular, advances in MR and video-see-through technologies have significantly enhanced XR’s potential for productive and creative work, making music in XR increasingly viable. Recent work has shown that such applications cannot only provide immersive means for single-user musical creativity [1, 2], but can also increase the sense of co-presence [3], namely the feeling of “being there” with another remote person while making music together [4, 5]. This enables a more immersive experience of making music together in real time, commonly referred to as “jamming” among musicians, and, when done in a remote setting, falls within the field of Networked Music Performance (NMP). Such remote jam sessions may, in some situations, e.g., the recent COVID pandemic, be especially valuable for musicians, as the option of meeting in person may be unavailable. Musicians engaged in such real-time jam sessions often improvise, a vital part of musical creativity, which places high demands on audio latency and quality [4, 6].

Recent work has shown that such applications cannot only provide immersive means for single-user musical creativity [1, 2], but can also increase the sense of co-presence [3], namely the feeling of “being there” with another remote person while making music together [4, 5]. This enables a more immersive experience of making music together in real time, commonly referred to as “jamming” among musicians, and, when done in a remote setting, falls within the field of Networked Music Performance (NMP). Such remote jam sessions may, in some situations, e.g., the recent COVID pandemic, be especially valuable for musicians, as the option of meeting in person may be unavailable. Musicians engaged in such real-time jam sessions often improvise, a vital part of musical creativity, which places high demands on audio latency and quality [4, 6].

XR-mediated NMP is often discussed in terms of communication latency, packet loss, interaction techniques, and the representation of remote musicians, for example, through volumetric or point-cloud renderings [7]. However, comparatively little attention has been paid to the surrounding 3D spaces in which musicians collaborate and experience telepresence. This spatial dimension is particularly relevant in XR, as musicians may either remain situated in their physical surroundings or perform inside fully Virtual Environments (VEs) that can be selected, customized, and potentially shared.

Designing such environments, however, is non-trivial. In AR, virtual content, such as remote musicians, is embedded into the performer’s physical surroundings. In VR, by contrast, musicians can be placed in familiar musical settings, such as studios or stages, as well as in abstract, natural, or otherwise inaccessible environments, such as spaceships or underwater worlds. Moreover, VR environments can be experienced either collaboratively, with multiple musicians sharing the same virtual space, or individually, with each musician performing in a different environment while remaining connected through the shared musical interaction. Consequently, the surrounding space becomes an integral component of the collaborative musical experience rather than merely a visual backdrop.

To investigate the role of the surrounding space in XR-mediated collaborative music making, we conducted a laboratory study comparing two representative settings using qualitative and quantitative methods. In the AR condition, musicians remained situated in their physical laboratory surroundings while interacting through pass-through video and 3D point-cloud representations of their remote partners. In the VR condition, musicians performed in customizable virtual spaces, with the option to share the same space or independently select different ones, whilst seeing the same point cloud as in AR. By comparing these two settings (see Figure 2 for more detailed POV screenshots), we investigate how the design of the surrounding space influences creativity support, affect, co-presence, involvement/presence, and flow during remote musical improvisation.

papers.title: From Counterfactual Edits to Human Narratives: LLM-Driven Interpretations for Recommender System Explanations
papers.abstract: Recommender systems increasingly influence what users discover and consume online, yet the decision logic behind their outputs often remains opaque. Counterfactual explanation (CFX) methods provide an effective way to show which changes to a user's interaction history would alter a recommendation. In recommendation settings, however, CFXs often require many edits, producing long, low-level lists that are hard for users to interpret. Moreover, most evaluations emphasize edit counts while largely overlooking whether the resulting CFXs are coherent and actionable for users. We argue that this gap between generating valid CFXs and communicating model behavior stems from the lack of user-centered abstraction and limited qualitative evaluation. To bridge this gap, we investigate large language models as mediators that summarize raw CFX interaction edit lists into concise natural language explanations describing higher-level preference patterns. We optimize these mediators for correctness, informativeness, and linguistic quality through preference optimization, and evaluate the resulting explanations with human-calibrated metrics derived from separate human-labeled datasets. On the MovieLens-1M dataset, across multiple counterfactual generators and language models, the resulting summaries achieve high overall linguistic quality, while the strongest semantic results are obtained with high-success CFX methods such as ACCENT and SPINRec. Direct Preference Optimization improves the semantic metrics in almost all evaluated settings.

papers.intro:
Recommender systems curate what users see, click, and watch (Afchar et al., 2022; Bauer et al., 2024), yet users often have little insight into why a particular item is suggested. As recommendations become ubiquitous across online platforms, explanations that improve user trust (Peintner et al., 2023), accountability (Ribeiro et al., 2016; Ser et al., 2024), and informed decision-making (Yu et al., 2025; Mohammadi et al., 2024) are increasingly important.

Counterfactual explanations (CFXs) have recently emerged as a promising mechanism for transparency in recommender systems (Wachter et al., 2017). By identifying minimal changes to a user’s interaction history that would alter the recommendation outcome, they offer actionable “what-if” reasoning aligned with human intuition (Freiesleben, 2022; Aryal and Keane, 2024). However, in practice, CFXs for recommenders often require modifying a large number of historical interactions. As illustrated in Figure 1, altering even a single top-ranked recommendation in the MovieLens-1M dataset11 1 https://grouplens.org/datasets/movielens/1m/ (ML-1M) may require removing dozens of past interactions. This observation exposes a fundamental mismatch between algorithmic minimality and human interpretability (Wachter et al., 2017). Although a counterfactual may be minimal under an optimization objective, it is typically presented as a list of low-level perturbations such as item removals. Long edit sets can therefore overwhelm users and limit practical use. This raises the core challenge we address: how can large counterfactual edit sets be turned into concise natural language explanations (NLEs) while preserving the counterfactual grounding?

We propose an approach in which large language models (LLMs) act as mediators between counterfactual generators and users. LLMs are well suited to this role because, unlike fixed heuristics, they offer flexibility in how raw interaction data is communicated and can handle free-form text descriptions. Rather than replacing counterfactual reasoning, the mediator summarizes raw interaction edits into concise, human-centered NLEs. papers.title: Prompt2Echo (P2Echo): Text-Prompted Multi-View Echocardiography Segmentation with One Model
papers.abstract: Automated segmentation in multi-view echocardiography is essential for comprehensive cardiac assessment, yet remains challenging due to substantial anatomical and appearance variability across standard acoustic windows. In this paper, we present P2Echo, a unified framework capable of segmenting diverse cardiac structures across multiple standard echocardiographic views using a single model controlled by structured view-aware text prompts. Unlike recent foundation model adaptations that rely on implicit latent priors, P2Echo explicitly conditions the segmentation process via a novel Dynamic Image-Text Alignment (DyITA) module. DyITA integrates a differentiable routing mechanism and token differential operators to dynamically modulate decoder features according to the requested view and target structure. This allows the network to adaptively switch its processing pathways for different views without architectural changes. Extensive experiments on a large-scale internal dataset (seen during training) and held-out evaluation on three external datasets demonstrate that P2Echo matches or exceeds both view-specific specialists and state-of-the-art universal models at a fraction of their computational cost, offering an efficient, controllable solution for multi-plane cardiac analysis. Code is available at: https://github.com/moeinheidari7829/P2Echo.

papers.intro:
Echocardiography is the primary non-invasive modality for cardiac diagnosis, relying on a standard set of acoustic windows (e.g., the Apical 2-, 3-, and 4-Chamber (A2C/2CH, A3C/3CH, A4C/4CH) and Parasternal Long/Short Axis (PLAX, PSAX) views) to visualize complex anatomy [1]. Although multi-view echocardiographic examinations provide complementary information, manual interpretation is time-consuming and prone to inter-observer variability. To enable objective and reproducible quantification of cardiac structure and function, automated analysis is essential, with accurate cardiac segmentation serving as a key foundational step. However, current automated solutions are largely siloed due to the dramatic anatomical appearance shifts between views; traditional deep learning models fail to generalize across planes [2]. This necessitates training separate specialist models for each view [3], leading to redundant development, high maintenance costs, and inconsistent performance across the clinical workflow. As summarized in Figure 1, multi-view echocardiography segmentation is complicated by several interacting sources of variability. First, the appearance and geometry of the same cardiac structure can change substantially across acoustic windows [1, 3], while only a subset of structures is visible in each view. Second, differences in scanners, acquisition settings, and clinical centers introduce additional domain shifts that alter image appearance even within the same view [4]. Inter-subject anatomical variability further changes chamber size, shape, and relative position. Finally, the characteristic speckle pattern of ultrasound, together with acoustic shadowing and signal dropout, can substantially weaken anatomical boundaries. Consequently, a unified model must simultaneously accommodate view-conditioned anatomy, heterogeneous acquisition domains, and locally ambiguous boundaries rather than learning a single view-agnostic appearance representation.

To address this redundancy, recent research has moved toward unified, multi-view segmentation. Early attempts utilized multi-branch architectures, where dedicated encoders process specific views before fusing information through cross-view dependency modeling [5, 6]. While effective, these designs increase model complexity and remain architecturally rigid, as adding a new view requires adding a new parallel branch. Alternatively, universal models attempt to learn a single view-agnostic representation from pooled data. However, empirical evidence shows that when classic architectures are trained on combined multi-plane data, their performance significantly decreases compared to plane-specific training. Without explicit conditioning, these models often converge to an average solution that degrades per-view accuracy, failing to capture the unique geometric details of conflicting views (e.g., the circular left ventricle in short-axis vs. the bullet-shaped ventricle in apical views) [1]. The rise of Foundation Models has introduced new paradigms for universal segmentation. SAM-based approaches, such as SAMUS [7] and EchoONE [1], adapt the Segment Anything Model (SAM) [8] for ultrasound by incorporating adapter layers or latent prompt generators. While EchoONE achieves multi-view capabilities, its dense prompts are derived from clustering-based structural prototypes, making the resulting guidance dependent on how well these learned priors represent the input anatomy and difficult to control explicitly. Parallel to this, text-guided segmentation methods have shown that natural language can serve as an explicit control signal, from MedCLIP-SAMv2 [9] to Grounding DINO-US-SAM [10], which pairs a LoRA-tuned Grounding DINO detector with SAM2 to segment multiple organs across 18 ultrasound datasets from free-form prompts. In these methods, language primarily guides target localization or visual-prompt generation before mask decoding, failing to continuously modulate decoder features at multiple spatial resolutions, as required to resolve the cross-view appearance variance of the same anatomical class in multi-view echocardiography.

In this work, we propose P2Echo (Prompt2Echo), a unified framework that leverages structured textual prompts to explicitly condition and control a single segmentation model across diverse echocardiographic views. Unlike prototype-derived latent priors, which are learned implicitly and cannot be directly specified by users, P2Echo employs view-specific text descriptions (e.g., “Apical 4 Chamber Left Ventricle”) as explicit conditioning signals. The operator can directly define the desired view and target structure, while P2Echo dynamically modulates decoder features according to the provided textual guidance. Central to our approach is the Dynamic Image-Text Alignment (DyITA) module. Rather than simple post-hoc fusion, DyITA integrates text guidance directly into the decoder blocks via a novel dynamic routing mechanism, allowing the model to "switch" its attention patterns based on the requested anatomy and view. It replaces multiple specialist models with a single network that is explicitly controllable via structured textual prompts. ➋ We introduce the DyITA module. papers.title: The Isoperimetric Flow and Synthetic Scalar Curvature for Causal Variational Principles
papers.abstract: An isoperimetric flow is introduced in the setting of causal variational principles. Describing the whole space by the support of a minimizing measure, we define an area functional on subsets by a surface layer integral. Mean curvature is defined via the first variation of this area functional. Using the method of minimizing movement, the isoperimetric flow is constructed as a Lipschitz curve of measures with prescribed volume change. As illustrating examples, we introduce and analyze ``smeared variants'' of the mean curvature flow in Euclidean space and on a Riemannian manifold. In these examples, it is shown that our area functional coincides with the usual area up to specified curvature corrections. As an application of our general results, by analyzing the volume and area of small isoperimetric balls, we introduce notions of local dimension and synthetic scalar curvature.

papers.intro:
Geometric notions such as surface area, dimension and curvature are traditionally formulated in terms of an underlying metric structure. In the smooth setting, they are closely tied to the differential geometry of Riemannian manifolds, while various extensions to non-smooth spaces have been developed within metric geometry and geometric measure theory. A different approach is to investigate to what extent geometric quantities can be defined directly in terms of a measure and a prescribed interaction between points, without requiring an underlying metric or differentiable structure.

Geometric notions such as surface area, dimension and curvature are traditionally formulated in terms of an underlying metric structure. In the smooth setting, they are closely tied to the differential geometry of Riemannian manifolds, while various extensions to non-smooth spaces have been developed within metric geometry and geometric measure theory. A different approach is to investigate to what extent geometric quantities can be defined directly in terms of a measure and a prescribed interaction between points, without requiring an underlying metric or differentiable structure.

The present paper develops such an approach in the framework of nonlocal interaction kernels. Starting from a non-negative kernel, we introduce a notion of nonlocal surface area and study the associated isoperimetric evolution. We then investigate how its small-scale behavior can be used to characterize geometric quantities, in particular dimension and scalar curvature. The underlying principle is to quantify the interaction between a measurable set and its complement, thereby obtaining a nonlocal analogue of classical surface area. In contrast to the local perimeter, this quantity incorporates a regularization at the scale determined by the interaction kernel. For suitable kernels on smooth manifolds, the corresponding asymptotic expansions recover classical geometric quantities, with higher-order terms encoding curvature contributions.

papers.title: Data Quality Challenges in Multimodal Tourism Recommender Systems
papers.abstract: Modern recommender systems increasingly consider diverse data modalities to enhance model performance. However, the quality of the underlying multimodal data (e.g. data from social media platforms) has received limited attention so far. Focusing on tourism recommendation, we examine real-world challenges encountered when using datasets from Yelp and Instagram. Issues include noise from fake reviews, hallucinated content from LLMs, modality contradictions, and demographic bias. We outline future directions such as quality-aware fusion, structured and controlled LLM-based content generation to reduce hallucinations, and user group differentiation to improve the robustness and reliability of multimodal recommendation systems.

papers.title: LUMIR: Decoupled Multimodal Representation Learning from Heterogeneous Data for Next-POI Recommendation
papers.abstract: As multimodal tourism-related information collected from heterogeneous data sources has become increasingly available, learning effective representations has attracted attention for improving recommendation performance. Existing approaches often tightly couple multimodal fusion with the architecture and optimization objective of a specific downstream model, which limits the generality and reusability of the learned representations. To address these limitations, we propose LUMIR, a decoupled multimodal representation learning framework based on contrastive learning. Multimodal information collected from heterogeneous data sources is first semantically unified into a shared textual representation space using large language models (LLMs). An interaction-aware fusion mechanism is then designed to model cross-modal interactions, while sequential signals are incorporated as a structural constraint to guide representation learning. To evaluate the learned representations, experiments are conducted on a multimodal point-of-interest (POI) dataset under the next-POI recommendation setting across multiple sequential recommendation backbones. The results show that LUMIR consistently outperforms existing multimodal fusion baselines in both accuracy-oriented and beyond-accuracy metrics, demonstrating that decoupling representation learning from downstream optimization provides an effective paradigm for learning reusable multimodal representations. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/wzehui/LUMIR.

papers.title: Few-Shot Residual Adaptation of Pretrained Latent World Models
papers.abstract: Pretrained latent world models can support visual planning and control, but their predictions may fail when physical dynamics change at deployment. We study whether such models can adapt from only a few interactions without modifying their pretrained weights or identifying the changed physical parameters. We introduce a few-shot residual adaptation approach that learns self-supervised corrections from latent prediction errors. The corrections are applied both inside the latent predictor and directly to its predicted latent state, while the pretrained world model remains frozen. We evaluate the approach in simulation and on a real robot under center-of-mass and friction shifts. These changes reduce the success of the frozen model to near zero. Using three interaction episodes for adaptation, our dual-site approach recovers 90\% success under the center-of-mass shift and 100\% under the modified friction on the real robot. Ablations show that correcting both locations outperforms single-site adaptation. Our diagnostics further suggest that much of the learned correction reduces a general prediction mismatch, while successful control also depends on shift-specific information captured during adaptation.

papers.intro:
World models predict how observations evolve under robot actions and have been used to support planning and control [7, 4, 25]. Latent world models are particularly promising because they can learn task-relevant representations without predicting every pixel, enabling efficient model-based control from visual observations [1, 29, 5]. A central challenge is that a model trained under one set of physical conditions may be deployed under another. Changes in center of mass, friction, payload, actuator properties, or contact dynamics can alter the effect of the same action even when the task, visual appearance, and goal remain unchanged [14, 15, 2]. Existing approaches often address this mismatch by retraining the model [13], estimating physical parameters [14, 2], adapting a policy [15, 11], or randomizing dynamics during training [18]. These strategies can be effective, but they may require substantial data, access to the training procedure, a suitable parameterization of the dynamics, or prior knowledge about the deployment shift.

In this work, we study how a pretrained latent world model can be efficiently adapted from a few interactions. We keep the pretrained model frozen and learn lightweight residual corrections from its prediction errors. These corrections are trained self-supervised from observed transitions, requiring neither rewards nor knowledge of the changed physical parameters. We inject them at two points in the latent dynamics pipeline: within the predictor and on its predicted latent state. We evaluate this setting in simulation and on a real robot under shifted center-of-mass and modified friction setting. These changes reduce the success of the frozen world model to near zero, while adaptation from only three interaction episodes recovers most of the lost performance. We find that adapting both inside the predictor and at its output works better than adapting either location alone. Our diagnostics further show that much of the correction reduces a general prediction mismatch, while the large control gap between general- and shifted-dynamics adapters suggests that some of the learned correction depends on the dynamics seen during adaptation.

papers.title: Convergence of an adaptive multilevel stochastic Galerkin FEM driven by a residual-based error estimator
papers.abstract: In this paper we analyze a residual-based a posteriori error estimation strategy and adaptive multilevel algorithms for a class of parametric elliptic PDEs, where the diffusion coefficient depends on countably many uncertainty parameters. Under a saturation assumption on the parametric approximation space, we propose a computable residual-based error estimator. We also introduce the notion of K-compatibility of finite element meshes, which ensures that only the triangulations with comparable mesh sizes are used, and incorporate this concept into the adaptive algorithm. We prove that the estimator is reliable and satisfies K-dependent stability and reduction properties. These results underpin our convergence analysis of the adaptive multilevel algorithm: we show that the algorithm drives both the a posteriori error estimator and the true approximation error to zero. Numerical experiments illustrate and confirm the theoretical findings.

SGFEM approximations combine generalized polynomial chaos (gPC) expansions in the stochastic variables/parameters with finite element discretizations of the expansion coefficients. The approximations (and the algorithms that generate them) are termed single-level if the same finite element mesh is used for all expansion coefficients, and multilevel otherwise. Single-level algorithms have emerged in [20], while multilevel approximations have been considered in [16, 22], among other works. Flexibility is the main advantage of multilevel methods, especially in the context of adaptivity, since each spatial coefficient in the gPC expansion is allowed to reside in a finite element space associated with its own appropriately chosen mesh. Thus, multilevel algorithms can successfully tackle problems where some gPC expansion coefficients require a highly refined mesh to approximate the solution accurately, while a coarser mesh suffices for other gPC coefficients.

papers.title: RF3DGS: Reflection-Free 3D Gaussian Splatting with Self-Priors
papers.abstract: 3D reflection removal is crucial in applications demanding high-fidelity visualization, such as museum exhibitions. In this work, we propose Reflection-Free 3D Gaussian Splatting (RF3DGS), a novel method for superior reflection removal. RF3DGS exclusively leverages a widely-adopted photometric prior for reflection removal: that the minimum pixel intensity across multi-view images corresponding to the same 3D point strongly correlates with reflection-free information. However, generalizing this principle to a 3D Gaussian Splatting within a multi-view context is non-trivial. To address this, RF3DGS first optimizes a vanilla 3DGS model using a geometric prior to estimate a coarse, reflection-free depth map for each view. Leveraging these depth maps and photometric prior, a 3D warping process aggregates reflection-free information from auxiliary views to construct a clean transmission pseudo-label for a given reference view. This pseudo-label provides a robust self-supervised signal for optimization. We further introduce an Adaptive Twin Rendering (ATR) loss to synergistically utilize this pseudo-label while preserving high-frequency details from the original, reflection-degraded images. By adeptly fusing these internal 3D self-priors with the ATR loss, RF3DGS demonstrates state-of-the-art reflection removal performance across both synthetic and real-world scenarios. Furthermore, we establish the first 3D reflection removal benchmark, based on the Unity rendering engine, for rigorous quantitative evaluation.

To inherit the robustness and overcome the weaknesses of current 3D reflection removal methods, we propose a novel reflection-free 3DGS method for the 3D reflection removal task. The proposed method simplifies the capture process by requiring only a monocular sRGB video, easily obtained with any mobile phone or DSLR camera, without relying on specialized photography techniques such as capturing flash or no-flash RAW images [47]. Inspired by Li et al. [24], we leverage the Photometric Prior in real-world reflection scenarios: for a given 3D scene point, the minimum intensity value across all captured views strongly corresponds to reflection-free information. Since pixel values from the captured views must be accurately projected back into 3D space, obtaining precise depth maps is crucial to effectively apply the photometric prior. Benefiting from explicit depth estimation in 3DGS, we can efficiently generate depth maps for each captured view by optimizing a vanilla 3DGS model under reflection conditions. To ensure the depth maps contain as pure reflection-free depth information as possible, we incorporate a Geometric Prior—also used by NeRFReN [10]—within 3DGS, which encourages smoothness in the rendered depth maps. This geometric prior assumes that the depth map of the transmitted component should be locally smoother than that of the reflection-degraded one. Utilizing these refined depth maps, we project all captured views back into the 3D space and apply the photometric prior, then re-render each view with preliminary clean transmission information. Due to the flaws of depth maps and imperfect projections, current reflection-free views still have inevitable artifacts, as shown in Fig. 4. We propose an Adaptive Twin Rending (ATR) loss to achieve this joint supervision, encouraging the 3DGS model to effectively capture the clean transmission information from preliminary reflection-free views and maintain the original 3D consistency for a reflection-degraded scene.

papers.title: Influence of the branching geometry on SPION propagation: coupling of experiment and simulation
papers.abstract: Magnetic Drug Targeting (MDT) is an emerging therapeutic concept in cancer medicine, where superparamagnetic iron oxide nanoparticles (SPIONs) are used as carriers for medication. Their magnetic properties allow for the manipulation of particle transport within the vascular structure and thus targeted delivery to the tumor site. To develop effective concepts for particle steering and accumulation, a detailed understanding of the particle--flow interaction, especially at asymmetric vascular bifurcations, is needed. Based on hierarchical scaling laws, generalized bifurcation geometries with varying degrees of asymmetry were derived and additively manufactured. The particle distribution was investigated by in situ optical measurements under different flow conditions and magnetic field configurations and compared with Lagrangian particle and Volume of Fluid Simulations (VoFS). While the particle mass partition followed the hydraulic flow split in asymmetric bifurcations, density-driven stratification dominated in the symmetric bifurcation, where one daughter branch received only a minor fraction of the particle mass at low flow rates despite carrying half of the flow. The Lagrangian model reproduced the predominantly advective propagation, whereas only the VoFS approach captured the stratification-induced asymmetry. Magnetic actuation counteracted the stratification, reversed the passive branch preference and increased particle retention. From a molecular communication perspective, bifurcation geometry, collective volume effects and magnetic actuation thus jointly determine the received particle signal at vascular bifurcations.

papers.intro:
Magnetic drug targeting (MDT) aims for efficient localized drug delivery by using SPION as magnetically steerable carriers. At the tumor site, SPION are accumulated by the magnetic field and release the medication. On their way, particles have to pass successive vascular bifurcations where they are affected by local flow partitioning. From a MC (MC) perspective, SPION can be interpreted as information carriers propagating through a flow-driven vascular channel, where the received particle signal is governed by the underlying hydrodynamics, the injection process, particle-specific transport mechanisms, and external magnetic actuation. Experimental MC testbeds have established the use of SPION in controlled pipe-flow systems [7], while recent studies have investigated effects such as pulsatile flow [8], injection design [Wille2025], and sedimentation [9]. In parallel, physical vessel models have been developed to study particle transport in branched vascular structures, demonstrating that vessel geometry and bifurcation topology can substantially affect particle distribution [2, 6, 1]. Accurate prediction of particle propagation therefore requires channel models that extend beyond straight vessels and idealized advection–diffusion transport. Existing approaches range from particle-based descriptions of nanoparticle transport in branched vessels [5] to experimentally validated MC models for complex vessel networks [4], but are based on idealised assumptions. However, experimentally grounded descriptions of how branch asymmetry affects SPION propagation and branch-specific concentration remain limited. This is particularly relevant because vascular networks exhibit non-uniform branching across spatial scales [Tekin2016], while concentrated SPION suspensions may show sedimentation and stratification behavior related to collective volume effects [9, 2]. Consequently, the relation between local hydrodynamic flow partitioning, particle redistribution, and magnetic steering at individual bifurcations remains insufficiently understood. In this work, we investigate SPION propagation through generalized single-bifurcation vessel models with systematically varied asymmetry. Based on previously introduced generalized vascular geometries [2], additively manufactured flow models are combined with in situ optical measurements under different inlet flow rates and magnetic-field conditions. The experimental results are compared with both a Lagrangian particle simulation and an Eulerian VoFS (VoFS) approach to distinguish predominantly advective particle transport from concentration-field effects such as stratification and sedimentation. By evaluating propagation time, temporal dispersion, branch-specific mass fraction, and post-peak washout, the study provides an experimentally grounded assessment of how branching asymmetry and stratification determine the passive particle routing, which of these mechanisms are captured by either simulation models and to which extent a magnetic field can reverse the passive routing towards the hydrodynamically disfavored branch.

papers.title: WINIC: An Automatic Cycle-Accurate Multi-Platform Microbenchmarking Tool for Instruction Performance Metrics
papers.abstract: Performance models allow developers to gain important insights into the interaction of their code with the hardware that executes it, and enable them to apply target-specific optimizations. To create in-core performance models for out-of-order processors, architecture-specific performance metrics like latency, throughput, and port binding of individual instructions are indispensable. For x86 microarchitectures, there already exist tools to automatically obtain those values; however, the extension of performance modeling tools like the Open Source Architecture Code Analyzer (OSACA) to support further architectures like RISC-V emphasizes the need for a multi-platform microbenchmarking tool. We present WINIC (What I Need Is Cycles), an automatic cross-platform microbenchmarking tool. Unlike previous tools, it can obtain throughput and operand-based latency metrics for most supported instructions of any 64-bit x86, AArch64, and RISC-V microarchitecture without the need for root permissions or extended system control levels. We cover the methodology of microbenchmarking and the approach of WINIC to collect cycle-accurate performance data for assembly instructions. We show that WINIC can be used to automatically obtain a vast number of accurate results and demonstrate for four target microarchitectures that our results match between 71% and 99% of the performance data of instructions obtained by similar tools and documentation. Furthermore, we investigate how operand-based metrics measured by WINIC can be used to improve the in-core performance predictions on selected micro-kernels, exemplarily for the Neoverse V2 microarchitecture.

papers.intro:
Optimizing large-scale scientific applications is critical for reducing their runtime and energy consumption. In this endeavor, performance modeling plays a vital role for understanding the interaction between the software and the hardware executing it. Although there exists a wide range of performance modeling tools, only so-called white-box models [1] reveal potential bottlenecks and allow users to gain insights on how to optimize their code. These tools require precise information on the underlying microarchitecture. In-core execution modeling requires performance characteristics of machine instructions, which is often the reason for large performance databases within the software. Such databases are tedious to create manually. In the best case, they capture enough performance-related metrics to enable building a well-founded performance model.

Although there exists a wide range of performance modeling tools, only so-called white-box models [1] reveal potential bottlenecks and allow users to gain insights on how to optimize their code. These tools require precise information on the underlying microarchitecture. In-core execution modeling requires performance characteristics of machine instructions, which is often the reason for large performance databases within the software. Such databases are tedious to create manually. In the best case, they capture enough performance-related metrics to enable building a well-founded performance model.

In this work, we propose WINIC (What I Need Is Cycles), a versatile microbenchmarking tool, designed to complement in-core performance modeling. It automatically measures throughput and operand-based latency on x86, AArch64, and RISC-V platforms while being able to run solely in user-space. We gather data for four state-of-the-art microarchitectures, consisting of two x86 microarchitectures, namely the AMD Zen 4 (“Genoa”) and Intel Ice Lake cores, the Arm-based Neoverse V2 used in the Grace CPU Superchip, and the Spacemit X60/K1 RISC-V microarchitecture used in the Banana Pi F3 CPU, and show that WINIC’s measured results match 71–99% of previously obtained performance numbers by other tools and references. Furthermore, we apply the operand-based latency measurements to the in-core model of the Open Source Architecture Code Analyzer (OSACA) [2, 3] and show how previously inaccurate predictions can be significantly improved by WINIC’s input.

The rest of this paper is structured as follows: In Section I-B, we give an overview of the existing related work on this topic. We discuss the design and performance metrics of modern out-of-order microarchitectures in Section II and go into detail about the design and usage of WINIC in Section III; in particular, the automated benchmarking of operand-based latencies. Section IV evaluates the metrics obtained with WINIC by comparing them to existing data, and Section V shows how these metrics can be used to improve OSACA’s predictions. Finally, in Section VI, we summarize the paper and give an outlook on future work.

nanoBench [9] is a microbenchmarking tool for x86-only. It executes benchmarking kernels and then uses the RDMSR and RDPMC instructions to read core-local performance counters, which store the number of core cycles or of μ\muops dispatched on a specific port. Those values are then used to determine throughput, latency, and port usage of the executed instructions. A database with results for recent Intel and AMD microarchitectures is available at uops.info [10].

iBench [11] is a tool for measuring the latency and throughput of single instructions purely based on runtime and instruction count. It can execute loop kernels manually written by the user and report the number of clock cycles elapsed per instruction. Currently, it only provides templates for x86 and AArch64. WINIC is based on iBench, but adds support for RISC-V and generates the benchmark kernels automatically.

Table I compares the capabilities of state-of-the-art microbenchmarking tools. Important features are the supported architectures (x86, AArch64, RISC-V) and metrics (latency, per-operand latency, throughput, port usage), as well as automatic benchmark generation, the possibility to run the tool in user-space mode, and the dependence on hardware performance counters. While it is desirable to check all boxes in this comparison, no tool currently can provide this. Although nanoBench can provide all capabilities for Intel architectures, the concept of using events of hardware performance units (PMUs) for determining port bindings is not applicable to other CPU architectures and, therefore, limits the port derivation feature of this tool to Intel hardware. WINIC aims for a different approach that can be transferred to all ISAs, using generic measurement techniques available to all platforms and we plan to extend its capabilities of port usage derivation soon.

papers.title: Davenport Constants of High-Dimensional Integer Sets
papers.abstract: The Davenport constant of a finite set of integer vectors is the maximum length of an irreducible zero-sum sequence over that set. For nonempty sets closed under negation, it equals the largest $\ell_1$-norm of a Graver basis element of the matrix formed by those vectors. We study extremal and average-case versions in growing dimension, with applications to integer programming. For integer cubes $[-R,R]^d \cap \mathbb{Z}^d$ and the sign cube $\{-1,1\}^d$, totally unimodular encodings improve on the upper bounds from direct circuit decomposition, while random perturbations of Hadamard matrices give new lower bounds. A key ingredient is a uniform affine Bernoulli variant of Nguyen and Wood's surjectivity theorem. In every sufficiently large dimension the sign-cube lower bound is $d^{d/2}2^{-d-o(d)}$, and the integer-cube lower bound is $R^d d^{d/2}2^{-o(d)}$ uniformly for polynomially bounded integer radii. For random sign-cube sequences of even length conditioned on summing to zero, we prove a sharp threshold from irreducibility to reducibility at $d\log d/\log 4$, far below the extremal scale. For fixed $p$ and $R$, we determine exact exponential rates for lattice $\ell_p$-balls when $p=1$, $R\geq3$, or $2\leq p<\infty$, $\lfloor R^p\rfloor\geq3$. For each fixed integer $k\geq3$, we determine the exponential rate of the worst-case $\ell_1$-distance from an optimal LP vertex to the nearest integer optimum in standard-form programs with ternary matrices having at most $k$ nonzero entries per column.
papers.intro:
The Davenport constant has roots in zero-sum theory over finite abelian groups and non-unique factorization: prime-ideal factorizations of irreducible algebraic integers give irreducible zero-sum sequences in their ideal class groups; see the survey [14]. We study the corresponding invariant for finite sets of integer vectors. For a finite 𝒳⊆ℤd\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^{d}, a nonempty zero-sum sequence over 𝒳\mathcal{X} is irreducible if no nonempty proper subsequence sums to zero. The Davenport constant 𝖣⁡(𝒳)\mathsf{D}(\mathcal{X}) is the maximum length of an irreducible sequence over 𝒳\mathcal{X}, counting repetitions, and is zero if no such sequence exists.

This choice is motivated by indecomposable integer relations in integer programming and by the geometric questions of Baeth and Geroldinger [4, p. 315, B.2(a)–(b)]. Our main regime is growing dimension at fixed radius, with cube bounds uniform for polynomially growing integer radii. papers.title: Empirical constraints on cosmic-ray scattering in NGC 1333 from dust polarisation
papers.abstract: Cosmic rays (CRs) regulate molecular-cloud ionization and chemistry. Gyro-resonant scattering by magnetic fluctuations sets their mean free path and, on larger scales, their effective diffusion coefficient. However, coefficients inferred from CR distributions averaged over cloud to Galactic scales leave local magnetic structure unresolved. We use the magnetic-field structure of NGC 1333 and its embedded protostellar core IRAS 4A to estimate local CR scattering rates and effective diffusion coefficients, $D(E)$, and examine their variation with environment and scale. We analyse JCMT/POL-2 maps of nine NGC 1333 regions and ALMA Band 7 maps of two IRAS 4A regions. We estimate plane-of-sky field strengths and derive fluctuation spectra from polarisation-angle structure functions. Where these spectra are sufficiently constrained, we apply quasi-linear gyro-resonant theory to calculate CR pitch-angle scattering rates and $D(E)$. The measured fluctuations constrain CR scattering over proton energy intervals of approximately 0.24-5.3 PeV in NGC 1333 and 10-57 TeV in IRAS 4A. Within these intervals, $D(E)$ spans approximately $3\times10^{28}$-$10^{31}\,{\rm cm^2\,s^{-1}}$. Scattering varies substantially between regions and is stronger where the magnetic-field angular dispersion is greater. Extrapolation to common energies suggests scattering in IRAS 4A is one to two orders of magnitude stronger than its surroundings. Within the directly probed intervals, the scattering mean free paths exceed the individual region sizes. The inferred diffusion coefficients therefore characterise local scattering conditions. A cloud-scale diffusive regime requires CRs to sample multiple regions with different scattering rates. Dust polarisation observations therefore provide constraints on CR scattering in clouds, connecting scattering to cloud-scale transport at energies accessible to $\gamma$-ray observatories.

papers.intro:
Cosmic rays (CRs) are an important source of ionization in molecular clouds. They have long been regarded as one of the few feedback agents capable of penetrating the densest regions, which are shielded from most ionizing interstellar radiation (Goldsmith and Langer 1978; Goldsmith 2001). By sustaining a residual ionization fraction in dense gas, CRs influence the coupling between gas and magnetic fields (Bergin et al. 1999; Padovani and Galli 2011; Bailey et al. 2017, e.g.), regulate ion-neutral chemistry (Desch et al. 2004; Indriolo et al. 2015; Gaches et al. 2019), and contribute to the thermal balance of star-forming material (Spitzer and Tomasko 1968, e.g.). Despite their importance, our understanding of the microphysics regulating CR propagation through molecular clouds is incomplete.

Despite their importance, our understanding of the microphysics regulating CR propagation through molecular clouds is incomplete.

In dense and/or weakly ionised clouds, CR transport is traditionally considered to transition from diffusion to ballistic propagation as gas density increases (Lagage and Cesarsky 1983; Felice and Kulsrud 2001; Ivlev et al. 2018; Cesarsky and Volk 1978). Ion-neutral damping of resonant magnetic fluctuations reduces CR scattering in these conditions (Ivlev et al. 2018). CR penetration then depends on energy losses and local magnetic geometry, including mirroring and focusing (Desch et al. 2004; Silsbee et al. 2018). However, diffusive behaviour may still play a role in regulating CR propagation, for example in the surface layers of dense substructure or in intermittent magnetic fields on clump scales (Yang et al. 2023; Chernyshov et al. 2024; Chernyshov et al. 2025), with potentially observable signatures (Ng et al. 2026).

On larger scales, the microphysics of CR propagation is unresolved. It is therefore generally treated using effective models characterised by a diffusion coefficient. The effective diffusion coefficients inferred from observations span more than four orders of magnitude. Estimates range from ≈2\approx 2–6×10266\times 10^{26} cm2 s-1 at 1 GeV over dense molecular clumps (Yang et al. 2023), through ≈2×1028\approx 2\times 10^{28} cm2 s-1 for GeV electrons in the star-forming disc of M 51 (Heesen et al. 2023), to ≳1031\gtrsim 10^{31} cm2 s-1 for 10–100 GeV protons in the Coma galaxy cluster (Wiener and Zweibel 2019). These estimates probe different environments, where the underlying transport microphysics need not be the same (Owen et al. 2023; Ruszkowski and Pfrommer 2023, for reviews, see). The diagnostics also differ. CR secondary-to-primary ratios, synchrotron and γ\gamma-ray emission, and ionization tracers probe different CR species, energies, and propagation scales (Strong et al. 2007; Padovani et al. 2009; Abeysekara et al. 2017; Heesen 2021; Luo et al. 2026, e.g.). It is therefore difficult to separate variations in CR propagation from the effects of gas density (Abrahams et al. 2017; Lai et al. 2026), magnetic-field structure (Beaumont et al. 2013; Crutcher 2012), astrochemistry (Latrille et al. 2025; Wakelam et al. 2005; Luo et al. 2024), and projection (Beaumont et al. 2013).

An alternative to these effective treatments is to follow individual CR particle trajectories through prescribed realisations of turbulent magnetic fields. Such test-particle simulations resolve gyro-scale wave-particle interactions directly and provide a stringent test of analytic transport theory (Giacalone and Jokipii 1999; Casse et al. 2001; Mertsch 2020, e.g.). However, their dynamic range is limited, and the turbulence must be specified a priori. They are therefore not tied to the magnetic structure of a particular cloud.

Such test-particle simulations resolve gyro-scale wave-particle interactions directly and provide a stringent test of analytic transport theory (Giacalone and Jokipii 1999; Casse et al. 2001; Mertsch 2020, e.g.). However, their dynamic range is limited, and the turbulence must be specified a priori. They are therefore not tied to the magnetic structure of a particular cloud.

This leaves a methodological gap between microphysical test-particle simulations and the effective diffusion coefficients used in large-scale models. The magnetic fluctuations in an individual cloud are not directly connected to the CR scattering rates or effective diffusion coefficients used to describe CR transport on larger scales. In large-scale models, the energy dependence of the diffusion coefficient is generally prescribed from a turbulence model, without being derived from the fluctuations actually present (Strong et al. 2007; Evoli et al. 2018, e.g.). This choice is consequential because different CR transport prescriptions produce substantial differences in galaxy star-formation rates, outflows and circumgalactic gas (Hopkins et al. 2021), as well as in observables such as radio synchrotron emission (Ponnada et al. 2024). The scale on which these models apply a diffusion coefficient also matters. A diffusion coefficient is meaningful only on scales larger than the CR scattering mean free path it implies. Whether it applies on the scale of a clump or cloud complex therefore depends on the scattering mean free path, even though the scattering itself occurs on gyro scales.

Bridging these regimes requires measuring magnetic fluctuations in a specific region and estimating their power at CR-resonant scales. In quasi-linear descriptions of CR transport (Jokipii 1966; Schlickeiser and Achatz 1993a; Schlickeiser 2002, e.g.), magnetic fluctuation power near the resonant scale sets the pitch-angle scattering rate, which in turn determines the parallel mean free path and diffusion coefficient (Schlickeiser and Achatz 1993b; Owen et al. 2021). Polarised sub-mm dust emission provides a way to constrain magnetic-field structure in star-forming clouds. Emission from aligned grains traces the plane-of-sky field orientation (Planck Collaboration et al. 2014; Pattle et al. 2023) and has provided broad insight into magnetic fields in these environments (Crutcher 2012; Li 2021, for reviews, see). Polarisation angle structure functions quantify angular dispersion as a function of scale, from which the turbulent magnetic-field component can be inferred. Estimates of the field strength and turbulent linewidth provide the additional quantities needed to estimate the local CR scattering rate (Davis 1951; Chandrasekhar and Fermi 1953; Hildebrand et al. 2009; Houde et al. 2009; Owen et al. 2021).

papers.title: VC-Dimension and Generalization in Geometric Machine Learning with Applications to Active Learning
papers.abstract: We compute the VC-dimension of metric ball classifiers in the model spaces of Riemannian geometry (Euclidean, spherical, hyperbolic) and present upper and lower bounds on the VC-dimension of metric balls in several other situations, including general normed vector spaces (potentially infinite VC-dimension), vector spaces with $\ell^p$-norms (VC-dimension grows at least linearly in the dimension, faster than Euclidean for $p=1$), flat tori, and general Riemannian manifolds (arbitrarily large VC-dimension after a conformal change). In several situations where the VC-dimension is large or even infinite, we prove generalization bounds under additional assumptions on the data distribution using covering arguments. Both in the VC-dimension and covering setting, we consider data on low-dimensional subsets of high-dimensional Euclidean spaces. As an application, we consider coverage-based algorithms in active learning.

Making decisions based on incomplete information can lead to disaster [Sha97]. The science of statistics studies what we can say about a ground truth based on limited information, and how confident we can be in our assertions, assuming that we are given ‘random’ examples of the underlying truth. In this article, we compute and estimate the VC-dimension of several geometric hypothesis classes. Geometric machine learning leverages progress in well-studied fields like Riemannian geometry and spectral geometry for the purposes of data science, for instance by embedding data in non-Euclidean spaces or by recovering the intrinsic geometry of data in a Euclidean space using data graph approximations to a ‘data manifold’. Our focus is on classifiers based on distance, the coarsest geometric quantity. Specifically, we study the VC-dimension of the class of metric ball classifiers {1Br​(x):x∈X,r>0}\{1_{B_{r}(x)}:x\in X,r>0\} in various metric spaces XX and for fixed or variable r>0r>0 and both open and closed balls. papers.title: Fermat ProbCover: Coverage-Based Active Learning on Fermat Distance Graphs
papers.abstract: Active learning aims to reduce annotation cost by selecting the most informative examples for labeling. In the low-budget regime, where uncertainty-based methods often fail, coverage-based active learning methods such as ProbCover have been shown to be effective. However, these methods typically rely on Euclidean distance, which may not adequately capture the underlying geometry of data. In this article, we propose PC-Fermat, a coverage-based active learning method that replaces Euclidean coverage neighborhoods with neighborhoods defined by a Fermat distance, i.e., a data-adaptive distance that reflects the underlying distribution of the data points. To facilitate computation, we construct a weighted Euclidean neighborhood graph and use a truncated shortest-path algorithm to compute the Fermat coverage graph. We also establish sufficient conditions under which this construction exactly preserves the Fermat coverage computed on the complete graph. Finally, we evaluate PC-Fermat on eight classification datasets across varying labeling budgets, with particular emphasis on the very low-budget regime. Our experimental results demonstrate that PC-Fermat outperforms several existing active learning methods on the majority of the datasets.

papers.intro:
The remarkable success of machine learning–particularly deep learning–has arguably been driven by the availability of large amounts of labeled data. However, obtaining sufficient amounts of labeled data for real-world applications is often expensive, time-consuming, and subject to ethical and practical considerations [1, 2]. Active learning [3] seeks to address this challenge by reducing the amount of labeled data required for effective model training. Specifically, given a fixed labeling budget of bb examples, active learning methods aim to select a subset of bb examples from an unlabeled dataset for annotation, with the goal of maximizing the predictive performance of a model trained on the resulting labeled data.

Specifically, given a fixed labeling budget of bb examples, active learning methods aim to select a subset of bb examples from an unlabeled dataset for annotation, with the goal of maximizing the predictive performance of a model trained on the resulting labeled data.

We distinguish one-shot coreset-selection methods from adaptive batch-selection methods in active learning. One-shot, coreset-selection methods [4] identify the set of examples for labeling up front, prior to any data labeling or model training. In contrast, adaptive batch-selection methods repeat a three-step cycle at each iteration: (i) train a model on the current labeled set, (ii) adaptively select unlabeled examples for labeling, and (iii) update the labeled set. In either setting, one can think of the active learning methods as defining a criterion (or acquisition function) that quantifies the utility of including a currently unlabeled example in the set to be labeled. Coreset selection methods are useful for batch-selection methods, at least as an initial step and for maintaining data diversity.

Acquisition functions for active learning can generally be classified into uncertainty-based [3, 5, 6, 7, 8] and representation-based [9, 10] criteria. Within the adaptive, batch-mode setting of active learning, uncertainty-based methods prioritize samples for which the current model is least confident, allowing the classifier to refine its decision boundaries and to maximize the added value of new annotation. Representation-based criteria, on the other hand, seek to select samples from diverse regions of the data distribution, ensuring that all regions of the input space are adequately covered or “represented” in the labeled set.

Within the adaptive, batch-mode setting of active learning, uncertainty-based methods prioritize samples for which the current model is least confident, allowing the classifier to refine its decision boundaries and to maximize the added value of new annotation. Representation-based criteria, on the other hand, seek to select samples from diverse regions of the data distribution, ensuring that all regions of the input space are adequately covered or “represented” in the labeled set.

One of the key challenges in the practical application of active learning is to balance uncertainty-based and representation-based query strategies, a problem that is often viewed as an exploration-exploitation trade-off. Representation-based methods encourage exploration by selecting samples that provide broad coverage of the underlying data distribution, whereas uncertainty-based methods promote exploitation by querying samples near the model’s decision boundary to refine its predictions. This balance is particularly important in the low-budget regime, where many uncertainty-based active learning strategies may fail to outperform random sampling [9, 10]. In particular, models trained on only a small number of labeled examples can produce unreliable uncertainty estimates, limiting the effectiveness of uncertainty-based selection. In contrast, coreset-selection methods prioritize representative sample selection and can achieve better performance in low-budget settings. These observations highlight the importance of prioritizing exploration over exploitation during the early stages of active learning, analogous to early-stage reinforcement learning.

We focus on one-shot coreset-selection methods for representation-based active learning to support effective learning under limited labeling budgets. Among such methods, ProbCover [9] provides a metric-based approach to coreset selection that seeks to maximize dataset coverage by selecting samples that effectively cover the underlying data distribution. In more technical terms, ProbCover produces a coverage graph of ϵ\epsilon-nearest neighbor distances to tabulate the extent to which a selected coreset “covers” the dataset. Importantly, ProbCover does not require a particular distance metric; rather, it simply relies on a metric structure over the representation space. This observation motivates our approach: instead of modifying the ProbCover selection mechanism, we investigate how its performance can be improved by equipping it with a data-adaptive metric that better captures the underlying geometry of high-dimensional data.

papers.title: Benchmarking LLM Next-Step Recommendations with Knowledge Space Theory
papers.abstract: Selecting an LLM for next-step recommendation requires benchmarks that reflect the intended educational task and domain. We present a benchmarking method that uses Knowledge Space Theory (KST) as a formal evaluation reference. Given a task catalogue and an existing prerequisite relation, the method derives admissible knowledge states and the complete set of immediate next steps for each state. Recommendations generated by a model under a specified prompt are compared with these reference sets. A sample evaluation study uses 2,400 responses from six models across four mathematics domains, four prompt conditions, and two catalogue orders. Exact-set accuracy was 61.3% with descriptions only, 62.8% when models were asked to reconstruct prerequisites, 96.3% with supplied prerequisite relations, and 98.2% with the complete knowledge space. Performance varied across models and domains, and recommendation sets agreed across the two presentations in 85.25% of pairs. The benchmark supports comparisons of model-prompt combinations against a context-specific reference. Its scores describe structural recommendation accuracy under the evaluated conditions; they do not establish learning benefit or the necessity of using an LLM for selection.

papers.intro:
Building LLM-based digital learning tools presents a practical selection problem: Which large language model (LLM) and with which prompt is suitable for a particular educational task? For learning recommendation, a relevant capability is selecting content that fits a learner’s current knowledge and the prerequisite relations of underlying content domain. A general model score offers limited guidance about this requirement. A task-specific benchmark can instead estimate how often a candidate model with a specific prompt recovers the complete set of structurally admissible next learning steps. Such evidence connects the decision-support aims of learning analytics (Siemens and Baker, 2012) with evidence for model and prompt selection.

LLMs appear especially attractive for recommendation tasks. They can interpret competency descriptions, produce accessible explanations, and be integrated easily without training a domain-specific generator. Recent work has explored LLMs as learning assistants and generators of research-informed formative feedback (Steinert et al., 2024; Kasneci et al., 2023). Yet, a fluent recommendation can conceal a structural error. A model may treat two tasks as parallel when a given curriculum defines one as prerequisite to the other, omit feasible next tasks, or recommend an already mastered task. Evaluations based on perceived plausibility or text quality do not directly establish whether a generated recommendation fits the intended progression.

The validity of a learning recommendation depends on its context. Some prerequisites reflect the mathematical operations required by a task: for example, determining a linear function’s equation from its graph involves identifying its slope and intercept. Other dependencies reflect the instructional sequence adopted by a curriculum or classroom. A benchmark for recommendation therefore needs an explicit account of the progression intended in a specific setting. This allows the same evaluation procedure to be applied to different content domains in different educational context without treating one instructional sequence as universally correct.

papers.title: Early--Narrow and Late--Wide Populations of GRB X-ray Flares
papers.abstract: The physical origin of gamma-ray burst (GRB) X-ray flares remains debated, particularly whether they arise from prolonged central-engine activity or from variability in the external shock. Building on our previous analysis of 89 Swift GRBs with measured redshifts, we investigate the rest-frame temporal properties of X-ray flares detected in 61 bursts. We apply a multivariate Gaussian Mixture Model to rest-frame peak times and widths. We identify two statistically distinct populations: early-narrow flares (80%), with characteristic peak times of approximately 10^2 s and w/t_pk <= 1, and late-wide flares (20%), with characteristic peak times of ~ 10^3.5 s and w/t_pk >= 2. Of the 61 single or first flares, 55 belong to the early-narrow population and only 6 to the late-wide population. Of the 36 second flares, 23 (64%) belong to the early-narrow population, with shorter waiting times, whereas 13 (36%) belong to the late-wide population, with substantially longer waiting times. The width-peak-time correlation remains significant for early-narrow flares but not for late-wide flares. Furthermore, we find no correlation between flare width and energy. We find a decline of flare luminosity with peak time, driven primarily by the early-narrow population, but not statistically significant for late-wide flares. These results imply that a simple shift in time, potentially associated with later episodes of central-engine activity, cannot explain the distinction between the two flare populations. On the other hand, the peak times are consistent with expectations from an accretion disk formed following the collapse of a stellar-size massive star. Combined with our previous finding that flare properties are independent of the presence of an X-ray plateau, these results favor prolonged accretion-driven central-engine activity over external-shock variability as the primary origin of X-ray flares.

papers.intro:
Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) typically consist of two emission phases: the prompt burst of γ\gamma-rays and a longer-lasting afterglow. The prompt phase shows strong variability, whereas the afterglow is generally smoother and less variable, occasionally interrupted by X-ray flares whose origin and connection to the prompt emission remain a subject of active investigation. Following the launch of the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory (hereafter Swift; Gehrels et al. 16), systematic X-ray afterglow observations revealed that these flares appear as sudden, high-amplitude flux variations during the afterglow.

The origin of X-ray flares and their connection to the prompt phase remain open questions. Observationally, flares share several properties with prompt pulses, such as: (i) hard spectra [3, 50, 13]; (ii) hard-to-soft spectral evolution [14]; (iii) similar intensity ratios between successive emission episodes [4]; (iv) a positive correlation between spectral lag and luminosity [38]; (v) a correlation between pulse rise times and the minimum variability timescale [52]; and (vi) a power-law-tailed waiting-time distribution extending from prompt γ\gamma-ray pulses to late X-ray flares, up to ∼103\sim 10^{3} s consistent with a common time-dependent Poisson process [20] 11 1 Note that in that sample, a cutoff of ∼103\sim 10^{3} s for GRBs with known redshift was taken, due to lack of sufficient data at later times.. Despite these similarities, there are notable differences between prompt pulses and flares. The number of flares rarely matches the number of prompt pulses, and flare widths increase approximately linearly with time, whereas prompt pulses are narrower and do not exhibit this temporal broadening [4, 5, 38]. Additionally, Saji et al. [51] reported that flare durations correlate positively with their minimum variability timescale and negatively with peak flux, a trend absent in the prompt emission. Moreover, the late prompt pulses appear longer, more asymmetric, and more widely separated than early ones [22, 19, e.g.,], further highlighting both connections and distinctions between the two emission phases. These differences indicate that flares are not simply a late extension of the prompt emission and motivate detailed comparisons to constrain their physical origin.

Proposed mechanisms include continued central engine activity [7, 40], delayed reactivation of the central engine [36, 26, 37, 54, 8, 18], and delayed magnetic dissipation during ejecta deceleration [17].

Alternative models rely on external outflow characteristics, such as refreshed shocks [49, 31], patchy shells [49, 59, e.g.,], or density fluctuations in the circumburst medium [55, 7]. Other scenarios include slightly misaligned lines of sight to structured jets [12], or episodic accretion onto a black hole, as described in accretion disk models [26, 45, 47]. In the later framework, instabilities or fragmentations within the accretion disk can lead to intermittent accretion episodes, producing the observed X-ray flares.

Several studies have suggested that the temporal structure of X-ray flares may reflect intermittent or fragmented accretion processes operating over a broad range of timescales. In particular, episodic accretion models predict asymmetric emission episodes with rapid rise phases followed by slower decays, naturally producing variability patterns similar to those observed in both prompt pulses and X-ray flares [43, 26, 45, 47, 28]. The stochastic waiting-time behavior observed from prompt pulses to X-ray flares [20] further suggests that GRB central engines may operate through intermittent episodes of activity, possibly associated with episodic accretion, rather than through a single continuous emission phase. Whether different flare populations occupy distinct regimes within this common stochastic process therefore remains unexplored.

[12], can reproduce only the early (<1000<1000 s) flares, highlighting the importance of distinguishing between these populations when evaluating flare origins.

papers.title: SpecValley: Aggregation as Spectral Valley in Dense Heterophilic Graphs
papers.abstract: Node classification in heterophilic graphs remains an open problem: aggregating over neighbourhoods can damp precisely the part of the signal that carries the labels. The field has answered with ever more expressive propagation operators, leaving the aggregation step that precedes them fixed by degree normalisation. However, degree normalisation acts as a spectral valley in its own right, attenuating a fixed middle band whose position at lambda equal 1 is set by the normalisation rather than by the data, exactly where the eigenvalues of dense graphs accumulate. We therefore begin with the representations rather than the propagation, in two stages: a learnable aggregation followed by an ordinary spectral filter. The first, SpecValley learns the position, sharpness and flank gains of the valley for every graph. We show formally how the aggregation operator and downstream filter interact. We establish that the response 1 minus lambda of degree normalisation vanishes exactly at that accumulation point. A spectral energy budget shows that what aggregation removes from a band, no linear spectral filter can recover. Crowding alone says nothing about the benefit. That is decided by how much label energy the valley removes, which we measure for every graph. SpecValley achieves strong results across heterophilic benchmarks, and a controlled ablation over aggregation operators and downstream filters attributes the gain to aggregation rather than the filter.

papers.title: Universal Fold Caustics in Anharmonic Matter-wave Lenses
papers.abstract: Caustics provide a universal connection between classical ray focusing and structured wave patterns. We theoretically investigate this connection in non-linear matter waves focused by a short-duration anharmonic lens acting on a Bose-Einstein condensate. A semi-classical description shows how the leading cubic aberration transforms the harmonic focal point into a fold caustic, whose local wave field is described by an Airy canonical integral. Three-dimensional Gross-Pitaevskii simulations show that mean-field interactions modify the near-focus density and longitudinal momentum distribution, producing a secondary momentum-space feature absent from the non-interacting evolution. We quantify the information about the effective interaction strength carried by the $1D$ distribution using classical Fisher information and maximum-likelihood estimation. We obtain a relative uncertainty of $2.7\times10^{-3}$ for a sample of $10^5$ detected points along $z$. These results establish a framework for studying interaction-driven departures from single-particle caustic universality and promote matter-wave lenses as a sensitive probe of mean-field interactions.

papers.intro:
In optical systems anharmonicities and aberrations are described by the caustic formalism [6]. In geometrical optics, caustics arise when neighbouring rays converge and the ray density becomes singular. Wave optics regularizes those singularities into finite diffraction patterns whose local structure is governed by universal canonical forms [6]. In particular, the canonical form near a generic fold caustic is described by an Airy function[1]. Thus, a singularity predicted by ray optics gives rise to a characteristic and physically measurable interference pattern.

The same mechanism can be applied to matter waves. Bose-Einstein Condensates (BEC) provide coherent matter-waves which spatial and momentum distributions can be shaped with techniques inherited from optical imaging and interferometry [3, 21]. Matter-wave caustics have been investigated in a range of settings, building on the broader theory of wave catastrophe [8, 26, 22, 14]. For a condensed Bose gas, the question is therefore not whether an Airy pattern can occur, but under which conditions a generalized, anharmonic lens realizes the universal fold regime. A further question is the extent the many-body interactions modify this pattern in a realistic system, and whether the resulting dynamics can be exploited for quantum sensing.
