The characteristic Airy length is set by the cubic lens coefficient, while the higher order contribution and condensate envelope provide controlled corrections. We then include mean-field interactions within a Gross-Pitaevskii Equation (GPE) simulation and show that the density enhancement associated to the caustic amplifies non-linear matter-wave dynamics, producing a systematic departure from the single-particle Airy universality. Finally, we quantify the information about the interaction strength carried by the resulting spatial fringe distribution and show that the caustic provides a novel, sensitive probe of the mean-field interactions.

papers.title: A Taxonomy of Failing Bug Reproduction Tests on SWT-Bench
papers.abstract:
Automatic Program Repair (APR) tools require high-quality test generation models to validate candidate patches. Despite the advancements of automated bug reproduction testing tools, they continue to struggle with issues of higher complexity. These struggles may be caused by a framework's lack of problem-specific context. We address the unclassified nature of these framework failures by providing a taxonomy of bug reproduction tests. This study uses the AssertFlip and OpenHands frameworks, the two highest-scoring open-source tools on SWT-Bench Verified. The significance of model selection on the causes of failure is also explored by utilizing GPT-5-mini and GPT-4o-mini on both tools. The error traces of these frameworks are categorized to determine granular modes of failure. Through this process, mechanical and implementation failures were the most common failure classes.
  Overall, a tool's generation approach has a significant impact on precision and coverage, while the selection of the model alters the quality and quantity of generated tests. Specifically, more powerful models with higher reasoning capability tended to present fewer failures due to a lack of technical or problem-specific context. Our experiment also shows evidence that our taxonomy can be used as concrete guidance to augment the issue description to improve the generation quality.
papers.intro:
The costly nature of program repair spurred the development of the Automated Program Repair (APR) subfield. APR tools automatically generate patches for software bugs when provided with an issue description, ground-truth tests, and a buggy codebase [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]. The effectiveness of these tools depends on the availability and quality of comprehensive contextual information, particularly high-quality bug-reproduction tests that validate candidate patches. To address this dependency, automated bug reproduction test generation has emerged as a complementary research area, providing the necessary test suites that APR systems require. Recent advances in Large Language Models for Software Engineering (LLM4SE) have catalyzed progress in this domain, leveraging the capacity of LLMs to both generate and evaluate test cases. Open-source frameworks such as AssertFlip, (a hybrid LLM-and-rule-based bug reproduction test tool) [7] and OpenHands (a general-purpose agentic platform) [8] exemplify this trend, enabling researchers to generate bug-reproduction tests at scale through locally executable, LLM-driven approaches.

Despite these advancements, current state-of-the-art LLM-driven bug reproduction frameworks exhibit substantial limitations when faced with complex software issues, particularly those requiring deep comprehension of external library semantics and intricate API interactions. Empirical evidence from the SWT-Bench Verified benchmark reveals that even top-performing open-source frameworks, AssertFlip (45.5% resolution rate) and OpenHands (62.4% resolution rate) with GPT-5-mini, ranking fourth and seventh respectively on the leaderboard [9], fail to reproduce more than one-third of the test cases. More importantly, the underlying causes of these failures remain uncharacterized in existing literature. Without a systematic understanding of failure patterns, practitioners cannot effectively diagnose weaknesses in their approaches, nor can researchers identify targeted interventions to advance the state of the art. A comprehensive taxonomy of bug reproduction test failures would address this gap by providing: (1) a structured framework for analyzing tool limitations, (2) insights into how tool choices and model selection influence failure patterns, and (3) an evidence base for developing targeted mitigation strategies. Such a taxonomy can transition bug reproduction research from incremental performance improvements to principled, failure-informed design.

This study addresses these gaps through a systematic empirical analysis of bug reproduction test failures across multiple dimensions. We examine two leading open-source frameworks, AssertFlip and OpenHands. To isolate the effects of model selection on failure patterns, we evaluate the frameworks using GPT-4o-mini and GPT-5-mini. This controlled experimental design enables us to disentangle tool-specific limitations from model-dependent weaknesses. We analyze 435 failing test instances across all tool-model configurations and manually categorize each failure. Our granular analysis reveals not only which failure patterns dominate, but also how the distribution of these patterns shifts as a function of tool architecture and model reasoning capacity. In addition, we investigate whether simple template-based augmentation guided by our taxonomy can remediate the identified failure patterns. Specifically, we apply a targeted method to a representative sample of failing instances, augmenting issue descriptions with failure-class-specific guidance derived from our taxonomy.

papers.title: SPARK: Semantic-preserving Prompt Mutation for Code Generation using Consensus-based Verification Framework
papers.abstract: Automated code generation with large language models (LLMs) has improved in recent years. With the lack of test cases in real-world usages, generated code is not automatically verifiable and often requires manual validation. Previous studies have leveraged consensus verification, where code solutions and corresponding test cases are generated and evaluated based on functional consistency. Building on this, SPARK incorporates semantic-preserving mutations to problem descriptions such as paraphrasing, grammatical adjustments, function renaming, and other alterations to enhance the robustness and correctness of LLM-generated code. For each mutated description, SPARK generates a set of code solutions and test cases. These candidate solutions are evaluated using consensus-based verification, where the solutions' quality is measured by how consistently they pass generated tests. We assess the effectiveness of SPARK on three benchmarks (LiveCodeBench, BigCodeBench, and DLBench) across three LLMs (o4-mini, DeepSeek-R1-Basic, and Gemini-2.5-Pro). Our evaluation demonstrates that SPARK outperforms state-of-the-art consensus-based verification approaches by up to 4.1%. Our generalization experiment highlights the practical potential of SPARK as an effective strategy for enhancing the reliability and correctness of LLM-based code generation systems in scenarios where traditional validation resources are scarce, while our qualitative analysis shows insight into how SPARK's mutation helps LLMs generate better code solutions.

papers.intro:
Automated code generation [1, 2] with large language models (LLMs) [3, 4, 5, 6] has advanced rapidly in recent years, offering promising tools for software development. Despite these gains, reliably producing a single correct, executable solution remains a significant challenge [7, 1, 8]. Many models achieve high success rates when allowed to generate multiple candidate solutions, as measured by metrics such as pass@k (the probability that at least one of the top-k generated solutions passes the test suite) [9, 10]. However, their top-ranked outputs often fail to meet correctness requirements in practice [11]. This gap highlights the practical difficulty of selecting a reliable solution from multiple generated candidates, especially in real-world scenarios where comprehensive, human-written test suites are scarce or unavailable [12, 13, 14].

Automated code generation [1, 2] with large language models (LLMs) [3, 4, 5, 6] has advanced rapidly in recent years, offering promising tools for software development. Despite these gains, reliably producing a single correct, executable solution remains a significant challenge [7, 1, 8]. Many models achieve high success rates when allowed to generate multiple candidate solutions, as measured by metrics such as pass@k (the probability that at least one of the top-k generated solutions passes the test suite) [9, 10]. However, their top-ranked outputs often fail to meet correctness requirements in practice [11]. This gap highlights the practical difficulty of selecting a reliable solution from multiple generated candidates, especially in real-world scenarios where comprehensive, human-written test suites are scarce or unavailable [12, 13, 14].

To address the lack of ground-truth tests in practice, prior work such as the CodeT framework [15] leverages generated corresponding test cases to verify code solutions. Inspired by consensus-based algorithms [16] such as RANSAC [17], this dual agreement approach can identify groups of solutions that consistently pass groups of generated test cases and thus exhibit highly cohesive functionality. CodeT demonstrated improvements in code generation benchmarks without relying on hand-crafted test cases. However, since CodeT relies on a single prompt, the generated solutions are often tied to a single LLM’s understanding of that one specification, leading to some misinterpretation. Figure 1 illustrates such a failure: when tasked with computing the mean and median from a JSON file and writing the results to a CSV, the original prompt repeatedly fails validation because the solution outputs a field header while the validation suite expects a key header. This scenario demonstrates how single-prompt generation can fail due to subtle specification ambiguities.

To mitigate this shortcoming, we propose SPARK , which introduces semantic-preserving prompt mutations to systematically create diverse, semantically equivalent variants of the original problem description. These instances increase diversity in both generated solutions and tests, improving the chances that more candidate matches the intended specification. Concretely, SPARK uses a common, language-focused LLM (GPT-4o) to apply controlled changes in phrasing, grammatical structure, function naming, and other lexical/syntactic features (see Table I). papers.title: The PAU Survey: Dissecting strong-lensing systems with narrow-band photometric redshifts
papers.abstract: Wide-field imaging surveys such as Euclid will identify large samples of strong-lens candidates, whose scientific use requires redshifts for both deflectors and lensed sources. Source redshifts are challenging because faint arcs are blended with foreground light. We test lens-model-informed photometry on eight known strong lenses, using broad-band models to define component regions, point-reflection subtraction to reduce contamination, and PAU Survey narrow bands combined with five HSC or CFHT broad bands. BCNz estimates separate lens and source redshift distributions without imposing their expected ordering. All eight lens redshift peaks agree with spectroscopy within $|\delta_z|\leq0.014$, where $\delta_z=(z_b-z_{\rm spec})/(1+z_{\rm spec})$. Four source peaks, all at $z_{\rm s}^{\rm spec}\leq1.23$, agree within $|\delta_z|\leq0.025$. Symmetric subtraction reduces the median source $|\delta_z|$ from 0.336 to 0.071. At $|\delta_z|<0.05$, narrow- plus broad-band photometry yields eight lens and four source matches, versus three and two using EAZY with broad bands alone. These results demonstrate component redshift recovery in blended systems and support redshift-based lens-candidate assessment alongside morphology and colour. Larger narrow-band surveys, including J-PAS, could extend this approach, pending uncertainty calibration and blind candidate tests.

papers.intro:
Strong gravitational lensing is sensitive to both the mass distribution of the lens and the angular-diameter distances between the observer, lens, and source, making it a powerful probe of galaxy structure and cosmology. Its astrophysical applications include constraining the total mass distributions of galaxies, encompassing both dark and luminous matter (Sonnenfeld et al., 2019, e.g.), investigating magnified high-redshift sources (van der Wel and others, 2013, e.g.), detecting dark matter subhaloes (Vegetti et al., 2012; He et al., 2023; Nightingale et al., 2024, e.g.), and placing statistical constraints on low-mass halo populations (Gilman et al., 2020; He et al., 2022, e.g.). Cosmological applications range from measuring H0H_{0} through time-delay cosmography (TDCOSMO Collaboration et al., 2025) and constraining dark energy using double-source-plane lenses (Collett and Auger, 2014) to testing cosmological models through lensing distance ratios combined with stellar kinematics (Cao et al., 2012; Cao et al., 2015). Accurate and reliable redshift measurements for both lenses and sources are crucial for these applications and for fully exploiting the rapidly growing samples of strong gravitational lenses.

Wide-field strong-lens searches combine automated candidate selection with visual grading and, where available, spectroscopic validation. In HSC-SSP, SuGOHI progressed from YattaLens, which combines lens-light subtraction, arc detection, colour selection, and lens modelling (Sonnenfeld et al., 2018; Wong et al., 2022), to convolutional neural networks (Jaelani et al., 2024). The latter approach identified 43 Grade-A and 269 Grade-B candidates in SuGOHI-X after visual inspection (Jaelani et al., 2024). KiDS searches likewise adopted neural networks (Petrillo et al., 2017) and subsequently transformer architectures through TEGLIE (Grespan et al., 2024). Transformers use self-attention to capture spatial relationships across images, complementing the architectures used in earlier searches (Vaswani et al., 2017; Dosovitskiy et al., 2021). Recent DES Year-6 and Euclid Q1 searches demonstrate the application of vision transformers to large imaging samples (González et al., 2026; Euclid Collaboration et al., 2026b). The DES search alone examined approximately 236 million image cutouts (González et al., 2026). These methods have greatly expanded candidate catalogues, increasing the need for efficient physical validation.

Expert inspection remains valuable for recognising complex lensing configurations and rejecting contaminants that are difficult to represent in automated training sets. However, its selection function is difficult to quantify and exhaustive grading becomes costly as samples grow. Moreover, morphology and colour provide little direct information on the relative redshifts of the deflector and candidate source. Only a small fraction of high-ranking candidates currently have spectroscopic validation (Sonnenfeld et al., 2018; Wong et al., 2022), leaving a gap between efficient image-based discovery and secure physical confirmation.

Spectroscopic follow-up provides the most direct way to confirm the redshifts of strong-lens systems, but it is observationally expensive and cannot be obtained for every candidate expected from future wide-field surveys, such as Vera C. Rubin Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST). The Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) is a highly multiplexed spectroscopic facility capable of observing up to 5,000 targets simultaneously using robotically positioned optical fibres (DESI Collaboration and others, 2022). However, even when DESI successfully measures the lens redshift, foreground-light contamination, limited signal-to-noise ratio, and wavelength coverage can still prevent the recovery of the background source redshift (Huang et al., 2025).

Photometric redshifts provide complementary information and already support precision cosmology: DES Year 6 combined multi-band photometry with clustering-redshift measurements to calibrate its weak-lensing source redshift distributions (Yin and others, 2025). For strong lenses, combining broad- and narrow-band imaging offers additional spectral information. The PAU Survey (PAUS) uses 40 narrow bands spanning approximately 45004500–85008500 Å to sample spectral energy distributions as low-resolution spectra (Padilla et al., 2019; Eriksen et al., 2019). The narrow bands localise continuum breaks and emission-line features, while broad bands constrain the overall continuum shape. Compared with broad-band colours alone, this dense wavelength sampling helps distinguish spectral features that would otherwise be smeared across a filter, while retaining the scalability of imaging surveys. In COSMOS, this combination achieved σ68/(1+z)=0.0037\sigma_{68}/(1+z)=0.0037 for the best-measured half of galaxies with iAB<22.5i_{\rm AB}<22.5 (Eriksen et al., 2019), with further improvements from ancillary photometry and refined modelling (Alarcon et al., 2021). This spectral information, obtained through imaging, makes PAUS an attractive test bed for redshift-based assessment of strong-lens candidates.

Bright, red early-type galaxies dominate the deflector population and can usually be handled well by photometric-redshift pipelines. In contrast, the lensed source is relatively faint and is not isolated from the deflector light. By construction it appears around the Einstein radius, typically 11–22 arcsec from the deflector centre, which in a seeing-limited ground-based image is one to two full widths at half maximum. The lensed source image is superposed on the deflector’s envelope, which at that radius is both bright and steeply falling. A circular or polygonal region placed on the arc measures the sum of the two. Extracting the source colours through lens modelling can still have 75% photo-z outlier fraction when lens surface brightness is higher than the source at the image position (Langeroodi et al., 2023). However, early-type galaxies are among the most morphologically symmetric galaxy populations. Their point asymmetries are substantially lower than those of spiral, irregular, and star-forming galaxies (Conselice et al., 2000; Conselice, 2003). This symmetry can be exploited to remove the deflector contamination without any assumption about the source’s own spectral energy distribution.

papers.title: Dimensional Crossover and Correlated Spin Dynamics in the Chain-Like van der Waals Antiferromagnet AgCrP$_2$S$_6$
papers.abstract:
We report a comprehensive investigation of the magnetic properties and spin dynamics of the chain-like van der Waals antiferromagnet AgCrP$_2$S$_6$ using magnetization, magnetic susceptibility, and $^{31}$P nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR). The magnetic susceptibility exhibits a broad maximum near 250 K, characteristic of strong short-range antiferromagnetic correlations in a low-dimensional system. A classical Fisher-chain analysis gives an effective intrachain exchange scale $J/k_B\approx 140$ K, while a quantum $S=3/2$ nearest-neighbor-chain calculation yields $J/k_B\approx 114$ K. A constrained AF-FM zig-zag-chain calculation is also compatible with the susceptibility, supporting a dominant quasi one dimensional antiferromagnetic exchange scale of order 100 K.
  $^{31}$P NMR measurements provide microscopic insight into both static and dynamic spin correlations. The $K-\chi$ relation displays two distinct linear regimes separated near $T^\ast\approx 250$ K, with different slopes indicating a change in the effective transferred hyperfine couplings. Below $T_{N}$, the relaxation follows $1/T_1\propto T^5$, consistent with magnon-mediated relaxation in the ordered state. The temperature dependence of the internal hyperfine field yields a critical exponent $\beta\approx 0.36$, consistent with three-dimensional universality.
  Together, these results establish AgCrP$_2$S$_6$ as a quasi-one-dimensional $S=3/2$ antiferromagnet embedded in a layered van der Waals host, in which local probes directly resolve the crossover from correlated intrachain spin dynamics to anisotropic three-dimensional magnetic order. More broadly, AgCrP$_2$S$_6$ provides a useful van der Waals platform for studying dimensional crossover, correlated spin dynamics, and hyperfine-coupling evolution in low-dimensional antiferromagnets.

papers.intro:
Low-dimensional quantum magnets provide an exciting platform for exploring correlation-driven phenomena that deviate from conventional three-dimensional (3D) magnetic behavior [1, 2]. In one-dimensional (1D) systems, thermal and quantum fluctuations strongly suppress long-range magnetic order, leading instead to extended regimes dominated by short-range spin correlations and collective excitations [3, 2]. When weak interchain interactions are present, these correlated spin chains may eventually develop long-range magnetic order at a temperature TNT_{\mathrm{N}} much smaller than the dominant intrachain exchange interaction JJ, producing a dimensional crossover from 1D correlated behavior to 3D magnetic order [4, 5]. Understanding how such correlated low-dimensional spin fluctuations evolve into long-range order remains a central problem in condensed matter physics.

Low-dimensional quantum magnets provide an exciting platform for exploring correlation-driven phenomena that deviate from conventional three-dimensional (3D) magnetic behavior [1, 2]. In one-dimensional (1D) systems, thermal and quantum fluctuations strongly suppress long-range magnetic order, leading instead to extended regimes dominated by short-range spin correlations and collective excitations [3, 2]. When weak interchain interactions are present, these correlated spin chains may eventually develop long-range magnetic order at a temperature TNT_{\mathrm{N}} much smaller than the dominant intrachain exchange interaction JJ, producing a dimensional crossover from 1D correlated behavior to 3D magnetic order [4, 5]. Understanding how such correlated low-dimensional spin fluctuations evolve into long-range order remains a central problem in condensed matter physics.

Theoretical studies of quasi-1D Heisenberg antiferromagnets show that the onset of long-range order is controlled by weak interchain coupling J⟂J_{\perp}. Within random-phase approximation (RPA) approaches, the ordering condition is J⟂​χ1​D​(Q,TN)∼1J_{\perp}\chi_{1D}(Q,T_{\mathrm{N}})\sim 1, where χ1​D\chi_{1D} is the susceptibility of an isolated spin chain at the ordering wave vector QQ [4, 5]. Consequently, even very small interchain interactions can stabilize 3D magnetic order once the intrachain correlation length becomes sufficiently large. The ratio TN/JT_{\mathrm{N}}/J therefore provides a useful measure of the exchange anisotropy and dimensionality of the magnetic interactions [4, 5]. Experimental realizations of quasi-1D antiferromagnets span a wide range of spin values, from strongly quantum S=1/2S=1/2 systems such as Sr2CuO3 and KCuF3 [6, 7, 8] to higher-spin compounds where quantum fluctuations are reduced but pronounced dimensional crossover effects persist [9, 10]. At sufficiently low energies, half-integer antiferromagnetic spin chains may also be described within the Tomonaga–Luttinger-liquid framework, which has been investigated experimentally in several quasi-one-dimensional magnetic systems. [11, 12]

Layered van der Waals (vdW) magnets have recently emerged as a versatile platform for realizing anisotropic magnetic interactions and reduced dimensionality [13, 14, 15]. The weak interlayer bonding in these materials enables strong directional dependence of exchange pathways within the layers and provides opportunities to tune magnetic properties through strain, pressure, or thickness reduction [16, 17]. The ability to isolate atomic layers and construct heterostructures makes vdW magnets particularly attractive for fundamental studies of low-dimensional magnetism and potential applications in magnonic devices and quantum technologies [18, 19]. While much attention has focused on two-dimensional (2D) vdW magnets with honeycomb lattices [20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26, 27], comparatively fewer systems host intrinsically chain-like magnetic networks embedded within layered structures. Such materials combine quasi-1D exchange anisotropy with the structural flexibility of vdW crystals, making them particularly attractive for investigating dimensional crossover phenomena [28].

AgCrP2S6 belongs to the family of metal thiophosphates related to the MMPX3X_{3} compounds [29, 28]. It crystallizes in the monoclinic space group P​2/aP2/a and adopts a layered vdW structure. Within each layer, the Ag and Cr atoms occupy a honeycomb-like lattice. The magnetic Cr3+ ions (S=3/2S=3/2) are coordinated by sulfur in distorted octahedral environments within each layer and the layers are separated by van der Waals gaps. A notable feature of this compound is the pronounced anisotropy of Cr–Cr distances. Along the crystallographic aa-axis, the Cr ions are separated by a short distance of approximately 3.33.3 Å, forming well-defined magnetic chains, whereas the in-plane separations perpendicular to the chains are significantly larger (∼9.5\sim 9.5 Å). The interlayer separation is intermediate (∼6.7\sim 6.7 Å), reflecting the layered van der Waals structure [29]. This hierarchy of distances naturally favors dominant intrachain superexchange interactions along the short bonds and much weaker interchain and interlayer couplings. The resulting hierarchy of magnetic interactions is illustrated schematically in Fig. 1, where the dominant intrachain exchange JJ along the crystallographic aa direction is distinguished from the weaker interchain J⟂J_{\perp} and interlayer couplings JcJ_{c}. This quasi-one-dimensional exchange topology, embedded within a layered van der Waals lattice, makes AgCrP2S6 a particularly appealing platform for investigating how low-dimensional spin correlations evolve into long-range order.

papers.title: Design of Self-Folding Origami Architectures for Biomedical Implants: A Finite Element Simulation Framework
papers.abstract: Minimally invasive brain implants require compact deployment geometries and controlled shape transformation for delivery through confined vessels. Origami-inspired structures enable large shape changes from compact to tailored deployed configurations, but implementation at microscale dimensions remains challenging, as conventional designs rely on predefined mountain and valley folds that become increasingly difficult to fabricate and assemble as unit-cell size is reduced to meet clinical requirements. To address this, we propose a self-folding methodology based on thermally induced stresses in thin-film bimetallic composites. Pairing the shape memory alloy Nitinol (NiTi) with molybdenum or stainless steel (SS316L) exploits their differing thermal expansion coefficients to generate localized hinge bending, enabling deterministic, autonomous folding into prescribed mountain and valley configurations. Using finite element simulations, we systematically optimize hinge length, layer thickness, width, and shape, identifying a hinge geometry achieving a ~50% reduction in unit-cell dimensions relative to previously reported designs. Integration into a complete waterbomb origami unit cell confirms that the strip-level folding mechanism scales to produce coordinated, self-folding deformation across the tessellated structure. These results demonstrate the feasibility of stress-induced, self-folding thin-film origami architectures built from clinically established biomaterials, providing a scalable design framework for next-generation, active neurovascular implants with integrated sensing and monitoring functionality.

papers.title: Microscopic derivation of the classical KMS condition for one-dimensional Bose gases
papers.abstract: The Kubo--Martin--Schwinger (KMS) condition provides an intrinsic characterization of thermal equilibrium, both in quantum and classical statistical mechanics. In this work, we establish stability of the KMS condition through the quantum-to-classical limit for one-dimensional defocusing Bose gases. More precisely, we consider scaled quantum KMS states in the (mean-field) semiclassical regime and prove that every associated Wigner measure satisfies the classical KMS condition corresponding to the nonlinear Schr\"odinger Hamiltonian. This result extends to an infinite-dimensional setting an earlier derivation of the classical KMS condition for finite-dimensional Bose--Hubbard systems. It also provides a complementary perspective on the derivation of nonlinear Gibbs measures from many-body quantum statistical mechanics.

papers.title: When do all iterates of $x^2 + a$ have maximal Galois group?
papers.abstract:
We provide an (in our opinion) simpler proof of the main results of [Stoll1992,Li2020,Li2021] on the question for which integers $a$ the Galois groups of all iterates of $x^2 + a$ are maximal (equivalently, the associated arboreal Galois representation is surjective). At the same time, we extend the results to rational parameters $a$. The main result states that for a subset of rational numbers of relative density $1/2$ in the complement of a certain open interval, the maximality of the Galois group of the second iterate is sufficient for the arboreal Galois representation to be surjective. We also discuss experimental evidence suggesting that a similar statement involving the fourth iterate may hold in general.
  The results were obtained in collaboration with Claude (Anthropic's AI model); they are also formalized in Lean (except for the experimental evidence).

papers.title: Cost controllability and predictive control of input-constrained monotone systems on Hilbert spaces
papers.abstract: Cost controllability, relating controllability and a performance measure like the stage cost in model predictive control (MPC), is a key tool in the stability and suboptimality analysis of closed-loop systems. We establish cost controllability for maximal monotone control systems subject to input constraints, a class encompassing finite- and infinite-dimensional port-Hamiltonian systems with colocated input and output. To this end, we employ a recently proposed saturated feedback to derive state-dependent bounds on the closed-loop cost. Our main result is that cost controllability holds globally with semiglobal exponential rate. We first establish this result in continuous time and then extend it to sampled-data systems. Whereas a qualitative detectability-like property is sufficient for asymptotic convergence of the controller, cost controllability requires quantitative rates. We provide two verifiable conditions ensuring cost controllability with explicit exponential rates: coercivity of the sum of system operator and output injection, and exponential detectability of the linear part. Moreover, under the coercivity condition, the resulting MPC scheme without terminal conditions renders the equilibrium globally asymptotically stable with semiglobal exponential rate already for prediction horizon two. We illustrate our results by a nonlinear finite-dimensional system, a semilinear heat equation and a nonlinearly damped wave equation.
papers.intro:
Model predictive control (MPC) computes a feedback law by iteratively solving finite-horizon optimal control problems and applying the first portion of the optimal control function, see, e.g., (Grüne and Pannek, 2017; Rawlings et al., 2017). Asymptotic stability of the MPC closed loop may be enforced by terminal costs and constraints, which, however, are often hard to construct, in particular for nonlinear partial differential equations. Without (stabilizing) terminal conditions, the stability and performance analysis of MPC (Grimm et al., 2005; Grüne, 2009) usually rests on a controllability assumption in terms of the stage cost, called cost controllability. Loosely speaking, it requires, for every initial state, an admissible control such that the stage cost along the resulting trajectory decays according to a fixed 𝒦​ℒ0\mathcal{KL}_{0}-bound depending only on the initial cost. For bounds linear in the initial cost, the minimal stabilizing horizon can be computed by a linear program (Grüne et al., 2010; Worthmann, 2011), and this analysis was extended to continuous time in Reble and Allgöwer (2012).

Model predictive control (MPC) computes a feedback law by iteratively solving finite-horizon optimal control problems and applying the first portion of the optimal control function, see, e.g., (Grüne and Pannek, 2017; Rawlings et al., 2017). Asymptotic stability of the MPC closed loop may be enforced by terminal costs and constraints, which, however, are often hard to construct, in particular for nonlinear partial differential equations. Without (stabilizing) terminal conditions, the stability and performance analysis of MPC (Grimm et al., 2005; Grüne, 2009) usually rests on a controllability assumption in terms of the stage cost, called cost controllability. For bounds linear in the initial cost, the minimal stabilizing horizon can be computed by a linear program (Grüne et al., 2010; Worthmann, 2011), and this analysis was extended to continuous time in Reble and Allgöwer (2012).

Verifying cost controllability in applications can be challenging, in particular under input constraints, and considerable work has been devoted to particular system classes. Coron et al. (2020) derived sufficient conditions in terms of homogeneous approximations, Worthmann et al. (2016) established cost controllability for nonholonomic mobile robots by explicit open-loop maneuvers, and Müller and Worthmann (2017) showed that the design of the stage cost is decisive, as quadratic costs may fail to asymptotically stabilize the MPC closed loop, whereas suitably designed costs succeed (Coron et al., 2020; Rosenfelder et al., 2023). In infinite dimensions, cost controllability and MPC without terminal conditions were studied for heat and wave equations in Altmüller and Grüne (2012); Altmüller et al. (2010), with emphasis on stage costs allowing for small stabilizing horizons. Receding horizon stabilization of infinite-dimensional systems was considered in Ito and Kunisch (2002) and established for Burgers and wave equations in Azmi and Kunisch (2016); Azmi and Kunisch (2018). A second line of research connects MPC with passivity and dissipativity. Closed-loop stability may be enforced by a passivity-based constraint (Raff et al., 2007), dissipativity is central to economic MPC, see, e.g., (Angeli et al., 2012), and for port-Hamiltonian, hence dissipative, systems, optimal control problems with the supplied energy as cost exhibit turnpike phenomena (Schaller et al., 2021).

Contribution and outline. We show that maximal monotone control systems under input constraints are globally cost controllable with semiglobal exponential rate, such that MPC stability theory directly becomes applicable. Our contributions are threefold. (i) Using the saturated feedback as admissible control, we prove cost controllability in continuous time (Theorems 4.5 and 4.9) and for the sampled-data system (Corollary 5.2), with explicit semiglobal exponential rates under coercivity or exponential detectability. (ii) Under coercivity of M+B​B∗M+BB^{*}, MPC without terminal conditions renders the equilibrium globally asymptotically stable with semiglobal exponential rate already for the shortest horizon N=2N=2 and every sampling period (Theorem 5.5). (iii) The results apply to nonlinear partial differential equations, as illustrated by a semilinear heat equation and a nonlinearly damped wave equation (Examples 4.7 and 4.10). After recalling the system class and the saturated feedback in Section 2, we reduce cost controllability to a state decay estimate in Section 3, verify this estimate in Section 4, derive the MPC guarantees in Section 5 and conclude in Section 6.

papers.title: The Unused Input: The Initial State as a Conditioning Interface for Recurrent TSFMs
papers.abstract: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) forecast unseen series without task-specific training. Increasingly they are built on recurrent backbones, whose constant per-step cost makes long-context inference cheap, and which, unlike transformers, carry a state. A recurrent backbone computes its prediction from two inputs: the observed context window and the initial recurrent state. In practice only the first is utilised and the initial state is unused by convention. We ask whether the initial state can be utilised in recurrent TSFMs. Using the xLSTM-based zero-shot forecaster TiRex as a case study, we freeze the backbone and train only a small head that writes a context vector into the initial state, so that any change in accuracy is attributable to the injected state rather than to adapted weights. A spectral summary of the input window, learned once and applied unchanged to every series, lowers mean GiftEval MASE by 0.175%, with every seed improving, which neither a parameter-matched LoRA adapter nor a learnable static state reproduces. An embedding of text attached to each series, evaluated on six MoTime datasets, reveals two roles for the state. As a per-dataset adaptation surface, a static state lowers MASE by 0.04-6.96% of the zero-shot baseline (8-70% of the gain of full fine-tuning). As a channel for exogenous information, the text-conditioned state lowers it by a further 0.15-0.41% of the zero-shot baseline on four of six datasets and, combined with a LoRA adapter, exceeds full fine-tuning, which has no access to the text, on one of them. In TiRex, the effect concentrates in the mLSTM blocks and is strongest at short context. The results are preliminary and the improvements small, but they point to the initial state as a direction for further research.
papers.intro:
Time series foundation models, pretrained once and applied across many forecasting tasks without further training, have become a standard tool for zero-shot forecasting (Das et al., 2024; Ansari et al., 2024; Woo et al., 2024; Cohen et al., 2024). Many are built on recurrent architectures, like TiRex (Auer et al., 2025a; Podest et al., 2026) on xLSTM (Beck et al., 2024), TSMamba (Ma et al., 2024) and Mamba4Cast (Bhethanabhotla et al., 2024) on Mamba, and others on gated DeltaNet (Hartl et al., 2026). A recurrent forecaster produces its forecast as a function of two inputs: the context window it observes, and the initial state it starts from. In practice only the first is used; the initial state is set to a fixed default that holds no information about the series being forecast. We investigate this unused initial state, taking TiRex as a case study.

Prompt and prefix tuning adapt a frozen model by optimising a sequence of trained vectors that its inputs attend to, leaving its weights unchanged (Lester et al., 2021; Li and Liang, 2021); recent work shows that similar conditioning mechanisms extend to time series forecasters (Ahamed et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2025). Initialising the state of classical RNNs is known to be beneficial, both for forecasting and systems-modelling tasks (Mohajerin and Waslander, 2017; Mohajerin and Waslander, 2019), and for conditioning on context more broadly (Wenke and Fleming, 2019), and the Temporal Fusion Transformer initialises its LSTM from static covariates (Lim et al., 2021). In NLP, Kang et al. (2025) extend this idea to modern state space models, adapting them by directly tuning states rather than prepending prompts, and Galim et al. (2025) show that, for state space models, tuning the initial state of a frozen model is at least as expressive as prefix tuning. To our knowledge, we are the first to study the initial state of a frozen, pretrained recurrent time series foundation model as a conditioning interface, and to characterise how the injected state behaves.

Our contributions are: (1) using TiRex, we show the recurrent initial state is a usable conditioning interface that can improve a frozen time series foundation model; (2) we condition on a spectral summary of the input window and on a CLIP-aligned (Radford et al., 2021) embedding of exogenous text, comparing each against a parameter-matched LoRA adapter (Hu et al., 2022) and an expressivity-matched static state; and (3) we characterise the behaviour of the injected state, whose influence in TiRex is strongest at short context and diminishes as data accumulates, and localises to the matrix memory of its underlying xLSTM (the mLSTM blocks).

papers.title: Universal Approximation Theorem for Metaplectic Neural Operators
papers.abstract: We prove universal approximation for metaplectic neural operators on nonempty bounded Lipschitz domains. The nonlocal branches are whole-space metaplectic multipliers with zero extension and restriction, associated with any fixed free symplectic matrix. Assuming a smooth, globally Lipschitz, nonpolynomial activation, we obtain compact-uniform approximation of continuous operators from $C^s$ to $C^r$ and from $H^s$ to $H^r$ in the respective output norms, for arbitrary nonnegative integers $s,r$ and finite input and output channel dimensions. In the Sobolev setting, compact input sets must additionally be uniformly bounded in $L^\infty$. One hidden operator layer with one nonlocal branch suffices. A single scalar symbol atom and finitely many positional features are prescribed by the transform and domain independently of the target operator, compact set and accuracy. The proof combines averaging neural operator theory with an exact chirp-conjugated averaging identity and derivative estimates. The result includes Fourier and fixed nondegenerate fractional Fourier multiplier constructions.

papers.intro:
Neural operators approximate nonlinear maps between function spaces. A typical target is the solution operator of a partial differential equation, which maps a coefficient field, a forcing term or initial data to the corresponding solution. The dependence on the input need not be local: changing the data in one region may affect the solution elsewhere. The mathematical analysis of neural operators must account both for the finite-dimensional nonlinear approximation performed within the network and for the mechanism by which information is transferred between different points of the domain. This paper studies the latter mechanism for neural operators whose nonlocal branches are multipliers with respect to a prescribed metaplectic transform. We ask whether fixing this transform preserves universal approximation, including approximation in norms that control derivatives of the output. Approximation in such norms is relevant when the predicted field is used to compute gradients or other derivative-dependent quantities.

Metaplectic analysis provides a common setting for Fourier and fractional Fourier transforms. Metaplectic operators implement linear symplectic changes of position and frequency and, up to constant phase factors, include Fourier transforms, fractional Fourier transforms, dilations and multiplication by quadratic phases [16, 13, 12]. Prescribing such a transform fixes the coordinates in which the multiplier acts. On the whole space, a metaplectic multiplier need not be translation invariant, even though a Fourier multiplier is. The free symplectic class considered here includes linear couplings of position and frequency beyond the scalar rotations associated with fractional Fourier transforms. This broader class permits a common approximation question for several choices of transform: which nonlocal operations are sufficient when the transform itself is fixed?

The classical properties of metaplectic operators describe the linear branch, but universality also depends on the admissible symbols, positional inputs and nonlinear maps. We therefore work with prescribed finite families of symbol atoms and positional features, and with finite neural networks for the local maps. The objective is to establish universal approximation within this architecture for every fixed free transform. The construction rests on spatial averaging, which Lanthaler, Li and Stuart [22] identified as a sufficient nonlocal operation for universality. Averaging gathers features of the input over the domain and makes the resulting finite vector available to the pointwise maps. Here the averaging operation must be realized by the prescribed metaplectic branch and used in a way compatible with the componentwise activation.

papers.title: Plug-and-Play ADMM for Inverse Problems with Flow Matching Denoiser
papers.abstract: Plug-and-Play (PnP) methods with generative priors have achieved strong performance in inverse problems, with recent flow matching models enabling fast and scalable reconstruction. However, a key challenge in PnP methods is maintaining consistency between data fidelity updates and the learned generative prior, as data-consistency steps can move iterates away from the flow trajectory. We propose an ADMM-based PnP framework for flow matching priors that enforces stronger consistency between the measurement model and the prior through auxiliary variables and dual updates. In addition, we introduce a trajectory correction mechanism that restores consistency with the flow via a combination of deterministic and stochastic projections. Our method provides a more principled integration of flow priors within PnP frameworks, achieving high-quality reconstructions with reduced computational cost.

Challenges: Despite their strong empirical performance, integrating generative priors within PnP frameworks remains challenging. A key difficulty arises from the interaction between the data-consistency step and the learned prior. In standard PnP algorithms, the data-consistency update (e.g., a gradient or proximal step with respect to l⁡(𝐲,𝐱)l({\mathbf{y}};{\mathbf{x}})) can move the iterate away from the data manifold or the learned flow trajectory, thereby degrading the effectiveness of the prior s⁡(𝐱)s({\mathbf{x}}). Following the data-consistency step, we project the iterate back toward the flow trajectory using a weighted combination of stochastic and deterministic projections. By combining ADMM with our trajectory correction, we achieve a more robust integration of flow-matching priors within PnP frameworks, leading to strong reconstruction performance and significant reduction of computational cost, runtime, and memory footprint compared to existing approaches (section 4.2 and table 2). papers.title: From Show Programs to Linked Data
papers.abstract: Many heritage institutions hold extensive collections of show programs. Too numerous to be cataloged individually, they remain difficult to access and are still largely undigitized. This paper presents a workflow for transforming such documents into structured, interoperable data by combining vision-language models (VLMs), a custom extension of the Linked Art ontology for the performing arts, and different approaches for automatic semantic data annotation. Using the Festival d'Avignon programs (1947--present), preserved at the Biblioth{\`e}que nationale de France, as a case study, we demonstrate how VLMs achieve more than 98% text transcription accuracy from heterogeneous heritage document images and how constraining large language model generation through a knowledge graph significantly reduces hallucinations in semantic annotation. We argue that this workflow opens new possibilities for large-scale, interoperable performing arts historiography, including the creation of catalogues raisonn{\'e}s for performing artists, a form of scholarship common in visual arts but absent in performing arts studies.

papers.title: Optimization-Based Path Planning for Industrial Manipulators: Experimental Validation in Additive Manufacturing
papers.abstract: Robotic additive manufacturing requires joint paths that reconcile robot feasibility with process-specific geometry. We develop an offline optimization-based path planner that combines joint-path regularity and self-collision penalties with process costs and constraints, so that a new process enters through its own reference, residuals, and tolerances. Full-path and boundary-coupled chunked optimization handle references of different lengths. Iterative Weight Tuning (IWT) determines the cost weights from the gaps between Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) and their targets. In carbon-fiber winding and robotic 3D printing, the planned paths meet the geometric tolerances and all KPI targets, and both paths are executed on a UR10e, without extrusion for printing, with joint-level tracking recorded during execution.

In additive manufacturing, robot configurations must accommodate the process geometry and tolerances along an ordered reference while respecting joint limits, self-collision clearance, and path continuity [2]. The planner must therefore translate the ordered process reference into a joint-space path that respects these requirements.

Once a path is fixed, execution introduces timing and feedback requirements. Optimal control and Model Predictive Control (MPC) address these requirements with custom trajectory-optimization and MPC formulations [10] and with robust tube MPC which handles model uncertainty through corridor-based planning [11]. Receding-horizon optimization supports reactive motion within its horizon, while coordinating configurations over the complete manufacturing reference would require the same process geometry together with execution models and timing assumptions.

Learned models offer another way to generate candidate paths or initialize numerical optimization. Motion Policy Networks learn reactive motion from depth observations [12], while DiffusionSeeder and Planning with Environment Representation, Sampling, and Trajectory Optimization (PRESTO) generate candidate paths for numerical refinement [13, 14]. Reinforcement Learning (RL) has also been combined with conventional planning and neural inverse kinematics for redundant manipulators [15], and with inverse-Jacobian control for simulated deburring [16]. At the execution stage, data-driven trajectory generation and compensation have targeted residual vibration and tracking error in pick-and-place tasks [17]. For winding and printing, a learned planner would need training tasks and inputs or rewards that represent the process geometry. Its paths would also need to be checked against the relevant tolerances.

Manufacturing planners incorporate process tolerances [2], optimize orientation and timing [18], and enforce coupled-system constraints [19]. Graph-based methods address winding sequences [20]. The question here is how core-relative fiber references and prescribed nozzle poses can each be converted into joint paths while coupling process agreement, path regularity, and clearance over the ordered samples. Pointwise inverse kinematics does not couple these path-wide requirements, so we integrate their residuals and constraints in a common robot-stage optimization. This coupling introduces one weight per cost term. The weights trade process agreement against regularity and clearance, while acceptance is decided by process tolerances, so manual tuning must be repeated for each process. Constrained Bayesian optimization has tuned the parameters of a contouring planner jointly with low-level controller gains against motion performance metrics [21], and NMPC weights have been tuned with Bayesian optimization [22] and adapted across repeated winding tasks [23]. We therefore pair the formulation with Iterative Weight Tuning (IWT), which determines the weights from the gaps between the evaluated metrics and their tolerances. The contributions of this work are as follows: 1. A process-aware joint-path formulation that couples winding fiber alignment or printing nozzle poses with joint regularity, self-clearance, and joint bounds. Both applications use forward kinematics to evaluate their process residuals within a common robot-stage optimization. 2. An adaptation of our Iterative Weight Tuning (IWT) method [23] to select robot and process cost weights for both winding and printing. Empirical sensitivities relate weight changes to robot and process Key Performance Indicator (KPI) errors, enabling regularized norm-optimal updates without differentiating through the path optimizer. The tuning uses clearance and fiber-alignment KPIs for winding and position- and orientation-tracking KPIs for printing. 3. A two-stage winding planner that converts groove transitions into a sequence of contact points and fiber directions in the core frame. The robot stage uses that fixed sequence to plan the motion of the core while accounting for fiber–robot clearance and enforcing an angular tolerance at groove endpoints. 4. A printing implementation that limits the number of active configurations per optimization. Fixed neighboring configurations and joint-difference penalties couple adjacent chunks, and alternating forward and reverse sweeps propagate the boundary updates.

papers.title: Chain of Physics: Supporting Fault Diagnosis with Engineering-Inspired Large Language Model Reasoning
papers.abstract: Fault diagnosis in complex systems requires linking observed changes in physical quantities to the failure mechanisms that produce them. Experienced engineers perform this task by combining sensor information with knowledge of system behavior and fault propagation. Large Language Models (LLMs) can support this process, but their diagnostic reasoning depends on the availability of asset-specific engineering knowledge and on how this knowledge is represented and used during inference. This work introduces Chain of Physics (CoP), an LLM-based fault-diagnosis framework built around a Constrained Knowledge Graph (CKG) generated automatically from asset-specific reference documentation. CoP addresses failure-sensor association from textual engineering knowledge. The CKG stores diagnostic chains connecting failure modes, changes in physical quantities, and monitoring sensors. During inference, semantically similar graph paths are retrieved for each question and used as both information and in-context examples for the reasoning process. Candidate failure modes are extracted from the question and analysed independently through dedicated LLM calls, which generate plausible failure-to-observation chains. A final decision module compares these chains with the available answer choices. CoP is evaluated on the FailureSensorIQ benchmark across four industrial asset classes and three LLMs. Compared with direct prompting and conventional Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), CoP improves diagnostic accuracy across all evaluated models, with gains ranging from 7.8 to 19.6 percentage points and from 11.7 to 18.2 percentage points, respectively. The results show that structured engineering knowledge can improve LLM-based diagnostic reasoning when graph retrieval is combined with in-context examples of fault propagation.

papers.intro:
Fault diagnosis in complex systems requires identifying the failure mechanisms responsible for an observed deviation from nominal behavior. Experienced engineers and technicians perform this task by combining available measurements with their knowledge of system behavior and reasoning about the physical quantities through which failure effects become observable International Organization for Standardization (2018). These relationships link observed sensor behavior to specific failure mechanisms, enabling Fault Detection and Isolation (FDI) and supplying diagnostic information for downstream health assessment and maintenance decisions in Prognostics and Health Management (PHM) frameworks Jardine et al. (2006). In industrial applications, the knowledge required for this process is generally distributed across technical manuals, reference documents, troubleshooting procedures, maintenance records, and accumulated expert experience Kang et al. (2026). Its interpretation and integration therefore remain largely dependent on experienced personnel, who must retrieve and reconcile information scattered across heterogeneous technical documents and information systems Wang et al. (2024a); Razaq et al. (2026). The problem considered in this work focuses specifically on diagnosis from engineering knowledge, not on the direct classification of measured sensor signals. Given a textual description of a failure mode or sensor observation, the objective is to recover the relevant failure–sensor association and the physical relationships that connect them. The task can therefore be viewed as knowledge association from engineering text, requiring the relationships among failure mechanisms, their physical effects, and the corresponding sensing modalities to be established from textual information.

The increasing interest in Large Language Models (LLMs) introduces the possibility of assisting engineers in this knowledge-intensive task Han et al. (2025). Through natural-language interaction, LLMs can process technical information, interpret diagnostic questions, and formulate possible explanations without requiring a dedicated model for each asset Razaq et al. (2026). Despite the strong push towards Artificial Intelligence (AI) adoption and the proliferation of AI initiatives across industrial sectors, the integration of LLMs into fault diagnosis remains challenging. Conventional task-specific models generally require representative labelled data and retraining when new assets or failure conditions are introduced, limiting their applicability in industrial settings. LLMs offer greater flexibility, but often lack the asset-specific and practical engineering knowledge required to interpret abnormal conditions correctly. This limitation can lead to hallucinated or physically inconsistent diagnostic explanations, particularly when the model must establish relationships between failure mechanisms, their effects on system behavior, and the available sensor measurements Ma et al. (2026). Their effective deployment therefore requires incorporating established engineering knowledge and guiding the reasoning process according to the physical relationships governing the system.

One of the most widely adopted approaches to incorporate external engineering knowledge into LLM inference is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) Lukens et al. (2025). By retrieving relevant passages from technical documentation, RAG can provide information beyond that acquired during pre-training without requiring task-specific model training. Nevertheless, the availability of relevant information does not guarantee that the model can reconstruct the physical sequence linking a fault to its measurable effects. However, in fault diagnosis, these relationships are central to the reasoning process: a failure affects one or more physical quantities, its effects may propagate through the system, and the resulting changes are detected by specific sensors. Representing this sequence explicitly may therefore provide a more suitable basis for diagnostic reasoning than supplying unstructured technical information alone. This type of explicit failure-to-observation reasoning has a long tradition in engineering diagnosis, including qualitative physics and model-based diagnosis de Kleer and Williams (1987), Signed Directed Graph (SDG) representations Kramer and Palowitch (1987), and Failure Mode and Symptoms Analysis (FMSA) International Organization for Standardization (2012). These approaches similarly rely on structured relationships between failure mechanisms, their physical manifestations, and the observations through which they can be detected. In recent years, Knowledge Graphs (KGs) have emerged as a possible means of representing this type of diagnostic structure through explicit entities and relationships Ibrahim et al. (2024). For fault diagnosis, a KG can represent the progression from a failure mode to the physical changes and the measurements through which those changes become observable. Even more, the close integration of LLMs and KGs is increasingly being investigated for industrial fault diagnosis Martinez-Gil et al. (2022). In fact, LLMs provide natural language processing and reasoning capabilities, while KGs organize domain knowledge into explicit entities and relationships. Their integration allows diagnostic systems to retrieve and use structured engineering knowledge during inference, supporting more informed and interpretable diagnostic reasoning. Still, the practical integration of LLMs and KGs into an industrial diagnostic framework presents two main difficulties Pan et al. (2024). First, manually constructing asset-specific knowledge representations requires considerable engineering effort, particularly when multiple systems and failure mechanisms are considered. Second, a graph containing relevant entities and generic relationships does not necessarily preserve the physical sequence required for diagnostic reasoning.

One of the most widely adopted approaches to incorporate external engineering knowledge into LLM inference is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) Lukens et al. (2025). By retrieving relevant passages from technical documentation, RAG can provide information beyond that acquired during pre-training without requiring task-specific model training. Nevertheless, the availability of relevant information does not guarantee that the model can reconstruct the physical sequence linking a fault to its measurable effects. However, in fault diagnosis, these relationships are central to the reasoning process: a failure affects one or more physical quantities, its effects may propagate through the system, and the resulting changes are detected by specific sensors. Representing this sequence explicitly may therefore provide a more suitable basis for diagnostic reasoning than supplying unstructured technical information alone. papers.title: Physics-Constrained Autoencoder for Interpretable Health Representation Learning in Turbofan Engines
papers.abstract: Health Indices (HIs) summarize degradation from operational data and support diagnostic and prognostic tasks in Prognostics and Health Management (PHM). Their usefulness depends on capturing degradation and interpreting system condition. Autoencoders learn such representations from unlabelled monitoring data; however, when training is driven only by reconstruction, the physical meaning of latent variables remains undefined, limiting their interpretation and diagnostic value. This work proposes a physics-constrained autoencoder that embeds system knowledge as an inductive bias in the decoder architecture and as a learning bias in the loss function. The decoder contains differentiable physical equations that receive latent variables and operating conditions as inputs, structurally guiding each latent variable to represent a predefined physical quantity and enabling component-level analysis before aggregation into a system-level HI.The methodology is benchmarked on the N-CMAPSS dataset against alternative representations. Reconstruction reaches an $R^2$ of 0.9993 and an MAE of 0.0036, comparable to fully data-driven models. After operating-condition correction, the inferred physical quantities track degradation, and their aggregation produces an HI with a Spearman correlation of 0.9791 with the ground truth, an RMSE of 0.0286, and an MAE of 0.0233. The methodology is further evaluated using a single model trained across four datasets representing distinct degradation scenarios. This model preserves component-level signatures that distinguish compression-side from expansion-side degradation without diagnostic labels.Finally, the proposed framework enables degradation trends to be visualized on component maps, providing a health representation in a form familiar to engine operators and domain experts.

papers.intro:
Prognostics and Health Management (PHM) has progressively reshaped the way operational data are processed and used in industrial settings Zio (2022). The increasing availability of sensors, embedded computing resources, and advanced data-processing methodologies has made it possible to move beyond traditional maintenance strategies, enabling informed asset management based on predictive decision-making Kordestani et al. (2021). In this context, PHM provides a structured framework for transforming raw monitoring data into actionable information supporting fault detection, diagnosis, prognosis, and health-aware asset management Hu et al. (2022). The main objectives of PHM can therefore be formulated as (i) assessing the current condition of an asset through diagnostics, (ii) anticipating its future degradation through prognostics, and (iii) supporting maintenance and operational decisions through health management Jardine et al. (2006).

The emergence of PHM is commonly associated with the aerospace and defence sectors, where the need for safer, more available, and more cost-effective systems has always been particularly demanding Hess et al. (2005); Jimenez-Roa et al. (2026). Aircraft systems and mission-critical platforms, including turbofan engines Xu et al. (2026), missile guidance systems Hu et al. (2024), and flight-control actuators Baldo et al. (2025), have motivated the development of integrated monitoring capabilities able to detect incipient faults, estimate Remaining Useful Life (RUL), and support logistics and maintenance planning. Since then, PHM has expanded well beyond its initial aeronautic domain, spanning a plethora of applications. Today, PHM methodologies are investigated and applied in several industrial sectors, including actuation systems Bertolino et al. (2023), space Aimasso et al. (2022), automotive applications Bustos et al. (2026), batteries Alcibar et al. (2026), and process industries Hu et al. (2022).

A central concept in this context is the Health Index (HI), which is commonly introduced as a representation of the degradation state of an asset measured through a normalized version of a health indicator. In other words, it can be defined as a compact representation of asset condition designed to track degradation progression and support downstream diagnostic and prognostic tasks. In practical applications, HIs have been obtained through different strategies, including the selection of degradation-sensitive features, the use of model residuals, the fusion of multiple condition-monitoring signals, and the learning of latent degradation representations from data Zhou et al. (2022); Chen et al. (2025); Ge et al. (2025).

Among data-driven approaches, autoencoders have become a widely adopted solution for unsupervised health representation learning. Their encoder–decoder structure allows high-dimensional monitoring data to be compressed into a compact latent representation and reconstructed from it Bengio et al. (2013). In PHM, the latent variables or a post-processed function of the latent space (e.g., a latent dynamical model) can then be used as an indicator of degradation and, consequently, as an HI. This makes autoencoder-based approaches particularly attractive when health-state labels are unavailable, run-to-failure data are limited, or the degradation state is only indirectly observed through sensor measurements, a combination frequently encountered in industrial applications González-Muñiz et al. (2022); de Pater and Mitici (2023).

(2022); de Pater and Mitici (2023).

Despite the intuitive appeal of using a latent representation as a degradation descriptor, a standard autoencoder is designed and optimized primarily for reconstruction. As a consequence, its latent coordinates are not guaranteed to correspond to physically meaningful degradation mechanisms. In fact, they may encode operating conditions, sensor drift, noise, mission-related trends, or dataset-specific correlations that help reconstruct the input data without necessarily describing the health state of the asset. This limitation is especially significant from a user perspective, considering the vital role of HI as key metrics that operators rely on to evaluate asset condition and determine the necessity of intervention. When an HI is obtained from a black-box latent space, its physical meaning may remain unclear even when the reconstruction performance of the model is satisfactory. Moreover, even when a learned latent representation tracks degradation accurately, it may provide little information about the physical source of that degradation or the component responsible for the observed change. Such ambiguities can reduce trustworthiness, especially in safety-critical applications where operators need to understand why a model indicates degradation and whether this indication is consistent with known system behaviour. Obtaining HIs that are predictive, interpretable, physically consistent, and usable by domain experts is therefore critical for the further adoption of PHM systems in industrial settings Nor et al. (2021).

papers.title: Where to Approximate in Neurosymbolic Inference?
papers.abstract: Probabilistic neurosymbolic methods rely on weighted model counting (WMC) to combine neural predictors with symbolic constraints. Exact WMC is #P-hard and typically scales poorly, so many methods resort to approximations. By unifying existing approaches under a three-step bottom-up approximate compilation pipeline, we study where approximation budget is best allocated. Inspired by tensor networks, we instantiate two steps with tensor train decompositions and derive new pipelines that exactly multiply approximated factors and recompress their products via SVD- or interpolation-based schemes. Across six tasks in Sudoku, arithmetic reasoning, and scene understanding, and across increasing problem sizes, our pipelines produce WMC estimates orders-of-magnitude more accurate than prior methods. This translates into stronger downstream learning on tasks where reasoning relies on tight interactions between symbolic factors, where cruder approximations ignore these dependencies. Our pipelines open novel design space for effective approximate compilation of challenging probabilistic reasoning tasks.

papers.intro:
Probabilistic neurosymbolic (NeSy) systems combine neural perception with symbolic constraints, to enable learning from weak supervision [34, 67] or to inject symbolic knowledge into structured prediction pipelines [1]. Inference involves solving the weighted model count (WMC) problem [7]: computing the probability that a neural distribution over discrete concepts satisfies a constraint. Computing the WMC exactly is #P-hard in general [56]. One approach for solving practical instances tractably is circuit compilation which compiles the constraint into a logical circuit, a process also called knowledge compilation [15], while the neural distribution is turned into a probabilistic circuit [63, 9, 1]. Then, under certain structural properties, these circuits can be efficiently multiplied and summed over to yield the exact WMC [51, 64]. The same structural properties and multiplication operation are also behind popular bottom-up strategies for knowledge compilation [46, 14].

The same structural properties and multiplication operation are also behind popular bottom-up strategies for knowledge compilation [46, 14].

However, compilation is itself hard, and exactly multiplying several compiled circuits blows up exponentially in the number of factors [64]. This implies that compilation strategies can hit a wall on many real-world NeSy problems. Even compiling a 9×99\times 9 Sudoku board, often used in benchmarks [4, 66], as a constraint is out of reach for all exact compilers. Without surprise, many NeSy methods focused on approximate computation of the WMC [59, 53, 8, 16]. However, these approaches have carried over with different perspectives and from different communities. As such, the problem of understanding where and when to approximate in a systematic way is still open.

In this paper, we provide a unified view over many NeSy pipelines and we identify three stages at which approximations can enter (Figure 1): (I) compiling each factor exactly or with a relaxed circuit, (II) multiplying factors exactly or via a recompression that controls size growth, and (III) combining remaining factors under an independence assumption. Many existing methods fit in this categorization, sometimes mixing several approximations. Independence (fuzzy) approximations are by far the most common [5, 58, 2] and are well known to support effective learning [58, 32], yet their inference fidelity is not well-studied. Stages (I) and (II) are far less explored. Drawing on the close connection between tensor networks and circuits [30], we instantiate stages (I) and (II) using tensor train (TT) decompositions. TTs have been used in NeSy to approximate and compress isolated factors [8] but not in a full compilation pipeline. We show how approximate tensor trains can be used for inference and compilation, deriving novel APRICOT pipelines.

papers.title: Mesoscopic derivation of predator-prey dynamics via diffusive fast-reaction asymptotics: cross-diffusion and fear effects
papers.abstract: We propose a kinetic derivation of a spatial predator-prey model with cross-diffusion interactions and a Beddington-DeAngelis functional response. At the mesoscopic level, we divide the two populations into distinct behavioral states: prey can be active or hidden in a refuge, while predators can be either searching or handling. The microscopic state of each subpopulation is described in terms of group size and a continuous directional velocity variable, with state transitions governed by suitable Boltzmann-type interaction operators. By combining a diffusive scaling with a slow-fast formulation of the kinetic reaction operators, we formally derive a macroscopic reaction-cross-diffusion system for the total population densities of prey and predators. The limiting model consistently recovers the Beddington-DeAngelis functional response along with its associated nonlinear diffusion terms. Crucially, the kinetic upscaling yields a predator-dependent prey growth term taking a logistic form with an effective carrying capacity. This carrying capacity depends non-monotonically on predator density because prey redistribute between active and refuge states. Since density-dependent competition acts separately within these behavioral states, intermediate predator levels reduce aggregate crowding and thereby increase the effective carrying capacity of the total prey population. Overall, our derivation provides a mechanistic link connecting predator-induced behavioral shifts, refuge use, and macroscopic cross-diffusion.

papers.intro:
Spatial movement and behavioral responses to interspecific interactions are closely connected in ecological systems. In predator–prey communities, individuals may change their activity or habitat use in response to predation risk, prey availability, or feeding requirements. At the population level, these responses can produce spatial fluxes that depend on the densities of both species. Cross-diffusion systems provide a mathematical framework for describing such effects, allowing the movement of one population to depend on the spatial distribution of another. A central modeling question is how the resulting nonlinear diffusion terms can be related to specific ecological processes, and how these processes also affect the reaction terms governing population growth and trophic interactions.

A mechanism for deriving cross-diffusion consists in distinguishing behavioral states within each population and assuming that transitions between these states occur on a faster time scale than demographic processes [26, 13, 19, 8, 20, 25, 14, 18, 23, 9]. When individuals in different states have different movement characteristics, eliminating the fast processes leads to effective diffusion terms that depend on the local population densities. The same reduction also determines the effective reaction terms, since reproduction, competition, and predation act on populations whose distribution among behavioral states is constrained by the fast dynamics. This approach has been applied to predator–prey systems involving Holling-type II and Beddington–DeAngelis functional responses [13, 19, 42]. In particular, following the mechanistic derivation of Geritz and Gyllenberg [22], Desvillettes and Soresina [19] obtained a non-triangular cross-diffusion system from a four-component reaction–diffusion model accounting for active and hidden prey, together with searching and handling predators. These derivations establish a connection between behavioral transitions, functional responses, and nonlinear spatial movement.

Kinetic theory provides a complementary framework for connecting elementary interaction mechanisms with collective behaviors [3, 4, 21, 24] in population dynamics. In this setting, a population is described through a distribution function over suitable microscopic variables, and interactions are encoded by operators (typically, Boltzmann and Fokker–Planck-type operators) specifying how these variables change. Macroscopic quantities are then recovered as moments of the distribution functions [35]. There is a vast literature of kinetic models for living systems in which the microscopic traits of individuals are characterized by their internal state, or activity [2, 10], also in the context of population dynamics [28]. For predator–prey interactions, Toscani and Zanella [44] recently introduced an alternative description in which the microscopic variable represents the size of the interacting groups and the first moments of the mesoscopic solutions satisfy the Lotka–Volterra equations. Additional developments of this approach include the kinetic models studied in [7, 45]. Going further, spatial kinetic descriptions allow movement and interactions to be considered within the same framework, with effective diffusion equations obtained through suitable asymptotic scalings. We mention, for example, the recent work [11] (whose approach is similar to ours, although based on the use of individuals’ microscopic velocities for the kinetic variable, rather than the size of interacting groups), where predation is modeled at the kinetic level by a sequence of behavioral transitions and the use of slow–fast dynamics allows for the derivation of predator–prey standard diffusion models with Holling-type II and type III functional responses. Similarly, in the framework of reacting gas mixtures, Martalò and Travaglini [31] derived a reaction–cross-diffusion system from kinetic equations, illustrating how cross-diffusion can also emerge from microscopic interactions occurring on different time scales.
