Each species is divided into two behavioral states: prey can be active or hidden in a refuge, while predators can be searching or handling. Building on the group-size approach of [44], we describe each subpopulation by a distribution function and represent the relevant interactions through Boltzmann-type operators. The interaction rules account for prey capture, predator-induced refuge use, return to activity, transitions between searching and handling, and competition within each prey state. Birth and death processes are included through additional linear drift operators. We then introduce spatial transport and relaxation operators to describe movement within each behavioral state.

By combining a diffusive scaling with a slow–fast formulation of the kinetic reaction operators, we formally derive a macroscopic reaction–cross-diffusion system for the total prey and predator densities. The scaling distinguishes dominant relaxation, fast behavioral transitions, and slow demographic processes, thereby making explicit the hierarchy of time scales underlying the reduction. In particular, convergence to local kinetic equilibrium for each distribution provides at leading order a link between the corresponding flux and concentration gradient, while the behavioral transitions impose at intermediate scales additional relations between the state densities, allowing going beyond the usual quadratic terms prescribed by Boltzmann operators and recovering more complex nonlinearities in the combined diffusion–fast-reaction limit. Specifically, the limiting system recovers the Beddington–DeAngelis functional response and the nonlinear diffusion structure obtained in [19], together with a novel prey-growth term determined by the demographic assumptions at the kinetic level. As a byproduct, if no state dichotomy in the prey is assumed, we are also able to recover the Holling-type II structure of [13]. The derivation thus relates the macroscopic coefficients and nonlinearities to the underlying interaction rules and clarifies how the behavioral mechanisms contribute to both spatial movement and population dynamics. To our knowledge, this is the first derivation of this kind for cross-diffusion predator–prey models. Moreover, in contrast to previous works on reacting gas mixtures [31], where a nonstandard rescaling of time and space is introduced to bring the linear relaxation operator to order 𝒪⁡(ε2)\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{2}), rather than the usual 𝒪⁡(ε)\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon) order in diffusive limits (thus leading to a Hilbert expansion with no first-order kinetic correction), we show that cross-diffusion emerges under a standard parabolic rescaling of space and time, allowing us to close the moment equations already at the first-order kinetic correction of the Hilbert expansion.

papers.title: Integrability of the horizontal mean curvature near characteristic points in the Heisenberg group
papers.abstract: We investigate the local integrability of the horizontal mean curvature near characteristic points of surfaces in the first Heisenberg group. We prove that, for every embedded surface of class $C^{2,\alpha}$, with $\alpha>0$, the horizontal mean curvature is locally integrable with respect to (any) Riemannian surface measure, without any assumption on the structure of the characteristic set. We further establish that the horizontal unit normal belongs to $BV_{\mathrm{loc}}$ and characterize its $W^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ regularity in terms of the vanishing one-dimensional Hausdorff measure of the characteristic set. Finally, we answer an open question by Danielli, Garofalo and Nhieu by constructing a $C^2$ surface with a unique characteristic point whose horizontal mean curvature fails to be locally integrable, thus showing that the additional H\"older regularity cannot, in general, be replaced by $C^2$ regularity.

papers.title: Distributionally Robust Indirect-Feedback Stochastic MPC with Gelbrich Ambiguity Sets
papers.abstract: Stochastic model predictive control uses disturbance statistics to set safety margins. Errors in these statistics can invalidate the safety guarantees. This paper therefore describes the uncertainty in the disturbance mean and covariance by a prescribed Gelbrich ambiguity set. This contains distributions of any shape whose moments are close in the Gelbrich distance to the nominal values, including distributions with unbounded support. For linear time-invariant systems with additive disturbances, we build on the indirect feedback paradigm, propagate this moment uncertainty along the error dynamics, and obtain a closed-form constraint tightening that is computed offline. Robustness enters as a single additive term that grows with the size of the ambiguity set, so the online problem remains a quadratic program. Recursive feasibility and closed-loop satisfaction of conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) constraints hold for every disturbance distribution in the set. We illustrate the method on a linearized planar quadrotor.
papers.intro:
Ensuring satisfaction of state and input constraints is challenging when the system is affected by unknown random disturbances. The usual way to address this is to use safety margins based on the mean and variance of the disturbance. Errors in these statistics can invalidate the risk guarantee the margins were meant to provide.

Ensuring satisfaction of state and input constraints is challenging when the system is affected by unknown random disturbances. The usual way to address this is to use safety margins based on the mean and variance of the disturbance. Errors in these statistics can invalidate the risk guarantee the margins were meant to provide.

A standard approach in stochastic model predictive control (SMPC) [1, 2] tightens constraints using the first two moments of the disturbance. We build on indirect-feedback stochastic MPC (IF-SMPC) [3], in which the nominal trajectory is never reset to the measurement. This separates the error dynamics from the online control decisions, allowing uncertainty bounds to be computed offline. The resulting guarantee, however, is stated for the assumed moments. Distributionally robust MPC removes that reliance by optimizing against a set of distributions [4, 5]. In this paper, we combine IF-SMPC with a Gelbrich ambiguity set on the disturbance. The Gelbrich set bounds deviations in the mean and covariance without prescribing the shape of the distribution, so unbounded disturbances with finite second moments are admitted. A closed-form expression for the worst-case conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) over a Gelbrich set [6] turns the propagated moment uncertainty into a deterministic constraint tightening.

The main contributions of this paper are as follows. • We construct an offline bound on how moment uncertainty accumulates over time and use it to determine constraint margins. Robustness enters as a single additive term that grows with the size of the ambiguity set, so the online problem remains a quadratic program. • We prove that, under the stated assumptions, the proposed controller is recursively feasible and satisfies each prescribed CVaR constraint, and hence the corresponding chance constraint, at every time step for every disturbance law in the ambiguity set. • We test the controller on a linearized planar quadrotor that flies into the corner between a wall and the floor, varying the disturbance moments and distribution shape. The baseline exceeds the risk limit in some tested cases, while the empirical CVaR of the proposed controller stays below it throughout.

A related MPC approach with distributionally robust CVaR constraints is Wasserstein tube MPC [11], which propagates a Wasserstein tube exactly for noise with compact polyhedral support. Optimal-transport ambiguity-set propagation [12] is the closest approach to the proposed offline propagation. An indirect-feedback scheme with Wasserstein DR-CVaR constraints [13] restores recursive feasibility by softening the CVaR constraint. A later moment-based DR-MPC [14] calibrates a radius on the second moment from data and restores feasibility by interpolating the initial state; in contrast, the proposed method uses a prescribed radius. Gelbrich ambiguity has also been used to robustify a quadratic cost under hard convex constraints [5], rather than a risk constraint.

Distributionally robust density steering [16] uses the same closed form with a Gelbrich outer approximation over a finite horizon, optimizing feedback gains in a semidefinite program. In contrast, this paper propagates a Gelbrich ball offline along the indirect-feedback error dynamics, and the tightened nominal constraints need no slack variables.

papers.title: CURRENT: A Recurrent Neural Network for Concurrent Spatial and Temporal Super-Resolution of 4D Flow MRI
papers.abstract:
Objective: To improve the spatial and temporal resolution of aortic 4D flow MRI through a unified deep learning framework for post-acquisition super-resolution (SR) of reconstructed velocity vector fields.
  Methods: We propose CURRENT, a recurrent neural network that performs spatial and temporal SR with a single network architecture. Supervised training was conducted using paired low- and high-resolution datasets generated by embedding computational fluid dynamics simulations of aortic flow into in vivo thoracic MRI backgrounds, followed by controlled spatial and temporal downsampling. CURRENT was evaluated for two-fold spatial and temporal SR against 4DFlowNet and for two-fold spatiotemporal SR against sequential spatial and temporal SR pipelines based on 4DFlowNet. Image-based and k-space-based quantitative metrics were considered and conventional interpolation were used as baselines. In addition, the impact of CURRENT's spatiotemporal SR on physics-informed relative pressure estimation was assessed. Finally, the ability of CURRENT to generalize from synthetic training data to in vivo acquisitions was investigated.
  Results: CURRENT achieved superior spatial SR performance and comparable temporal SR performance to dedicated 4DFlowNet models while providing a unified solution for both tasks. Simultaneous spatiotemporal SR using CURRENT yielded more accurate relative pressure estimates than either spatial or temporal SR alone and outperformed sequential 4DFlowNet-based spatial and temporal SR approaches. Furthermore, the proposed model demonstrated promising generalization to in vivo 4D flow MRI data despite being trained exclusively on synthetic datasets.
  Conclusion: CURRENT provides a unified framework for spatial and temporal SR of 4D flow MRI. The proposed approach has the potential to enhance physics-based analysis and broaden the applicability of accelerated 4D flow MRI.

papers.title: STarlight Acquisition and Reflection toward Interferometry (STARI) mission
papers.abstract: We introduce the NASA-funded mission STARI (STarlight Acquisition and Reflection toward Interferometry), a two-spacecraft technology demonstrator for future long-baseline interferometers. STARI will perform, to our knowledge, the first in-space transfer of starlight between free-flying spacecraft, a critical step toward long-baseline space interferometry. Two propulsive 8U CubeSats in low Earth orbit will fly in formation with separations up to 200 m: one relays a narrow stellar beam to the other, where an off-axis parabola reimages it into a single-mode fiber. Using differential GNSS, visible LED beacons, and fast-steering mirrors in closed-loop control, we aim to sustain diffraction-limited, high-throughput fiber coupling during formation flight. STARI, targeting launch in 2029, is designed to mature key technologies needed for future mission concepts such as the Large Interferometer for Exoplanets (LIFE), which would seek atmospheric biomarkers on nearby Earth-like exoplanets.

papers.intro:
Long-baseline interferometry bypasses the diffraction limit of a single filled aperture by coherently combining light collected across a much larger physical baseline. Ground-based interferometers have demonstrated milli-arcsecond imaging of stellar surfaces and circumstellar environments [1], but atmosphere, weather, and geography limit both sensitivity and baseline flexibility. Space interferometry removes these barriers and is especially compelling for future mid-infrared nulling missions that could measure atmospheric biomarkers on nearby terrestrial exoplanets [2, 3, 4]. Recent formation-flying interferometry roadmaps and exoplanet-interferometry study reports identify flight validation of beam transfer, optical coupling, path-length stability, and coordinated spacecraft control as a key step toward such observatories [5, 6]. The remaining challenge is not conceptual, but practical: future space interferometers require precision formation control, beam transfer, optical coupling, autonomous operations, and flight-proven performance data at the system level.

STARI is a pathfinder mission built around one essential operation for a future distributed optical interferometer: collect starlight on one free-flying spacecraft, transport that beam across tens to hundreds of meters, and inject it into a single-mode fiber on another spacecraft. Figure 1 illustrates the present handoff concept. The mission is not itself an interferometer. It deliberately omits a combiner and delay line so that the project can concentrate on the flight demonstrations that are difficult to reproduce on the ground: relative navigation in low Earth orbit, optical beam handoff, closed-loop fine steering, coupling stability, station-keeping using propulsion maneuvers, low platform jitter, and autonomous coordinated two-spacecraft operations.

A 2024 SPIE paper described STARI during its pre-Phase-A CubeSat stage [7] before being officially selected for funding, with a start date of December 2024. A 2025 SmallSat/SRR update captured the first NASA-funded baseline: a 6U-class design, a ∼100\sim 100 m starlight-transfer demonstration, a reference-laser-assisted acquisition concept, and a maturing ConOps for transitions between standby and science relative orbits. Since then, the mission has carried out the System Requirements Review (SRR) in Ann Arbor in December 2025 and passed after responding to action items identified by the review committee; the project then carried out an internal preliminary design review (PDR) in May 2026 on the campus of Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute in Troy, New York. Here in the 2026 SPIE proceedings, we summarize the present design and the main changes since 2024, with emphasis on how the subsystem trades are converging toward a flight experiment.

papers.title: Just Image Transformers with Late-Stage Pixel Refinement
papers.abstract: Recent work on latent-free diffusion transformers has demonstrated the feasibility of training image generators without a latent VAE. This avoids compression artifacts from the VAE and simplifies the training pipeline. In particular, JiT showed that even a standard transformer can be trained to generate images when the model is trained to predict the final image ($x$-prediction). Even though JiT unlocks training efficiency comparable to latent models, it still suffers from reduced image quality likely arising from modeling the image as a collection of large patches. In this work, we revisit JiT and show that adding simple convolutional pixel-pathway layers in a post-training phase significantly improves generation quality. Moreover, we show that the added pixel-pathway does not need to be active in the early denoising stages, and can be activated as late as in the last $20\%$ of the denoising process. Our experiments on ImageNet@256 show improvements compared to the original JiT results, achieving an FID of $1.78$ (from $2.34$ with corrected sampling), without using additional losses.

papers.intro:
Recent advances (Li and He, 2026; Yu et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026c; Ma et al., 2026c; Chen et al., 2026b; Guo et al., 2026; You et al., 2026) in latent-free generation avoid the bottleneck of latent-based methods by training diffusion models directly in pixel space. Such pixel-space diffusion transformers (pDiTs) take an RGB image as input and predict a denoising step in pixel space. Li and He (2026) observe that the v-prediction objective commonly used to train diffusion transformers requires the network to predict off-manifold targets because of the added noise component. They instead propose predicting the final image (x-prediction), thereby keeping the prediction targets on the manifold of real images. Their experiments show that, where v-prediction fails with large patches, x-prediction succeeds with patches of up to 32×3232\times 32 pixels. Their model is a standard image transformer that divides an image into large, non-overlapping patches, hence the name Just Image Transformer (JiT).

Although these results show that simple large-patch transformers can be trained directly in pixel space, we find that JiT outputs lack sharpness and show subtle patch-boundary artifacts (see Figs. 1 and 2). We hypothesize that these issues mainly arise from the architectural choices. In fact, JiT independently decodes final patch tokens into non-overlapping pixel patches. This requires consistency across patch boundaries to be established through global patch-level attention. Moreover, the output head has no direct access to the noisy input 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t}, so recoverable fine detail must pass through the input bottleneck and the entire transformer backbone. These architectural choices place the burden of resolving local dependencies, such as edge continuation and texture alignment, on a large-patch transformer, which is inefficient use of global attention and transformer capacity. This motivates using dedicated local processing that communicates across patch boundaries.

We augment the patch-level transformer with a pixel-level pathway and study its late activation. We also revisit the timestep-sampling and loss-weighting strategies used during training. Our contributions are as follows: 1. Post-training refinement. We improve JiT models by adding a pixel-level pathway consisting of only a few convolutional blocks on top of the big-patch transformer. Unlike previous work, we do so in a post-training manner, showing it’s possible to pre-train just a transformer backbone using an xx-prediction objective and add pixel refinement in a shorter fine-tuning stage. 2. We revisit the training protocol, showing that the timestep distribution during training has an effect on learning fine details and the timesteps near the clean endpoint benefit from better coverage. We also experiment with different head configurations and revisit the generation procedure of JiT, proposing a correction for the final denoising steps.

papers.title: Using Proof Dependencies to Manage Verification Projects
papers.abstract:
Verification technology now scales to sizable projects, but techniques for managing such projects fall short. There are no effective ways to assess the progress made so far and to determine which verification tasks to perform next. A key issue is that the successful run of a verification tool provides little indication about what has actually been achieved. The guarantees provided depend on the specifications of the verified code as well as any unverified assumptions made in the proofs, e.g., about the behavior of unverified libraries. Manual inspection of specifications and assumptions to determine progress is error-prone and prohibitively expensive.
  In this paper, we present automated techniques to assess and guide verification projects. All of these techniques employ an automatic proof dependency analysis that computes, for each proof obligation in a project, the specifications, statements, and assumptions that are needed to prove it. We show that this analysis enables effective proof audits by determining all assumptions a proof depends on. We also use it to determine which statements in a program are constrained by the provided specifications, which indicates how strong a specification is. Based on these two insights, we propose a novel progress metric for verification projects and show how to use it to guide verification projects to maximize progress.
  We implement our approach in the symbolic execution backend of Viper and lift it to the Go verifier Gobra. Our evaluation on real-world benchmarks, including a verified Internet router, shows that the dependency analysis is sound and sufficiently precise, that our progress metric accurately reflects the state of a verification project over time, and that our guidance outperforms standard bottom-up and top-down verification strategies.

Various projects have demonstrated that verification technology now scales to sizable applications (Chakarov et al., 2025; Pereira et al., 2025; Protzenko et al., 2020; LeBlanc et al., 2025). However, with growing size and complexity, managing verification projects becomes increasingly challenging (Brugger et al., 2026; Mugnier et al., 2025; Oliveira et al., 2025). A key issue in project management is to assess the progress achieved so far and to steer the effort toward project completion. Both are surprisingly difficult for deductive verification projects, due to three main challenges.

First, software systems interact with libraries, the operating system, database systems, and other components, many of which remain unverified for the time being. Consequently, the proof of a software system is based on assumptions about unverified code, e.g., about the possible result values of a library call. In practice, assumptions are also used to work around shortcomings of verification technology, e.g., to supply complex mathematical facts. Assumptions weaken the guarantees given by verification and are a common cause of unsound verification results (Fonseca et al., 2017). Therefore, in order to assess the progress made in a verification project and to ensure the validity of the obtained proofs, it is crucial to perform proof audits, where all assumptions are identified and reviewed.

Assumptions are typically scattered throughout the codebase, for instance, in the form of unverified components or explicit assume statements. However, many of the assumptions in a codebase are irrelevant for the audit of a given proof because the verified property does not depend on them. Hence, to make proof audits efficient, it is necessary to automatically identify those assumptions that may actually affect the validity of the proof. This task is complicated by the fact that the impact of an assumption may be indirect and not visible in the code. For example, using a data structure invariant in the proof of a method mm is sound only if all operations on the data structure maintain the invariant. Any assumption in the verification of these operations indirectly also impacts mm’s proof, even if mm does not call the operations directly. The challenge is thus to precisely identify all relevant assumptions for a proof audit. In particular, a syntactic analysis would flag too many irrelevant assumptions and make audits inefficient.

Second, progress in a verification project depends not only on the amount of verified code but crucially also on the properties that have been proved. Most existing verification tools check memory safety and the absence of crashes by default; all other relevant properties, such as functional correctness, termination, and information flow security, are checked only if required by user-provided specifications. Hence, the successful run of a verification tool alone does not provide any indication whether such properties have been proved. In whole-program analyses, properties are typically specified globally and can be reviewed manually. In contrast, modular verification associates a specification with each method of a program; manually reviewing all of them each time a project manager needs to assess progress is infeasible. The challenge is to measure progress in verification projects automatically, taking into account the three main progress indicators: the amount of verified code, the strength of the specification, and the assumptions made in the proofs.

Third, the scope of a verification project is often not precisely defined because one could always eliminate one more assumption, verify another library method, or prove additional properties. Therefore, verification projects often aim at giving the strongest guarantees that can be achieved within the project’s resource constraints. Project managers try to prioritize verification tasks that have the largest effect on the overall progress. For instance, they may decide to eliminate an assumption that affects many proofs or verify a method that is being called frequently. However, predicting the impact of a change is difficult when specifications are decentral and proof dependencies are not obvious. The challenge is to automatically provide guidance on which tasks to prioritize.

Existing work on proof auditing (Tomb and Joshi, 2025; Schröer et al., 2025) extracts proof dependencies, in particular on assumptions, from the UNSAT core provided by an SMT solver. However, this work may miss crucial assumptions because it does not track indirect dependencies, such as those introduced by method calls or data structure invariants. On a technical level, these existing techniques have been designed for verifiers that produce a single verification condition for each method, such that the UNSAT core for this verification condition contains all relevant information. Yet, many state-of-the-art verifiers employ symbolic execution (Jacobs et al., 2011; Müller et al., 2016; Santos et al., 2020), which verifies each path through a method separately and produces many SMT queries in the process. This complicates the extraction of precise information about the assumptions used in the proof.

To the best of our knowledge, there is no prior work on measuring progress or providing semantic guidance in verification projects. Several approaches (Goldweber et al., 2024; Lahiri, 2024; Baksys et al., 2025) address the subproblem of assessing the strength of specifications by checking whether they are strong enough to verify test cases or client code. These approaches require comprehensive test suites that need to be annotated with loop invariants and ghost code, which incurs substantial manual effort. Another line of work (Le et al., 2018; Goldweber et al., 2024; Knüppel et al., 2021; Amaral et al., 2025) assesses specification quality by attempting to verify mutations of the program. They consider a specification to be sufficiently strong if verification fails for the mutated code, which is computationally expensive since one verifies many mutations of each method. Moreover, one cannot distinguish the “good” case where a specification indeed rules out a mutation from the “bad” case where verification fails for other reasons, for instance, because the mutation requires a slightly different loop invariant.

papers.title: Ender: Visual Scaffolding for Geometric Proof Comprehension
papers.abstract: Geometric proof is a foundational but notoriously difficult topic in secondary mathematics, primarily due to the high cognitive load required to integrate visual diagrams with logical text. As proofs evolve, tracking the initial givens and an expanding set of derived truths can easily overwhelm working memory. While established scaffolding techniques are often visual and diagram-based, current digital learning environments mostly rely on static, text-heavy interfaces that force students to manage these complex mental models on their own. This paper introduces Ender, an interactive rendering system designed to visualize the logical status of two-column proofs. Ender's design is grounded in four literature-derived requirements: (1) diagram annotation, (2) structural tracing, (3) support for partial or incorrect work, and (4) synchronization between the diagram and text. To evaluate the system, we conducted a between-subjects, think-aloud experiment with 12 secondary school students in the United States, comparing Ender against a traditional digital proof interface. Our results indicate that students using Ender performed significantly better on proof comprehension tasks--specifically in identifying and correcting logical errors. These findings suggest that dynamic visual scaffolding may ease the working memory burden of digital interfaces, offering a promising building block for future AI-based proof tutoring systems.

papers.intro:
Geometric proof is a key concept in secondary school mathematics, yet it remains one of the most difficult to learn [69, 72, 64]. A primary source of this difficulty is the high cognitive load required to coordinate two distinct representations: the visual diagram and the logical text. While the diagram provides spatial intuition, the text demands rigorous deduction. Novices frequently struggle to connect these modes, often viewing the diagram as a static picture rather than a dynamic representation of logical truths. They lose track of the evolving state of the proof, leading to errors where they confuse “surface features”—such as the orientation or size of a shape—with the underlying logical structure [14, 71, 20, 8].

Because proof diagrams are typically under-specified [42], these scaffolds serve as critical bookkeeping mechanisms that allow students to visually track logical information as it is established. This kind of dynamic marking comes naturally with pen and paper, where a diagram can be freely annotated as reasoning unfolds. papers.title: Adaptive catalyst discovery emerges from composable scientific intelligence
papers.abstract: Catalysis underpins chemical manufacturing, yet knowledge for catalyst design remains dispersed across experimental observations, computational data and catalysis subdisciplines. To overcome this challenge, we present Composable Catalytic Intelligence (CatAI), a physics-grounded modular AI framework that learns 1.8 million structure-property relations and organizes them into 30 physicochemical encoders. This reusable intermediate layer enables task-specific models to guide catalyst discovery for targeted reactions and objectives. Across benchmark tasks, CatAI achieves a 7.8% lower task-averaged prediction error than the next-best models. In experimental validation, CatAI identified a new confined-passable pocket catalyst applicable in industrial homogeneous polymer synthesis with 9 times the activity of the commercial benchmark. In parallel, it guided autonomous closed-loop optimization of a highly active Cu-based geminal-atom photocatalyst for C-O coupling reactions surpassing the traditional Ni-based systems. This approach connects property-level data to catalytic objectives, supporting physicochemical knowledge reuse across mechanistically distinct systems through computational screening and iterative model-experiment feedback.

papers.title: Investigation of the timing performance of double-sided $p$-type 3D silicon sensors produced by CNM
papers.abstract: We investigate the timing performance and spatial uniformity of double-sided $p$-type 3D silicon sensors produced by the Centro Nacional de Microelectr\'onica (CNM). Three sensor layouts are studied: hexagonal and square geometries with an inter-electrode spacing of \SI{30}{\micro\meter}, and a hexagonal geometry with an inter-electrode spacing of \SI{50}{\micro\meter}. The sensors are characterized using a \SI{1064}{\nano\meter} infrared laser and a custom two-stage wide-band readout. Measurements with a $^{90}$Sr source are used to establish a minimum-ionizing-particle-like reference for the laser signal. The timing resolution improves with increasing bias voltage for all three layouts. Two-dimensional laser scans are used to study the position dependence of the timing response and to quantify its uniformity. Among the investigated devices, the square \SI{30}{\micro\meter} geometry shows the best overall timing performance at the highest measured bias voltage.
papers.intro:
The High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC) will operate under challenging conditions, with a nominal bunch-crossing frequency of 40 MHz and up to approximately 200 proton–proton interactions per bunch crossing. The high pileup environment presents significant challenges for event reconstruction, while the accumulated radiation exposure requires silicon tracking detectors to exhibit high radiation hardness. Although precise timing information is not a baseline requirement for the inner tracking detectors, it could provide additional benefits for pileup mitigation and event reconstruction. Therefore, radiation-tolerant silicon sensors with fast timing capabilities are of interest for future tracking applications.

papers.title: RiSE-Drive: Risk-Sensitive Long-Horizon Candidate Evaluation for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
papers.abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving systems increasingly rely on generating multiple trajectory candidates and selecting one for execution. In this setting, a central challenge is no longer only candidate generation, but how to evaluate candidates according to their long-horizon consequences under uncertainty. Existing methods still mainly use deterministic point scores, heuristic subscores, or single-outcome evaluations, which makes it difficult to capture delayed failures, tail risk, and ranking instability under plausible future perturbations. We present RiSE-Drive, a framework for risk-sensitive long-horizon candidate evaluation in end-to-end autonomous driving. RiSE-Drive first performs candidate-conditioned latent future rollout, then estimates long-horizon outcome distributions instead of single scalar scores, and finally ranks candidates using a tail-risk-aware and perturbation-robust decision criterion. This reformulates candidate scoring from deterministic oracle-style evaluation into distributional outcome assessment with explicit risk control. As a result, the evaluator is encouraged to prefer candidates that are not only strong under nominal conditions, but also reliable under long-horizon rollout and safety-critical deviations. Experiments on the NAVSIM-v1 and NAVSIM-v2 benchmarks, as well as the closed-loop HUGSIM benchmark, show that RiSE-Drive achieves state-of-the-art performance and significantly improves the robustness of candidate selection.

End-to-end autonomous driving aims to map raw multi-view observations directly to a safe, rule-compliant, and route-progressive future ego trajectory in a unified learned planner (Jiang et al., 2023; Chitta et al., 2023; Hu et al., 2023; Weng et al., 2024). Modern systems increasingly adopt a generate-and-select paradigm, where a proposal module enumerates multiple feasible futures and a selector chooses one for execution (Li et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025a; Kirby et al., 2026; Guo et al., 2025). Under behavior-grounded evaluation such as NAVSIM and NAVSIM-v2 (Dauner et al., 2024; Cao et al., 2025), the central challenge is therefore not only to generate plausible candidates, but to evaluate which candidate remains best under long-horizon interactions and future uncertainty.

papers.title: Economic Benefits of Cross-Border Electricity Trade and Domestic Electricity Production in Switzerland
papers.abstract: This paper assesses the economic benefits of cross-border electricity trade in the context of rising energy prices and geopolitical uncertainty. Switzerland provides a particularly compelling case because of its geographical location and limited integration into the EU electricity market. We first use the Nexus-e framework to simulate the generation capacity and transmission grid expansion required under autarky and free-trade scenarios. Based on these capacity configurations, a fundamental power market model simulates wholesale market outcomes under projected demand and generation conditions for 2040. By jointly accounting for consumer and producer surplus, as well as investments in generation capacity and grid infrastructure, we provide a comprehensive assessment of the welfare effects of cross-border electricity trade, leading to an estimated EUR 1.5 billion gain. More specifically, open access to cross-border electricity trade implies a EUR 1.8 billion transfer from largely publicly owned producers to consumers. Finally, we provide an illustrative, non-causal mapping of broader macroeconomic effects. Under a price-convergence assumption, the implied demand adjustment corresponds to a GDP-equivalent effect of approximately EUR 7 billion.
papers.intro:
Cross-border electricity trade is of critical importance to Switzerland. Over the 2015–2025 period, the country had a positive power trade balance, with net exports averaging about 1.7 TWh per year.11 1 Data provided by Bundesamt für Energie BFE. Cross-border power trading generates significant economic value for Switzerland and for its flexible hydropower capacity in particular, allowing for the optimal utilization of power infrastructure. In addition, international trade strongly supports security of supply. However, considering only the average yearly trade balance provides only a partial picture of the Swiss power system and can be misleading regarding the country’s energy autonomy. When restricting the trade balance to the winter months, the data reveal a different situation. With net winter imports averaging 4.2 TWh, the Confederation relies heavily on the European power market to satisfy domestic electricity demand. At the end of winter, remaining hydropower reserves averaged 1.5 TWh, representing only one third of the required imports and highlighting the crucial importance of access to international electricity markets.

Against this background, this paper evaluates the economic and financial implications of pursuing a policy of full autarky, compared to an open-trade scenario under comparable security-of-supply constraints. To ensure transparent and reproducible results, we rely on simulation models, and, more specifically, the outcomes of a fundamental power market model as the cornerstone of our analysis. Switzerland is a particularly suitable case study for several reasons. First, the country, while being geographically located in the heart of Europe, is not integrated into the European power market or the more efficient Flow-Based Market Coupling system and instead relies on bilateral and multilateral agreements. In other words, Switzerland currently lies in an intermediate and temporary situation. Second, the power landscape of Switzerland, with significant hydropower storage capacity and its lack of sufficient domestic production during the winter months, makes it a particularly compelling case for our research question. Third, the relatively small size of its electricity market compared with those of neighboring countries allows us to abstract from second-order international effects. Finally, reliable benchmarks based on the existing literature are available. Within these environments, we use the CentIv and Cascades models from the Nexus-e framework (Gjorgiev et al., 2022) to simulate the cost-efficient development of generation capacity required to meet demand and the grid expansion within Swiss borders that is needed to achieve satisfactory power system security, respectively. The resulting generation and transmission configurations are then used as inputs to BKW’s fundamental price-forecasting model to simulate wholesale market outcomes. This process yields hourly power demand and prices for both the autarky and trade scenarios in 2040, providing the basis of our economic analysis.

papers.title: BODYinTRANSIT-Lab: A Multimodal Dataset for Investigating Sensory-Driven Transformations in Body Perception and Affective Experiences
papers.abstract: Multimodal datasets that combine synchronised behavioural and physiological signals with subjective affective and body perception measures are still rare. This limits both the understanding of embodied experience and the development of computational models that infer subjective states from sensor data. We introduce BODYinTRANSIT-Lab, a multimodal dataset that addresses this gap by capturing affective, perceptual, and behavioural responses to the Footsteps Illusion. In this closed-loop paradigm, participants perform walking tasks while receiving real-time manipulated auditory feedback of their own footsteps intended to alter perceived body weight. The dataset comprises synchronised recordings from 101 participants recruited through systematic stratification by eating-disorder symptomatology and physical activity level. BODYinTRANSIT-Lab combines full-body kinematics with electromyography, electrocardiography, respiration, and electrodermal activity. Its annotations capture both immediate and post-trial experience, including within-trial perceived-weight ratings, post-trial assessments of body feelings and affective experience, 3D avatar body visualisations, and quantitative body maps. Psychological, behavioural, demographic, and social measures provide further information about factors that may influence individual responses. We provide a deep learning benchmark that uses walking kinematics to classify relative affective valence and perceived weight within subjects. On within-session, segment-level splits, the baseline model achieved mean balanced accuracies of 45.9% for affective valence and 44.5% for perceived weight. The BODYinTRANSIT-Lab dataset provides an experimentally controlled resource for cognitive neuroscience and affective computing research, with potential applications in affect-aware interactive systems, health and well-being technologies, and creative embodied experiences.

papers.intro:
Our perception of our own body shapes how we move, feel, and interact with the world [22]. Because this perception is continuously updated by sensory integration, it can change even when the physical body does not [4, 16]. By deliberately manipulating multisensory feedback, interactive technologies can reshape mental body representations [43, 44, 45, 32, 30] and induce Body Transformation Experiences (BTEs). BTEs involve temporary changes in how individuals perceive their bodies, including appearance, size, weight, ownership, and physical capabilities [64]. These transformations can alter affective experience, cognition, and behaviour, with potential implications for health and well-being [18, 45, 32]. Understanding how these experiences relate to measurable bodily responses, and why those responses differ across individuals, is therefore an important problem for affective computing.

The Footsteps Illusion offers a compelling setting for investigating this relationship during everyday movement. By modifying the frequency spectrum of self-generated footstep sounds in real time, auditory feedback can alter how heavy or light people perceive their bodies to be, alongside changes in emotional state and gait [55]. Walking has a dual role in this paradigm: it generates the sensory feedback that shapes bodily experience, while also providing a behavioural signal through which that experience can be investigated. This action-dependent feedback loop brings body perception, affect and movement into the same experimental setting, making the paradigm particularly suitable for examining how subjective bodily experience relates to measurable behavioural responses [60, 12].

However, the experience elicited by altered bodily feedback cannot be inferred from the manipulation alone. Responses to the Footsteps Illusion vary with body-related beliefs and aspirations, eating-disorder symptomatology, physical activity, and social context [57, 12, 13]. The same feedback may therefore have different perceptual and affective significance for different people. For affective computing, this raises two connected questions: how do self-reported changes in body perception and affect relate to recorded kinematic and physiological signals, and which individual characteristics are associated with variation in these responses? Addressing these questions requires an experimental record that connects the applied feedback, reported experience, movement, physiology, and participant characteristics.

papers.title: MammothDP: Private Boosted Decision Trees Ready for Trusted Hardware and Leakage-free Hyperparameters
papers.abstract: Data spaces like the European Health Data Space (EHDS) require the protection of sensitive data in studies during the data's processing and the study's release alike. In this work, we investigate how to implement this mandate using established trusted execution environments (TEEs) and timing side-channel hardening to protect the processing even under a compromised server, and the state-of-the-art differential privacy (DP) notion to protect the release of studies on tabular data. This combined setup could seem to complete the picture, but in fact raises unexpected security challenges that we mitigate by introducing MammothDP: a significant milestone towards a holistic machine learning system based on the recent gradient boosted decision tree learner S-BDT that is provably DP if used within a privacy filter, timing side-channel hardened, and deployed on a TEE. To achieve a strong privacy-utility tradeoff, we introduce two novel components: an early stopping criterion that adaptively selects the number of trees without any privacy overhead, and an improved rollback protection that is no longer vulnerable under timing side-channel attacks.

papers.title: New Constraints on the Ultrahigh Energy Neutrino Flux from the First Array-Wide Search with the Askaryan Radio Array
papers.abstract: Ultrahigh energy neutrinos ($E_\nu \gtrsim 100$ PeV) are detectable through Askaryan emission---the nanosecond-scale radio impulse emitted by relativistic particle cascades in a dielectric medium. The Askaryan Radio Array (ARA), an Askaryan detector array located at the South Pole, has been taking data for more than a decade. We present the first array-wide search for diffuse ultrahigh energy neutrinos with ARA. The search found no events on an expected background of $0.13\pm0.01\text{ (stat.)}^{+0.05}_{-0.06}\text{ (syst.)}$ events. The resulting upper limit is the most stringent from $50$ EeV to $1000$ EeV and provides the first constraints on the flux reported by the KM3NeT Collaboration that are complementary to optical Cherenkov and particle detectors. This limit also constrains UHECR source models, and excludes some models with trans-GZK proton populations at the $90\%$ confidence level. This represents the largest Askaryan detector dataset ever analyzed, demonstrating the feasibility and sensitivity of searches with large detector arrays acting as a single observatory. It also underscores the high acceptance and exposure of Askaryan detector arrays to ultrahigh energy neutrinos.

papers.title: Analysis Methodology of the Search for Ultrahigh Energy Neutrinos in 10.6 Years of Askaryan Radio Array Data
papers.abstract: The Askaryan Radio Array (ARA) is an in-ice radio observatory at the South Pole designed to detect ultrahigh energy (UHE) neutrinos through Askaryan emission produced by interactions of neutrinos and their secondary particles. In this paper, we present the detailed methodology of the first array-wide search for a diffuse UHE neutrino flux using data from all five ARA stations. The dataset considered represents $10.6$ years of livetime and is three times larger than previous ARA neutrino searches. This search achieves a $28\%$ analysis efficiency for a neutrino flux corresponding to the current experimental upper limits. No neutrino candidates are observed on an expected background of $0.13\pm0.01\text{ (stat.)}^{+0.05}_{-0.06}\text{ (syst.)}$ events. We set a new upper limit on the diffuse UHE neutrino flux, which is the most stringent from $50$ EeV to $1000$ EeV. We also discuss lessons learned for future searches on large radio arrays.

papers.title: Stochastic Discrete Variable Representation: Tensor Network Eigenstates on General Potential Energy Surfaces
papers.abstract: Tensor network states such as tree tensor network states (TTNS) or matrix product states (MPS) allow very compact representations of high-dimensional wave functions. Using them efficiently relies on a compact representation of the Hamiltonian, and many methods are limited to the sum-of-products (SOP) form. General potential energy surfaces (PESs) do not have this form. To overcome this issue, a stochastic discrete variable representation (SDVR) is presented. The matrix elements of the potential operator in the node-local basis are estimated stochastically by importance sampling of grid configurations. The estimator of the matrix elements is unbiased, and the PES is only evaluated pointwise. The variance is reduced by representing parts of the potential with a 2-mode representation and only sampling the remainder. Sampling noise biases the eigenvalues. A noise-control scheme mitigates this bias. Final energies are obtained from an unbiased variational Monte Carlo estimator. The method is demonstrated by calculating vibrational states of CH3 (6D) and acetonitrile (12D), as well as the zero-point vibrational energy of uracil (30D). For all three systems, the energies agree with the exact references to sub-wavenumber accuracy.

Third, collocation[73, 74, 75, 59] requires the Schrödinger equation to hold at a set of points. It needs no matrix elements of the Hamiltonian, and the PES is evaluated exactly at these points.

papers.title: TanCRAFT: Context-Reasoned Anticipatory Feedback for Assembly Tasks
papers.abstract: Preventing human error in physical assembly tasks requires assistance systems that can intervene before mistakes are made. This is especially challenging in settings where users are free to choose the construction order and correctness depends on the evolving assembly rather than a fixed next step. We present TanCRAFT, a four-stage real-time predictive assistance system that tracks the scene state, reasons about the current partial assembly, forecasts the near-future motion of manipulated pieces, and intervenes when the predicted placement is incompatible with the target. We instantiate our framework and confirm its effectiveness in a controlled tangram assembly task through offline benchmarks and a within-subject user study. Our findings show that the predictive feedback significantly reduces mistakes relative to unguided and reactive sessions, while yielding the lowest mean perceived workload and shortest mean completion time. Overall, these results demonstrate the value of predictive feedback for error prevention and provide a step toward cost-aware assistance for automation and human-robot workcells.

papers.intro:
Human error remains a significant contributor to failures and quality defects in manual assembly, industrial production, and human-robot workcells [1, 2, 3]. While some mistakes are easily reversed, others are costly once completed. The cost therefore depends not only on whether errors are detected, but also on when. For example, a misplaced component or unsafe action may be easy to correct before commitment, but costly, time-consuming, or even unsafe after completion. This motivates the need for assistance systems that go beyond post-hoc error detection and are capable of real-time error forecasting and prevention.

Anticipating errors is challenging because systems must infer human actions, intentions, and potential mistakes from external observations. Moreover, anticipation alone is insufficient for assistance, as it does not address how a system should act to prevent the mistake. In this context, previous predictive-assistance methods anticipate supportive robot behaviors or human assembly actions [4, 5]. TRAFA [6] extends prediction to proactive error feedback but operates in a sequential task with a fixed next correct action. Still, many real scenarios, such as kit or furniture assembly, are far less constrained, letting users choose their own strategy, revise placements, and manipulate pieces without committing them. This freedom makes interaction more natural, but error anticipation substantially harder. To address this challenge, we propose TanCRAFT, a real-time predictive assistance framework for non-sequential assembly comprising four stages: Track, Reason, Forecast, and Intervene.

papers.title: The Case for AI-Enabled Gate Monitoring as Farm Security in the UK: A PRISMA-Guided Review of the Evidence on Rural Crime, Livestock Predation and Farm Access
papers.abstract: Farm security in the UK rests on thinner evidence than its cost suggests. We ran a PRISMA guided review: twelve searches of Web of Science and Scopus on 2nd -4th November 2026 returned 1,183 records (761 unique), and grey-literature and hand-searches added 35 assessed sources. We synthesised 96 database records and 24 grey sources narratively. UK peer-reviewed evidence is small (16 records), and the main UK survey of crime and farmer mental health has 80 responses. Cost estimates rest on insurer claims: NFU Mutual put UK rural crime at {\pounds}41.5 million in 2025, with livestock theft up almost 30% to about {\pounds}4.5 million and dog attacks on livestock costing {\pounds}1.95 million. The Home Office states that agricultural crime cannot be separately identified in its central data. We found no independent evaluation of cameras, sensors, trackers or marking; light and sound deterrents lost effect within one to five months in a systematic review of anti-predator interventions; and no study examined how often farm gates are left open or what follows. Camera-trap AI papers report accuracy on ecological datasets, none at a farm gate in the records we found, and in one comparison machine learning detected 41% of wildlife against 81% for analysts. We argue, as an inference from these gaps and not as a demonstrated effect, that continuous gate-level AI-mediated monitoring, as implemented in Fieldmark AI, would be highly beneficial for UK farm security. It would create the farm-level, time-stamped record that no official source holds, verify events that periodic human checks miss, resolve whether foxes, dogs or people were responsible, and give every other security measure something to be tested against. No study has yet shown that it reduces loss, and we set out the evaluation needed to show it.

papers.title: Monochromatic or rainbow triangles in the triangular lattice
papers.abstract: Erd\H{o}s, Graham, Montgomery, Rothschild, Spencer, and Straus conjectured that for each non-equilateral triangle $\operatorname{T}$, every 2-coloring of the plane contains a congruent copy of $\operatorname{T}$ with monochromatic vertex set. We confirm this conjecture for triangles with a ratio $\sqrt{7/3}$ between two side lengths. We further prove that every coloring of the plane, regardless of the number of colors used, contains congruent copies of 36 specific triangles with monochromatic or rainbow vertex sets, partially answering a question of Geh\'er, Sagdeev, and T\'oth. Both these results were obtained by considering finite configurations on the triangular lattice.

papers.title: How Much of Your VLA Is kNN
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models now exceed 95% success on the LIBERO simulation benchmark, yet it remains unclear how much of this performance requires generalization beyond the training demonstrations. In this work, we show that retrieving nearby demonstrations and reusing their action chunks achieves a success rate of 91.7 % on LIBERO without policy training. Under LIBERO-Plus perturbations, retrieval shows the smallest drop of all evaluated policies. Across nine publicly available VLAs, fine-tuning mostly makes the vision-language backbone a better retrieval key, and the actions of the VLAs remain close to the demonstrations. In addition, we introduce Local Action Consistency (LAC), an offline metric that measures whether nearby observations in representation space are also associated with similar future actions. We show that LAC tracks the success rate of retrieval and can guide the training of a retrieval key. Our evaluation and source code are available at https://github.com/sereact/lerobot_knn.

papers.title: Closed-Form Gaussian Information Projection for Embedded Simplices and Simplicial Mixtures
papers.abstract: We study Gaussian approximation of Dirichlet--Gaussian probability density functions on embedded simplices. We derive the unique information projection onto the family of nondegenerate ambient Gaussian probability density functions, obtaining closed-form expressions for the optimal Gaussian and the minimum divergence for arbitrary positive Dirichlet parameters. The minimum divergence depends only on the intrinsic simplex dimension and Dirichlet parameters, is invariant up to an affine isomorphism, independent of the ambient dimension, and independent of the normal covariance. Furthermore, by joint convexity of Kullback--Leibler divergence, we establish explicit intrinsic dimension-dependent sharp upper bounds for finite Gaussian Mixture with shared component weights. For uniform probability density functions, these bounds reduce to dimension-dependent constants. The results provide closed-form Gaussian Mixture constructions and rigorous approximation guarantees for probability density functions associated with embedded simplicial complexes. A numerical example on a circular curve illustrates the theoretical results and their connections to geometric Gaussian Mixture representations.

papers.title: Plumbline: When the Loss Lies, Validating LLM Training Correctly
papers.abstract: Correctness is a prerequisite for training large language models (LLMs) at scale, yet it is hard to ensure: a fault can sit in any part of a run, and how it shows differs across frameworks and the libraries they depend on. Some failures are loud and some are silent, and both take time to detect and trace. A single fault can waste a long run: the run crashes late, or the model scores lower only at the final evaluation. We present Plumbline, a correctness validation system for LLM training, used in production at Amazon. Plumbline checks each part of the training lifecycle, from the data a run trains on to the model it serves, down to the new layers each model brings and up to whole runs. Its diagnosis reuses these checks to trace failures to their root causes. Both rest on a systematic correctness methodology designed to carry across models and frameworks. Plumbline supports two agentic use cases: Day-0 onboarding, which validates the training of a newly released model before teams rely on it, and root-cause tracing of training failures. Across 3 frameworks and 5 models, it found 61 problems, 32 of them silent. Of these, 42 are fixed or reported upstream, 8 of them first raised by us. We further group the 61 into seven failure patterns that show where training breaks, and report how problems recur across frameworks and models.

papers.intro:
Teams that train large language models (LLMs) commonly build on released model checkpoints and open-source training frameworks. Errors in such training can arise in the user’s code and configuration, in the framework, and in the libraries and hardware beneath it Hu et al. (2024); Jiang et al. (2025b). These errors are costly to resolve: on one production platform, diagnosing an escalated training failure took 34.7 hours on average and more than a day in 41.9% of cases Jiang et al. (2025b).

These costs argue for validating training correctness before a long run, instead of discovering errors after a run fails or a trained model underperforms. A fault can sit in any part of a run and need not show in the loss, so we check each part on its own against what correct training produces. Our contributions are: • Plumbline, a correctness validation system for LLM training. Its checks cover a run at three levels: each stage of its lifecycle, from its data to the model it serves; one training step under each supported setting; and whole runs. Its diagnosis reuses the checks at smaller scale, with tools that record what a run did, to trace a failure to its root cause. • A systematic correctness methodology designed to carry across models and frameworks. It follows two principles. Under correctness first, each check tests the training a user would run against a reference not produced by the code under test, under rules fixed per system version, with bounds above measured noise. Under modularity, each check tests one part on its own, so the checks run alone or together as a full scan, and a new model or framework changes how a check connects to it, not what it tests. papers.title: Feedback Vertex Set, Max Cut, and Edge Coloring on the Strong Product of a Graph and a Path
papers.abstract:
We examine the computational complexity of well-known problems on subgraphs of the strong product of two paths. Namely, for Max Cut we show NP-hardness on induced subgraphs of $P \boxtimes P$ answering a question by Dvo\v{r}\'ak, Huynh, Joret, Liu, and Wood (2021). For 3-Edge Coloring we show NP-hardness on subgraphs of $P \boxtimes P$ and that it is equivalent to 3-Edge Coloring on planar graphs for induced subgraphs of $P \boxtimes P$. It is a long standing open question whether 3-Edge Coloring on planar graphs is NP-hard.
  As a second contribution, we consider graphs of the form $G \boxtimes P$ and show that Feedback Vertex Set on these graphs is FPT in the clique-width of $G$. Furthermore, we show that it can be solved in polynomial time if $G$ is chordal or co-comparable and that the computational complexity depends on the parity of $P$ if $G$ is bipartite. Namely, it is solvable in polynomial time if $P$ has an even number of vertices but is NP-complete otherwise. For Max Cut, we show that it can be solved in polynomial time if $G$ is bipartite.

In our most restricted setting, the input is a graph GG and an integer ℓ\ell and the task is to solve the problem on G⊠PℓG\boxtimes P_{\ell}, i.e., the strong product of GG with a path on ℓ\ell vertices. It is not hard to see that for every ℓ≥2\ell\geq 2 the full product G⊠PℓG\boxtimes P_{\ell} admits a proper 33-edge-coloring if and only if G⊠PℓG\boxtimes P_{\ell} has maximum degree at most 33. Thus, the 3-Edge Coloring problem on G⊠PℓG\boxtimes P_{\ell} becomes trivial for every ℓ≥2\ell\geq 2.

papers.title: Constraints on Lorentz Invariance Violation from PeV Gamma Rays of Cygnus X-3 Observed by LHAASO
papers.abstract: The Large High Altitude Air Shower Observatory (LHAASO) has detected photons with energies up to 3.7 PeV from the binary system Cygnus X-3 during a flaring episode. The combination of such extreme photon energies and the large source distance provides a sensitive probe of Lorentz invariance violation (LIV). In superluminal LIV scenarios, high-energy photons can become unstable and rapidly decay, resulting in a sharp spectral cutoff. However, the observed hard intrinsic spectrum of Cygnus X-3 exhibits no evidence for such a feature. This absence enables us to place stringent constraints on LIV, with the second-order LIV energy scale constrained to be above 10^{-2}M_{pl}, improving previous limits by nearly an order of magnitude.

papers.title: Ultra-high-energy cosmic rays require metal-rich sources
papers.abstract: The elemental composition of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) must be evaluated at a given rigidity rather than energy to compare with candidate elemental abundances, such as those of low-energy cosmic rays seeding the acceleration of UHECRs. We determine the UHECR composition from fits to Pierre Auger Observatory data and evaluate the resulting abundances at fixed rigidity. We identify two classes of solutions consistent with measurements above $10^{17.8}$ eV: one in which the hydrogen flux at Earth is dominated by secondary nucleons produced by photodisintegration of heavier nuclei in extragalactic photon fields, and a second in which this contribution is less pronounced. Only the latter, which yields a mixture of primary and secondary protons at Earth, allows a hydrogen abundance at the source comparable to that of low-energy cosmic rays. However, both classes of solutions require an overabundance of nuclei in the silicon-iron group. Other source models from the literature also fail to reproduce the full elemental composition. The metallicity of UHECRs thus differs markedly from that of all candidate seed populations considered, leaving the origin of the heavy-element excess unresolved.

papers.title: The exponent $3/4$ for the exceptional sets of the equations $K/n=1/x+1/y+1/z$
papers.abstract: For $K\ge4$ let $E_K(N)$ be the number of integers $2\le n\le N$ for which $K/n=1/x+1/y+1/z$ has no solution in positive integers; $K=4$ is the Erd\H{o}s-Straus equation. We prove that $E_K(N)\le N\exp(-c((\log N)^3/K)^{1/4})$ with absolute constants $c,B>0$, uniformly for $4\le K\le(\log N)^3/B$. This improves the exponent $2/3$ of Vaughan's bound of 1970. The bound is non-trivial for $K$ up to a constant times $(\log N)^3$, which is, up to a factor $(\log\log N)^{2+o(1)}$, the scale at which, by work of Pomerance and Weingartner, exceptional primes become common. The sieve is combinatorial: a truncated inclusion-exclusion over the classes of parametric solutions, whose second moment is the partition function of a two-copy polymer gas, bounded by a real form of the Koteck\'y-Preiss criterion. Averaging over the residue classes of the small primes gives the family its full mass, and summing each cluster in a random order bounds the cluster sums. Since a divisor of an exception is an exception, nothing about the small primes themselves is needed, and the sieve can use the classes of the whole family of parametric solutions, one triple per class. All constants are explicit, and the whole proof has been checked in the proof assistant Lean 4.

papers.title: Filamentary dynamics in fan-like structures in high-altitude lightning discharges
papers.abstract: We present LOFAR radio telescope measurements revealing that high-altitude negative leaders (HANLs) exhibit behavior completely different from the current paradigm of negative leader propagation. Our data show that the fan at the tip of a propagating HANL is formed by filaments that behave like smoothly advancing negative leaders. These negative leader filaments appear to have moderate conductivity, remain thin (radius $\sim1$ m), grow continuously at $\sim10^5$ m/s over hundreds of meters, and emit VHF radiation persistently. The observations show that the filaments making up the fan in front of a propagating negative leader are not necessarily streamers, as commonly assumed. Previous work suggesting to observe streamers at the tips of negative leaders should be re-examined in light of these new findings

papers.title: Elastic-WAM: Adaptive Spatiotemporal Imagination for Efficient Robot Control
papers.abstract: World-Action Models improve robot control by predicting future visual dynamics, but iterative video denoising incurs substantial inference overhead. Recent approaches reduce this cost through partial future denoising, yet typically rely on fixed refinement budgets. Our empirical observations reveal that preferred refinement depths vary across tasks and states, while different future regions exhibit varying relevance to action generation. Motivated by these findings, we propose Elastic-WAM, which adaptively allocates world refinement computation across temporal denoising time and spatial future space. A unified spatiotemporal refinement demand field governs when to stop world refinement, how far to advance each denoising step, and which regions to refresh. We parameterize this field with a shared temporal basis and spatial amplitudes, and learn it through a three-stage action-grounded supervised procedure. At inference, the learned field guides recurrent sparse world refinement to improve task success while reducing inference overhead. Evaluations across diverse simulation benchmarks and real-world long-horizon manipulation demonstrate state-of-the-art control performance with reduced inference latency.

World-Action Models (WAMs) have shown that predicting future visual dynamics can improve robot control [37, 3, 1, 31, 9]. However, iterative denoising of future videos incurs substantial inference overhead [2, 20]. Recent studies show that intermediate video representations can already support action prediction without complete denoising [25, 24, 19]. Explicit video generation can even be removed at inference while retaining future prediction as a training objective [40]. Nevertheless, these approaches typically adopt a fixed future refinement budget, regardless of the current task or execution state [13, 10]. Consequently, a fixed budget may waste computation in some states while limiting action quality in others [30].

Even within the same task, different states favor different refinement depths, as shown in Fig. (a.2). Beyond refinement depth, action-to-video attention maps reveal uneven attention across future video regions (shown in Fig. (a.3)), motivating selective refinement of regions most relevant to action generation [38]. Together, these observations motivate adaptive allocation of world refinement computation across both temporal denoising time and spatial future video regions.

papers.title: Characterizing Fixed-Treewidth Planar Graphs
papers.abstract: We give the first inductive characterization of planar graphs of treewidth $k$ for each $k \geq 3$. Our definition generalizes the well-known inductive definition of planar $3$-trees and the recent definition of so-called planar quasi-$4$-trees [F\"orster, 2024]. As a key step, which may be of independent interest, we show that every planar triangulation $G$ of treewidth $k$ admits a tree decomposition of width $k$ where each adhesion set induces a cycle in $G$. As an application of planar quasi-$4$-trees, we show that planar graphs of treewidth at most $4$ have vertex arboricity at most $2$. That is, the vertex-set of every planar graph of treewidth at most $4$ can be partitioned into two sets that each induce a forest.

papers.intro:
Undoubtedly, treewidth is one of the most important parameters in algorithmic and structural graph theory. Numerous investigations are concerned with graphs of small treewidth and their combinatorial properties. The treewidth of a graph can be defined in several, seemingly different ways, e. g., via tree decompositions, chordal completions, clique-sums, or a variant of the cops-and-robber game (see for example this survey [5]). A very simple and accessible definition involves the edge-maximal graphs of treewidth kk, so-called kk-trees, which are defined starting with Kk+1K_{k+1}, and inductively adding a new vertex connected to exactly the vertices of some kk-clique of the so-far constructed graph.

Planar graphs form a second central pillar of graph theory, both from a theoretical and practical point of view. While a planar graph can have arbitrarily large treewidth, a widespread and worthwhile approach is to consider planar graphs of small treewidth. As all graphs of treewidth at most 22 are planar, the combination of planarity and small treewidth becomes interesting starting with treewidth 33. In fact, planar graphs of treewidth at most 33 are well understood. These are exactly the subgraphs of planar 33-trees also known as stacked triangulations or Apollonian networks [28, 34]. In particular it is well known that every planar 33-tree can be obtained by starting with a triangle and then repeatedly adding a vertex to an inner face and connecting it to the vertices incident to the face (see for example [4]).

Since then, it was shown that various subclasses of planar graphs have vertex arboricity at most 22, such as triangle-free planar graphs [16], planar graphs without 44-cycles [35], and planar graphs of degeneracy at most 33 [12], which include planar 3-trees. For general planar graphs, however, Chartrand and Kronk [15] show that 33 is indeed tight by showing that the dual of the Tutte graph [39] has vertex arboricity 33. Since the dual of the Tutte graph has treewidth 55, this leaves the question open whether planar graphs of treewidth at most 44 have vertex arboricity at most 22. We utilize planar quasi-44-trees to show that this is indeed the case.

papers.title: Revealing Hidden Excitation in the Core of NGC 4696: New Infrared Diagnostic Diagrams with JWST
papers.abstract: The warm molecular and ionized gas in filamentary nebulae of cool-core BCGs provide a sensitive probe of the poorly understood exchange of energy between the ICM, cold molecular gas, and AGN feedback. Optical line ratios commonly yield similar LINER-like classifications across these systems, but do not resolve how the excitation of warm molecular gas varies between compact nuclear structures and surrounding filaments. We present JWST/NIRSpec integral-field spectroscopy of the central $3''\times3''$ ($620\times620~{\rm pc^2}$) of the Centaurus cluster BCG, NGC~4696. The NIR data resolve H$I$ and ro-vibrational H$_2$ emission across compact nuclear apertures, a circumnuclear swirl, and filamentary structures. H$_2$ excitation diagrams yield characteristic low-excitation temperatures of $T_{\rm ex}\simeq1.8-2.2\times10^3$~K, while curvature at higher energies requires hotter or non-thermal components. The H$_2$/Pa$\alpha$ balance varies strongly: filamentary regions have H$_2$ 1-0 S(1)/Pa$\alpha$ ratios 4-8 times higher than the compact nuclear apertures. In contrast, matched-aperture optical diagnostic diagrams show substantially less regional separation, with all regions occupying a low-ionization locus. We thus introduce new spatially resolved NIR diagnostic diagrams that reveal distinct molecular excitation conditions across the nucleus, swirl, and filaments. Ratios are broadly consistent with contributions from AGN-related photoionization, ICM-related cooling radiation, and non-radiative heating, although the present data do not uniquely determine their relative importance. These results demonstrate how spatially resolved NIR spectroscopy reveals excitation variations hidden in conventional optical classifications, providing a new route to constrain the multiphase cooling-feedback cycle in cluster cores.

papers.intro:
Understanding how the most massive galaxies nurture, disrupt, or recycle their gas is crucial to understanding galaxy formation and evolution. Brightest cluster galaxies (BCGs) are the most luminous galaxies in their host clusters and reside near the minima of the cluster gravitational potentials, where they interact strongly with the surrounding intracluster medium (ICM) through processes dominated by active galactic nucleus (AGN) feedback [36, 68]. The hot, X-ray-emitting ICM loses energy via radiation and should, in theory, cool rapidly, leading to massive star formation in cluster cores. However, mechanical energy released by the central supermassive black hole in the form of jets heats the ICM, inflating cavities and driving processes such as turbulence, shock waves and sound waves that inhibit runaway cooling [68, 41, e.g.]. This feedback loop is thought to be self-regulating, with cold gas condensing from the ICM via thermal instabilities and raining back onto the AGN to fuel its continued activity, maintaining balance on kiloparsec to sub-parsec scales [99, 95]. Metals produced by star formation and stellar evolution enrich the ICM, and their distribution is then reshaped by large-scale motions such as bulk sloshing and uplift, which move gas away from the centre, form eddies and filamentary structures, and promote dust grain formation and energy redistribution in cluster cores [15, 75, 95, 42, e.g.].

Their coherent morphologies often closely trace radio bubbles and X-ray cavities, and individual filaments can exhibit ordered kinematics along their lengths. Magnetic tension and magnetic draping may therefore play an important role in supporting filaments and enabling their survival within the hot ICM [32]. Although cool-core BCG filaments can contain substantial cold-gas masses, star formation is often spatially offset from both the densest molecular gas and the brightest line-emitting structures. In many cool-core BCGs, low-ionization, LINER-like optical spectra and strong molecular emission cannot be explained by pure stellar H ii-region photoionization alone [47, 27, 25, 45, 72, e.g.,]. papers.title: Beyond the Fast Rotators: A JWST Multi-Cycle Treasury Survey of Substellar Weather
papers.abstract: Atmospheric variability provides a unique window into the three-dimensional structure, dynamics, and evolution of brown dwarf and giant exoplanet atmospheres. Recent JWST time-resolved spectroscopic observations have revealed complex wavelength-dependent variability, offering unprecedented insights into cloud structures, thermal perturbations, and atmospheric chemistry. However, existing programs have focused primarily on individual benchmarks and specific scientific questions, resulting in heterogeneous spectral and temporal coverage and leaving important regions of the substellar population underexplored, particularly across a broad range of rotation periods, spectral types, and viewing geometries. A JWST Multi-Cycle Treasury program could systematically investigate substellar weather across a diverse, well-characterized population. By combining broad infrared spectroscopic coverage with observations spanning multiple rotations and strategically selected epochs, this program would constrain the contributions of different physical mechanisms while investigating how atmospheric structures depend on rotation, viewing geometry, and fundamental physical properties. Extended monitoring would also improve rotational-period determinations and reveal how atmospheric features evolve from rotation to rotation and over longer timescales. This coordinated effort would provide a consistently designed and uniformly processed dataset of time-resolved spectra and variability diagnostics, enabling population-level comparisons, testing predictions from three-dimensional circulation models, and establishing a framework for interpreting the atmospheric diversity and evolution of brown dwarfs and directly imaged giant exoplanets.
papers.intro:
Atmospheric dynamics shape the observed properties of planetary atmospheres, as illustrated by the evolving cloud bands, storms, and vortices of Solar System gas giants [36, 34]. Brown dwarfs provide an opportunity to investigate analogous processes beyond the Solar System, across a much broader range of temperatures, gravities, and rotational regimes. However, unlike Solar System planets, their atmospheres remain spatially unresolved, making time-resolved observations essential for probing their three-dimensional structure and evolution. Over the past decades, photometric and spectroscopic surveys have established atmospheric variability as a widespread phenomenon among brown dwarfs (e.g., [17, 33, 8, 27, 42]). Ground-based monitoring, HST, and Spitzer have revealed diverse variability amplitudes, rotation periods, and evolving light-curve morphologies, while JWST now enables their characterization across a much broader infrared wavelength range, probing a wider range of atmospheric pressures.
