Despite these advances, our understanding of the physical mechanisms driving substellar variability remains incomplete. Heterogeneous condensate clouds are commonly invoked to explain rotationally modulated brightness variations ([5, 25, 4]), while thermal perturbations, atmospheric circulation, and thermochemical disequilibrium may also contribute ([41, 21, 26, 30]). Recent JWST observations have begun to reveal wavelength- and molecule-dependent variability that cloud heterogeneity alone cannot always explain, highlighting the complexity of the underlying atmospheric processes [6, 26, 11, 30, 28, 29, 35].

A comprehensive understanding of substellar weather requires moving beyond individual benchmark objects and limited observational configurations. The diversity of rotation periods, viewing geometries, atmospheric properties, and light-curve morphologies raises fundamental questions about how atmospheric structures form, evolve, and manifest in time-resolved observations. Addressing these questions requires a coordinated observational framework that samples a broader range of physical parameters, combines complementary atmospheric diagnostics, and characterizes variability over appropriate temporal baselines. A JWST Multi-Cycle Treasury program envisions a total of order 1,500 hours, sampling spectral type (L, T, Y), rotation (2-22 hr, [40]), and viewing geometry (close to pole-on or equator objects), with repeated multi-rotation observations of selected targets across cycles to study the weather and climate of substellar objects.

papers.title: A TESS Disappearing Act: The Vanishing Transits of TOI-2535 b
papers.abstract: Planetary transits require a fortuitous alignment between a planet's orbit and our line of sight, but dynamical interactions can render this geometric coincidence only temporary. We report the discovery of the hot Jupiter TOI-2535 b, the first confirmed planet orbiting a single star whose transits have been directly observed to disappear. Over seven years of photometry from NASA's Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS), the planet's transit chord traversed and eventually moved off the stellar disk entirely, with an impact parameter changing at the rate of $\dot{b} = 0.16\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$. The transit mid-times also show significant departures of $\pm 6$ hours from a linear ephemeris. Joint modeling of the transit timing and duration variations (TTVs and TDVs) and NEID radial-velocity data indicates the presence of a nearby, mutually inclined ($i_\mathrm{mut} \gtrsim 5^\circ$) planetary perturber, with the TDV being primarily due to precession of the planets' orbital planes. Our dynamical modeling reveals that the perturber is likely of Saturn-mass or greater and in a mean-motion resonance with TOI-2535 b, making this an unusual system that contains two short-period giant planets. The TDVs measured for TOI-2535 b represent one of the most extreme examples of planet-planet interactions driving orbital evolution on human timescales.

papers.intro:
In multi-planet systems, time-varying gravitational interactions between planets drive changes in the planets’ orbital elements. For planets that transit their host stars, these deviations from a Keplerian orbit can be detected through changes in the transit mid-times (transit timing variations; TTVs) or shapes (transit duration variations; TDVs). For a review of TTVs and TDVs, see [1]. Because a planet is only observed to transit when its orbit normal is within a few degrees of the sky plane, even small changes in a planet’s orbital inclination can result in measurable changes in its transit shape. For sufficiently large inclination changes, a planet may only have the correct transit geometry for a fraction of its dynamical evolution; if the variation is fast enough and we are lucky to catch the planet in the right phase of its inclination evolution, we may see its transits appear or disappear.

Circumbinary planets frequently exhibit rapid changes in their transit impact parameters [31, 95, 57, e.g.,], because the planet’s orbit normal is precessing around the stellar binary’s orbit normal, and because the stars themselves present a “moving target” for the planetary transit. As a result, even a small misalignment between the two orbits leads to intervals when the planet may transit both, one, or neither of its host stars.

In this Letter, we present the discovery of TOI-2535 b, a hot Jupiter with an orbital period of Porb=8.236P_{\mathrm{orb}}=8.236 days that is the first planet directly observed to have ceased transiting. Transits observed from TESS and with telescopes on the ground reveal that the planet’s orbital inclination has changed so rapidly that the transit chord has likely traversed more than half the stellar disk, crossing the stellar equator before progressing to a grazing and finally non-transiting configuration, over the seven year observing baseline. The transit mid-times also deviate significantly from a linear ephemeris, with TTVs of ±\pm6 hours, some of the largest ever seen for a short-period giant planet. These transit variations indicate that TOI-2535 b is in or near a mean-motion resonance with an inclined planetary companion, making it an unusual system both in containing a hot Jupiter with a nearby planet, as well as in having two closely separated planets with significant mutual inclinations.

papers.abstract: Transit timing variations are a powerful method for detecting non-transiting planets, particularly in systems near mean-motion resonances. We investigate the ultra-short-period hot Jupiter TOI-2109 b using 87 transit epochs spanning two decades (2006-2025), combining observations from TESS, CHEOPS, HST, and ground-based photometry. We compare five timing models representing different physical scenarios: a linear ephemeris, orbital decay, apsidal precession, a sinusoidal model, and a two-planet n-body dynamical model. The orbital-decay fit yields $\dot{P} = -3.96 \pm 2.05$ ms yr$^{-1}$, providing no significant evidence for ongoing orbital decay. The sinusoidal model reveals a periodic transit-timing-variation signal with an amplitude of $\approx 44\,s$. Dynamical modelling favours an additional non-transiting companion near the 7:3 mean-motion resonance with an orbital period of $1.57813\pm 8.9\times10^{-5}$ days and a mass of $0.70 \pm 0.02\,M_{\rm Jup}$. The two-planet model yields $\Delta \mathrm{BIC}=4.95$ relative to the sinusoidal model, indicating positive evidence that the observed transit timing variations are best explained by gravitational perturbations from an additional planet.

In multi-planet systems, mean-motion resonances (MMRs), in which the orbital periods of two planets follow a simple integer ratio, play a key role in determining long-term orbital stability and driving TTVs. papers.title: CIALLO: Learning Shared Intent Representations for Cross-Embodiment Manipulation
papers.abstract: Robot demonstrations contain reusable manipulation knowledge, but transferring this knowledge across embodiments requires representations that bridge differences in control interfaces. Action reconstruction alone does not ensure that similar behaviors across robots share a representation. To address this gap, we introduce CIALLO, an action codec that aligns actions, visual changes, and observation-grounded language in a shared space of short-horizon behavioral intent. An embodiment-conditioned decoder maps this intent back to robot-specific actions, allowing a shared representation to support different control interfaces. After pretraining on eight embodiments, CIALLO adapts to a new robot from one recording of at most 10 seconds by updating only its embodiment embeddings. The calibrated codec then remains frozen while a policy learns to predict intent from observations and instructions. We instantiate this policy with Qwen3.5-4B to form Qwen-CIALLO, whose backbone requires no large-scale robot-action pretraining before policy finetuning. With 20 demonstrations per task, Qwen-CIALLO achieves 76.7\% average success across real SO-101 and single-arm Piper robots, compared with 70.0\% for fully finetuned $\pi_0$. In simulation, we additionally finetune the action decoder, achieving 97.3\% success on LIBERO and 52.7\% on RoboTwin 2.0. The LIBERO policy also achieves 80.8\% on LIBERO-Plus without further finetuning. Together, these results support a shared action codec as a transferable control interface that separates embodiment calibration from task learning.

A grasp demonstrated by one robot can teach another what to reach for and how an object should move, even when their joint coordinates and control rates differ. Cross-embodiment learning seeks to reuse experience from existing robots to provide control knowledge for a new body [32, 14, 27]. Pretrained vision-language models supply broad semantic knowledge [22, 2], but grounding that knowledge in an unfamiliar action interface still requires substantial amounts of robot demonstration data. A reusable action codec could make these demonstrations more useful for task learning by reducing the need to adapt the underlying control representation.

Similar motions can be expressed as end effector displacements or joint angles, with different dimensions, numbers of arms, and temporal resolutions. Shared action layouts and embodiment-specific modules allow policies to consume heterogeneous data [14, 27, 46]. Yet action reconstruction alone, even with embodiment-conditioned encoding and decoding, does not require similar behaviors across robots to have similar representations. Visual changes and grounded language connect different control sequences that produce similar visual effects or serve compatible task goals. We therefore align action representations through these shared cues to learn a codec that transfers across embodiments with only brief calibration.

CIALLO separates a shared representation of short-horizon behavior, intent, from the body and control schema used to realize it. Building on latent action learning and action–vision alignment [49, 5, 52, 6], CIALLO aligns actions, visual changes, and observation-grounded language in one space. The visual and text branches anchor actions to their effects and task context, encouraging nearby representations for compatible behaviors across embodiments. papers.title: Finite Numerical Joyce Transport and Derived Hall Scattering Groupoid
papers.abstract: Let $\mathcal{D}$ be a triangulated category over a finite field $k$ satisftying certain finiteness conditions. Let $\Sigma$ be a connected component of the space of numerical stability conditions on $\mathcal{D}$ with one element $\sigma\in\Sigma$ satisfying the support property and the finite counting condition. We prove that each of the Joyce elements with respect to $\sigma_1\in\Sigma$ is a finite rational Lie polynomial in those of any other $\sigma_0\in\Sigma$, so the generated Lie subalgebra $\mathfrak{L}_\sigma,\sigma\in\Sigma$ in the uncompleted derived Hall algebra $\mathcal{H}(\mathcal{D})$ is constant on $\Sigma$. Our proof combines completions on strict sectors with a uniform mass bound for successive local substitutions. We use the method of Hall scattering diagrams on phase categories to provide a realization of the transform of Joyce elements. For the finite-length case, we also give an alternative proof using finite-length hearts instead of phase categories. As an application, we explicit the generators of the Lie subalgebra $\mathfrak{L}$ in the Dynkin case.

papers.title: Inertial swarmalators with finite-range coupling in two dimensions
papers.abstract: We study swarmalators with inertia and finite-range coupling in two dimensions. For attractive phase coupling an energy function forbids sustained motion; for repulsive coupling every steady state obeys an exact sum rule. When position and phase share a mass $m$, a mode is destabilized by inertia if and only if $\Re s>-m(\Im s)^2$, where $s$ is its overdamped eigenvalue; this yields the Hopf boundary of the one-dimensional inertial swarmalator in closed form, with an exceptional point as its large-mass limit. In two dimensions, uniform phase waves are transversely unstable and break into filaments. Inertia sets filaments that are stable without it into motion through a supercritical Hopf bifurcation, a two-dimensional analog of the one-dimensional thrashing wave, while a separate, irregularly moving state coexists with the static filament below threshold. Simulations show a moving filament network carrying an extensive population of $\pm1$ phase defects.

papers.intro:
Swarmalators are mobile oscillators whose positions and phases are coupled in both directions [1, 2, 3]. They generalize earlier models of mobile oscillators, in which motion affects synchronization but not the reverse [4, 5], and of chemotactic oscillators, in which the coupling acts both ways [6, 7]. Swarmalator behavior has been identified in a wide range of systems. In biology, Japanese tree frogs adjust their calling and their spatial arrangement together in choruses [8]. Vinegar eels (Turbatrix aceti) synchronize their body undulations in dense swarms at the edge of a drop, where the resulting metachronal waves drive fluid circulation [9, 10]. Sperm cells self-organize into vortex arrays through hydrodynamic entrainment [11], and spinning starfish embryos assemble into living chiral crystals [12]. Physical realizations are equally varied. Magnetic Janus colloids under a rotating field link the synchronization of their rotations to self-assembly [13]. Coupled magnetic domain walls move faster when their precessions synchronize, and the authors of that study interpret them as swarmalators [14]. Chemical micromotors synchronize spontaneously while they move [15], and synchronization has been found in collectively moving inanimate and living active matter alike [16]. Magnetically actuated microrobot collectives switch between reconfigurable collective states [17]. Feedback-controlled colloids realize tunable swarmalators whose coupling is hydrodynamic and therefore decays with distance [18]. Small robots and drones have been programmed to sync and swarm, with reciprocal or non-reciprocal couplings [19, 20].

Two features recur across these platforms. Their interactions are short-ranged, being hydrodynamic, steric or limited by line of sight. In macroscopic realizations such as robots, drones and vibrated granular particles, momentum is moreover not negligible [21, 22]. Most swarmalator theory nevertheless assumes all-to-all coupling and overdamped motion. Within that setting the original 2D model and its extensions show ring and splintered states [1, 23], active phase waves [24], chiral and non-uniform behavior [25], and the effects of thermal noise [26], delays [27] and non-reciprocal coupling [28, 29]; swarmalators have also been studied in three and higher dimensions [30, 31, 32]. Much of the analytic progress has come from simplified models: the one-dimensional (1D) ring model [33, 34, 35, 36, 37], its normal-form derivation from chemotactic oscillators [38, 6], and a two-dimensional (2D) model on a periodic plane in which the dynamics separates into coupled Kuramoto models [39].

Two physical ingredients have been studied only separately and only in 1D. The first is inertia. O’Keeffe recently showed that adding a mass to the 1D ring model leaves the synchronization and desynchronization thresholds unchanged, but turns the static phase wave into an unsteady “thrashing” wave through a subcritical Hopf bifurcation [40]. This parallels the role of inertia in the Kuramoto model, where it produces hysteresis and discontinuous transitions [41, 42, 43]. In the 1D swarmalator model every overdamped attractor is static, so the unsteadiness there is produced by inertia alone. The study is confined to one spatial dimension, and it closes by suggesting that the model be explored in two or three dimensions [40]. To our knowledge, whether inertia produces analogous unsteady states in higher-dimensional swarmalator models has not been examined: the recent review of the field discusses inertia only for Kuramoto oscillators [2], and the studies of swarmalators in two and more dimensions cited above do not include it. The second is finite interaction range. Sar, O’Keeffe and Ghosh tuned the coupling range of the 1D model and found multiple “sync dots”, higher-winding waves and an unsteady state at short range [44]. In 2D, a finite cutoff has been imposed on the spatial interaction only [45], and a short-range repulsion added to otherwise global couplings produces oscillatory states [46]; in both cases the phase coupling remains global. Finite-range rules in both channels have been combined with self-propelled, run-and-tumble disks, where they produce gel, labyrinth and frustrated phase-separated states [47] and modify ratchet transport on asymmetric substrates [48]; there the motion is driven by self-propulsion, whereas in our model it is generated by the couplings alone. Distance-independent topological coupling in 2D produces local vortices [49], and winding numbers have been used to classify transitions in 2D swarmalator systems [50].

(ii) The positional and phase dynamics follow from one pair potential, with mobilities J′J^{\prime} and K′K^{\prime} that may have either sign. (iii) Position and phase carry the same mass mm. Figure 1 previews the collective states the model produces: static clusters for attractive phase coupling, and for repulsive coupling a persistently moving network of phase-wave filaments that gives way to a phase-disordered liquid as the repulsion grows. Feature (ii) is shared by the 1D ring model [33, 40], so several of our exact results apply to it as well.

This lets us answer, for a two-dimensional model, the question raised by the 1D study. Three features of the 1D picture do not carry over. First, the local bifurcation is supercritical rather than subcritical; the hysteresis comes from a separate, irregularly moving state that coexists with the static filament below the threshold. Second, the 1D static wave itself has no stable 2D analog, because a uniform phase wave in the plane breaks up into filaments for every mass. Third, with finite-range repulsive phase coupling the overdamped system is already persistently active, so that in the bulk inertia reshapes the unsteady state rather than creating it. Our model extends the gradient structure of the ring model to the plane. It is not the solvable 2D model of Ref. [39] to which Ref. [40] points, and the inertial dynamics of that model remain open.

papers.title: Anosov representations from cyclic Higgs bundles
papers.abstract: For every complex simple Lie group G (not of type $E_8$) we construct the minimal Slodowy slice, which is a half-dimensional slice in the character variety of a closed surface group into G, containing the composition of Fuchsian representations with the minimal representation of $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ in G and invariant under the mapping class group action. This slice is defined via cyclic Higgs bundles, and we show that when G is not of type $E_8$, the corresponding representations are Anosov, so in particular discrete and faithful, and dominate some Fuchsian representation. For each of these Higgs bundles, we consider the equivariant harmonic map to the symmetric space, and we show it is an embedding and a quasi-isometric embedding with regard to the induced metric. From the cyclicity of these Higgs bundles we are also able to construct an auxiliary harmonic map to a pseudoriemannian symmetric space $G/G^\sigma$ which is also an embedding. Our techniques also apply to harmonic Higgs bundles over the unit disk satisfying a certain completeness condition. These techniques also apply to two other families of cyclic Higgs bundles.

papers.intro:
The non-Abelian Hodge correspondence defines a bijection between geometric objects, which are representations of surface groups into a complex Lie group GG, and algebraic objects, which are GG-Higgs bundles over a Riemann surface. This correspondence is realized in one direction by constructing equivariant harmonic maps and on the other direction by resolving a PDE called Hitchin’s equation. In particular, this correspondence does not translate every property of a Higgs bundle well to its associated representation.

papers.title: Complexity of Deciding Existence of Maltsev Polymorphisms of Finite Relational Structures
papers.abstract: In this article, we show that the problem of deciding whether a finite relational structure $\mathbf{A}$ admits a Maltsev polymorphism is a computational problem, which can be solved in polynomial time. We provide a proof of this result by reducing the problem to deciding whether a binary relational structure, associated with $\mathbf{A}$ admits such a polymorphism. In our construction of such an algorithm, we make an extensive use of a property of binary relations, which is implied by the existence of a Maltsev polymorphism, the so-called rectangularity property.

papers.intro:
It was shown in [5] that deciding if a relational structure admits any of the following polymorphism is NP-complete; a semilattice polymorphism, a conservative semilattice polymorphism, a commutative semigroup polymorphism. Relational structures and digraphs with majority/ near unanimity polymorphism have studied in [2], [5], [9], [11], [13], and [14]. However, deciding whether a relational structure 𝐀\mathbf{A} admit a Maltsev polymorphism seemed to be a more challenging problem. On the algebraic side, the complexity of deciding whether an idempotent algebra has Maltsev term has been investigated ([10], [12], [15], [17]). However, a polynomial procedure to recognize whether, given as its input relational structure, that structure has a Maltsev polymorphism remained unknown. Establishing the presence of Maltsev polymorphisms would, for instance show that any instance of the constraint satisfaction problem having as 𝐀\mathbf{A} as its template, is solvable in polynomial time (see [3]).

In particular, we do not work under the so-called “promise of a Maltsev operation.” As will become clear in the paper, the key ingredient in the construction of the said algorithm is the rectangularity property of the product of two Maltsev algebras. The failure of rectangularity will immediately preclude the existence of a Maltsev polymorphism of 𝐀\mathbf{A} and this property can be verified in deterministic logarithmic space in n=|A|n=|A|.

papers.title: $G_2'$-Slodowy Slices II: Anosov Representations
papers.abstract: We find \emph{exotic} connected components of Anosov representations of surface groups in the higher rank group $G=G_2'$ that are neither $\iota$-Fuchsian deformations nor higher rank Teichm\"uller spaces. These representations are found through the non-abelian Hodge correspondence via $G_2'$-Higgs bundles that we call \emph{$\alpha$-bundles} and \emph{$\beta$-bundles}, which are particular cyclic Higgs bundles in the Slodowy slices of the $\mathfrak{sl}_2$-triples associated to the simple roots $\alpha$ and $\beta$ of $\mathfrak{g}_2^{\mathbb{C}}$. We first prove that (most) $\beta$-bundles that are also Hodge bundles are $P_{\beta}$-Anosov and $\alpha$-bundles are $P_{\alpha}$-Anosov. The strategy employed is new, geometric, and general. For $\sigma \in \{\alpha, \beta\}$, we then show the locally homogeneous $(G_2', G_2'/P_{\sigma})$-manifold ${\mathscr{M}}_{\sigma}(\rho)$ recently described in arXiv:2510.12757, for the representation $\rho:\pi_1S\rightarrow G_2'$ associated to a $\sigma$-bundle, coincides up to finite cover with the corresponding geometric structure for $\rho$ defined via domains of discontinuity by Guichard-Wienhard and Kapovich-Leeb-Porti. Consequently, we find that $\pi_1({\mathscr{M}}_{\sigma}(\rho))$ is an invariant for the connected component of $\rho$ in the space of $P_{\sigma}$-Anosov representations. After verifying the folklore result that the $G_2'$-character variety has exactly three connected components, we conclude lower bounds for the number of connected components of $P_{\sigma}$-Anosov representations in the two non-Hitchin components, most of which are exotic.

papers.title: A Virgo Environmental Survey Tracing Ionised Gas Emission (VESTIGE). XXIII. NGC 4569 past orbit reconstruction with ORFEO
papers.abstract: Extended ionised gas tails can preserve a dynamical record of a galaxy's recent interaction with the intracluster medium (ICM). Recovering that history from the observed tail requires solving an inverse dynamical problem tied to the physical conditions for gas removal. We present the first application of ORFEO to NGC 4569, using the sky positions and line-of-sight (LOS) velocities of the galaxy and 94 H$\alpha$-emitting regions to reconstruct its recent orbit and tail chronology. The model combines data with gas surface-density constraints, a spherical Virgo Cluster A gravitational potential derived with MG-MAMPOSSt, and an X-ray-based ICM density profile. For an assumed LOS distance, it infers its orbit and ram-pressure history. At the fiducial distance $d_0=16.5$ Mpc, ORFEO recovers a coherent phase-space sequence with a dynamical tail age $T_{\rm tail}=250^{+37}_{-19}$ Myr. The ram-pressure maximum occurred at $t_{P_{\rm ram},{\rm peak}}=-163^{+11}_{-15}$ Myr, close to the nearest approach to the Virgo Cluster A centre at $305^{+19}_{-25}$ kpc, placing NGC 4569 after peak ram pressure. Scanning the LOS distance does not select a unique solution but separates comparably fitting reconstructions into a low-distance post-peak branch and a high-distance pre-peak branch. Comparison with an independent stripping threshold at the observed disc truncation radius favours the low-distance solutions and supports a post-stripping interpretation. On this branch, ORFEO recovers the mostly west-to-east projected motion inferred from the H$\alpha$ morphology and is consistent with previous constraints on the interaction chronology. Requiring only $\sim10$--11 min of wall-clock time for NGC 4569, ORFEO provides a computationally inexpensive inverse framework for deriving orbital, tail, and ram-pressure histories that can guide tailored simulations and be extended to larger samples of stripped galaxies.

papers.intro:
Galaxies in dense environments differ systematically from their field counterparts. Dense environments contain a higher fraction of early-type galaxies (Dressler 1980), while cluster spirals have lower atomic gas content (Haynes & Giovanelli 1984; Cayatte et al. 1990; Solanes et al. 2001; Gavazzi et al. 2005); H i-deficient systems can also show reduced molecular-gas reservoirs (Fumagalli et al. 2009; Boselli et al. 2014b) and star-formation activity (Kennicutt 1983; Gavazzi et al. 1998; Lewis et al. 2002; Gómez et al. 2003; Boselli et al. 2014c). These trends demonstrate the important role of environment in regulating galaxy evolution (Peng et al. 2010, see e.g.), but the present-day state of a galaxy does not by itself identify the physical process or interaction history that produced it.

These trends demonstrate the important role of environment in regulating galaxy evolution (Peng et al. 2010, see e.g.), but the present-day state of a galaxy does not by itself identify the physical process or interaction history that produced it.

Several mechanisms can drive this transformation (Boselli & Gavazzi 2006; Boselli & Gavazzi 2014; Cortese et al. 2021, see reviews by), and their different physical action gives rise to different characteristic timescales. Gravitational interactions with nearby galaxies and with the global cluster potential can perturb both the stellar and gaseous components (Merritt 1983; Byrd & Valtonen 1990; Moore et al. 1998); repeated high-speed encounters in particular can produce cumulative transformations over several Gyr (Moore et al. 1998; Boselli & Gavazzi 2006). Starvation instead suppresses the replenishment of the cold interstellar medium (Larson et al. 1980), so star formation declines gradually as the existing gas reservoir is consumed over several Gyr (Boselli et al. 2006; Boselli et al. 2014c). Ram-pressure stripping (RPS), by contrast, acts directly on the interstellar medium when the pressure exerted by the intracluster medium (ICM) overcomes the gravitational restoring force of the galaxy (Gunn & Gott 1972; Boselli et al. 2022), and can remove gas on sub-Gyr timescales, producing truncated star-forming discs and extended gaseous tails (Koopmann & Kenney 2004; Boselli et al. 2006; Crowl & Kenney 2008; Cortese et al. 2012; Boselli et al. 2014c; Boselli et al. 2016b; Fossati et al. 2018; Boselli et al. 2022; Boselli et al. 2023b). The timing and effectiveness of environmental processing also depend on the accretion history and orbit of a galaxy. Environmental effects can begin before cluster infall, through pre-processing in groups (McGee et al. 2009; De Lucia et al. 2012; Fossati et al. 2019) or suppression of gas replenishment in the cluster outskirts (Bahé et al. 2013; Ayromlou et al. 2021), and continue after cluster entry through interactions with other galaxies and with the global cluster potential. RPS is particularly tied to the galaxy trajectory: it becomes more effective where the galaxy encounters denser ICM and high relative velocities, and therefore changes in strength and timing as these conditions vary along the orbit (Gunn & Gott 1972; Boselli et al. 2022).

papers.title: Model-Based Authoring of SOC Simulation Exercises for Cybersecurity Education
papers.abstract: Cybersecurity training and classroom exercises with a virtual Security Operations Center (SOC) combine alerts, evidence, timeline entries, learner tasks, and assessment items that must remain consistent across an evolving incident. This paper presents a model-based authoring method in which a technical and educational specification is used to construct an incident exercise model and a large language model (LLM) generates selected scenario text based on that model. The incident exercise model combines an incident model of events, objects, and evidence with an exercise orchestration model of SOC alerts, timeline entries, learner tasks, and assessment items. The method is implemented in a Virtual SOC prototype and evaluated using a phishing-to-ransomware reference exercise. Its incident exercise model contains eight incident events, eight incident objects, six evidence items, seven alerts in five batches, 13 timeline entries including 12 learner tasks, and five representative assessment items. GLM-5.3-generated alert descriptions are inserted and a separate validator checks references, ordering, evidence links, assessment completeness, and selected fixed fields. Validation is demonstrated with reference data, resulting in true-negative outcomes for valid data and true-positive outcomes for deliberately placed inconsistencies. The resulting exercise package is executable within the Virtual SOC learner environment. Overall, the evaluation indicates consistency across the involved model elements and establishes the feasibility of the model-based and generative approach.

papers.title: Continuous Angular Control in Text-to-Image Generation via Geometric Token Encoding
papers.abstract:
Text-to-image diffusion models can render a photorealistic analog clock but cannot control the time it displays. Across four pretrained models, fewer than 1% of generated clocks place both hands within 6 degrees of the requested time; the models instead collapse onto visually dominant configurations such as the canonical 10:10 pose. The same failure appears when a specific fraction of a circular object is requested, where models return complete or conventionally sliced objects. We observe that these two failures share a geometric structure: both target quantities can be parameterized by angular variables.
  We introduce a geometric token encoding framework that conditions generation directly on these angles. Each angular component is encoded as a periodic sine-cosine feature and projected into a role-specific token embedding that is injected into the prompt before a frozen text encoder. To spatially ground these tokens without requiring localization input at inference, we introduce Stochastic Localization Relaxation (SLR), which stochastically relaxes attention supervision from component-level to object-level to unconstrained localization during training. For clocks, we additionally introduce a hand-swap preference objective that discourages assigning the correct angles to the wrong hand roles. On analog clocks our method reaches 63-78% Acc@6 degrees across evaluation methods, compared with below 1% for the baselines. On circular-fraction generation, it achieves 89.5% Acc@0.10, while maintaining 88.8% on unseen object categories and 84.9% on unseen target values, compared with roughly 20% for pretrained baselines.

These observations expose a limitation of natural-language conditioning. Language is effective for describing semantic content, appearance, and scene context, but provides an unreliable interface for precise numerical and geometric control. A model may understand that the requested object is a clock or a pizza without faithfully representing the particular time or fraction specified in the prompt. Clock time is jointly determined by the orientations of the hour and minute hands, while a circular fraction is specified by the angular boundaries of its visible sector. This common structure suggests that these quantities should be represented directly in angular space rather than expressed only through language.

papers.title: Asymptotic Robustness of HDG Schemes for the Convection-Diffusion Equation
papers.abstract: The convection-diffusion problem has been studied extensively as an important model for convection-dominated problems. The problem becomes more challenging when the convecting velocity is no longer Lipschitz and merely has Sobolev regularity. In this paper, we use Boyer's extension of the DiPerna--Lions theory for the transport equation to study the vanishing diffusion limit of discretizations of the convection-diffusion equation with Sobolev velocity. In the case of flux-adapted boundary conditions, we prove that a continuous Galerkin discretization converges strongly to the renormalized solution of the transport equation as the diffusion coefficient and mesh size go to zero, without requiring any relationship between them. We refer to this unconditional strong convergence as asymptotic robustness. In the case of Dirichlet boundary conditions, we use the renormalization theory and barrier arguments to prove that a piecewise constant hybridizable discontinuous Galerkin scheme is asymptotically robust, while the continuous Galerkin scheme may fail to converge. Our results indicate that the asymptotic robustness of schemes for the convection-diffusion problem depends on the realization of the boundary conditions as opposed to internal layers.

papers.title: Continuous 3D Spatial Transcriptomics Reconstruction via Histology-Informed Implicit Neural Representations
papers.abstract: Three-dimensional spatial transcriptomics (3D ST) enables the analysis of gene-expression patterns across tissue depths. However, 3D ST measurements are acquired from discrete 2D tissue sections, which are often sparsely sampled due to high acquisition costs. To address this limitation, we propose a histology-informed multi-task implicit neural representation (HIM-INR) for continuous 3D gene-expression reconstruction from sparse ST observations. HIM-INR jointly reconstructs gene-expression profiles and histological representations using an INR with a shared backbone, leveraging densely sampled histological images as auxiliary spatial supervision. Once trained, HIM-INR predicts gene expression at arbitrary 3D coordinates without requiring histological images. Experiments on two 3D ST datasets demonstrate improved reconstruction over existing methods, particularly as the number of missing ST sections increases.

papers.intro:
Three-dimensional spatial transcriptomics (3D ST) [1] has emerged as a promising approach for investigating the spatial organization of gene expression within tissues. Building on conventional 2D ST [2], which measures gene expression in individual tissue sections, 3D ST enables the characterization of molecular interactions across tissue depths and the spatial extent and connectivity of pathological regions. Such capabilities offer new opportunities to investigate cell-to-cell communication across sections, characterize tumor invasion and inflammatory infiltration, and reveal spatial relationships between tissue architecture and molecular states that cannot be fully captured by individual 2D sections [1, 3].

Building on conventional 2D ST [2], which measures gene expression in individual tissue sections, 3D ST enables the characterization of molecular interactions across tissue depths and the spatial extent and connectivity of pathological regions. Such capabilities offer new opportunities to investigate cell-to-cell communication across sections, characterize tumor invasion and inflammatory infiltration, and reveal spatial relationships between tissue architecture and molecular states that cannot be fully captured by individual 2D sections [1, 3].

Despite the potential of 3D ST, gene expression is measured only on discrete tissue sections. Furthermore, the high cost of ST measurements restricts the number of sections that can be profiled, resulting in sparse observations along the tissue depth axis. Previous studies have aligned ST measurements from serial tissue sections into a common spatial coordinate system to reconstruct tissue structures along the depth axis [4, 5]. However, gene-expression information remains restricted to the observed sections, leaving the continuous distribution of gene expression between them unresolved.

These limitations motivate the reconstruction of a continuous 3D gene-expression field from sparsely and discretely observed ST sections. However, this task remains challenging. While gene expression can vary substantially with changes in tissue structure across sections, no direct information on gene expression is available between sparsely sampled ST sections. Consequently, not only conventional neighborhood-based interpolation methods but also deep learning-based approaches [6, 7] that model nonlinear relationships between spatial positions and gene expression face difficulties in accurately reconstructing gene expression in unobserved regions.

Gene-expression patterns are known to be associated with tissue structure and morphology [8, 9]. Moreover, histological images are commonly acquired alongside ST measurements and are often available from more densely sampled tissue sections due to their substantially lower acquisition cost [10]. We base our method on an INR model, which represents continuous signals by learning a function that maps spatial coordinates to corresponding signal values [11]. Using the INR as a shared backbone, our framework jointly reconstructs gene-expression profiles and histological representations extracted using a pretrained pathology foundation model designed to capture tissue morphology [12]. By incorporating histological reconstruction as an auxiliary task, the shared INR backbone receives additional spatial supervision from densely sampled histological sections, even at locations where ST measurements are unavailable. This encourages the model to capture continuous variations in tissue morphology and learn shared spatial representations for gene-expression and histological reconstruction. papers.title: Right for the Wrong Reasons? Evaluating Plausibility and Behavioral Change in Explanation-Guided Learning
papers.abstract: Explanation-Guided Learning (EGL) promises models that are not only accurate but also rely on task-relevant evidence. However, whether improved agreement between model explanations and human-provided rationales also implies a changed decision strategy remains unclear. We study this tension under controlled synthetic shortcut introduction using a constructed shortcut dataset. Inspired by real-world applications, our benchmark covers shortcuts of different kinds, including localized, background-based, and global cues. This allows us to evaluate whether different EGL objectives produce behavioral changesand explanatory changes. Across these axes, we find that the effects of EGL are strongly objective-specific. Rationale-based data augmentation provides the clearest robustness gains when shortcut evidence can be separated from task-relevant foreground information, reaching average accuracy improvements of up to +4.8 percentage points (pp) together with increased foreground reliance. Attribution-constraining objectives primarily improve explanation plausibility, increasing Importance Mass by up to +14 pp on average, but provide weaker and less consistent behavioral correction, with average accuracy gains of at most +1.6 pp. Moreover, neither improved robustness nor improved plausibility reliably implies higher perturbation-based fidelity. Overall, our results show that EGL can be useful, but its success cannot be inferred from rationale agreement alone and should instead be evaluated along complementary behavioral and explanation-level axes. We publicly release all experimental results to enable further analysis (https://right-for-wrong-reasons.dfki.de/).

Ever more complex machine learning models are deployed in high-stakes domains such as medicine and finance, where opaque decision processes complicate human oversight and may obscure biases encoded by the model. In response, the community has developed a broad range of methods for explaining model predictions. This growing emphasis on transparency is also reflected in regulation such as the EU AI Act, which establishes transparency requirements for high-risk AI systems [7].

In response, the community has developed a broad range of methods for explaining model predictions. This growing emphasis on transparency is also reflected in regulation such as the EU AI Act, which establishes transparency requirements for high-risk AI systems [7].

While explanations are commonly used as post-hoc diagnostic tools, transparency can also be pursued during model design or training, for example through inherently interpretable architectures. A complementary strategy is to retain flexible models but guide them during training toward user-specified evidence. This idea underlies Explanation-Guided Learning (EGL), which augments the classification loss with auxiliary objectives derived from user-provided rationales [8, 19]. In its classical form, such guidance directly constrains model explanations to align with these rationales, aiming to encourage models to base their predictions on task-relevant evidence and follow the aspiration of being “right for the right reasons.” However, whether optimizing explanations actually changes the model’s decision strategy in this intended way remains an empirical question. The promise of explanation-guided training has led to a growing body of work in computer vision and natural language processing [8, 21, 25, 31, 34].

Assessing whether EGL fulfills its intended goals is further complicated by a gap between the apparent quality of an explanation and the model behavior it is meant to reflect. Plausibility, i.e. agreement between an explanation and human annotations, does not necessarily imply fidelity, i.e. causal relevance of the highlighted features to the model’s decision [4, 9]22 2 The terms faithfulness and fidelity are used interchangeably in this work.. A model may therefore be trained to produce plausible explanations while still relying on shortcuts or spurious correlations [10]. For EGL, this raises a central question: do objectives that improve rationale agreement also induce the intended behavioral changes, such as greater robustness, reduced shortcut reliance, and more faithful explanations, or do they primarily optimize the appearance of explanations? This question is especially relevant when comparing classical attribution-constraining objectives with rationale-based data-augmentation objectives, since both use rationales during training but may affect the learned model differently. Yet prior work has mostly considered isolated shortcut settings and often emphasizes plausibility metrics, leaving the relation between objective type, model behavior, and explanation quality insufficiently understood.

We conduct a multi-axis evaluation of EGL under controlled synthetic shortcut bias. To this end, we construct a benchmark that injects three shortcut types: localized patch cues, class-correlated backgrounds, and global color-cast cues. Using this benchmark, we compare several EGL objectives for a convolutional and a transformer-based model, distinguishing attribution-constraining objectives from rationale-based data-augmentation objectives. We evaluate the resulting models along four complementary axes, grouped into behavioral and explanation-level effects: robustness to shortcut shift (RQ1) and reliance on foreground versus shortcut evidence (RQ2) as behavioral axes, and explanation plausibility with respect to object masks (RQ3) and explanation fidelity to the model’s decision process (RQ4) as explanation-level axes. Our results show that these desiderata can diverge substantially. The Attribution-constraining objectives yield the clearest plausibility gains, whereas rationale-based data-augmentation objectives are more effective for improving robustness and reducing shortcut reliance in separable shortcut settings. These findings show that evaluating EGL primarily through explanation plausibility is insufficient: improved rationale agreement does not show that the model relies on the intended features, and objectives that directly intervene on the training data may be more effective for changing model behavior than attribution alignment.

papers.title: Properties of the Dichromatic Polynomial
papers.abstract:
The chromatic polynomial is a well-studied function of graphs whose coefficients, factorization, and other properties are well-known to encode structural information about the underlying graph. An analogous notion of graph colouring exists for directed graphs which is also well-studied, but little is yet known about the corresponding dichromatic polynomial.
  We investigate properties of the dichromatic polynomial, including its coefficient interpretations, root-dense regions, and asymptotic growth. We also show that chordal digraphs' polynomials split into linear factors in a way analogous to the undirected case, confirm a conjecture on dichromatic uniqueness posed by Gonz\'alez-Moreno et al., and study the density of dichromatic polynomials within certain larger families of polynomials.

papers.intro:
Graph colourings have been a major area of study in the field of combinatorics since at least the early 1900s. In particular, Birkhoff [6] first showed that the number of ways to properly colour a given graph with nn colours is a polynomial in nn, called the chromatic polynomial, which satisfies a recursive edge deletion-contraction property. In 1982, Neumann-Lara [20] defined a generalization of graph colourings to digraphs: in the undirected case, a colouring is proper if there are no monochromatic edges, while in the directed case, it is proper if there are no monochromatic directed cycles. Under this interpretation, directed graph colouring is a generalization of undirected graph colouring, since an undirected graph may be represented as a directed graph with the same colouring rules by replacing each edge with a pair of arcs in opposite directions. In 2011, Harutyunyan [12] established some interesting properties of the dichromatic polynomial, defined to be the Neumann-Lara analogue of the chromatic polynomial, and in 2022 González-Moreno et. al. [8] further investigated the dichromatic polynomial, including establishing a deletion-contraction relation.

papers.title: First results from a borehole network for the seismic characterization of the Einstein Telescope Euregio Meuse-Rhine candidate site
papers.abstract: The low-frequency sensitivity of the Einstein Telescope depends on the seismic environment of its site, both through the mechanical coupling of ground motion to the test masses and through Newtonian noise. We present the first results of the seismic characterization of the Euregio Meuse-Rhine candidate site based on a network of recently instrumented boreholes covering the first seven months of 2026 at four underground stations and their co-located surface sensors. Two of these boreholes were deliberately sited next to railway infrastructure, so that the levels reported here describe how anthropogenic transients propagate to depth at different distances from the source. The analysis was carried out with \texttt{SiteChar}, a Python framework developed for this work to provide a common processing pipeline across different sensors, networks and observation periods. It processes the data in sequential chunks and separates the noise floor from the contribution of transients. We present a characterization of the catalogue of observed transients and a tentative classification. These measurements form part of an integrated site characterization approach that combines the observed seismic field with three-dimensional geological and wave-propagation models to predict Newtonian noise and ultimately guide its mitigation at the Euregio Meuse-Rhine candidate site.

papers.intro:
The Einstein Telescope (ET) is designed to extend the observation band of gravitational wave detectors down to a few Hertz [24, 13]. This extension makes the characterization of the underground seismic environment a central element of site assessment. The dedicated cryogenic low-frequency interferometer is designed to target approximately the 3–30 Hz band, enabling science including early warning for binary neutron-star mergers, observations of intermediate-mass black holes, and improved tests of gravity in the strong-field regime [1]. This is also the frequency band in which detector performance is most closely coupled to the local environment.

Below roughly 10 Hz [2], the seismic environment enters the sensitivity budget through two distinct mechanisms. First, ground motion couples mechanically to the test masses through the suspension chain. Seismic isolation attenuates this transmission, while underground siting provides an additional reduction by taking advantage of the lower seismic motion at depth. Second, fluctuations in the local mass density associated with the same ground motion exert a gravitational force directly on the test masses, called Newtonian noise (NN), which no isolation system can shield [10]. Careful site selection can reduce this contribution, while active subtraction using arrays of auxiliary sensors provides an additional mitigation route. Current ET sensitivity projections anticipate the need for NN mitigation in the low-frequency detector, motivating substantial effort toward the optimisation of the auxiliary sensor arrays [9, 5, 3, 4, 26, 27], toward next-generation and alternative sensing technologies [8, 22, 25], and toward neural-network subtraction methods [28, 14]. A prototype cancellation system has also been deployed at Virgo [18, 17] for testing. The central question for site characterization is therefore not simply how quiet a site is, but whether its seismic environment can be sufficiently characterized and modelled to predict its impact on ET and to design an effective NN mitigation system.

An explicitly integrated approach to site characterization is crucial for the EMR candidate site. Rather than treating geology, seismic observations, and NN modelling as separate activities, the EMR strategy is to combine the measured seismic field with a detailed three-dimensional geological model and physics-based simulations of seismic wave propagation. The resulting displacement field can then be translated into gravitational perturbations at the detector test masses, including the influence of the underground infrastructure, and used to develop and optimize mitigation strategies. A distinctive feature of the EMR site characterization program is therefore the development of this integrated, site-specific modelling chain, connecting geological structure, measured seismic fields, wave propagation, NN prediction, and mitigation. This approach is designed to move beyond the characterization of individual site properties towards a physics-based prediction of how the complete underground environment affects ET performance.

A further aspect of the seismic environment concerns its non-stationary component. Anthropogenic activity in the surrounding area produces transient disturbances that are superimposed on the ambient background, and whose contribution is not captured by long-term averaged spectra. Their characterization, in terms of spectral signature, occurrence statistics and spatial extent, is therefore a natural complement to the description of the background field and provides part of the input needed for a realistic description of the environment in which the detector would operate.

papers.title: Virtual Two-Step Nilpotency of the Fundamental Groups of Special Quasi-Projective Varieties
papers.abstract: We prove that the fundamental group of every smooth connected complex quasi-projective variety that is special in the sense of Campana is virtually nilpotent of class at most two. This establishes the two-step nilpotency conjecture of Cao--Deng--Hacon--P\u{a}un, a quasi-projective analogue of Campana's almost abelian conjecture for special compact K\"ahler manifolds. Examples of Cadorel--Deng--Yamanoi show that the step bound is sharp. On a suitable finite etale cover, we construct a canonical second Albanese map to a torus torsor over an abelian variety. The proof reduces to showing that the kernel of the induced map on fundamental groups is finite. Using good minimal models and meridian groups of projective pairs, we show that an infinite kernel would yield a saturated rank-one subsheaf of logarithmic differentials whose Iitaka dimension contradicts specialness.

papers.title: Earth Embeddings in Environmental Remote Sensing
papers.abstract: Earth observations from satellite platforms have profoundly transformed research and applications across numerous domains. However, uneven observation coverage and frequent data gaps continue to limit their ability to capture Earth's surface dynamics. Moreover, processing multi-modal Earth observations requires substantial computational resources and sophisticated data harmonization frameworks, which may not be readily accessible to many remote sensing practitioners. Earth embeddings have emerged as promising solutions to these challenges. As general-purpose representations converted from multi-source Earth observations, Earth embeddings can support a wide range of downstream tasks with no requirement of task-specific feature design and preprocessing. In this study, we first introduce the theoretical foundations of Earth embeddings. Then, we review several representative Earth embedding products. We next examine the applications of Earth embeddings across six major domains of environmental remote sensing. Finally, we systematically assess the performance of Earth embeddings in four downstream tasks, including hyperspectral image classification, individual tree crown segmentation, crop yield prediction, and aboveground biomass mapping. Our review and case studies suggest that, despite several advantages over conventional Earth observation data, current Earth embeddings do not always outperform remote sensing imagery or hand-crafted features. Earth embeddings should not be viewed as a direct replacement for conventional EO data, but rather as representations that provide stable information across space and time. Remote sensing practitioners may consider evaluating Earth embeddings' suitability for specific tasks and using them strategically, rather than assuming superior performance by default.

papers.title: Hx2Dx: From Anamnesis to Diagnosis - A Multimodal Arena for Conversational Clinical Reasoning in LLMs
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve expert-level diagnostic accuracy in static evaluations, where the model receives a curated vignette or case report that already condenses the diagnostically relevant findings. Such evaluations measure inference over already selected evidence; the evaluations do not account for the inquiry used to obtain it. In clinical practice, however, diagnosis is an iterative process of inquiry. Clinicians take the patient's history, or anamnesis (Hx), through targeted questioning, examine the patient, and request and interpret tests, progressively narrowing the differential until they reach a final diagnosis (Dx). We introduce Hx2Dx ARENA, an interactive benchmark of 1'000 clinical cases from the New England Journal of Medicine (NEJM). Each case is a simulated encounter that proceeds from initial presentation through history taking and physical examination to diagnostic workup. We evaluate open- and closed-source LLMs under multiple configurations. Performance varies considerably across models in the interactive setting, and every model loses diagnostic accuracy relative to the static setting, where the full case is presented upfront. The ability to ask the right questions accounts for much of both the gap between models and the loss of accuracy: diagnosis improves as questions become more targeted and build a more complete clinical picture. LLMs thus reason well once the relevant data are available but remain limited in hypothesis-driven information gathering, in knowing what to ask in order to know. Closing this gap is a prerequisite for their safe integration into real-world diagnostic workflows.

papers.title: Physics-informed Bayesian optimization of high-order harmonic generation in gases
papers.abstract: Optimization of high-order harmonic generation in gases is essential for attosecond science. Improving conversion efficiency from the infrared driving laser to the extreme-ultraviolet high-order harmonic radiation requires balancing microscopic single-atom dipole responses with macroscopic phase matching. The resulting conversion-efficiency landscape exhibits complex structures, such as the hyperbolic ridge in the pressure-length space, which can be difficult to accurately reconstruct using conventional Bayesian optimization. Here, we introduce a physics-informed Bayesian optimization framework that incorporates known physical scaling relations through nonlinear transformations of the search space. We first demonstrate the approach in the two-dimensional pressure-length space, where a direct grid scan enables detailed validation of the reconstructed landscape, before extending it to four dimensions, where exhaustive scanning becomes computationally impractical. In four dimensions, incorporating the pulse-duration scaling and a square-root transformation of conversion efficiency further improves the accuracy of the reconstructed landscape, as validated against an independent reference dataset. We also employ a threshold-based acquisition strategy to identify extended high-efficiency operating regions rather than isolated optimal points. Together, these results demonstrate that incorporating physical knowledge into Bayesian optimization improves the exploration and reconstruction of multidimensional high-order harmonic generation landscapes, extending its capabilities beyond locating individual optima.

papers.intro:
High-order harmonic generation (HHG) is a widely used method for producing coherent, short-pulse extreme-ultraviolet (XUV) radiation for fundamental studies of ultrafast electron dynamics [32, 25] and for applications such as coherent imaging [66] or coincidence spectroscopy [40]. In a typical gas-based HHG experiment [39, 20, 8], an intense femtosecond infrared (IR) laser is focused into a gaseous target. This leads to the generation of a broad comb of discrete peaks at odd multiples of the laser frequency, reaching across the XUV range and potentially extending even into the soft-X-ray regime [53, 47]. In the time domain, the coherent superposition of high harmonics forms an attosecond pulse train [44, 1]. The optimal operation of HHG sources is essential for addressing future challenges in chirality, quantum optics, and spin dynamics [61], with a recent perspective highlighting broader developments in HHG sources and their applications to quantum phenomena [15]. This requires advanced optimization techniques, as HHG is inherently a multiscale problem [18], involving both the microscopic response of individual atoms to the driving laser field and the macroscopic propagation and buildup of the generated harmonic radiation. The interplay between these processes determines the overall IR-to-XUV conversion efficiency (further referred to only as conversion efficiency), which remains relatively low, typically on the order of 10−710^{-7} to 10−410^{-4} [58, 9, 57, 41, 7, 46, 63].

Microscopically, HHG originates from the nonlinear response of individual atoms to the strong driving field. This interaction is described quantum mechanically by the time-dependent Schrödinger equation (TDSE) [12, 11, 59]. Its essential physics can, however, be captured by the simplified semiclassical three-step model [16, 33], which describes HHG in terms of tunnel ionization, acceleration in the continuum, and recombination. First, the intense laser field distorts the atomic potential sufficiently for an electron to tunnel ionize. The electron is then accelerated by the field and gains kinetic energy. When the oscillating field reverses, the electron can be driven back toward its parent ion, recombine, and release its accumulated energy as a high-energy photon. Repetition of this process over successive half-cycles gives rise to the characteristic HHG spectrum, consisting of a broad plateau of harmonic orders with comparable intensity followed by a sharp high-energy cutoff. Electrons that do not recombine with their parent ion instead contribute to the partial ionization of the medium.

The macroscopic buildup of the harmonic field is governed by phase matching, which depends on both propagation-induced phase shifts and the phase of the microscopic atomic response. Accordingly, the wave-vector mismatch contains contributions from neutral-gas dispersion, plasma dispersion due to laser-induced free electrons, the intensity-dependent atomic dipole phase, and the geometric phase associated with focusing [14, 22, 28, 10]. The macroscopic HHG process also exhibits geometrical scale invariance, whereby the driving-laser pulse energy, focusing geometry, gas pressure, and interaction length can be scaled according to specific relations while preserving the harmonic conversion efficiency [28]. Phase-matching and absorption considerations further reveal a characteristic hyperbolic relation between the pressure and medium length corresponding to optimal conversion efficiency [63, 4]. A related dependence has recently been identified for the driving-pulse duration: at a given intensity, experiments and simulations show that the conversion efficiency is maximized at a particular pulse duration, and that this maximum scales approximately with the inverse square root of that duration [64].

While these scaling relations provide valuable guidance for identifying favorable operating conditions, maximizing the conversion efficiency requires the simultaneous optimization of several interdependent gas and laser parameters [63]. Although low-dimensional parameter spaces can be explored using direct numerical scans, the computational cost increases rapidly with the number of optimization variables, making exhaustive exploration increasingly impractical. Beyond identifying optimal conditions, reconstructing the conversion-efficiency landscape is valuable for understanding the dependence on different operating parameters and identifying extended regions of favorable conditions. This motivates approaches that can efficiently locate high-efficiency conditions while accurately reconstructing multidimensional HHG landscapes using a limited number of simulations.

In recent years, it has increasingly been applied to computationally and experimentally expensive laser–matter interaction problems [52, 29, 13, 65, 60, 56, 19, 5, 35], including waveform control and polarization gating for attosecond pulse generation [13]. However, the potential of BO for efficiently optimizing and accurately reconstructing the multidimensional conversion-efficiency landscape in gas-based HHG remains largely unexplored.

In recent years, it has increasingly been applied to computationally and experimentally expensive laser–matter interaction problems [52, 29, 13, 65, 60, 56, 19, 5, 35], including waveform control and polarization gating for attosecond pulse generation [13]. However, the potential of BO for efficiently optimizing and accurately reconstructing the multidimensional conversion-efficiency landscape in gas-based HHG remains largely unexplored.

BO constructs a probabilistic surrogate model of the quantity to be optimized from a limited number of evaluations and uses an acquisition function to iteratively select new points that are most informative or promising for locating the optimum [51, 21]. By balancing exploration of uncertain regions with exploitation of promising ones, BO can identify high-performing conditions with substantially fewer evaluations than exhaustive parameter scans. However, standard BO does not inherently account for known physical structure in the parameter space. Commonly, Gaussian processes (GPs) [50] are used as surrogate models, describing correlations between points based on their Euclidean distance in the chosen parameter space. Consequently, the choice of coordinates influences how accurately the GP can represent the underlying physical landscape.

papers.title: Adversarial risk analysis with fully probabilistic designs
papers.abstract: Adversarial risk analysis (ARA) informs decision-makers when facing intelligent opponents and uncertain outcomes, enabling an analyst to model beliefs about the opponents' preferences, capabilities, beliefs, and the strategic calculations that opponents employ. Major applications cover reliability and risk analysis of critical infrastructures in presence of adversarial threats. In such domains, ARA mitigates typical common knowledge assumptions of standard game-theoretic approaches. However, ARA entails complex modelling and computations. To alleviate these, we explore its combination with fully probabilistic design (FPD), a control theory methodology supporting an agent in choosing the decision distribution that achieves the outcomes with a distribution closest to its ideal. We use FPD to model and forecast the opponent's decisions within an ARA setting and present how to handle security games within this ARA-FPD framework, covering both single and multiple stage problems.

papers.intro:
Numerous reliability and risk analysis settings, specially when dealing with critical infrastructures, comprise decisions by adversaries affecting the security, safety and acceptability of systems, see the reviews by Hausken et al. (2025) and Guikema and Aven (2010), as well as references therein. Examples in reliability include life testing problems (Lindley and Singpurwalla, 1993); warranty analysis (Singpurwalla and Wilson, 1993); optimal maintenance (Jackson and Pascual, 2008); reliability demonstration (Rufo et al., 2014); and software reliability testing (Soyer et al., 2025). Examples in risk analysis include transportation network protection (Quijano et al., 2018), nuclear power power plant protection (Zhao et al., 2020) or counterterrorism protection of complex infrastructures (Hausken, 2010).

Decision making when facing intelligent opponents with non-aligned or misaligned objectives is frequently formulated within standard game-theoretic perspectives which, from a computational point of view, are based on approximating Nash equilibria and related refinements (Menache and Ozdaglar, 2011). The underlying assumptions to these perspectives usually entail that agents know not only their payoffs, preferences, beliefs, and feasible actions, but also those of their opponents, usually designated common knowledge (CK) assumptions. Alternatively, in games with incomplete information (Harsanyi, 1967) it is habitually assumed that each agent has a probability distribution over certain opponents’ features, designated types, characterizing their beliefs and preferences. This distribution is considered to be known by all players, a specific CK assumption called the common prior hypothesis, allowing for a symmetric joint normative analysis of the game in which players maximize expected utilities, and expect other players to do the same, leading to Bayes-Nash equilibria. General CK assumptions have been critically reviewed, e.g., in Raiffa et al. (2002) or Heap and Varoufakis (2004), whereas common prior assumptions were discussed by Antos and Pfeffer (2010), Sákovics (2001) or Angeletos and Lian (2018), to name but a few. In their reviews of game theoretic approaches to reliability and risk analysis, Hausken et al. (2025) and Hunt and Zhuang (2024) argue that developing methodology addressing cases with lack of full knowledge and full rationality are important topics for further development.

The underlying assumptions to these perspectives usually entail that agents know not only their payoffs, preferences, beliefs, and feasible actions, but also those of their opponents, usually designated common knowledge (CK) assumptions. Alternatively, in games with incomplete information (Harsanyi, 1967) it is habitually assumed that each agent has a probability distribution over certain opponents’ features, designated types, characterizing their beliefs and preferences. This distribution is considered to be known by all players, a specific CK assumption called the common prior hypothesis, allowing for a symmetric joint normative analysis of the game in which players maximize expected utilities, and expect other players to do the same, leading to Bayes-Nash equilibria. General CK assumptions have been critically reviewed, e.g., in Raiffa et al. (2002) or Heap and Varoufakis (2004), whereas common prior assumptions were discussed by Antos and Pfeffer (2010), Sákovics (2001) or Angeletos and Lian (2018), to name but a few. In their reviews of game theoretic approaches to reliability and risk analysis, Hausken et al. (2025) and Hunt and Zhuang (2024) argue that developing methodology addressing cases with lack of full knowledge and full rationality are important topics for further development.

Adversarial risk analysis (ARA) (Insua et al., 2009; Banks et al., 2015) is a decision-analytic approach to games that employs distributions to model the goals, resources, beliefs, preferences, and reasoning of an attacker precisely aiming to address such lack of full knowledge and rationality issues. Within ARA, a defender solves the problem from the perspective of her attacker, while placing subjective probability distributions over all the attacker’s unknown problem elements. This gives her a distribution over the attacker’s actions, accounting for the uncertainty she may have about her adversary’s actions, enabling her to maximize expected utility to find her optimal protective action. Banks et al. (2020) provide a detailed conceptual comparison between ARA and key game theoretic solutions, including Nash and Bayes-Nash equilibria. Since its proposal, ARA has been used to model a variety of problems, mainly in the security risk domain, including routing in the presence of improvised explosive devices (Wang and Banks, 2011), international piracy (Sevillano et al., 2012), counter-terrorist online surveillance (Gil and Parra-Arnau, 2019), enhanced combat modelling (Roponen and Salo, 2016), and cybersecurity (Wang and Neil, 2021). Reliability applications include Insua et al. (2018) and González-Ortega et al. (2021). However, ARA entails involved modelling and computational issues. In particular, to account for the uncertainty about the attacker, sophisticated probability distributions need to be assessed, including random utilities, demanding complex reasoning. Furthermore, the ARA methodology entails simulations from the attacker’s perspective and then optimization of the defender’s problem, potentially leading to expensive computations.

This paper studies how these issues are alleviated with the help of the control-theoretic methodology of Fully Probabilistic Design (FPD) (Kárný and Guy, 2006), introducing a novel ARA-FPD approach. Within stochastic control problems, FPD of decision rules supports the decision-making of an agent while expressing its decision objectives through an ideal distribution that describes the consequences sought by such agent (Kárný, 2022). Here, FPD will be used to facilitate forecasting the attacker’s actions within ARA settings, greatly alleviating the aforementioned modelling and computational issues by, on the one hand, mitigating the need to extract very detailed information about the attacker’s preferences, limiting the focus to his ideals, and, on the other hand, avoiding repeated costly optimizations adapting FPD explicit optimization results.

papers.title: ASPIRE: An Agentic System-Identification Platform for Iterative Reasoning and Exploration
papers.abstract: System identification requires expert decisions on the identification method, incorporation of prior physical knowledge, and model validation. We propose ASPIRE, a framework for nonlinear system identification in which a large language model agent selects and executes the identification method. ASPIRE constructs closed-form, nonlinear static or dynamic models from measured data, optionally supplemented by a system description, the intended use of the model, and physical requirements expressed formally or in natural language. Each model includes its parameters, an estimation record, an interpretation of its terms, and an error evaluated on test data inaccessible to the agent. Formal physical requirements are verified independently. ASPIRE operates autonomously or interactively, allowing the agent to ask questions and the user to request further analyses and identification rounds. We evaluate ASPIRE on three measured systems: a mobile robot, a rotational system with dry friction, and a laboratory fermenter. Each system is tested with and without a description, in five runs per task. All 30 runs delivered valid models, at a cost of 0.96 to 3.38 US dollars per run. An assessment by the authors found that, for the 30 models recommended by the agent, one per run, the interpretation of the model and the documentation of its structure selection and parameter estimation fully satisfied 132 of 150 assessed items and partly satisfied 18. The most frequent discrepancy, found in nine models, concerned inaccurate or unsupported claims about model structure selection.

papers.intro:
In industrial applications, white-box models based on closed-form mathematical expressions are usually preferred to black-box models. Closed-form models relate inputs, states, and outputs through a small set of named parameters and, as such, are useful wherever a model must be interpreted, checked against physical knowledge, extrapolated beyond the range of the data, or embedded in model-based control. Obtaining such models from measured data requires several decisions by an expert: the identification method, the model class, how prior physical knowledge enters the estimation, the estimation criterion, and the validation procedure that matches the model’s intended use. Techniques such as symbolic regression (SR) and sparse regression automate the search for model structure [3, 7], and some SR tools allow for incorporating physical requirements and prior knowledge [20, 5, 6, 23, 44].

Agents based on large language models (LLMs) that write and execute code can choose the identification method: they can inspect the data, propose model structures informed by physical knowledge, implement a fitting procedure, or call an existing SR package and iterate. Recent systems couple LLM-proposed equation structures with numerical parameter fitting [36, 11], give an LLM a fixed set of code-execution tools for equation discovery [43], or let an agent apply physics-based analysis tools to infer properties of the system and then configure existing SR and sparse-regression packages accordingly [48]. In system identification, ASIA [32] delegates the choice of the model class, the training algorithm, and the hyperparameters to an autonomous coding agent.

Existing agentic equation-discovery methods have several limitations: they do not support the specification and verification of physics-based requirements, evaluation on test data inaccessible to the agent, and documentation of the identification procedure. Furthermore, each delivered model should include a record of its structure and parameter estimation, distinguishing estimated parameters, fixed constants, and parameters derived from other parameters. The record should contain sufficient information to check the reported identification procedure against the executed code and execution logs. To the best of our knowledge, no published framework combines these features with agent-selected identification methods and a protocol for reporting variability across repeated runs.

It is unrelated to the robot-skill system of the same name [27]., a framework for system identification using LLM agents. ASPIRE constructs closed-form static or dynamic models from measured data, optionally supplemented by a system description, the model’s intended use, and physical requirements expressed formally or in natural language. The agent selects and executes the identification method, which may involve physically motivated model structures, symbolic or sparse regression, or custom estimation code. Each candidate model is accompanied by its parameter values, estimation procedure, interpretation, limitations, and test error. The agent also recommends one of the candidates. ASPIRE supports autonomous and interactive operation; in the latter, the agent can request information from the user, who can also request analyses and further identification rounds. The framework consists of one or more LLM agents responsible for identification and a software harness that executes their commands, enforces computational budgets, checks and evaluates candidate models, and records the identification runs.
