In summary, the main contributions of this paper are:

• We introduce ASPIRE, an agentic framework for system identification in which LLM agents autonomously select, implement, and execute identification methods to obtain nonlinear closed-form models from measured data. Unlike systems based on predefined modeling pipelines or restricted toolboxes, ASPIRE allows the agent to develop and compare alternative model structures and estimation procedures, including methods not specified in advance. • We integrate physical knowledge and user interaction into agentic system identification. Users can specify the intended application, physical requirements, and available knowledge about the system, while the agent can request clarifications, explain its results, and revise models based on user feedback. Formal physical requirements are checked independently of the agent, including properties such as monotonicity, equilibrium conditions, and physically consistent behavior under specified operating conditions, which cannot be assessed by predictive accuracy alone. • We develop an identification framework that separates autonomous model construction from independent model verification and evaluation. The framework prevents agents from accessing test data, verifies formal physical requirements, and retains executable models, parameter estimation records, and execution logs. This separation enables the identification procedure and its results to be examined and reproduced, despite the agent’s freedom to choose its methods. • We demonstrate the framework on three experimentally measured systems: a mobile robot, a rotational system with dry friction, and a laboratory fermenter. Repeated experiments with and without system descriptions investigate the agent’s ability to identify models from data alone and to incorporate prior physical knowledge. The results show that the agent can construct models with competitive predictive accuracy while satisfying physical requirements that are not enforced by conventional symbolic regression and sparse identification methods. The experiments also quantify run-to-run variability and computational cost.

papers.title: Hybridization-brightened interlayer excitons in multilayer WSe2 controlled by sliding ferroelectricity
papers.abstract: Interlayer excitons (IXs) combine spatially separated electron and hole wavefunctions with electrically tunable dipole moments, but their reduced wavefunction overlap generally limits optical emission, particularly for high-energy states. Here we report a bright, spectrally narrow high-energy interlayer exciton (h-IX) near 2.23 eV in few-layer WSe2 and investigate how its optical activity evolves with layer number and sliding-ferroelectric polarization. In pristine 2H-WSe2, we observe thickness-dependent brightening of high-energy exciton emission. GW-BSE calculations reveal mixed intralayer and interlayer configurations with enhanced optical weight, suggesting that multilayer hybridization contributes to the observed brightening. In parallel-stacked 3L/3L WSe2 containing a sliding-ferroelectric interface, the h-IX exhibits polarization-dependent energies and Stark responses that distinguish Pup and Pdown domains. Electric-field-driven domain-wall motion produces hysteretic transfer of spectral weight between the two h-IX branches, enabling optical tracking of ferroelectric switching. These results establish multilayer hybridization as a route to optically active high-energy interlayer excitons and sliding ferroelectricity as a complementary degree of freedom for controlling their energy, dipole and emission.

papers.title: An automated approach to structure theorems for minimally repetitive rich words
papers.abstract: Recent work on repetitions in rich words has led to the intensive study of the family of infinite rich words $\{{\mathbf u}_d:d\geq 2\}$, where ${\mathbf u}_d$ is the fixed point of the morphism $\varphi_d:\Sigma_d^*\rightarrow \Sigma_d^*$ defined by $\varphi_d(i)=\tt{0}(i+1)$ for $i\in\{\tt{0},\ldots,d-2\}$ and $\varphi_d(d-1)=\tt{0}(d-1)(d-1)$. For $d=2$ and $d=3$, it is known that the repetition threshold for infinite $d$-ary rich words is equal to the asymptotic critical exponent $E^*({\mathbf u}_{2d-1})$. Moreover, the structure of ${\mathbf u}_{2d-1}$ underlies the structure of all ``minimally repetitive'' $d$-ary rich words: there is a real number $t_d>E^*({\mathbf u}_{2d-1})$ such that every infinite $t_d$-power-free $d$-ary rich word contains the language of $\pi({\mathbf u}_{2d-1})$ for one of finitely many morphisms $\pi:\Sigma_{2d-1}^*\rightarrow \Sigma_d^*$. We conjecture that a similar situation holds for all $d\geq 2$, and prove this for the first unknown case $d=4$. To do this, we develop a new approach for proving such structure theorems. Two key new concepts are ``compatibility'' of return words to palindromes in recurrent rich words, and ``$t$-persistent repetitions''. They facilitate the automation of several aspects of the proofs which were previously done laboriously by hand. We first demonstrate our approach by giving a much shorter proof of the known structure theorem for infinite $\tfrac{16}{7}$-power-free ternary rich words. Then we prove a new structure theorem: every infinite $2.12$-power-free quaternary rich word contains the language of one of seven distinct words of the form $\pi({\mathbf u}_7)$, up to permutation of the letters. We prove that all seven words are rich and have critical exponent $E^*({\mathbf u}_7)$, so the repetition threshold for quaternary rich words is $E^*({\mathbf u}_7)\doteq 2.1197196907$.

papers.intro:
Since the completion of the proof of Dejean’s theorem [12, 30], which describes the boundary between avoidable and unavoidable repetitions in infinite words over a fixed alphabet, there has been much research on determining the analogous “repetition threshold” for more restricted classes of infinite words. This includes work on episturmian words [19], balanced words [13, 22, 29], rich words [10, 11], and words with given factor complexity [9, 27, 32]. In this paper, we continue the study of repetitions in infinite rich words.

A finite word ww of length nn is called rich if it contains exactly n+1n+1 distinct palindromes as factors, including the empty word. Such words are “rich” in palindromes, as every word of length nn contains at most n+1n+1 distinct palindromes as factors. An infinite word is rich if all of its (finite) factors are rich. Since their introduction about two decades ago [15], much work has been done on rich words from many different perspectives. • Examples of infinite rich words include episturmian words [15], complementary-symmetric Rote words [5], and words coding symmetric dd-interval exchange [1]. • There are characterizations of infinite rich words in terms of complete return words [24], a relation between factor and palindromic complexity [6], and bi-extensions of bispecial factors [2]. • Upper and lower bounds on the number of rich words of length nn over an alphabet of size dd have been established [25, 31]. An asymptotically accurate count is not yet known. • Morphisms preserving richness have been studied by several authors [3, 14, 24]. A complete characterization of such morphisms is not yet known.

papers.title: Learning from First Discrepancies with Joint Reset and Pilot Guarantees
papers.abstract: A run that stops at its first wrong decision shows the queries and their correct labels up to and including that decision, and nothing after it. We study how many such runs are needed for learning. Each run tests a hypothesis, the pilot, chosen beforehand from a fixed binary class of VC dimension at most $d$, on a fresh record of at most $D$ queries drawn from one unknown distribution that does not depend on the pilot. The terminal information of a record is shown only if the pilot makes no discrepancy, and a bounded loss, fixed in advance, is attached to the position where a hypothesis stops. If the discrepancy probabilities of members of the class have infimum at most $f$ and their risks have infimum at most $r$, one learner uses $\widetilde O((d+1)[D(f+\varepsilon)+r]/\varepsilon^2)$ runs and $\widetilde O(D(1+f/\varepsilon))$ distinct pilots on every history. It returns a member of the class and an interval of width at most $\varepsilon$ containing, with probability at least $1-\delta$, both the output's risk and the optimal risk. We also treat unknown ceilings and expected costs. Lower bounds for finite classes show that each order is necessary in the worst case, possibly on different instances, at positive dimension, small accuracy and fixed confidence. The learner enumerates label patterns of the class on displayed queries, possibly in exponential time; the results, under standard measurability conditions, concern statistical resources only. The proof combines a gain computable from stopped displays, exponential weights, a sparse depth-robust graph and a harmonic-mean bound.
papers.intro:
Many checking procedures go through a sequence of items and stop at the first item that is handled incorrectly. When a candidate decision rule is run on such a sequence, the run reveals the items and their correct labels up to and including the first item on which the rule is wrong; the later items, and any outcome attached to the end of the sequence, remain hidden. This paper studies how to learn a good rule when this is the only feedback. The learner must choose which rule to run before it sees the sequence, and an early mistake hides everything that follows. Even when every revealed label is correct, minimizing the empirical error on the prefixes observed so far need not produce a good rule, because the behaviour that matters for the loss of a candidate may lie beyond those prefixes, which were determined by the rules that happened to be run. Learning therefore requires deliberate exploration.

papers.title: Measuring Robustness and Efficiency in a Connectome-Constrained Fly Visual System Model: Linking an Adversarial and a Perceptual Illusion
papers.abstract: Biological visual systems compute reliably under tight metabolic and wiring constraints, whereas artificial vision systems consume far more energy and can be sensitive to adversarial perturbations. Whether networks with brain-like wiring are more robust at lower computational cost is unclear. We address this by benchmarking a task-optimized, continuous-time recurrent neural network of the fly visual system constrained by its synaptic connectome (FlyNet) against artificial neural networks. We compare it against CNNs, RAFT, and continuous-time recurrent neural networks without detailed connectome constraints (sCTRNN, CTRNN) on a collision-detection task within a differentiable 3D rendering pipeline. FlyNet is adversarially vulnerable but, relative to its compute, more robust to common video corruptions than RAFT, while using up to five orders of magnitude fewer FLOPs. The CTRNNs remain more robust than FlyNet across almost all tested perturbations, suggesting that connectome constraints benefit efficiency, through their low edge count, over robustness. Recurrence improves robustness to white-box attacks in RAFT and temporal context improves robustness to common corruptions. FlyNet's position and velocity representations degrade under adversarial textures but recover under counterfactual textures that restore correct classification while staying equally far from training, ruling out unfamiliar textures as the cause of failure. The reverse-phi illusion similarly disrupts these representations and inverts the same low-level motion statistic as the adversarial textures. Optimizing this input statistic alone, without access to the network, suffices to induce classification failure, attributing both perturbations to the same circuit vulnerability. Connectome-constrained models can thus surface adversarial failure mechanisms as testable hypotheses about biological perceptual vulnerabilities.

papers.intro:
Biological neural systems compute reliably despite stochastic components and variable inputs [1], and do so under tight metabolic and wiring constraints [2, 3]. But these systems are not perturbation-proof: Classical visual illusions expose the limits of computational mechanisms of biological perception [4]. Artificial neural networks, by contrast, consume vastly more energy [5] and can fail under various perturbations [6, 7, 8, 9]. Do artificial and biological neural networks specialized for the same task share the same failure modes? Linking both has been hard because the systems one can attack with gradients are not biologically wired. To our knowledge, no perceptual illusion has yet been tied to an adversarial stimulus in the same system at the level of a computation both exploit.

Robustness — the ability to maintain reliable computation under perturbations — of a biological neural network can now directly be evaluated with FlyNet [10], a fly visual system model constrained by real synaptic wiring. It was trained on motion detection, an ecologically essential task for the fly, using the Sintel optical flow dataset [11] and recapitulates single-neuron response properties across three decades of experimental research, without training on that data. In artificial networks, robustness is linked to specific architectural features — recurrence [12, 13, 14], global processing [15, 16], and continuous-time dynamics [17, 18]. FlyNet has little of these: it uses continuous-time dynamics but has sparse recurrence and primarily local connectivity, reflecting the predominantly feedforward organization of the fly optic lobe. Any robustness it exhibits might therefore arise from properties other than recurrence or global integration, possibly shaped through evolution under tight metabolic constraints [2, 3]. Does biological wiring contribute to robustness, to efficiency, or to both?

We designed a behaviorally grounded, looming-based collision-detection task to evaluate robustness in both connectome-constrained networks and conventional optic-flow models. We implemented the task in a fully differentiable 3D rendering pipeline, in which textured objects follow parametric trajectories toward the observer. Rather than optimizing perturbations in pixel-space — where they lose effectiveness under geometric transformations [19, 20] — we optimize textures directly in 3D scene space, ensuring physical consistency across frames as objects scale during looming. We evaluate models under both adversarial attacks and common video perturbations (e.g., flicker, fog), and pair each robustness measurement with computational cost in FLOPs per inference to characterize robustness relative to efficiency.

The main contributions of our work are: • A differentiable 3D rendering pipeline for a binary collision detection task (approaching objects that hit or miss the observer) in which adversarial attacks optimize object textures for differentiable motion-perception models. • A direct comparison of gradient-based adversarial attacks and the reverse-phi illusion on the same connectome-constrained, task-optimized model of the fly visual system (FlyNet). • Using counterfactual restoration, we find textures equally far from the training distribution that recover classification accuracy and position and velocity readouts, linking failure to motion-code disruption, not unfamiliar textures. • We identify the computation both perturbations exploit: Adversarial textures and reverse-phi both invert the Hassenstein–Reichardt correlation between radially neighboring inputs, and optimizing this statistic alone is sufficient to induce or reverse classification failure. • We benchmark robustness–efficiency trade-offs across architectures with different inductive biases (recurrence, global signals, continuous-time dynamics) under adversarial attacks and common video perturbations. • We find that FlyNet and sCTRNN have higher robustness per order of magnitude of compute than every other architecture on common video corruptions of the collision-detection task.

papers.title: Good Practices for Measuring the Interfacial Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya Interaction by Brillouin Light Scattering and Magneto-Optical Kerr Effect
papers.abstract: The interfacial Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction (iDMI) is a key ingredient for stabilizing chiral magnetic states, such as skyrmions and chiral domain walls, which are key building blocks for next-generation spintronic technologies. Despite its importance, the quantitative determination of the iDMI constant, $D$, is often plagued by significant discrepancies. This paper establishes a set of good practices for measuring iDMI using two primary techniques: Brillouin Light Scattering (BLS) and the Magneto-Optical Kerr Effect (MOKE). Through the analysis of Co/Pt-based heterostructures, this work provides a comprehensive roadmap for measurement procedures, data evaluation, and uncertainty analysis. Our analysis highlights the crucial role of magnetic parameters used to extract the iDMI constant and propagation of their uncertainties, and the measurement model for enhancing measurement reliability. The proposed methodology provides a practical framework for improving the consistency and reproducibility of iDMI measurements across different laboratories and experimental techniques.

The development of next-generation spintronic technologies, such as racetrack memory and logic-in-memory architectures, relies on the energy-efficient manipulation of chiral magnetic states like chiral domain walls (DWs) and skyrmions [1, 2]. These textures are particularly attractive as information carriers because electric currents can drive them with high efficiency. A fundamental requirement for stabilizing these topological spin structures is the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction (DMI).

These textures are particularly attractive as information carriers because electric currents can drive them with high efficiency. A fundamental requirement for stabilizing these topological spin structures is the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction (DMI).

Originally proposed in the 1950s to explain weak ferromagnetism in bulk antiferromagnets like α\alpha-Fe2O3 [3, 4], the DMI is a key ingredient for non-collinear or helical magnetic states in various systems, including spin glasses, orthoferrites, manganites, and superconducting cuprates [5, 6, 7, 8]. While the DMI often cancels out in bulk materials due to crystal inversion symmetry, a finite contribution emerges when this symmetry is broken. In thin-film heterostructures, symmetry breaking occurs at the interface between a ferromagnet (FM) and a heavy metal (HM) with strong spin-orbit coupling [9]. In these systems, the interaction becomes interfacial in nature (iDMI), therefore its strength DD is inversely proportional to the magnetic layer thickness [10, 9]. The iDMI is crucial for stabilizing Néel-type domain walls with a fixed chirality [11, 12], which are energetically favored over traditional Bloch walls and enable fast current-driven dynamics [13, 14].

However, despite its technological importance, quantitatively determining the iDMI constant DD remains challenging. Recent literature, including our review [15, 16, 17, 18] and our international interlaboratory round-robin comparison conducted across European, US, and Asian metrology and research institutes [19], reports notable discrepancies in DD values for nominally identical material systems, particularly when evaluated using different experimental techniques.

However, despite its technological importance, quantitatively determining the iDMI constant DD remains challenging. Recent literature, including our review [15, 16, 17, 18] and our international interlaboratory round-robin comparison conducted across European, US, and Asian metrology and research institutes [19], reports notable discrepancies in DD values for nominally identical material systems, particularly when evaluated using different experimental techniques.

To address these inconsistencies, this work aims to establish concrete, step-by-step measurement protocols and good practices that minimize uncertainty and maximize interlaboratory reproducibility for measuring iDMI. We focus on two of the most prevalent techniques in the field [18], which were already employed in the round-robin comparison: Brillouin Light Scattering (BLS) and the Magneto-Optical Kerr Effect (MOKE). While BLS relies on the non-reciprocity of spin-wave dispersion [10, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26], MOKE characterizes iDMI through domain wall dynamics within the thermally activated creep regime [27, 28, 29, 30, 31, 32]. While we leave the detailed discussion of quantitative discrepancies between the two methods [19] for future work, here we focus on overcoming common pitfalls in the measurement procedures, data evaluation and uncertainty analysis. Particular key roles are attributed to the magnetic field reversal for BLS and minimum bubble size for MOKE. Furthermore, we determine spatial iDMI statistics, assess their impact on uncertainty, and correlate the results with sample homogeneity, a factor often neglected due to the substantial laboratory time required. Overall, the proposed protocols ensure reliable and reproducible results for both methods and offer a practical roadmap toward the standardized characterization of iDMI in chiral magnetic systems.

To address these inconsistencies, this work aims to establish concrete, step-by-step measurement protocols and good practices that minimize uncertainty and maximize interlaboratory reproducibility for measuring iDMI. We focus on two of the most prevalent techniques in the field [18], which were already employed in the round-robin comparison: Brillouin Light Scattering (BLS) and the Magneto-Optical Kerr Effect (MOKE). While BLS relies on the non-reciprocity of spin-wave dispersion [10, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26], MOKE characterizes iDMI through domain wall dynamics within the thermally activated creep regime [27, 28, 29, 30, 31, 32]. While we leave the detailed discussion of quantitative discrepancies between the two methods [19] for future work, here we focus on overcoming common pitfalls in the measurement procedures, data evaluation and uncertainty analysis. Particular key roles are attributed to the magnetic field reversal for BLS and minimum bubble size for MOKE. Furthermore, we determine spatial iDMI statistics, assess their impact on uncertainty, and correlate the results with sample homogeneity, a factor often neglected due to the substantial laboratory time required. Overall, the proposed protocols ensure reliable and reproducible results for both methods and offer a practical roadmap toward the standardized characterization of iDMI in chiral magnetic systems.

papers.title: The chemical DNA of the Magellanic Clouds -- VII. The lithium abundance in the Small Magellanic Cloud and the discovery of 4 lithium-rich stars
papers.abstract: Measuring lithium abundance in galaxies beyond the Milky Way (MW) remains a challenging task. In these systems, only stars close to the tip of the red giant branch (RGB) are sufficiently bright to be observed spectroscopically.Their A(Li) are expected to be altered by mixing episodes that occur during the stellar evolution, making the interpretation of measured abundances more complex. In this context, we present A(Li) of 209 RGB stars in the Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC),observed with FLAMES@VLT. Approximately one-third of the sample shows a Li line detected at a significance level above 5sigma, while about half of the sample has detections above 3sigma; for the remaining stars, only upper limits can be derived. This sample exhibits a significant star-to-star scatter in A(Li). Using theoretical models, we find that the observed scatter can be likely explained by the combination of 2 effects.First,our stars span a wide range of ages, masses, [Fe/H]. Thermohaline mixing, one of the leading mechanisms proposed to explain the extra mixing occurring at the RGB bump, predicts different levels of A(Li) depletion depending on stellar mass and [Fe/H], naturally contributing to the observed scatter in A(Li). Second, in the SMC, the enrichment in A(Li) driven by novae is expected to occur at lower [Fe/H] than in the MW, because the SMC has experienced a lower star formation efficiency than the MW. This is also supported by the rise of A(Li) with decreasing age, as measured in 3 SMC globular clusters. Furthermore, we report the first identification of 4 low-mass Li-rich giant stars in the SMC, reinforcing the existence of Li-rich stars in extra-galactic systems. All these results demonstrate that A(Li) measured in stars close to the RGB tip, still provide valuable constraints on both stellar/galactic chemical evolution of A(Li) in external galaxies.

For decades the standard interpretation of the Spite plateau was that the measured abundance reflects the abundance of Li produced in the Big Bang nucleosynthesis. This view is in conflict with the value of A(Li) derived from standard Big Bang nucleosynthesis and the baryon-to-photon ratio determined by the Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe and Planck satellites (Pitrou et al. 2018, A(Li)∼\sim2.7 dex,). At higher metallicities than those of the Spite plateau, A(Li) starts to increase up to the meteoritic value (Lodders et al. 2009, A(Li) =3.33 dex,) at solar metallicity and exhibiting a large star-to-star scatter. In fact, additional sources of Li production may operate on long timescales (several Gyr), thus providing fresh Li when [Fe/H] is already high ([Fe/H]>>–0.8 dex). These sources include novae (Starrfield et al. 1978b; D’Antona and Matteucci 1991b), asymptotic giant branch (AGB) stars (Cameron and Fowler 1971), ν\nu process during core-collapse supernovae explosions (Matteucci et al. 1995) and high-energy Galactic cosmic rays (Reeves et al. 1970; Prantzos 2012). Novae in particular are considered an efficient source of Li and are able to explain the rise in A(Li) observed in thin disk stars (Romano et al. 1999; Grisoni et al. 2019; Romano et al. 2021). Usually the upper envelope of A(Li) distribution in the thin disk star is considered as diagnostic of the true A(Li) (Cescutti and Molaro 2019; Romano et al. 2021; Nguyen et al. 2025b, see e.g.), while the large A(Li) star-to-star scatter observed at any evolutionary stage is usually interpreted as depletion caused by stellar interior mixing processes.

A further complication of this complex picture is the existence of a small number of stars with A(Li) that are significantly higher than those of most of the stars at the same evolutionary stage and metallicity. The origin of these rare Li-rich stars (Deepak and Reddy 2019; Martell et al. 2021, ∼\sim1%,) is still debated and they could be explained with internal or external processes. Internal processes require the onset of the Cameron-Fowler mechanism (Cameron 1955; Cameron and Fowler 1971) able of preserving the Li7{}^{7}{\rm Li} produced by the decay of Be7\rm{}^{7}Be. This mechanism can work in low-mass stars whenever a mechanism carries Be7\rm{}^{7}Be to cooler stellar regions. An external channel to create Li-rich stars is the mass transfer process in a binary system where the companion star is able to produce fresh Li through the Cameron-Fowler mechanism. This scenario is usually invoked to explain the existence of metal-poor, low-mass Li-rich stars before the RGB bump where no mechanism are able to onset the Cameron-Fowler mechanism. Another possible mechanism, able to explain the most metal-rich Li-rich stars, is the engulfment of small bodies, i.e. rocky planets, hot Jupiters, and brown dwarfs (Siess and Livio 1999).

A(Li) in external galaxies, in turn, is crucial for understanding (i) whether these systems were born with the same initial A(Li) measured in the Milky Way (MW), and (ii) the role of novae and sources of Li production to the chemical evolution history of galaxies with star formation efficiencies differing from that of the MW. At present, our knowledge of A(Li) outside our Galaxy is extremely limited because of the challenging of these observations. For stellar populations older than ∼\sim1-2 Gyr, the only observable stars are those near the RGB tip, which have already experienced extra-mixing episodes. Such mixing dramatically reduces the surface A(Li), making the Li resonance line at 6707.8 Å virtually absent or undetectable. On the other hand, for younger stellar populations, Li measurements can be carried out, in particular in bright AGB stars and carbon stars (Plez et al. 1993; Smith et al. 1995; Hatzidimitriou et al. 2003, see e.g.), providing information about the recent Li enrichment in external galaxies with an ongoing star formation, e.g. the Magellanic Clouds. papers.title: A large radiatively loud anti-glitch in 1E 2259+586 with a protracted recovery
papers.abstract:
Context. Anti-glitches are rare and enigmatic timing anomalies. High-cadence monitoring has revealed radiatively quiet anti-glitches in several pulsar populations, but radiatively loud anti-glitches and their links to magnetospheric activity remain poorly understood. Aims. We characterize a new, large anti-glitch in the magnetar 1E 2259+586 and compare its phenomenology with other magnetars. Methods. We analyze timing, flux, pulse-profile evolution, and spectra using EP, NICER, and IXPE X-ray observations. Results. We report a 2025 anti-glitch in 1E 2259+586, the largest in this source, with $\Delta
u\approx-1.174(7)	imes10^{-7}$ Hz and $\Delta
u/
u\approx-8.19(4)	imes10^{-7}$. Unlike its 2019 anti-glitch, this event was radiatively loud: the persistent X-ray flux roughly doubled (~106% increase), followed by a recovery exceeding 320 days. The pulse profile changed modestly but significantly: the valley between the main and secondary peaks became shallower and then recovered with the flux. Spectral properties also changed, and Fermi-GBM detected a short soft gamma-ray burst near the event. These features resemble the radiatively loud 2012 anti-glitch. Conclusions. 1E 2259+586 is unique among magnetars: its anti-glitch rate is comparable to normal spin-up glitch rates, and its anti-glitches can be radiatively loud or relatively quiescent. The fractional anti-glitch amplitudes appear to increase monotonically; further verification is needed. Regular monitoring of 1E 2259+586 is essential for understanding anti-glitch mechanisms.

papers.intro:
Magnetars are a rare and extreme class of young, isolated neutron stars. Observationally, they are characterized by long spin periods (P∼1P\sim 1–12​s12\,\mathrm{s}) and large spin-down rates (P˙∼10−13\dot{P}\sim 10^{-13}–10−10​s​s−110^{-10}\,\mathrm{s\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}}). These rotational parameters imply ultra-strong surface dipole magnetic fields (B∼1014B\sim 10^{14}–1015​G10^{15}\,\mathrm{G}) and characteristic ages on the order of a few thousand years (Olausen and Kaspi 2014). Historically, they first appeared under the names of soft gamma-ray repeaters (SGRs) and anomalous X-ray pulsars (AXPs) (Mazets et al. 1979; Fahlman and Gregory 1981). Unlike ordinary radio pulsars, whose emission is powered by the loss of rotational energy, the generally accepted magnetar model posits that both the persistent and transient emissions of magnetars are primarily driven by the decay and instability of their ultra-strong magnetic fields (Thompson and Duncan 1995; Thompson and Duncan 1996). To date, approximately 30 confirmed and candidate magnetars have been cataloged, with a comprehensive and regularly updated listing available in the McGill Magnetar Catalog 11 1 http://www.physics.mcgill.ca/~pulsar/magnetar/main.html (Olausen and Kaspi 2014).

Similar to canonical rotation-powered pulsars (RPPs), magnetars also experience glitches—sudden spin-up of their spin frequency (Dib and Kaspi 2014). Uniquely, however, magnetars appear to be the favored hosts for anti-glitches (sudden spin-down events) (Archibald et al. 2013). Although growing observational data have recently identified this behavior in an accreting ultra-luminous X-ray pulsar (NGC 300 ULX-1) and some RPPs (Ray et al. 2019; Zhou et al. 2024; Tuo et al. 2024; Wang et al. 2025), magnetars remain the most prolific sources of anti-glitches. Moreover, unlike the radiatively quiet behavior typically associated with RPPs, magnetar anti-glitches are generally accompanied by energetic activities such as bursts and profound radiative variations (Archibald et al. 2017; Ge et al. 2024). Furthermore, as the only confirmed origin of fast radio bursts (FRBs) to date (Andersen et al. 2020; Bochenek et al. 2020), magnetars exhibit anti-glitches that appear to be intrinsically linked to FRB emissions (Younes et al. 2023). However, the absolute scarcity of recorded magnetar anti-glitch events severely restricts our understanding of the complex internal structures and radiation mechanisms of these extreme objects.

1E 2259+586, the first AXP identified, exhibits a spin period of approximately 7 s and is spatially associated with the supernova remnant (SNR) CTB 109 (Fahlman and Gregory 1981). Based on its spin-down rate, the inferred surface dipole magnetic field strength is estimated to be 5.9×1013​ G5.9\times 10^{13}\text{\,G}. In 2013, Archibald et al. (2013) reported an anti-glitch in this source, which was accompanied by short X-ray bursts, a significant flux enhancement, and variations in both the first frequency derivative (ν˙\dot{\nu}) and the pulse profile. Additionally, using archival data from the Rossi X-ray Timing Explorer (RXTE), Dib and Kaspi (2014) and İçdem et al. (2012) reported a prominent timing discontinuity that occurred in 2009. If fitted with a standard glitch model, this event similarly yields a negative frequency jump (Δ​ν<0\Delta\nu<0). Furthermore, the 2009 event exhibited significant changes in the pulse profile (detected in an observation), X-ray flux (in two observations), and the frequency derivative (Dib and Kaspi 2014). Strikingly, in 2020, Younes et al. (2020) reported a radiatively quiet anti-glitch from this source, during which neither the pulse profile nor the pulsed flux exhibited any significant alterations.

papers.title: Profinite groups with finite conjugacy classes of commutators
papers.abstract:
It was shown in a recent work by Senise and Shumyatsky that if $G$ is a finite group such that $|x^G|\leq m$ whenever $x$ is a commutator of prime power order, then $G''$ has $m$-bounded order. In this paper, we examine the following question: given a profinite group $G$ such that $|x^G|$ is finite whenever $x$ is a commutator of prime power order, does it follow that $G''$ is finite? We show that, in general, the answer to this is negative. The main result obtained in this paper is the following theorem:
  Let $G$ be a profinite group in which $|x^G|$ is finite whenever $x$ is a commutator of prime power order. Assume that $\pi(G)$ is finite. Then: (1) The second commutator subgroup $G''$ is finite; (2) $G$ has an open normal subgroup of nilpotency class at most $3$.

papers.title: Optimality Guarantees for Minimum Variance Subset Selection via Semidefinite Programming
papers.abstract: Given a set of data points in Euclidean space and a prescribed cardinality $k$, the minimum variance $k$-subset problem asks for $k$ points minimizing their average squared distance from their centroid. We develop a semidefinite programming (SDP) framework for exact recovery and global optimization. First, we show that the natural SDP relaxation fails Slater's condition. Identifying the proper face containing its feasible region yields an equivalent, lower-dimensional, strictly feasible formulation that enjoys strong duality. A primal--dual characterization of optimality then gives geometric necessary and sufficient conditions under which the SDP relaxation is guaranteed to be tight. These conditions reveal how tightness depends on the internal geometry of the selected subset and on its separation from the remaining points. Second, we embed the SDP relaxation in a branch-and-cut algorithm combining first-order optimization, valid inequalities and dimension-reducing branching. Extensive experiments on public data sets, with up to 1,500 points and different values of $k$, show that the method strongly outperforms general-purpose exact solvers as the number of points and cardinality increase.

papers.intro:
Given a set of nn points in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} and an integer 1<k<n1<k<n, the minimum variance kk-subset problem (MVkkSP) asks for kk points minimizing the sum of their squared Euclidean distances to their centroid. An optimal subset is thus the group of kk points of minimum variance, hence the most cohesive one, and its centroid a representative estimated from this group. Both aspects have been studied. Finding kk points that form a small set under a given measure, the variance among others, is a classical problem in computational geometry Aggarwal et al. (1991). In robust statistics, the centroid of an optimal subset is the impartial trimmed mean Gordaliza (1991), a location estimate insensitive to outliers obtained by discarding the n−kn-k observations whose removal minimizes the variance of the remaining ones. These two aspects meet in the analysis of measurement data, where a known number of identical objects is observed under Gaussian noise among unrelated ones. There, an optimal subset identifies these objects, and its centroid is the maximum-likelihood estimate of their common characteristics Kel’manov and Pyatkin (2011).

From an optimization perspective, the MVkkSP can be formulated as a binary quadratic program with a cardinality constraint, and is closely related to several well-studied problems in the literature. In particular, it admits an equivalent formulation as the problem of finding the heaviest kk-subgraph Billionnet et al. (2017); Pereira and da Cunha (2026); Malick and Roupin (2012); Sotirov (2020) in a complete graph whose edge weights are given by the negative squared Euclidean distances between the data points. The MVkkSP is also related to the maximum diversity problem Duarte and Martí (2007); Martí et al. (2010); Martínez-Gavara et al. (2026), which seeks to select kk points that maximize the sum of pairwise distances among them, in contrast to the present problem, which minimizes variance. It is further connected to the minimum sum-of-squares clustering (MSSC) problem Aloise et al. (2012); Piccialli and Sudoso (2025); Sudoso and Aloise (2026), which partitions all data points into clusters and minimizes the sum of within-cluster squared deviations. Unlike MSSC, however, the MVkkSP focuses on selecting a single subset of fixed cardinality, without requiring a partition of the entire dataset.

Its mathematical programming formulation as a binary quadratic program with a cardinality constraint leads to a nonconvex optimization problem whose standard linear relaxations provide weak bounds and lead to large branch-and-bound trees Malick and Roupin (2012); Pereira and da Cunha (2026). These challenges motivate the development of stronger formulations and bounding techniques that better exploit the quadratic structure of the problem. In particular, semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxations have proven effective for a variety of quadratic combinatorial optimization problems, including max-cut Hrga and Povh (2021); Gusmeroli et al. (2022) and clique-related problems Ames (2014); Sudoso (2025), by providing strong bounds that can be embedded in branch-and-bound schemes to tackle large instances.

We study the MVkkSP from both theoretical and algorithmic perspectives, with the goal of solving the problem to global optimality. Our main contributions are as follows.

• We show that the natural SDP relaxation fails Slater’s condition because its affine constraints restrict feasibility to a proper face of the positive semidefinite cone. We explicitly identify this face and perform one facial reduction step, obtaining an equivalent, smaller SDP relaxation that is strictly feasible and satisfies strong duality. • Using strong duality, we derive optimality conditions and translate them into geometric sufficient and necessary conditions for tightness. For a candidate subset whose points are equidistant from its centroid, we prove that the SDP relaxation recovers it when its diameter is smaller than both its separation from the unselected points and the separation among the unselected points. For arbitrary subsets, we introduce an internal shape parameter and an adjusted separation measure that together yield a polynomial-time checkable sufficient condition for exact recovery. We also derive a necessary condition requiring every unselected point to lie sufficiently far from the centroid. • We validate the theory on synthetic instances with progressively perturbed planted solutions. The sufficient condition certifies exact recovery under substantial perturbations, while the necessary condition provides a useful indication of lost planted optimality. • We exploit the facially reduced SDP relaxation algorithmically by embedding it within a branch-and-cut framework. To handle large-scale instances, the SDP relaxation is approximately solved by a first-order method, together with a post-processing procedure that provides valid lower bounds. These bounds are further strengthened by separating valid inequalities and adding them through a cutting-plane scheme. Branching produces child relaxations of the same form and smaller dimension. • We benchmark the exact method on datasets with up to 1,5001{,}500 points across a wide range of dimensions and cardinality parameters. The proposed approach is compared with state-of-the-art general-purpose global optimization solvers and substantially outperforms them on the most challenging instances.

papers.title: Softness is something you also need! Why compliance helps control: information metrics of a passive walker with compliant ankle
papers.abstract:
A great gap in adaptivity, flexibility, and dexterity still exists between intelligent robots, whether they are made of rigid or (partially) compliant components, and their naturally evolved animal and vegetal counterparts. One reason could be of `paradigm' nature. On the one hand, most robots (both rigid and soft) are still designed by following a `Cartesian' approach, with top-down control and a clear mind-body separation. Designing artificial agents on the basis of the principles that we observe in biology is not an easy task. The principles of organization of animals and plants rely on morphological computation and emergence of fit behaviors from loosely coupled networks of embodied agents.
  Modeling and control require radically new approaches. In this paper we briefly recall and explain some seminal mathematical results linking information metrics and dynamics of the agents, already published years ago; we integrate them with some recent methods developed by us and by the community, we highlight some brief remarks about their relevance and we hint to our current and near future work towards finding concrete and efficient ways for the modeling and control of completely or partially compliant artificial agents and for a better understanding of physical intelligence in nature. We present a technical note summarizing phase-space volume calculations for inverted-pendulum and passive-dynamic walking models, following our proposed framework. Starting from the McGeer compass gait, we introduce knee-ankle compliance, foot-rocker effects, and a Ruina-style compass gait with distributed leg inertia. Standard heel-strike maps are derived and used in the estimation of viable phase-space volumes $W(\gamma)$, based on a state-dependent Monte-Carlo and Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces methods. We show how the methods based on RKHS allow deeper and more subtle analysis.

papers.title: On Monotonicity in Mean Field Games Induced by Discount Factor Transformations
papers.abstract: This paper is devoted to the well-posedness of a class of infinite horizon discounted Mean Field Games (MFGs) problems, where both an exponential discount and a so-called cheap control factors are present simultaneously, and scale in a possibly different way. We introduce a new class of transformations of variables, at the level of both the MFG PDE and the corresponding FBSDE systems. We then show how these transformations reveal a new mechanism that generates semiconvexity estimates for the value function and ensures the existence of mean field equilibria, as long as the parameters land in a suitable regime, that we quantitatively describe. This new mechanism demonstrates furthermore how discount factors lead to a source of strong displacement monotonicity for the Lagrangian, without any initial monotonicity assumptions on the running costs. Consequently, in such regimes of parameters uniqueness of solutions manifests. Our approach uses a Lagrangian point of view, which lets us treat general non-separable Lagrangians and both deterministic and idiosyncratic noise driven models in a transparent, unified way. For a specific class of quadratic Lagrangians, using turnpike-type methods, we further obtain an exponential contractivity estimate for the mean field equilibria.

papers.intro:
The theory of Mean Field Games (MFGs) was initiated by Lasry–Lions in [31, 30, 32] on the one hand, and independently by Huang–Malhamé–Caines in [25]. In the following years, some of the pillars of the theory were presented in a series of lectures by P.-L. Lions at Collège de France. The main objective of MFGs is to describe the behaviour of limits of Nash equilibria associated to symmetric stochastic differential games when the number of agents tends to infinity. As such, an MFG is typically described by the value function of a typical infinitesimal representative agent, and the time evolution of the overall agent distribution. This paper deals with infinite horizon discounted MFGs, and as follows we present the mathematical formulations of the models.

papers.title: On the Spectral Estimation of VARMA Processes
papers.abstract: We consider the problem of estimating the power spectral density of a Vector-valued Autoregressive Moving-Average (VARMA) process. A well-established approach to accomplishing this task consists of formulating a moment problem that selects the spectral density maximizing an entropy-like index while matching certain moments of the underlying process. However, existing methods assume that the moving-average (MA) component is either fixed or scalar, thereby reducing the class of ARMA models over which the optimal spectral density is sought. In this paper, we propose a new moment problem, based on the notion of transportation entropy, for learning the spectral density of a VARMA process without fixing the MA component or restricting it to be scalar.
papers.intro:
Autoregressive Moving-Average (ARMA) processes have wide applications in different domains, including systems and control [1, 2], signal processing [3], time series analysis [4], and finance [5]. From the perspective of identification and control, these processes have rational spectra which can approximate any continuous spectral density if the order of the model is sufficiently large. Moreover, standard realization theory can convert the ARMA model into a state-space form which is convenient, e.g., for the purpose of filtering.

Autoregressive Moving-Average (ARMA) processes have wide applications in different domains, including systems and control [1, 2], signal processing [3], time series analysis [4], and finance [5]. From the perspective of identification and control, these processes have rational spectra which can approximate any continuous spectral density if the order of the model is sufficiently large. Moreover, standard realization theory can convert the ARMA model into a state-space form which is convenient, e.g., for the purpose of filtering.

It is often the case that the spectral density of ARMA processes must be identified from data. For scalar processes, a well-posed problem of jointly estimating the AR and MA parameters was formulated in [6, 7] as maximizing the entropy of the process with equality constraints of covariance and cepstral matching (i.e., the moment equations). The sample version of the latter can readily be obtained from a finite-length realization of the underlying process. It was shown that the correspondence between the covariances and the AR parameters is a smooth bijection, and the same holds for the correspondence between the cepstral coefficients and the MA parameters. The cepstral coefficients are also called logarithmic moments because they are the Fourier coefficients of log⁡Φ\log\Phi where Φ\Phi (assumed to be positive) denotes the spectral density of the process.

For vector-valued ARMA (VARMA) processes, the model parameters become matrices, and the estimation problem becomes more challenging. A number of attempts have been made to extend the Maximum Entropy framework to the multivariate case. The first setup considered the case where the MA part is fixed a priori, and certain divergence indices are minimized subject to matricial covariance constraints; see, e.g., [8, 9, 10]. However, if we want to jointly estimate the matricial AR and MA parameters from the data, the standard Maximum Entropy method [11] works only with scalar logarithmic moments [12, 13, 1], bringing about VARMA models with scalar MA parts, i.e., the MA parameters have the form of a scalar times the identity matrix. We remark that the scalar logarithmic moments of a vector-valued process with a matricial spectral density Φ\Phi (assumed to be positive definite) were first defined in [14] as the Fourier coefficients of logdetΦ\log\det\Phi. These quantities were utilized in the spectral estimation of VARMA process in later works that are cited above. It is worth noting that assuming the MA component to be fixed or scalar reduces the class of ARMA models over which the optimal spectral density is sought, potentially resulting in a spectral estimator that is not always satisfactory.

One may be tempted to use the matricial logarithm for positive definite matrices to define a kind of matricial cepstral coefficients and hope to generalize the multivariate spectral estimation method with the scalar logarithmic moments. As we will see, however, it is not possible to go through the Lagrange dual analysis of the corresponding Maximum Entropy problem, because the optimal primal variable (which is a function) cannot be expressed in terms of the dual variable. Notice that a successful dual analysis is the key to obtaining a finite-dimensional dual problem, which serves as a practical tool for estimating the parameters characterizing the spectral density. The same happens if we consider the more general notion of ν\nu-entropy (parametrized by a positive integer ν\nu) proposed in [15, 16] for the scalar case.

Hence, the major obstacle in estimating a VARMA process by means of a moment problem is to find a suitable definition of the cepstral coefficients for a vector-valued process, and this is precisely the motivation behind the current work. Inspired by recent results on optimal transportation between Gaussian processes [17, 18, 8], we define a new concept of matricial cepstral coefficients using a spectral factor WW of the spectral density of the process. For this reason, they are termed “WW-cepstral coefficients”. These coefficients are naturally compatible with the transportation entropy derived from the transportation (Hellinger) distance between two spectral densities. We show that this new Maximum Entropy formulation is amenable to Lagrange dual analysis, and the dual problem becomes well-posed after incorporating an appropriate design of regularization. Then we derive a spectral estimator, based on the proposed Maximum Entropy problem, which uses only a finite sample path of the underlying process. The advantage of our VARMA spectral estimator is illustrated by numerical experiments.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Sec. II introduces the VARMA spectral estimation problem and two possible Maximum Entropy formulations, and explains the difficulty. Sec. III introduces the transportation entropy and the WW-cepstral coefficients and formulates the new Maximum Entropy problem. A detailed dual analysis is carried out. Sec. IV regularizes the dual optimization problem and investigates its well-posedness property. Sec. V provides a spectral estimation procedure based on the regularized dual problem and a finite sample path of a random process, with a discussion of the statistical consistency of the estimator. Sec. VI illustrates our VARMA spectral estimator in comparison with some alternative ones through numerical simulations. Sec. VII concludes the paper.

papers.title: When Reasoning looks like Hidden Understanding: How Chain-of-Thought Fosters Anthropomorphism, Perceptions of Epistemic Superiority, and Cognitive Deference
papers.abstract: As AI-based products permeate society, specifically systems using generative models, a belief system is emerging about what these products are and what they can and cannot do. One common belief concerns the perception of the form of language as evidence of 'understanding' language. As these generative models reproduce linguistic patterns rather than understand meaning, interpreting these patterns as evidence of understanding is a misattribution. This misconception is extended by the notion that generative models can 'explain their reasoning.' Anecdotally, these misconceptions which mistake the form of language for its meaning are driving cognitive deference to AI systems in a way that displaces human agency. Such mistakes involve attributions of cognitive properties to the system, allowing them to be treated like intentional 'minds'. Importantly, perceived epistemic authority and superiority make that 'mind' worth deferring to. Anthropomorphism in tandem with epistemic authority and superiority, we argue, increases the risk that users generalise from narrow task performance to broader competencies, committing the "fallacy of composition". This paper explores misconceptions of Chain of Thought (CoT) reasoning as sufficient transparent 'explanation'. We explore how anthropomorphism acts as a vehicle for cognitive deference of decision-making and perceptions of epistemic superiority in AI systems. Finally, we explore CoT's ramifications using medicine as an example. Taken together, we conclude that explainability operationalised through CoT is highly problematic and undercuts the very ethical principles it is intended to serve. While CoT may be valuable for improving output accuracy and moderation, we suggest that the practice of asking models to provide user facing reasons for their outputs should be actively discouraged, and AI literacy training should explicitly caution against its use.

papers.intro:
Through the use of terminology from brain and cognitive sciences, artificial intelligence (AI) systems are often mistakenly granted biological and cognitive qualities, distorting system understanding and fueling anthropomorphism. Meanwhile, fields that study how the brain enables cognition and behaviour borrow concepts from information and computation, reducing the brain’s complexity to that of a calculating machine (Baria and Cross, 2021). The ‘computer is a brain simile’ is emblematic of broader pattern of conceptual borrowing to deal with arising explanandum (Floridi and Nobre, 2024). In innovative fields lacking a settled vocabulary, it is generally reasonable to import terms and explanans from other disciplines to describe new phenomena. Such borrowing is useful, but never neutral. Concepts carry additional information from their original contexts, assumptions, and metaphors. When transferred across domains, they can clarify and connect ideas, but they can also introduce hidden assumptions and misleading associations. Conceptual borrowing risks making machines seem cognitive, allowing for over trust, anthropomorphism, misplaced responsibility, and distorted views of both AI and cognition.

When transferred across domains, they can clarify and connect ideas, but they can also introduce hidden assumptions and misleading associations. Conceptual borrowing risks making machines seem cognitive, allowing for over trust, anthropomorphism, misplaced responsibility, and distorted views of both AI and cognition.

Chain of Thought (CoT) is an example of conceptual borrowing, as the term is used to reflect human ‘reasoning’ and ‘thinking’. CoT technically refers to the intermediate tokens a reasoning model (e.g., o3, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Gemini 3, DeepSeek R1, Grok 3) generates before its final output. These models are trained to generate CoT tokens that are semantically related to rational, logical, stepwise responses, which are subsequently used to condition the tokens in the final output context. The practical purpose of CoT is to give the model additional intermediate computational space. CoT thereby helps the model expand, correct, or disambiguate imperfect user prompts, improve final-output benchmark performance and accuracy, and make outputs easier to steer, evaluate, and moderate (Chen et al., 2026; Wei et al., 2022). It is contentious whether these steps correspond to reasoning or the model’s actual causal processes which generated the specific output at all – a problem that was already apparent in more traditional machine learning approaches (Ghassemi et al., 2021). Studies show that CoT is not always faithful because it may not meaningfully represent the actual process the model used to derive its final output (Turpin et al., 2023; Anthropic, 2025a; Chua and Evans, 2025).

CoT technically refers to the intermediate tokens a reasoning model (e.g., o3, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Gemini 3, DeepSeek R1, Grok 3) generates before its final output. It is contentious whether these steps correspond to reasoning or the model’s actual causal processes which generated the specific output at all – a problem that was already apparent in more traditional machine learning approaches (Ghassemi et al., 2021). Studies show that CoT is not always faithful because it may not meaningfully represent the actual process the model used to derive its final output (Turpin et al., 2023; Anthropic, 2025a; Chua and Evans, 2025).

However, CoT is not just a technical feature; it is widely used as a communicative interface, presenting a representation of the model’s process in familiar higher level “steps,” “reasoning,” and “thought.” In real-world applications, users often do not see the full CoT. It may be hidden or summarised by a smaller model or display only brief status labels such as “reflecting”, “planning”, “analysing”, or “evaluating”. These summaries are seemingly user-facing interface devices, not necessarily faithful records of the model’s internal causal process. This framing may make outputs seem more transparent and trustworthy, even when the generated explanation is partial, filtered, or unfaithful. Further, explanations that are partial or filtered can determine degree of belief, such that these types of explanations require imagination for application and subsequently inflate confidence in the explanation (Koehler, 1991). Thus, CoT matters not only because it may misdescribe how models work, but because it can shape how users interpret, trust, and attribute cognitive capacities to systems.

If CoT, and user facing summaries of CoT, can falsely present outputs as the product of human-like reasoning, then its use in widely adopted systems may contribute to the acceptance of broader anthropomorphising practices now common across the industry. Many companies continue to overtly anthropomorphise tools without signs of developing accessible technical communication or novel explanations that advance concepts from beyond brain and cognitive sciences (Anthropic, 2025b; Anthropic, 2025a; OpenAI, 2026). Some speculate that this narrative is an explicit marketing strategy deployed to increase user trust, perceived intelligence, and product familiarity, while obscuring technical limitations, accountability, and the underlying nature of the systems (Bender and Hanna, 2025; Inie et al., 2026).

Ethics frameworks have unintentionally played into the narrative by taking the terminology supplied by computer science (e.g., ‘explainability’) at face value, allowing the metaphor to be obfuscated (Floridi et al., 2018; Amann et al., 2020). The ethical motivation for explainability has stemmed from commitments to informed consent and accountability, advocating for the assurance of a user understanding the reasoning behind a particular piece of information that they would use to guide their decision-making. In the context of informed consent, some have argued that a person’s informed consent requires that person’s knowledge of the stepwise process by which an AI system provided a specific output (Amann et al., 2020). Notwithstanding the valid moral motivations for seeking such assurance, the problem is that post hoc explanations of all kinds have never been conclusively proven to be reliable as a means of consistently demonstrating the computational process by which a particular output is reached (Ghassemi et al., 2021). All of these problems have been present throughout the modern history of traditional AI systems; present generative models now substantially worsen a problem that was never actually resolved.

papers.title: Bi-Hamiltonian structure and conserved quantities of the Yajima-Oikawa-Newell system
papers.abstract:
We study the Hamiltonian and bi-Hamiltonian structure of the Yajima-Oikawa-Newell (YON) system, an integrable model of long wave-short wave interaction depending on two real parameters $\alpha$ and $ eta$, which reduces to the Yajima-Oikawa system for $\alpha=0$ and to the Newell system for $ eta=0$. For $\alpha
eq0$, a constant shift of the long wave maps the YON system into the Newell system, for which two nonlocal Hamiltonian operators are known. We show that, for $\alpha
eq0$, the system admits no local Hamiltonian operator homogeneous in its natural grading and polynomial in $ eta$. A nonlocal gauge transformation built on the potential of the long wave makes the first of the known operators local for a single value of its parameter: the transformed system is Hamiltonian, for every $\alpha
eq0$ and every $ eta$, with respect to a local, non-degenerate Poisson operator, which is the Lie-Poisson structure of the $\mathfrak{sl}(2)$ current algebra. From a recursion operator advancing the hierarchy by two steps, given in explicit weakly nonlocal form, we construct a second, weakly nonlocal Hamiltonian structure, whose nonlocal tail is generated by the three autonomous Lie point symmetries of the system, and prove that both structures are compatible. Since the recursion operator admits no square root and the first structure has no Casimirs, the Lenard-Magri chain splits into two families, seeded by the two simplest conserved quantities. Every flow of both families is local, and all the corresponding Hamiltonians are in involution. As by-products, we relate the Lie point symmetries of the system to its conserved quantities via Noether's theorem, and obtain the conserved densities in closed form by asymptotic diagonalisation of the Lax pair.

Some conservation laws of Eqs. (1) were obtained in [7] by means of the multiplier method of Anco and Bluman [14, 15], as no variational formulation of the YON system was known. For its two reductions, on the other hand, a Hamiltonian theory is available. The YO system (2) is well known to be bi-Hamiltonian, being a reduction of the constrained KP hierarchy [16, 17], and Liu [18] showed that the Newell system (3) is a modification of it, the two systems being related by a Miura-type map, and gave two Hamiltonian operators for the Newell hierarchy. Both of them are nonlocal in the variables (S,S∗,L)(S,S^{*},L): the first one is weakly nonlocal, with a tail built on the phase symmetry, whereas the second one involves inverses of differential operators. To the best of our knowledge, these results have not been related to the YON system, and it is not known whether the nonlocality of these operators can be avoided. The purpose of this paper is to address both questions.

As we will see, the nonlocality is unavoidable in the original variables, but it is not intrinsic. For α≠0\alpha\neq 0, the shift of LL mentioned above reduces the YON system to the Newell system, so that the operators of [18] apply to it. We first show that the natural local candidates, namely operators that are homogeneous in the grading of the system and compatible with its U⁡(1)U(1) invariance, all fail to be Poisson as soon as α≠0\alpha\neq 0. A phase gauge on the potential of the long wave, very much in the spirit of the gauge transformations relating the members of the derivative NLS family [19, 20, 21, 22, 23], then turns the first operator of [18] into a local one, and it does so for a single value of the gauge parameter. In that gauge the operator is linear in the fields, and it is in fact the Lie–Poisson structure of the 𝔰​𝔩​(2)\mathfrak{sl}(2) current algebra, which makes its Jacobi identity manifest. Taking this local, non-degenerate operator as the first structure, we construct a recursion operator for the hierarchy in explicit, weakly nonlocal form and, from it, a second Hamiltonian structure, also weakly nonlocal, which lies one step above the pair of [18] and whose nonlocal tail is generated by the three autonomous Lie point symmetries of the system. The resulting picture has some features that are worth pointing out from the start. The recursion operator advances the hierarchy by two steps rather than one, as in the YO case, and admits no square root, so that the hierarchy splits into two families; and, since the first structure has no Casimirs, the Lenard–Magri chain cannot be started, as usual, from a Casimir, but has to be seeded by the two simplest conserved quantities.

papers.title: Conformal Risk Control for QoT-Aware Lightpath Feasibility Under Technology-Driven Domain Shift
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML)-based regression models support operational decision-making in optical networks but typically expose only point predictions, which carry no statistically controlled information about their reliability. This paper proposes a post-hoc conformal risk control (CRC) framework that keeps a pretrained AI/ML regressor fixed, provides a finite-sample guarantee on uncertainty band miscoverage, and maps the band to operational decisions through policy rules. The guarantee applies to interval miscoverage, while decision-error rates are evaluated empirically. We instantiate the framework for quality of transmission (QoT)-aware lightpath (LP) feasibility assessment, in which a regressor predicts optical signal-to-noise ratio (OSNR) under domain shifts caused by fiber, amplifier, and switching upgrades. Feature shift contribution scores identify the LP features whose relation to QoT changes the most across a technology transition, and two policies translate the bands into feasibility decisions, allowing operators to tune the trade-off between conservatively rejecting or aggressively accepting LP realizations. Experiments on open space-division multiplexing (SDM) QoT datasets over the CONUS topology show that, for a target coverage of 90%, the uncertainty bands meet the target in all 170 trials spanning 17 domain shifts and ten calibration-test partitions, whereas a source-only quantile regression (QR) baseline meets it in none. Under severe shifts, the efficiency-oriented (EO) policy empirically improves zero-shot (ZS) feasibility-decision accuracy from about 85% to above 99%, approaching a transfer learning (TL) policy while avoiding retraining. The framework provides finite-sample control of uncertainty band miscoverage for regression-based optical network decision support, with potential applications beyond QoT-aware LP feasibility assessment.

papers.intro:
Optical transport networks are evolving toward increasingly agile and heterogeneous infrastructures, driven by coherent transceivers, flexible-grid elastic optical networking, and emerging SDM technologies [1, 2]. These advances expand the control-plane design space by introducing degrees of freedom in routing, modulation-format selection, and spectrum/spatial/waveband allocation, but they also intensify the need for fast and reliable physical-layer feasibility assessment [3]. In particular, QoT estimation for unestablished LP is a key enabler of impairment-aware provisioning, reconfiguration, and monitoring in dynamic optical networks [4, 5], and AI/ML regressors can approximate analytical QoT models with high accuracy when detailed physical-layer modeling is too expensive or impractical.

Optical transport networks are evolving toward increasingly agile and heterogeneous infrastructures, driven by coherent transceivers, flexible-grid elastic optical networking, and emerging SDM technologies [1, 2]. These advances expand the control-plane design space by introducing degrees of freedom in routing, modulation-format selection, and spectrum/spatial/waveband allocation, but they also intensify the need for fast and reliable physical-layer feasibility assessment [3]. In particular, QoT estimation for unestablished LP is a key enabler of impairment-aware provisioning, reconfiguration, and monitoring in dynamic optical networks [4, 5], and AI/ML regressors can approximate analytical QoT models with high accuracy when detailed physical-layer modeling is too expensive or impractical.

Operational deployment, however, demands more than the strong average accuracy typically observed during model development [6]. A trustworthy model must also remain reliable when deployment conditions depart from the training data, and expose how much confidence each individual prediction deserves. Network evolution stresses both requirements at once. Differences between training and operational conditions arise from unintentional processes, such as component aging, and from intentional interventions, such as technology upgrades [7]. The latter are usually the more demanding case, because an upgrade in fiber, amplifier, or switching technology modifies not only the distribution of the LP descriptors, but also their underlying relationship with QoT. Such a source–target domain shift silently erodes the accuracy of a regressor trained on the pre-upgrade infrastructure, and a point prediction gives no signal that it has occurred.

Existing work has studied accuracy loss under domain shift and the reliability of individual predictions separately, and neither line of work assesses their impact on operational decisions. Domain shift mitigation methods recover target-domain accuracy, through retraining or adapting the model [8, 9, 10, 11], but require the ability to update the predictor and sufficient target-domain data to update it. Uncertainty-aware methods, in turn, are frequently model-specific or heuristic [12, 13, 14, 15, 16], and report a confidence value rather than committing to an operational choice. Complementing them, CP (CP) equips black-box AI/ML models with distribution-free uncertainty estimates under mild assumptions [17], applied post-hoc using held-out labeled target-domain dataset and without retraining, while its connection to CRC [18] extends conformal methods from coverage guarantees to broader, user-defined risk-control objectives. However, to the best of our knowledge, no prior work in the literature translates a risk-controlled uncertainty band into optical network decisions, precisely when a trained AI/ML model is reused after fiber, amplifier, or switching upgrades.

This paper closes that gap by proposing a post-hoc CRC decision-support framework that leaves the deployed regressor untouched, organized in three layers: (i) a fixed AI/ML regressor, (ii) a CRC layer that converts each point prediction into a risk-controlled uncertainty band from a small target-domain calibration set, and (iii) a policy layer that maps the prediction and band into an operational decision. First, we strengthen the statistical foundations of the conformal band. Whereas [19] sets its width to an empirical quantile of the calibration residuals, which controls coverage on average over calibration sets, in this work we select it through an LTT (LTT)-based CRC procedure [20] from an upper confidence bound on the miscoverage risk that holds uniformly over a grid of candidate widths. This yields the guarantee that, even with the specific and possibly small calibration set available, the selected band keeps the probability that the true QoT value falls outside the band below α\alpha, with confidence of at least 1−δ1-\delta. The statement remains valid even though the width is selected using that same calibration set. Second, we broaden the evaluation to 17 source–target scenarios grouped into six shift families, covering fiber, amplifier, and switching upgrades in isolation and in combination. While the transition studied in [19] changes fiber and amplifier jointly, our isolated evaluation results identify the amplifier as the dominant contributor. Third, we characterize each shift using feature shift contribution scores that identify the LP features whose relation to QoT changes the most, and we delimit what such feature-level scores can and cannot reveal about the impact on the deployed model. Fourth, we map the risk-controlled band to feasibility decisions through two policies, RA (RA), which prioritizes avoiding unsafe acceptance, and EO, which prioritizes avoiding overly conservative rejection. Their decision-error rates are assessed empirically.

papers.title: One Table, Many Queries: Benchmarking Generalist Tabular Models Across Generation, Imputation, and Prediction
papers.abstract: Generation, imputation, and prediction query different aspects of the same tabular distribution, but are usually evaluated separately. This leaves unclear which capabilities they share, how their training objectives interact, and whether one model can perform all three well. We introduce the One Table Benchmark (\ours{}), spanning 56 datasets, 46 registered methods, and 20 capability axes under aligned data splits and explicit task contracts. We compare task ranks on aligned support, train five backbones under all seven non-empty objective combinations on five datasets with three seeds, and contrast fixed-model profiles with specialist portfolios. Rank comparisons connect imputation and prediction through numerical recovery and dependence preservation, and link generation to both through predictive utility; distributional fidelity follows different, sometimes opposing, rankings. Objective interventions show the largest pooled gains from including the recipient's own objective. Generation has the broadest coverage of positive pooled auxiliary effects, while prediction shows potential to improve imputation and synthetic-data utility, with responses that vary across backbones. Cross-addition effects reveal that objective benefits need not add and depend on the objectives already present. Fixed-model comparisons expose corresponding utility--fidelity trade-offs: some generalists surpass specialist portfolios on utility, while fidelity continues to favor specialization. Frozen foundation models show strong prediction and numerical point imputation, together with promising synthetic-data utility, highlighting their potential across all three tasks. These findings motivate unified tabular models that share useful conditional information while improving categorical reconstruction and faithful joint sampling.

papers.intro:
Generation, imputation, and prediction use different aspects of the same tabular distribution. Generation produces complete records, imputation recovers missing features from observed information, and prediction infers a designated target. Each task has its own benchmarks and modeling traditions (Yang et al., 2024; Khan et al., 2025; Erickson et al., 2025), yet their common statistical foundation suggests opportunities for sharing learned capabilities. Understanding these relationships matters for building models that can serve several uses of a table, and for deciding when a task should benefit from training on another.

The conditional-query view makes this connection explicit: generation queries the joint distribution, while imputation and prediction query feature and target conditionals. Models increasingly support several of these interfaces (Ivanov et al., 2019; Jolicoeur-Martineau et al., 2024; Zhang and others, 2025), but existing task-wise evaluations provide limited insight into which capabilities are shared. Appendix reviews related benchmarks and generalist models.

papers.title: Data-Efficient Unlearning-Based Backdoor Detection in Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Detecting backdoor attacks in federated learning (FL) is challenging because malicious clients can manipulate the global model while preserving main-task performance. Static model-update statistics may therefore fail to clearly distinguish malicious from benign clients. Unlearning-based detectors instead probe client models through loss ascent on clean server data, but detection performance degrades with scarce proxy data. We propose Screening via Unlearning Response Analysis (SURA), a data-efficient detector. SURA reuses the same small clean proxy across multiple train-mode loss-ascent steps, strengthening client responses without additional clean data. For federated vision models with batch normalization (BN), repeated probing also changes BN running statistics and can confound endpoint measurements. SURA addresses this by restoring the shared pre-probe BN state only at readout while preserving the parameter changes induced by probing. This separates repeated probing from response measurement and removes BN drift and the interaction between parameter and BN-state changes from the readout. Across six backdoor attacks, SURA uses only 10 clean server images, outperforms methods under the same data budget, and approaches the robustness obtained with much larger proxy sets.
papers.intro:
Federated learning (FL) enables multiple clients to collaboratively train a shared model while keeping their raw data local [1]. However, because the server cannot directly inspect clients’ local training, malicious clients can poison their data or manipulate model updates to implant backdoors [2]. Backdoor attacks are particularly difficult to detect because they preserve performance on benign inputs while inducing attacker-chosen behavior on inputs containing an attack trigger pattern [3]. Existing server-side defenses commonly examine submitted updates using distances, similarities, clustering, or robust aggregation [4, 5, 6, 7]. However, because backdoored updates can remain statistically similar to benign ones, such update-based signals may provide limited separation between malicious and benign clients [8]. To overcome this limitation, we exploit unlearning-based detection that actively probes each client model with labeled, trigger-free server data (a clean proxy) and identifies suspicious clients from differences in their loss responses [9]. Fig. 1 illustrates this low-data setting and its impact on unlearning-based screening.
