We use probing to denote clean-loss ascent on the proxy and readout to denote the subsequent loss measurement. An endpoint readout measures loss after the final probe step. With few proxy images, shallow probing may be insufficiently discriminative, motivating deeper probing. For the vision models with batch normalization (BN) considered here, deeper train-mode probing also updates BN running means and variances [10]. As a result, the endpoint response mixes probe-induced parameter changes with BN-buffer drift and their interaction.

This leads to two core challenges. 1 Discriminative probing under scarce data. The probe must elicit sufficiently discriminative loss responses from only a handful of clean server samples without relying on a large proxy set. 2 Comparable response measurement. Client responses should be measured under a common BN reference rather than client-specific post-probe states. To address these challenges, we propose Screening via Unlearning Response Analysis (SURA). SURA first applies repeated loss-ascent probing to elicit informative client responses. It then restores the shared pre-probe global BN statistics only when measuring those responses, while preserving the parameter changes induced by probing. This design separates the probing process from the state used for response measurement and provides a common BN reference across clients. The separation allows deeper probing to amplify weak responses without forcing response measurement to inherit the BN state accumulated during probing. Our scope is limited to models with BN running statistics; extending the principle to architectures without stateful BN remains future work.

papers.title: Testing isotropy of random fields with values in abstract spaces
papers.abstract: We study the problem of testing isotropy, i.e., distributional invariance under orthogonal transformations, for random fields taking values in abstract spaces. We propose a novel approach based on computing local directional characteristics, which are uniformly distributed under the assumption of isotropy. Our work is motivated by an application in material science, where we are testing the isotropy of function-valued porosity profiles of paper sheets, whose morphology is resolved by $\mu$-CT imaging. While considerably more general, the presented methodology is competitive with existing isotropy tests for real-valued random fields.

papers.intro:
A random field is stationary if its distribution is shift-invariant, and it is isotropic if its distribution is invariant under any orthogonal transformation (rotation or reflection) at the origin. If the random field is both, stationary and isotropic, we call it motion-invariant. For the analysis of spatial data, the assumption of motion-invariance allows for strong simplifications (Cressie, 2015). In particular, the covariance between two locations depends only on their Euclidean distance. Consequently, several statistical tests have been proposed in the literature to decide whether the assumption of isotropy for random fields is justified by the data. See Weller and Hoeting (2016) for an overview of nonparametric tests. In recent years, further tests have been developed, including tests based on the excursion set of a given random field (Abaach et al., 2025; Azaïs et al., 2025), spectral domain tests (Weller and Hoeting, 2020; Eckle et al., 2026), and also isotropy tests on the sphere (Sahoo et al., 2019).

A critical gap is that existing literature addresses primarily real-valued random fields. While multivariate extensions are scarce (see e.g. Jona-Lasinio (2001)) there is currently a lack of methodology for high-dimensional or non-Euclidean data. Driven by an application in which we analyze local porosity profiles in paper-based materials represented as point-wise functional data, we aim to bridge this gap by introducing an isotropy test designed for random fields with values in abstract spaces. The analysis of local porosity in paper-based materials is of particular interest for industrial applications because it influences effective physical properties such as air permeance (Woudberg et al., 2018; Leitl et al., 2023). In general, porosity profiles are frequently used descriptors for analyzing the morphology of many functional materials, such as batteries (Hosseinzadeh et al., 2018; Dodell et al., 2025), fuel cells (Banerjee et al., 2016), or cement (Rimmelé et al., 2008).

papers.title: Decay rates for monotone operator flows in the space of probability measures
papers.abstract: Motivated by the mean-field dynamics of large populations of interacting agents, we study the long-time behavior of flows driven by monotone demicontinuous operators on the Wasserstein space. For cocoercive operators, we prove that the flow converges to a zero of the operator and that the operator residual and the metric speed decay as $o(t^{-1/2})$, so that the population comes to rest (the agents asymptotically stop moving). We also consider Tikhonov regularized flows of merely monotone demicontinuous operators and show that the operator residual and the metric speed tend to zero, with rate $O(1/t)$ when the Tikhonov parameter is $\alpha/t$ with $\alpha\geq 1$, and that the trajectory converges to the zero of minimal second moment, which is a Dirac mass, so that the agents reach consensus (all agents reach the same point). Finally, we study a discrete analogue for nonexpansive operators and show that the generated sequence converges to the fixed point closest to a reference Dirac mass; this fixed point is again a Dirac mass, so that consensus is also reached under this scheme. The main arguments rely on a specially tailored superposition principle, which represents the flow as a curve in a fixed Hilbert space of random trajectories, where the crucial estimates are derived.

papers.title: AI Alignment Is Neither Solvable nor Sufficient
papers.abstract: Humans and AI systems increasingly act within the same social and economic environments. Alignment, the goal of ensuring that AI systems act in accordance with human values, is widely regarded as a central challenge for ensuring that AI benefits society while avoiding harm. We argue that this endeavor is misguided. First, alignment is not well defined, as it presumes a sufficiently stable and identifiable set of human intentions or values. Second, where a concrete notion of alignment can be specified, it is not solvable. Third, where alignment appears solvable, solving it would not necessarily mitigate the negative consequences of AI. A key reason is that alignment is typically framed as a property of individual AI systems, while the resulting hybrid societies of humans and machines are complex systems shaped by interactions and feedback loops. Emergent risks, and not only those posed by individual misaligned systems, are therefore likely to become a major source of harm. We conclude that AI safety is an ongoing challenge and not a problem that can be solved once and for all by verifying a particular model property.

papers.title: Koszul duality and determinant formulas for affine hyperplane arrangements
papers.abstract: For real affine hyperplane arrangements, we prove Lam's determinant conjecture for the inverse Varchenko matrix restricted to bounded chambers. The proof combines Lam's comparison of twisted intersection forms with the period determinant formula of Varchenko, Loeser-Sabbah and Douai-Terao. For normal crossing arrangements, we introduce the taut path algebra and the chamber intersection algebra and establish a Koszul duality between them, yielding an explicit multivariate formula for the inverse Varchenko matrix. After specializing the parameters to $q$, its restriction to bounded chambers is a scalar multiple of the $q$-intersection matrix, proving a determinant conjecture of the authors. We also discuss how the Koszul duality results generalize to affine oriented matroids.

papers.title: From Search to Decision: How Post-Training Shapes Information-Seeking Capabilities in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Information seeking in large language model (LLM) systems increasingly involves decisions about when to acquire information, where to search, and how to evaluate and use evidence. Recent post-training methods have improved several such behaviors, but their objectives and evaluations span different tasks and system settings. This paper organizes research around six interrelated information-seeking capabilities and examines the learning signals, optimization methods, update loci, and credit-assignment mechanisms used to develop them. We synthesize empirical progress in targeted behaviors, end-to-end performance, search control, and generalization. Existing studies report gains in retrieval routing, query refinement, multi-tool exploration, evidence-grounded reasoning, and resource-aware search, although the scope of behavioral evidence varies across capabilities. We identify open challenges in estimating prospective retrieval utility, coordinating information-seeking decisions, and adapting to unfamiliar retrieval environments, and discuss evaluation practices for interpreting future progress.

papers.intro:
Large language models (LLMs) increasingly interact with external information sources to address knowledge-intensive tasks. In such systems, retrieval is no longer necessarily a fixed preprocessing step: models may decide whether to search, formulate queries, explore sources, evaluate and integrate evidence, and revise their next actions in response to observations (Asai et al., 2024; Jin et al., 2025). These interrelated decisions constitute information-seeking capabilities that can be shaped through post-training. Recent work has made progress on several of these capabilities. Retrieval-trigger and utility-aware training improve acquisition decisions (Labruna et al., 2025; Zou et al., 2026); query refinement and multi-tool coordination address information needs and exploration (Chen et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2025); evidence-grounded methods target support judgments and integration (Huang et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2025); and budget-aware policies improve the efficiency of iterative search (Sun et al., 2026b). These advances employ different supervision signals, optimization objectives, and update targets, making their contributions difficult to compare solely through downstream task scores. Existing surveys have examined retrieval–reasoning interactions (Li et al., 2025b; Wei et al., 2026), deep-search architectures and workflows (Xi et al., 2025), and reinforcement learning for agentic search and deep research (Lin et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025a). Related work has also reviewed credit assignment in agentic reinforcement learning (Zhang, 2026). However, these surveys primarily organize existing research around system architectures, retrieval processes, or optimization techniques, leaving the learning and empirical progress of individual information-seeking capabilities less systematically examined. To address this gap, we provide a capability-centered synthesis that connects the decisions models learn to make, the post-training mechanisms used to improve them, and the empirical evidence supporting their improvement. This perspective enables a systematic comparison of learning progress across capabilities, evaluation settings, and information environments.

papers.title: MEOW: Medical Open-World Interactive Segmentation
papers.abstract: In open-world recognition, machine learning models not only make predictions on unknown structures ("generalized open-set"), but also continually learn and improve from those predictions over time. Interactive segmentation, despite its access to user feedback, has so far remained confined to the open-set setting. In this work we introduce MEOW, the first framework that turns non-interactive segmentation backbones into interactive open-world learners without updating learnable model parameters. MEOW combines parameter-free transductive reasoning with memory consolidation to accumulate knowledge and thereby improve future performance. Focusing on medical data, we show that MEOW consistently improves its own predictions on classes never seen during training, and transfers zero-shot to unfamiliar domains, including micro-CT data and other imaging modalities.

papers.intro:
Recent advances in lifelong learning have fundamentally shifted how deep learning models are deployed in dynamic environments where data distributions and task definitions continuously evolve [1, 2]. When a static model trained on a closed-world distribution is deployed in the wild, it inevitably encounters out-of-distribution data. Processing these unseen distributions without adaptation degrades predictive performance [3]. In critical vision-tasks [4], e.g. medical image analysis [5] and autonomous driving [6], this may lead to fatal outcomes. Consequently, enabling models to continuously adapt during their operational lifetime is crucial for maintaining high reliability and performance.

However, model adaptation introduces various challenges concerning plasticity-stability trade-offs and catastrophic forgetting [7], as well as model complexity and prohibitive computational costs [8]. Another conceptual problem arises from the nature of the incoming data stream. Standard lifelong learning frameworks often assume a well-defined stream where novel tasks or classes are explicitly delineated and labeled by human experts. In practical settings, however, models must be able to handle completely novel, unknown classes and domains that emerge dynamically.

To succeed in such a dynamic environment, open-world (OW) learning has emerged as a highly relevant and pressing challenge. In OW-learning, a model must be able to operate in unknown domains, make predictions for unknown classes, and also actively learn and improve over time. This is usually achieved by leveraging knowledge directly from its own predictions on these unknowns.

In clinical environments, closed-world systems with fixed label spaces fail due to rare pathologies and domain shifts. They often yield hazardous, overconfident predictions when unknown structures are forced into predefined categories [9]. OW-learning addresses this by incorporating these unknowns into a model’s taxonomy. Moreover, it mitigates severe data scarcity caused by costly expert annotations, licensing constraints, and strict privacy regulations, as exhaustive labeling of every possible class is no longer required. By dynamically adapting to anatomical variations and unseen distributions, OW frameworks help bridge the gap toward safe, robust clinical deployment.

OW-learning combines multiple learning paradigms [10], including incremental, continual, transfer, out-of-distribution, few-shot, and open-set (OS) learning. Furthermore, desired properties encompass mechanisms for fast learning and unlearning at scale. Beyond these, OW systems must unify instance classification for existing classes with novelty detection and label management for new classes. While OS systems are limited to identifying or rejecting unknown classes, OW systems incrementally learn from their own predictions during deployment. Previously unknown classes become known once processed, thereby enhancing future performance. Beyond traditional tasks like classification or regression, OW recognition also extends to generative modeling, where models must adapt to generate samples from previously unseen distributions.

We focus on the 3D vision-task of open-world interactive segmentation (OW-IS), which has not been studied yet. In interactive segmentation (IS) [11, 12], a machine learning (ML) model takes user inputs like clicks or brushes to segment parts of an image. Self-training and pseudo-labeling schemes for OW systems often rely on gradient-based parameter updates, which are prone to confirming a model’s systematic biases, degrade representation stability, and require significant computational overhead. This motivates the need for an adaptation mechanism that can exploit a model’s own predictions to learn new classes and domains reliably, rapidly, and safely.

On top of the desired OW-properties mentioned above, our approach offers various favorable properties in terms of IS- and OW aspects, including flexible user interactions and a modular architecture. Most importantly, our method requires no gradient-based learning [13] to transform non-interactive, frozen-parameter models into flexible IS models while simultaneously enabling efficient OW-learning capabilities. Our main contributions are as follows: Interactive Segmentation: We introduce MEOW, a modular 3D IS system that is capable of handling sparse annotations (e.g., from clicks or brushes) in a flexible manner. In contrast to methods that are trained end-to-end using a fixed interaction strategy during training, our approach takes non-interactive off-the-shelf segmentation models and integrates them into our IS framework. Our system is invariant to diverse annotation styles, ensuring robust performance across different users. Apart from clicking and brushing interactions, our method further supports interactive hyperparameter tuning via sliders. Open-World Learning: We propose a solution to OW-IS, i.e., an IS system learning from its own predictions of novel structures. Notably, this also includes the selective removal of previously learned samples and domains. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first operational OW-IS framework. General Improvements: To enable efficient OW-IS for 3D data, we introduce modifications to PARMESAN, including improved feature compression, better memory search kernels, and more efficient test-time augmentation. We also improve its message passing approach for post-processing of raw predictions by implementing hierarchical message passing, thereby enhancing overall segmentation quality and robustness. Finally, we propose novel evaluation metrics that are useful for IS.

papers.title: Sharp weighted Riesz inequalities for harmonic mappings in the range 1<p<2
papers.abstract:
For $1<p<2$ and $c>0$, we determine the exact norm of the weighted analytic--coanalytic projection operator $F\mapsto(P_+F,\sqrt c\,P_-F)$ from $L^p(\T)$ to $L^p(\T;\ell_2^2)$. The sharp constant is \[
  a_{p,c}=\left(\frac{1+c+\sqrt{1+c^2+2c\cos(2\pi/p)}}{2\sin^2(\pi/p)}\right)^{1/2}. \] We construct an explicit plurisubharmonic minorant of the corresponding pointwise obstacle and obtain an origin-corrected inequality for arbitrary harmonic decompositions. The uncorrected inequality holds under an optimal angular condition at the origin. The scalar estimate underlying the construction is proved by angular minimization and a two-sided comparison with solutions of $y''=y$. An explicit family establishes sharpness.

papers.title: Commutators in free skew fields
papers.abstract: We characterise additive and multiplicative commutators in free skew fields in terms of traces and determinants of matrix evaluations. Namely, a noncommutative rational function is a sum of additive commutators if and only if all its matrix evaluations have trace zero, and it is a product of multiplicative commutators if and only if all its matrix evaluations have determinant one. As applications, we characterise pairs of noncommutative rational functions with equal operator or Frobenius norms, or with identical spectra. Finally, using valuations and free Poisson fields, we show that the identity and the generators of a free skew field cannot be expressed as a nonempty product of additive commutators, answering a question of Gardella and Thiel in the negative.

papers.intro:
Commutators measure the failure of commutativity, and their relationship with matrix invariants has been studied since the early days of matrix algebra. Shoda [Sho37] proved in characteristic 0 that a matrix is an additive commutator if and only if its trace vanishes; Albert and Muckenhoupt [AM57] extended this to arbitrary fields; see also [Suw23] for more recent work over commutative rings. For finite-dimensional simple algebras, Amitsur and Rowen [AR94] proved that every element of reduced trace zero is a sum of at most two additive commutators. The distinction between a single commutator and a sum of commutators is illustrated by the examples of Rosset and Rosset [RR00] and, more recently, Jang [Jan26]. In the free algebra, a noncommutative polynomial has zero trace at matrices of every size precisely when it is a sum of commutators. This observation appears in [KS08, BK09], and underlies the tracial Nullstellensatz of [KŠ14]. It is also closely related to the study of values of noncommutative polynomials and trace positivity; see, for instance, [Bre20, KSV23]. The invariant theory and trace identities of generic matrices were developed by Procesi [Pro76] and Razmyslov [Raz74], while rational identities in division algebras were investigated by Bergman [Ber76].

Amitsur’s theory of rational identities [Ami66] and the matricial approach to noncommutative rational functions of Helton, McCullough and Vinnikov [HMV06], and Kalyuzhnyi-Verbovetskyi and Vinnikov [KVV12, KVV14] allow one to translate questions in a free skew field into questions about matrix evaluations. The connection between factorisation in the free algebra and irreducibility of generic determinants was developed in [HKV18, HKV22]; generic spectral properties of rational evaluations were subsequently studied in [BV25]. Questions about pointwise rank, spectral and norm equivalences of noncommutative polynomials are considered in [SV25].

papers.title: Hamilton cycles in vertex-transitive graphs of prime-power order
papers.abstract: A graph is vertex-transitive if, for any two vertices, there is an automorphism mapping one to the other. We prove that every connected vertex-transitive graph of order $p^n$, where $p$ is a prime and $p^n\geq 3$, has a hamiltonian cycle. Our main tool extends Witte's theorem [JCTB (1986)] on Cayley digraphs of $p$-groups.

papers.intro:
A graph is vertex-transitive if its automorphism group acts transitively on its vertices. In 1969, Lovász [7] asked whether every finite connected vertex-transitive graph has a hamiltonian path. This question is still open, although it has been answered affirmatively in many special cases; see, for example, [8, 9, 5, 6, 10]. Only four connected vertex-transitive graphs on at least three vertices are known to have no hamiltonian cycle: the Petersen graph, the Coxeter graph, and the two graphs obtained from them by replacing each vertex with a triangle. None of these four graphs is a Cayley graph, and it is a folklore conjecture that every connected Cayley graph on at least three vertices has a hamiltonian cycle. We refer to [4] for a survey.

A graph is vertex-transitive if its automorphism group acts transitively on its vertices. In 1969, Lovász [7] asked whether every finite connected vertex-transitive graph has a hamiltonian path. This question is still open, although it has been answered affirmatively in many special cases; see, for example, [8, 9, 5, 6, 10]. Only four connected vertex-transitive graphs on at least three vertices are known to have no hamiltonian cycle: the Petersen graph, the Coxeter graph, and the two graphs obtained from them by replacing each vertex with a triangle. None of these four graphs is a Cayley graph, and it is a folklore conjecture that every connected Cayley graph on at least three vertices has a hamiltonian cycle. We refer to [4] for a survey.

Most partial results concern graphs of restricted order. For example, Du, Kutnar and Marušič [3] proved that, apart from the Petersen graph, every connected vertex-transitive graph of order p​qpq, where pp and qq are primes, has a hamiltonian cycle. For prime-power orders, the starting point is Witte’s theorem [14] that every strongly connected Cayley digraph of a nontrivial finite pp-group has a directed hamiltonian cycle. Marušič [11] proved that every vertex-transitive digraph of order pkp^{k} with k≤3k\leq 3 is a Cayley digraph, and that every connected vertex-transitive graph of these orders is hamiltonian. He also constructed non-Cayley vertex-transitive graphs of order pkp^{k} for every k≥4k\geq 4, so Witte’s theorem does not settle the prime-power case. Chen [1] and Zhang [15] proved that connected vertex-transitive digraphs of order p4p^{4} and p5p^{5}, respectively, have directed hamiltonian cycles. Both proofs lift hamiltonian cycles from quotient digraphs. To the best of our knowledge, the prime-power case has remained open for every exponent n≥6n\geq 6. We settle it in this paper.

papers.title: A linear programming approach to finite copula interpolation
papers.abstract: We consider exact and interval-valued interpolation of multivariate copulas at arbitrary finite configurations in the unit cube. We first characterize when the prescribed data are compatible with a quasi-copula and derive explicit extremal quasi-copula envelopes. The copula interpolation problem is thereby reduced to a copula sandwich problem between these envelopes. Restricting them to the canonical rectangular grid generated by the data coordinates yields a finite linear feasibility system whose elementary-volume constraints are encoded by a cell--vertex incidence matrix. Farkas' lemma then identifies the criterion of Omladi\v{c} and Stopar with an explicit certificate of infeasibility. Although this criterion is indexed by infinitely many formal cell combinations, we show that it suffices to test finitely many vertices of a sign-polytopal subdivision. We also extend the construction to $k$-increasing discrete quasi-copulas for $2\leq k\leq d$.

Copula interpolation under finitely many pointwise constraints has previously been studied in several forms. Best-possible bounds and existence results for copulas with a prescribed value at one point are closely related to the corresponding one-point quasi-copula bounds; see [10] and the references therein. The existence and construction of multivariate copulas attaining prescribed quasi-copula values at two arbitrary points were established in [6]. In the trivariate case, a linear-programming approach was used in [2] to treat prescribed values at several points: existence is guaranteed for two arbitrary points, whereas it may fail for three points. These results motivate the general finite interpolation problem considered here, in which both the number and the coordinates of the interpolation points are arbitrary.

Our starting point is the compatibility of finite data with the class of quasi-copulas. For exact data, the Fréchet–Hoeffding bounds and the directed Lipschitz inequalities give necessary compatibility conditions. We show that these conditions are also sufficient and construct explicitly the smallest and the greatest quasi-copulas interpolating the prescribed values. For interval-valued data, represented by lower and upper functions A,B:E→[0,1]A,B\colon E\to[0,1] satisfying A≤BA\leq B, we obtain analogous extremal lower and upper quasi-copula envelopes, denoted by Q¯A\underline{Q}_{A} and Q¯B\overline{Q}_{B}. The original finite interpolation constraints are then equivalent to the global sandwich condition Q¯A≤Q≤Q¯B\underline{Q}_{A}\leq Q\leq\overline{Q}_{B}. Consequently, the interval-valued copula interpolation problem is equivalent to the existence of a copula between these two quasi-copula envelopes.

papers.title: Memory of Initial States in Long-Time Dynamics Revealed by Non-Gaussianity
papers.abstract: In quantum dynamics of few-body observables in quadratic systems, information about the initial state is retained in long-time averages, as captured by the generalized Gibbs ensemble. Here, we show that this memory extends beyond the averages to temporal fluctuations around them. By generating a manifold of non-Gaussian initial states and quantifying their non-Gaussianity via the corresponding entropy, we find that the magnitude of temporal fluctuations is a smooth function of the initial-state non-Gaussianity. This relation explains the qualitatively different scaling of fluctuations observed after quantum quenches: exponentially small fluctuations for non-Gaussian initial states and polynomially small fluctuations for Gaussian initial states. Therefore, our results identify non-Gaussianity as a key to uncovering initial-state memory beyond long-time averages.

papers.title: On operators with infinitely many spectral components
papers.abstract: For a unital complex Banach algebra $\mathscr A$ and $n\in\mathbb N$, let $\mathcal C_n(\mathscr A)$ be the set of all elements whose spectrum has at least $n$ connected components, and let $\mathcal C_\infty(\mathscr A)=\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb N}\mathcal C_n(\mathscr A)$. We prove that $\mathcal C_\infty(\mathscr A)\neq\varnothing$ if and only if $\mathscr A$ contains a sequence of non-zero pairwise orthogonal idempotents, and that the number of components of a spectrum is always finite, $\aleph_0$ or $\mathfrak c$. This allows us to extend the spectral depth $d_\sigma(\mathscr A)$ to a cardinal-valued invariant with values in $\mathbb N\cup\{\aleph_0,\mathfrak c\}$. We show that $d_\sigma(\mathscr A)=\mathfrak c$ precisely when $\mathscr A$ contains a dyadic family of idempotents indexed by the full binary tree. In that case, some element has spectrum homeomorphic to the Cantor space $\mathbf 2^{\mathbb N}$. The supremum defining $d_\sigma(\mathscr A)$ is attained when the spectral classes of $\mathscr A$ are dense and when $\mathscr A$ is commutative, but not in general. We construct a unital complex Banach algebra with $d_\sigma(\mathscr A)=\aleph_0$ and $\mathcal C_\infty(\mathscr A)=\varnothing$. If $\Delta$ is the character space of a commutative $\mathscr A$ and $\pi_0(\Delta)$ is the space of all components of $\Delta$, then $d_\sigma(\mathscr A)=\card\bigl(\pi_0(\Delta)\bigr)$ when $\pi_0(\Delta)$ is finite, $d_\sigma(\mathscr A)=\aleph_0$ when $\pi_0(\Delta)$ is infinite and scattered, and $d_\sigma(\mathscr A)=\mathfrak c$ when $\pi_0(\Delta)$ is not scattered. We also prove that the spectral depth is additive with respect to finite direct sums and that the spectral classes are invariant under injective holomorphic functions.

papers.title: Metric-Aligned Group Relative Policy Optimization for Explainable Deepfake Detection
papers.abstract: Deepfake detectors are commonly evaluated on real/fake classification alone, but real-world applications require explanations of the visual evidence behind each prediction. Joint vision-language models struggle with authenticity assessment, producing "real" narratives for manipulated images. To address this, we propose a decoupled predict-then-explain pipeline as our submission to the ACM Multimedia 2026 Explainable Deepfake Detection Challenge, with methods trained and evaluated on the XPlainVerse benchmark. A vision-foundation-model ensemble first classifies the image, then a Qwen3-VL-8B model generates a decision-conditioned explanation of the visual evidence. For fake images, a second Qwen3-VL-8B compresses that text into a short non-expert summary without using the image. We further apply metric-aligned Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to optimize both explainers against the challenge criteria. Under matched conditions, GRPO raises complex BERTScore-F1 from 0.686 to 0.712 and also improves grounding (entity and evidence F1); our submission ranked first on complex BERTScore-F1 and seventh overall.

papers.intro:
The realism of synthetic imagery has advanced to the point where it is nearly indistinguishable from authentic content. This is particularly evident for deepfake imagery, whose low-cost creation is routinely misused for harmful ends, including misinformation and deliberate attacks on individuals’ reputations. Moving beyond straightforward identity replacement, modern generative pipelines enable nuanced person-centric edits that modify actions, object interactions, and overall scene semantics while preserving the subject’s identity (Gupta et al., 2025). As generation methods advance, detectors still struggle to generalize beyond the generators and manipulation methods seen during training (Guillaro et al., 2025; Han et al., 2025), making reliable identification of manipulated content increasingly demanding.

Despite this growing sophistication of synthetic content, deepfake detection systems are typically evaluated on classification accuracy alone: a detector need only output a binary real/fake label, without articulating which regions, objects, or attributes support that decision. This leaves a critical gap for real-world deployment, where both experts and non-expert users need to understand how an image was manipulated and which specific changes alter the style, semantics, or narrative of the scene, especially for localized edits to actions, interactions, or context, not merely whether it was flagged as synthetic.

In this paper, we present our solution to this challenge: a decoupled predict-then-explain pipeline that separates foundation-model detection from decision-conditioned explanation generation. This design provides the explainer with a predetermined authenticity decision, rather than relying on the autoregressive output to generate a class-specific narrative before deciding. Because token-level supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is only indirectly aligned with the sequence-level metrics used for evaluation, we follow the recent reinforcement-learning post-training trend (Ouyang et al., 2022; DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025) and further optimize explanations with GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) against the challenge’s semantic-similarity metrics. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: • We introduce a decoupled predict-then-explain pipeline for explainable deepfake detection. • The method tackles decision bias and related errors in combined decision and explanation generation. • We apply metric-aligned GRPO post-training for both complex and simple explanations, improving over SFT alone.

papers.title: Dynamics of R\'enyi entanglement entropies and Eigenstate Thermalization
papers.abstract: How is entanglement dynamics encoded in the eigenstates of the time-evolution operator? We address this question by focusing on R\'enyi entropy dynamics in deterministic chaotic Floquet models in arbitrary dimensions. Inspired by the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis (ETH), we employ spectral representations of reduced density matrix moments (purity and its higher-order generalizations) whose decay through spectral dephasing captures nonequilibrium entanglement growth. These representations closely resemble those governing local-observable dynamics, but involve eigenstates in a replicated Hilbert space and observables are replaced by subsystem permutation operators, such as the swap operator for R\'enyi-2. Focusing on R\'enyi-2, we combine exact random matrix theory calculations, established ETH results and numerical tests in 1D to formulate ETH-like ans\"atze for subsystem swap matrix elements in the replicated eigenbasis and their cross-correlations with initial-state overlap statistics. In the thermodynamic limit, purity dynamics is entirely determined by smooth slowly varying functions that emerge from such statistics, paralleling generalized ETH formulations in a single replica. In the limit of large subsystems, these functions exhibit a striking structural simplification: locality of the dynamics together with bulk spectral dephasing reduce their functional dependence to a single fundamental frequency. Our formalism provides a setting where ETH-like statements naturally coexist for both arbitrarily small and large subsystem sizes. We discuss extensions of our results to higher R\'enyi entropies. Beyond clarifying the spectral foundations of entanglement dynamics, these results lay some of the groundwork for future applications of spectral filter methods to the computation of R\'enyi evolution in deterministic systems.

papers.intro:
The eigenstate thermalization hypothesis (ETH) provides a central framework for understanding dynamics and thermalization in generic isolated quantum many-body systems. Its antecedents include von Neumann’s quantum ergodic theorem [1, *vonneumann_proof_2010], Berry’s random-wave conjecture [3], and early studies of matrix-element statistics in the energy eigenbasis [4, 5, 6, 7]. Its modern formulation was developed in the works of Deutsch and Srednicki [8, 9, 10]. Most notably, ETH provides a simple microscopic justification for the local emergence of thermal behaviour at late times under unitary dynamics [9, 10, 11]. Together with its related generalizations [10, 12, 13, 14], it also provides the information necessary to reconstruct the dynamics of correlation functions, even in the transient regime before local equilibrium is established.

papers.title: Mitigating oscillatory systematics in MeerKLASS L-band H i intensity maps
papers.abstract: HI intensity mapping is a promising probe of the large-scale structure of the Universe, but is limited by foregrounds and instrumental systematics. For the MeerKAT Large Area Synoptic Survey (MeerKLASS) L-band data, it is found that emission line stacking measurement reveals a type of systematics related to the instrument beam. Using simulations with a full-sky electromagnetic beam model, we show that the chromaticity and sidelobes of the MeerKAT beam modulate the frequency-smooth foreground emission and introduce oscillating structures that persist after foreground removal. The beam rotates with respect to the sky between two types of scans, and combining datasets with different beam orientations before foreground cleaning makes the residuals stronger. In MeerKLASS L-band data, processing these two types of scans separately significantly suppresses the oscillating residuals while preserving the stacked HI signal. The ratio of the HI signal amplitude to the systematic fluctuation amplitude increases by 81%. We find an oscillating structure in PCA mode 11 in our previous data processing, but simply removing this mode does not improve the stacked spectrum due to the signal loss. Our strategy can help mitigate spectral ripples that are induced by the beam in future MeerKAT and SKA-Mid surveys.

papers.intro:
The large-scale distribution of matter in the Universe, particularly that of dark matter, is one of the primary targets of modern cosmology, as it provides key constraints on cosmological models and fundamental physics. Although dark matter cannot be detected directly through electromagnetic radiation, its distribution can be inferred from observable tracers. Among these, the redshifted 21-cm emission from neutral hydrogen (H i) is particularly promising because most H i resides in dark matter haloes in the post-reionization Universe (z≲6z\lesssim 6; Villaescusa-Navarro et al. 2018). Therefore, the measurement of H i distribution probes the distribution of dark matter and helps us test the cosmological model (Bull et al., 2015). Since cosmological information is encoded in the large-scale fluctuations of the integrated H i emission, individual H i-bearing galaxies do not need to be resolved. Instead, the unresolved H i emission from many galaxies can be mapped over coarsely sampled sky areas, allowing efficient surveys of large cosmological volumes with relatively small-aperture telescopes. This technique trades angular resolution for survey speed and is known as H i intensity mapping (e.g. Madau et al. 1997; Bharadwaj et al. 2001; Chang et al. 2008; Wyithe et al. 2008).

One of the major challenges in H i intensity mapping is the removal of foreground contamination, which is dominated by Galactic synchrotron and free–free emission, together with their extragalactic counterparts. The foreground remains spectrally smooth and is predominantly described by a power law, but its amplitude varies at the Kelvin level across different lines of sight, as shown in MeerKLASS Collaboration et al. (2025). At z≲6z\lesssim 6, the foreground emission is at least four orders of magnitude brighter than the expected cosmological H i signal (Santos et al., 2015; Wolz et al., 2026). The cosmological H i signal exhibits more rapid frequency fluctuations due to the different frequencies corresponding to the 21 cm line at different redshifts. A variety of blind component separation methods have therefore been developed (Spinelli et al., 2022), such as Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and its multi-scale extension (Carucci et al., 2025); Independent Component Analysis (ICA; Chapman et al. 2012); Generalized Morphological Component Analysis (GMCA; Carucci et al. 2020); and the Generalized Needlet Internal Linear Combination (GNILC; Remazeilles et al. 2011; Olivari et al. 2016) method. A comprehensive overview and comparison of these foreground-cleaning methods is provided in Spinelli et al. (2026).

Over the past decade, H i intensity mapping observations have been carried out with various radio telescopes, including the Green Bank Telescope (Chang et al., 2010; Masui et al., 2013; Switzer et al., 2013; Wolz et al., 2022), the Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment (CHIME Collaboration et al., 2022; CHIME Collaboration et al., 2025), the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical Telescope (Li et al., 2023), and the Tianlai array (Zuo et al., 2021). Another important facility for H i intensity mapping is MeerKAT, a radio interferometer located in South Africa, consisting of 64 dishes, each 13.5 m in diameter, and serving as a precursor to the Square Kilometre Array (SKA). MeerKAT can perform H i intensity mapping in both interferometric and single-dish modes, allowing it to probe a wide range of spatial scales. In interferometric mode, MeerKAT has been used to measure the H i power spectrum on relatively small scales (Paul et al., 2026; Mazumder et al., 2025; Townsend et al., 2026). In single-dish mode, MeerKAT has conducted several H i intensity mapping campaigns, including the MeerKLASS L-band pilot survey (Wang et al., 2021; Cunnington et al., 2023; Carucci et al., 2025) and the subsequent L-band deep-field observations (MeerKLASS Collaboration et al., 2025; MeerKLASS Collaboration et al., 2026). In this work, we focus on the latter. The single-dish observations retain large-scale modes inaccessible to the interferometric measurements, while the long integration time of approximately 62 hours per dish provides improved sensitivity compared with previous MeerKLASS single-dish observations (MeerKLASS Collaboration et al., 2025; MeerKLASS Collaboration et al., 2026). However, the performance of foreground-cleaning methods is often degraded by instrumental systematics. One of the most important is the telescope beam, which exhibits frequency-dependent oscillations and complex sidelobe structures (Matshawule et al., 2021). These beam effects introduce additional spectral structure into the measured data which cannot be removed by PCA effectively (Spinelli et al., 2022; Spinelli et al., 2026).

In MeerKLASS Collaboration et al. (2025), the measured auto-power spectrum of the MeerKLASS L-band deep field was found to contain substantially more power than expected. This excess, which is later mitigated by performing internal cross-correlation between different H i datasets (MeerKLASS Collaboration et al., 2026), indicates that residual systematics may still be present in the data after foreground cleaning. However, a power spectrum is a statistical description of the fluctuations in the data and does not directly show the spatial or spectral structures responsible for the excess power. Stacking provides a complementary way to investigate these structures. Unlike the power spectrum, the stacking results can be directly examined as angular images and frequency spectra. This allows us to see how residual systematics vary across the sky and with frequency, providing a more direct way to investigate their properties and possible origins. Understanding and mitigating these systematics through stacking can therefore benefit not only the stacking measurement itself, but also power-spectrum analyses performed on the same data.

papers.title: The Dose Makes the Poison: Exposure-Aware Evaluation of Generative Drug Design
papers.abstract: Generative models are increasingly used to propose molecules for drug discovery. They can produce far more candidates than can be experimentally tested, making computational selection essential. Most selection methods rely on predicted molecular properties, such as potency and toxicity, but overlook how these properties translate into drug exposure at a given dose. As a result, molecules that appear promising on paper may require impractical doses or raise safety concerns. We investigate this gap by using physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) simulations to re-evaluate molecules selected from three PARP1-targeted generative pipelines. Of 60 shortlisted molecules, seven fail to achieve sufficient target exposure, while 28% of the remaining candidates show predicted safety risks at their required dose. Moreover, 85% of candidates with an achievable dose are outperformed by molecules overlooked during static selection. These findings suggest that accounting for dose and exposure can substantially change which generated molecules are considered promising for drug development.

papers.intro:
A challenge in computational drug discovery is deciding which molecules are worth pursuing. Generative models can explore large chemical spaces and propose thousands of candidates, but only a small fraction can be experimentally tested. Selecting promising molecules therefore requires computational methods to assess their properties before experimental validation. Most current workflows rely on predictions of potency, toxicity, and drug-like properties. Such predictions are widely used to benchmark generative models (Gao et al., 2022; Brown et al., 2019; Polykovskiy et al., 2020; García-Ortegón et al., 2022), guide molecular generation (Loeffler et al., 2024; Lee et al., 2023), and filter or rank candidates using multi-parameter scoring functions (Wager et al., 2010).

A challenge in computational drug discovery is deciding which molecules are worth pursuing. Generative models can explore large chemical spaces and propose thousands of candidates, but only a small fraction can be experimentally tested. Selecting promising molecules therefore requires computational methods to assess their properties before experimental validation. Most current workflows rely on predictions of potency, toxicity, and drug-like properties. Such predictions are widely used to benchmark generative models (Gao et al., 2022; Brown et al., 2019; Polykovskiy et al., 2020; García-Ortegón et al., 2022), guide molecular generation (Loeffler et al., 2024; Lee et al., 2023), and filter or rank candidates using multi-parameter scoring functions (Wager et al., 2010).

While useful, these predictions do not tell us whether a molecule will perform well at the dose needed for treatment. Both efficacy and toxicity depend on drug exposure, which is determined by the interaction of several properties, including potency, absorption, clearance, and protein binding (Maurer et al., 2020). For example, a molecule with high predicted potency may still require a large dose if it is rapidly cleared or poorly absorbed. Similarly, a molecule with weak predicted off-target activity may become a safety concern if the dose required for target engagement leads to high systemic exposure. Evaluating molecular properties independently can therefore miss important differences between candidates. Physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) models offer a way to account for these effects by simulating how drug concentrations change over time following administration. PBPK modeling is widely used in drug development, including for target pharmacology and dose prediction (Chen et al., 2021; Geci et al., 2024; Naga et al., 2022). Recent studies have also explored incorporating predicted pharmacokinetic properties or PBPK-derived exposure into molecular generation (van den Maagdenberg et al., 2025; Ramey et al., 2022), as well as improving potency while preserving favorable bioavailability and toxicity properties (Horne et al., 2024). In this work, we take a different approach. Rather than modifying the generative objective, we use PBPK simulations to examine whether molecules selected by conventional property-based screening remain promising once dose and exposure are considered.

We investigate this question using three PARP1-targeted generative pipelines: MOOD, a docking-guided diffusion model (Lee et al., 2023); REINVENT4-MPO, a recurrent neural network fine-tuned through reinforcement learning to optimize potency and ADME-related properties; and Mol2Mol, a seed-based approach that generates analogues of existing molecules. Both REINVENT4-MPO and Mol2Mol are implemented using the REINVENT4 framework (Loeffler et al., 2024). We treat these pipelines as separate case studies rather than a controlled comparison. For each pipeline, we apply the same property-based filters and static ranking procedure, then re-evaluate the shortlisted molecules using PBPK simulations. We estimate the dose needed to achieve sufficient target exposure and assess the associated safety margins for two liabilities relevant to PARP inhibitors.

papers.title: Personalized Affective Perception via Continual Learning in Human-Agent Negotiation
papers.abstract: Self-interested intelligent agents that negotiate with humans should interpret nonverbal expressions and adapt their behavior accordingly. However, generic facial-affect models degrade across individuals and contexts, creating a generalization gap. We introduce an affect-adaptive negotiation strategy that incorporates Continual Learning with Imagination for Facial Expression Recognition (CLIFER) to personalize valence-arousal perception in real time. Differential feedback converts changes in valence-arousal direction and intensity into adjustments of the agent's target utility. An asynchronous architecture updates CLIFER in the background during live interaction. In a counterbalanced within-subject study in which 66 participants negotiated with a humanoid robot, the CL-enabled agent achieved significantly higher individual utility and elicited higher participant concession rates than the FaceChannel baseline. The CL condition yielded significantly higher mean arousal estimates, alongside a broader output range. Participant utility and Nash distance did not change significantly between conditions. These outcomes support the practical value of coupling continual affective personalization with differential feedback for real-time negotiation.

papers.intro:
Negotiating resources, tasks, and conflicting interests is a fundamental capability for socially intelligent agents collaborating with humans [1, 2]. Traditionally, Automated Negotiation has been modeled with Game Theory and AI, viewing agents as rational utility maximizers that exchange offers based on fixed mathematical functions, heuristics, or reinforcement learning policies [3, 4]. Recent agents demonstrate sophisticated strategic reasoning in human-agent negotiation: from the tool-integrated ASTRA agent that performs dynamic offer optimization [5] to competitive bargaining models like ChargingBoul [6] and systems that analyze strategic trade-offs in multi-agent environments [7]. These approaches advance strategic decision-making, while situated human interaction also requires attention to individual preferences and affective cues [8, 9]. Balancing utility with human social acceptance is still a challenge [10, 11]. As embodied agents transition from industrial environments to unstructured social roles (e.g., mediators, tutors, and caretakers), affective intelligence becomes a functional necessity, and expressions serve as social signs of the interaction partner’s affective state. For example, a tense or serious expression may signal resistance before a rejection is verbalized. At the same time, a slight or mild smile may indicate mutual agreement [12, 13]. Recent work has begun to utilize this, with agents using affect for dispute resolution [14] and persuasion [15].

Affect perception is not only perspective-dependent but also highly personal. Models built on static datasets commonly fail to detect the dynamics of a social task in which the observer is an active participant. This failure creates what is known as a generalization gap [16]. Gunes et al. point out that high accuracy on static benchmarks does not guarantee functional adaptation in the wild. Generic models such as FaceChannel [17] provide a common affect representation, but contextual interpretation remains difficult [16]; for instance, a concentrated expression need not indicate anger. In a negotiation context, this is critical: if the agent misinterprets concentration as anger, it may alter its concession target in response to an ambiguous signal. This need for adaptation raises the plasticity-stability dilemma: the agent needs plasticity to learn the current participant’s idiosyncratic expressions, while excessive adaptation can lead to catastrophic forgetting of previously learned affective knowledge.

We address this challenge by adapting affect perception to observations from the ongoing negotiation, with generative replay to support retention of general affective representations. Our agent integrates continual learning (CL) to personalize affective perception. A CL-enabled system retains general knowledge while incrementally updating its parameters using the current participant’s facial observations [18, 19]. We pursue three objectives: (i) to enhance negotiation efficiency through personalized perception, (ii) to improve human-agent negotiation outcomes, and (iii) to validate continual learning as allowing real-time adaptation for affect understanding. To realize these objectives, we extend the Solver Agent [20, 21] from categorical affective feedback to differential feedback from continuous valence-arousal estimates. FaceChannel uses a fixed pretrained affect model, while CLIFER combines participant-specific demo training with continued adaptation during negotiation; both share the differential-feedback policy.

We compare these two perception conditions in human-agent negotiation under the following Research Questions (RQs):

• RQ1 (Affective Feedback): Does continual learning produce a behaviorally useful affective signal versus generic models? We analyze how personalized adaptation changes arousal/valence estimates and whether these representations produce affect signals influencing negotiation behavior. • RQ2 (Behavioral Influence): How does the agent’s personalized behavior influence human negotiation behavior? We examine whether an agent that adapts its affective feedback during the interaction induces a behavioral shift. We explore whether changes in human concession rates statistically mediate differences in agent utility. • RQ3 (Negotiation Efficiency): Does personalized affective perception enable the agent to gain higher individual utility without degrading joint optimality (Nash distance) in fewer negotiation rounds? We test whether adapting perception improves the agent’s return and negotiation speed, and examine the accompanying participant utility and Nash distance. We hypothesize that personalized affective feedback helps the agent adapt its strategy early and reach agreements efficiently. • RQ4 (Questionnaire Analysis): Do participants perceive the CL-enabled agent as more sophisticated? papers.title: Treewidth versus Hadwiger number: Graph classes with dominated balanced separators are quasi-linearly treewidth-Hadwiger bounded
papers.abstract: In a hereditary graph class $\mathcal{G}$, the treewidth of a graph in $\mathcal{G}$ is bounded by a function of the size of a largest clique minor of the graph if and only if the class $\mathcal{G}$ excludes some planar graph as an induced minor. Campbell et al. (arXiv 2024) conjectured that such a bounding function can always be chosen to be linear. We verify this conjecture for several classes of graphs (including even-hole-free graphs) and show that if a hereditary graph class $\mathcal{G}$ has dominated binary-weighted balanced separators, then the bounding function can be taken to be in ${O(h \log h)}$, where $h$ is the Hadwiger number. We say that $\mathcal{G}$ has dominated binary-weighted balanced separators if, for every ${G \in \mathcal{G}}$ and every $\mathsf{w} \colon V(G) \to \{0,1\}$, there is a set ${D \subseteq V(G)}$ of bounded size so that deleting the closed neighbourhood $N_G[D]$ of $D$ leaves each component with at most a fixed fraction of the total weight of $G$. Our result reduces the quasi-linear weakening of the conjecture of Campbell et al. to a conjecture of Gartland and Lokshtanov stating that every graph class excluding a planar graph as an induced minor admits dominated binary-weighted balanced separators.

papers.title: Characterization of BNLs 20 and 30 micrometer thick LGADs for the Electron Ion Collider
papers.abstract: The 20 and 30 micrometer thick Low-Gain Avalanche Detectors (LGADs) produced at Brookhaven National Laboratory (BNL) were evaluated. Detailed electrical measurements indicate well-formed and stable gain layers with consistently low leakage currents. Transient Current Technique (TCT) was used to evaluate the gain. Fast-laser timing studies demonstrate time resolutions at the level of a few tens of picoseconds. To assess operational longevity under realistic conditions for Electron-Ion Collider sub-detector systems, devices were irradiated with 30 MeV and 60 MeV protons to fluences of 10^13 to 10^14 neq/cm^2, enabling a focused study of radiation-induced effects on gain stability and timing performance.

papers.intro:
The next generation of high-energy physics (HEP) experiments relies on detector systems capable of timing resolutions of O(10 ps), together with position resolutions of O(10 μ\mum), to enable four-dimensional (4D) tracking in which both the spatial and temporal coordinates of charged particles are reconstructed [14, 3]. Low-Gain Avalanche Detectors (LGADs) have emerged as one of the leading silicon technologies for precision timing applications [13]. LGADs incorporate a highly doped multiplication layer that generates moderate internal gain through controlled avalanche multiplication, producing large and fast signals while maintaining the advantages of silicon-based tracking detectors. Recent developments in thin-LGADs [16], AC-LGADs [7], inverse LGADs (iLGADs) [1] and trench-isolated LGADs (TI-LGADs) [12, 24, 23] have expanded their use in high-rate environments where both spatial and temporal precision are required.

The Electron–Ion Collider (EIC), planned to begin operation in the early 2030s, will deliver luminosities between 1033 and 1034 cm-2s-1 and will operate with high event rates and dense forward particle fluxes [22], however, the event rates and particle fluxes are at EIC are not very high compared to the LHC, HL-LHC or RHIC. The AC-LGADs have been identified as a leading candidate technology for EIC far-forward instrumentation, barrel-time of flight (TOF) (strips) and an endcap-TOF (pixels), where they can provide the precise timing information needed for particle identification and 4D tracking. In this work, we study standard (DC-coupled) LGADs, which share the same gain layer and thus the same bulk gain and timing mechanism as AC-LGADs. We note that obtained results are specific to standard LGADs and may not directly apply to AC-LGADs. Extending this study to AC-LGADs is left for future work. The cumulative radiation exposure expected for EIC far-forward detectors is of the order of 1013 1 MeV neq/cm2 over ten years of operation [17]. This is significantly lower than the (1–3)×1015 neq/cm2 expected for the timing layers of the HL-LHC experiments, including the ATLAS-HGTD [9] and CMS-ETL [5].

Although LGADs have shown promising radiation tolerance, their gain layer degrades under proton and neutron irradiation, leading to higher leakage currents, reduced signal amplitude, and degraded timing resolution. Understanding this degradation in thin sensors is essential for designing timing layers that can operate reliably in the EIC environment. In particular, thin-LGADs offer a balance between fast charge collection and mechanical robustness, but their behaviour under irradiation with low and medium-energy protons remains insufficiently characterised. However, radiation effects of different proton energies on LGADs are summarized here [8].

The results provide guidance for the design and qualification of LGAD-based timing layers for the EIC and contribute to the broader understanding of LGAD performance in high-radiation environments.

papers.title: Integration by parts and DLR equations for SPDEs on the whole line
papers.abstract: We study a stochastic reaction-diffusion equation on the whole real line, driven by space-time white noise, with a possibly nonlocal diffusion operator, such as a fractional Laplacian, and a coercive potential with polynomial growth. On the whole line, unlike on bounded intervals, its invariant measures cannot be described by an explicit density with respect to a Gaussian measure. We set the equation in suitable weighted spaces and show that invariant and infinitesimally invariant measures coincide, as do reversible measures and solutions to an integration-by-parts formula. We then show that the reversible measures are exactly the Gibbs measures defined through the Dobrushin-Lanford-Ruelle equations, without any moment condition, thanks to a priori estimates that also yield a Fernique-type theorem, uniform with respect to translations. In this way, we connect the Da Prato-Zabczyk approach to invariant measures of SPDEs with the DLR approach from statistical mechanics to Gibbs measures. Finally, we prove the existence of a reflection positive reversible measure and, in analogy with the one-dimensional long-range Ising model, we show that the reversible measure is unique, ergodic and translation invariant when the kernel of the nonlocal operator has a finite first moment, while it can be non-unique, for suitable double-well potentials, when the kernel has a power-law decay with infinite first moment.

papers.title: Thermodynamically consistent neural constitutive models for elastoplasticity via eigen-representations
papers.abstract: Neural network material models can represent yield surfaces and hardening laws with far more flexibility than classical closed-form plasticity formulations, but training such a model end-to-end through an implicit return map introduces non-trivial challenges. This work presents a thermodynamically consistent neural constitutive model for rate-independent, isotropic elastoplasticity that jointly learns a flexible yield function together with its evolution laws. For non-associative flow, the yield function extends the convex flow potential by a jointly trained additive term, which renders the model thermodynamically consistent by construction. Isotropy and convexity are enforced simultaneously across all learnable components through a permutation-invariant, spectral (eigenvalue-based) representation. Training proceeds through a backward-Euler return map, with gradients propagated by the implicit function theorem together with an eigenvalue-degeneracy-aware scheme for safe differentiation. The robustness and generality of the approach are demonstrated by reproducing known constitutive models, including non-associative flow, learning material behavior from stress--strain data extracted from a full-field finite element simulation, and capturing unknown non-associative behavior from homogenized representative volume elements of a foam. Finally, the proposed neural plasticity model is evaluated within finite element simulations to solve boundary-value-problem under plane stress.

papers.intro:
Computational simulation of plastic materials is central to the design and analysis of a vast class of engineering systems subject to permanent, irreversible deformation history, ranging from metal forming and additive manufacturing to geo-mechanical engineering and structural analysis. At the core of these simulations is the constitutive model, which encodes the plastic material’s response to the deformation history, and governs how it evolves under loading. Conventionally, these constitutive models, be it micromechanically motivated or phenomenological, are formulated within rigorous physics-based frameworks that ensure thermodynamic consistency (Coleman and Noll, 1959; Coleman and Gurtin, 1967) together with other important principles of constitutive modeling, e.g., objectivity (Noll, 1958), also sometimes referred to as frame indifference (Coleman and Gurtin, 1967) along with the observed material symmetries.

Computational simulation of plastic materials is central to the design and analysis of a vast class of engineering systems subject to permanent, irreversible deformation history, ranging from metal forming and additive manufacturing to geo-mechanical engineering and structural analysis. At the core of these simulations is the constitutive model, which encodes the plastic material’s response to the deformation history, and governs how it evolves under loading. Conventionally, these constitutive models, be it micromechanically motivated or phenomenological, are formulated within rigorous physics-based frameworks that ensure thermodynamic consistency (Coleman and Noll, 1959; Coleman and Gurtin, 1967) together with other important principles of constitutive modeling, e.g., objectivity (Noll, 1958), also sometimes referred to as frame indifference (Coleman and Gurtin, 1967) along with the observed material symmetries.

These constitutive models address the three key ingredients of plasticity, namely an elastic storage mechanism, a yield criterion that delineates the onset of plasticity, and an evolution mechanism that describes how plasticity progresses upon yielding. Their formulation is typically parsimonious, relying on hand-crafted functional forms with a small number of parameters that are calibrated to capture specific material behaviors, such as yielding, hardening, and flow characteristics. The resulting models are well-understood, admit efficient return-mapping algorithms (Simo and Ortiz, 1985; Ortiz and Simo, 1986; Miehe, 1998a; Miehe, 1998b), and satisfy thermodynamic consistency by construction. Yet this parsimony also limits their expressive power, and extending them to capture complex yield or hardening behaviors can require expert re-derivation and re-implementation.

Yet this parsimony also limits their expressive power, and extending them to capture complex yield or hardening behaviors can require expert re-derivation and re-implementation.

The emergence of machine learning as a tool for constitutive modeling offers a route to overcoming this limitation in model expressivity. Neural networks, with their universal approximation properties (Cybenko, 1989; Hornik, 1991), can represent a wide range of complex, nonlinear functions. The earliest applications date back to the pioneering work of Ghaboussi et al. (1991) in the early 1990s, who used feedforward neural networks (FNNs) to learn constitutive relations directly from data. Widespread adoption, however, gained momentum only more than two decades later, as part of a broader shift toward data-driven approaches in computational mechanics, e.g., (Bessa et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2016). This shift was driven by advances in software ecosystems, automatic differentiation, and high-performance computing. Recurrent neural networks (RNNs), which carry an internal state that encodes the loading history, further enabled the modeling of path-dependent material behavior (Mozaffar et al., 2019; Bonatti and Mohr, 2021; Ghavamian and Simone, 2019). However, both FNN and RNN approaches treat the constitutive response as a data-driven phenomenological input-output map, with no structural mechanism ensuring thermodynamic admissibility.

Initial attempts to incorporate thermodynamics into constitutive models did so by embedding the constraints into the training objective, adding penalty or regularization terms that reward non-negative dissipation on the sampled data. The thermodynamics-based artificial neural networks (TANNs) of Masi et al. (2021); Masi and Stefanou (2022) embed a thermodynamic potential explicitly but penalize negative dissipation rates during training and do not guarantee this by construction. The hybrid models proposed in (Settgast et al., 2020; Malik et al., 2022) model the yield function and the evolution of internal state variables with neural networks. Vlassis and Sun (2021a); Vlassis and Sun (2021b) incorporate Sobolev-type training (Czarnecki et al., 2017) and component-based level-set parametrization. Weber et al. (2023) augment FNNs with physics-based training enhancements for rate-independent plasticity. He and Chen (2022) infer internal state variables from the hidden state of a recurrent network and enforce the dissipation inequality through a penalty term in the loss. In each of these cases, thermodynamic consistency is either not considered explicitly or is incorporated only as a training objective, rather than being guaranteed by the model formulation itself. Thus, it is satisfied only over the sampled loading states without offering any guarantee at unseen loading conditions.

Thus, it is satisfied only over the sampled loading states without offering any guarantee at unseen loading conditions.

A more robust way to ensure thermodynamic consistency is to build it into the model itself, using a classical constitutive framework as a foundation. In the case of hyperelasticity, this amounts to the existence of a free energy function, together with objectivity and appropriate material symmetries, cf. (Linka et al., 2021; Fuhg et al., 2022a; Kalina et al., 2023; Thakolkaran et al., 2022). Another important aspect in neural elasticity is the construction of polyconvex elastic potentials, building on the seminal contributions of Ball (1976); Ball (1977). A maturing line of work uses input-convex neural networks (ICNNs) (Amos et al., 2017) and closely related constraining mechanisms to guarantee polyconvexity (Klein et al., 2022; Linden et al., 2023; Taç et al., 2024) among many others. For the special case of isotropy, highly flexible polyconvex models based on ICNNs and principal stretches (Vijayakumaran et al., 2025; Tepole et al., 2025) or signed singular values (Geuken et al., 2025; Geuken et al., 2026) have been proposed.

Extending this approach to plasticity is more challenging. The model must simultaneously learn the yield surface that delineates the limits of the elastic regime, enforce thermodynamic consistency within the elastic regime, handle the evolution of internal state variables during plastic deformation, allow for non-associative flow when the material calls for it, and enforce material symmetry across every learnable component. Of these, thermodynamic consistency within the elastic regime is the best-understood requirement, thanks to the maturity of (hyper)elastic modeling, while internal variable evolution remains the most architecturally demanding.

papers.title: A phase-field model of viscous surfaces in fluids
papers.abstract: Viscous surfaces play a crucial role in biological and industrial multiphase flows, yet their simulation remains challenging due to complex rheology and topological changes. We present a thermodynamically consistent phase-field model for viscous surfaces in incompressible Navier-Stokes fluids, incorporating surface shear and dilatational viscosities via the Boussinesq-Scriven constitutive law. The diffuse-interface formulation is derived from a sharp-interface model and rigorously validated through matched asymptotic analysis, confirming recovery of the correct sharp-interface limit. We develop an unconditionally energy-dissipative time discretization, ensuring numerical stability. The model is validated through a quantitative benchmark against analytical solutions for surface flows on a rigid sphere, and a simulation of vesicle fusion showing preservation of energy dissipation across topological transitions. These results demonstrate that the framework enables robust, physically consistent simulations of complex surface dynamics, including large deformations and topological changes, without explicit surface tracking.

papers.title: Neural network scaling and generalization for 3D strain fields in heterogeneous materials
papers.abstract: Computational homogenization and coupled multiscale simulations of heterogeneous materials require repeated solution of mechanical fields on Representative Volume Elements, which becomes prohibitively expensive for high-resolution three-dimensional microstructures. Machine-learning surrogates can accelerate these computations, yet most existing approaches predict fields for fixed macroscopic loadings and provide limited guidance on how to scale network architectures for high-resolution 3D tensor-field prediction. This work presents a U-Net surrogate trained to predict the full 36-component strain localization tensor field in voxelized concrete mesostructures at resolutions up to $256^3$. Training localization tensors are generated with an FFT-based linear elastic solver, and an extensive hyperparameter optimization is performed to derive scaling rules and an accuracy-speed trade-off analysis. The results show that only network width and depth need to be scaled with problem complexity, while several conventional U-Net design choices, such as doubling channels after downsampling, are suboptimal for this problem. The final neural network achieves a Mean Absolute Error of 1.118% on both the validation and the held-out test sets, and an inference speedup of approximately 8.7x over the FFT-based solver on an Nvidia H100 GPU. Generalization experiments reveal transfer across aggregate volume fractions and highlight the importance of training on diverse morphologies. To safeguard reliability, a Maximum Mean Discrepancy metric computed on internal feature maps is proposed for detecting out-of-distribution microstructures without costly reference computations.

papers.intro:
In engineering applications, solid materials are generally considered homogeneous at the macroscopic scale, although most of them are heterogeneous at a finer scale. For instance, concrete is composed of aggregates embedded in a cementitious matrix and these two phases possess different mechanical properties, leading to non-uniform stress and strain fields that govern macroscopic performance and durability. The same principle applies to fiber-reinforced composites, and polycrystalline materials.

In engineering applications, solid materials are generally considered homogeneous at the macroscopic scale, although most of them are heterogeneous at a finer scale. For instance, concrete is composed of aggregates embedded in a cementitious matrix and these two phases possess different mechanical properties, leading to non-uniform stress and strain fields that govern macroscopic performance and durability. The same principle applies to fiber-reinforced composites, and polycrystalline materials.

Computational methods such as the Finite Element Method (FEM) and Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) based solvers [1, 2] can be used to compute stress and strain fields in heterogeneous materials. These fields are generally used for homogenization or coupled multiscale simulation purposes. In one-way homogenization, the objective is to derive a macroscopic effective material behavior that will be assigned to the equivalent homogeneous material in macroscopic models. In coupled multiscale approaches, such as FE² [3] and FE-FFT [4], there is no macroscopic constitutive law, and the material behavior is evaluated at each macroscopic integration point by computing and averaging the stress in a heterogeneous Representative Volume Element (RVE) subjected to the macroscopic strain. The multiscale methods can require a very large number of RVE computations depending on the size of the macroscopic mesh and the number of iterations necessary to reach convergence between the two scales (in staggered solving schemes). Unfortunately, for microstructures (or mesostructures) with complex geometries, the computational cost can be very large due to the high resolution required to resolve the fine details. Due to the numerous RVE computations and the potentially high computational cost of each of them, multiscale simulation approaches often lead to infeasible computational times even though these approaches have a tremendous potential to improve the accuracy of simulations by bridging multiple scales, which helps understand and predict complex physical phenomena involving the interaction between a macroscopic problem and microscopic (or mesoscopic) features.

In recent years, Machine Learning (ML) has emerged as a promising paradigm for accelerating the computations of stress and strain fields in heterogeneous materials [5, 6]. Instead of computing these fields on-the-fly for each new microstructure or new loading condition, a dataset is precomputed using traditional numerical methods (generally FEM or FFT-based solvers), an ML model is trained on this dataset, and then used as a surrogate for the numerical model. The computation using the surrogate is often faster than the original at the expense of an additional approximation error. This approach is particularly beneficial for multiscale simulations requiring numerous RVE computations for which the computational cost is critical, although ML surrogate models can be used on their own, to evaluate stress or strain fields in new microstructures and eventually to derive macroscopic effective behaviors. One important limitation is that the generalization outside the training data distribution is not guaranteed.
