In 2015, Liu et al. [7] trained multiple ML models including decision trees, random forests and support vector regression models to predict linear elastic strain fields in 3D microstructures and found that random forest was the best approach for their configuration, with a Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 13 %13\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}. In 2019, Yang et al. [8] discovered that neural networks, and particularly Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) were even better than random forest, reaching 3 %3\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} MAE on the same task. Khanolkar et al. [9] showed CNN capabilities on a wide range of microstructures. A CNN variation, the U-Net architecture [10], first developed for medical image segmentation purposes, was found to be very efficient at predicting stress and strain fields in composites [11, 12, 13, 14] and polycrystalline microstructures [15, 16, 17]. Yang et al. [18] used a generative adversarial training approach on a U-Net for similar tasks, and Monteiro Fernandes et al. [19] compared training based on a physics-informed loss function (minimization of the stress divergence) and training based on simulation data. Other studies have trained U-Nets on more complex microstructures with varying morphologies [20, 21] and volume fractions [22]. In addition to synthetic microstructures, CNNs are also able to predict stress fields in microstructures measured by X-ray tomography [23]. Researchers have successfully trained U-Nets to predict not only strain fields but also fracture patterns [24, 25]. Alternative architectures, including graph neural networks [26, 27], Fourier neural operators [28], difference-based networks [29], and hybrid convolution-attention U-Nets [30, 31] have also shown good capabilities.

Alternative architectures, including graph neural networks [26, 27], Fourier neural operators [28], difference-based networks [29], and hybrid convolution-attention U-Nets [30, 31] have also shown good capabilities.

Most existing ML surrogates for heterogeneous materials predict microscopic stress or strain fields for one or a few fixed macroscopic loadings, which limits their usefulness in multiscale frameworks where arbitrary loading paths must be evaluated. Predicting the full strain localization tensor instead provides a more general representation: a single network forward pass yields a microstructure-specific linear operator from which strain and stress fields can be reconstructed for any macroscopic strain in the linear elastic regime. The same concept extends to tangent operators in nonlinear problems, provided the prediction is conditioned on the current strain state. This tensorial formulation is therefore both physically grounded and computationally advantageous. Furthermore, while U-Nets have repeatedly been shown to perform well on field-prediction tasks, the literature lacks a systematic investigation of how their architecture should be scaled for high-resolution three-dimensional tensor fields, and how hyperparameters should be chosen to balance predictive accuracy against the computational speed required in multiscale simulations. The present work addresses these gaps by (1) training a parametric 3D U-Net to predict the complete 3636-component strain localization tensor in 64364^{3} to 2563256^{3} concrete mesostructures, (2) performing an extensive hyperparameter optimization to derive robust scaling rules and an accuracy-speed trade-off analysis, and (3) assessing the generalization limits of such surrogates when the training microstructural distribution is varied. The resulting model is intended as a fast, data-driven substitute for RVE solvers in coupled multiscale simulations, while highlighting the practical trade-offs that must be navigated when deploying machine-learning surrogates in computational mechanics.

papers.title: Towards funnel control on Riemannian manifolds
papers.abstract: Funnel control for time-invariant control-affine systems with relative degree one is transferred to the case of dynamical systems evolving on a Riemannian manifold. It is shown that, under some regularity assumptions, the classical proofs carry over. The regularity assumptions reflect the particularities of the nonlinear theory and degenerate in the classical Euclidean case.

papers.title: Orchestr.AI: A Unified Workflow for Training and Benchmarking of Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials
papers.abstract: Machine-learning force fields enable atomistic simulations at near-reference accuracy and substantially reduced computational cost, but their development remains fragmented across software frameworks with incompatible data formats, configuration schemes, dependencies, and execution procedures. Orchestr.AI addresses this limitation through a unified workflow that coordinates different MLIP software frameworks, referred to as engines, for data preparation, model training, fine-tuning, evaluation, and deployment. A common YAML interface defines each experiment, while engine-specific environment profiles preserve compatible software stacks and avoid dependency conflicts. The platform currently supports five MLIP model architectures, namely SchNet, PaiNN, NequIP, Allegro, and MACE, through their corresponding software implementations, providing automated configuration mapping and standardized dataset handling across these frameworks. Benchmarks on the rMD17 and 3BPA datasets show that Orchestr.AI reproduces the expected performance trends while enabling controlled cross-engine comparisons. Repeated executions with fixed configurations and engine profiles produce highly consistent results, demonstrating practical workflow reproducibility. Beyond training, Orchestr.AI provides modular architectural interfaces that connect trained models to ASE-based simulations, batch inference, epistemic uncertainty estimation, calibration, and active-learning workflows. The platform therefore provides a reproducible and extensible infrastructure for developing, comparing, and deploying machine-learning interatomic potentials, which we validate here through cross-engine accuracy and repeatability benchmarks.

papers.title: Early X-ray emission as an observational diagnostic of gamma-ray burst progenitors
papers.abstract: Identifying the progenitors of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) from the properties of their early high-energy emission detected by wide-field satellites is crucial for advancing our understanding of GRB physics and for multi-messenger astronomy. Current classification methods, which rely primarily on prompt emission properties, exhibit large scatter and are challenged by recently detected events. In this Letter, we propose a new method to classify GRB progenitors using their early X-ray emission, which is detectable by current wide-field X-ray monitors. We performed a systematic time-resolved spectral analysis of the X-ray steep decay phase for a sample of 23 collapsar-driven GRB candidates detected by the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory. We fitted the spectra over the $0.3 - 150 \, \rm keV$ energy range using both a physical synchrotron model and the empirical Band function, allowing us to constrain the spectral peak energy and the bolometric flux. We find a correlation between the rest-frame synchrotron cooling frequency, $\nu_{c,z}$, and the isotropic-equivalent luminosity, $L_{\rm iso}$, that is clearly separated from the $\nu_{c,z} - L_{\rm iso}$ relation followed by merger-driven GRB candidates. A similarly distinct separation is found in the correlation between the rest-frame peak energy, $E_{p,z}$, and $L_{\rm iso}$ obtained with the Band model. Finally, we provide a prescription for classifying fast X-ray transients detected by the Wide-field X-ray Telescope aboard the Einstein Probe mission, as its narrow energy range ($0.5 - 4 \, \rm keV$) limits spectral modelling to a simple power law. We show that the photon index and X-ray luminosity of the steep decay spectra clearly separate collapsar- and merger-driven candidate events, making them powerful diagnostics of GRB progenitors.

papers.intro:
Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) are the most luminous electromagnetic transients observed in the Universe. Their radiation is characterized by a short-lived and highly variable prompt emission phase, typically detected in the MeV domain, followed by a long-lasting afterglow observable across the electromagnetic spectrum. GRBs are extragalactic sources and are powered by ultra-relativistic, collimated jets. Based on the bimodal distribution of the prompt emission duration (Mazets et al., 1981; Kouveliotou et al., 1993), they have been suggested to originate from two distinct progenitor channels: the merger of compact objects (Eichler et al., 1989, short GRBs, T90≤2​sT_{90}\leq 2\,\rm s;) and the core collapse of massive stars (Woosley, 1993, long GRBs, T90>2​sT_{90}>2\,\rm s;).

However, a firm identification of the GRB progenitor requires additional observational evidence. In particular, the detection of associated thermal transients can provide direct constraints on the progenitor: a supernova (SN) supports a collapsar origin (Galama et al., 1998), whereas a kilonova (KN) indicates a compact binary merger origin (Li and Paczyński, 1998; Abbott et al., 2017c). Another complementary approach is to study the GRB host galaxy: collapsar progenitors are generally associated with star-forming environments (Fruchter et al., 2006), while merger-driven GRBs are found both in old and young stellar populations and at larger offsets from their host galaxies (Berger, 2011; Fong and Berger, 2013). Alternatively, gravitational wave (GW) detection can provide direct confirmation of the merger scenario, as demonstrated by the joint detection of GW 170817 and GRB 170817A from a binary neutron star (BNS) merger (Abbott et al., 2017a; Abbott et al., 2017b; Goldstein et al., 2017; Savchenko et al., 2017; Abbott et al., 2017c).

Furthermore, the limited detection horizons of optical telescopes for SNe and KNe restrict their identification to relatively nearby events (Levan et al., 2026), in contrast to the cosmological distances at which GRBs are detected. Similarly, the sensitivity of the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA detector network currently limits the detection of GWs from BNS mergers to distances of a few hundred Mpc.

papers.title: Planetary material is a major source of hydrogen in helium-atmosphere white dwarfs
papers.abstract: Many white dwarfs with helium-dominated atmospheres show traces of hydrogen in their spectra. On average, the total mass of hydrogen within their convective envelopes increases with age, but there is no consensus on the origin of such hydrogen. Hypotheses include upward diffusion from hidden reservoirs deep within the envelope, or accretion, alongside heavier elements, of planetary material. We construct a simple model that includes both pathways, and test it using two independent samples of helium-atmosphere DB white dwarfs from the DESI and SDSS spectroscopic surveys, selected to have Gaia colours BP-RP > -0.25, corresponding roughly to 10000 < $T_{\rm eff}$ < 19000K. We find that at least $22 \pm 2$ per cent of the helium-atmosphere white dwarfs with detectable hydrogen must have accreted some of it from their planetary systems, via ices, hydrated minerals or atmospheres. We thus demonstrate that planetary hydrogen is a necessary ingredient to explain the spectral evolution of white dwarfs as a population, rather than only extreme hydrogen-enriched cases.

White dwarfs are dense stellar remnants that have ceased nuclear fusion and whose destiny is to cool and crystallise (Mestel, 1952; Salpeter et al., 1961; Tremblay et al., 2019). Their intense gravitational fields (Schatzman, 1958) force atoms to stratify by mass, producing in most cases a core of carbon and oxygen surrounded by a helium-rich envelope and a thin outer layer of hydrogen (Althaus et al., 2010). The interplay between processes such as diffusion (Unglaub and Bues, 1998), stellar winds (Unglaub and Bues, 2000) and convection (MacDonald and Vennes, 1991; Rolland et al., 2018) determines the atmospheric composition of the star, and thus its spectral type. If the balance between these processes shifts, a white dwarf can change its appearance (Bédard, 2024). Similarly, if it begins accreting material from its environment, changes to its atmospheric composition may be detectable spectroscopically.

Most newly formed white dwarfs have sufficient amounts of primordial hydrogen (i.e. inherited from their prior evolution) to have hydrogen-dominated atmospheres during their whole lives, thus preserving their original spectral classification at all cooling ages. However, the fraction of helium-dominated atmosphere white dwarfs varies along the cooling sequence: they account for around 24 per cent of white dwarfs with cooling age ∼1\sim 1 Myr, falling to only about 8 per cent at ∼10\sim 10 Myr, rising again as high as 40 per cent when they reach several Gyr (Bédard et al., 2020; Cunningham et al., 2020; López-Sanjuan et al., 2022; Jiménez-Esteban et al., 2023; Torres et al., 2023; O’Brien et al., 2024; Kilic et al., 2025; Kilic et al., 2026a, e.g.). This phenomenon is termed spectral evolution and is linked to changes in the atmospheric hydrogen abundance.

Historically, the interstellar medium was considered as a potential source for external metal-enrichment of white dwarfs (Alcock and Illarionov, 1980), before accretion from remnant planetary systems was proposed as an alternative (Alcock et al., 1986). The interstellar scenario has since been decisively ruled out in favour of planetary systems, which can supply both hydrogen and metals (Farihi et al., 2010; Zuckerman et al., 2010). About 25–50 per cent of all white dwarfs are observed to accrete metals (Zuckerman et al., 2003; Koester et al., 2014; Manser et al., 2024; Ould Rouis et al., 2024) but, in most cases, that material appears dry and rocky (Trierweiler et al., 2023), adding only traces of hydrogen. However, water can survive within planetesimals throughout post-main-sequence evolution (Jura and Xu, 2010; Malamud and Perets, 2016; Malamud and Perets, 2017a; Malamud and Perets, 2017b), and the number of systems thought to be accreting large quantities of hydrogen is growing, with sources including water-rich asteroids (Farihi et al., 2013; Raddi et al., 2015), icy objects (Xu et al., 2017; Klein et al., 2021; Johnson et al., 2022; Sahu et al., 2025) and giant planets (Gänsicke et al., 2019; Schreiber et al., 2019). Crucially, while metals sink out of the convective envelope, accreted hydrogen accumulates.

It has been proposed that a large fraction of stars with trace hydrogen may have accreted water-rich debris at some point in their history (Raddi et al., 2015), as some heavily metal-enriched He-atm stars have large quantities of hydrogen, and excess photospheric oxygen after accounting for the metal oxides in dry rock. Hydrogen is detected almost twice as frequently at He-atm white dwarfs with photospheric metals than at those without, further supporting the hypothesis that accretion of planetary hydrogen is involved (Gentile Fusillo et al., 2017). papers.title: NuSTAR view of the NGC 4151 corona: thermal balance and astroparticle constraints
papers.abstract: I present a comprehensive analysis of all publicly available NuSTAR observations of the nearby Seyfert galaxy NGC 4151 (2012--2024). The hard X-ray continuum is well described by thermal Comptonization in a hot corona, with electron temperatures $kT_{\rm e} \approx 40-125$ keV and optical depths $\tau \approx 0.4-1.2$ (slab geometry). A clear anti-correlation between $kT_{\rm e}$ and $\tau$ is observed, consistent with a thermostat behavior with constant Compton parameter $\gamma \approx 3.12$ calculated according to Sunyaev and Titarchuk (1980). Variability on timescales of hours constrains the size of the emitting region to $R \approx 250-1200 r_{\rm g}$, corresponding to moderate compactness values $\ell \lesssim 4$. The source occupies the same region of the compactness--temperature plane as other local Seyferts, with no evidence for pair runaway. I then explore two astroparticle implications. The IceCube neutrino excess reported toward NGC 4151 corresponds to $L_\nu/L_X \approx 0.3\%$, an energetically negligible contribution that does not alter the observed coronal energy balance. An additional injection of pairs from the hypothetical X17 boson cannot produce significant changes, unless the injection rate exceeds the photoproduction one, but no anomalies were found in the present data set. The NuSTAR data thus provide no evidence for either a significant neutrino cooling channel or an X17-related pair injection in the corona of NGC 4151.

papers.intro:
The NuSTAR satellite (Harrison et al., 2013), launched in 2012, is the first instrument focusing X-rays above 10 keV. It is placed in low-Earth orbit, where the background is low. These two factors determined an improvement of the hard X-rays sensitivity up to two orders of magnitude with respect to previous hard X-rays satellites. On the focal plane, there are two CdZnTe pixellated detectors, named FPMA and FPMB (Focal Plane Module A, B). The nominal energy range is 3−78.43-78.4 keV, with 0.40.4 keV resolution at 1010 keV. Its superb performance makes it the best instrument available to date to study the hot corona of active galactic nuclei (AGN, e.g. Fabian et al. 2015).

papers.title: A Lightweight Differentiable Method for Real-Time Skin Rendering and Digitization
papers.abstract: Inverse rendering for skin typically relies on offline path tracing to estimate physical properties, which fail to map directly to the approximate shaders utilized in interactive applications, such as game engines. We bridge this gap by directly estimating subsurface scattering parameters tailored for real-time rendering pipelines. We introduce a differentiable Screen-Space Subsurface Scattering (SSSS) framework that enables the joint optimization of spatially varying base textures and scattering distances. To account for local variations in skin thickness, we estimate these parameters across distinct facial regions, generating a blended profile map ready for production runtime engines. Our pipeline utilizes a low-cost, single-light, single-view capture setup designed for accessible and practical appearance acquisition. Optimization is driven by a masked loss function targeting regions where subsurface scattering effects are dominant. We validate our approach on a real-world dataset of $45$ individuals across the Monk Skin Tone Scale, ensuring demographic generalization. Furthermore, we complement this evaluation with synthetic data, a multi-light setup validating our single-light assumption, and a tilted-view configuration confirming angular consistency. Results demonstrate that our method effectively recovers scattering parameters from lightweight inputs, yielding realistic skin appearance directly compatible with standard real-time shaders.

papers.intro:
Accurately simulating human skin remains a significant challenge in computer graphics due to its physical complexity and the high sensitivity of the human visual system to facial appearance. As a layered, anisotropic, and spatially varying medium, skin involves intricate subsurface scattering, fine-scale geometric details, and directionally dependent light transport. To meet the computational constraints of interactive applications, the industry often relies on screen-space approximations rather than full volumetric path tracing. However, the perceptual sensitivity of observers ensures that even subtle rendering inaccuracies appear unnatural. Additionally, the global diversity of skin tones demands methods that generalize across the full spectrum of human pigmentation while maintaining both physical plausibility and real-time performance.

Accurately simulating human skin remains a significant challenge in computer graphics due to its physical complexity and the high sensitivity of the human visual system to facial appearance. As a layered, anisotropic, and spatially varying medium, skin involves intricate subsurface scattering, fine-scale geometric details, and directionally dependent light transport. To meet the computational constraints of interactive applications, the industry often relies on screen-space approximations rather than full volumetric path tracing. However, the perceptual sensitivity of observers ensures that even subtle rendering inaccuracies appear unnatural. Additionally, the global diversity of skin tones demands methods that generalize across the full spectrum of human pigmentation while maintaining both physical plausibility and real-time performance.

Traditional approaches for capturing skin optical properties often require sophisticated hardware, such as hyperspectral sensors or polarimetric imaging systems [23, 1, 32]. While these methods yield accurate results, they are typically expensive, restricted to controlled laboratory settings, and produce physical parameters (e.g., extinction coefficients) that do not map directly to real-time shaders. Furthermore, they often struggle to scale across the diverse facial expressions and skin tones encountered in real-world scenarios. To address these limitations, we introduce a low-cost, replicable single-view, single-light capture setup. Our compact configuration facilitates the practical acquisition of skin appearance without requiring specialized environments.

To address these limitations, we introduce a low-cost, replicable single-view, single-light capture setup. Our compact configuration facilitates the practical acquisition of skin appearance without requiring specialized environments.

Instead of estimating offline physical parameters like absorption or extinction coefficients through complex path-tracing intermediaries, we directly optimize the specific parameters used in real-time rendering pipelines. We ground our approach in the Bidirectional Subsurface Scattering Reflectance Distribution Function (BSSRDF), specifically utilizing the Burley Normalized Diffusion profile [6], the standard for real-time physically based skin shading. To enable optimization, we implement a differentiable version of the Screen-Space Subsurface Scattering (SSSS) algorithm incorporating this profile. This model provides control via the scattering distance parameter, which governs the distance light travels beneath the surface. Tuning this parameter manually is difficult due to its strong coupling with material appearance and the lack of direct visual references. Our approach automates this process by directly optimizing scattering distance textures from photographic data, enabling efficient and plausible appearance reconstruction.

Our approach automates this process by directly optimizing scattering distance textures from photographic data, enabling efficient and plausible appearance reconstruction.

Prior work frequently underexplores skin tone diversity, focusing primarily on mid-range tones and resulting in biased models that generalize poorly across lighter or darker skin. To address this limitation and drive representative skin modeling, we anchor our framework in the Monk Skin Tone Scale [35] (Fig. 2). Unlike traditional scales designed primarily for dermatological UV response (e.g., Fitzpatrick [14]), the Monk scale provides a perceptually balanced distribution covering the broad spectrum of human skin tones. Our primary goal is to leverage this scale to deliver a lightweight differentiable inverse rendering method that is physically grounded, equitable across diverse populations, and directly compatible with real-time production pipelines.

papers.title: Entropy: the Route from the Gaussian Field to the Statistical Mechanics of the Thermal Radiation
papers.abstract:
Maximum Entropy or canonical typicality applied to the electromagnetic field can provide starting points for arriving at the Bose distribution of the photon numbers of thermal radiation, but they rely on statistical postulates whose experimental testability is controversial.
  Here we start from experimentally verifiable assumption of Gaussianity of the electromagnetic field. We analyze the field by projecting it onto orthonormal time-frequency basis functions with unitary bandwidth duration product that represent field's orthogonal time-frequency modes. Through the Glauber-Surashdan representation, we see that the joint density operator of the modes in the photon number basis factorize into diagonal density operators with geometric coefficients of individual modes, while the mean photon occupations of the modes remains still unknown. The independent imposition of Clausius' relation on each one of the entropies and energies of the modes leads to Bose's mean photon occupancy.
  Thus, our main claim is that for the first time Bose statistics is recovered in the paper under explicit, experimentally verifiable statistical assumptions, without assuming any statistical postulate that is not directly experimentally verifiable.
  From the mean occupation numbers, the Boltzmann distribution of the energy of matter particles of the material that generates/absorbes the radiation is then derived by retracing in the backward direction the Einstein-Feynman detailed balance.
papers.intro:
Entropy Maximization (MaxEnt) with expected energy constraint is the basic assumption from which Bose derives his famous occupancy statistics of photons [1]. Later, Jaynes [2] interpreted the MaxEnt principle as a general inference principle of statistical mechanics from which the equilibrium probability distributions are derived. The MaxEnt principle has found widespread applications and has been supported by axiomatic consistency arguments [3]. However, its status as a fundamental principle of statistical mechanics remains controversial. Friedman and Shimony [4] and Diaconis and Shimony [5] identified limitations of the MaxEnt prescription, while Uffink [6] challenged the claimed uniqueness of its axiomatic justification. These criticisms emphasize the distinction between a principle for assigning probabilities from incomplete information and a physical explanation of the statistical behavior of microscopic systems.

An alternative route to the photon number spectral distribution of thermal radiation is provided by canonical typicality. It establishes concentration of reduced states with respect to the uniform (Haar) measure over the energy-constrained pure states of the universe, comprising the system and its environment [7, 8]. This framework has also been applied to quantum fields in [9], where an individual mode (the system) is separated from the remaining modes (the environment). However, the cited works do not provide an experimental procedure for testing whether the global pure states produced by a radiation source are distributed according to this uniform measure.

The approach proposed in this paper requires neither the MaxEnt assumption nor the assumption about Haar-uniform sampling of global pure quantum states, as we take as unique assumption the circular Gaussianity of the field complex envelopes. We hasten to point out that Gaussianity of thermal radiation is well established [10], but here we follow the converse route: starting from a classical Gaussian field with an initially unknown energy spectral density, we recover the geometric photon statistics of thermal radiation and subsequently determine the equilibrium spectrum through Clausius’ relation. In this context, the Central Limit Theorem (CLT) provides microscopic sufficient conditions on the radiating material for Gaussianity of the field. The relevance of these conditions is illustrated by Macovei [11], who predicts non-geometric, even sub-Poissonian, photon statistics for radiation emitted by small ensembles of atoms in thermal equilibrium with their environment.

papers.title: Efficient control of multi-agent robust MDPs through tensor trees
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a tensor-based framework for controller synthesis of stochastic multi-agent systems under temporal logic specifications that couple the agents, such as one agent reaching its goal only after another agent has reached its own. The agents are modeled as robust Markov decision processes (RMDPs), whose transition probabilities are only known to lie in an ambiguity set, for instance due to abstraction errors, learned models, or uncertain parameters. We show that the decoupled nature of the ambiguity sets allows one to decompose the computation of a lower bound on the satisfaction probabilities into per-agent factors, so that only the per-agent ambiguity sets need to be stored. This leads to improved memory complexity compared to monolithic approaches. We compare our approach with state-of-the-art approaches based on approximate simulation relations and with interval MDP abstractions. On a four-agent ordered reach-avoid benchmark, our approach certifies a lower bound twice as high as the simulation relation- based approach with 20 times less memory, and needs about 200 times less memory than the interval MDP abstraction, even at a resolution with about a million times more joint cells.

papers.intro:
Teams of autonomous agents increasingly operate in domains where failures are costly or dangerous, such as warehouse logistics [1] and disaster response with unmanned aerial vehicles [2]. These agents may be required to complete tasks that constrain them jointly. For instance, robots carry packages in a convoy through a shared corridor, or drones reach their designated zones in a given order. Temporal logic specifications express such tasks formally, as requirements on the order and timing of events along the agents’ behaviours [3, 4]. Agents’ motion is subject to random disturbances, and the models used for control design are only approximate. Under uncertainty, a controller may fail the task, which can damage goods, delay a rescue operation, or endanger people nearby. Controllers therefore need guarantees that hold despite this uncertainty before they are deployed. Correct-by-design control synthesis provides such guarantees. It computes a controller together with a formal guarantee that the controlled system satisfies a temporal logic specification [4].

For stochastic systems, the guarantee is a certified lower bound on the probability that the specification is satisfied [5, 6]. Arguably, the state-of-the-art approach to compute such guarantees is to rely on finite-model formal approximations of the continuous-state system, called abstractions [7, 8]. However, the transition probabilities of such finite models are often known only within sets, due to abstraction errors [7, 9], estimation from data, or uncertain parameters [10]. Robust Markov decision processes (RMDPs) model these uncertainties by an ambiguity set for each state and input: a set of transition distributions that contains those of the true system [11, 10]. Interval MDPs are a widely used instance [12, 7, 13]. For multi-agent systems, the specification is evaluated on the joint behaviour of the agents. Specification-decomposition-based methods split the team specification into per-agent tasks [14], or start from local tasks for each agent, possibly with synchronization [15]. Compositional methods treat each agent separately against assumptions on other agents [16]. These methods do not yet address specifications that couple the agents. For such specifications, a common approach is dynamic programming on the product of the agents’ state spaces [17], whose memory and running time grow exponentially with the number of agents. The key research gap we will address in this paper is to certify a lower bound for multi-agent systems under such specifications without this exponential cost.

papers.title: Learn-To-Propagate: Distributionally Robust Motion Planning for Nonlinear Uncertain Systems
papers.abstract: Motion planning for stochastic systems aims to find a sequence of control inputs that drives a system to a goal set while avoiding unsafe states with high probability. Existing approaches, however, are either restricted to linear dynamics with perfect knowledge of the underlying distributions or lack formal correctness guarantees. To address these limitations, we propose \emph{Learn-To-Propagate Distributionally-Robust Forest (L2P-DR-Forest)}, a distributionally-robust sampling-based planning algorithm for \emph{nonlinear} stochastic systems with \emph{unknown} initial state and process noise distributions. Our approach leverages recent advances in optimal transport to learn ambiguity sets that contain the true system distributions with high confidence. We develop an efficient method for propagating these sets through the system dynamics and for verifying their safety. We then integrate these techniques into a novel sampling-based planning algorithm to grow a forest of search trees in the system's state space while accounting for and mitigating the growth of ambiguity-sets radii. We prove that the algorithm is correct, i.e., every returned plan satisfies the specifications with the prescribed confidence, and, under some feasibility and distributional assumptions, is probabilistically complete. Evaluations on several robotic benchmarks demonstrate that our algorithm significantly outperforms existing methods while providing formal guarantees with high confidence.

papers.intro:
Motion planning has become a central problem in robotics, enabling autonomous systems to operate safely in complex environments while avoiding obstacles. Applications span domains such as autonomous driving, aerial navigation, and robotic surgery. In this context, sampling-based algorithms have emerged as particularly successful approaches (Cortés and Siméon, 2020), where samples from the state and control spaces are used to efficiently construct search trees and compute collision-free trajectories. However, real-world robotic systems are often subject to uncertainty arising from process and measurement noise, external disturbances, and imperfect knowledge of the system dynamics. Unfortunately, existing approaches either rely on linear-Gaussian assumptions to obtain tractable safety guarantees or accommodate more general uncertainty at the expense of formal correctness guarantees (Blackmore et al., 2011; Luders et al., 2010; Luders et al., 2013; Ho et al., 2022; Prattis et al., 2026; Dai et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020). This work aims to bridge this gap by developing a motion planning framework for uncertain systems that provides both correctness and completeness guarantees.

This work aims to bridge this gap by developing a motion planning framework for uncertain systems that provides both correctness and completeness guarantees.

Among approaches that seek formal safety guarantees under uncertain disturbances, two broad directions have emerged. The first assumes that disturbances have bounded support, reducing safety checks to a worst-case reachability problem (Wu et al., 2022; Danielson et al., 2020). While effective in some settings, these methods often become overly conservative when the support of the uncertainty is large. A second direction relies on distributionally robust optimization (DRO) (Mohajerin Esfahani and Kuhn, 2018), constructing sets of plausible probability distributions, referred to as ambiguity sets, and evaluating worst-case probabilities over these sets (Summers, 2018; Hakobyan and Yang, 2020; Renganathan et al., 2020; Lindemann et al., 2021; Gracia et al., 2026). Yet, most existing DRO-based approaches are limited to linear or locally linearized systems, can be overly conservative, and either require a predefined ambiguity set or face challenges in learning sufficiently tight ambiguity sets from data. To address these limitations, we show how recent advances in Wasserstein-based distribution learning (Figueiredo et al., 2026; Fournier and Guillin, 2015) and nonlinear uncertainty propagation (Figueiredo et al., 2025) can be combined to enable safe motion planning for nonlinear stochastic systems with unknown disturbance distributions.

Leveraging recent results in optimal transport, our approach estimates a compact ambiguity set centered around a discrete distribution that is guaranteed, with high probability, to contain the true underlying system distributions. Critically, Wasserstein ambiguity sets admit a highly tractable propagation rule through Lipschitz continuous dynamics, with their radii expanding at most linearly with the Lipschitz constant of the dynamics. Consequently, these sets can be efficiently propagated while preserving computable bounds on distributional uncertainty, avoiding the need for relearning at every propagation step. This property enables rapid exploration of the planning tree and substantially reduces the computational burden associated with exhaustive sampling. Combined with existing DRO results (Gao and Kleywegt, 2023), this allows us to synthesize motion plans that carry formal collision-avoidance guarantees despite underlying distributional uncertainty.

In contrast, comparable methods that do not provide formal safety guarantees exhibit substantially lower reliability.

papers.title: Switching reconstruction of signed graphs: net-degree and balance
papers.abstract: The switching reconstruction problem for $2$-edge-colored graphs, introduced by Bondy and Mercier, asks whether such a graph is determined up to isomorphism by the multiset of the graphs obtained by exchanging the colors of the edges at each vertex; for complete underlying graphs it is the vertex-switching reconstruction problem of Stanley. We study this problem in the language of signed graphs, where the net-degree of a vertex and the notion of balance come naturally into play. We prove that a signed graph on $n\neq4$ vertices is reconstructible when its net-degrees are all positive, all negative or all zero, which generalizes the reconstructibility of regular graphs in Stanley's problem. For connected balanced signed graphs, whose switching reconstruction problem we show to be equivalent to that of connected graphs with a distinguished bipartition of the vertex set, we prove reconstructibility when the two parts of the bipartition differ in size by more than two, and when all net-degrees are non-negative.

papers.intro:
In 2011, Bondy and Mercier [4, Section 6] introduced the switching reconstruction problem for 22-edge-colored graphs: the switching of such a graph at a vertex vv exchanges the colors of the edges incident with vv, the switching deck is the multiset of the isomorphism classes of the nn graphs obtained by switching at each vertex, where nn is the order of the graph, and the question is whether the graph is determined, up to isomorphism, by its deck. When the underlying graph is complete and the two colors are read as “edge” and “non-edge”, this is the vertex-switching reconstruction problem posed by Stanley in 1985 [20].

In 2011, Bondy and Mercier [4, Section 6] introduced the switching reconstruction problem for 22-edge-colored graphs: the switching of such a graph at a vertex vv exchanges the colors of the edges incident with vv, the switching deck is the multiset of the isomorphism classes of the nn graphs obtained by switching at each vertex, where nn is the order of the graph, and the question is whether the graph is determined, up to isomorphism, by its deck. When the underlying graph is complete and the two colors are read as “edge” and “non-edge”, this is the vertex-switching reconstruction problem posed by Stanley in 1985 [20].

Stanley’s problem is a variant of the classical reconstruction problem of Kelly and Ulam, see [3] for a survey; the latter problem was considered for balanced signed graphs by Harary [9]. Stanley asked whether every graph on at least five vertices is reconstructible; the question is still open, and appears as a conjecture in Bondy’s list of beautiful conjectures in graph theory [2]. Stanley proved that graphs on n≢0(mod4)n\not\equiv 0\pmod{4} vertices are reconstructible, and the conjecture is known for disconnected [7, 10], regular and triangle-free graphs [7], for graphs whose degrees satisfy suitable conditions [10, 12], and, by computer search, for n<16n<16 [18]; moreover, the number of subgraphs with fewer than n/2n/2 vertices isomorphic to a given graph is reconstructible, a switching analogue of Kelly’s Lemma [7]. papers.title: From Bias to Positionality: A critical grammar for Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Bias has become a default lens for understanding what machine learning systems do and how we should relate to them. Bias is at root a deviation from a standard; in decision making systems we can supply a standard from outside: a law, a protected attribute, a benchmark, a statistical property. However, even there, biased is often used as a shorthand, without stating what the position taken is - a silent ``relative to''. In a general use of language models, nothing supplies the standard: there is no decision to audit and no counterfactual output, so the shorthand fails. We argue that positionality -- the located, articulated, owned and contestable position from which anything is said -- is the better grammar for the question these models now force: who is speaking, from where? Against the vendors' answer of nowhere and the seductive possibility of everywhere, we argue that when a model is taken as-if speaking, it speaks from somewhere, and this means positionality can describe models, and the way they are believed beyond their warrant, even though they are not accountable speakers. A model's positionality is laminar -- laid down across corpus, tuning, system prompt, application and the live conversation. We separate three sets of factors: the positionality of a model's creators, the behaviour they intend for it, and the behaviour it enacts, and situate current work within this matrix. This lets us highlight what each stratum inherits from the one below, with ruptures and collapses where that inheritance is disavowed. We then return to where models speak from, and discuss the implications for how models are made, read and held accountable.
papers.intro:
Bias is an effective framing for issues with decision making systems: the standard is supplied from outside — by law, a protected attribute, a benchmark, through principles of non-discrimination (Gerards and Borgesius, 2022; Zuiderveen Borgesius, 2020); (European Union, 2026, Article 4a). In AI systems more generally, biases range from this statistical representativeness (Zhou et al., 2022; Buolamwini and Gebru, 2018; Selbst et al., 2019; Green and Viljoen, 2020; Raji et al., 2020; Barocas et al., 2019) through the production of gendered text and images (Guilbeault et al., 2024; Bolukbasi et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2018; Bianchi et al., 2023; Prates et al., 2020; Birhane et al., 2024; Qadri et al., 2023; Sheng et al., 2019) and into wider cultural productions (Kommers et al., 2026; Cremaschi et al., 2025; Noble, 2018; Bunz, 2019; Daryani et al., 2025; Navneet et al., 2026; Jiang et al., 2023; Srinivasan and Uchino, 2021). However, bias is often under-defined in the literature (Ghosh and Wilson, 2025), and it works as shorthand - there is always a silent ’… relative to’. As commonly deployed, the term bias presupposes positionality, but does not clearly articulate it. In this paper, we contend that bias is the wrong grammar for what large language models (LLMs) do and how we relate to them. Instead, positionality fits better: it is a concept that already comes with practices of owning, articulating, costing and contesting a position, and avoids the presupposition of an unbiased position.

In language models, particularly when used for cultural production, there is no clear reference point to build bias relative to. Bias can be measured in limited situations: the insertion of pronouns into template documents (Zhao et al., 2018), roundtrip translations (Prates et al., 2020), choice of gender or style when generating images (Bianchi et al., 2023; Guilbeault et al., 2024), ideology (Cremaschi et al., 2025; Buyl et al., 2024) – but even discussing ideology brings us into the realm where bias breaks down: there is no decision to audit, no counterfactual output, no protected attribute to test around. Further, part of cultural production is actually having a voice: the deviation from neutrality is precisely what is valued (Kommers et al., 2026; Srinivasan and Uchino, 2021). Without a clear standard to build bias relative to, what matters is the position taken in the assemblage of model, system and user.

Language models are increasingly taken as if they are speaking – even if they lack the conditions of accountability to be a true speaker (Gómez, 2026; Zhang, 2026) – and in this frame it makes sense to ask where the speech comes from. The default answer has been nowhere: the position of the vendors, that their models are even-handed, apolitical instruments with no positions of their own, except some bias that may be reduced (OpenAI, 2025b; Anthropic, 2025), as an approximation of neutrality (Fisher et al., 2025). In contrast, Neuman (Neuman, 2026) argues that language models offer the possibility of a view from everywhere, as they contain "representations of many social identities without personally inhabiting any one of them", giving a "moral standpoint unavailable to individual human reasoners". While there is something compelling to the idea that models are "condensates of human culture" (Neuman, 2026), and have a unique point to speak from, we argue it is important to treat it as somewhere. LLMs have a credibility excess (Fricker, 2007; Bondy, 2010; Zhang, 2026), where they are seen as more authoritative than warranted; this makes it relevant to ask what is the somewhere from which they speak, rather than falling back on the abstracted nowhere and everywhere.

Positionality keeps the question "who is speaking, from where?" open, framing the shaping of a model as taking a position rather than removing a defect. Models take a particular, sedimented, composite position — laid down in a corpus, filtered by raters, written into a specification, steered by a deployer, bent by the conversation — that can be located, articulated, owned and contested, even without "a singular human social position." (Neuman, 2026). We explore what it means to take seriously the idea that a language model has a positionality, and ask what that is. Philosophically, this draws on a cosmopolitical worldview (Stengers, 2005), an avoidance of flattening towards a single consensus through keeping open multiple, divergent worlds. Alongside questions of the ideologies they encode (Buyl et al., 2024; Cremaschi et al., 2025; Kröger and Barkett, 2025), or the values they embody (Birhane et al., 2021), positionality offers a generative, diagnostic grammar to discuss multiple aspects of the operation of language models and their socio-technical embedding.

papers.title: Non-closed products in branch and weakly branch groups
papers.abstract: We prove that the first Grigorchuk group and the Gupta-Sidki $3$-group are not double coset separable, disproving a conjecture of Grigorchuk, Leemann and Nagnibeda. More generally, every finitely generated regular branch group with bounded activity contains two finitely generated, profinitely closed subgroups with trivial intersection whose product is not closed. Every infinite finitely generated subgroup of the first Grigorchuk group or the Gupta-Sidki $3$-group also fails to be double coset separable. We extend the construction to the $p$-Basilica groups and, using polynomial activity, to the long-range group, whose derived subgroup we prove to be finitely generated. Under an additional hypothesis on finite quotients, we determine the closure of the product. Membership in the constructed product is decidable in the first Grigorchuk group.

papers.title: Deep Learning for Operator Maps in Optimal Liquidation
papers.abstract: We analyze the solution map of a optimal execution problem in which price dynamics are subject to a general transient impact kernel. Given the structure of the optimal trading strategy derived by Abi Jaber and Neuman in \cite{https://doi.org/10.1111/mafi.12465}, we show that the strategy is locally Lipschitz continuous with respect to the underlying model parameters governing temporary and transient price impact as well as the fundamental price process. Continuity of this map justifies the application of neural-net based approximations which take model parameters as inputs. We propose a method generating samples of the transient price impact kernel for the purposes of creating training data, and a method of projecting the kernel to a finite dimensional representation appropriate for input to a neural net, and a dimensional reduction based on the relationship between inventory and trade signal. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the trained neural net and use it to quantify the potential financial costs associated with misspecifying the transient impact kernel.

papers.intro:
The market trading phenomenon known as price impact can affect the value of asset holdings, depending on the schedule of submitted trades. Indeed, present and future prices of an asset will typically be lower if a trader makes a sequence of large sell actions than they would have been otherwise. Such effects manifest as a cost to the trader when employing a liquidation program. Therefore, in order to ensure efficient trade prices, these effects need to be incorporated into market model assumptions when designing trade algorithms.

Therefore, in order to ensure efficient trade prices, these effects need to be incorporated into market model assumptions when designing trade algorithms.

Extensive empirical analysis of price impact effects and associated dynamics has been carried out in works such as [10], [3], [18], and [7]. Each of these works analyzes trade and quote data, or tick-by-tick data, to estimate models that capture the relationship between trade volumes and price dynamics. Further empirical analysis and modeling that consider phenomena beyond price impact can be found in [33], [26], and [11].

Further empirical analysis and modeling that consider phenomena beyond price impact can be found in [33], [26], and [11].

Preliminary work on investigating the effects of price impact on optimal trade scheduling appears in [9] and [2]. These works show how to balance the tradeoff between the cost of trading quickly due to price impact and the risk of trading slowly due to random future price changes. These findings come from framing the agent’s liquidation objective as a dynamic stochastic control problem and then computing the optimal strategy for a risk-neutral or risk-averse trader. In the last few decades, the literature on optimal liquidation has extended significantly to include additional types of price impact and market features beyond price impact. See, for example, [13] and [27] which incorporate a signal into the dynamics of the price process. The stochasticity of price impact and volatility is considered in, for example, [4], [17], [14], and [6].

Transient price impact and resilience are effects that quantify how prices revert back to pre-trade values after having been subjected to impact due to market activity. Adapting optimal trading strategies to account for transient price impact has been explored in works such as [5], [16], and [20]. A very general form of transient price impact is considered in [1] on which the model of the present work is based. In that paper, the authors characterize the optimal strategy in terms of a backward stochastic differential equation (BSDE) and an operator-valued Riccati equation. In this work, we derive several regularity properties of the solution map that justify the application of a type of universal approximation theorem, thereby facilitating the training of a recurrent neural network (RNN) to learn how to compute the optimal trading strategy as a function of the infinite-dimensional model parameters.

Other work has applied machine learning techniques to algorithmic trading problems. Each of [32], [12], [31], and [28] considers a reinforcement learning (RL) paradigm in the context of optimal trade execution, either to take advantage of statistical arbitrage or to liquidate a large block of shares. Similar techniques are applied in [23] to devise optimal market making strategies. In [15], instead of approaching the problem via RL, a neural net (NN) is trained to take model parameters and states as inputs. This NN represents the agent’s value function, which is used in a dynamic programming sense to compute the optimal strategy, unlike our work in which the RNN represents the agent’s trading strategy directly.

A closely related approach is developed in [29], where they consider a similar optimal liquidation framework with transient impact. Their method first uses an in-context operator network to infer an unknown price-impact operator from observed trajectories and then trains a separate neural-network policy for the inferred environment. Their numerical experiments consider exponential and power-law kernels. By contrast, in this paper we assume that the kernel is given and train a single RNN to approximate the solution directly across a broad class of admissible kernels.

papers.title: Sub-Ice: semi-automated mapping of basal channels from ice shelf surface elevation data
papers.abstract: Basal channels, troughs carved into ice shelf bases by buoyant plumes, modulate basal melt and can weaken ice shelves. Through hydrostatic adjustment they have a surface expression, yet their geometry is largely mapped manually, limiting the number of channels studied and the consistency between mappings. We present Sub-Ice, a semi-automated tool that maps basal channels from surface digital elevation models. From user-defined start and end points, Sub-Ice traces the channel centerline by iteratively locating elevation minima, extracts cross-sectional profiles and delineates channel edges using one of three methods (slope threshold, profile knee point or peak prominence), producing georeferenced centerlines and edges and along-channel width and depth. Applied to 34 channels on Roi Baudouin Ice Shelf, East Antarctica, Sub-Ice centerlines differ from manually digitized ones by a median of 132 m, at the upper end of the differences between manual records from different years (74-132 m), while following the channel trough more closely. Absolute channel widths depend on the edge method and the width of the edge search window, which we calibrate against a slope-based criterion. Rather than seeking a single "true" edge, Sub-Ice applies explicit, reproducible criteria, enabling consistent comparison of channel geometry across channels, ice shelves and time.

papers.intro:
Ice shelves (the floating extensions of an ice sheet) exert a backstress on the glaciers and ice streams that feed them, slowing the flow of ice toward the sea. A reduction in this buttressing effect due to ice shelf thinning or break-up can trigger an acceleration of upstream ice discharge and, in turn, an indirect contribution to sea level rise (Rignot and others,, 2004; Fürst and others,, 2016). A key driver of ice shelf thinning is ocean-driven basal melting, and one of its most visible consequences at the ice shelf base is the formation of basal melt channels: elongated, kilometer-scale troughs carved by buoyant water plumes. This buoyant water can originate from subglacial discharge at the grounding line (Le Brocq and others,, 2013) or from ocean water intruding beneath the shelf and concentrating in pre-existing basal topography (Gladish and others,, 2012; Millgate and others,, 2013). Once established, channels tend to be self-sustaining and can persist over decades. Basal melt channels are widespread around the Antarctic continent and have been documented beneath ice shelves across a wide range of oceanographic and glaciological settings (Alley and others,, 2016). Their relevance to ice shelf stability extends beyond their role as a signature of ocean forcing. Locally thinned ice above a channel concentrates strain (Lilien and others,, 2025), and channels have been linked to basal and surface crevassing (Rignot and Steffen,, 2008; Vaughan and others,, 2012; Alley and others,, 2016), the weakening of ice shelf shear margins (Alley and others,, 2019; Lhermitte and others,, 2020; Miele and others,, 2023), and transverse fractures that can propagate across the shelf (Dow and others,, 2018). Channel-driven fracture has been directly associated with ice shelf calving events: for example, in 2016 the calving of iceberg C-33 from the Nansen Ice Shelf followed a transverse fracture that developed above a basal channel (Dow and others,, 2018; Dow and others,, 2024), and in 2021 iceberg D-29 calved from Roi Baudouin Ice Shelf following the joining of two channel-associated fractures (Jackson and others,, in press). Basal melt channels are, in this sense, “both indicators of change and modulators of ice-shelf stability” (Alley and others,, 2023). Recently, it was shown that channelized melt beneath Antarctic ice shelves has been substantially underestimated, warranting further investigation into the link between basal channel dynamics and large-scale ice shelf stability (Zinck and others,, 2026).

Studying basal channels is inherently difficult because they form at the ice-ocean interface, tens to hundreds of meters below the surface. In-situ measurements from ground-penetrating radar (GPR) surveys (Langley and others,, 2014; Drews and others,, 2017), boreholes (Stanton and others,, 2013) and autonomous underwater vehicles (Dutrieux and others,, 2014; Wåhlin and others,, 2024) provide the most direct view of channel geometry and the ocean conditions within channels, but their coverage is limited in space and time. Numerical models offer insight into the plume dynamics and thermodynamics driving channel formation and evolution (Jenkins,, 2011; Gladish and others,, 2012; Sergienko,, 2013; Millgate and others,, 2013; Drews,, 2015; Stubblefield and others,, 2023), but are limited by the scarcity of observations at the ice-ocean interface. Remote sensing provides a complementary route to spatially distributed and temporally repeated observations. Although melting takes place at the ice shelf base, basal channels have a visible surface expression due to hydrostatic adjustment: because the ice above a channel is thinner than the surrounding shelf, the surface is slightly depressed, typically by only a few meters across channels several kilometers wide. This surface expression is a dampened reflection of the basal geometry, which can be considerably more complex (Langley and others,, 2014), and narrow channels can be held out of hydrostatic equilibrium by bridging stresses (Drews,, 2015). Large channels, however, are close to hydrostatic equilibrium, and their surface expression therefore provides a useful first-order measure of channel position, shape and evolution.

Remote sensing studies have exploited both optical imagery, in which channels appear as subtle brightness contrasts, and digital elevation models (DEMs), in which they appear as topographic lows. Alley and others, (2016) compiled the first Antarctic-wide inventory of basal channel distribution, identifying channels manually in MODIS mosaics and Landsat 8 imagery. They quantified channel abundance by length and density (channel length per ice shelf area) rather than by channel area, as they found channel edges diffuse and difficult to identify consistently. Subsequent studies have focused on the temporal evolution of individual channels or channel systems. Chartrand and Howat, (2020) traced the migration of a large channel on the Getz Ice Shelf by locating local minima in DEMs and altimetry profiles, which were then manually edited and smoothed into centerlines. Alley and others, (2024) manually digitized the centerlines of 12 large channels in West Antarctica over five decades of Landsat imagery, showing that ice-flow-independent lateral migration constitutes a novel proxy for changes in ocean forcing. Similarly, Jackson and others, (in press) manually mapped the centerlines of 11 channels on Roi Baudouin Ice Shelf annually from 2002 to 2021. Advances in altimetry now also allow channelized melt to be resolved directly: Lowery and others, (2025) derived monthly melt maps of the Pine Island Glacier ice shelf from CryoSat-2 DEMs, showing that melt varies both across and along its largest channels. Detailed channel geometries (centerlines, edges and cross-sectional shape) have thus been mapped for only a small number of channels, and a consistent record of basal channel geometry beyond individual ice shelves is still lacking.

papers.title: The Impact of a Magnetic Field on stochastically generated g-modes
papers.abstract: Magnetic fields have been proposed as a mechanism for suppressing low-frequency gravity modes in stellar interiors, providing a means of constraining internal magnetic field strengths. However, previous suppression criteria have largely relied on linear theory. Here, we use two-dimensional nonlinear magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations in a core convecting star to investigate the interaction of gravity waves with magnetic fields of varying strengths and geometries. Using both global and local field geometries, we find that amplitude reduction is gradual and frequency dependent, with low-frequency modes preferentially attenuated while higher-frequency modes can be amplified. In order to achieve significant suppression we require a magnetic field strength at least an order of magnitude larger than predicted by commonly used linear criteria. Its likely that this difference arises because magnetic fields can themselves excite waves through Maxwell stresses, offsetting magnetic attenuation. Our results demonstrate that strong magnetic modifications to wave propagation do not necessarily result in equivalent suppression of the global oscillation spectrum. The linear criteria typically used to infer field strengths based on mode suppression does not capture all relevant physics and should be used with care.

Magnetic fields are ubiquitous in stellar astrophysics, being either frozen into a star’s interior during formation (a ’fossil’ field) or actively generated by dynamo action [54, 25, 71]. In intermediate mass and massive main sequence stars with convective cores, a dynamo occurs within the convective core and the radiative region is then threaded by the fossil field or possibly regenerated locally by e.g. the Tayler-Spruit dynamo [70, 56, 21]. If the field is fossil in nature it is likely predominantly dipolar, since diffusion would have would act on the smallest scales first, though smaller scale fields could still exist.

During the main-sequence, these fields can significantly influence a star’s internal structure and evolution, affecting the rotation profile [70], chemical stratification [47], convective overshoot [7] and surface abundances [26]. Therefore, internal magnetic fields are likely very important in stellar evolution. Unfortunately, we have little observational constraints on fields in these stars, with large scale stable fields having only been observed in ≈10%\approx 10\% of massive stars [82, 33, 14]. Observational constraints on deeper magnetic fields would therefore, be very useful and are just becoming available [76, 72, 38].

Internal gravity waves (IGWs) are also present in stably stratified stellar radiative regions, such as the envelopes of intermediate mass/massive stars [57, 40, 60]. After generation at core-radiative boundaries (CRBs) they are able to affect angular momentum redistribution [83, 73, 29] and chemical mixing [30, 61, 77]. These waves also give rise to standing gravity modes (g-modes) which can be used by asteroseismologists to probe the deep interior and infer quantities such as core mass [1, 2] near core rotation rate [75] and chemical stratification [50, 55].

papers.title: An Analytical Model of Compute-limited Multistage Training Pipelines
papers.abstract: Modern foundation models are trained through multiple stages, yet how these stages interact and how compute should be allocated across them remain poorly understood. We introduce an analytically tractable high-dimensional model combining unsupervised pretraining with a linear autoencoder, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with noisy stepwise labels, and reinforcement learning (RL) with sparse episodic rewards. Using random matrix theory and an operator-projection closure, we derive approximate low-dimensional learning dynamics that closely match simulations. We show that finite pretraining data imposes a representation-dependent performance limit, with Bayes classification error scaling as the inverse square root of the pretraining sample ratio, and observe the same exponent in asymptotic SFT and RL errors. Better pretraining also reduces sensitivity to noisy supervision. SFT initialization shortens the initial RL plateau induced by sparse rewards, an effect we also observe in OLMo-2 1B on GSM8K. Longer SFT warm starts additionally improve asymptotic RL performance. Optimizing compute across all three stages reveals that the optimal allocation depends on supervision quality and total budget, with a non-monotonic dependence of the RL compute share on budget. Finally, a complementary compositional model shows how RL selectively strengthens task-relevant pretrained skills while largely preserving unused skills. Together, these results identify mechanisms linking representation quality, feedback structure, and compute allocation in multistage training.

Alongside the transition to multistage training pipelines, foundation models reflect a second shift from a sample-complexity–centric view of learning to a compute-centric one. Whereas classical theory treats data as the limiting resource and implicitly assumes unbounded compute, modern foundation models invert this assumption: data is abundant, compute is limited, and performance scales predictably with model size and training compute, as evidenced by large-scale empirical scaling laws Kaplan et al. (2020); Hoffmann et al. (2022). In this compute-limited regime, models are rarely trained to convergence, and performance is instead determined by how a fixed computational budget is allocated across model capacity and multiple training stages.

papers.title: Everything in its right place: attention is a radio head
papers.abstract: Attention, the core of language models, is a digital calculation over tokens: an exponential selects them, a division normalizes and a positional code sets the order. We show that attention can instead emerge from the synchronization of a receiver with its context tokens. Each past token is an oscillator whose state carries its content and whose frequency drifts with its age. The present token selects them by content, aligning an antenna with its query, and by position, setting the frequency of a receiver with its dial. Solving Kuramoto's problem for this receiver yields an attention layer in closed form with two phases: above a critical coupling set by the context, the receiver locks and its weights normalize; below it, it stays silent and its weights sum to less than one. Trained networks use both phases to select, abstain and count, fail where the theory predicts and keep reading far beyond the training length. Each part of attention finds its place in one device, a radio head: it tunes in to what to hear and when, and stays silent when nothing relevant is on air.

papers.title: Project Progress Desk: Know Where All Your Claude Code and Codex Projects Stand at a Glance
papers.abstract: Codex and Claude Code let developers work on many projects in parallel, but keeping track of them still means switching between chats, terminal sessions and providers. We present Project Progress Desk, a local desktop interface that brings overall progress, blockers and pending decisions into one view. Users can see which projects need attention, inspect what remains, and compare earlier approaches before choosing how to continue. Agent receipts link reported outcomes to each project's weighted acceptance checklist; the overview distinguishes receipt-supported progress from dated estimates. We describe daily use across 36 projects, including a choice between two implementations based on their recorded outcomes. At the demo, attendees will explore 30 simulated projects, trace completed work to overall progress, and watch a coding agent's new result update the overview.

papers.title: Disentangling Multimodal Rotary Positional Embedding in Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Vision-language models widely adopt Multimodal Rotary Position Embedding (MRoPE), an extension of Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) that incorporates temporal, height, and width axes to encode the spatial structure of visual tokens. However, MRoPE also assigns height and width coordinates to text tokens that lack inherent spatial structure, introducing spatial positional effects into text-vision attention. Existing MRoPE variants explore different frequency allocations and coordinate layouts, with their designs suggesting different intuitions about these cross-modal effects: they may provide useful spatial references for associating language with visual regions, or introduce unnecessary positional preferences that hinder text-vision interactions. In this work, we disentangle intra-visual spatial structure from cross-modal spatial effects to investigate this question. We identify a constraint of shared coordinate layouts that prevents eliminating cross-modal spatial effects while preserving intra-visual spatial encoding, and develop controlled experiments to isolate their respective contributions. Our results across multiple model scales, MRoPE variants, and benchmarks show that cross-modal spatial effects provide little additional benefit as spatial references and can even impair model performance, while intra-visual spatial encoding remains useful for fine-grained grounding.

One adoption in vision-language models (VLMs), hereafter referred to as vanilla RoPE, assigns one-dimensional position indices to a flattened sequence of text and visual tokens. Multimodal Rotary Position Embedding (MRoPE) [23] extends this formulation by introducing three positional axes: temporal, height, and width. papers.title: The RSI Tax: When Recursive Self-Improvement Is Not Worth the Cost
papers.abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) seeks to improve an agent using its own task experience. Its practical value depends on whether performance gains justify the full cost of self-improvement and task execution. We evaluate this trade-off on continual task streams, scoring each task before its feedback is used for subsequent updates. We define the \emph{RSI Tax} as the token cost of the self-improvement process and include it alongside task-execution costs in end-to-end evaluation. Across six methods and two language models, a bounded-note baseline matches or exceeds the observed accuracy of Meta-Harness, EvoSkill, and RRSI, with mean total-token savings of 65.6-71.0\%. We decompose the RSI Tax into verification, exploration, and writing costs, and track subsequent use of the associated state or artifact. For these three RSI methods, verification accounts for 74.8--93.6% of the aggregate RSI Tax. A substantial share of the RSI Tax is also associated with states or artifacts that are not used later in the evaluated streams. These results expose a practical limitation of costly RSI procedures: improvements in the deployed agent need not justify the expense of the improvement process. They motivate RSI objectives that jointly optimize the RSI Tax and expected task-execution cost while ensuring continued growth in agent capabilities across the task stream.

papers.title: A posteriori error estimates for higher-order BDF methods for parabolic partial differential equations
papers.abstract: We derive a posteriori error estimates for parabolic problems discretized by conforming finite elements in space and by the backward differentiation formula of order $k$ in time, with variable step-sizes for $k \le 3$ and constant step-size for $k = 4$. The key ingredient of the analysis is a polynomial $(k+1)$-point time reconstruction of degree $k$ of the approximate solution combined with the elliptic reconstruction. We conclude upper a posteriori error bounds in $L^\infty(L^2) \cap L^2(H^1)$ and in $L^\infty(H^1) \cap H^1(L^2)$. Numerical experiments for $k = 1, \dots, 4$ with linear and quadratic finite elements confirm the optimal orders of the estimators in time and in space.

papers.title: Beyond Accuracy: Physics-Informed Evaluation of ANN-based Power Flow Solvers under System Shift
papers.abstract: Recent advances in artificial deep learning-based power flow (PF) solvers have primarily focused on improving estimation accuracy, while their physical feasibility and operational reliability under realistic system variations remain insufficiently evaluated. This paper proposes a physics-informed evaluation framework for deep learning-based PF solvers under topology and load distribution shifts. Beyond conventional voltage-domain errors, the framework incorporates KCL gaps, branch-flow gaps, KVL residuals, continuous feasibility scores, and strict, practical, and relaxed PF feasibility rates. Four case studies are designed to investigate topology shifts, mixed topology training, load distribution shifts, and combined topology distribution shifts. Eight ANN architectures, including graph input models, load-only baselines, and physics-informed neural networks, are evaluated under consistent settings. The results demonstrate that low estimation errors do not necessarily correspond to physically feasible or operationally reliable PF solutions, particularly under combined system shifts. The proposed framework establishes an initial foundation and analysis for the development and verification of trustworthy deep learning-based PF solvers, providing support for their reliable deployment in future AI-enabled power system analysis.

papers.intro:
Deep learning-based power flow (PF) solvers have attracted increasing attention as fast data-driven alternatives to conventional model-based PF methods. These solvers are particularly attractive because they require less detailed topology information and are relatively robust to noisy, erroneous, or missing measurements [1]. However, most existing deep learning-based PF solvers are primarily developed and evaluated based on accuracy, whereas their practical reliability in real grid analysis remains insufficiently examined. In particular, accurate estimates of voltage magnitudes and phase angles, or even values within acceptable limits, do not necessarily guarantee a physically feasible or secure operating state, since the corresponding solution may still violate operational constraints such as line PF limits. Therefore, the lack of systematic verification of physical consistency and operational feasibility under realistic system changes may introduce additional reliability risks and hinder the practical deployment of deep learning-based PF solvers [2].

Basic deep learning-based PF solvers primarily focus on learning an accurate input–output mapping, where ANNs are trained on historical datasets and then used to rapidly estimate DC PF results [3]. Physics-informed neural network (PINN)-based PF solvers have further been developed by embedding simplified admittance matrices, thereby improving calculation accuracy and robustness [4]. For large scale power grids, PowerFlowNet [5] employs graph neural networks (GNNs) by representing power systems as graphs and achieves performance comparable to the traditional Newton–Raphson method. Similarly, a model-driven graph convolutional neural network is developed based on a simplified linear power flow model to enhance both interpretability and accuracy [6]. The application of deep learning-based PF solvers in distribution networks is investigated in [7], where three deep neural networks are proposed to approximate PF results in three phase unbalanced distribution networks. For unbalanced distribution networks, the PowerFlowMultiNet is introduced as a multigraph GNN with separate phase-wise graphs to capture phase-specific operating characteristics, while a message-passing strategy is adopted to model time-dependent features [8]. To further enhance deep learning-based AC PF solvers for distribution networks, line losses are incorporated into the loss function in [9], and Kirchhoff’s laws and active power balance constraints are incorporated into the training process, which also reduces training time [10]. In addition, considering the growing importance of data privacy, a privacy-preserving deep learning-based PF method is proposed to maintain calculation accuracy while protecting sensitive data [11]. Nevertheless, existing deep learning-based PF solvers mainly emphasise prediction accuracy and the incorporation of physical constraints during training or in the loss function.

papers.title: When does text encoding matter for language modeling?
papers.abstract: UTF-8's role as the de facto encoding standard in language models introduces cross-lingual inequities due to its variable-length design. However, the effect that this encoding choice has on model performance remains largely unexamined. In this work, we investigate how text encoding impacts the performance of byte-level language models, comparing UTF-8 with a wide range of other encoding strategies, including other Unicode-based approaches, language-specific encodings, and our own customized encodings. To facilitate our analysis, we propose Aether: a hybrid encoding scheme that uses script-specific encodings for our target setting while maintaining full Unicode coverage through UTF-8 fallbacks, using this framework to model four orthographically diverse languages. Surprisingly, we find that while languages with information-dense characters (Chinese, Korean) significantly benefit from compressive encodings, languages whose characters carry less information individually (Georgian, Tamil) are largely insensitive to encoding choice. In light of these findings, we argue that text encoding should be a language-specific design decision, rather than a universal default.

papers.intro:
Subword tokenization (i.e. BPE; Gage, 1994; Sennrich et al., 2016) has long been the dominant approach to tokenization (Mielke et al., 2021), but there is growing interest in byte-level tokenization (Tay et al., 2022; Xue et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2024, inter alia) as a way to overcome the shortcomings of subword tokenization (Bostrom and Durrett, 2020; Beinborn and Pinter, 2023; Wang et al., 2025; Chai et al., 2024). While these methods aim to reduce inductive biases carried by subword tokens, the inherent biases of the bytes used as the bases for language models instead are often overlooked. The de facto standard for converting text into bytes in modern computing applications is UTF-8, a variable length encoding scheme capable of expressing all Unicode codepoints using 1∼\sim4 bytes; due to its ubiquity, it is also the primary method for converting text into language modeling inputs. However, UTF-8 introduces inefficiencies (Moon et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2026a) and unfairness (Petrov et al., 2023; Arnett et al., 2024), leading some to argue that it is suboptimal for NLP applications van der Goot (2026).
