In this work, we present a systematic comparison of encoding methods for byte-level language modeling, based on a wide range (16) of encoding methods spanning Unicode-based encodings, language-specific encodings, and our own proposed custom encodings (Figure 1). To enable controlled comparisons within a target script, we propose Aether tokenizers (Alternative Encoding Tokenizers for Hybrid Encoding Representations), which apply script-specific encodings when relevant while applying UTF-8 as a back-off encoding for other text. Using Aether tokenizers, we train “byte”-level models on four orthographically distinct languages (Chinese, Korean, Georgian, Tamil) with 38 unique language-encoding pairs.

However, these studies are limited to a single alternative encoding designed to improve the UTF-8 baseline on a specific dimension, leaving many aspects of how encoding choice affects language modeling unexplored. In this work, we present a systematic comparison of encoding methods for byte-level language modeling, based on a wide range (16) of encoding methods spanning Unicode-based encodings, language-specific encodings, and our own proposed custom encodings (Figure 1). To enable controlled comparisons within a target script, we propose Aether tokenizers (Alternative Encoding Tokenizers for Hybrid Encoding Representations), which apply script-specific encodings when relevant while applying UTF-8 as a back-off encoding for other text. Using Aether tokenizers, we train “byte”-level models on four orthographically distinct languages (Chinese, Korean, Georgian, Tamil) with 38 unique language-encoding pairs.

Our experiments reveal two distinct patterns. For Chinese and Korean, encoding choice has a clear impact on performance, with more compressive encodings yielding significantly better results. In contrast, all encodings perform similarly for Georgian and Tamil, even when their compression rates differ by up to ∼7×{\sim}7\times and ∼8×{\sim}8\times, respectively. We hypothesize that these divergent results stem from differences in the orthographic granularity of the underlying scripts. Specifically, when characters individually encode meaningful information (as in Chinese and Korean), compression appears to heavily impact performance, while characters that carry little information in isolation (like Tamil and Georgian) are largely insensitive to encoding selection. Given these script-specific trends, we argue that text encoding should be treated as a deliberate design choice that accounts for these properties rather than accepted as a universal default.

papers.title: Automatic Continuity for projective clone homomorphisms
papers.abstract: We show that every projective clone homomorphism from a closed function clone containing the automorphism group of a countable homogeneous Ramsey structure $\Delta$ in a finite relational language is uniformly continuous. This answers, for such structures, open questions previously raised by Barto, Bodirsky, Marimon, Pongr\'acz, and the second author in several papers (Bodirsky, Pinsker, Pongr\'acz, J. Symb. Log. 2021; Barto, Pinsker, SIAM J. Comput. 2020; Marimon, Pinsker, arXiv:2512.01086). Consequently, the polymorphism clone of a first-order reduct $\Gamma$ of $\Delta$ admits a projective clone homomorphism if and only if $\Gamma$ primitively positively interprets all finite structures; in other words, this ability of $\Gamma$ is characterised by the absence of non-trivial identities in its polymorphism clone, a purely algebraic condition.sence of non-trivial identities in its polymorphism clone, i.e., a purely algebraic condition.

A constraint satisfaction problem asks whether a finite collection of local requirements can be satisfied simultaneously. Formally, fix a relational structure Γ\Gamma in a finite relational language. The problem CSP⁡(Γ)\CSP(\Gamma) takes as input a finite structure in the same language and asks whether it admits a homomorphism to Γ\Gamma. Equivalently, the input is a conjunction of atomic formulas, and the task is to find an assignment satisfying them in Γ\Gamma. For example, choosing the complete graph K3K_{3} as the template gives graph 3-colourability. Varying the template changes the available constraints and, with them, the complexity of the problem.

A pp-interpretation represents one structure inside a finite power of another: its domain is a quotient of a pp-definable set, and both equality on the quotient and the basic relations have pp-definable preimages. If Γ\Gamma pp-interprets Λ\Lambda, then CSP⁡(Λ)\CSP(\Lambda) reduces to CSP⁡(Γ)\CSP(\Gamma) in polynomial time, by replacing variables with tuples and constraints with their defining formulas. papers.title: Decision-Focused Learning via Neural Optimization Layers for Battery-Assisted Grid-Import Smoothing in AI Data Centers
papers.abstract: Rapid AI data-center power fluctuations challenge grid integration. Sustained grid-import smoothing requires allocating limited battery power and energy under uncertain demand. We formulate risk-aware BESS scheduling that coordinates advance reserve commitments and demand-responsive dispatch, accounting for operating costs, grid-ramp penalties, and their conditional value-at-risk. We develop battery scheduling decision-focused learning (BS-DFL) with a constraint-aware neural optimization layer trained directly from this objective without optimal-solution labels. The trained layer is then frozen to guide demand-predictor learning through scheduling costs and ramping risk, enabling solver-free rolling-horizon scheduling. In a 10,000-minute simulation using loads derived from measured AI workloads, BS-DFL reduces mean absolute minute-to-minute grid-import changes by 71.70% and total scheduling cost by 18.01% relative to an MSE-trained predictor coupled with a mixed-integer linear programming solver, with an average decision time of 18.77 ms.

papers.intro:
The rapid growth of AI data centers introduces highly variable electricity loads, creating challenges for grid-compatible operation and power-ramp management [1]. Behind-the-meter battery energy storage systems (BESSs) can mitigate rapid load fluctuations without modifying computational workload schedules [2]. However, sustained grid-import smoothing is constrained by battery power and energy limits, requiring careful scheduling of charging and discharging flexibility. Predictive scheduling is therefore needed to mitigate current grid-import fluctuations while preserving sufficient power and energy headroom for future uncertain demand.

Behind-the-meter battery energy storage systems (BESSs) can mitigate rapid load fluctuations without modifying computational workload schedules [2]. However, sustained grid-import smoothing is constrained by battery power and energy limits, requiring careful scheduling of charging and discharging flexibility. Predictive scheduling is therefore needed to mitigate current grid-import fluctuations while preserving sufficient power and energy headroom for future uncertain demand.

Existing studies have developed battery-assisted ramp-rate control for AI data centers [3]. At the scheduling level, coordinated workload shifting, battery dispatch, and reserve allocation have been investigated to balance operating costs and grid-ramping risk [4]. To guide advance battery scheduling, neural load forecasts have been combined with robust model predictive control for peak shaving [5], while probabilistic load forecasts support capacity allocation between peak shaving and frequency containment reserves [6]. Nevertheless, prediction errors of similar magnitude can lead to substantially different scheduling costs and grid-ramp violations, depending on the battery’s available power and energy flexibility.

Nevertheless, prediction errors of similar magnitude can lead to substantially different scheduling costs and grid-ramp violations, depending on the battery’s available power and energy flexibility.

Conventional forecasting approaches typically minimize statistical prediction losses, such as mean squared error, without explicitly considering their impact on downstream battery scheduling decisions. This motivates decision-focused learning (DFL), which incorporates downstream scheduling costs into predictor training [7]. DFL has been applied to BESS reserve-market participation [8], PV-battery scheduling [9], and AI data-center workload scheduling under distribution-grid constraints [10]. These methods rely on differentiable convex optimization layers, limiting their direct application to scheduling with discrete decisions. To accommodate such decisions, surrogate-loss and black-box differentiation methods have been applied to battery scheduling [11]. Other approaches include perturbation-based learning for energy storage arbitrage [12] and supervised neural optimizer for battery peak shaving and energy cost reduction [13]. However, these approaches often rely on optimization solvers during training or deployment, which can limit training scalability for large or complex problems and the responsiveness of real-time battery scheduling.

papers.title: Mutual Linearity in Nonlinear Population Dynamics
papers.abstract: Mutual Linearity in Nonlinear Population DynamicsMutual linearity, the persistence of affine relations among stationary observables under arbitrarily strong changes of one transition rate, is known for Markov jump processes and chemical reaction networks. We show that generalized Lotka--Volterra dynamics form a new class of mutually linear systems, even though species can go extinct and attractors can be chaotic. Any change to one species' equation acts on the others as one effective press and keeps all abundances affinely related: piecewise across extinctions, and as time averages on chaotic attractors.

papers.title: Two Communities, One Problem: Branch-and-Bound vs. A* for Resource-Constrained Project Scheduling
papers.abstract: Branch-and-Bound (B&B) and $A^*$ are popular exact search methods originating from Operations Research and Artificial Intelligence, respectively. Although the two methods share fundamental search principles, their different ways of exploring the search space can lead to substantially different computational performance. We investigate these differences using the Resource-Constrained Project Scheduling Problem (RCPSP) as an exemplary problem setting. We first establish the relationships between mixed-integer linear programming, state-action, and timed Petri-net representations. Since B&B and $A^*$ admit numerous algorithmic enhancements, we focus on relatively basic implementations. This allows us to examine the fundamental differences between the methods rather than compare the performance of state-of-the-art solvers. By using the same lower bound and best-first node selection, we isolate the effects of the search mechanisms, particularly the identification of equivalent states reached through different scheduling decision sequences. Experiments on 480 benchmark RCPSP instances show that graph-based $A^*$ substantially outperforms the B&B variants considered. With additional pruning rules, $A^*$ proves optimality for all 480 instances, compared with 445 for best-first B&B under the same time and memory limits. Depth-first B&B uses less memory and can find feasible solutions even when the search does not finish within the time limit. Stronger linear programming relaxations reduce the search space but introduce considerable computational overhead. Our findings highlight the importance of duplicate-state detection and clarify the computational trade-offs between the search approaches. These insights can help researchers select an appropriate method and identify opportunities to incorporate effective mechanisms from one approach into the other.

Because even moderately sized instances can be difficult to solve optimally, the RCPSP is important both as a practical scheduling problem and as a benchmark for exact optimization methods.

Two mature research traditions approach this problem from different perspectives (details are presented in Section 2). In Operations Research (OR), exact methods commonly explore a tree of restricted subproblems or partial schedules using Branch-and-Bound (B&B). Lower bounds are used to eliminate subproblems that cannot improve the best complete schedule found so far. In Artificial Intelligence (AI), the problem can instead be represented as a state-space graph and solved using A∗A^{*}, which expands states in best-first order according to an admissible evaluation function and merges equivalent states reached through different decision sequences. At a sufficiently abstract level, A∗A^{*} can be represented within general formulations of B&B (Nau et al., 1984). This theoretical relationship, however, does not explain how the concrete algorithms used in OR and AI differ when applied to the same scheduling problem. In practice, B&B in its ordinary variant (Nau et al., 1984, see, ordinary B&B in) explores a tree of subsets of feasible solutions implicitly defined by partial schedules, whereas graph-based A∗A^{*} systematically searches a graph, detecting and merging duplicate states reached through different decision sequences. B&B may also use the best feasible solution found so far to prune nodes. Existing comparisons are often affected by differences in problem representation, lower-bound strength, node-selection strategy, or algorithm-specific enhancements. Consequently, it remains unclear how much of the observed performance difference is caused by the different search mechanisms themselves.

This study aims to explain the fundamental computational trade-offs between these two widely used exact-search paradigms and to provide a basis for selecting, improving, or combining them. Its purpose is therefore not to determine whether a basic implementation of either method outperforms state-of-the-art RCPSP solvers. Instead, our contributions are threefold. First, we develop a common modeling foundation for the comparison by presenting mixed-integer linear programming (MILP), state-action, and timed Petri-net representations of the RCPSP and establishing the relationships between their schedules, states, and search graphs. Second, we provide a mechanistic and formal comparison of B&B and A∗A^{*} under identical lower-bound information and best-first node selection. The analysis identifies how duplicate states, pruning, repeated heuristic evaluations, and memory requirements affect the two searches. Finally, we conduct a controlled empirical study on benchmark RCPSP instances, comparing computational time, generated and expanded nodes, lower-bound evaluations, and memory use. The experiments examine how instance characteristics and the search mechanisms influence the relative performance of the two methods.

papers.title: Collision Avoidance and Collision Detection Strategies to Counteract Large-Scale FMCW Automotive Radar Interference
papers.abstract: Automotive radars operating in dense traffic environments may experience significant mutual interference, potentially degrading sensing reliability for advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS). This issue motivates the development of techniques to mitigate interference among multiple radar-equipped vehicles sharing the same spectrum. This paper investigates interference mitigation strategies for uncoordinated radar networks through system-level simulation. Two approaches are considered: frame-by-frame collision avoidance (FbF-CA), which exploits idle intervals to measure the perceived interference and possibly adapt the operating frequency, and frame-by-frame collision detection (FbF-CD), which estimates interference during transmission based on observed chirp collisions. An event-driven radar network simulator is used to model realistic highway traffic and radar interactions. Results show that collision avoidance provides higher robustness when a larger bandwidth is available, while collision detection is more effective under bandwidth-limited conditions. The analysis highlights the trade-off between collision avoidance and collision detection mitigation strategies and provides design insights for scalable automotive radar deployments.

For these reasons, modern vehicles are increasingly equipped with multiple FMCW (FMCW)-based radar sensors operating in the millimeter-wave bands in the 76–81 GHz band, with regional variations. However, the growing penetration of radar-equipped vehicles also introduces new challenges. Radar signals transmitted by nearby vehicles may overlap in time and frequency, generating interference that can affect sensing reliability. In FMCW automotive radars, such interference can produce signal components that resemble legitimate reflections, potentially leading to corrupted chirps, degraded sensing performance, or even the detection of false targets. This problem is further exacerbated by the fact that automotive radars typically operate in a shared spectrum with limited coordination among devices. As radar adoption continues to increase, the probability that multiple sensors operate simultaneously within the same spectrum increases, raising concerns about the scalability of current radar spectrum allocations in dense traffic scenarios [1].

Focusing on proactive approaches, they can be broadly categorized into coordination-based and uncoordinated techniques. Coordination-based solutions rely on explicit cooperation among radar devices but require communication and standardization across different manufacturers, which may limit their practical deployment [7]. papers.title: Dual-Parabola Interpolator: A Low-Bias Peak Estimator for Distributed Radar Synchronization
papers.abstract: Coherent distributed radar processing requires accurate wireless synchronization. Two-way time transfer (TWTT) obtains reception timestamps from sampled matched-filter peaks, but interpolation bias limits accuracy even when noise is reduced by higher signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) or averaging. Three-point parabolic interpolation is attractive for its simple, explicit formula; reducing its bias generally requires more elaborate fitting, such as higher-order polynomials, or a model tailored to a particular peak shape. A practical alternative should retain this simplicity and interpretability while approaching the low bias of more flexible fits. We propose the Dual-Parabola Interpolator (DPI), which combines two parabolic estimates from five amplitude samples near the matched-filter peak. An adaptive weight cancels the leading interpolation error without requiring a waveform-specific peak model or a correction table. Simulations over flat and standardized multipath channels show bias comparable to a five-point quartic fit, with essentially the same standard deviation as the other interpolators and an execution cost close to a three-point parabolic fit. This combination is useful for TWTT in urban or other multipath settings, where channel distortion prevents reliance on a nominal peak shape.

papers.title: Trust, but verify, audit and attribute: a human-in-the-loop framework for checking AI-produced research results
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems now produce research results in bulk: in October 2026 a single laboratory released more than 700 AI-generated mathematics manuscripts, only part of them with machine-checked proofs. Such volumes will be checked mostly by AI agents that call specialised software. A passing check certifies only the artefact that was checked. For proofs translated into the proof assistant Lean, it has been shown that this artefact may state something other than the author's text, and that deciding whether a translation is faithful is undecidable in general. The human researcher therefore stays in the loop, and human and AI contributions must be recorded. We propose a domain-independent, human-in-the-loop framework for checking AI-produced results. Validated, agent-usable tools with different grounds of trust check the results; a fidelity audit asks whether each check addressed the claim as stated; the human decides at fixed points; and a dialog report attributes the work to the human and to the AI. We describe two automatic implementations of the tool layer, for mathematics (Wolfram Language, MATLAB, Lean) and statistics (Python and R), and run the mathematical one on a two-claim example. An ambiguous claim was split into two readings, one refuted and one proved.

papers.title: Preserving Cultural Records: A Large-Scale Benchmark and Visual-Prior Routing Network for Ancient Book Image Restoration
papers.abstract: Ancient books preserve invaluable cultural heritage, yet their images often suffer from complex degradations caused by long-term ageing, environmental exposure, and physical damage. Existing ancient book image restoration benchmarks are limited in scale and rely on simplified degradation simulations, which cannot fully represent real-world degradation patterns and restrict the generalization ability of restoration models. To address these challenges, we introduce AncBench, a large-scale synthetic paired benchmark containing 100K aligned clean-degraded image pairs. AncBench models realistic composite degradations through a comprehensive degradation pipeline that considers material ageing, paper texture variation, blur, staining, water-induced geometric distortion, and local occlusion. Furthermore, we propose AncRestore, a degradation-aware visual-prior routing network for ancient book image restoration. AncRestore first learns degradation representations from degraded images and then dynamically selects and integrates suitable visual priors according to different degradation characteristics. Guided by these degradation cues, a dynamic routing mechanism combines expert-wise and region-wise routing strategies adaptively adjusts the contribution of these priors across different regions, enabling the model to recover both global appearance and local text details. Extensive experiments show that AncRestore effectively suppresses composite degradations while preserving text structures and enhancing restoration quality against other methods, highlighting its application potential for intelligent ancient book image restoration in cultural heritage preservation.

papers.title: INTENT: Out-of-Sample, Out-of-Time, and Cold-Start Evaluation on User Event Sequences
papers.abstract: Banks now train foundation models on ordered sequences of customer events such as transactions, app sessions, and authorizations. Deployed, such a model predicts forward in time, often for customers and merchants absent from training, yet each is evaluated on private data, so no two can be compared. Public benchmarks for such sequences rarely test a period the model has not seen; recommendation studies usually hold out each user's last events instead. We present INTENT (INTEraction, Novelty, and Transfer evaluation for next-action prediction), a public benchmark that scores a model in seven cells defined by whether the user, the period, and the target item appeared in training. An audit of 59 public dataset families retains five datasets; the most common defect is the lack of a calendar timestamp that orders events. No date lies within the time span of all five datasets, so each is split at its own cutoff, chosen by one rule fixed before any model is evaluated. Summed over the datasets, every cell holds at least 111,769 users. In reference results the cell determines the best model: a transformer leads on seen items after the cutoff but scores zero on new items, a variant that embeds item metadata helps mainly on MicroLens, and repeating the user's last item leads on new items in four of five datasets. This parameter-free control also shows that on three datasets most of the score lost after the cutoff reflects changed behavior rather than the model. The pipeline, the cutoff rule, and the per-cell user counts are publicly available.

papers.title: SHINE: Shear inference environment - Generative forward modelling for radio weak gravitational lensing
papers.abstract: Next-generation radio interferometers, such as SKA, will observe the radio sky with unprecedented sensitivity and resolution enabling weak gravitational lensing studies using radio data, which not only complement optical observations but also probe higher redshifts. However, traditional shear estimation methods, based on measuring the ellipticity of observed galaxies, are not directly applicable to radio interferometric data. Interferometric observations are acquired in the Fourier domain, where galaxy images are delocalised, making shape measurements non-trivial. Furthermore, deconvolution methods such as CLEAN can introduce systematic errors when converting observations to the image domain, biasing shear estimates. To address these challenges, we propose a cosmic shear inference method based on forward generative modelling, which avoids explicit shape measurements. Our forward model simulates galaxy images, applies the shear transformation and, by including the instrumental response of the radio interferometer, simulates the visibilities of observed galaxies, with the likelihood explicitly defined in Fourier space. Using Monte Carlo sampling algorithms, we estimate the posterior distribution of the cosmic shear conditioned on a set of galaxy observations that share a common shear. We obtain unbiased shear estimates with sub-percent accuracy when applied to parametric galaxy simulations. We compare our method to state-of-the-art shear estimators, demonstrating a reduction in uncertainty of up to 3 times and no apparent multiplicative bias. We then show that applying this parametric model to COSMOS galaxies with realistic morphologies introduces a bias in the shear estimate over 10{\sigma}. Finally, we demonstrate that, by incorporating a generative forward model based on an autoencoder architecture trained on real galaxy images, we can mitigate this bias to below the 2{\sigma} level.

papers.title: The distribution of small gaps between zeros of the Riemann zeta function
papers.abstract: Let $0<\gamma_1\leq \gamma_2\leq \cdots$ be the ordinates of the non-trivial zeros $\rho_n$ of the Riemann zeta function in the upper half-plane, counted with multiplicity. Selberg proved unconditionally that there exists $\lambda_0<1$ such that a positive proportion of the zeros $\rho_n$ satisfy $\gamma_{n+1}-\gamma_n\leq 2\pi \lambda_0/\log \gamma_n$. Simoni\v{c}, Trudgian and Turnage-Butterbaugh were the first to obtain an explicit value in Selberg's theorem, showing that $\lambda_0=1- 10^{-3\cdot 10^{13}}$ is admissible. This was considerably improved by Zhao who showed that $\lambda_0= 1-2.36\cdot 10^{-6}$ is admissible. In this paper, we use a different approach, based on an unconditional variant of Montgomery's pair correlation method, to obtain a substantial improvement of these results, showing unconditionally that $\lambda_0=0.7892<4/5$ is admissible.

papers.title: Comparative Evaluation of Deep Learning Models for Geographic Atrophy Segmentation in En Face OCT Images
papers.abstract: Background: Geographic atrophy (GA) is an advanced form of age-related macular degeneration (AMD). It causes irreversible vision loss due to progressive degeneration of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and photoreceptors. Accurate segmentation of GA in en-face image is crucial for early diagnosis, monitoring disease progression, and developing personalized treatment strategies. However, existing deep learning approaches are typically evaluated using single architectures and single-device datasets, limiting insight into relative performance and cross-device robustness. Methods: We trained and systematically compared five deep learning architectures for GA segmentation: Nested U-Net, ResU-Net, nnUnet, Swin-Unet and MedSegDiff model, together with a thresholding based classical baseline. The models were trained on a dataset of en-face OCT images derived from 269 OCT volumes from two different devices, following a three-step preprocessing technique involving normalization and inpainting to enhance the quality of the en-face images. Results: On the fixed held-out validation set comprising OCT scans from both Cirrus (R) (Carl Zeiss Meditec, Inc., USA) and Spectralis (R) (Heidelberg Engineering, Germany) devices, nnUnet achieved the highest mean Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.8882 +/- 0.0033. The other models yielded the following Dice scores: Nested U-Net (0.7932 +/- 0.0423), ResU-Net (0.8453 +/- 0.0074), Swin-Unet (0.6886 +/- 0.0294), and Diffusion model (0.7959 +/- 0.0242). Conclusions: nnUnet framework, demonstrated most reliable performance for GA segmentation in en-face OCT under limited data conditions. It offers the best balance of accuracy, stability, and efficiency for GA quantification.

authors.institution: IRCCS Azienda Ospedliero-Universitaria di Bologna Policlinico di Sant'Orsola

authors.institution: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique

papers.title: AGN feedback destroying group cool cores --- a case study on IC 2476 with a remnant radio AGN and an exceptionally low abundance
papers.abstract: We present results from deep XMM-Newton observations ($\sim$180 ksec) of the galaxy group IC 2476 in the X-GAP sample, capturing a rare AGN feedback regime, where the central radio AGN has ceased activity but the radio lobes are still detectable. The hot intragroup medium of IC 2476 features a compact cool core, with a size of ~10 kpc, and a moderate X-ray luminosity of $\sim3.4\times10^{40}$ erg/s. We measured an unusually low temperature of $\sim$0.45 keV within the cool core. We measured an exceptionally low abundance of below ~0.2 solar, even in the central region. The X-ray surface brightness of the group is not symmetric and shows a clear depression in the region overlaid with the eastern radio lobe, suggesting the presence of an X-ray cavity. The scaled entropy of the hot gas within 0.1 r500 of IC 2476 is among the highest in X-ray galaxy groups with a similar system temperature. Our study suggests that the past powerful radio AGN outburst in IC 2476 has disrupted the cool core and the X-ray cavity has dissipated or mixed with the surrounding hot gas since the shutdown of the central AGN. A large cool core may be gradually re-established in the absence of AGN activity. This system therefore provides a great example of AGN feedback destroying the group cool core, even with a moderate radio luminosity at present.

papers.title: Limit theorems for dispersing billiards with infinite cusps
papers.abstract: Extending Lenci's work in CMP (2002), Chaos (2003), we present new insights into semi-dispersing billiards with infinite cusps. We investigate the Convergence to Stable Processes (CSP) and Functional Central Limit Theorems (FCLT) both for the collision map and for the billiard flow. Whereas the billiard map always preserves an infinite measure equivalent to Lebesgue, the billiard flow preserves the Lebesgue measure, which is either finite or infinite depending on the finiteness of the area of the billiard table. When the reference measure is infinite, the usual LLN fails, but we are able to prove the CSP and FCLT. We also prove classical FCLT for the flow when the area of the billiard table is finite. These results are obtained through a precise study of the properties of the billiard map, combined with a general approach based on induction and on coupling involving point processes.

papers.title: Event-based analysis of neuromorphic feedback systems
papers.abstract: This article investigates the existence and stability of periodic behavior arising in the feedback interconnection of neuromorphic systems, which evolve according to continuous dynamics but interact only through discrete events. Exploiting the event-driven nature of this interaction, each system is modeled by an operator that maps the history of events to the delay of its response. Building on the fading-memory properties of these operators, the article develops a small-gain result establishing the existence, uniqueness, and robustness of periodic one-to-one rhythms.

papers.title: Data-driven regional traffic simulation from heterogeneous mobility sources
papers.abstract: Regional traffic simulators increasingly combine mobile-phone, road-sensor and GPS data, but what each source contributes is rarely clear. We present an agent-based simulator of daily traffic in Emilia-Romagna, Italy: phone data give trips and their timing, half of the road sensors set the traffic level, all sensors correct it locally, and GPS traces guide route choice. We measure what each source adds against predictors without simulation, on sensors kept out of parameter calibration in winter 2020 and partly shared with it in summer 2021; as these sensors informed some modelling choices, the evaluation is not fully independent. Total traffic is within 1% of observations in winter and 10% in summer, and the simulator ranks roads better than a road-type predictor (Spearman 0.67-0.68 against 0.41-0.48, winter). GPS improves this ranking, sensors improve local estimates, and timing comes mostly from the demand. Single-road errors remain similar to those of simple predictors, and the test of specific origin-destination pairings was underpowered and inconclusive. These findings provide a practical framework for assessing the contribution and limitations of heterogeneous data sources in regional traffic simulation.

papers.title: From Prediction to Action: Learning Physical Context for Deformable Linear Object Manipulation
papers.abstract: A representation that accurately predicts a deformable object's response is not necessarily the one most useful for choosing manipulation actions. We study this distinction between predictive utility and decision utility in planar single-grasp shape control of Deformable Linear Objects (DLOs). As a common decision backbone, we introduce Geometry-Pointer-Flow (GPF), a geometry-grounded policy that separates grasp-location selection from grasp-conditioned motion generation. Its geometry-only variant reduces one-step executed shape error by 32.8% relative to a DLO-specific diffusion policy, while using 18.7 times fewer parameters and achieving approximately 193 times faster inference. On this backbone, we compare physical context represented by ground-truth parameters, estimated parameters, and learned interaction-history representations, for both forward prediction and executed control. For prediction, ground-truth physical parameters reduce next-shape error by 15.8% over geometry alone, and estimated parameters are slightly more predictive than interaction history. This ordering does not carry over to control: estimated parameters provide no detectable one-step control gain, whereas history-conditioned GPF reduces executed error by 9.9% relative to geometry-only GPF across 470 paired simulation trials. In closed loop, interaction history improves strict-threshold attainment in simulation and yields the strongest zero-shot performance on hardware. All policies are trained exclusively in simulation and transferred to the physical robot without real-world training or fine-tuning. These results show that physical context should be evaluated by the decisions it supports rather than by predictive accuracy alone. Code will be released upon acceptance.

authors.name: Chengxiao Dong

papers.title: Phragm\'en-Lindel\"of theorems for parabolic equations of p-laplacian-type
papers.abstract: We consider rigidity properties of ancient solutions to parabolic equations of $p$-Laplacian-type. We start with the degenerate range $p>2$. First, a solution which is bounded above in an intrinsic backward paraboloid is either bounded in an entire half-space, or grows in space at least like a power with a sharp, explicit exponent. This relies on the expansion of positivity and on the Comparison Principle. Then, we turn to the growth in time. Positivity in the paraboloid alone yields no upper rate: we present explicit self-similar solutions, positive in the paraboloid, with $u(0,-T)\simeq T^{\beta}$ for every $\beta\le0$ and every $\beta\ge1$. For solutions bounded below in the paraboloid, we prove a dichotomy for the infimum of $u(\cdot,-T)$ on a ball whose radius is a fixed fraction of that of the paraboloid at time $-T$: either it is of order $T$ along a sequence of times, or it grows sublinearly, like $T^{\zeta}$ with $\zeta<1$ explicit. In the second case, a Harnack-type argument shows that the supremum on the same ball grows at most linearly. Then, we carry out the same program in the singular, supercritical range $\frac{2N}{N+1}<p<2$, where the picture is similar but several roles are reversed. In space, the iteration via the Comparison Principle can only be started from a point lying above an explicit slope, and explicit solutions show that nothing better than a cone bound can be expected below it. The self-similar profiles are unique but only local, and positivity in the paraboloid is compatible with every exponent $\beta\le1$ and with no exponent in $(1,\frac1{2-p})$. In time, the dichotomy is replaced by an a priori linear bound for the infimum. Similarities and differences between the two ranges are collected at the end of the work.

papers.title: Tracing early galaxies back in time: implications for the dearth of galaxies beyond z~15
papers.abstract: Although the James Webb Space Telescope has pushed the observational frontier to $z\sim14$, the onset of star formation in the earliest galaxies remains beyond direct reach, making the star formation histories (SFH) of observed galaxies a key tool for probing earlier epochs. We develop and validate a new SFH model based on an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, capable of reproducing the bursty star formation expected in high-redshift galaxies. Tested on the SPHINX$^{20}$ mock catalogs, it accurately recovers stellar masses and SFRs and reconstructs cumulative SFHs at population level; the formation redshift is well constrained at $z\gtrsim9$ but not at $z\sim8$. Applied to 400 galaxies at $9<z<15$ from the UNICORN/GOODS-South sample, we find that sources observed at $z<10$ typically reached 20% of their stellar mass no earlier than $z\sim12$, disfavoring a clear evolutionary link to spectroscopically confirmed galaxies at $z\gtrsim13$. Among 218 galaxies at $10<z<15$, only 28 had formed 20% of their stellar mass by $z=15$, with a median formation redshift $z_{\rm form,20\%}=16.9^{+1.1}_{-1.1}$, and 24% of our sample had already reached $10^7$M$_{\odot}$ by $z=15$. At $z=17$, only 11 of these 28 galaxies had reached 20% of their stellar mass. The derived survey areas required to detect them are consistent with or slightly more optimistic than previous constraints at the bright end, and larger than some literature estimates at the faint end. At $z=20$, a single galaxy had formed 20% of its stellar mass, yielding a tentative constraint of one object at $M_{\rm UV}=-18.1\pm0.6$ per $\sim200$\,arcmin$^2$. Our results suggest a relatively slow decline in star formation activity between $z\sim15$ and $z\sim17$, followed by a more rapid decline up to $z\sim20$.

papers.title: AFNO: Universal Certifiably-Arbitrage-Free Operator Learning Framework for European Call-Price Surfaces
papers.abstract:
Neural operators (NOs) have been introduced as deep learning-powered solutions to the computational bottleneck of solving families of problems. Once trained, an NO can rapidly output approximate solutions, avoiding the need to rerun classical solvers. However, standard NO architectures cannot guarantee static no-arbitrage when predicting European call-price surfaces from market or model features and, as we verify experimentally, can yield negative PnL in downstream trading tasks.
  We introduce a certifiably arbitrage-free (AF) and universal encoder-decoder NO framework, continuously mapping inputs from a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) $\mathcal{H}$ over any fixed subset of $[0,\infty)^2$ to a convex combination of arbitrage-free European call-price surfaces by continuously solving an approximate nearest-neighbour problem. We show that a nearest arbitrage-free correction of an unconstrained predicted surface need not exist, implying that no-arbitrage cannot, in general, be restored through post-processing. Further, we show that standard NOs, such as the FNO and certain encoder-decoder NOs, admit parameter configurations whose outputs violate static no-arbitrage. Thus, out-of-the-box NOs generally cannot be certifiably restricted to arbitrage-free configurations, but may only be guided towards them through PINN-type regularization during training.

authors.name: Raeid Saqur
authors.institution: Mathematical Institute of the Slovak Academy of Sciences

papers.title: Face lattices of polytopes and bipolar polytopes
papers.abstract: We show that the face lattice of every convex polytope $Q$ is, on the combinatorial level, the vertex set of a polytope one dimension higher: the faces of $Q$ are the vertices of a \emph{bipolar polytope} $W(\mathcal{F}(Q))$, and the intervals of the face lattice are its faces. Here a bipolar polytope is a polytope with two distinguished vertices, the poles, such that every facet contains exactly one of them and an intersection property holds. The vertices of every bipolar polytope carry a lattice order whose intervals are the faces, and this lattice is the face lattice of the vertex figure at either pole; conversely, every atomistic and coatomistic lattice that is an abstract polytope arises in this way. Geometrically, the polar of the Cayley polytope of $Q$ and $Q^\circ$ is a convex realization of $W(\mathcal{F}(Q))$ whenever the normal fan and the face fan of $Q$ satisfy a certain interval condition; this holds for cubes and cross-polytopes and for suitable realizations of all polytopes of dimension at most three. Finally, every combinatorial type of $3$-polytope has a realization that decomposes into convex bipolar polytopes, one for each vertex.

authors.name: Jan Pavlik
authors.institution: Slovak University of Technology in Bratislava

papers.title: Thales's theorem in higher dimensions
papers.abstract: In the Euclidean plane, Thales's theorem is equivalent to the statement that a quadrilateral with two opposite right angles has a circumscribed circle. We generalize the latter to higher dimensions: a convex polytope with two distinguished vertices, the \emph{poles}, such that the faces spanned by the two poles are perpendicular, is inscribed in the sphere whose diameter joins its poles. These \emph{orthogonally bipolar} polytopes are exactly the bipolar polytopes of a companion paper that arise as cutouts by orthogonal projections. As an application we show that for a polytope $P$ and a point $B$, the balls with diameters $[V,B]$, $V$ a vertex of $P$, cover $P$, and that the power diagram of their boundary spheres refines this covering to a tiling. Further, we investigate the properties of orthogonally bipolar polytopes, their characterization, and their application to tilings: in dimension three, the cutouts of $P$ by the orthogonal projections of $B$ onto its faces tile $P$ by orthogonally bipolar polytopes exactly when every such projection lies in the relative interior of its face. Finally, we propose an interpretation of the topic in political science.

authors.name: Jan Pavlik
authors.institution: Slovak University of Technology in Bratislava

papers.title: From Worst-Case to Smoothed Complexity in Continuous Optimization
papers.abstract: Worst-case complexity bounds often fail to reflect the practical performance of optimization algorithms, while average-case complexity heavily relies on the distribution of the input. In this work, we develop a smoothed-analysis framework for classical continuous optimization algorithms by studying their behaviour on random perturbations of arbitrary functions. Our main contribution is to apply methods suited for non-degenerate functions to perturbations of degenerate functions, thereby recovering the faster best-known rates for the non-degenerate class. We derive smoothed complexity guarantees for several standard methods, including (Accelerated) Gradient Descent, Conjugate Gradient, and Newton-type methods, under various settings including nonconvex ones, and show that these bounds can substantially improve upon their worst-case guarantees, bringing them closer to the practical behaviour of the respective methods.

authors.name: Coralia Cartis
authors.institution: Mathematical Institute of the Slovak Academy of Sciences

papers.title: Explanation-Aware Fairness Beyond Output Parity: Joint Output-Attribution Regularization for Medical Image Classification
papers.abstract: Output-level fairness does not constrain whether demographic groups rely on similar predictive contributions in representation space. For a nonlinear encoder with a linear head, we show that outcome-conditioned output score disparity equals the signed sum of feature attribution differences across subgroups by allowing small prediction gaps to arise through cancellation effect. We test whether an attribution disparity penalty complements output-level equalized odds based fairness surrogates. Across 960 DINOv2-LoRA models on HAM10000 and Harvard-GF datasets for gender and race fairness, attribution augmentation increases utility-fairness trade-off performance for hypervolume in six different settings with paired 95% confidence intervals and relative gains of 1.49-10.57%. Under a predefined utility constraint, augmented model families also achieve 9.0-38.7% lower equalized odds difference, lower attribution disparity, and reduced cancellation ratio while preserving predictive utility. These results support attribution fairness as a complementary explanation-aware constraint on output fairness.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Deep Neural Networks: Methods, Frameworks, and Perspectives
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks underpin fundamental tasks in a wide range of signal domains, such as image, audio, and language processing. However, their internal mechanisms are notably difficult to interpret. Internal activations are structured signals transformed across layers that may encode a multitude of interdependent relationships, as individual neurons frequently represent multiple underlying concepts. Mechanistic interpretability aims to uncover the internal mechanisms of neural networks by identifying components whose activations are causally responsible for specific behaviors. In such a context, this article provides an overview of advances in mechanistic interpretability for the analysis of causal inference in deep neural networks.

papers.title: High-precision abundance analysis of a unique CEMP-no star in Sculptor
papers.abstract: The Carbon-Enhanced Metal-Poor stars (CEMP-no, low barium) are commonly accepted as the direct descendants of Population III (Pop III) stars which either ended their lives as faint supernovae (SNe; E_SN < 10^51 erg) or were fast-rotating stars (spinstars). While CEMP-no stars are common in the Milky Way (MW) and ultra-faint dwarf galaxies (UFDs), they are surprisingly rare in dwarf spheroidal galaxies (dSphs). This could hide an environmental dependence of the properties of Pop III stars, highlighting the importance of high-resolution studies of CEMP-no stars in dSphs. Here we present the first detailed study of a CEMP-no star with [Fe/H] < -3 in the Sculptor dSph. The high-resolution VLT/UVES spectra allowed us to derive one of the most precise abundance patterns obtained for a star belonging to a dwarf galaxy, providing chemical abundances for 17 elements and 4 upper limits. This star, DR20080, is extremely metal-poor, [Fe/H] = -3.26, and clearly enhanced in carbon, [C/Fe] = +1.60 (after correcting for internal mixing). Furthermore, it has low [Ba/Fe] = -1.28. The oxygen abundance of DR20080 ([O/Fe] = +1.53) is significantly higher than the average found in CEMP-no stars in the MW, while the iron-peak elements are under-abundant ([Mn/Fe] = -1.02; [Ni/Fe] = -0.45). The abundance pattern of DR20080 was compared to theoretical yield predictions of Pop III and Pop II SNe to infer the properties of its progenitor. The best result points toward a double Pop III progenitor scenario, with the major contributor to the abundance pattern being a Pop III faint SN with mass m_PopIII = 43 M_0 and explosion energy E_SN = 0.6 x 10^51 erg, while the minor contributor is a Pop III hypernova of m_PopIII = 19.4 M_0 and E_SN = 10 x 10^51 erg. The unique properties of DR20080 have never before been observed in Sculptor or in any other environment within the MW and its satellite system.

authors.name: Ioanna Koutsouridou
authors.institution: Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare, Sezione di Firenze

papers.title: The UV luminosity function at 1.6 < z < 2.2 from UVCANDELS
papers.abstract: We present an analysis of the rest-frame UV luminosity function (LF) of galaxies at $1.6<z<2.2$ using the UVCANDELS F435W imaging data. Restricting our analysis to sources above $30\%$ completeness to minimize uncertainties at the faint end, we construct a catalog of 5,212 galaxies at $1.6<z<2.2$ down to an absolute magnitude of $M_{\rm UV} = -16.8$, using well-tested photometric redshifts. We perform a maximum likelihood estimate to derive the best-fit Schechter parameters of the UV LF at a median redshift of $z\sim1.9$. We report a best-fit faint-end slope of $\alpha = -1.586 \pm 0.042$. Splitting the sample into two redshift bins, we obtain $\alpha=-1.488 \pm 0.055$ at $z\sim1.75$ and $\alpha=-1.604 \pm 0.066$ at $z\sim2.05$ ($\sim1.4\sigma$ difference), alongside a $\sim2.3\sigma$ brightening in $M^{*}$. Integrating our best-fit LF down to $M_{\rm UV} = -15$, we derive $\rho_{\rm UV} = (1.821 \pm 0.037) \times 10^{26}\ \rm erg\ s^{-1}\ Hz^{-1}\ Mpc^{-3}$ at $z\sim1.9$. Combining our F435W measurements with previous UVCANDELS F275W results and other literature data, we model the redshift evolution of $\rho_{\rm UV}$ from $z\sim0$ to $z\sim10$.

authors.name: Shamuhawu Hailanhazi
authors.institution: University of Chinese Academy of Sciences

authors.name: Christopher J. Conselice
authors.institution: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique

papers.title: Deformable Texture Maps: Compiling Dynamic Microgeometry into Neural Textures
papers.abstract: Deformable material surfaces, such as cloth, owe their appearance to fine-scale geometries that restructure under deformation. Even when coarse simulation models efficiently recover this microstructure, explicitly instantiating and rendering it remains expensive. We introduce Deformable Texture Maps (DTM), a representation that compiles deformation-driven microgeometry into a continuous and compact neural texture. Our model maps texture coordinates and local deformations to intrinsic maps describing opacity, surface normals, depth, and material identity. This captures the occlusion and visibility changes generated by deformation. At runtime, these maps provide a common texture-space representation of deformation-driven fine-scale structure that can be evaluated directly on coarse deforming surfaces. Since our representation encodes geometric attributes rather than radiance, lighting and material response remain decoupled from the learned model. This allows us to apply relighting, as well as shading and material editing without retraining. We further introduce a persistent texture-space rendering strategy that caches these intrinsic maps and selectively updates them as deformation changes. This effectively decouples neural evaluation from frame rendering and enables their reuse across frames and conventional rendering effects. We demonstrate our approach on yarn-based textiles, where non-linear material stretch and shear induce changes in yarn geometry, spacing and occlusion. We build our model by, first, sweeping tileable yarn patches through deformation space, then, rendering the detailed geometry into a canonical texture-space, and finally, compressing the resulting maps into a single neural representation. Our resulting model can be evaluated directly on arbitrary coarse garment meshes and integrated with conventional shading pipelines, keeping appearance authorable at render time.

papers.title: G\"odel's Incompleteness Theorems in Grounded Arithmetic
papers.abstract: Reflective Grounded Arithmetic (RGA) is a paracomplete arithmetic in which every term is a program and truth is grounded evaluation. RGA discharges a hypothesis only when it proves the hypothesis decided. This paper shows, in a machine-checked Isabelle/HOL development, how G\"odel's incompleteness theorems hold for RGA and for systems built on it. RGA's implication is material and RGA has the disjunction property, so the implications the textbook proof of the second theorem uses fail while its entailments and rules hold: G\"odel's proof survives as entailments. RGA does not prove its consistency sentence Con, and RGA derives its own second theorem as the entailment $\mathit{Con}\vdash\neg\mathit{Pr}(\ulcorner\mathit{Con}\urcorner)$ and as one sentence quantified over proofs. The second theorem is then proved once, for every G\"odel extension of RGA: an entailment relation on RGA's language, closed under RGA's rules, with a checker that meets three structural conditions, NEC, D3 and EXPL as proof transformers, D1 as closed acceptance, and consistency. D2 is not among the conditions. RGA with its checker is one instance. Inductive Grounded Arithmetic (IGA), RGA with ground induction, is another, its checker adding one rule detector, and IGA does not derive its consistency sentence for it. Adoption, a reflection rule whose premise is a derived warrant that the checker accepts computed proofs of every instance of a universal, gives consistent extensions RGA$^+$ and IGA$^+$. RGA$^+$ derives RGA's consistency sentence and IGA$^+$ derives RGA's and IGA's, so each strictly extends its base, and IGA$^+$ both. The second theorem holds at every adopted notation claim, and adopting Turing's code for that claim's checker derives its consistency sentence, so no claim certifies itself. Whether IGA alone derives RGA's consistency sentence is open, and the paper names what two routes to an answer need.

papers.title: Hierarchical interfacial anchoring for durable perovskite solar cells
papers.abstract: Although inverted perovskite solar cells now deliver certified efficiencies approaching their single-junction limits, their practical deployment remains constrained by the thermo-mechanical fragility of buried interfaces under realistic temperature fluctuations. Here, we identify thermo-mechanically driven, stress-accumulation-dominated adhesion failure at self-assembled monolayer-based buried interfaces as a critical failure mode in inverted perovskite solar cells. To address this issue, we propose an interfacial robustness design strategy based on a homometallic halide pretreatment, which constructs a chemically compatible and highly anchorable interfacial environment on transparent conductive oxides to guide the ordered assembly of SAMs. This interfacial treatment increases the density of surface hydroxyl species and enables hierarchical multipoint interfacial anchoring dominated by metal-oxygen coordination, with Cl- induced hydrogen-bonding interactions acting cooperatively, thereby enhancing anchoring robustness and improving tolerance to thermo-mechanical stress accumulation. With this interfacial strategy, the devices achieve a power conversion efficiency of 27.3% (26.9% certified) and retain 94% of their initial efficiency after 400 temperature cycles between -40 and 85 degrees C (ISOS-T-3). These results demonstrate that rational regulation of buried interfacial anchoring architectures can simultaneously enhance device efficiency and long-term operational reliability, offering a viable pathway toward high-efficiency and durable perovskite photovoltaics.

authors.name: Zuhong Zhang
authors.institution: Kunming University of Science and Technology

authors.name: Zhihao Li
authors.institution: Qingdao University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Mixed Signals: Weight-Space Programming for EEG and ECG
papers.abstract: Weight-space programming allows language models to read a trained neural network's weights and edit them. This opens the door to ``training'' by reasoning rather than through gradient descent. Prior work has demonstrated its functionality and promise for game-playing networks and fixing specific failures in language models, even extending to diffusion models. In this work, we present its applicability to models trained on biosignal data, specifically EEG and ECG data. We show that frontier models are not only able to debug specific faults planted in biosignal-based models without being told what these faults are, but are even capable of writing all the weights of a network from scratch, given only the architecture, the task, and a minimal set of training subjects. In particular, in one set of experiments, a language model was able to match standard gradient-descent training using $6\times$ fewer training subjects, through reasoning alone and without any gradient descent step. Networks written by Claude Opus 5.5 also scored higher than classic hand-crafted EEG pipelines (alpha band power, and common spatial patterns with linear discriminant analysis) when built from the same 5 subjects. We also highlight some of the limitations, which include the inability of language models to improve already well-trained classification models, and their incapacity to reliably recognize, from the weights alone, the task a network was trained on. Overall, our results indicate that weight-space programming can be useful for small networks, such as those deployed on edge devices and wearables, but the concept still requires further investigation before it can be used in practice.

papers.title: On the Existence of an Equilibrium Density Profile for Massive Collisional Star Clusters
papers.abstract: The dynamical evolution of massive, dense star clusters is governed by a complex interplay of multiple physical processes, including two-body relaxation, strong encounters, stellar evolution, and galactic tides, superimposed on the orbital motion of individual stars and binaries within the cluster potential. These processes can alter the internal evolution of individual stars and binaries, produce exotic stellar objects, and collectively determine the global structural evolution of the cluster. In this paper, we use the Monte Carlo star cluster evolution code CMC-COSMIC to study how the density profiles of dense star clusters evolve under the combined effects of these processes. We find that for a given initial mass and binding energy, cluster models converge toward a characteristic density profile largely independent of their initial density distributions. This convergence occurs during the late-time, quasi-static phase of evolution, when gravitational contraction is balanced by energy generated through black hole binaries in the cluster core. The shape of this profile is well represented by a King profile with W_0=6.8 but with the virial radius of the final cluster larger than the initial by a factor of about 7. We further show that this equilibrium profile is dynamically stable, i.e., perturbations away from it decay through the cluster's natural dynamical evolution, driving the system back toward the equilibrium profile.

papers.title: Optimal Last-Iterate Bounds for Nonexpansive Stochastic Approximation
papers.abstract: We establish last-iterate mean-square residual bounds for nonexpansive stochastic approximation (SA), or stochastic Krasnoselskii-Mann (KM) iterations. In particular, we consider fixed-point mappings that are nonexpansive with respect to the Euclidean norm, and focus on polynomially decaying stepsizes. We study three conditions on the conditional second moment of the noise, and obtain bounds that are optimal up to logarithmic factors in each case. When it scales linearly with the squared residual, the best rate is $O(1/k^{1-\epsilon})$ for any $\epsilon>0$. In this case, for all considered stepsizes, our bounds match those of the noiseless KM iteration. When it is bounded by a constant, the best rate is $O(\log^2 k/\sqrt{k})$. When it scales affinely with the squared norm of the iterate, the best rate is $O(1/k^{1/2-\epsilon})$, and the mean-square residual can diverge if the stepsizes are not square-summable. Thus, unlike for contractive SA, square-summable stepsizes are necessary for nonexpansive SA. We demonstrate how various algorithms with cocoercive maps, such as stochastic gradient descent, linear SA, and learning in cocoercive games, fit into our framework, and how the different noise conditions arise in each of them.

papers.title: Invariant measures, Gelfand pairs and integral representations
papers.abstract:
We prove that whenever a Gelfand pair acts cocompactly on a locally compact space, there is a measure relatively invariant under a "parabolic" subgroup. That result seems new even for simple Lie groups, in which case it admits a much more direct proof.
  Along the way, we obtain for general Gelfand pairs a variant of Furstenberg's invariant ray theorem for minimal parabolics. We use this to establish an integral representation theorem for positive spherical functions in complete generality, extending the Harish-Chandra representation. A similar representation theorem is given for positive harmonic functions.

papers.title: Classical Tensor Codes and Quantum Tanner Codes Achieve Capacity on Erasure Channels
papers.abstract: We show that on the classical erasure channel, the tensor product of two capacity-achieving code families is itself capacity-achieving under mild conditions. We also prove that duals of tensor products of independent uniform random binary linear codes achieve erasure capacity. Using these local codes, for every erasure probability $\rho\in(0,1/2)$ and every rate gap $\varepsilon>0$, we obtain a family of binary quantum Tanner codes of rate at least $1-2\rho-\varepsilon$. For fixed $\rho$ and $\varepsilon$, these codes have bounded check weights, minimum distance growing linearly with the blocklength, and a linear-time erasure decoder whose decoding error decays exponentially with the blocklength.

papers.title: Hierarchical Graph Representation Learning with Pooling-Induced Substructures
papers.abstract: Hierarchical graph-level tasks that require reasoning over substructures that extend beyond local neighborhoods are posing challenges for standard Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). While graph pooling aims to address this by coarsening graphs into hierarchical representations, existing methods often fail to explicitly preserve the substructures they induce, leading to inconsistent empirical performance. Moreover, evaluating such approaches remains challenging due to the lack of benchmarks with explicit hierarchical structure. We propose Pooled-Substructure-Aware GNNs, an approach to graph pooling that explicitly preserves and processes substructures uncovered by structure-based pooling schemes. We show that this design enhances the expressive power of pooling-based GNNs in the sense of the Weisfeiler-Lehman (WL) test. To enable principled evaluation, we introduce two new synthetic datasets with controllable hierarchical structure and propose a metric to characterize the prevalence of hierarchical patterns in real-world graph-level benchmarks. On tasks with relevant hierarchical structure, our approach outperforms matched pooling baselines, while remaining competitive on structurally simpler benchmarks. Code and datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/lsbicego/PSA-GNN/.

authors.name: Xiaowen Dong
authors.institution: University of Science and Technology Beijing

papers.title: Stagewise and interpretable emergence of inside-outside computation in Transformer-based language models
papers.abstract: Variability in syntactic structure and parsing ambiguity are fundamental aspects of natural language which modern LLMs have to learn to deal with proficiently. Previous "post-mortem" studies have shown that fully trained Transformers indeed approximate canonical parsing algorithms such as inside-outside, but little is established theoretically about how this is actually learned. Here, we make a first step towards addressing this by studying the learning dynamics in synthetic context-free grammars with variable parse tree topology. The stagewise learning curves are fully interpretable, in the sense that all of the loss stages a) can be computed analytically, and b) can be clearly associated to the representation of a hidden latent tree variable, which allows to lift ambiguity and utilize information from wider contexts. By probing representations, we visualize the emergence of inside-outside computation across depth and during training: while during early stages local (bigram/trigram) information is used and involves only a few initial layers, gradually the Transformer develops an encoder-decoder structure where the most abstract latent information is encoded in the middle, and the latter half of the network is used to progressively refine the final token prediction. This organization of computation is reminiscent of findings in real-world LLMs, and importantly applies here to a synthetic model which allows full analytical control of the data statistics, thus opening the door to theoretical progress.

papers.title: Discovering Equations for the Thermodynamics of South Asian Monsoon Precipitation
papers.abstract: South Asian monsoon precipitation depends on the thermodynamic structure of the lower troposphere, but how its ingredients combine to shape precipitation remains unclear, partly because this dependence is nonlocal in the vertical. We use symbolic distillation, which combines neural networks and symbolic regression, to discover interpretable precipitation equations from 21 years of June-August reanalysis data. Neural networks first learn the vertical thermodynamic structure most relevant to precipitation, condensing each variable into a single interpretable feature not tied to a particular vertical grid. Then, symbolic regression derives closed-form equations from these features and the surface state. Our best equation explains 1.5 times as much precipitation variance as a widely used buoyancy-based diagnostic and recovers about 85% of neural network skill while using about a thousand times fewer parameters. Unlike the buoyancy diagnostic, which adds moisture and instability, the equations treat them as competing controls, with the heaviest precipitation occurring when the lower free troposphere is humid. Over ocean, sensible heating is associated with additional precipitation mainly when near-surface air is warm and moist, improving predicted precipitation and its diurnal cycle. Although the learned features were optimized only for precipitation prediction, the equations largely respond to each feature as expected from convective physics, consistent with the reanalysis. These responses reduce the dependence of monsoon precipitation on the entire vertical column to a few simple, testable constraints that could guide data-driven precipitation models to make them more physically consistent.

papers.title: SinkState: On-the-Fly SVD of Recurrent States for Efficient Hybrid LLM Serving
papers.abstract: Hybrid models combine softmax attention with linear attention, which compresses history into fixed-size recurrent states to balance model quality and inference efficiency. However, linear attention has not pushed this compression to its limit: we find that the queries, keys, and values of linear layers concentrate in a stable, low-dimensional subspace, a phenomenon we call the linear attention sink, so each state is effectively low-rank, with a rank that varies across states. Yet existing serving systems keep these redundant states dense, reading and rewriting them in full at every decoding step, so their memory traffic grows with the batch size and dominates the decoding cost. Thus SinkState stores each recurrent state in an adaptive low-rank form throughout inference with buffered updates and a local SVD restricted to the top subspace. SinkState further consolidates the remaining components asynchronously on the CPU. On four hybrid models with Mamba-2 and Gated DeltaNet (GDN) layers, from 4B to 120B parameters, SinkState reduces the peak memory of recurrent states by up to 2.6x (1.9x on average) and speeds up decoding by up to 1.58x (1.25x on average) over Mamba-SSM and FLA, while maintaining accuracy.

papers.title: On the proof of Falconer distance conjecture
papers.abstract: We are able to catch the main idea from OpenAI's recent release and present a proof of Falconer distance conjecture in our own words. Arguments are judiciously simplified and carefully designed for graduate-level readers.

papers.title: Data4Cyber: Labeled Cyber-Physical Datasets for Distribution-Grid Management Systems Under Representative OT Attacks
papers.abstract: Cyberattacks against power systems increasingly exploit industrial communication and control dependencies arising from distributed energy resources (DER), remote management, and market-based incentives. Progress on intrusion detection is constrained by a lack of public datasets that align operational technology (OT) network telemetry with physical measurements and control context. Data4Cyber is a labeled cyber-physical dataset recorded in a laboratory distribution management system (DMS) for self-consumption optimization with photovoltaic generation, battery storage, controllable loads, and substation metering. It captures synchronized process measurements, controller context, price incentives, and packet captures (Modbus/TCP and MQTT) across one benign baseline and six attack scenarios spanning protocol-semantic Modbus manipulation, man-in-the-middle (MitM) false-data injection, and MQTT price manipulation. Its fixed 1 s time base, phase-resolved labels, and state-oriented representation support temporally blocked stateful-detector evaluation. Baseline results show that high recall alone is insufficient: several detectors achieve sensitivity through alarm saturation. Context-driven attacks require process-aware interpretation rather than single-channel thresholding.

authors.name: Lennart Bader
authors.institution: Fraunhofer Institute for Communication, Information Processing and Ergonomics

authors.name: Marawan Emara
authors.institution: Fraunhofer Institute for Communication, Information Processing and Ergonomics

authors.name: Martin Serror
