papers.title: Universal Multichannel Coherence-Mediated Thermal Transport in Carbon Allotropes: Experimental Evidence and Scaling Laws
papers.abstract:
Understanding thermal transport in structurally disordered carbon materials remains a fundamental challenge because conventional models based on a single coherence contribution cannot accurately describe heat conduction over a broad temperature range. In this work, the thermal conductivity of graphene oxide (GO), thermally reduced graphene oxide (trGO), GO-hydrated fullerene composites (GO-HyFn), expanded graphite (EG), and EG-multiwalled carbon nanotube (MWCNT) composites was measured between 4.5 and 300 K. Despite substantial differences in density, porosity, graphitic ordering, and microstructure, all materials exhibit glass-like temperature dependence of thermal conductivity.
  The experimental results demonstrate that the conventional two-channel model, comprising a Peierls contribution and a single thermally activated coherence term, systematically fails to reproduce the observed temperature dependence. To resolve this discrepancy, we propose a generalized multichannel phenomenological model in which the coherence contribution consists of up to three Arrhenius-type channels with distinct activation energies. Depending on the structural state, two or three coherence channels are required to accurately describe the thermal conductivity.
  A key finding is the reproducible hierarchy of activation energies across diverse carbon allotropes, following approximately (E2 ~ 4E1 and E3 ~ (12-25)E1). While the channel amplitudes increase with material density, the activation energies remain nearly invariant, indicating universal vibrational energy scales. The proposed framework also consistently describes published data for other disordered carbon materials. These results provide experimental evidence for multichannel coherence-mediated heat transport and establish a unified phenomenological bridge between structural hierarchy with thermal transport in disordered carbon solids.

papers.title: Proportional Neuro-Impulsive Control of SISO LTI Systems
papers.abstract: This paper explores a controller that is at the crossroads of neuromorphic, i.e., spike-based, and impulsive control systems. The controller consists of a single integrate-and-fire-like neuron that generates an input proportional to the system output when the neuron variable reaches a threshold. We prove that any static output-feedback stabilizable single-input single-output (SISO) linear time-invariant (LTI) plant can be made semi-globally asymptotically stable (sGAS) in closed loop with the proposed neuro-impulsive controller. This improves on existing fixed-amplitude neuromorphic controllers, which only achieve practical stability, but at the price of using graded spiking inputs. Moreover, we provide an algorithm for choosing appropriate controller parameters given a set of admissible initial conditions. A numerical example of an inverted pendulum linearized around its upright equilibrium illustrates the method.

papers.title: Excitable Behaviours of a First-Order High-Pass Neuron Model
papers.abstract: With the rise of neuromorphic technologies, simple and tunable neuron models are needed to analyse and design spiking systems. However, the simplest neuron models, e.g., Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) models, usually fail to capture the excitable behaviours of biological neurons. This could be a significant limitation, as excitability enables reliable spike timing under parametric uncertainties. Recently, a minimal excitable model, the so-called High-Pass Model (HPM), was introduced in neuroengineering. It simply consists of a static sigmoid with a high-pass filter in positive feedback. Given its novelty, it is still unclear how easily the HPM can be tuned, and how much of the excitable behaviours of a biophysical neuron it can reproduce. To address these questions, we investigate the tunability of a first-order HPM sub- and supra-rheobase, i.e., below and above the onset of the tonic spiking regime (where the neuron spikes periodically), and compare its behaviours with those of a simple Hodgkin-Huxley-type Conductance-Based Model (CBM). Below rheobase, both models fire spikes in response to transient inputs, including post-inhibitory rebound spikes. Above rheobase, an affine reparametrization of the input of the HPM suffices to fit its frequency-current curve to that of a CBM. The two models mostly differ near their respective rheobases, where the first-order HPM lacks bistability and spike latency. We suggest that modifying the frequency-selective element of the HPM may be sufficient to overcome this limitation. These results highlight the potential of the HPM as a fundamental computational primitive in neuromorphic, spike-based technologies.

papers.title: Compact plasma-based extreme compression of relativistic electron beams
papers.abstract: Accelerated particle beams are essential tools of modern science and technology with applications ranging from medicine [1], to light sources [2], to high-energy physics [3]. Over time, as accelerator-based experiments become more sophisticated and probe natural phenomena with greater temporal resolution, there is an increasing demand on beam parameters, in particular on bunch duration. Experiments have been proposed that require beams with 1-2 orders of magnitude shorter durations than what is possible with current state-of-the-art technology. However, state-of-the-art temporal bunch compressors force a trade-off between how short an electron bunch can be made and how well its transverse quality survives the strong bending magnets required to do so -- a limitation that stands as a grand challenge for accelerator physics to-date [4]. In this experiment, we demonstrate a new, compact compression technique for generating ultrashort, high-peak-current electron bunches that circumvents this trade-off using plasma wakefield acceleration. Just as chirped pulse amplification unlocked ultrashort, high-power laser pulses and the technologies that followed from them, here we demonstrate an analogous chirp-and-compress strategy applied to relativistic electron beams by using the extreme electric fields of a plasma wakefield in place of a stretcher-amplifier, thereby unlocking the path to ultrashort, extremely high-current electron beams. We demonstrate the first application of this plasma-compressed bunch using it to drive single-microbunch free electron lasing at optical wavelengths in a single, meter-scale undulator module, producing radiation pulses roughly four orders of magnitude more energetic than the first beam-driven, plasma-based free electron laser demonstration at the same accelerator facility [5, 6].

papers.title: Modal-Augmented Chebyshev Physics-Informed Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Power Systems
papers.abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) offer a promising alternative to numerical integration for power system dynamic simulation; however, their conventional architectures can struggle to capture electromechanical oscillations. Although physics-informed Kolmogorov-Arnold networks (PIKANs) offer an alternative, their B-spline implementations incur substantial training costs. To address these limitations, this paper investigates Chebyshev PIKANs (c-PIKANs) and proposes a modal-augmented c-PIKAN (mac-PIKAN) based on a trial solution that incorporates the closed-form modal response of the linearized swing equation. First, the modal response is used to capture the dominant oscillatory dynamics. Then, a c-PIKAN learns a nonlinear correction weighted by a quadratic time-dependent factor, ensuring that the initial rotor angle and speed are satisfied exactly. Evaluations on the single-machine infinite-bus benchmark demonstrate the computational efficiency of c-PIKAN and show that mac-PIKAN reduces PINN rotor-angle and frequency errors from 1.59% to 0.29% and from 5.26% to 0.99%, respectively, while maintaining higher accuracy across training-data sizes and at lower damping levels.

papers.title: Large-area Spatially Aligned Anchors
papers.abstract: Extended Reality (XR) technologies, including Virtual Reality (VR) and Augmented Reality (AR), offer immersive experiences merging digital content with the real world. Achieving precise spatial tracking over large areas is a critical challenge in XR development. This paper addresses the drift issue, caused by small errors accumulating over time leading to a discrepancy between the real and virtual worlds. Tackling this issue is crucial for co-located XR experiences where virtual and physical elements interact seamlessly. Building upon the locally accurate spatial anchors, we propose a solution that extends this accuracy to larger areas by exploiting an external, drift-corrected tracking method as a ground truth. During the preparation stage, anchors are placed inside the headset and inside the external tracking method simultaneously, yielding 3D-3D correspondences. Both anchor clouds, and thus tracking methods, are aligned using a suitable cloud registration method during the operational stage. Our method enhances user comfort and mobility by leveraging the headset's built-in tracking capabilities during the operational stage, allowing standalone functionality. Additionally, this method can be used with any XR headset that supports spatial anchors and with any drift-free external tracking method. Empirical evaluation demonstrates the system's effectiveness in aligning virtual content with the real world and expanding the accurate tracking area. In addition, the alignment is evaluated by comparing the camera poses of both tracking methods. This approach may benefit a wide range of industries and applications, including manufacturing and construction, education, and entertainment.

papers.title: Noetherian connected braided Hopf algebras are affine
papers.abstract:
The well-known Wu--Zhang question asks whether every Noetherian Hopf algebra over a field is affine (finitely generated as an algebra). In this paper, we extend this fundamental problem to the braided setting within the monoidal category ${}_{H}^{H}\mathcal{YD}$ of left Yetter--Drinfel'd modules over a Hopf algebra $H$. By developing term-rewriting methods based on reduction orderings and prime-word factorizations in free prebraided algebras, we establish explicit expansions for YD-triangular comultiplications. We prove that if $(\mathbb{K}\langle X \rangle, \epsilon)$ is an augmented free algebra in ${}_{H}^{H}\mathcal{YD}$ and $I \subseteq \ker \epsilon$ is an ideal invariant under a YD-triangular comultiplication, then every $I$-reducible letter---and consequently every non-empty word in $\langle X \rangle$---can be expressed modulo $I$ as a linear combination of products of $I$-irreducible letters strictly smaller with respect to the reduction order.
  As a primary consequence, we prove that any right Noetherian connected prebraided Hopf algebra $B$ in ${}_{H}^{H}\mathcal{YD}$ is affine, generated by the image of a finite set $X_{I}$ of $I$-irreducible letters. As an application, we show that the braided component $B = A^{\mathrm{co}\,\pi}$ of a right Noetherian Radford biproduct $A = B \sharp H$ is affine whenever $A_{(0)} \subseteq \jmath(H)$, reducing the affineness of $A$ entirely to that of $H$.

papers.title: Tuning and Mapping of Two-Tone Optomechanical Instability up to the Physical Limits
papers.abstract: We report on the compete theory describing the two-tone instability proper to optomechanical back-action-evading experiments. We address all possible mistunings (including power imbalance of the two pumps), as well as the device imperfections (finite mechanical quality factor, and sideband resolution). We illustrate the importance of power mistuning and sideband resolution, the latter being particularly relevant in finding the back-action-evading "sweet spot". The model is compared to experiments performed up to an extremely high cooperativity, of almost a 100. This has been made possible thanks to a fine-tuning procedure, which is presented. The agreement theory-experiment is very good, and the limiting factor is unraveled: cavity frequency noise. Besides, we discover at very high drive powers new self-driven states, which all share the characteristic feature of presenting a mechanical comb spectrum; as if the synchronization of the responses to the two drives (which occurs at lower powers) was destroyed by nonlinear effects. We believe that our work is extremely relevant to the implementation of back-action-evading experiments, as well as other related two-tone schemes.

papers.title: DASWeave: Weaving Evidence across Speaking Conditions for Multimodal Depression, Anxiety, and Stress Screening
papers.abstract: Multimodal screening for depression, anxiety, and stress in children and adolescents uses verbal and nonverbal behaviour. Most existing multimodal methods learn from a single recording or interview. Yet a participant's behaviour changes with the speaking condition, and these changes hold evidence that is invisible in a single recording. We propose DASWeave to bring this evidence into a neural network that encodes each response and then combines all responses of a participant. We train supervised trees to find which behavioural statistics matter for screening, both within each response and in how they change across conditions. We feed the tree outputs into the network both before and after this combination. We fine-tune a large language model to relate what a participant says to how they say it across conditions, and feed its representation into the network after the combination. The language model reads behaviour as text descriptions. We therefore derive additional training targets for the network from a multimodal large language model that takes in the audio-visual features directly. On the official hidden test set of the ACM Multimedia 2026 AdoDAS Grand Challenge (Track 1), DASWeave ranks second among 95 eligible teams. Its mean F1 is 27.1% higher than that of the official audio-visual baseline. It also has the highest mean AUROC among the top five teams. Ablation studies on the validation set show that the supervised trees and the fine-tuned language model contribute most to mean F1.

papers.title: Thermodynamic signatures of a nearby quantum critical endpoint in UTe$_2$ under intense magnetic field
papers.abstract: Several unconventional superconducting phases have been discovered in the vicinity of metamagnetism in the heavy-fermion paramagnet UTe$_2$ under magnetic field. To describe the mechanism of magnetic-field-induced superconductivity, a challenge is to characterize the quantum critical magnetic properties at the metamagnetic transition. In this work, we investigate the thermodynamic properties of UTe$_2$ under magnetic fields up to 60~T applied in the crystallographic $\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{c}$ plane. Magnetization and magnetostriction experiments have been performed under magnetic fields tilted by an angle $\theta\lesssim42^\circ$ from $\mathbf{b}$ toward $\mathbf{c}$. They support that a quantum critical endpoint at the field angle $\theta_{QCEP}\simeq(70\pm10)^\circ$ and magnetic field $\mu_0H_{QCEP}\simeq(75\pm10)$~T terminates the metamagnetic transition line. A pseudo-gap in the magnetic susceptibility is related with the metamagnetic transition observed in magnetic fields for $\theta<\theta_{QCEP}$. The possible relation between the quantum critical endpoint and the development of magnetic-field-induced superconductivity is discussed.

papers.title: YTShorts-92K: An Interpretable Multimodal Dataset of YouTube Shorts
papers.abstract: Short-form video has become one of the dominant formats of online content, yet large-scale datasets enabling the analysis of what makes these videos successful remain limited. Existing resources often focus on post-publication popularity signals or rely on non-interpretable representations such as high-dimensional embeddings. Here, we introduce YTShorts-92K, a dataset of 92,654 YouTube Shorts collected from 345 creators and spanning 12 manually defined content categories. Each video is enriched with an interpretable multimodal feature set covering metadata, textual information, visual characteristics from frames and thumbnails, and cross-modal consistency measures. We describe the collection methodology, data cleaning process, and feature extraction pipeline, followed by descriptive analyses of the diversity of creators, topics, and extracted features. This dataset offers a reusable resource for studying short-form video content, online attention, and multimodal content analysis.

authors.name: Artur Vlaszov
authors.institution: Budapest University of Technology and Economics

papers.title: Evolution of cooperation in enterprise resource-sharing networks with dynamic participation and adaptive decision-making
papers.abstract: Resource sharing among enterprises is an important mechanism for improving resource utilization efficiency and facilitating collaborative development. However, the emergence and sustainability of cooperative behavior depend critically on whether enterprises choose to participate in resource-sharing activities and how they balance cooperation and competition in their decision-making processes. To investigate these issues, we develop an evolutionary cooperation model on the enterprise resource-sharing network that integrates participation status, decision-making modes, and cooperative strategies within a unified framework. Specifically, enterprises dynamically switch between active and dormant states according to their aspiration levels, while Q-learning is employed to enable adaptive selection between payoff-driven and conformist decision-making modes. Meanwhile, interactions between resource-sharing and non-sharing in active enterprises are characterized by the snowdrift game. Through extensive simulations, we systematically examine the effects of the payoff parameter, the reinforcement-learning parameters, the participation and Q-learning mechanism, and network size on enterprise participation and the evolution of cooperation. The results show that an intermediate aspiration level is most favorable for sustaining enterprise participation and facilitating the emergence of cooperation. Moreover, the dynamic activation mechanism effectively mitigates the decline in cooperation under high cost-to-benefit ratios, allowing the system to sustain a decent level of cooperative behavior. These findings highlight the important roles of dynamic participation and adaptive decision-making in shaping the evolution of resource-sharing cooperation and provide a new modeling framework to understand the emergence and persistence of cooperation in complex enterprise networks.

authors.name: Attila Szolnoki
authors.institution: Institute for Technical Physics and Materials Science

papers.title: On the Nonemptiness of the Core: Connecting Cooperative Games and Asset Pricing
papers.abstract:
We show that the Bondareva--Shapley theorem for infinite cooperative games can be derived from a version of the fundamental theorem of asset pricing. The link is the Choquet extension of a game, viewed as a possibly nonlinear pricing rule on the space of measurable simple payoffs. Under this identification, balancedness translates into no arbitrage, and a linear functional dominated by the pricing rule yields an allocation in the anti-core; the core statement follows by duality.
  Applying the arbitrage-free pricing theorem of Cornet (2025), we recover the characterization of the nonvacuity of the core initiated by Schmeidler (1967) and established in full generality by Bartl and Pinter (2023) for bounded-below games. Unlike the earlier derivation in Cornet (2025), our argument does not require the game to have bounded variation or the collection of coalitions to be a $\sigma$-algebra.

papers.title: Network-Co-Designed Dynamic Sparsification for Dependable Distributed Robot Learning over 3GPP Networks
papers.abstract: Robot fleets performing distributed learning often face volatile uplink conditions like bandwidth variation, packet loss, and latency spikes that delay or destabilize training. We propose a network-co-designed dynamic sparsification loop that couples model-update compression to network-facing byte budgets and time constraints. We describe two realizations: (i) a standards-aligned SA6/5GC mapping that leverages CAPIF with NEF/PCF/NWDAF, enriched with AI-specific semantics; and (ii) a VASEAL-style role-reversed loop where the learning system exposes learning-state feedback and receives bounded, time-limited control intents. We implement the mechanism in an asynchronous federated reinforcement learning framework with heterogeneous simulated quadruped robots and reproducible uplink impairments via emulated network links. Results indicate that substantial communication reduction is achievable under dynamic constraints without materially degrading learning progress in the studied setting.

authors.name: Boldizsar Bunda
authors.institution: Budapest University of Technology and Economics

papers.title: Nonnegative weak tilings and the Coven-Meyerowitz condition (T2)
papers.abstract: We develop a general method, in finite cyclic groups, for constructing nonnegative rational functions $f$, normalized by $f(0)=1$, that satisfy the Coven-Meyerowitz condition $(T1)$ but fail $(T2)$, such that $f$ is a weak complement for a set tile $A$. Motivated by the unsupported-divisor questions in arXiv:2507.11672, we show that if a set tile $A$ admits an unsupported divisor, then a suitable dilation of $A$ admits such a rational weak complement $f$. Using this method, we construct an explicit example in the group $\mathbb{Z}_{180}$. The weak complements in our explicit perturbative constructions are not positive definite because of restrictions on the Fourier support of the perturbations. Thus these constructions do not resolve the proposed extension of the Coven-Meyerowitz conditions to positive-definite weak tilings (arXiv:2411.03854, Problem 1.2).

authors.name: Gergely Kiss
authors.institution: HUN-REN Alfréd Rényi Institute of Mathematics

authors.name: Mate Matolcsi
authors.institution: HUN-REN Alfréd Rényi Institute of Mathematics

papers.title: Estimating multidimensional poverty under incomplete data in North Macedonia
papers.abstract: Multidimensional Poverty Indices (MPIs) are available for more than 100 countries, but rarely below the national or regional level. Local estimates require knowing how deprivations overlap within households, yet the sources that cover every locality, such as censuses and geospatial data, cannot be linked at the household level. We show how to measure local multidimensional poverty under such incomplete data, using North Macedonia as a case study. Combining settlement-level access to services with municipal census data, we pair an independence-based point estimate with sharp bounds over all joint distributions consistent with the data. We find that, nationally, 5.01 percent of households are multidimensionally poor, with bounds of 2.01 to 17.44 percent. Also, poverty is concentrated in small rural municipalities, which are poorer than nearly all municipalities of the capital city under any dependence structure. Validating our index against official statistics, the Global MPI, and a fieldwork deprivation index indicates that the socio-economic part of the index is consistent with external measures of deprivation, while the geographic part captures a distinct dimension of remoteness. Our approach thus presents a promising way to measure multidimensional poverty at the local level in countries where linked household data are unavailable.

papers.title: HiPFuse: Real-Time LiDAR Semantic Segmentation for Robotic Perception on Edge Devices
papers.abstract: Real-time robotic perception requires accurate LiDAR semantics under limited resources. Bird's-eye-view (BEV) aggregation is efficient but can mix differently labeled surfaces in columns. We present HiPFuse, a point-BEV fusion framework that exchanges point and height-partitioned BEV features across horizontal scales, combining point-wise detail with 2D spatial context from one LiDAR scan. Fixed height assignments preserve separate vertical aggregation groups, with auxiliary supervision of initial BEV features using targets from the same 3D cells. A dual-scale BEV context module adds broader context from a coarser grid. On SemanticKITTI and MCD, HiPFuse achieves 63.7% and 62.5% mIoU at 14.2 and 22.4 FPS on Jetson AGX Orin, respectively, exceeding the 10 Hz scan rate. Separate training and evaluation show indoor applicability. Replacing only the baseline semantic front end with HiPFuse in fixed robotic systems reduces odometry absolute trajectory error RMSE by 10.6% on average across two outdoor sequences and increases accepted-loop recall by 8.7 percentage points on SemanticKITTI. Qualitative semantic maps show more continuous road labeling. Our code is available at https://github.com/haiyang2022/HiPFuse.

papers.title: Sharp Proximity Bounds for Integer Programs with Few Rows
papers.abstract: We study the proximity between an optimal vertex of a standard form linear program with constraint matrix $A\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times n}$ and an optimal integer solution. When $m = 2$, we prove the sharp infinity-norm bound $\Delta-1$, where $\Delta$ is the largest absolute maximal minor of $A$. When $m = 1$, we express the difference between an optimal LP vertex and an optimal integer solution as a nonnegative combination of certain generators in the kernel of $A$ with a bounded coefficient sum. This implies sharp proximity bounds for all norms when $m=1$. Combining this representation with its known counterpart for Hilbert bases due to Sissokho, we develop techniques that transfer results from $m=1$ to $m=2$. Along the way, for $m=2$, we prove that such a representation exists for an extended Gomory group relaxation and obtain the sharp infinity-norm bound $\Delta$ for Graver basis elements. We also present a new short proof of Sissokho's result and lower bounds on the proximity for all $m$ and $\Delta$.

papers.title: DEIA: Evidence-Grounded Crash Repair with Change-Aware Test Design for HarmonyOS ArkTS
papers.abstract:
Mobile crash repair requires more than identifying a source edit. Developers must establish how the edit relates to the reported failure and whether the modified application can be built, launched, and exercised without disrupting valid behavior. In HarmonyOS applications, this assessment also depends on platform-specific packaging and runtime execution.
  To address this need, we present DEIA, an evidence-grounded workflow for HarmonyOS crash repair. DEIA constructs a bounded source-evidence package, uses a large language model to propose content-anchored edits, and relies on a deterministic writer to materialize and check the patch. It derives fail-to-pass (F2P) obligations from the reported fault and pass-to-pass (P2P) obligations from the potential impact of the patch. A stage-level ledger links the patch, test obligations, runtime observations, and candidate-generation cost.
  We evaluate DEIA on 30 repair tasks from 24 HarmonyOS applications and compare it with an OpenHands-based workflow on 29 matched tasks. DEIA's first-added-line location exactly matches the curated reference in 25/29 tasks (86.2%), compared with 19/29 (65.5%) for OpenHands, a difference of 20.7 percentage points. DEIA also uses 81.5% fewer tokens, makes 60.8% fewer model calls, and takes 34.9% less candidate-generation time on average. Only two of the 58 behavior-specific P2P obligations were executed, both for one repair pattern; comprehensive behavior preservation therefore remains unestablished.

papers.title: Aeroelastically Constrained Optimal Path Planning of a Fixed-Wing Airborne Wind Energy System
papers.abstract: Multi-megawatt fixed-wing airborne wind energy systems (AWES) use an aircraft with large, slender wings that deform over the pumping cycle. To harvest maximum energy, the cycle is usually designed by means of dedicated reference trajectory optimization routines. It is well known that such routines rely heavily on the system model and that close alignment between the model and the physical system is required for the results to hold in practice. Nevertheless, the wing is usually treated as rigid and structural limits are respected indirectly through upper bounding of states and inputs. In this work, we directly enforce bounds on the elastic deflection and twist of the wing in the power-maximizing periodic optimal control problem. To that end, we model the wing by root-clamped modes, loaded by strip-theory aerodynamics and by the gravitational and inertial loads of the manoeuvring aircraft. To keep the problem tractable, the modal dynamics are replaced by their quasi-static equilibrium, which enters every discretization interval as algebraic constraints. For a multi-megawatt reference aircraft, the elastic twist near the wing tips reaches $1.03^\circ$ along the optimal rigid-wing trajectory. With a twist limit of $0.6^\circ$, the optimal trajectory delivers $31\,\%$ less mean power than the rigid-wing one, mainly through a lower tether tension during reel-out. Rigid-wing trajectory optimization can thus overestimate the power that the wing limits permit. Forward simulations that retain the modal dynamics demonstrate that the quasi-static deflection and twist deviate from the dynamic ones by less than $2\,\%$ of their limits. This work shows that elastic deformation can be accounted for in the trajectory optimization and that, depending on the wing limits, it can strongly reduce the achievable power.

papers.title: Numerical Investigations on Bitumen Liberation from Oil Sands Lump
papers.abstract: The dynamic liberation and digestion of viscous oil-solid aggregates under turbulent flow is a critical transport phenomenon in multiphase chemical processes, including slurry transport, soil remediation, and industrial extraction. A primary industrial application of this phenomenon is oil sands hydrotransport, where pipelines are widely utilized to simultaneously transport and extract bitumen from lump ore. However, optimizing operating conditions requires a fundamental understanding of the localized hydrodynamic mechanisms governing detachment. To address this, a three-dimensional (3D) Eulerian-Eulerian (E-E) CFD approach coupled with k-omega SST turbulence model has been utilized to investigate bitumen detachment dynamics from complex solid matrices. Six numerical cases were analyzed across lump diameters (D) of 4 and 5 cm and particle Reynolds numbers (Re_p) between 2000 and 4000. The simulation results reveal that bitumen liberation is a shear-driven process, occurring only when the shear stresses exerted by the flow on the lump surface exceed a critical threshold value. The bitumen liberation rate increases with higher Re_p and smaller D, due to enhanced local shear forces and reduced particle shielding. Based on these mechanistic insights, a novel semi-empirical shear-driven model was formulated. The proposed model demonstrates excellent predictive accuracy when validated against experimental liberation data, with an error less than 8.3%. Overall, these findings clarify the fluid-particle interactions governing bitumen detachment and offer a robust, physics-based tool for predicting recovery efficiency in industrial hydrotransport operations.

authors.name: Xuehua Zhang
authors.institution: Max Planck University of Twente Center for Complex Fluid Dynamics

papers.title: Control Barrier Functions for Counting Tasks in Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: Multi-agent systems increasingly operate in dynamic environments and execute complex tasks that require coordination, posing significant computational challenges. Counting tasks, which require a minimum number of agents to satisfy a given condition, arise naturally in such systems. Examples include surveillance tasks, where at least m drones must continuously monitor a critical area, and emergency-response tasks, where at least m robots must converge to an incident location. The identities of the agents assigned to these tasks may change dynamically depending on their states, input bounds, and individual objectives. In this work, we propose a control barrier function (CBF)-based framework for enforcing counting invariance and counting convergence tasks, without explicitly assigning agents or enumerating all possible subteams. We develop a recursion-based method for constructing differentiable CBFs for counting tasks. The resulting CBF constraints are incorporated into quadratic programs, enabling online controller synthesis. Numerical experiments demonstrate scalability to large multi-agent systems, while a multi-drone emergency-response case study illustrates the satisfaction of counting tasks.

authors.name: Siyuan Liu
authors.institution: Qingdao University of Science and Technology

papers.title: MediPFN: Amortized In-Context Nuisance Learning and Inference for Causal Mediation Analysis
papers.abstract: Causal mediation analysis decomposes a treatment effect into indirect pathways through mediators and direct pathways through other processes. Tabular foundation models perform classification and regression through in-context learning, providing estimates of conditional means and propensity scores used in causal mediation analysis. Constructing confidence intervals from these estimates requires accounting for uncertainty introduced by fitting and combining several nuisance functions. We introduce MediPFN, an amortized inference framework that adapts a pretrained tabular foundation model to nuisance prediction and combines its predictions through a cross-fitted influence-function estimator. A separate head learns quantiles of the estimator's standardized error from simulated tables with known indirect effects. Supervised fine-tuning, symmetrization, and independent calibration then produce a confidence interval. We establish coverage bounds for the resulting intervals under standard assumptions. Across experiments, MediPFN attains coverage closer to the nominal level than several comparators. It also reduces the computational cost of uncertainty quantification, running 59.1 times faster than bootstrap in matched comparisons.

papers.title: Towards Design of Efficient Neuromorphic Controllers
papers.abstract: One of the major sources of inspiration for neuromorphic engineering is the central nervous system, which is orders of magnitude more efficient than classical digital clock-based computers. Neuromorphic control aims at recreating this efficiency in control systems, combined with (formal) stability and performance guarantees. In our previous work [1], we have established formal guarantees for the emulation of static output feedback controllers implemented using integrate-and-fire neurons. In this paper, we investigate the ``efficiency'' of the resulting controllers in terms of sparse spiking activity. By changing the network structure of our original implementation, foregoing the unit gain assumption made in our previous work, we will establish that the chosen architecture of the spiking controller significantly affects its sparsity and discuss the implications of these observations for the efficient implementation of spiking controllers.

papers.title: Online Adaptive Clustering in Robust Distributed Model Predictive Control
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a dynamic clustering framework for tube-based model predictive control (MPC) of coupled multi-agent systems. Agents within a cluster coordinate their dynamics explicitly, while couplings from agents outside the cluster are treated as bounded disturbances. For each admissible cluster, we construct a state-dependent mismatch measure from a robust upper bound on its predicted closed-loop cost and an optimistic, partition-independent lower bound. Combining this mismatch with a communication penalty enables online selection of the clustering topology, ranging from centralized to fully decentralized operation. The resulting switching controller is shown to preserve recursive feasibility and constraint satisfaction, and to render the closed-loop system practically asymptotically stable. Furthermore, the mismatch provides an upper bound on the finite-horizon performance difference with respect to centralized MPC. An eight-agent spring--damper example illustrates how the controller adapts cooperation while maintaining performance close to centralized MPC with reduced communication.

authors.name: Stefan van Dijk
authors.institution: Amsterdam UMC Location University of Amsterdam

papers.title: Passive ladder-network representation of the radiation impedance of a spherical cap on a rigid sphere
papers.abstract: A loudspeaker in a closed box is modeled as a rigid sphere with an axially moving cap. For an axisymmetric cone-velocity profile, its radiation impedance is written as a network. Each spherical-harmonic mode has an impedance rational in frequency, realized exactly as a finite passive ladder of masses and compliances terminated in a resistance. Ideal transformers set by Legendre coefficients couple these ladders; truncated modes reduce to a residual mass. Despite the different geometry, the impedance resembles that of a baffled piston but, at equal volume velocity, has half its low-frequency resistance and about three quarters of its radiation mass.

papers.title: TITAN DR1: The Type Ia Supernova Trove from ATLAS in the Nearby Universe - Host Galaxies I: Associations, Redshifts and Derived Properties
papers.abstract: We present the host-galaxy catalogue for TITAN DR1, a sample of 8378 spectroscopically confirmed Type Ia supernovae (SNe~Ia) at $z \lesssim 0.15$ -- the largest homogeneous low-redshift SN Ia sample assembled to date. We describe the association of each SN with its host, the compilation of redshifts, measurements of uniform far-ultraviolet to mid-infrared (FUV--MIR) photometry, and the derivation of host properties through spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting. Combining four host-association methods with manual vetting, we securely identify hosts for 7856 SNe~Ia (93.8\%). We compile host-galaxy spectroscopic redshifts for 5522 objects and provide CMB-frame and peculiar-velocity-corrected redshifts. \rev{PSF-matched} photometry is measured for 7568 host galaxies, including both global fluxes and local optical-only fluxes within a fixed 1.5~kpc aperture centred on the SN; \texttt{Bagpipes} returns successful global fits for \rev{all} hosts and local fits for 7329. Stellar mass and rest-frame $g-z$ colour are robustly measured from optical data alone, whereas reliable estimates of star-formation rate, dust attenuation, and mass-weighted age require broader wavelength coverage to break age--dust degeneracies\rev{, and are reported for 5827 hosts}; in our redshift range, MIR data suffice and far-IR coverage is not required. The hosts span a representative low-redshift galaxy population, with a median stellar mass of $\log_{10}(M_*/M_\odot)=10.22$ (\rev{60\%} high-mass; $\log_{10}(M_*/M_\odot)>10$), \rev{71\%} star-forming ($\log_{10}(\mathrm{sSFR}/\mathrm{yr}^{-1}) > -10.5$), and an approximately exponential $A_V$ distribution. This catalogue provides the foundation for forthcoming analyses of the luminosity step and the broader role of galaxy environment in SN~Ia standardization and cosmology.

papers.title: Angular momentum transport in a newborn protostar--disc system: magnetic braking, spiral arms and the magneto-rotational instability
papers.abstract: Angular momentum transport in young protostar--disc systems involves magnetic braking, magneto-rotational turbulence and gravitational instability, mechanisms that are usually studied separately and on different scales. We present a three-dimensional non-ideal magnetohydrodynamic simulation, including Ohmic and ambipolar diffusion, that follows the collapse of a $1~M_\odot$ dense core continuously from the cloud scale to the formation of the protostar, and then the resulting protostar--disc system for $\sim 64~\mathrm{yr}$ at a resolution of $\sim 10^{-4}~\mathrm{AU}$ at the protostellar surface. We decompose the azimuthally averaged angular momentum budget into Reynolds, Maxwell and gravitational torques, each split into a radial and a meridional component, over a quasi-steady phase of the evolution. The collapse produces a thick disc an order of magnitude more massive than the protostar, whose specific angular momentum decreases as it accretes. Accretion through the disc is vertically layered, with accreting and decreting layers at the same radius, a pattern set layer by layer by the torques. The transport separates into three regimes delimited by the coupling of the magnetic field to the gas. Magnetic braking operates in the envelope. Maxwell stresses dominate inside $\sim 0.1~\mathrm{AU}$, where the field recouples and the magneto-rotational instability develops. In the ambipolar dead zone that makes up the bulk of the disc, the Reynolds stress dominates, carried by $m=2$ spiral arms in a marginally unstable disc, with the gravitational stress as a secondary contributor. Meridional transport is as important as radial transport, so that a one-dimensional viscous model fitted to the net mass flux would require a negative $\alpha$ over part of the disc.

papers.title: Shape Perturbation of the Galerkin Boundary Element Dirichlet-to-Neumann Matrix on Moving Polygons
papers.abstract: For nonlocal interface evolution problems such as the Mullins-Sekerka flow, certain parametric schemes discretize only the interface and approximate the Dirichlet-to-Neumann map by boundary elements. Their error analysis requires bounds on how this discrete operator changes as the polygon moves. In that analysis, the polygons are only Lipschitz and close to a smooth curve only in a Lipschitz norm, the perturbations are controlled only in the energy norm, and the kernels are singular on the diagonal. We study the symmetric Galerkin boundary element matrix on the polygons in a Lipschitz neighborhood of a smooth reference curve. Its first variation, tested against discrete Neumann solutions, is bounded by the energy norm of the perturbation alone. The second-order remainder of the associated mass form is bounded by the product of the energy norm and the Lipschitz norm of the perturbation, so that only one of the two factors needs a uniform bound. On the interpolating polygon, the matrix is consistent with the continuous operator without the logarithmic loss that a pointwise comparison of the kernels would suggest, and its shape derivative is consistent with that of the continuous operator. All bounds are uniform in the mesh size and depend only on the constants of the reference curve.

papers.title: Learning a model of non-stationary nuisances with non-local correlations for object detection
papers.abstract: We tackle the problem of detecting faint objects in multivariate data corrupted by a strong and spatially correlated nuisance component in the low-sample regime. Standard covariance-based models often yield unstable or ill-conditioned estimators of the nuisance statistics, severely degrading detection performance. We propose a data-driven approach based on sparse precision matrix modeling, where the precision matrix is approximated through a pivoted sparse Cholesky factorization whose non-zeros coefficients are learned by maximum likelihood. This yields a low-complexity yet expressive statistical model of the nuisance. Building on this model, we derive a generalized likelihood ratio test for faint source detection enabling direct control of the false alarm rate. The approach is evaluated on an astrophysical application: the detection of exoplanets by high contrast imaging, where it achieves state-of-the-art performance.

papers.title: Emergent Biological Capabilities in a Foundation Model for Molecular Interactions
papers.abstract: Foundation models trained on large unlabeled corpora develop emergent capabilities, tasks that go beyond the training objective. We extend this paradigm to multimodal biology with Bonbon, a foundation model for molecular interactions trained on approximately 3.2 trillion tokens of paired protein-ligand sequences. From a single representation space, Bonbon exhibits three zero-shot emergent capabilities at hierarchical levels of resolution: functional (mechanism of action), residue (binding site localization, including orthosteric/allosteric discrimination), and bond (covalent versus non-covalent engagement). All three capabilities generalize to out-of-distribution complexes. Bonbon was trained on protein-ligand sequences alone, without any task-specific supervision and without structural coordinates. We conducted controlled scaling experiments across six model scales from 42M to 1.6B parameters; every capability evaluated shows a sharp jump at the largest scale on continuous metrics, even as pretraining loss decreases smoothly. This demonstrates that loss-based scaling laws alone are insufficient to predict when zero-shot emergent capabilities become available. The capabilities reported here emerge after training at a 1:2,000 parameter-to-token ratio to accommodate the sparsity of paired biological interaction data. The same frozen representations achieve state-of-the-art binding and affinity prediction at five orders of magnitude greater speed than co-folding methods. In prospective wet-lab validation across nine disease targets spanning seven protein families, Bonbon achieves a 61.5% dose-response hit rate on de novo compounds, yielding structurally novel molecules not previously reported to inhibit these proteins, including for out-of-distribution targets.

papers.title: Point defects and primary radiation damage in Co-free Fe-Ni-Cr-Mn high-entropy alloys from molecular dynamics
papers.abstract: Co-free Fe-Ni-Cr-Mn high-entropy alloys (HEAs) are candidates for nuclear structural applications. We used molecular dynamics with the EAM-21 potential, stiffened at short range, to study five HEAs that have been irradiated experimentally: Fe37Ni34Cr16Mn13 (ES1), Fe35Ni35Cr15Mn15 (P35), Fe46Ni22Cr15Mn17 (Y3), Fe27Ni28Cr18Mn27 (Kumar) and Fe30Ni30Cr10Mn30 (C30). They were compared with pure Ni, Fe60Ni40, the Fe70Ni10Cr20 model alloy of 316L, and Fe50Ni34Cr16, which is ES1 with Mn replaced by Fe. We calculated stacking fault energies, threshold displacement energies, point-defect formation and migration energies, and 1015 displacement cascades from 5 to 40 keV at 300 and 823 K. The stacking fault energy follows the Ni content: 19-44 mJ/m^2 in the alloys and 113 mJ/m^2 in Ni. Compared with the Mn-free alloys, the HEAs have lower threshold displacement energies (48-56 against 64-74 eV) and lower dumbbell formation energies, and Mn is the element most transported by interstitials. All the concentrated alloys leave about the same number of Frenkel pairs, 56-72 at 40 keV, half the number in Ni. At 40 keV, 54-58% of the interstitials are in clusters in the HEAs, against 67-71% in Fe60Ni40, Fe70Ni10Cr20 and Fe50Ni34Cr16 and 82% in Ni. At the same cluster size, clusters of 4-12 interstitials are faulted about half as often in the HEAs, and this does not follow the stacking fault energy. The surviving interstitials are enriched in Mn in the HEAs and in Ni in the Mn-free alloys, and depleted in Cr. The results support direct loop formation in cascades in Fe60Ni40 and Fe70Ni10Cr20 and less of it in ES1.

papers.title: Chiral Superconductivity Indifferent to Parent Topology in the Square-Lattice Hofstadter-Hubbard Model
papers.abstract: We study a $\pi$-flux square-lattice $t$-$t'$ Hofstadter-Hubbard model proposed to be realizable in twisted moir\'e bilayers. By tuning $U$ and $t'$ at half filling, ground-state density-matrix renormalization group simulations (DMRG) and a parton analysis identify an integer quantum Hall (IQH) phase, a chiral spin liquid (CSL), and an antiferromagnet (AFM) in the phase diagram, while charge and spin fluctuations from finite-temperature determinant quantum Monte Carlo (DQMC) suggest a closing charge gap but an open spin gap at the IQH-CSL boundary, consistent with the topological criticality expected there. This model therefore produces a phase diagram hosting weakly correlated band topology (IQH), intrinsic topological order (CSL), and conventional symmetry breaking (AFM) side by side. Upon doping any of these three parent phases, a single chiral topological superconductor with spin Chern number $C_s=-2$ occupies nearly the entire phase diagram. DMRG, DQMC, and weak-coupling perturbation theory agree on its pairing symmetry. This shows that doping the topological band of our model robustly induces the same paired state throughout the phase diagram regardless of the character of the underlying correlated half-filled state and its magnetic fluctuations, whether an IQH, a spin liquid or a weakly fluctuating AFM.

authors.name: Leon Balents
authors.institution: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique

papers.title: Accretion variability as a probe of black holes and their environments: Light curve signatures of a single hot spot
papers.abstract:
The compact radio source at the centre of the Milky Way, Sagittarius A*, exhibits temporal broadband brightness variability. The observed timescales of such fluctuations, ranging from minutes to hours on horizon scales, arise from the complex interplay of gravitation, plasma, and light propagation processes in the immediate vicinity of the supermassive black hole. Kinetic and fluid simulations associate this variability with turbulence and the formation of magnetised, localised plasma structures.
  Focusing on a single fluctuating compact emission region, a 'hot spot', we study how intrinsic source fluctuations map onto different regions of the observer's screen. Our aim is to identify distinct imprints of light propagation effects, which encode information both about the source and the underlying space-time geometry.
  We simulate image time series by propagating the emitted light to a distant observer's sky plane in Minkowski, Schwarzschild, and Kerr space-times. We then compute the corresponding observed light curves and power spectra, both for the full observed images and for selected angular sectors of the observer's sky plane.
  We derive a semi-analytical model for the power spectrum of a fluctuating hot spot in flat space-time, reproducing all qualitative features of curved-space-time spectra at moderate inclinations. Moreover, we describe how such power spectra are affected by space-time geometry, inclination, and source velocity, and show that orthogonal two-sector angular decompositions of the sky plane provide information on system orientation and lensing effects.
  The physical effects highlighted in this paper are expected to be present in the timing signature of accretion-flow variability, as observed by current instruments and future photometric and interferometric facilities. Further work is needed to investigate if our conclusions hold for realistic disc configurations.

authors.name: C. Deffayet
authors.institution: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique

papers.title: N -phase flow simulations using X-Mesh and an explicit marker interface representation
papers.abstract: We present a marker-based X-Mesh framework for incompressible N-phase flow simulations with sharp, explicitly tracked interfaces. The interface is represented by Lagrangian marker chains, while the computational mesh is deformed so that selected mesh edges conform to the tracked geometry without changing mesh connectivity. This combination preserves the advantages of body-fitted finite element discretizations while allowing highly distorted and nearly degenerated elements to capture fine interfacial features on relatively coarse meshes without requiring mesh refinement. The arbitrary Lagrangian-Eulerian (ALE) finite element solver uses a pressure field that is continuous within each phase and discontinuous across the fitted interface. Surface tension is introduced through a variational membrane, so the pressure jump is resolved without prescribing a curvature-dependent correction; a Young wall energy provides the corresponding treatment of fluid-fluid-solid triple points. Topological changes are handled geometrically from the marker representation. Numerical experiments illustrate the ability of the approach to transport complex interfaces and to control topology changes through marker-based feature-size criteria.

papers.title: Neuromodulation Through Intrinsic Noise
papers.abstract: Neuromodulation, the modulation of excitability through the regulation of neuronal parameters, is a key tool in neuromorphic control design. This paper investigates how spiking excitability can be modulated by intrinsic noise. Focusing on a simplified memristive neuron model, we show that intrinsic noise plays distinct functional roles depending on the feedback pathways: Intrinsic noise in the fast excitatory feedback shapes the nature of excitability and modulates the sensitivity of the neuron to external/internal stimuli, whereas that in the slow inhibitory feedback provides internal stimuli that can trigger stochastic spiking. We expect these findings to guide the design of neuromorphic systems that harness intrinsic noise to exploit beneficial stochastic phenomena, such as stochastic resonance.

papers.title: Dual-Space Preconditioning for Variational Inequalities and Root-Finding Problems
papers.abstract: This paper develops a dual-space preconditioning framework for variational inequalities and root-finding problems beyond classical cocoercivity and Lipschitz continuity assumptions. To this end, we introduce both a novel cocoercivity-type condition and a relaxed Lipschitz continuity condition, and derive convergence of deterministic and stochastic methods under these generalized conditions. For isotropic preconditioners, the resulting algorithms can be interpreted as variable-stepsize variants of classical methods, extending recent analyses based on $(L_0, L_1)$-type growth conditions while allowing simpler proofs and larger stepsize ranges. We also show that the framework naturally handles variational inequalities through weak Minty-type arguments. Finally, we study the associated continuous-time dynamics and derive a variational and optimal control interpretation of the preconditioned flow. Overall, the results show that dual-space preconditioning provides a flexible mechanism for designing and analyzing operator methods beyond the standard Euclidean Lipschitz setting.

papers.title: Loops and mirrors
papers.abstract: For a smooth affine complex variety X we construct a Q-algebra LH(X), loop cohomology, in terms of the formal-loop space of X. We conjecture that it is isomorphic to the symplectic cohomology of X. The degree-zero loop cohomology subalgebra is finitely generated for polarized log Calabi-Yau X, constructing an intrinsic mirror affine coordinate ring. Its polyvector algebra is identified with the full loop cohomology algebra for a positive log Calabi-Yau pair with maximal boundary and smooth loop mirror, proving a form of mirror symmetry. In this case we further identify the degree-zero loop cohomology algebra with the Gross-Siebert intrinsic mirror algebra. Assuming in addition that X is a surface, we prove that the full loop and symplectic cohomology algebras agree.

papers.title: Smoothed Least-Absolute Conditional Multidimensional Scaling via Iteratively Reweighted Majorization
papers.abstract: Conditional multidimensional scaling combines latent coordinates with observed covariates to fit pairwise dissimilarities. We develop a smoothed l1 formulation using the shifted Charbonnier loss. We prove residualwise sharpness of the quadratic loss majorizer, monotonicity, compact containment, and stationarity of noncollapsed accumulation points. A uniform additive bound quantifies approximation to exact least-absolute conditional stress. The experiments use paired contamination, separately calibrated loss parameters, combined-configuration recovery, and direct checks of the theorem's inequalities.

papers.title: What to Predict for Efficient Scheduling on Parallel Machines
papers.abstract: We study learning-augmented algorithms for scheduling on multiple parallel machines under the objectives of minimizing the makespan or the total weighted completion time. We assume that the algorithm has access to noisy information (the prediction) about an optimal solution, expressed through a solution encoding that implicitly quantifies both the amount of information provided and the nature of noise (errors in the prediction). Our central question is to determine the maximum level of noise that still allows for efficiently recovering this optimal solution. We observe that information guiding greedy scheduling to optimality or revealing the optimal assignment of tasks to machines is very sensitive to noise, and prove that recovering an optimal solution from solution encodings capturing either is computationally hard, even for a small (non-constant) number of errors. On the positive side, we show that an order-based encoding, which leads to errors that are dispersed locally, is robust to noise. We present a dynamic programming framework that utilizes this encoding and solves optimally several classical scheduling problems, including makespan and total weighted completion time minimization on identical or unrelated machines.

papers.title: Decisions by Discrimination: Differential Evidence for Medical Reasoning
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly studied for clinical decision support, and medical question answering provides a testbed for evaluating this capability. In particular, medical multiple-choice questions (MCQs) reflect a core challenge in clinical decision-making: plausible options often share overlapping evidence, while only a few decisive factors distinguish the correct option from incorrect ones. However, existing retrieval-based and reasoning-oriented methods mainly focus on supplying broadly relevant knowledge or eliciting reasoning paths, rather than identifying the compact differential evidence that separates confusing alternatives. In this work, we present a retrieval-grounded differential evidence framework for medical MCQs. Our method extracts option-specific pieces of differential evidence and organizes them into concise evidence prompts for answer selection. This design better aligns external knowledge with differential reasoning while reducing irrelevant context. Experiments show consistent accuracy gains across multiple datasets and target LLMs. Ablation studies further show that our framework outperforms both directly using retrieved evidence chunks and closed-source LLM-generated general hints, and that its improvements are not solely explained by answer-proximal guidance, but are consistent with differential evidence serving as a compact aid for reasoning over competing alternatives. Our findings also offer insights for medical reasoning and other decision-making settings with multiple possible choices.

papers.title: Robust State-Parameter Estimation in Second-Order Th\'evenin Batteries
papers.abstract: We propose a scheme for estimating the full states and parameters of a second-order Th\'evenin battery model, using distinct features of the measured current. An identification step, run during suitable rest intervals, identifies the resistances and capacitances of the two RC branches from the voltage relaxation by linear least squares, without knowledge of the open-circuit voltage (OCV) map. An online estimator then runs continuously: the polarization voltages are estimated by open-loop observers; the series resistance is updated at current jumps using least squares; the state of charge (SOC) is propagated by Coulomb counting using the current capacity estimate, and both estimates are updated periodically by a sliding-window regression. We show that the identification is exact under a mild rank condition, that the series resistance is recovered at the first current jump, and that the online state and capacity estimates converge exponentially under verifiable excitation conditions. We also establish robustness of the online estimator under bounded process disturbances and measurement noise.

papers.title: On Algebraic LNE models of complex affine algebraic curves
papers.abstract: We give a sufficient condition for an affine complex curve to have an algebraic complex LNE model.

authors.name: Karolina Zajac
authors.institution: Pontifical University of John Paul II in Kraków

papers.title: The Monophonic Directed Convexities
papers.abstract: Graph Convexity is a topic with many papers in the literature, especially on the $P_3$, geodesic, and monophonic convexities in undirected graphs. Regarding directed graphs, Erd{\H o}s et al. in 1972 and Chartrand and Zhang in 2000 obtained the first results on the $P_3$ and geodesic convexities for directed graphs, respectively. In this paper, we start the investigation of monophonic convexity on directed graphs. We define two convexities, the monophonic and the strong monophonic directed convexities, related to the minimal and the induced directed paths, respectively. We show that deciding whether a set is convex is polynomial-time solvable in the monophonic convexity, but coNP-complete in the strong monophonic convexity. For both convexities, we prove that the hull number is NP-complete even in DAGs. Regarding the monophonic convexity, we prove that the hull number is polynomial time solvable in tournaments, but the interval number is NP-complete in tournaments and also in bipartite oriented graphs.

papers.title: Do They Do as They Are Told? Investigating Coding Agents' Adherence to Explicit Instructions in Context Files
papers.abstract: Developers increasingly rely on agent context files (ACFs), persistent, project-scoped artifacts such as AGENTS.md, to steer the behavior of autonomous coding agents without renegotiating expectations at every interaction. Yet this governance mechanism rests on an untested assumption: that instructions written into an ACF are actually carried out, rather than ignored or loosely followed. Existing studies describe what ACFs contain, but not whether individual instructions are followed, leaving open which guidance can be trusted. We address this gap through an empirical study of real-world ACF snapshots and their linked agent-generated commits: characterizing the explicit, actionable instructions ACFs encode, operationalizing them into executable measurement scripts, and using these scripts to assess instruction-level compliance. We find that most observable instructions can be operationalized and that agents follow ACF guidance more often than not, but adherence splits sharply between instructions followed consistently and those never respected, with differences across instruction categories and coding agents. This split shows where ACF guidance works and where it does not, pointing to instruction types that may need rewriting and to agents that may need enforcement beyond the ACF. These findings lay the groundwork for systematic approaches to specifying, verifying, and enforcing project-specific instructions in autonomous software development.

authors.name: Yutaro Kashiwa
authors.institution: Nara Institute of Science and Technology

papers.title: Prior Probabilities for Constrained Hypotheses: Invariance, Neutrality, and Model Search
papers.abstract: When testing hypotheses with equality and inequality constraints using Bayes factors, the hypotheses are commonly assigned equal prior probabilities. The resulting posterior probabilities depend on how the analyst divides the parameter space into hypotheses: splitting one hypothesis into two changes the posterior probabilities of the other hypotheses, and a hypothesis can receive more posterior probability than a hypothesis that contains it. An alternative is considered where the prior probabilities of the hypotheses follow from a single prior distribution on the parameters. Prior probabilities of the equality constrained subspaces are taken from the Bayesian variable selection literature, and prior probabilities of the inequality constrained regions within these subspaces are given by their relative complexities under the encompassing prior. Under this complexity-induced prior, posterior probabilities do not depend on how the hypotheses are divided, are coherent across nested hypotheses, and agree with those from an exploratory model search over the same subspaces. In return, inequality constraints do not increase the posterior probability of a hypothesis relative to the null hypothesis. The prior is therefore suited for analysts who want to test constrained hypotheses without favoring specific constraints a priori, while the potential gain in evidence for the constraints remains quantified by the Bayes factor.

papers.title: You Can Have It All: Small sparse induced-universal graphs for minor-closed classes
papers.abstract:
We show that, for every fixed proper minor-closed graph class $\mathcal{G}$ and every positive integer $n$, there exists a graph $U_n$ with $n^{1+o(1)}$ vertices and edges such that every $n$-vertex graph in $\mathcal{G}$ is isomorphic to an induced subgraph of $U_n$.
  This result generalizes and unifies the results of Dujmovi\'c et al. (J. ACM 2021) on induced-universal graphs and the results of Esperet, Joret, and Morin (J. London Math. Soc. 2023) on sparse induced-universal graphs from planar graphs to all proper minor-closed graph classes. It simultaneously improves the previous bounds for the number of vertices in induced-universal graphs (previously $O(n^2)$ obtained as a corollary of a result of DeVos et al. (J. Comb. Theory, Ser. {B} 2004) and a result of Gavoille and Labourel (ESA 2007)) and the number of edges in subgraph-universal graphs (previously $O(n^{3/2})$ by Babai et al. (Theory and Practice of Combinatorics 1982)).

authors.name: Cyril Gavoille
authors.institution: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique

papers.title: Compositional random forest
papers.abstract: Compositional data have been analysed in the literature from three main points of view: directly on the simplex, in log-ratio coordinates, and as directional data on the unit sphere. In this paper, we construct a random forest framework for compositional responses that accommodates all three. Random forests are ensembles of decision trees, and the split criterion determines how each tree grows. We use the log-likelihood gain as the split criterion and consider distributions defined on the different spaces in which compositions can be represented. The Dirichlet likelihood has been studied in the literature, but its covariance is fixed by its mean up to a single scalar, and its maximum likelihood estimator has no closed form. To obtain more flexible criteria, we use two well-known transformations. First, the square-root transformation maps compositions onto the unit sphere, where existing directional distributions require numerical estimation. We introduce a tangent-normal (TN) distribution, which shares its parameters with the Kent distribution, and construct a split criterion whose gain is computed from additive sufficient statistics: the shape parameters are maximised out in closed form, up to an exponentially small truncation constant, so that no parameter is estimated iteratively. Second, the log-ratio transformation maps compositions to Euclidean space, where the multivariate logistic-normal distribution has a flexible covariance and a closed-form maximum log-likelihood, also based on additive sufficient statistics. Both criteria respond to a shift of the mean, measured relative to the covariance, and to a change in the covariance itself. In simulations, the most accurate forest depended on the covariance structure of the composition. The TN forest was the most accurate in two of the three designs.

papers.title: FP64 Performance and the Limits of Ozaki Emulation on HPC Systems
papers.abstract:
A growing industry narrative holds that native double precision can be deprioritized in HPC accelerators, on the hypothesis that low-precision tensor cores can emulate FP64 on demand, and that most HPC workloads are bandwidth-bound. This paper evaluates some of those claims and explores the importance of FP64 in scientific computing. We show roofline profiling data of representative HPC workloads, across a variety of common computational motifs, to evaluate the arithmetic-intensity and accuracy requirements of these workloads. We also consider FP64 emulation via the Ozaki method to ascertain some of the possibilities and limitations of these approaches.
  These results indicate that Ozaki emulation should not be evaluated as a general replacement for FP64, but as an optimization for the subset of workloads whose dominant computation is sufficiently large, dense, and GEMM-shaped. Our analysis indicates this is less than 10\% of the HPC ecosystem. Furthermore, even in this favorable regime, standalone GEMM speedup is not enough to accelerate (or avoid performance regression) for the application: numerical behavior, workspace requirements, matrix shape, and integration overhead determine whether the benefit survives at application scale. This paper characterizes those boundaries empirically. Furthermore, we show that dense GEMM accounts for only a small fraction of FP64 computation across HPC workloads, leaving most application-level FP64 work beyond the reach of GEMM-based emulation.

papers.title: Continuous Horizon Forecasting
papers.abstract: Multi-horizon forecasting has been dominated by discrete forecast strategies that treat model outputs as fixed-vectors or recurrently create them. In this paper, we introduce the Continuous Horizon (CH) strategy that generalizes upon recursive, direct, and multi-step strategies by redefining forecasts as a continuous operator and the forecast horizon as a query variable rather than an index. We present the theoretical foundations for the CH strategy, a Universal Operator Approximation Theorem, and a continuous-horizon bias-variance decomposition that formally proves the estimation variance improvements of CH over the discrete strategies. We validate the CH strategy empirically through a simulation study, and on 16 large-scale datasets from the M-series benchmark, showing how CH achieves competitive RMSE accuracy, while uniquely enabling parallel inference, targeted horizon querying, and interpolation and extrapolation across unseen horizons.

papers.title: The Ordinary Days of Extraordinary Blazar 3C 454.3
papers.abstract: The blazar 3C 454.3 (z = 0.859) is one of the brightest and most variable flat-spectrum radio quasars in the sky. Here, we present a multi-wavelength analysis of this enigmatic object in its quiescent states during June 2022 and May 2023 coincident with its first X-ray polarimetric and hard X-ray observations with International X-ray Polarimetric Explorer (IXPE) and Nuclear Spectroscopic Telescope Array (NuSTAR). Though no X-ray polarization was detected, NuSTAR detected the source on all occasions during this period. We generated five broadband spectral energy distributions (SEDs)of the blazar using quasi-simultaneous observations taken with the Fermi-Large Area Telescope, NuSTAR, and Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory. The hard X-ray flux measured by NuSTAR exhibited mild flux variations. The SEDs were modeled with a one-zone leptonic emission framework using the JetSet package. The optical-ultraviolet spectrum of 3C 454.3 revealed an upturn which we reproduced with the standard accretion disk model. The X-ray to gamma-ray spectrum of 3C 454 was found to be well explained by the external Compton (EC) process with the seed photons provided by the BLR and accretion disk. These results provide intriguing clues about the multi-wavelength behavior of 3C 454.3 during its quiescent activity state.

papers.title: The unavoidable minor in graphs of uncountable edge-connectivity
papers.abstract: For any given uncountable cardinal $\kappa$, we show that every $\kappa$-edge-connected graph admits a minor embedding of the graph $T_{\kappa}\star1$ (the $\kappa$-regular tree with a new apex vertex adjacent to all its nodes), which is itself $\kappa$-edge-connected. This extends a previous result of Kurkofka regarding unavoidable minors of $\aleph_0$-edge-connected graphs to all uncountable cardinalities $\kappa$.

papers.title: Unified Ott--Antonsen Framework for Stability and Bifurcations in Ring Swarmalators
papers.abstract: Swarmalators, a prototypical model that integrates temporal rhythms with spatial swarming, have been widely used to explore the collective dynamics observed in active-matter systems. Although numerical simulations have revealed a variety of collective states, a general theoretical framework for the stability and bifurcations of the states remains unavailable. Here, by the model of one-dimensional ring-structured swarmalators with general distributions of natural frequencies and velocities, we conduct a systematic theoretical analysis of the stability and bifurcations of four representative collective states observed in simulations: the desynchronization state, the phase-wave state, the synchronization state, and the mixed state. We show that the macroscopic dynamics are governed by a low-dimensional invariant manifold, namely the generalized Ott--Antonsen manifold, and further establish that the same manifold underlies the collective dynamics of high-dimensional agent models, thereby unifying these seemingly different descriptions within a common reduction framework. Building on this connection, we derive stability conditions and bifurcation boundaries for the collective states and construct a bifurcation diagram in the two-parameter coupling plane, with theoretical predictions validated by large-scale numerical simulations. Our results clarify the dynamical origins of state selection in swarmalator systems and provide a theoretical foundation for analyzing nonequilibrium phase transitions in active-matter systems with coupled internal rhythms and spatial motions.

papers.title: Uncertainty-Aware Hybrid Offline Reinforcement Learning with Online Action Selection Enabled by Sparse Gaussian-Process Critics
papers.abstract: Start-ups and grade changes remain largely operator-driven, while developing and maintaining dynamic models for model-based control requires substantial engineering effort. Hybrid Offline Learning and Online Optimisation (HOFLON) uses one-step offline reinforcement learning to select actions from historical transition data. In its original implementation, the online objective combines the predicted return from a tree-ensemble critic with an adversarial-autoencoder (AAE) penalty for unfamiliar state-action pairs. We examine the effect of this penalty and replace the critic and AAE with a sparse variational Gaussian-process (sGP) critic. Actions maximise $\mu - \kappa\sigma$, an uncertainty-adjusted estimate of the return from one action followed by the historical operating practice. On the HOFLON polymerisation-reactor benchmark, removing the AAE from HOFLON led to 4 failed start-ups in 15 runs over five critics. At its published weight, the variation in the AAE penalty is four orders of magnitude smaller than the variation in the tree-ensemble critic. Nevertheless, it changes actions when the predicted returns of competing candidates are nearly equal, and paired runs with and without the penalty diverged from the first move. With a Mat\'ern-5/2 sGP critic, $\kappa = 0$ led to failure in 13 of 15 runs, whereas with $\kappa = 3$ none of 15 runs (five critics, three noise realisations) failed. The median and lowest returns were 13,464 and 13,398 (HOFLON: 13,393 and 12,411). A squared-exponential sGP critic with learned inducing inputs needed $\kappa \geq 3$ to remain within the empirical data support in steady state, and then settled with a temperature offset of 2.0 K.

papers.title: Isolation Is Not Confidentiality: Security Boundaries of Geometric Access Control in RAG
papers.abstract:
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems increasingly rely on vector databases containing documents governed by different access-control policies. Recent search-preserving geometric approaches enforce such access control by structuring the embedding space so that transformed embeddings, which we call protected representations, remain retrievable without exposing information across policy boundaries.
  We provide a unified security analysis of this paradigm, covering policy isolation, representation confidentiality, query forgery resistance, and policy-membership hiding. We consider both a curious cloud service provider observing the protected representations stored in the vector database and a curious user holding aligned pairs of original embeddings and protected representations. Evaluating the available implementations of the works proposing these geometric transformation mechanisms across three encoders, we find that geometric transformations preserve retrieval utility and provide strong policy isolation, but do not provide the other security properties. A curious user can recover the original embeddings from a few hundred pairs and forge policy-compatible queries at a higher cost that grows with encoder dimension for secret per-policy transformations. Moreover, policy-dependent geometry can leak policy membership even when unauthorized retrieval is prevented. These results show that policy isolation, confidentiality, forgery resistance, and membership hiding are distinct security objectives.

authors.name: Steve Nouyep
authors.institution: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique

authors.name: Sebastien Salva
authors.institution: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique

papers.title: Obvious Group Manipulations and Top Trading Cycles
papers.abstract: We introduce a group version of non-obvious manipulability, which is stronger than the original definition by Troyan and Morrill (2020) and weaker than group strategy-proofness, and study its implications in Shapley-Scarf housing markets. We provide several characterizations of the Top Trading Cycles mechanism using the new condition.

papers.title: Uneven Self-Reported AI Use: An Embedded Case Study Across Eleven Teams in a Software Organization
papers.abstract: This paper presents a descriptive, embedded single-case study examining self-reported AI use within a software organization. The study draws on 98 structured interview records collected across 11 teams, using ten standardized team-level instruments (n = 65) and one instrument with distinct response anchors (n = 33). Among respondents assessed using standardized instruments, 36 of 65 (55.4%) reported AI-use frequency scores of 4 or 5 on a five-point scale. Team-level proportions varied from 20.0% (1/5) to 71.4% (5/7). A record-level cross-tabulation revealed limited awareness or understanding of organizational AI policies across both frequency groups: 86.1% (31/36) of respondents scoring 4-5 and 96.6% (28/29) of those scoring 0-3 reported either no policy awareness or uncertainty about policy details. In the group assessed using the distinct instrument, 31 of 33 respondents (93.9%) scored 4 or 5. Although the pooled proportion reached 68.4% (67/98), differences in response anchors limit direct comparability, making the standardized-instrument results the primary analytical reference.
