papers.title: SAIL: Self-Adaptive Index Learning with Hybrid Models (Extended Version)
papers.abstract: Learned index structures have demonstrated a significant improvement in query performance over traditional index structures. The majority of learned indexes use a uniform node structure throughout their index structures. A few studies show that combining multiple types of node structures can lead to indexes that better adapt to local key-set distributions, hence yielding query efficiency gains. Following this line of work, we propose a learned index structure named SAIL that supports a wide range of different candidate node structures for both leaf and inner nodes, selected via cost models based on data driven approximations. We design an efficient construction algorithm that recursively partitions the key-set to be fitted by the candidate node types. Experiments demonstrate that SAIL achieves 2x improvement over existing learned indexes in query time, with similar memory consumption and index build times.

papers.title: Sharp asymptotic stability of the incompressible porous medium equation on the whole plane
papers.abstract: We study the asymptotic stability of the steady state $e_s(x)=-x_2$ of the incompressible porous media equation in $\mathbb R^2$. For every $s>2$, we prove that sufficiently small initial perturbations $\theta_0\in H^s(\mathbb R^2)$ of $e_s$ generate unique global solutions $\rho=e_s+\theta$, where $\theta$ remains uniformly bounded in $H^s$ and converges strongly to zero in $H^s$ as $t\to\infty$. The main innovations of this work are threefold. First, exploiting the structure of the equation, we construct a weighted energy that eliminates the need to control $\|\nabla u^2\|_{L^1_tL^\infty_x}$. Second, rather than estimating the anisotropic commutators directly, we study the integral terms containing these commutators and establish suitable bounds through refined computations in frequency space. Third, we establish convergence in the highest-order $H^s$ norm under uniform energy bounds involving only an $L^\infty_tH^s_x$ bound on $\theta$ and an $L^2_tH^s_x$ bound on $\mathcal R_1\theta$.

papers.title: Solomonoff Induction with Reflective Oracles
papers.abstract: We study predictive properties of a reflective variant of Solomonoff induction formulated using reflective oracles (Fallenstein et al. 2015, Wyeth et al. 2025). We show that the resulting optimal predictor succeeds against computable predictive strategies that specify only part of the data-generating process. The argument relies on the fact that hypotheses computable from the predictor's own conditional probabilities remain within the reflective hypothesis class. In particular, the predictor learns incomplete models specified by computable interval restrictions on next-bit probabilities. We also establish weighted forms of unbiasedness and calibration. Finally, we discuss whether an optimal predictor's conditional probabilities suffice to compute every hypothesis in the reflective class.

papers.title: AgentScript-Eval: Benchmarking LLMs and Agents for Code Generation in an Enterprise DSL
papers.abstract: Domain-specific languages (DSLs) are widely used in enterprise software, giving a compact interface to complex tasks, from data access to infrastructure automation. Platforms increasingly extend them to agents, where a developer declares the topics, permitted actions, and guardrails of an agent rather than writing general-purpose code. Large language models (LLMs) write general-purpose code well, but that ability has been measured almost entirely on languages abundant in public pretraining data, and enterprise DSLs are neither abundant nor public. We introduce AgentScript-Eval, an execution-graded benchmark of 100 real tasks for AgentScript, the declarative DSL that Salesforce uses in Agentforce to build conversational agents. Tasks span authoring an agent from a specification, debugging a broken definition, and optimizing a working one. Evaluating five models zero-shot, we find that the regime is hard: the best model reaches only 25.0% pass@3, and every model scores 0% on authoring from scratch. We further find that model scale and price are weak predictors of success -- a 31B open-weight model attains the highest compilation rate of any model tested (48.0%) and matches the strongest frontier model on partial-credit accuracy at the lowest token cost. Adding an agentic compile-and-edit loop is the single largest lever, roughly doubling partial-credit accuracy. Beyond that gain, the wording of domain guidance matters more than its packaging. The same skill pack scores 28% as plain documentation but only 14% as a live plugin. Rewriting one skill inside that plugin then raises it to 37%, our best result, with catalog and tooling untouched. Larger models did not reliably outperform smaller ones; what mattered was the harness surrounding the model and the guidance supplied to it.

papers.title: Scattering Resonances of Plane-Embedded Cavities: A Finite Element DtN Approach
papers.abstract: While scattering resonances of plane-embedded cavities have wide-ranging engineering applications, numerical results for such configurations remain virtually unexplored. We present an effective finite element approach for computing these resonances. The unbounded domain is truncated using a Dirichlet-to-Neumann(DtN) boundary operator, recasting the problem as the eigenvalue problem of a holomorphic Fredholm operator function. Discretization is carried out using Lagrange finite elements with a truncated DtN expansion, and convergence is rigorously proven using Karma's approximation theory. The resulting non-linear matrix eigenvalue system is computed using a multi-step parallel spectral indicator method. Numerical experiments confirm the theoretical predictions and provide benchmark solutions for future investigations.

authors.name: Bo Gong
authors.institution: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China

authors.name: Takumi Sato
authors.institution: Tohoku Medical and Pharmaceutical University Hospital

papers.title: Sufficient Dimension Reduction with Multimodal Predictor Objects
papers.abstract: We study the regression of a scalar response $Y$ on a Euclidean predictor $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^p$ and a random predictor object $\mathcal{Z}$ in a general metric space under arbitrary structural dependence. We introduce a joint sufficient dimension reduction $(\mathbf{B}^\top\mathbf{X}, \mathcal{G}_Z)$ constructed via a sequential conditional independence framework, which differs fundamentally from the ordinary central subspace of $Y \mid \mathbf{X}$. Methodologically, $\mathcal{Z}$ is embedded into a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, and a regularized kernel-response envelope model extracts a finite-dimensional reduction of the feature map. Partial adaptive estimation then recovers the Euclidean reduction conditional on the first-stage coordinates. We establish root-$n$ consistency rates for the first-stage envelope subspace under a shrinking regularizer, alongside large-sample consistency for the second-stage Euclidean subspace estimator. Simulations and two real-data applications illustrate the utility and flexibility of the proposed method.

papers.title: End-state-assisted tunneling at a topological insulator STM tip
papers.abstract: Recent spin-sensitive scanning tunneling experiments with topological-insulator tips motivate a microscopic understanding of how tip geometry controls current delivery. We show that topological end states mediate resonant tunneling through the gap opened by interedge hybridization in a quantum spin Hall tip. An asymmetric termination gives oppositely spin-polarized helical paths unequal effective lengths and resonance widths. Within an independent-path description, their transmitted-current imbalance vanishes at a matched resonance and becomes finite away from it. Coupling these directional channels to a $d$-wave altermagnet yields a spin-dependent interference contrast. Hybridized end states along a stepped termination provide multiple tunneling resonances. Our results establish end-state-mediated tunneling as a transport mechanism for STM with strongly confined topological tips.

authors.name: Bin Zhou
authors.institution: University of Tennessee Health Science Center

papers.title: Opacity of Discrete Event Systems under Sensor Attacks
papers.abstract: Many information control problems in discrete event systems can be addressed using strong opacity, weak opacity, and non-opacity. These opacities depend on observations. If cyber attackers can attack sensors (or observation channels), then opacities will change. An opaque system may become not opaque, or a not opaque system may become opaque. Therefore, it is important to investigate opacities under sensor attacks. In this paper, we consider opacities under sensor attacks for two settings. The first one is the user has prior knowledge of sensor attacks in which the opacities are called as W-CA-opacities. The second one is the user has no prior knowledge of sensor attacks, and opacities are called as N-CA-opacities. For the former, we construct an augmented automaton that integrates the information of sensor attacks and then converts W-CA-opacities into classical opacities to solve the verification problem. For the latter, we construct the observers for the given system without sensor attacks and with sensor attacks, respectively. We then do the parallel operation on these two observers to obtain a method of verifying N-CA opacities. Furthermore, by adopting the detector technique, we find polynomial algorithms for verifying weak opacity and non opacity for both settings.

papers.title: AURA: Auditory Spatial Intelligence via a Unified Representation from a General-Audio Encoder through Complete Alignment
papers.abstract: Answering spatial questions about multi-source scenes requires a model both to identify each sound and to locate it. Existing spatial audio-language models obtain spatial information from a dedicated encoder, which separates spatial and semantic processing into distinct feature spaces. We study whether a general-audio codec trained without spatial supervision can serve both purposes. A controlled layer-wise analysis shows that the frozen codec retains spatial information, with lateral cues carried by the difference between the two ear channels. This information, however, is not readily accessible: in dual-source scenes, a model trained on these features predicts left/right at chance and, on the remaining axes, assigns the detected direction to the queried and the non-queried source equally often. We attribute this failure to an audio--text information asymmetry, in which the audio contains both sources while the answer describes only the queried one. A controlled $2\times2$ experiment shows that either completing the scene description or exposing the inter-channel difference lifts left/right accuracy above chance, whereas binding directions to the queried source requires both. Building on these findings, AURA keeps the codec and the language model frozen and exceeds the strongest dedicated system on SpatialSoundQA by 10.31 points in dual-source direction accuracy, with about 40\% of its trainable parameters.

authors.name: Hongli Cao
authors.institution: Affiliated Hospital of Southwest Medical University

authors.name: Liang An
authors.institution: State Key Laboratory Fluid Power and Mechatronic Systems

papers.title: Cascading Contingency Analysis of Modern Power Systems Using a Stochastic Hybrid Systems Framework
papers.abstract: This paper presents a cascading contingency analysis and risk assessment framework that incorporates probabilistic mode transitions motivated by stochastic hybrid system (SHS) concepts together with power-flow-based stress evaluation. A two-stage modeling approach is adopted in which sensitivity-based analysis is first used to identify candidate cascading transitions, followed by DC power flow re-evaluation to accurately capture post-contingency stress redistribution, islanding behavior, and load shedding. A probabilistic propagation model is constructed using mode-dependent transition probabilities derived from line loading conditions. A Cascading Risk Index (CRI) is introduced to quantify the expected load shedding accumulated over cascade progression. Case studies on the IEEE 39-bus system demonstrate that the proposed framework captures diverse cascading routes under multiple initiating outages and identifies critical propagation patterns that are not revealed by N-1/N-2 screening. The results highlight the importance of SHS modeling in assessing cascading risk and providing a scalable framework for resilience evaluation in modern power systems.

papers.title: FaST: Factored Synthesis of Transitions for Offline Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Synthetic data augmentation promises to scale offline reinforcement learning beyond fixed logged datasets, but leading diffusion-based generators model the transition tuple (state, action, next state, reward, terminal) as a monolith: no single factor can be natively redrawn in isolation. We present FaST (Factored Synthesis of Transitions), which factors transitions via the chain rule into state, action, dynamics, reward, and terminal stages, fitting each with an estimator matched to its statistical properties. Across twelve D4RL locomotion and maze benchmarks, TD3+BC and IQL agents trained on FaST transitions match the SynthER diffusion baseline while generating transitions over 90x faster. The explicit action-given-state conditional can also be re-queried for a fixed state, enabling targeted action synthesis: drawing N candidate actions per generated state and keeping the highest-advantage one under a value function fit to the same data, thereby synthesizing improved behavior during generation rather than filtering for it post-hoc. Best-of-10 synthesis beats training on real data on 11 of 12 medium and medium-replay settings (+8.9 D4RL points on average, up to +28.4), and is competitive with advantage-filtered SynthER at a fraction of its generation cost. On expert mixtures both mechanisms degrade identically, tracing the failure to the advantage estimate itself rather than to either targeting mechanism.

papers.title: An Accurate Modulation-Assisted Method for Phasor Estimation Under Decaying DC Offsets
papers.abstract: Decaying DC (DDC) offsets severely compromise the accurate estimation of current phasors immediately following power grid fault occurrence. Consequently, conventional full-cycle discrete Fourier transform (FCDFT) algorithms experience decaying oscillatory magnitude errors, potentially causing distance relays to malfunction. This paper introduces a modulation-assisted technique designed to precisely eliminate the DDC components from fault current signals. By multiplying the fault signal with a high-frequency carrier and applying consecutive sliding Fourier projections, the proposed method effectively isolates the DDC signal while entirely rejecting higher-order harmonic interference. It utilizes a direct algebraic solution derived from a robust forward-difference operation across just three sequential projections to estimate and extract the DDC parameters. Furthermore, the algorithm seamlessly processes both single and multiple DDC components by dynamically tracking them as one equivalent first-order mode. Extensive evaluations are conducted to validate the proposed method accuracy. The proposed algorithm limits the maximum overshoot (MO) to 0.62% (0.59% for $k \geq 8$) for the evaluated DDC cases, and to 2.47% (0.95% at 20 dB for $k = 8$) under noisy conditions.

papers.title: Discrete Model-Based Diffusion for Combinatorial Optimization in Multi-Robot Task Allocation
papers.abstract: Decision making in multi-agent and multi-robot systems often involves discrete decision variables, leading to NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems that must be solved within seconds for near real-time implementation. Denoising diffusion has emerged as a powerful tool for such problems, but existing approaches face a trade-off: Model-Based Diffusion (MBD) incorporates diffusion in sampling-based optimization (SBO) without training but only over continuous spaces, while existing diffusion-based combinatorial solvers operate over discrete spaces but require offline training. To this end, we propose Discrete Model-Based Diffusion (Discrete MBD), a training-free SBO method that directly optimizes discrete variables by approximating categorical reverse transition distributions through Monte Carlo sampling. We establish a finite-step lower bound on the probability of finding a global minimizer and show that this bound converges to one as the number of denoising steps increases. Extensive experiments on generic integer programs and heterogeneous multi-robot coalition formation and scheduling demonstrate that Discrete MBD outperforms SBO baselines in nearly all settings while achieving solution quality competitive with that of mixed-integer programming and reinforcement learning methods at a fraction of their computational cost.

papers.title: Giant Radio Galaxies from the Third Data Release of the LOFAR Two-metre Sky Survey (LoTSS-DR3): Physical Characteristics and Environments
papers.abstract: Giant radio galaxies (GRGs) are radio-loud active galactic nuclei (AGN) with projected linear sizes exceeding 0.7 Mpc, offering insights into the evolution of large-scale radio jets and their environments. We present 2333 GRGs from the LOFAR Two-metre Sky Survey Data Release 3 (LoTSS-DR3), with projected sizes of 0.7-2.9 Mpc, redshifts of $0.126 \leq z \leq 3.517$, and 150-MHz radio luminosities of $1.72 \times 10^{24}$-$3.04 \times 10^{28}$ W Hz$^{-1}$. Of these, 726 ($\sim 31\%$) lie at $z \geq 1$. We investigate their radio properties, lobe energetics, equipartition pressures, black hole masses, mid-infrared colours, and environments. Equipartition pressure decreases with increasing projected size, consistent with declining lobe energy density as radio structures expand, while its positive correlation with redshift persists after controlling for radio power and projected size. WISE colours highlight the diversity of the host-galaxy population, with approximately 75% of sources with available photometry falling within the empirical AGN/HERG region. For BCG-hosted GRGs, physical projected size shows no significant dependence on cluster mass. Although the normalized projected half-size, $D/(2r_{500})$, decreases with increasing cluster mass, this trend is consistent with the expected self-similar scaling of cluster radius rather than an independent suppression of radio-source growth in massive clusters. The substantial high-redshift population provides an opportunity to investigate GRGs at early cosmic epochs, although surface-brightness dimming and inverse-Compton losses against the cosmic microwave background can limit their detectability.

papers.title: Min-CSPs on Complete Instances III: Nearly Optimal Characterizations of Approximation for Symmetric CSPs
papers.abstract:
This paper studies complete Min-$k$-CSPs: an instance on $n$ variables has one nontrivial constraint for every $k$-set of variables (so $\binom{n}{k}$ constraints in total), and the goal is to find an assignment that minimizes the number of unsatisfied constraints. They are motivated by the connections to machine learning and data science, as well as the possibility of being testbeds for new algorithmic techniques. Previous recent results presented polynomial-time algorithms for the decision version of every complete Boolean $k$-CSP, which is a necessary condition for any multiplicative approximations for the minimization version, but nontrivial approximation results have been limited to fragile CSPs, 2-SAT, and NAE-3-SAT, leaving the approximability of most complete Boolean Min-CSPs open, including complete Min-$k$-SAT.
  In this paper, we resolve this question, up to nearly matching factors, for the natural class of symmetric Boolean predicates. Given $A \subseteq \{0, \dots, k\}$, Min-CSP($A$) is a Min-$k$-CSP where each constraint is specified by $k$ literals and is satisfied if the number of true literals belongs to $A$. Let $w(A)$ be the maximum number of consecutive integers in $A$. Our main results for complete Min-CSP($A$) are (1) a QPTAS for $w(A) \leq 2$ and (2) an $\widetilde{O}(n^{w(A)-3})$-approximation for $w(A) \geq 3$, as well as almost matching hardness results for the latter. Our QPTAS for $w(A)=2$ significantly improves the previous $O(1)$-approximation for Min-2-SAT and the $\operatorname{polylog}(n)$-approximation for Min-NAE-3-SAT, as well as extends the PTAS for fragile CSPs (i.e., $w(A) = 1$).

papers.title: Discrete-Time Stochastic Control Beyond i.i.d. Noise
papers.abstract: We study discrete-time stochastic control problems where the noise driving the state dynamics is a stationary infinite-order chain rather than an i.i.d. sequence. We formulate the problem as a controlled Markov process by enlarging the state space to include the posterior distribution of the noise given the state-action history. Assuming that the sensitivity of the noise transition kernel to past noise values decays exponentially, we show that the expected total variation distance between the full-history and finite-memory noise filters decays at rate $\sqrt{N}\rho^{\sqrt{N}}$. We use this result to construct finite-memory control models and establish explicit near-optimality bounds for their policies. Finally, under suitable ergodicity conditions, we show that Q-learning converges to the optimal solution of the approximate model, so the same performance bounds apply to the learned policies.

papers.title: Parabolic induction and pullback of perverse sheaves on Vogan varieties
papers.abstract: Let $M$ be a Levi subgroup of a quasisplit connected reductive group $G$ over a $p$-adic field. Vogan's geometric perspective on the local Langlands correspondence fixes a perfect pairing between the Grothendieck group of representations of $G$ and its pure inner forms with a fixed infinitesimal parameter and the Grothendieck group of equivariant perverse sheaves on the associated Vogan variety. Granting a list of desiderata for the enhanced local Langlands correspondence, we show that parabolic induction $\mathrm{Ind}_M^G$ is the transpose of geometric restriction $\xi^*$ with respect to this pairing if and only if the $p$-adic analogue of the Kazhdan--Lusztig hypothesis and the expected multiplicity formula for tempered induction both hold. The identity refines to one for each pure inner form of $G$.

papers.title: Irrationality and Noether--Lefschetz loci in the moduli space of K3 surfaces
papers.abstract: The goal of this paper is twofold. First, we construct examples of families of surfaces where the locus of points in the base with constant degree of irrationality is not constructible. Second, we explore the notion of gonality loci in the moduli space of K3 surfaces, which are characterized by the existence of a smooth curve with fixed gonality. Among various results, we prove that polarized gonality loci are always unions of Noether--Lefschetz divisors.

papers.title: EoSAlign: An Open-Source Software for Calculating, Comparing, and Aligning Pressure Under Extreme Conditions
papers.abstract: Accurate pressure determination is essential in high pressure experiments. Inconsistencies among pressure scales limit direct comparisons and contribute to uncertainty in measured properties, such as, phase boundaries, melting conditions, and thermodynamic models, especially above 100 GPa where existing scales diverge by >10 GPa. EoSAlign, an open-source software, can calculate, compare, and align pressures using a range of published calibrations. EoSAlign calculates pressure from experimental measurements (such as volume (A^3), Raman shift (cm^-1), or luminescence peak position (nm)) and it can be used to compare pressure values from different pressure standards. Using EoSAlign, we fit and align the bridgmanite and post-perovskite equations of state to a common scale, enabling us to reduce pressure scale related differences. EoSAlign can be applied to any high pressure data analysis to compare experimental results, improve consistency between studies, and advance our understanding of planetary interiors and high pressure physics.

papers.title: The Supercritical Ten Martini Problem
papers.abstract: We solve the ten martini problem for the positive-Lyapunov part of the spectrum of any nonconstant real analytic one-frequency Schr\"odinger operator. The proof uses the intrinsic symplectic structure of the dual center of Ge--Jitomirskaya [28] and extends the Kotani--almost-reducibility strategy of Ge--Jitomirskaya--You [30] from two-dimensional centers to arbitrary finite center dimension.

papers.title: Darmok: Championship Cryptic Crossword Solving via Constraint Tightening and Resilient Orchestration
papers.abstract:
We present Darmok, the first automated system to reach superhuman performance on British cryptic crosswords. Unlike American-style crosswords, cryptic clues disguise an unmarked definition and compositional wordplay beneath a misleading surface reading, sparse grids leave nearly half of each word's letters unchecked, and tournament rules rank a grid with even a single wrong or blank square behind all error-free solutions regardless of speed. Competing alongside an elite human field at the 55th Times Crossword Championship in London, Darmok solved all seven championship puzzles error-free and finished faster than every human competitor in every round. It solved the Final puzzle in 6m 52s, a full 3m 13s ahead of the human champion.
  Today's frontier AI models can on average solve a whole puzzle in a single try with comparable accuracy and speed. However, cloud API calls still stall, time out, trigger safety refusals, or get stuck in reasoning loops. To simultaneously achieve tournament-grade accuracy, speed, and reliability, Darmok cross-checks clues across three independent models in rounds; uses verified crossing letters to unlock harder clues; and uses a whole-puzzle model and dictionary lookups to fill any remaining gaps without overwriting confirmed words. This design maintained near-zero-error performance across a five-month daily evaluation period. Under normal benchmark conditions, removing backup models, fallback steps, or elaborate prompt instructions barely changes accuracy, making the architecture appear over-engineered. Yet during both the worst days of daily operation and a severe slowdown of our primary model in the live Championship Final, the backup paths carried the solve, showing that as foundation models master the average case, the central challenge in building complex AI systems shifts to resilience in the worst case.

papers.title: When Should Agents Remember? Falsification-Gated Self-Evolution for LLM Agents
papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly operate in long-horizon, verifier-rich environments, but current self-improvement mechanisms often write episode-derived lessons directly into memory, making local success an unreliable signal for reusable and safe knowledge. This paper addresses the core question of when an experience-derived behavioral update should be admitted into persistent agent state. We propose Falsification-Gated Self-Evolution (FGSE), a verifier-grounded framework that represents each candidate lesson as a structured hypothesis with an explicit precondition, behavior change, expected effect, and verifier. FGSE applies the hypothesis only in a temporary state, tests it on target-transfer, falsification, and archived-regression probes, and then commits, refines, or rejects it according to measured gain and risk. Across web, app, tool-use, and long-term memory benchmarks, FGSE achieves strong task performance, including 39.8 WebArena success rate, 78.8 AppWorld average completion, and 0.724/0.487 Pass$^1$ on $\tau$-Retail/$\tau$-Airline, while reducing falsification failures to 5.0%, regression damage to 1.3%, and harmful committed updates to 3.6%. These results suggest that testing memory updates as hypotheses supports more reliable long-term adaptation.

papers.title: Synapse-Control: Making Agent Experience Actionable with Lightweight Runtime Control
papers.abstract: Large language model agents reuse execution experience to improve reliability on complex tool-based tasks. Systems such as Sentry call large models to generate failure diagnoses before retrieving advice, adding inference cost to experience reuse. We present Synapse-Control, an agent runtime whose lightweight control plane selects advice and determines when to send it to the task-executing model. Rules shortlist relevant advice, and a lightweight 1.7B classifier fine-tuned on teacher-labeled state-suggestion pairs scores those candidates instead of generating a diagnosis. Micro-contracts encode reusable interface checks, such as required arguments or valid options, without prescribing complete task programs. A Prompt Value Table records earlier guidance and feedback to limit repeated suggestions through cooldown and token-budget checks. Across 1,308 attempts per method in AppWorld and WebShop, Synapse-Control achieves 270 successes (29.8% more than Base), replaces 4,987 generative diagnosis calls, and reduces auxiliary control time relative to Sentry by 50.2% and 51.0%, respectively.

papers.title: DisasterAgent: An Evidence-Driven Agent for Verifiable Disaster Report Generation From Remote Sensing Imagery
papers.abstract: Remote sensing disaster assessment is moving from simple damage classification toward comprehensive report-level analysis. In this setting, responders need not only damage descriptions but also verifiable evidence to guide response and recovery. Recent vision-language models (VLMs) and tool-augmented agents offer strong multimodal reasoning and perception, but they struggle to provide the evidence required for high-stakes verification. To address these limitations, we propose DisasterAgent, an evidence-driven agent that uses a Perception-Augmentation-Generation workflow to generate verifiable disaster reports from bitemporal optical imagery. DisasterAgent first invokes a specialized vision expert toolkit in the perception phase to build a Spatiotemporal Perception Graph (STPG), serving as a structured memory to store and organize disaster-induced changes across space and time. Evidence-based Augmentation (EA) then extracts evidence from the STPG, attaching inline citations that form a closed evidence loop from each statement to the supporting visual evidence. Extensive experiments on the DisasterM3 and RSCC benchmarks demonstrate that DisasterAgent consistently outperforms general-domain VLMs, remote sensing-specialized models, and existing remote sensing agents. Notably, compared with the original model, it improves the average score for disaster report generation on DisasterM3 by 13.5\% and ST5-SCS on RSCC by 15.34\%, providing a more accurate and verifiable solution for disaster emergency response. The code will be available at https://github.com/ZhijianLi2003/DisasterAgent.

papers.title: Kinetic Non-Equilibrium Receptivity Analysis of Hypersonic Flows via a Complex Linearized Unified Gas-Kinetic Scheme
papers.abstract: In the near-space regime, local rarefaction near the leading-edge shock and wall degrades Navier-Stokes-based stability and receptivity analyses due to velocity slip, temperature jumps, and non-equilibrium transport. The unified gas-kinetic scheme (UGKS) provides a multiscale kinetic description spanning continuum to rarefied regimes. Building on this, a complex linearized UGKS (CLUGKS) is developed: first-order perturbations of the discrete UGKS residual are formulated under a time-harmonic assumption with complex amplitudes, converting disturbance equations into a steady elliptic system solved via pseudo-time marching with LU-SGS acceleration. Consequently, kinetic shock structures, wall slip, temperature jumps, and non-Fourier heat fluxes are inherently captured without hybrid coupling. Three benchmarks verify the framework: a standing acoustic wave at an isothermal wall, a Mach 2 normal shock interacting with an obliquely incident acoustic wave, and freestream acoustic receptivity of a hypersonic blunt wedge. The scheme is applied to argon blunt-wedge flows at equivalent altitudes of 40 km and 50 km. At 40 km, UGKS and Navier-Stokes wall responses agree well in period and phase, while wall slip sustains a weakly positive spatial growth rate in UGKS downstream. At 50 km, intensified rarefaction produces a kinetic temperature precursor and a thickened, merged shock layer; while wall-pressure responses remain close, significant deviations emerge in temperature and heat-flux disturbances. These findings show that while continuum models capture dominant wall-pressure signatures under moderate rarefaction, resolving kinetic non-equilibrium across the shock-particularly its thermal footprint-is essential at higher altitudes.

papers.title: FAME-QP: A GPU-Accelerated Quadratic-Programming Solver for Real-Time Model Predictive Control
papers.abstract: We present FAME-QP, a GPU-accelerated solver for dense quadratic programs arising in linear model predictive control. FAME-QP combines constraint-dependent operator representations with fused single- and two-kernel iterations replayed through CUDA graphs, automatically selecting the execution configuration through device calibration and problem-specific timing. It probes a cached operator bank to select the initial penalty and updates operators lazily when problem matrices change. Numerical benchmarks and simulated humanoid and quadrotor control experiments demonstrate reduced latency relative to competing GPU solvers while maintaining solution accuracy and control performance.

papers.title: Explicit restricted isometries with $k=m^{2/3-o(1)}$
papers.abstract: We construct an explicit family of real $m\times n$ restricted isometries with $m\to\infty$, $m/n\to 0$, $\delta_k\to 0$, and $k=m^{2/3-o(1)}$. We combine Gershgorin's circle theorem with a flat RIP estimate to reduce the problem to choosing a large vertex set in a strongly regular graph with the property that every small subset spans few edges. We select this vertex set using an incidence geometric result due to Zahl. The proof only uses the entrywise absolute value of the Gram matrix despite the conventional wisdom that such proof techniques exhibit a barrier of $m^{1/2}$. We prove that this barrier is actually $m^{2/3}$, and we show that our particular construction exhibits the same barrier.

papers.title: JAX-WAVE: A Differentiable Physics-Supervised Framework for Inverse Wave Design in Heterogeneous Media
papers.abstract: Designing a prescribed wave field in a heterogeneous medium requires an initial pressure distribution that compensates for the medium's propagation response. Repeated numerical inversion solves this task afresh for each target and environment. We introduce JAX-WAVE for amortized inverse wave design: a shared neural network maps desired terminal fields and known wave-speed maps directly to bounded initial pressures. Training through a differentiable finite-difference time-domain solver uses the physical design objective without requiring optimized control labels. Linear propagation and symmetric pressure bounds imply an exact sign-reversal relation for the regularized optimum. A shared-weight projection enforces this relation, preserves feasibility, and satisfies an exact identity for the paired-sign objective. We characterize the discrete propagator and its weighted adjoint to connect learning, numerical inversion, and optimality assessment. On an independent confirmation set, three trained models achieve unseen-material errors of 25.24% for geometric targets and 4.77% for reachable targets. Matched-capacity comparisons show improved reconstruction with the sign parameterization. Within a 5 ms median online budget, the learned map reduces mean error by 45% relative to accelerated numerical inversion on the heterogeneous benchmark; longer numerical solves recover greater accuracy. The results establish a reusable inverse-design procedure and show how its accuracy and computational value depend on target structure and query workload.

papers.title: On L\'{e}vy type subgroups of the symmetric group of $\omega$ associated with simple density functions
papers.abstract: The L\'{e}vy group, introduced by L\'{e}vy in (L\'{e}vy (1951)), is defined by \[\mathcal{L} = \left\{\sigma\in aut : \lim_n \frac{|\{k\in n : \sigma(k)\notin n\}|}{n} = 0\right\},\] where $aut$ denotes the group of all permutations of $\omega$. This group happens to be closely connected with the notion of asymptotic density as it consists of permutations that map sets with an asymptotic density back to sets with the same density. Our aim is to replicate the construction by replacing $n$ in the denominator by $g(n)$ for a function $g:\omega\to [0,\infty)$ with $g(n)\to \infty$ (weight), which leads us a class of L\'{e}vy type groups. Specifically we define simple L\'{e}vy group with weight $g$ as \[\mathcal{L}_g = \left\{\sigma\in aut : \lim_n \frac{|\{k\in n : \sigma(k)\notin n\}|}{g(n)} = 0\right\}.\] As a natural consequence we first study its relationship with the notion of simple density functions (which had been introduced in \cite{gd2} as a general class of density functions by similar manner) paving way for the class of simple density functions and ideals $\mathcal{I}_g$. We have $\mathcal{L}_g = aut$ if and only if $n/g(n)\to 0$ (just like $\mathcal{I}_g = 2^{\omega}$ if and only if $n/g(n)\to 0$). The relation between simple density functions and simple L\'{e}vy groups is in expected line. What seems more interesting is the comparative study of these groups. We start with the relation between $\mathcal{L}$ and $\mathcal{L}_g$ and constructing suitable examples it is shown that strict inclusions and incomparability may occur. Finally we come up with an interesting observation that there are continuum many pairwise incomparable simple L\'{e}vy groups, each of which is incomparable with $\mathcal{L}$.

papers.title: Sharp Sample Complexity of KL-Regularized Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: KL-regularized reinforcement learning, the objective behind maximum-entropy RL and RL from human feedback, is variational inference in the graphical model of "control as inference": the regularized optimal policy is a posterior over trajectories, and the suboptimality of a policy is $\beta$ times a KL divergence between path measures. However, it is not known how many samples it takes to learn this posterior, even with a generative model. Earlier $1/\epsilon$ guarantees scale with $H^5$ in the effective horizon $H$, and no lower bound for MDPs depends on the temperature $\beta$. In this work, we show that for a discounted MDP with $K$ state-action pairs, the plug-in estimator finds a policy that is $\epsilon$-optimal from every initial state with $\widetilde{O}(KH^3/(\epsilon\max\{\epsilon,\beta\}) + KH)$ samples, and that no algorithm, even one that chooses where to sample, can do with fewer when $\epsilon \lesssim \min\{H, H^2/\beta\}$. For $\epsilon < \beta$ this is a $1/\epsilon$ rate with the same horizon dependence as unregularized RL. We also find the exact asymptotic constant of the plug-in estimator, a Fisher-weighted variance of the estimated soft Q-function. The estimator is locally asymptotically minimax among methods that sample every pair equally often, and we give the allocation of samples that is optimal among adaptive designs. Simulations on small MDPs match the rates and the constants.

papers.title: Point-in-Time Encoders for Earnings Calls
papers.abstract: Text encoders turn earnings calls into vectors for search, for language models that answer from retrieved passages, and for forecasting models. A live retriever can use an encoder trained once on all available text, as finance retrievers are, but a backtest needs an encoder that read no text written after the date of each vector. To address this look-ahead bias, from 412,248 calls we train vintages under four pretraining recipes, with yearly cutoffs from 2010 to 2024, and each vintage reads only text dated on or before its cutoff. We then fine-tune each vintage on the question-answer pairs of the calls themselves. The vintages we train on calls alone, with 33.8M parameters, retrieve answers on held-out calls better than the general retrievers we tested in every test quarter. Their vectors also raise by about half the rank correlation between next-day returns and forecasts built from past returns and firm size. When each vintage continues the previous one, a later vintage retrieves better on earlier quarters than the vintage available at the time, and a point-in-time language model that answers from the passages the later vintage retrieves inherits the gain. The 2024 vintage of our families also forecasts earnings surprises better, although the interval of this gain includes zero on calls that no vintage read. It forecasts returns no better, so point-in-time vintages matter most for retrieval and little for forecasts of returns.

papers.title: Agent Benchmarks Stop Ranking Before They Run Out of Tasks
papers.abstract: Data-science and ML-engineering agents are evaluated on benchmarks such as MLE-bench, ALE-Bench, SWE-fficiency and AlgoTune, whose tasks yield a quantity (a Kaggle metric, contest score or speedup). When one stops separating the best models, the usual remedy is a harder version. Re-scoring released runs of eight benchmarks, including SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench for breadth, we find much of this saturation lies in the measurement, not the tasks. Most agent benchmarks reduce a run to one pass/fail bit, which fails in two ways. It is too coarse: neighbouring top-ten agents on SWE-bench Verified differ by less than its tests' errors, and correcting them reorders neighbours no more than deleting a random sixth of each agent's passes. It is capped at the reference: ALE-Bench's top ten, separated by contest score, tie when graded against the median human, although nearly half the runs beat that human. On fixed tasks, a higher bar only moves the problem; graded credit fixes it. We derive a clipped log-ratio score with dated anchors and cost as a separate axis. In a Terminal-Bench re-run, pass/fail-tied models differ over tenfold on the quantity the tests discard.

papers.title: Reciprocal mirror map derivatives, euler-twisted Gromov-Witten invariants, and instanton counts via quantum Serre duality
papers.abstract: We study mirror map derivatives as a means of relating the genus zero Gromov-Witten theories of an anticanonical Calabi-Yau hypersurface in a smooth, almost minimal Fano variety and the local Calabi-Yau formed from the total space of the Fano's canonical bundle with the euler-twisted theory of the ambient Fano. A precise relationship between reciprocal mirror map derivatives is obtained from the non-equivariant limit of quantum Serre duality for the euler-twisted theory of the ambient Fano as formulated by Iritani, Mann, & Mignon. This allows us to express the generating series of 3-point euler-twisted invariants as the derivative of the local mirror map with respect to the closed one. In low dimensions, this series is shown to be a modular form of Eisenstein type which has arisen before in this area. We prove integrality of the twisted invariants from this identification. The regularized small quantum $D$-module of the Fano is reducible, and we show it is equivalent to an inhomogeneous Picard-Fuchs equation governed by this generating series. The reciprocal mirror map derivative is then shown to be a generating function of local 3-point invariants, which recovers some known results for local Calabi-Yau threefolds and proves a conjecture of the second named author and A. Malmendier in previous work on local fourfolds. Explicit calculations for $\mathbb{P}^2,\mathbb{P}^3$ and $\mathbb{P}^4$ illustrate these relationships, which includes the vanishing of positive-degree ordinary genus-zero invariants for anticanonical elliptic curves and K3 surfaces, the recovery of the quintic threefold's instanton numbers, and finally some formulas for genus-zero invariants of local projective spaces.

papers.title: Coupled Cluster Simulations of Vibrational Circular Dichroism Spectra
papers.abstract: We report the first simulations of vibrational circular dichroism (VCD) spectra at the coupled-cluster level of theory. Using a generalization of Stephens's pioneering magnetic-field perturbation theory framework for the magnetic-dipole vibrational transition moment to biorthonormal wave functions, we have derived generalized expressions for the corresponding atomic axial tensors (AATs) and velocity-gauge atomic polar tensors that collapse to Stephens's expressions for real, Hermitian states. Adapting these exact-state expressions to coupled-cluster left- and right-hand biorthonormal wave functions and using our recently developed density-based formulation yields compact equations that involve only perturbed ground-state amplitudes, as well as unperturbed and perturbed, unrelaxed one-electron densities; two-electron-density contributions vanish exactly. We have validated the resulting AATs by comparison with our previous configuration interaction formulation for a two-electron system, size-intensivity tests, a translational sum rule, and other tests. Simulated VCD spectra for (S)-3-chloro-1-butyne at the coupled-cluster singles and doubles level with the correlation-consistent triple-zeta basis set reveal significant discrepancies between length and velocity gauges. We find that the addition of large-exponent functions via a core-valence basis set for the Hartree--Fock reference components yields substantially improved gauge invariance without the need for gauge-including atomic orbitals.

papers.title: Elastic Landau states as martensite nuclei in austenite
papers.abstract: In this article, we investigate the geometric closure of austenite--martensite interfaces. Classical compatibility conditions permit stress-free interfaces between the two phases: the condition $\lambda_2 = 1$ admits planar interfaces, whereas the cofactor conditions additionally admit curved interfaces. However, neither, guarantees the geometric closure of these interfaces. We identify two-parameter families of martensitic deformations that overcome this limitation and enable the formation of closed, stress-free martensite nuclei embedded in an austenite matrix. A main result is the interpretation of the classical deformation modes of simple shear and pure shear as martensitic phase transformations. These correspond to cubic to monoclinic-II and cubic to orthorhombic transformations, respectively. The former naturally satisfies the \emph{extreme compatibility conditions}, which are stronger than the cofactor conditions, and gives rise to \emph{elastic Landau states}, a self-accommodating martensitic nuclei embedded in austenite. We show that these states can be assembled to form arbitrarily shaped, stress-free martensitic islands surrounded by austenite. Such states can arise even in conventional shape memory alloys that do not satisfy supercompatibility, provided hierarchical twinning produces an average deformation that is a simple shear. The theory provides a geometric mechanism for self-accommodation. Its predicted deformation gradients agree with those reconstructed from experimentally observed microstructures. This agreement suggests that these microstructures originate from simple shear.

papers.title: Accelerating matrix-free fast diagonalization and preconditioned linear solvers for higher-order finite element discretized elliptic problems on distributed GPUs
papers.abstract: The time to solution of an iterative solver depends on the number of iterations and the cost per iteration. This paper develops algorithms that reduce both for elliptic problems discretized with high-order continuous finite elements on distributed GPUs, implemented in a unified matrix-free code supporting CUDA, HIP and SYCL. A distributed direct fast-diagonalization (FD) Poisson solver provides exact solutions on tensor-product meshes with direction-wise grading and coefficients varying along one coordinate direction. Its tensor data stay distributed, moved between slab layouts by collective transposes or kept in place by a Schur-complement approach. It is also an exact coarse solver. A two-level hybrid Schwarz preconditioner with FD cell solves (HS-FD) is extended to 2:1 hanging-node octrees with exact local cell inverses, while a \(p\)-multigrid preconditioner with Chebyshev--Jacobi smoothing (CJ-\(p\)MG) resolves hanging-node constraints at every level within fused kernels. Both approaches exploit FP32, where cell shapes and coefficients allow, within an FP64 conjugate-gradient iteration, adaptively select replicated or distributed coarse levels, support block solves for multiple right-hand sides and determine all parameters from the operator without case-specific tuning. Comparisons with Jacobi-preconditioned conjugate gradients (Jacobi PCG), MFEM, nekRS and deal.II span uniform, graded and octree meshes, layered coefficients, and four applications across NVIDIA, AMD and Intel GPUs. The direct solver is two to three orders of magnitude faster than Jacobi PCG on uniform meshes. HS-FD converges in 11 iterations for an octree generalized Poisson problem across 8 to 1024 MI250X graphics compute dies. The results guide solver selection by mesh structure and coefficients

papers.title: Tolerance complexes of chordal graphs and squarefree symbolic powers
papers.abstract: For a simplicial complex $K$ and an integer $t\ge0$, the $t$-tolerance complex $\mathcal{T}_t(K)$ consists of the sets that become faces of $K$ after deleting at most $t$ of their elements. Kim and Lew conjectured that if $K$ is $d$-Leray, then $\mathcal{T}_t(K)$ is $(\eta(d+1,t+1)-1)$-Leray (the Leray conjecture), and that if $K$ is $d$-collapsible, then $\mathcal{T}_t(K)$ is $(\eta(d+1,t+1)-1)$-collapsible (the collapsibility conjecture), where $\eta$ is the Erd\H{o}s--Gallai number. We prove the collapsibility conjecture for $d=1$ when $t\le3$ or $\dim K\le4$, and for all $t$ when $K$ is the clique complex of a subtree graph of a spider, a class of chordal graphs containing all interval and split graphs; in particular, it holds for nerves of finite families of intervals. For every $d$, we prove both conjectures when $K$ has at most $d+1$ facets, when $K$ has nonzero homology in its top dimension, and when the Stanley--Reisner ideal of $K$ is squarefree stable. The Stanley--Reisner ideal of $\mathcal{T}_t(K)$ is the $(t+1)$-st squarefree symbolic power of that of $K$, so the Leray conjecture becomes a regularity bound. Using this, we prove the Leray conjecture for flag complexes when $t\le3$, and for all $t$ for independence complexes of bipartite and chordal graphs, and we show that it is preserved under joins. We also construct chordal graphs $H$ for which the Leray number of $\mathcal{T}_t(\mathrm{Cl}(H))$ exceeds its Helly dimension by an arbitrarily large amount, and others for which it depends on the field. Finally, we reduce the case $t=1$ of the Leray bound for $d$-collapsible complexes to a question on intersections of links.

papers.title: EJAI: Judgment-Preserving Civic AI for Data Center Environmental Justice
papers.abstract: Communities in the United States and around the world are contesting data centers, the physical infrastructure of AI. These disputes pose environmental justice issues: residents must weigh unevenly distributed burdens using evidence scattered across metrics, corporate claims, policy documents, and public testimony. A formative study with 10 users showed that dashboards and single-agent AI can settle questions before people examine that evidence. Here we present EJAI, a source-grounded system that links an interactive map, retrieved evidence, missing-data statements, and two stakeholder personas that allow people to inspect evidence and form their own policy recommendations. In a small functional benchmark of 21 queries, retrieved evidence supported 98.4% of factual claims and the system acknowledged missing evidence in 32 of 33 cases. Persona alignment carried a grounding cost: the Corporate Executive omitted some evidence that conflicted with its assigned priorities. In a within-subjects study, 15 participants acting as residents prepared for a simulated town hall. Some checked cited AI claims while treating map metrics as official, some made conditional recommendations with safeguards such as water-use disclosure, and some found the personas simplified or biased. Our results suggest that civic AI can support preparation for public reasoning when it makes evidence, gaps, and disagreement open to inspection, and that corpus imbalance and two-sided personas remain open justice concerns.

authors.name: Snehalkumar 'Neil' S. Gaikwad
authors.institution: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill

papers.intro:
As AI expansion drives demand for data center infrastructure (Li et al., 2025), several North Carolina governments have paused approvals for data centers. On October 6, 2026, the Raleigh City Council voted 7–1 to pause approvals for certain large data centers for six months, as residents asked how working-class neighborhoods would be protected and how they would have a real voice (Holiday, 2026). In 2026, Durham County adopted a nine-month pause (Michaels and Chen, 2026), Orange County adopted a one-year pause (Chen, 2026), and Charlotte extended its pause to as late as October 2027 (Beebe, 2026). Developers and some local officials emphasize tax revenue, jobs, and investment, while residents and advocates raise concerns about water use, electricity demand, land conversion, emissions, noise, and utility costs (Ngata et al., 2025; George and Conteh, 2026). These disputes raise environmental justice concerns because burdens and benefits may fall unevenly across communities (Ngata et al., 2025; George and Conteh, 2026; Hajiesmaili et al., 2025). We treat data center siting as an environmental justice problem grounded in broader concerns with distribution, recognition, and participation. Residents must evaluate burdens using evidence that is fragmented, technical, incomplete, and shaped by institutional interests.

As AI expansion drives demand for data center infrastructure (Li et al., 2025), several North Carolina governments have paused approvals for data centers. On October 6, 2026, the Raleigh City Council voted 7–1 to pause approvals for certain large data centers for six months, as residents asked how working-class neighborhoods would be protected and how they would have a real voice (Holiday, 2026). In 2026, Durham County adopted a nine-month pause (Michaels and Chen, 2026), Orange County adopted a one-year pause (Chen, 2026), and Charlotte extended its pause to as late as October 2027 (Beebe, 2026). Developers and some local officials emphasize tax revenue, jobs, and investment, while residents and advocates raise concerns about water use, electricity demand, land conversion, emissions, noise, and utility costs (Ngata et al., 2025; George and Conteh, 2026). These disputes raise environmental justice concerns because burdens and benefits may fall unevenly across communities (Ngata et al., 2025; George and Conteh, 2026; Hajiesmaili et al., 2025). We treat data center siting as an environmental justice problem grounded in broader concerns with distribution, recognition, and participation. Residents must evaluate burdens using evidence that is fragmented, technical, incomplete, and shaped by institutional interests.

Reasoning about these disputes requires connecting metrics, facility records, corporate claims, policy documents, and community testimony (Fusi et al., 2023; Ngata et al., 2025), work often performed by advocates, journalists, and community organizations as civic data intermediaries (Qiao et al., 2025; Davis and Ramírez-Andreotta, 2021). Dashboards can show where facilities are located and which counties have high burdens (Chokki et al., 2022; McIntyre et al., 2025), but they typically present metrics without local context. LLM assistants can explain terminology and summarize documents (Liu et al., 2024), but authoritative answers may encourage overreliance without verification. Neither is designed to help residents examine evidence while forming their own view. Could a resident who learns of a proposed data center at a public meeting get help inspecting the evidence for their county, seeing what is missing, comparing how stakeholders interpret the same evidence, and reaching their own recommendation?

Reasoning about these disputes requires connecting metrics, facility records, corporate claims, policy documents, and community testimony (Fusi et al., 2023; Ngata et al., 2025), work often performed by advocates, journalists, and community organizations as civic data intermediaries (Qiao et al., 2025; Davis and Ramírez-Andreotta, 2021). Dashboards can show where facilities are located and which counties have high burdens (Chokki et al., 2022; McIntyre et al., 2025), but they typically present metrics without local context. LLM assistants can explain terminology and summarize documents (Liu et al., 2024), but authoritative answers may encourage overreliance without verification. Neither is designed to help residents examine evidence while forming their own view. Could a resident who learns of a proposed data center at a public meeting get help inspecting the evidence for their county, seeing what is missing, comparing how stakeholders interpret the same evidence, and reaching their own recommendation?

Critical research on AI’s societal impacts has documented the environmental costs of AI infrastructure (Valdivia, 2025; Domínguez Hernández et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025) and argued that the public should have democratic control over how AI is developed (Bogiatzis-Gibbons, 2024; Valdivia, 2025). Within HCI, scholars have called for balancing efficiency and ease of use with environmental justice (Soden et al., 2025). We build on this work by asking how an interactive visualization–LLM system can help the public scrutinize the infrastructure AI depends on and support civic judgment about it. We call this design aim judgment-preserving civic AI: LLM systems that help people inspect evidence, recognize uncertainty, compare interpretations, and form their own civic recommendations. Drawing on Sen’s capability approach and his account of democracy as public reasoning (Sen, 1999; Sen, 2009), we design for four civic capabilities: engaging with local evidence; understanding what it means and what it leaves out; interacting with competing interpretations; and preparing to act through questions, conditions, and recommendations.

papers.title: Improved Bounds for Online Matching with Random Edge Arrivals
papers.abstract: We study the unweighted online matching problem with random edge arrivals, where each edge arrives at an independent time drawn uniformly from $[0,1]$, and the algorithm must immediately and irrevocably accept or reject it while maintaining a matching. Guruganesh and Singla (IPCO, 2017) first broke the $1/2$ barrier of the naive Greedy algorithm by giving a $(1/2+\varepsilon)$-competitive algorithm for a small constant $\varepsilon>0$, a guarantee that has remained the best known for nearly a decade. We give a simple three-phase algorithm that achieves a competitive ratio of $0.5445$ by deliberately rejecting selected early edges to reserve their endpoints for later matching opportunities. With a different choice of parameters, the same algorithm is $0.5535$-competitive on triangle-free graphs, including bipartite graphs. We also establish competitive ratio upper bounds below $0.6964$ for general graphs and $0.7043$ for bipartite graphs via exact rational evaluation of an optimal-policy recurrence on fixed graphs, even when the input graph is known up to isomorphism.

papers.title: Bridging Graph and Pairwise Learning for Gene Regulatory Network Inference from scRNA-seq Data
papers.abstract: Motivation: Gene regulatory networks (GRNs) capture the underlying interactions through which transcription factors (TFs) regulate genes. Based on gene expression data, existing GRN inference approaches generally fall into two categories: graph-based methods, which model the GRN as a whole graph, and pairwise-based methods, which decompose the GRN into individual TF-target gene pairs for modeling. However, each approach exhibits limitations that are precisely the strengths of its counterpart. Graph-based methods tend to overfit due to their reliance on a single training graph, whereas pairwise-based methods benefit from abundant TF-target training pairs. In contrast, pairwise-based methods overlook the global topological structure, which is essential for comprehensively capturing regulatory mechanisms. Results: To address these limitations, we propose scGPL, an end-to-end unified framework that jointly models global regulatory topology and local interactions. scGPL extracts macro-level features from the global regulatory graph and introduces a dynamic, importance-guided subgraph sampling mechanism to capture fine-grained local dependencies. By fusing global representations with subgraph-enhanced local features, our framework bridges the gap between the two paradigms, incorporating essential whole-graph topological dependencies while retaining the data abundance advantage of pairwise methods. Extensive experiments on seven benchmark datasets demonstrate that scGPL consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance, with up to 13.7% improvement over the strongest baseline, validating the effectiveness of our integrative design. Availability and implementation: The source code is maintained on GitHub (https://github.com/talent-hang/scGPL), and the datasets and versioned releases are archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21608485 for reproducibility.

papers.title: Forecast Projection and Decision Regret: Theory and Evidence from Battery Arbitrage
papers.abstract: Decision-focused learning trains forecasts for the decisions they lead to, but forecasts are often projected onto known bounds before use. We study the resulting mismatch in battery arbitrage. When a battery starts and ends the day at the same charge level, a common shift in prices affects its schedule only through round-trip losses. As a result, decision-focused losses identify the forecast level only weakly. For the SPO+ and perturbed Fenchel-Young losses, we characterize the preferred level by a throughput-matching condition. Projecting forecasts onto a price cap can then remove profitable spreads and increase regret, even as prediction error falls. We give bounds on the change in regret, a dual-threshold condition under which a raw-optimal schedule remains optimal after clipping, and a general version of the mechanism for other problems with a conservation constraint. On 1,158 holdout days of the Indian day-ahead market, an equal-weight average of three statistical forecasts outperforms the five decision-focused variants tested. On 53 later days, with 62% of price blocks at the cap, no variant outperforms the regression or the equal-weight average, although most differences from the average are not significant. The results suggest that forecast post-processing should be treated as part of the predict-then-optimize pipeline.

papers.title: Counterexamples to the buckling eigenvalue-ratio conjecture in every dimension
papers.abstract: In 1999, Ashbaugh formulated the conjecture that the ball maximizes the ratio of the first two clamped buckling eigenvalues among bounded domains in Euclidean space. We disprove this conjecture in every dimension $d\ge2$ by constructing smooth connected domains with finitely many interior holes. The key observation is that a zero-value constraint on a concentric sphere close to the boundary of a ball increases the first two eigenvalues by the same relative amount to first order, whereas their ratio increases strictly at second order. A quantitative surface penalty and logarithmic cutoffs transfer this strict inequality to smooth perforated domains. The construction gives explicit geometric parameters depending only on the dimension \(d\).

papers.title: DOBB: Dynamic Oriented Bounding Boxes for Multi-Agent Collision Avoidance under State Uncertainty and Heterogeneous Dynamics
papers.abstract: Learning-based decentralized collision avoidance must remain reliable under state-estimation uncertainty and heterogeneous agent dynamics. Existing methods typically address these factors through training-domain variation or by exposing uncertainty and capability estimates to the policy at runtime. However, both leave the policy to infer how these quantities should alter the physical separation required for safe interaction, which can couple collision-avoidance behavior to relationships learned from the training distribution. We introduce the Dynamic Oriented Bounding Box (DOBB), an online geometric representation that maps the current state estimate, uncertainty, and agent-specific response characteristics into a dynamic, direction-dependent safety margin. We derive geometric features that jointly characterize the relative configuration and severity of interactions between agents' DOBBs, along with a reward function that preserves the physical interpretation of those interactions. Across four evaluation environments, DOBB achieves the lowest mean total failure rate of 2.6%. This performance persists under out-of-distribution shifts in actuation dynamics and state-estimation uncertainty, with collision-based failure remaining at or below 2.3% in every tested condition. We attribute this robustness to the geometric abstraction of the safety margin, which is less coupled to the specific uncertainty and actuation regimes encountered during training.

papers.title: Coxeter cubes on the graph associahedron and separable elements
papers.abstract: A Coxeter cube is a Boolean lattice inside a finite Coxeter group $W$ such that every square is a Coxeter square in the sense of Dyer and Wang. A Coxeter cube of full dimension based at the identity, which we call a based cube, is the same as a partition of the positive roots into inversion sets with one simple root in each block. These partitions were studied by Dimitrov, Gigliotti, Ossip, Paquette and Wehlau under the name of fine decompositions, and by Hohlweg and Pons as partitions of $w_0$. We show that the based cubes of $W$ form a point configuration in the graph associahedron $K(\Gamma)$ of the Coxeter diagram $\Gamma$ of $W$. The vertices of $K(\Gamma)$ are the based cubes whose blocks are parabolic. Every other based cube lies in the interior of an edge or of a cubical face, and we count the based cubes on each edge using the Coxeter arrangement. We also characterize the elements of $W$ that occur as vertices of based cubes. For the cubes at the vertices of $K(\Gamma)$ these are exactly the separable elements of Gaetz and Gao, and for arbitrary based cubes they satisfy a similar condition.

papers.title: On the topology of some linear systems of hyperelliptic curves in Hirzebruch surfaces
papers.abstract: Following a program suggested by Dolgachev and Libgober in 1981, we study the topology of the locus of smooth sections of linear systems of hyperelliptic curves on Hirzebruch surfaces. Our primary interest is the computation of various flavors of ``enriched monodromy representations''. Within this class of examples, we find that a variety of behaviors occur - in some situations the enriched monodromy faithfully captures the fundamental group, and in others it does not. Our arguments mainly leverage algebro-geometric techniques to compute cohomological obstructions to families of embeddings.

papers.title: Bounded point evaluations in spaces of several complex variables
papers.abstract: The focus of this manuscript is existence criteria for bounded point evaluations and bounded point derivations. In the single variable setting conditions for the existence of bounded point evaluations and derivations are known for many spaces of functions; however, in the several variable case far less is known. In this manuscript, we consider Campanato spaces, which contain many other function spaces as special cases, and prove sufficient conditions for the existence of bounded point evaluations in these spaces that are analogs of known results for the single variable case. We also demonstrate that for certain cases these sufficient conditions are also necessary.

papers.title: A Theory of Cross-Validation Variance
papers.abstract: Cross-validation estimates predictive performance by repeatedly splitting the data into training and validation sets, fitting the model on the first and evaluating it on the second. Every observation influences the estimate in two roles, through its own evaluation when it is held out and through the models it helps fit when it trains. The random splits determine its weight in each role. From this representation, we prove an exact finite-sample identity for the variance of the cross-validated estimate. For a given splitting scheme with a common training set size, the variance is a function of these weights, with constants of the model, the metric, and the population. It covers metrics averaged over observations, such as mean squared error, and over case--control pairs, such as the AUC. The identity shows which schemes to use. The variance decomposes into sampling variance, which depends only on the training size, and variance due to the random fold splitting, which arises when the weights change from one draw of the splits to the next. K-fold cross-validation, whose weights are equal across observations by design, is therefore variance optimal at first order; Monte Carlo and bootstrap cross-validation are not. The first-order variance of K-fold does not depend on K, and under reasonable conditions on the model leave-one-out has the smallest variance of any K-fold scheme. For the AUC the same holds for leave-pair-out, which evaluates every case--control pair. Finally, we show the cross-validated estimate is asymptotically normal with the identity's full variance. Together, these results provide a general theoretical foundation for inference on cross-validated performance and establish principles for selecting variance-optimal cross-validation designs.

papers.title: Location Matters: Sparse Latent-Variance Attacks for Face Privacy against Diffusion Personalization
papers.abstract: Text-to-image diffusion models can learn and reproduce an individual's identity from only a few reference photos, creating risks of unauthorized and misleading content generation. Proactive defenses address this risk by adding adversarial perturbations to facial images before release, thereby disrupting identity acquisition during downstream personalization. However, existing methods typically rely on dense $L_\infty$-bounded perturbations, whose accumulated distortions can become visible around facial structures. Recent methods improve protected-image quality, but often at the cost of reduced protection effectiveness. In this paper, we propose Sparse Encoder Attack on Latent Variance (SEAL), a sparse adversarial protection framework that modifies only 5% of the spatial locations in a facial image. SEAL combines a differentiable top-k masking scheme that jointly optimizes perturbation locations and values with a variance-oriented objective over the frozen VAE encoder's latent distribution to disrupt identity-consistent representations. A saliency-guided dispersion penalty further discourages perturbation concentration in perceptually salient facial regions. Experiments on CelebA-HQ and VGGFace2 show that SEAL achieves the best protected-image quality among the compared methods, exceeding 41 dB PSNR with 0.97 SSIM and at most 0.07 LPIPS, while reducing identity similarity to at most 0.15 after diffusion personalization. These results demonstrate that sparse location optimization enables strong identity protection while preserving high visual quality. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Lvxan/SEAL

papers.title: HandsOnAid: Building and Evaluating an Offline First-Aid Assistant for Emergency Response Scenarios
papers.abstract: Emergencies can occur where there is no phone signal and no ambulance nearby. A small language model on a phone can be helpful in such situations, but its advice needs to be safe and accurate. We built HandsOnAid, a 4-bit Gemma 2B model fine-tuned with QLoRA on FirstAidQA dataset, a corpus of 5,550 first-aid question-answer pairs. We compared seven configurations, including the base, 4-bit and 8-bit fine-tuned models, and versions with a length floor, safety gate, or retrieval. We used a 41-pair question-answer bank with medically reviewed references that followed ANZCOR guidelines, and a strict 0-5 score rubric, with twelve safety overrides. Four frontier LLM judges (GPT-5.6 Sol, Claude Opus 5, DeepSeek V4 Pro, GLM-5.3) blindly scored every answer, with 45 hidden controls used to check judge reliability. Fine-tuning improved the mean score by +1.08 over the base model to 2.34. The best configuration scored 2.51 out of 5 which was the fine-tuned 4-bit model with retrieval. A medical professional also conducted a blind evaluation of 40 answers across the base, the 4-bit fine-tuned, and the retrieval configurations, and the scores were similar to the LLM judges' average scores. A keyword audit found limited coverage of several details of ANZCOR guidelines in the training corpus, that are required by the rubric, which suggests that missing information in the training data could be a cause of the low scores. On a smartphone device (Pixel 7 Pro) with six CPU threads and no network connection, the 4-bit fine-tuned model produced its first displayable text in 6.86 seconds and a complete answer in 14.88 seconds on average over ten questions.

papers.title: ICLayout-Bench: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Custom Circuit Layout Design
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are being explored for circuit design, but their ability to produce high-quality custom layouts has not been extensively evaluated. ICLayout-Bench is a benchmark in which agents use electronic design automation (EDA) tools to construct and optimize GDSII layouts from transistor-level circuit netlists. These layouts are evaluated using physical verification, parasitic extraction, and post-layout simulation. Layouts that pass the physical and functional checks are scored on electrical performance and area. The benchmark includes 165 tasks across 13 process design kits (PDKs), covering technology nodes from 3 nm to 180 nm. The tasks span analog, mixed-signal, and digital circuits in open-source and commercial EDA flows. The experiments evaluate 22 configurations spanning seven models on 21 public and 19 private tasks. Mean layout scores range from 4.22 to 80.26 on public tasks and from 1.43 to 67.01 on private tasks, on a 100-point scale. Higher reasoning effort does not consistently improve mean scores, and configurations with comparable scores can incur substantially different model costs.

papers.title: Uniform Resolvent Estimates for the Dunkl Laplacian
papers.abstract:
Let \(\Lk=-\Dk\) denote the nonnegative Dunkl Laplacian associated with a finite reflection group and a nonnegative multiplicity function \(\kappa\), and let $
N=d+2\gk\geq 3 $
be the corresponding homogeneous dimension. We establish uniform \(L_\kappa^p(\mathbb{R}^d)\)-\(L_\kappa^q(\mathbb{R}^d)\) resolvent estimates for \(\Lk\) whenever \[ \frac{2}{N+1} \leq \frac{1}{p}-\frac{1}{q} \leq \frac{2}{N}, \quad \frac{2N}{N+3}<p<\frac{2N}{N+1}, \quad \frac{2N}{N-1}<q<\frac{2N}{N-3}, \] where the last upper bound is interpreted as \(q<\infty\) when \(N=3\). Remarkably, this admissible range coincides with the corresponding range for the Euclidean Laplacian \(-\Delta\) in dimension \(N\).

papers.title: An additively idempotent semiring of least order generating a limit variety
papers.abstract:
We construct an additively idempotent semiring of order five that generates
  a limit variety and is not strongly nonfinitely based. The generated variety
  has exactly two maximal proper subvarieties, both hereditarily finitely based.
  We also prove that no ai-semiring of order at most four generates a limit
  variety. Consequently, five is the least possible order of a finite
  ai-semiring generating a limit variety.

papers.title: Whittaker supermodules for the Takiff superalgebra \mathfrak{osp}(1|2)
papers.abstract: In this article, we classify all simple Whittaker supermodules over the Takiff Lie superalgebra \(\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{osp}(1|2)\otimes\mathbb C[t]/(t^2)\), associated with Whittaker characters defined on the even part of its positive nilpotent subalgebra.

papers.title: MMDM: Measuring Massive Multitask Decision Making
papers.abstract: System-1 Decision Models directly make structured probabilistic decisions over query-specified options given a state in a single forward pass, without autoregressively generating reasoning trajectories or textual responses. Recent evaluations cover diverse tasks but often rely on existing benchmarks, where prior exposure to test material can obscure generalization. Moreover, real-world decision making often involves long contexts, large option spaces, and complex logical dependencies, challenges that existing benchmarks do not adequately capture together. Thus, we introduce MMDM (Massive Multitask Decision Making), a benchmark of 5,448 high-quality questions across 16 task categories, combining newly constructed tasks with source-grounded recompositions and rewrites for single-select, multi-select, and soft-label decision making in fresh contexts. It covers realistic scenarios such as agent state tracking, tool and skill selection, preference judgments, and rubric scoring, with option spaces ranging from 2 to 1,024 and inputs extending to 64,817 tokens. With MMDM, we conduct a comprehensive quantitative evaluation of 28 decision models, showing that many perform well on common knowledge yet struggle with interdependent options, constrained decisions, and multi-select tasks. For example, Perplexity Decider-V1.2 reaches 78.75% Hard Single-select Accuracy on world knowledge, but only 53.95% on option logic and 47.95% on constraint planning, while the best Hard Multi-select Accuracy across all models is 36.81%. These results highlight joint reasoning, constraint-aware selection, and complete multi-select recovery as key priorities for decision model development, with MMDM providing a testbed for measuring this progress.
