papers.title: Euclidean Ramsey Theory for Lines and Finite Configurations
papers.abstract: A classical question in Euclidean Ramsey theory, posed by Erd\H{o}s, Graham, Montgomery, Rothschild, Spencer, and Straus, asks which finite configurations $X\subset\mathbb E^2$ must appear in blue under every red--blue coloring of the plane having no red pair of points distance one apart. For $m \ge 2$, let $\ell_m$ denote the line of $m$ points with consecutive points distance one apart. Tsaturian showed that $\ell_5$ is unavoidable; we improve this to $\ell_7$. Additionally, we show that in every three-coloring of the plane in which two colors contain no $\ell_2$, the third color must contain an $\ell_3$. To conclude our discussion on lines, we prove several related results on two-colorings of higher-dimensional Euclidean spaces where both colors avoid longer lines. Our methods also extend to other point configurations. In any two-coloring of the plane in which one color contains no $\ell_2$, we show that the other color must contain both a regular pentagon of side length one and a unit square together with its center. We also prove that every two-coloring of three-dimensional space contains either a monochromatic unit square or a monochromatic noncoplanar tetrahedron with four edges of length one and two of length $\sqrt{2}$. Our proofs combine Sz\'ekely's averaging inequalities for distance-avoiding sets with the Fourier-analytic and linear-programming methods of de Oliveira Filho and Vallentin, together with a theorem on rotation-invariant measures from OpenAI's recent work on the Hadwiger-Nelson problem.

authors.name: Yumo Liu
authors.institution: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China

papers.title: BARS: Budget-Aware Sequential Sampling with Refusal for Majority Identification under Unknown Distributions
papers.abstract: Repeated sampling with majority selection is an effective means of enforcing self-consistency in large language models. Recently, a variant has also been introduced that terminates early to save costs when the output distribution is favorable. But it still cannot yield a correct confidence estimate from the answer distribution. For this issue, we formalize this as majority identification under an unknown distribution with a budget and a target error rate, and propose BARS, a sequential rule certifying the top-two gap and returning an early stop, a budgeted majority vote, or a refusal when feasibility cannot be established. A refusal is a statement about the rule and its budget, not a claim that a question is unanswerable, and it tells practitioners when to widen the budget or switch models. A certified mode carries proven bounds on the joint answering error and on refusing an instance the budget could handle, while a practical mode, used in our experiments, replaces them with empirical calibration. On synthetic instances drawn from known distributions over thousands of seeds, the difficulty-driven behavior is recovered and the price of the certified mode is measured.On GSM8K the practical mode draws 22.3\% fewer samples than fixed-8 sampling over the same pool, refused questions included, at the cost of declining 18.8\% of the questions. On MATH, it greatly improves the accuracy of its output answers into 82.5\% at the cost of honestly refusing to answer half of the difficult questions that the model itself is unable to solve.

papers.title: Scott spectra of distributive continuous lattices
papers.abstract: Let \(L\) be a distributive continuous lattice. We prove that the hull--kernel topology on \(\Spec(L)\) is the Scott topology of the inclusion order if and only if \(\sigma(L^{\op})=\upsilon(L^{\op})\). The necessary implication and the algebraic case are known. We prove sufficiency for arbitrary distributive continuous lattices, thereby obtaining the spectrum characterization requested by Lawson and Mislove. The proof embeds \(L\) into a continuous lattice that is both a frame and a coframe, and transfers the Scott topology of the spectrum along the induced map of spectra.

papers.title: IntentTwin: Deconfounding Candidate Support and the Oracle-to-Deployment Gap in Offline Web Behavior Prediction
papers.abstract: Offline web-behavior benchmarks frequently insert the demonstrated action into a finite candidate set and then measure reranking. We show that this protocol can create a candidate-support confound: when the target is outside training support while all distractors are sampled from that support, support membership identifies the gold action without modeling behavior. We formalize this effect with support-identifiability rate (SIR), construct support-balanced candidate sets, and evaluate a target-free dual-path proposer that combines support retrieval with open-vocabulary DOM/LM proposals. On filtered OPeRA (4,282/469/992 train/dev/test steps), the original protocol has SIR 1.0000 on target-OOV rows and a support-only rule reaches 1.0000 OOV Exact@1. Support balancing reduces SIR to 0.0000; the strongest conditional reranker obtains 0.7214 overall Exact@1, 0.7988 on IV rows, and 0.5668 on OOV rows. The target-free dual-path system reaches Proposal Recall@16 0.6915 and end-to-end Exact@1 0.5212, compared with oracle conditional Exact@1 0.7450. On Mind2Web, the same audit yields SIR 0.2380 and an oracle-to-proposal gap of 0.2125. A 200-row semantic audit labels 0.7150 of exact-key OOV targets as semantically novel, 0.2450 as locator/string variation, and 0.0400 as ambiguous (Cohen's $\kappa=0.8173$). These measurements show why support composition must be controlled alongside candidate accuracy when offline results are used to reason about deployment.

authors.name: Shuhao Hu
authors.institution: Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications

papers.title: Trajectory-Regularized Distribution Distillation for One-Step Generation
papers.abstract: Distilling flow matching models for one-step generation generally follows two paradigms. Trajectory alignment supervises the student with the teacher's probability flow ODE, but its performance degrades under very small sampling budgets. Distribution matching directly optimizes the generated distribution, but estimating its reverse Kullback-Leibler gradient typically requires a separate network to track the evolving student score. We propose trajectory-regularized distribution distillation (TRD), which combines distribution-level and trajectory-level supervision through a momentum-mixture policy predicted in a single student forward pass. This policy serves simultaneously as a one-step generator, an estimator of the student's marginal velocity that removes the need for a second trainable network in distribution matching, and a closed-form time-dependent velocity field supervised along the teacher ODE trajectory. Experiments on SANA-1.6B and Stable Diffusion 3.5 show that TRD outperforms representative consistency and distribution matching baselines in generation quality and training efficiency for both one-step and few-step generation, with a trade-off in sample diversity.

papers.title: Divisibility graphs of semigroups as weighted poset blow-ups
papers.abstract: We develop a structural theory of divisibility graphs of arbitrary semigroups. For a semigroup $S$, let $S/{\mathcal J}$ be the poset of Green's ${\mathcal J}$-classes ordered by inclusion of principal ideals,and equip each $\mathcal {J}$-class $J$ with the weight $|J|$. We prove that the divisibility graph ${\operatorname{Div}}(S)$ is obtained from the comparability directed graph $Comp(S/{\mathcal J})$ by replacing each $\mathcal J$-class with a complete symmetric graph of order $|J|$ and by replacing each directed edge $J_u$ to $J_v$ in $Comp(S/{\mathcal J})$ with all directed edges from every element of $J_u$ to every element of $J_v$. Consequently, ${\operatorname{Div}}(S)$ is determined, up to isomorphism, by the weighted poset $(S/\mathcal {J},\{ J \}_{J\in S/{\mathcal J}})$. This yields structural descriptions of its strongly connected components, maximal unilaterally connected subgraphs. The main contribution is the reduction of divisibility graph problems to weighted quotient-poset problems. As applications, we obtain reconstruction and isomorphism criteria and prove an inheritance theorem for divisibility $D$-saturated subsemigroups.

papers.title: One Byte, One Token: Byteifying a 27B Hybrid-Attention LLM with Self-Generated Data
papers.abstract: Byte-level BPE fragments Chinese text (for Qwen3.8 on Chinese Wikipedia, 3.84 bytes per token on average; 64% of tokens are single characters) and hides spelling from the model. We ask whether an already-trained 27B subword model can be converted directly into a pure byte-level model (one byte, one token), without a patching structure or a local encoder, while keeping most of its ability. Starting from Qwen3.8-27B (48 Gated DeltaNet layers + 16 full-attention layers), we shrink the vocabulary from 248,320 to 384 entries (the 256 byte symbols already in the BPE vocabulary plus special ids), leave every other weight untouched, and continue training in a two-stage curriculum (encoding first, then reading) on 4.77 GB of supervised bytes: all dialogue/behavioral supervision is generated on-policy by the original model itself (character dictionary, word dictionary, general dialogue, coding sessions), and knowledge reading uses encyclopedia text (54% of supervised bytes). Training takes 178.6 h on 8xH200. On the same GPU and serving stack, the byte model's gap to the original falls within the paired bootstrap interval on MATH-500, HumanEval+, MMLU-Pro and non-thinking GSM8K, and it loses 4-6 points on C-Eval, thinking-mode GSM8K and non-thinking IFEval. Without thinking it leads on every character-level task (CUTE 75.2 -> 84.0, EXECUTE-zho 81.6 -> 93.9, our Chinese character suite 54.4 -> 64.0), but lookup knowledge about Chinese characters such as pronunciation and stroke count drops, and thinking does not recover it. The cost is throughput: per-step speed is identical, but each step yields 3-5x less output; Chinese characters per second is about 1/4 of the original, and prefill at 64K bytes is 6.5x slower. We also document four byte-model failure modes (greedy runaway, sampling breaking UTF-8, ineffective penalty terms on a small vocabulary, repetition) and their fixes.

papers.title: When to Start Denoising? Adaptive Denoising Entry for Generative Video Compression
papers.abstract: Generative video compression offers a promising solution for compressing and reconstructing videos under extremely low bitrate constraints, among which the diffusion-based solutions still achieve the best performance by providing the powerful generative latent prior. However, their effectiveness critically depends on when the compressed latent is introduced into the diffusion process, which directly governs the trade-off between reconstruction fidelity and perceptual realism. To address this limitation, we identify denoising start-timestep selection as a key factor governing this trade-off and formulate it as a geometric optimization problem. Based on this formulation, we propose a novel adaptive diffusion entry method for generative video compression (ADE-GVC), the first timestep-aware generative video compression framework, featuring a lightweight predictor that estimates an adaptive denoising start point from the compressed latent. A temporal adapter further extracts compression-aware conditions and injects them into a pretrained video diffusion model, enabling the reconstruction of videos with both high fidelity and realism. More importantly, we observe a strong quantitative relationship between the predicted timesteps and the distortion between the original and compressed latents, providing empirical support for our optimization formulation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ADE-GVC achieves the state-of-the-art performance on perceptual metrics and substantially improves reconstruction realism over existing generative video compression methods. Notably, our ADE-GVC achieves an average bitrate savings of 40.99\% (on DISTS) and 95.24\% (on PSNR) compared to the latest open-source baseline GLC-Video.

papers.title: Critical geometry of triconnected clusters in percolation
papers.abstract: We investigate the critical geometry of triconnected clusters in percolation, which remain connected after the removal of any two sites. By combining biconnected-component decomposition with the SPQR decomposition of graphs, we develop an efficient algorithm for identifying triconnected clusters in large systems. Extensive Monte Carlo simulations yield estimates of the fractal dimension $d_3=1.2308(3)$, $1.083(2)$, and $0.77(2)$ in dimensions $d=2$, $3$, and $4$, respectively, revealing a systematic decrease of $d_3$ with increasing $d$. In dimension $d=6$, the largest triconnected cluster grows logarithmically with system size, whereas on complete graphs, corresponding to $d=\infty$, it approaches a finite size. Both behaviors indicate a vanishing fractal dimension, $d_3=0$, for $d\geq6$. Furthermore, the singular contribution to the susceptibility-like quantity associated with the second moment of the triconnected-cluster size distribution scales as $\chi\sim L^{2d_3-d}$. Consequently, it vanishes for $d\geq3$, leaving a finite asymptotic susceptibility, in contrast to the divergent behavior observed in standard percolation.

papers.title: Scaling Shapley Energy Attribution to Large LLM Batches
papers.abstract:
LLM services have become essential infrastructure for applications such as chat assistants and coding agents. Service providers need to attribute resource consumption to individual requests for purposes such as billing. Among these resources, energy is a key metric for assessing the cost of serving each request. However, serving engines batch requests together, and GPUs report only aggregate energy consumption. Providers typically estimate each request's share in proportion to its token consumption, but this approach can produce substantially unfair estimates. The Shapley value provides a principled solution to fair energy allocation, but computing it directly requires $2^N-1$ GPU runs for $N$ requests, which is infeasible for large batches.
  To address this problem, we propose StepSplit. Across GPU generations, we observe that the energy consumed by each inference step, a forward pass over a batch, consists of a shared energy, largely due to reading model weights, and a request-specific energy. We derive a closed-form Shapley value: each request is charged its own energy plus an equal part of the shared energy of every step in which it participates. A microbenchmark of 2.5-17.8 minutes calibrates both parts of the step energy once per model and GPU configuration. Under static batching, StepSplit uses this closed form in a single pass over the scheduler log. Under continuous batching, removing a request can change how the remaining requests are batched, so StepSplit adds a correction to the closed form, computed by replaying the scheduler on a CPU. We evaluate StepSplit against Shapley values measured using 529,513 GPU runs. Under static batching with batch sizes of 8-256, StepSplit achieves an $L_1$ error of 0.4-4.3%, compared with 13.4-61.3% for token-proportional allocation. Under continuous batching with 8-128 requests, the corresponding errors are 0.5-6.4% and 20.6-71.7%.

papers.title: SFU-Sim: Bit-Exact Reverse Engineering of NVIDIA MUFU and Validation of PTX Paths
papers.abstract: Reproducing the numerical behavior of a GPU requires predicting the exact output of special function instructions. Vendor documents give only the function semantics and error bounds. These do not fix the output bit pattern. We present SFU-Sim, which builds bit-exact models of NVIDIA multi-function unit (MUFU) instructions by black-box reverse engineering on real GPUs. We first model a single bare MUFU instruction. We then add the surrounding operations found in the disassembly to model full PTX paths. The model covers 12 common MUFU forms and two BF16 forms on the tested Blackwell GPU. Using SIN/COS as a complete case study, we show how we analyze the PTX-to-SASS compilation path and recover the segment structure, the equivalent coefficient tables, and the finite-width arithmetic. On NVIDIA GPUs of three architectures (Ampere, Ada Lovelace, and Blackwell), we exhaustively compare every tested PTX path over its specified input domain. FP16 and FP32 paths cover all $2^{16}$ and $2^{32}$ input encodings, respectively. The model output matches the hardware bit for bit, with zero mismatches. SFU-Sim computes each output directly from its input. It needs neither a lookup table of all inputs nor access to a physical GPU. It can serve as a bit-exact special function component for instruction simulators. It can also serve as an arithmetic reference for hardware design and functional verification that target the same numerical behavior. SFU-Sim and its validation programs are open source at https://github.com/hzX40000000/SFU-Sim

authors.name: Haozhi Xie
authors.institution: State Key Laboratory of Optoelectronic Materials and Technology

papers.title: An Accelerated Dynamic Stochastic Primal-Dual Method for Multi-stage Stochastic Optimization
papers.abstract: We consider multi-stage stochastic optimization problems with smooth convex stage costs and linear linking constraints. Dynamic stochastic approximation (DSA), a stochastic first-order method, uses a recursive structure whose memory requirement grows only linearly with the number of stages. Its implementation, however, requires an exact solution of the proximal subproblem associated with the stage cost, and this subproblem often admits no closed-form solution. To resolve this issue, we develop an accelerated dynamic stochastic primal-dual (A-DSPD) framework that retains the recursive value-function structure and only requires the gradient of the stage cost. Within this framework, each stagewise saddle-point subproblem is solved by an inexact accelerated stochastic primal-dual method (iASPD), which applies Nesterov acceleration to the smooth stage cost and uses recursively generated stochastic $\epsilon$-subgradients for the nonsmooth downstream value function. For the stochastic composite saddle-point problem, after $N$ primal-dual updates, iASPD yields optimality and feasibility bounds in which the contribution of the smooth stage cost decays at a faster rate $O(1/N^2)$, while the terms associated with stochastic $\epsilon$-subgradients of the nonsmooth value function decay as $O(1/\sqrt{N})$, up to the prescribed oracle inexactness. We also develop bounds for the stochastic $\epsilon$-subgradient estimators and the dual iterates, which yield complexity guarantees for A-DSPD. Specifically, A-DSPD computes an $\epsilon$-solution using $O(1/\epsilon^4)$ sampled scenarios and $O(1/\epsilon^5)$ primal-dual updates for three-stage problems. We further extend the method and its convergence analysis to problems with an arbitrary finite number of stages. Numerical experiments on three-stage stochastic portfolio models illustrate the empirical advantage of the proposed method.

authors.name: Bin Zhou
authors.institution: University of Tennessee Health Science Center

papers.title: Regularity Estimates for a Nonhomogeneous Free Boundary Interface Problem
papers.abstract:
In this work, we establish regularity properties for minimizers of a novel nonhomogeneous interface problem with a free boundary, formulated in Orlicz-Sobolev spaces. The nonlinear terms fulfill Lieberman-type structural assumptions with subcritical growth. The principal difficulties stem from the nonhomogeneous framework and the lack of suitable representation formulas. Our findings extend recent contributions in the field and provide new insights even in the particular case of the Laplacian.
  Keywords: Free Boundary Problems; Orlicz-Spaces; Nonhomogeneous Operator; Transmission Problem; Regularity.

papers.title: Convex monohedral tilings: a sharp neighbor bound and rigidity in the equality case
papers.abstract: We study both side-to-side and non-side-to-side convex monohedral tilings of the Euclidean plane in which every tile has the same number of neighbors. Reflections are allowed, point contacts count as neighbors, and no periodicity assumption is imposed. Combining boundary estimates for sums of face curvatures, angle-incidence counts and side-length matching, we prove that the common neighbor number satisfies $N\le21$ and classify all equality cases. Equality holds precisely when the prototile is a $30^\circ$-$30^\circ$-$120^\circ$ triangle and the entire tiling is similar to the central subdivision of the standard equilateral triangular tiling. This resolves the open problem on the maximum common number of neighbors recorded in Adams's The Tiling Book.

papers.title: MISO-BR: An Open Corpus for Misogyny Detection in Brazilian Portuguese
papers.abstract: Misogyny is among the most prevalent forms of online hate speech directed at Brazilian users, yet open and auditable resources dedicated to it in Brazilian Portuguese remain scarce. We introduce MISO-BR, an open, documented and versioned corpus of 896 balanced social media texts annotated for binary misogyny, released with its construction protocol and reproducible baselines. The corpus combines lexicon- and target-guided scraping from X with items imported from OLID-BR, a large language model triage stage whose prompt and decoding parameters are released, and manual annotation by three annotators following a written guide. Inter-annotator reliability reaches a Fleiss' kappa of 0.788 over 816 items. Under a single fixed protocol we compare four classical classifiers (Multinomial and Bernoulli Naive Bayes, a linear SVM and a random forest) with fine-tuned BERTimbau Base and Large. The classical models cluster between 0.651 and 0.676 macro-F1 and are precision-oriented but recall-poor. The transformers reach 0.833 macro-F1 and accuracy (Wilson 95% CI for accuracy [0.77, 0.88]), a gap of roughly 16 points, while Base and Large are indistinguishable on the test set despite a 2.6x difference in training cost. We argue that the value of the resource lies less in its headline scores than in the auditability of its pipeline, and we state three limits that users must reckon with: the artificial class balance, whose effect on precision under realistic prevalence we quantify; the association between provenance and label, which the released source field makes measurable; and the selection bias induced by lexicon-guided sampling and automatic triage. The corpus, annotation guide, models and experimental scripts are publicly available.

papers.title: Exploring Post-Hoc Disentanglement of Audio Foundation Models for Music Similarity
papers.abstract: Audio foundation models like CLAP, MuQ, and MERT excel at capturing general musical similarity. On the other hand, their entangled latent spaces limit interpretability and fine-grained attribute control. Conditional Similarity Networks (CSN) address this by pairing a backbone representation model with learned masks that gate the embedding space into attribute-specific subspaces. However, existing methods train the backbone from scratch, rather than leveraging pretrained foundation models. We instead present a systematic study of post-hoc disentanglement, adapting CSN to gate frozen pretrained embeddings. We evaluate adding trainable parameters to adapt the embedding under different masking and pooling regimes across two datasets. Our findings show that minimal adaptation capacity is sufficient for post-hoc gating to improve both attribute-specific disentanglement and overall retrieval performance, while pooling, masking, and depth choices yield limited additional gains.

papers.title: A Variable-metric Inexact Progressive Hedging Algorithm with a Lagged Stopping Criterion for Multistage Stochastic Variational Inequalities
papers.abstract: The progressive hedging algorithm (PHA) solves multistage stochastic variational inequalities (SVIs) by independently solving regularized scenario subproblems and enforcing nonanticipativity through primal-dual updates. Since these subproblems are often solved iteratively, practical implementations need stopping criteria that control errors while preserving convergence. We propose iVMPHA-Lag, a variable-metric inexact PHA with a lagged stopping criterion for monotone SVIs. The method allows scenario block metrics to vary across outer iterations while remaining compatible with nonanticipativity. For each scenario, an error budget combines a positive fraction of the previous budget with a progress measure from the preceding outer iteration. This gives a stopping tolerance fixed before the inner iterations begin, so each scenario can check its criterion independently without a prescribed summable tolerance sequence. With positive initial budgets and a positive inexactness parameter, we prove finite inner termination provided the inner solver produces valid approximations whose residual and enlargement errors tend to zero. Under suitable conditions, we establish global convergence of the primal-dual iterates and local $R$-linear convergence under metric subregularity at the limit point. Numerical experiments on synthetic strongly monotone box-constrained SVIs show that iVMPHA-Lag with adaptive metrics uses fewer scenario evaluations and less time on average than exact PHA and the competing inexact methods among the tested configurations in all four baseline regimes. Its average time advantage over the competing inexact methods persists across the tested problem sizes. Further comparisons show that metric adaptation improves efficiency over the fixed scalar configuration, while lagged stopping and positive budget retention reduce inner computational work.

papers.title: The Fermat--Torricelli problem under isosceles orthogonality-type conditions
papers.abstract:
The location problem studied by Weber \cite{Weber} leads to the Fermat--Torricelli problem of minimizing sums of distances. Ben\'{i}tez, Fern\'{a}ndez and Soriano \cite{BFS} proved that a real normed space of dimension at least three is an inner-product space if and only if every triple of points has a Fermat--Torricelli median in its convex hull. Pakhrou \cite{Pakhrou} showed that it suffices to test equilateral triangles. We establish a characterization using triangles $\{0,x,y\}$ satisfying
  \[
  \|x+y\|=\lambda\|x-y\|,\qquad \forall\,\lambda>2/3,
  \]
  with the parameter fixed in each characterization. The case of parameter one gives an isosceles orthogonality criterion. The proof combines radial rescaling with the transfer of planar minimality to the ambient space, without completeness or regularity assumptions on the norm.

papers.title: Projection-Based Partial Correlation Inference Beyond Sparsity
papers.abstract: Valid inference for partial correlation in high-dimensional Gaussian models is challenging when the conditioning variables exhibit dense dependence and conventional sparsity assumptions are inappropriate. We develop a target-specific projection framework for estimating and testing a population partial correlation without requiring coordinate sparsity. A population quadratic criterion characterizes the information retained by a linear reduction and is maximized by a one-dimensional projection. Under a rank-one alignment condition, this optimal projection preserves the original partial correlation. To obtain a feasible procedure, we estimate the optimal direction using diagonal ridge regularization on an independent training sample. Under conditions on regularized effective dimension and target-specific ridge bias, we establish a quantitative direction-estimation rate in the covariance-induced prediction norm. We further show that, under alignment, the induced partial-correlation error is second order in the direction error. These results yield oracle equivalence and asymptotic normality for the feasible split-sample estimator, as well as asymptotically valid testing of the original zero-partial-correlation null. Exact finite-sample \(F\)-calibration holds under the projected null. An explicit coordinate-dense Gaussian model verifies the required rates even when the dimension exceeds the sample size. Numerical experiments illustrate the finite-sample performance of the proposed procedures.

papers.title: Unified Far-field and Near-field Codebook Design for XL-array Systems
papers.abstract: While extremely large-scale antenna arrays (XL-arrays) hold immense promise for next-generation wireless networks, the paradigm shift encompassing new near-field communications renders conventional discrete Fourier transform (DFT)-based Type-I codebooks inefficient. Meanwhile, existing near-field alternatives usually impose prohibitively high storage and/or feedback burdens. To tackle these challenges, we propose in this letter a unified codebook applicable to both far-field and near-field XL-array systems. Our key idea is to express the near-field channel steering vector in an equivalent form, which is a Hadamard product of an angular vector and a curvature-related vector. This new representation allows direct reuse of the legacy Type-I codebook for angle quantization, while only a lightweight auxiliary codebook is newly added for additional curvature quantization. Subsequently, we optimize the auxiliary curvature codebook by maximizing the average beamforming gain given the information of user distribution. By leveraging the local monotonicity of the beamforming gain with respect to curvature mismatch, the optimization problem is further reduced to a quantization-error minimization problem, for which suboptimal curvature codewords are obtained. Numerical results demonstrate that the proposed unified codebook achieves near-optimal beamforming performance that approaches its upper bound based on perfect channel state information (CSI), while significantly reducing the required feedback overhead as compared to various benchmark schemes.

authors.name: Changsheng You
authors.institution: Southern University of Science and Technology

papers.title: $\mathbb{R}$-linear unitary preservers of C$^*$-algebras
papers.abstract: We study the structure of general $\mathbb{R}$-linear unitary preservers between unital C$^*$-algebras. Representing any unital $\mathbb{R}$-linear unitary preserver in terms of three $\mathbb{R}$-linear maps on the self-adjoint part of the domain yields a canonical decomposition into a Jordan-type summand and a purely non-Jordan summand. When the domain is abelian, we completely classify the purely non-Jordan summand via type $\mathrm{I}_2$ JW-algebras. For unital C$^*$-algebras with no two-dimensional irreducible representations, we characterize a natural class of purely non-Jordan unitary preservers governed by pairs of Jordan $*$-homomorphisms.

authors.name: Wenming Wu
authors.institution: Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences & Peking Union Medical College

authors.name: Wei Yuan
authors.institution: Shaanxi University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Euclidean and Hermitian Self-Orthogonal Codes from Divisible Codes
papers.abstract: Self-orthogonality and divisibility are two fundamental properties of linear codes, and the relationship between them has long been of interest. Huffman and Pless (2003) showed that every binary \(4\)-divisible code is Euclidean self-orthogonal, that a ternary code is Euclidean self-orthogonal if and only if it is \(3\)-divisible, and that a quaternary code is Hermitian self-orthogonal if and only if it is \(2\)-divisible. The general case remained open for a long time. In 2024, Li and Heng settled the odd-characteristic case, proving that every \(p\)-divisible code over \(\F_{p^m}\), with \(p\) odd, that contains the all-one vector is Euclidean self-orthogonal. In this paper we treat the even-characteristic case: we prove that every \(4\)-divisible code over \(\F_{2^m}\) containing the all-one vector is Euclidean self-orthogonal. We also prove that, for every prime \(p\), every \(p\)-divisible linear code over \(\F_{q^2}\), where \(q=p^m\), that contains the all-one vector is Hermitian self-orthogonal. These criteria make the construction of self-orthogonal codes from divisible codes simple and efficient. As applications, we recover the known Euclidean and Hermitian self-orthogonality of generalized Reed--Muller codes and obtain several infinite families of new Euclidean and Hermitian self-orthogonal codes, which give rise to infinite families of quantum codes with excellent parameters.

papers.title: Can KV Cache Be Reused Across Model Updates? A DeepSeek-V4-Flash Case Study
papers.abstract: Reusing key--value (KV) caches across language model updates could avoid repeated computation of shared context, but changes in model weights raise a fundamental question about what these caches preserve. We investigate direct cache reuse across four model updates, with a detailed study of DeepSeek-V4-Flash to Flash-0731. Our central finding is that caches can retain useful task information without faithfully reproducing the updated model's behavior. Retrieval accuracy varies substantially across updates, ranging from near-native performance to large losses. With source caches already available, reuse achieves median time-to-first-token speedups of $2.10$--$5.08\times$ on three longer-prefix QA benchmarks. To characterize the behavioral differences behind these outcomes, we introduce Functional Cache Divergence, which compares next-token distributions under reused and native caches. Direct KV cache reuse better preserves native model behavior in natural-text continuation, whereas compatibility degrades with increasing prefix length in single-token retrieval tasks. Answer-margin analyses help explain how correct retrieval decisions survive substantial internal state changes. Yet even agreement on the first generated token does not ensure agreement in answer content or stopping behavior. These findings establish task utility and fidelity to native inference as distinct criteria for evaluating cross-version KV cache reuse.

papers.title: Geodesically Semiconvex Approximations in the Wasserstein Space and Applications to Flow Interchange
papers.abstract:
We study the approximation of functionals by geodesically semiconvex functionals in the Wasserstein space, with applications to dissipation estimates along the Jordan-Kinderlehrer-Otto (JKO) scheme.
  For the potential and interaction energies, the approximation problem reduces to approximate the underlying potentials in Euclidean space. For the internal energies, we construct approximations by decomposing truncated functionals into differences of geodesically convex functionals and applying Moreau-Yosida regularization to the second component. Under suitable assumptions, we establish strong quantitative convergence of the gradient of the first variation in weighted \(L^2\) space. These approximations may enable us to obtain dissipation estimates along the JKO scheme for functionals that are not geodesically semiconvex. We illustrate this approach by deriving an \(L^{m+1}\) bound for the JKO scheme of fast diffusion equation, and by establishing internal energy dissipation for the JKO scheme of Fokker-Planck equation.

papers.title: Uncovering the Blind Spots of OKS-mAP: A Unified Protocol for Occlusion, Joint-Angle, and Temporal Evaluation of 2D Pose Estimators
papers.abstract: The dominant metric for 2D human pose estimation, OKS-mAP, has three blind spots: it does not distinguish visible from occluded keypoints, does not measure joint-angle error, and is silent on the temporal stability of tracking-free per-frame inference. We propose a supplementary protocol with three modules: (M1) OKS-mAP stratified by ground-truth visibility, with Delta_occ = mAP(v=1) - mAP(full), quantifying how much the aggregate metric masks occlusion-specific differences; (M2) joint-angle error (RMSE/MAE/P95) plus knee-valgus detection consistency; (M3) frame-to-frame displacement, median-filter residual jitter, and jump rate, before and after OneEuro smoothing. We ran it on four datasets (COCO val2017, CrowdPose, OCHuman, PoseTrack18) and four models from two architecture families (YOLO11s-pose, an occlusion-domain fine-tuned variant, ViTPose-B/L), under a common detector-free oracle protocol and an open-source harness. Delta_occ is negative in every combination (-0.19 to -0.47): aggregate mAP overestimates occluded-scene performance in every tested combination. Joint-angle error is amplified in occluded layers; angle metrics reveal differences mAP cannot localize, e.g., the smaller occlusion-trained model significantly outperforming a larger transformer in occluded elbows. On PoseTrack18 val, raw jitter matched between the two YOLO models; pixel-domain OneEuro smoothing cut jump rates 9-10% at no matched-scope AP cost; residual jitter persists after detector removal; the transformer pair's jump rate is significantly lower; smoothing benefits replicate across architectures. Stratified mAP tracks full mAP closely (sign-consistency 1.0, 12/12), serving magnitude diagnosis rather than re-ranking; angle-metric difference vectors (especially knee) partially diverge, suggesting independent information. The protocol and harness are open-sourced, complementing rather than replacing OKS-mAP.

papers.title: Geometric Hammocks: Surface Laminations and the Ziegler Spectrum of String Algebras
papers.abstract: We give the first complete topological, geometric, and ergodic classification of the Ziegler spectrum $\Zg(\Lambda)$ of a non-domestic string algebra $\Lambda$ over an algebraically closed field of arbitrary cardinality, via a dictionary with Thurston's theory of geodesic laminations on a cusped hyperbolic surface. This is a model-theoretic counterpart of Haiden--Katzarkov--Kontsevich's realization (\emph{Publ.\ Math.\ IHES} 2017) of stability conditions on the bounded derived category of a gentle algebra via flat surfaces: pure-injective modules correspond to admissible geodesics, and the Ziegler topology to a corridor quotient of Chabauty space. Three consequences follow. The Krull--Gabriel dimension equals the surface's topological accumulation depth, and the string closure with all higher Cantor--Bendixson strata is globally homeomorphic to an explicit corridor space, with the pushout map to $\Zg(\Lambda)$ a homeomorphism if and only if $\Lambda$ is domestic. Prefix-free dyadic blocks in the geometric perfect core verify Puninski's cardinality-free two-chain criterion, resolving the open problem of superdecomposable pure-injectives over uncountable fields for all non-domestic string and special biserial algebras. Three purely algebraic invariants on the perfect core---localized pp-shape entropy, a $K_0$-weighted pressure function satisfying an algebraic Ruelle--Walters Variational Principle, and a pp-bifurcation index with a Gauss--Bonnet simplicity obstruction---strictly separate uncountable iso-entropic and iso-pressure families, and the inverse limit of the quotient pp-lattice recovers the transversal Cantor cross-section.

papers.title: SpatialSR: Spatial Resolution-Centric Pipeline for Arbitrary-Scale Remote Sensing Super-Resolution
papers.abstract: Although remote sensing image arbitrary-scale super-resolution (RSI-ASSR) methods support reconstruction at arbitrary or continuous scales, they predominantly condition on the relative scale factor and have not sufficiently investigated the absolute spatial resolution itself as a reconstruction prior, thereby disregarding the inherent spatial context of objects, which frequently leads to spatial-related distortions and compromised performance in downstream remote sensing applications. To address these challenges, we introduce SpatialSR, a SRe-centric arbitrary-scale RSISR method that leverages the spatial resolution (SRe) of remote sensing images (RSI) as an essential prior for super-resolution reconstruction. Distinct from existing SR methods, SpatialSR aims to restore high-resolution remote sensing images with a target SRe (typically set to 0.1m/pixel to align with the metadata of commonly used downstream task datasets). Specifically, we design a Spatial Resolution Estimation Module (SREM) to estimate the SRe of low-resolution (LR) images, thereby dynamically determining the required arbitrary scaling factor. Next, we employ a pretrained SRe-to-image diffusion model to extract SRe-specified texture-style codes, which are further incorporated into a carefully designed Resolution-aware Style Consistency Module (RSCM) to constrain the SRe-aware texture consistency of reconstructed images. Furthermore, to overcome the high computational expense inherent in diffusion-based SR methods, we wrap the iterative diffusion process as a Trajectory Consistency (TC) loss, which enables comparable reconstructed texture quality of the generative model in SpatialSR within a single step. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed SpatialSR achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on commonly used RSISR and downstream (image classification and segmentation tasks) datasets.

papers.title: Minimum Synthesis Time for Single-Deletion Correcting Codes of Prescribed Size
papers.abstract: DNA is a promising medium for data storage, but the high cost of DNA synthesis remains a major obstacle to its widespread deployment. In the reference-based synthesis model, synthesis time is measured by the length of the reference sequence. Previous studies have analyzed code sizes under synthesis-time constraints and constructed cost-constrained codes, including codes that correct deletions. In this paper, we study the minimum synthesis time for codes of prescribed size, considering both unrestricted codes and single-deletion correcting codes. We establish finite-length lower bounds valid for arbitrary reference sequences and upper bounds using existing $q$-ary differential VT codes. For fixed $q\geq3$, $A>0$, and $R\in(0,1)$, we determine the minimum synthesis time up to an $O(1)$ term when the code size is $M_n=\lfloor Aq^{Rn}\rfloor$. The corresponding redundancy is $(1-R)n\log_2q-\log_2A+o(1)$ bits. In particular, for these code sizes, the minimum synthesis time for single-deletion correcting codes exceeds that for unrestricted codes by a term proportional to $\ln n$, and we determine its coefficient. We also derive upper and lower bounds for code sizes $\lfloor q^n/(nq^{s_n})\rfloor$, where $s_n\to\infty$ and $s_n=o(n)$. These sizes correspond to redundancy $\log_2 n+s_n\log_2q+o(1)$ bits. For code sizes $\lfloor q^n/(nq^c)\rfloor$ with fixed constant $c$, the redundancy is $\log_2 n+c\log_2q+o(1)$ bits. We give conditions under which single-deletion correcting codes exist or do not exist for all sufficiently large $n$, together with bounds on the minimum synthesis time. These results show how code size and the single-deletion correcting constraint affect synthesis time and provide theoretical guidance for the construction of cost-constrained codes.

authors.name: Wenjun Yu
