papers.title: Newton non-degenerate holomorphic foliations and their separatrices
papers.abstract: In this paper we study germs of holomorphic foliations in the complex plane that are Newton non-degenerate. This is an algebraic condition attached to the Newton polygon of the foliation, analogous to the one defined by Kouchnirenko for analytic curves and, more generally, hypersurfaces. As in this case, the condition of Newton non-degeneracy for foliations can be identified through the comparison of two numerical invariants: the Newton number - a computation involving simple geometric data of the Newton polygon - and the Milnor number. The Newton number is never greater than the Milnor number, and the foliation is Newton non-degenerate if and only if they are equal. The assumption that a foliation is Newton non-degenerate imposes conditions on its set of separatrices. We prove that, under this hypothesis, the foliation has no weak separatrices and, hence, all its separatrices are analytic. We also give a description of the set of separatrices of a Newton non-degenerate foliation, which is sufficient to characterize the foliation as Newton non-degenerate when it is of generalized curve type. This allows us to prove that the property of being Newton non-degenerate is topologically invariant for foliations of generalized curve type.

papers.title: Uniform symmetric spectral finiteness of semialgebraic cones
papers.abstract: Cone-constrained eigenvalues of a matrix are defined through a complementarity problem constrained by a closed convex cone. We show that every closed semialgebraic convex cone is uniformly symmetrically spectrally finite; that is, the cone spectra, the sets of the cone-constrained eigenvalues, of symmetric matrices relative to the cone are uniformly finite with respect to the matrices. The uniform bound is explicit, and as an application, we derive a uniform bound for the cardinality of spectra of symmetric matrices relative to L\"{o}wner cones. In addition, using the uniform finiteness of cone spectra, we also show the uniform finiteness of the number of singular values relative to two closed semialgebraic convex cones. For non-semialgebraic cones, we observe two contrasting phenomena. On the one hand, we show that the exponential cone is uniformly symmetrically spectrally finite. On the other hand, we provide a closed non-semialgebraic convex cone such that the associated cone spectra of symmetric matrices are finite but are not uniformly finite.

papers.title: Feedback Design in the Shadow of Strategic Communication
papers.abstract: We study optimal feedback design when evaluations affect subsequent strategic communication within organizations. A firm designs public feedback about an employee's potential before the employee communicates private information about project-specific circumstances to a manager. While more informative feedback helps the manager make better decisions, it can also intensify preference conflicts and undermine the credibility of subsequent communication. We characterize the optimal feedback policy. First, full disclosure is either optimal for all prior beliefs or strictly suboptimal for all of them. In particular, it is optimal when preference conflicts are sufficiently small or sufficiently large. Second, when full disclosure is suboptimal, no disclosure is optimal for some priors, while partial disclosure is strictly optimal for some priors if and only if the number of messages in equilibrium communication varies with posterior beliefs. Third, optimal partial disclosure can conclusively identify low-potential employees when high potential is rare, but high-potential employees when it is common.

papers.title: Joint Activation and Weight Quantization for Learned Image Compression
papers.abstract: Learned image compression (LIC) models achieve competitive rate-distortion performance with increasingly large networks, making network quantization important for efficient deployment. Directly quantizing LIC models remains difficult in post-training quantization (PTQ) because compression performance is highly sensitive to quantization noise. Existing methods typically focus on optimizing either the weights or the activations, resulting in substantial rate-distortion degradation. To address this limitation, we introduce a two-stage pipeline that uses SmoothQuant to balance activation and weight ranges, followed by GPTQ to adapt the transformed weights. The proposed joint search framework optimizes the balancing transformation and adapted weights under the rate-distortion objective, accounting for the coupling between the two stages. Experiments across multiple LIC architectures and activation quantization configurations show that the joint search strategy consistently reduces rate-distortion degradation after quantization.

papers.title: The strongly local part of nonlinear Dirichlet structures and its energy measures
papers.abstract: This paper substantially extends the results of Sasaya (2026, JFA): we propose a framework for nonlinear generalizations of regular Dirichlet forms and prove that each energy in this framework has a largest strongly local part. We also prove the existence and uniqueness of canonical energy measures of this part, which satisfy convexity and locality properties and, under additional assumptions, certain chain rules in one variable. In particular, our framework requires neither $p$-homogeneity nor strong locality. Moreover, under a Ball--Carlen--Lieb-type upper bound, we prove more detailed chain rules for the directional derivatives of these energy measures. Our framework is applicable both to $p$-energy forms on fractals and to a class of symmetric nonlinear Dirichlet forms in the sense of Cipriani and Grillo~\cite{CG2003}, including those of Orlicz--Sobolev and variable-exponent Sobolev type.

papers.title: Online Graph Coloring: Competitive Ratios Separating Randomized and Deterministic Algorithms
papers.abstract:
We study online coloring, focusing on the competitive ratio. The best previously known results were (1) a lower bound of $\Omega(n / \log^2 n)$ for both deterministic and randomized algorithms by Halld\'{o}rsson and Szegedy (1994), (2) an upper bound of $O(n / \log n)$ for randomized algorithms by Halld\'{o}rsson (1997), and (3) an upper bound of $O(n / \log \log n)$ for deterministic algorithms by Kawarabayashi, Yoneda, and Yoneda (2025). In this paper, we improve these results as follows:
  1. A new lower bound of $\Omega(n / \log n)$ for deterministic algorithms.
  2. A new upper bound of $O(n (\log \log n)^2 / \log^2 n)$ for randomized algorithms.
  3. A new upper bound of $O(n / (\log \log n)^{2-\varepsilon})$ for deterministic algorithms for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$.
  For randomized algorithms, we nearly close the gap between the lower and upper bounds; the remaining gap is only $O((\log \log n)^2)$.
  We establish the asymptotic separation between randomized and deterministic online graph coloring. Against an oblivious adversary, a polynomial-time randomized algorithm achieves a competitive ratio asymptotically smaller than any deterministic algorithm can guarantee, even with unlimited computation.

papers.title: Elliptic hypergeometric sum/integrals for orthogonal groups and Seiberg duality on the lens space
papers.abstract: We derive new transformation formulas for elliptic hypergeometric sum/integrals associated with the orthogonal groups $\mathrm{SO}(N)$. The sum/integrals are written in terms of the lens elliptic gamma function, which depends on an integer $r\geq 1$ in addition to the usual complex variables, and they reduce to the elliptic hypergeometric integrals of Spiridonov and Vartanov for $r=1$. The derivation uses the $BC_n\leftrightarrow BC_{\tilde n}$ transformation formula proven in our previous paper, together with a duplication formula for the lens elliptic gamma function proven here. The duplication formula takes a different form depending on whether $r$ is even or odd. Physically, the new transformations show that the supersymmetric lens indices on $S^1\times S^3/\mathbb{Z}_r$ of the 4d $\mathcal{N}=1$ $\mathrm{SO}(N)$ and $\mathrm{SO}(N_f-N+4)$ gauge theories related by Seiberg duality are equal for odd $r$. For even $r$, where the lens index depends on the global form of the gauge group, they show the equality of the contributions from flat connections whose holonomies lie in a common maximal torus. The $BC_n$ formula itself gives the corresponding statement for the symplectic groups.

papers.title: A proof of the constant-width numerical range conjecture
papers.abstract: We prove the conjecture of Chien, Nakazato, and Meng that the numerical range of a finite complex matrix has constant width $d$ if and only if it is a closed disk of radius $d/2$, with a singleton allowed when $d=0$. For $d>0$, the characteristic polynomial of the associated Hermitian pencil and its translate by $d$ have a nonconstant common divisor over $\mathbb{C}(\zeta)$. At points on the unit circle where the factorization can be evaluated, every root of the common divisor equals the smallest eigenvalue. A coefficient of the divisor thus gives a rational formula for that eigenvalue. The characteristic equation forces this rational function to be a Laurent polynomial with exponents in $\{-1,0,1\}$. Antipodal symmetry then makes the midpoint of the extreme eigenvalues a first harmonic, giving the support function of a disk. We also obtain the corresponding quadratic factor of the Kippenhahn polynomial.

papers.title: Ratio-of-mediator-probability weighting for causal mediation analysis: estimation, extensions, and practical guidance
papers.abstract: Ratio-of-mediator-probability weighting (RMPW) estimates natural direct and indirect effects by reweighting mediator distributions across treatment conditions rather than modeling the outcome, thereby accommodating treatment-by-mediator interaction. This article brings existing RMPW methods together within a common estimation framework, incorporates a heteroskedastic normal model for continuous mediators, and extends two-step variance estimation to multiple parametric weight components. The framework is illustrated using a national health survey to decompose disparities in cigarette smoking by sexual-minority status and a randomized welfare-to-work experiment to examine pathways from program assignment through employment to maternal depressive symptoms. Targeted simulations evaluate model specification, alternative weighting strategies, treatment-selection adjustment, weight stability, variance estimation, and continuous treatments. Parametric RMPW performed well when models were adequately specified and weights were stable, but correct specification alone did not prevent unstable estimation from concentrated weights. Stratification-based weighting provided some robustness to model misspecification. Standard errors that treated estimated weights as fixed were unreliable, whereas two-step and bootstrap inference performed well under appropriate conditions. The results provide practical guidance for selecting weighting strategies, diagnosing instability, and conducting inference. The methods are implemented in the community-contributed Stata command mmwsmed.

papers.title: FERN: Cross-Benchmark Table Retrieval for Text-to-SQL with Frozen Retrievers and Learned Ranking
papers.abstract: Text-to-SQL systems over large pooled catalogs must first retrieve the tables a question needs. We compare against the published table recall of RASL, which uses Claude 3.5 models to extract keywords and select tables, on pooled BIRD, Spider, and Fiben catalogs. FERN (Feature-Engineered Ranking with No generative LLM) instead fuses three frozen retrievers into 100 candidates, describes each with up to 120 features, and reorders them with LightGBM rankers fitted once on BIRD's training questions. On Spider, where it was not fitted, its candidate pool alone reaches RASL's published recall at fifteen tables (98.0), and the ranker raises the share of questions with every gold table in the top five (complete@5) from 83.9% to 95.6%. At five tables, FERN's recall is within one point of RASL's on Spider (96.7 vs 97.0) and on BIRD with its evidence hints (96.6 vs 97.5), and 8.2 points below on BIRD without them (89.3). On 121 real BEAVER questions, without BEAVER fitting, its recall at fifteen (82.1) falls between two BEAVER-trained retrievers (80.8, 84.5), but its complete@15 is below both (49.6 vs 54.5 and 62.0). On Fiben, it falls far short at fifteen tables (54.2 vs 69.2, different question sets), although its recall at fifty is numerically close to RASL's question-only retrieval result (80.7 vs 79.4). On BIRD dev with evidence, non-retrieval features raise complete@5 by 7.7 points over retrieval signals alone. On BIRD dev, median latency is 208 ms per question on one A100, without hosted model calls.

papers.title: A Cross-Scenario Survey and Analysis of Self-Evolving Multimodal Agents
papers.abstract: Recent work shows that multimodal agents increasingly self-improve without recurring human annotation. However, each self-improvement mechanism is designed and evaluated within a single scenario, leaving its preconditions unverified under cross-scenario transfer. This survey investigates the structural source of asymmetric mechanism transfer across four scenarios: multimodal reasoning, multimodal generation, GUI and Web navigation, and embodied manipulation. We first formalize the self-evolving multimodal agent by four criteria and a differentia of self-reference, and adopt the three-stage self-evolving loop of experience generation, feedback acquisition, and update consolidation as our analytical framework to position the scenarios along ceilings on rollout count and feedback fidelity. Comparing self-evolving with fixed loops within each scenario separates the limitations that the scenario imposes from those inherent in the self-evolving design. We then recast each mechanism as a trade-off that raises a scarce factor by presupposing a task-structural resource, such as output equivalence or checkable outcomes, and judge it portable, conditional, blocked, or redundant across scenarios. We attribute the asymmetry to divergent combinations of scarce factors and resources across opposite transfer directions, and identify the matched-budget measurements that could overturn these still untested verdicts.

papers.title: Analytic and optimized approximations to the median of the gamma distribution
papers.abstract:
The median $
u_\Gamma(\alpha)$ of the gamma distribution has no closed form, but its behavior at both ends is known: it is asymptotic to $2^{-1/\alpha}e^{-\gamma}$ (with $\gamma$ being the Euler-Mascheroni constant) as the shape parameter $\alpha 	o 0$, and approaches $\alpha - 1/3$ as $\alpha 	o \infty$. We write approximations as interpolations $(1 - g)
u_0 + g
u_\infty$ between two elementary-function bounds or approximations, each exact in one limit, with an interpolator $g(\alpha)$ going from 0 to 1, and compare three such forms: a first one between previously proven bounds, a second ending in an approximation from the beta median that is exact at $\alpha = 1$ but does not quite approach $\alpha - 1/3$ as $\alpha 	o \infty$, and a third one, between bounds proved here, that corrects the large-$\alpha$ end of the second. For each form, the ideal interpolator's slope at 0, approach to 1, and value at $\alpha = 1$ are derived in closed form. Rational interpolators with every coefficient set in closed form from these properties, with no numerical fitting, reach a worst relative error of 0.0011 over all $\alpha > 0$, with absolute error below 0.0002. Fitting some of these or other coefficients numerically to minimize the worst absolute-or-relative error then trades accuracy against complexity: the Pareto frontier reaches 0.000087 with two fitted constants and 0.000041 with five, and from two on uses degree-4 rationals of the second form with no $\alpha^2$ term in the numerator. The proofs that the end functions of the first and third forms are bounds are machine-checked in Lean 4.

papers.title: Multiple Control Barrier Functions for Geometric Hybrid Systems: Modeling and Safe Control Synthesis
papers.abstract: We formulate geometric hybrid dynamical systems with states on intrinsic manifolds and inputs in topological spaces using relaxed C1-control bundles. Within this framework, we establish a barrier certificate that guarantees forward invariance of a closed set for closed-loop systems. We introduce multiple control barrier functions and derive conditions that render their sublevel sets forward invariant. We then construct pointwise optimal safe control laws, establish regularity conditions for measurable selections, and use these laws to design safety filters for geometric hybrid systems on manifolds. A second-order bouncing-pendulum example illustrates the framework and results.

papers.title: Global regularity of axisymmetric Navier--Stokes equations under total slip and critical smallness
papers.abstract: We study the axisymmetric incompressible Navier--Stokes equations in a finite cylinder subject to the Navier--total--slip boundary condition, that is, the Navier slip condition with zero friction. We prove that the solution remains smooth for all time provided that the initial swirl $\Gamma_0 = r v_{\theta,0}$ has zero mean and an explicit smallness condition on the initial data holds. The condition involves $\Gamma = rv_\theta$ and the variables $V = v_\theta/\sqrt{r}$ and $\Omega = \omega_\theta/r$, and it is invariant under the natural scaling of the Navier--Stokes equations, hence critical. The total-slip condition produces a boundary term on the lateral wall that cannot be controlled by the dissipation alone; we overcome this with a sharp trace-type identity combined with a remainder controlled by $\|\Gamma\|_{L^2}$. In addition, the Robin-type boundary condition $\partial_r \Gamma = 2\Gamma$ destroys the maximum principle for $\Gamma$, and we replace it with a uniform $L^4$ bound. These estimates yield uniform $L^4$ bounds for the velocity, and regularity follows from the Ladyzhenskaya--Prodi--Serrin criterion together with boundary regularity results for the Navier slip condition.

papers.title: Splitting module-finite extensions over singular local rings
papers.abstract: We study when a module-finite extension of a singular local ring splits as a module over the base. On a Gorenstein curve of positive residue characteristic, weak normality forces splitting for every extension of finite projective dimension. In residue characteristic two the converse holds when two is zero or a nonzerodivisor. A missing square root in the prescribed base gives an explicit nonsplit extension of generic rank four. We obtain a second curve criterion by gluing retractions on the branches and determine all evaluation ideals for coordinate crossings and for \(x^2=y^2u z_1\cdots z_s\) in odd characteristic. For cubic extensions we prove a presentation theorem with arbitrarily many relations. It applies on the blow-up of an ideal generated by a regular sequence of length three, and on the blow-up of a three-dimensional local ring with a quadric tangent cone. A family of matrices satisfying the criterion exists over every residue field in the regular-sequence case.

papers.title: $\varphi$-symmetric Sasakian Lie algebras
papers.abstract: We study Sasakian Lie algebras with trivial centre for which the adjoint operator $\mathrm{ad}_\xi$ associated to the Reeb vector field $\xi$ has two-dimensional image. Their structure is governed by a K\"ahler-exact Lie algebra $\mathfrak{h}_1$ and a vector $H_0\in\mathfrak{h}_1$, and the cases $H_0=0$ and $H_0\neq0$ are of a different nature. For $H_0=0$ we prove that the Sasakian structure is $\varphi$-symmetric if and only if $\mathfrak{h}_1$ is locally symmetric. For $H_0\neq0$ and $\mathfrak{h}_1$ solvable, we prove that it is $\varphi$-symmetric if and only if $\mathfrak{h}_1$ is locally symmetric and a natural two-form $\rho_0$ on $\mathfrak{h}_1$ determined by $H_0$ is parallel. The latter condition is equivalent to the vanishing of the mixed root spaces attached to the distinguished root selected by $H_0$ in the associated normal $j$-algebra. As a consequence, every Sasakian Lie algebra in this class of dimension at most seven is $\varphi$-symmetric, which extends a result of Loiudice and Lotta in dimension five. This bound is sharp: in dimension nine we exhibit a Sasakian structure which is not $\varphi$-symmetric, even though its K\"ahler base is locally symmetric.

authors.name: Adrian Andrada
authors.institution: Consejo Nacional de Investigaciones Científicas y Técnicas

papers.title: Nucleation of water ice under weak ionization via clustering on negative ions
papers.abstract: Water-ice grains are shown to form spontaneously in a cold, weakly-ionized laboratory plasma with trace water admixture when neutrals and ions are cooled below $\sim$200 K. These conditions serve as an analog of ice nucleation in cold astrophysical and atmospheric environments. The ice grains form without the presence of particulate impurities, and do not form in the absence of ionization, indicating that nucleation is induced by ions. Time-resolved ion mass spectrometry provides separate detection of clusters of water molecules on both positive and negative ions. Hydrated negative ions, mainly $\mathrm{OH^-(H_2O)_n}$, grow to $\sim$200 amu, while hydrated positive ions, mainly $\mathrm{H^+(H_2O)_n}$, remain small and short-lived. As the temperature is reduced from room temperature toward 200 K, negative ion clusters grow in size and then drop sharply in abundance, consistent with the onset of rapid growth into macroscopic ice grains below a critical temperature. This indicates that hydrated negative ions are key precursors to ice nucleation in cold, weakly ionized environments, such as the Earth's mesosphere and protoplanetary disks, providing a concrete pathway for ice formation in environments where the nucleation mechanism has remained unresolved. This negative ion pathway is estimated to dominate over ice deposition on pre-existing dust grains in protoplanetary disk locations where there is sufficient UV to partially dissociate water molecules, and in addition, where negative ions such as OH- can form readily through electron attachment at low temperature.

papers.title: Pair localization in one-dimensional quasicrystals with spin-dependent hopping
papers.abstract: We investigate the quantum localization of two interacting particles moving in a one-dimensional quasicrystal with unequal hopping amplitudes. Using a two-body Green's function approach, we determine the localization phase diagram of attractively and repulsively bound pairs, showing that increasing the hopping amplitude of one constituent while keeping the other fixed raises the critical quasiperiodic strength, promoting pair delocalization. The localization threshold nevertheless remains bounded above by the Aubry-Andr\'e critical point of the slower constituent. Effective analytical descriptions capture pair localization in the limits of strong hopping imbalance and strong interactions. The dynamics of an initially on-site pair provides signatures of delocalization induced by unequal hopping amplitudes. In particular, the effective spreading exponent of the root-mean-square width of a pair distribution reveals a progression from localized to subdiffusive and eventually superdiffusive behavior as the hopping ratio increases. Our results establish unequal hopping amplitudes as a means of tuning the transport properties of interacting pairs in quasiperiodic lattices, with direct relevance to ultracold atoms in optical lattices.

papers.title: Parametric Proof-Carrying Compilation for Quantum Error-Correction
papers.abstract: We present PC-QEC, a proof-carrying compilation framework for quantum error correction parameterized by both code distance and syndrome-extraction scheme. It covers all four schemes---Standard, Flag, Shor and Knill---with circuit-level distance guarantees for every legal code distance in each proved family under the declared fault and readout contracts. The circuit-level model permits single-wire Pauli faults at every operation's qubit operands, capturing data errors, readout errors and ancilla faults that propagate into multi-qubit hook errors. For each family and scheme, code-algebra proofs and fault-aware Hoare proofs compose into a finite symbolic certificate whose size is independent of code distance. We demonstrate family-wide guarantees for five code families across all four schemes. For rotated Surface code, one Standard Scheme certificate proves a distance lower bound $d$ for every odd $d\ge3$ and checks in 214\,s on average. Lean 4 mechanizes the metatheory and exact circuit-level distances for canonical Surface, hypergraph-product (HGP) and Toric code families.

papers.title: Incorporating World Models in Decision Making for Next Best View Selection in Active Sensing
papers.abstract: Efficient robotic 3D reconstruction requires selecting views that contribute new surface measurements with few physical captures. Pretrained world models can guide this choice, but a predicted surface may not produce valid depth measurements under the operating conditions of the deployed sensor. We present a deployment adaptation methodology for next-best-view selection that learns a sensor-return adapter from limited local calibration data while keeping the pretrained predictor fixed. The adapter estimates measurement dropout over each predicted surface, allowing the selection method to favor views likely to fill gaps in the measured reconstruction. In a real-robot experiment with a structured-light sensor, the adapted method achieves higher measured surface coverage with 60% fewer captures than nominal selection. The adapted method recovers a surface region that the nominal method repeatedly targets but fails to measure. These results suggest that robots can reuse pretrained predictive models while adapting their decisions to local operating conditions in data-scarce environments.

papers.title: Molecular Gas Optics Using Vibrational Population Density Refraction
papers.abstract: Gas optics holds promise for development of advanced optical elements with 2-3 orders of magnitude higher damage threshold than any solid-state optics. Here, we demonstrate a new concept for refracting the laser beam using vibrationally excited molecules as gas optics instead of traditional control of thermodynamic gas temperature. The transient, vibrational population density grating is formed in a CO2 gas by interfering two mid-IR lasers to imprint spatial modulation in the linear refractive index (Delta n0 >=2x10-5) of the neutral gas via enhancement of the molecular polarizability. It is increased by pumping the asymmetric stretching mode of CO2 at optimal wavelengths to resonantly produce a highly nonequilibrium state that increases the effective vibrational mode temperature to greater than 2000 K in a room temperature gas. The measured beam steering efficiency of such a volume gas grating exceeds 90% that makes this approach a candidate for producing other large-aperture, high-throughput molecular optics elements, with expected damage thresholds 0.5-1 kJ/cm2, much-needed for future ultrahigh-power lasers.

papers.title: LLM-Assisted Advances in the Ropelength Problem
papers.abstract: This work summarizes some updates to the ropelength problem, concerning the shortest possible contour length of a unit-thickness knot, that were derived with the assistance of ChatGPT-5.6 Luna. The first of two main results is that the universal lower bound for a knot with crossing number C has been improved from $L\geq1.105C^{3/4}$ to $L\geq2.0996C^{3/4}$, achieved by further separating local and global terms in an optimization integral. The second main result is a bound relating ropelength to stick number (s), such that $L\geq\pi(s-1)$. This implies stronger lower bounds for the ropelengths of at least 41 torus knots, and a specific class of pretzel knots. Other results include an improved packing-based lower bound for T(Q,Q) links and an optimized standard parameterization for torus knots. There were many problems for which the LLM was unable to render assistance, for example in reducing the numerical coefficients or scalings of known universal upper bounds.

papers.title: Linear-size graphs at every strict dismantling level
papers.abstract: Dismantling reduces a graph to one vertex by successive deletions. At level zero, a vertex is eligible if one of its neighbours is adjacent to all its other neighbours. At level $k\geq1$, its neighbours must induce a graph dismantlable at level $k-1$. A graph has strict level $k$ if it admits a reduction at level $k$ and none at level $k-1$. For every $k\geq1$, we construct a graph of strict level $k$ with $3k+8$ vertices. Each step adds three vertices: the neighbours of one induce the preceding graph, and the other two provide the adjacencies used to rule out other first deletions at the lower level. A second construction gives a graph of order $4k+4$ at strict level $k$. Together the two families give the upper bound $\min\{4k+4,3k+8\}$ on the least order at strict level $k$.

papers.title: When Are Predictions Enough? An Evaluation Protocol for Frozen Expert Composition
papers.abstract: Practitioners often combine independently trained models while keeping their weights frozen. These experts are commonly combined through their final predictions, although their internal features may retain useful information that those predictions omit. We ask when combining features improves on combining predictions, and how to make that comparison fair. We introduce a reusable evaluation protocol, apply it to 21 frozen deepfake detectors from DF40 (Yan et al., 2024), and audit how evaluation choices change the conclusions. The protocol uses strong prediction baselines, compares simple and larger feature combiners, varies architecture and training data separately, and reports results by held-out generator with train/test overlap controls. Under leave-one-generator-out evaluation, logistic regression on the features of six architecture-diverse experts improves macro AUROC by 0.081 over the best tested prediction combiner in each fold, with gains on seven of eight generators. The larger network shows no clear improvement over the linear model (approximately 3.5M versus 10K parameters), suggesting that access to richer information matters more than additional combiner capacity on this pool. Features may help when they retain information that the predictions omit and that transfers to new generators. Predictions may be enough when the strongest prediction baseline already performs well, while neither approach reliably compensates for poor expert transfer. Weakening prediction baselines on the overlap-affected standard split inflates the apparent feature advantage by up to 0.172 AUROC. Overlap-aware evaluation also changes the estimated gain, though the contrast does not isolate overlap. Results by generator and expert pool show where the advantage holds, weakens, or reverses. Without these controls, the same benchmark can support different conclusions.

papers.title: Multivariate Bernstein duality for tournament Wright--Fisher diffusions
papers.abstract: We give a probabilistic proof of a multivariate Bernstein duality for a multivariate Wright--Fisher frequency process with selection encoded by a finite tournament. The construction includes nontransitive interactions, such as rock--paper--scissors selection. Its dual is a pure-jump process of coefficient functions in the multinomial Bernstein basis. Selection increases the Bernstein degree through a winner--loser averaging operator, whereas neutral resampling decreases it through a duplication operator. For the proof, we construct a continuous forward process independently of duality, use duality to establish uniqueness, and obtain a weak stochastic differential equation representation and invariance of the simplex faces. This provides a sampling-based treatment of the tournament specialization of multitype Bernstein duality, extending an open problem in the binary Kingman setting of Cordero, Hummel, and Schertzer (2022).

papers.title: Smooth actions of Baumslag-Solitar groups on the interval
papers.abstract: We study representations of the Baumslag-Solitar group $BS(m,n)=\langle a,b\mid ab^ma^{-1}=b^n\rangle$ inside the group of orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of the interval $[0,1]$. We prove that for integers $n,m\in \mathbb Z\setminus\{-1,0,1\}$, the group $BS(m,n)$ embeds into $\mathrm{Diff}_+^1([0,1])$ if and only if $|n|=|m|$. Furthermore, we show that for any $\alpha\in (0,1)$, the group $BS(m,n)$ embeds inside $\mathrm{Diff}_+^{1+\alpha}([0,1])$ if and only if $1=|m|=|n|$ or when $1=m\leq n$.

authors.name: Cristobal Rivas
authors.institution: Universidad de la República de Uruguay

papers.title: Spectral Constraints on Line-Seed Inverse-Compton Models for the MeV Feature in GRB 221009A
papers.abstract: We investigate inverse-Compton (IC) scattering of atomic and molecular line photons as an explanation of the evolving MeV spectral feature observed by Fermi-GBM in GRB 221009A. Detections of H$\alpha$ and Pa$\alpha$ emission from the host galaxy motivate hydrogen recombination seeds, with only indirect support for Ly$\alpha$. A marginal Mg XII feature in the late-time X-ray afterglow provides an event-specific motivation for metal-line seeds, whereas Si XIV, S XVI and iron K-shell transitions are motivated by historical reports of X-ray line features in other gamma-ray bursts. Strong late-time H$_2$ emission detected by the James Webb Space Telescope at the projected burst position motivates our most detailed spectral test. Assuming lateral illumination by the H$_2$ $1-0\,S(1)$ transition at $2.122\,\mu{\rm m}$, we calibrate lognormal electron distributions to reproduce the observed MeV photon centroids and widths. We also require IC emission from the ultraviolet (UV) photons driving molecular fluorescence to remain compatible with contemporaneous LAT observations. In a separate test including accompanying molecular transitions, the most favourable configuration, based on the Rh3o photodissociation-region model, approximately describes the MeV feature, although all tested configurations exceed the adopted central spectral references at some energies. For an assumed precursor UV budget, favourable interception substantially reduces the seed-photon energy deficit, but even under ideal excitation and internal escape assumptions, the reference-line photon density in the compact examples falls short of the required value by factors of approximately 4-9. Collisional de-excitation, infrared photon escape and electron cooling impose additional constraints on these configurations. Atomic candidates remain kinematically possible, but their local seed-photon supply is also unestablished.

papers.title: A Beltrami Mode in Extreme Fractional Hydrodynamics under Stochastic Forcing
papers.abstract: We construct an exact stochastic solution of the extreme order endpoint of adaptive fractional Navier Stokes (AFNS) hydrodynamics on the three-dimensional periodic torus. A helical Beltrami eigenfield reduces the nonlinear vector equation to a scalar Ornstein Uhlenbeck process when the white-in-time forcing is aligned with that eigenfield. The resulting invariant Gaussian law yields explicit formulas for the stationary energy, its fluctuations, temporal correlations, circulation, and helicity. Under the same forcing, the corresponding classical Navier Stokes mode has a stationary energy that diverges as the Reynolds number tends to infinity, while the Euler limit exhibits linear growth of the mean energy and has no invariant probability law. The construction isolates, without a cascade hypothesis, the statistical effect of the finite fractional dissipation retained at the extreme endpoint of AFNS.

papers.title: F3-AGI v4.0: Bioenergetically-Gated Active Inference, Metaplastic Preconditioning, and Residual Program Synthesis for Sample-Efficient Abstract Reasoning
papers.abstract: Few-shot abstract reasoning on ARC-AGI requires inducing algorithmic transformations from 2 to 5 demonstration pairs without task-specific pretraining. Because few-shot demonstrations under-constrain the hypothesis space, program synthesis suffers from the Rashomon effect (predictive multiplicity): heuristic search finds spurious programs with low training error that fail on test inputs, while unconstrained library growth degrades latency. We introduce F3-AGI v4.0, a CPU-native neuro-symbolic and active inference architecture comprising three mechanisms: (1) F3-Metabolic-Optim, combining mistake-gated plasticity, Fisher-EMA preconditioning, and virtual ATP gating; (2) Adaptive Complexity-Guided Program Synthesis (AACR) with a Cycle-3 ResidualPatchSynthesizer and smallest-pair early rejection; and (3) a 512D L2-normalized random projection driving Expected Free Energy (EFE) exploration with dead-signature pruning. Across three empirical studies: (i) on a synthetic 5-task class-incremental stream without replay, F3-Metabolic-Optim achieves 91.67% final accuracy with 9.17% forgetting, skipping 93.47% of updates, cutting L1 plasticity cost by 65.7%, and running 2.19x faster than EWC; (ii) on the 400-task ARC-AGI-1 public evaluation set (offline CPU, zero LLM calls), F3-AGI v4.0 solves 57/400 tasks (14.25% pass@2; 56/400 pass@1) with a mean latency of 1.62 s/task, decomposed into 19/50 (38.00%, 1.19 s/task, a 42.5x paired speedup over Horizon 2) on the 50-task calibration slice and 38/350 (10.86%) on the 350 strictly uninspected hold-out tasks (with 7 autonomous Cycle-3 patch solutions); and (iii) in a local 5-game (15-level) ARC-AGI-3-inspired interactive suite, our agent completes 15/15 levels with 89.44% level-weighted RHAE (90.72% unweighted).

papers.title: Third-Order Asymptotics for Fixed-Length Lossy Compression of Discrete Memoryless Sources
papers.abstract: This paper determines the third-order asymptotics of the logarithm of the minimum codebook size for fixed-length lossy compression of discrete memoryless sources. For an excess-distortion probability constraint $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ and every interior distortion level, we establish a third-order correction of $\frac12\log n+O(1)$, where $n$ is the blocklength. This sharpens the general bounds of Kostina and Verd\'u [IEEE Trans. Inf. Theory, 2012]. The main technical innovation lies in the converse for positive dispersion. Under a reverse change of measure, we retain the exponential weights associated with tilted information and distortion slack and control them jointly using the multivariate weighted-strip estimate of Scarlett, Martinez, and Guill\'en i F\`abregas [Proc. IEEE ISIT, 2015]. A pairing argument verifies the required covariance nondegeneracy uniformly over all reconstruction words whose distortion balls meet a typical set, yielding the matching converse.

papers.title: High degree covers and genericity
papers.abstract:
It is known that the genuine irreducible Iwahori-spherical representations of a tame $n$-fold Brylinski-Deligne cover of a $p$-adic split connected reductive group are all generic, when the degree $n$ is suitably large. This has been established by studying the the structure of the Gelfand-Graev representation as a module under the action of the Iwahori-Hecke algebra.
  In this paper, we present a different proof based on metaplectic Moy-Prasad theory.

papers.title: Thermodynamic Formalism for Non-Invariant Probabilities: Entropy, Divergence, Channels
papers.abstract: Let $\mathcal{M}$ and $\mathcal{M}_\sigma$ denote, respectively, the sets of Borel and $\sigma$-invariant probabilities on the uncountable set $\Omega=\{1,2,...,d\}^\mathbb{N}$. Given a H\"older Jacobian $J$, the dual Ruelle operator $\mu \in \mathcal{M} \mapsto \mathcal{L}_{J}^* (\mu)$ will play the role of a dynamical channel; generalizes the action of a stochastic matrix on probability vectors. Since $\mathcal{L}_{J}^*$ generally breaks $\sigma$-invariance, we introduce the \emph{ni-entropy} $h_{ni}(\mu)$ for non-invariant measures, employing the concept of the expected value function on cylinders of size one. $h_{ni}(\mu)$ differs from Shannon entropy but extends the Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy from $\mathcal{M}_\sigma$ to $\mathcal{M}$; $h_{ni}$ is concave and u.s.c. This leads us to the concept of ni-pressure $\mathcal{P}(A)$ of a potential $A:\Omega \to \mathbb{R}$. $\mu\in \mathcal{M}$ is not a density with respect to a dominating measure. We define an {\it ni-Kullback-Leibler divergence} $D_{ni}(\rho || \nu)$ not assuming absolute continuity. We investigate concepts of Information Theory such as Minimal Output Entropy, Donsker-Varadhan variational principle, a variational formula for $h_{ni}$, bounds for divergence, information projections, and their connections to the ni-pressure $\mathcal{P}$.

authors.name: Artur O. Lopes
authors.institution: Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul

authors.name: Elismar R. Oliveira
authors.institution: Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul

papers.title: A counterexample to the Erd\H{o}s--Mahler conjecture
papers.abstract: We disprove a 1939 conjecture of Erd\H{o}s and Mahler by constructing, for every real $\tau\ge4$, a Cantor set of numbers of irrationality exponent $\tau$, each having infinitely many regular continued-fraction convergents of the form $2^a/3^b$.

authors.name: Diego Marques
authors.institution: Consejo Nacional de Investigaciones Científicas y Técnicas

papers.title: No finite rulebook can certify every safe program: an impossibility theorem for gatekeeping AI agents
papers.abstract: An AI assistant writes small programs, and a gatekeeper must decide, from the code alone, whether each one may run. Suppose the rules are fixed: never perform a forbidden action, never let the output depend on a secret, always answer eventually. Can two rulebooks, one listing what is allowed and one listing what is not, both be complete, if every rule must be backed by evidence that a machine can check in finite time? We prove that they cannot. Checkable evidence can only establish what a finite record settles, and ``never'' and ``eventually'' are never settled by a finite record. For prohibitions the failure is one-sided: every violation can be caught by watching, but no safe program can be cleared for good. For confidentiality and responsiveness, neither side can be. We characterise exactly which rules about visible behaviour evidence can confirm, and we show that any sound rulebook of $n$ bits omits a compliant program of about $n$ bits. A time limit makes everything checkable, but only by running the program for essentially the whole limit, so a finite machine is not a feasible one. Finally, we show what a gatekeeper can still guarantee: not a verdict on every program, but a checkable list that contains everything it must allow and nothing it must refuse. Simulations on 2.2 million random programs and on self-referential adversaries show that the obstruction is adversarial rather than typical, and that the one error a longer test never removes is the liveness part of confidentiality.

papers.title: A new representation of effective diffusion in fluctuating periodic potentials through stochastic duality
papers.abstract: We revisit the classical problem of effective diffusion in fluctuating periodic force fields by combining homogenization with stochastic duality. We consider a specific class of fluctuations in which the internal state of the force field is independently redrawn from a fixed distribution at Poisson-distributed times. In the homogenization framework, the effective diffusion coefficient \(D_{\rm eff}\) is expressed in terms of a corrector function satisfying a backward Kolmogorov equation. For the redraw dynamics considered here, the equation governing the spatial derivative of the corrector can be reinterpreted as the stationary forward equation of a dual system obtained by reversing the force field, \(F\to-F\). This relation eliminates the corrector and yields a representation of \(D_{\rm eff}\) entirely in terms of stationary densities and probability currents of the physical and dual systems. We further introduce an auxiliary function \(Q(x)\) whose spatial variation is determined by the stationary current. When this current vanishes, \(Q(x)\) becomes independent of position and the effective diffusion coefficient reduces to the local relation \( D_{\rm eff}=L^2Q. \) This result generalizes the classical Lifson--Jackson relation to fluctuating periodic force fields. We verify the theory using analytical calculations, numerical solutions of the stationary equations, and direct simulations of the long-time particle displacement, including a driven system with nonzero stationary current.

papers.title: The WoW: A Large-Scale World Knowledge Corpus for Full-Lifecycle LLM Training
papers.abstract: Existing Chinese educational corpora often suffer from fragmented coverage and a lack of systematic organization. In this paper, we propose WoW (\textbf{Wo}rld Kno\textbf{w}ledge), a large-scale dataset designed for the full-cycle training of foundation models. The construction of this dataset is driven by an Educational Knowledge Graph, which serves as a taxonomic backbone for the systematic collection and completion of missing educational modules across all levels. Compared to previous versions, this iteration provides enhanced systematicity, superior quality, and a larger scale, while incorporating multimodal signals and supporting every stage of model development. Experiments demonstrate that WoW significantly improves model performance across diverse benchmarks. To facilitate community research, we further provide an interactive platform for graph-based data selection and retrieval.

papers.title: StatPrompt-LLM: A Lightweight Statistical Refinement for Foundation-Style Time-Series Forecasting
papers.abstract: Time-series forecasting has recently seen a paradigm shift with the introduction of foundation-style models that adapt large pretrained language architectures to sequential data. However, effectively exposing fundamental temporal structures, such as trend, scale, and temporal dependence, to these models remains an open challenge, particularly when the available observations are limited. In this paper, we conduct an exploratory empirical study across different generations of forecasting architectures and propose StatPrompt-LLM, a lightweight statistical refinement of Time-LLM. StatPrompt-LLM augments the existing Time-LLM prompting mechanism with dataset-level statistical information and introduces a zero-initialised autoregressive bypass as a complementary linear forecasting pathway. We evaluate our framework on electricity and meteorological time-series benchmarks, including ETTh1, ETTh2, and Weather, under full-prefix and reduced-prefix configurations. Under the 10% reduced-prefix configuration, StatPrompt-LLM achieved lower in-sample prediction errors than Time-LLM, with unweighted average relative reductions across datasets of 40.2% in MSE and 21.4% in MAE. Full-prefix results were more dataset-dependent. Ablation analyses revealed relatively modest and dataset-dependent changes when selected additional statistical descriptor groups were masked within the combined architecture. Computational profiling indicated additional model parameters and runtime overhead relative to Time-LLM.

papers.title: An Accelerated Power Method
papers.abstract: An Accelerated Power Method (APM) for locating the dominant eigen-pair of a real, symmetric matrix is presented. The algorithm is motivated by Nesterov's Accelerated Gradient Method (AGM) and a connection between the APM and the AGM holds, that is analogous to the relationship between the Conjugate Gradient and Lanczos methods. Theoretical convergence analysis shows that the APM is guaranteed to recover the dominant eigen-pair of a normalized semi-definite matrix at a rate no worse than the Power Method. For normalized indefinite matrices, the APM will recover an extremal eigen-pair, but not necessarily the dominant one, and the rate can be worse than the vanilla PM, depending upon the choice of acceleration parameter. Computational practicalities are discussed, including parameter tuning, and numerical experiments are also presented.

papers.title: Reinforcement Learning based control of Cancer Chemotherapy treatments
papers.abstract:
Reinforcement Learning has achieved tremendous success in recent years. Extending its scope from the traditional complex games such as Atari, Go, Pokeman, and Chess, reinforcement learning has caught researchers' attention on modelling real-life scenarios. Personalized medicine and the dynamic treatment regimen are two such preliminary research fields; researchers are focusing their mindsets currently. Estimating the optimal dynamic treatment regimens from the observational real clinical data is being popularized among the researchers, widening its scope towards more advanced versions of reinforcement learning algorithms.
  This research is about a research study that focused on reinforcement learning techniques that have been approached in the context of cancer chemotherapy treatments. Primarily this thesis addresses the result of the study by means of the state-of-the-art on reinforcement learning techniques used in generating the optimal policy for sequential treatments, including the existing online reinforcement learning approaches. Thereby a simulation for cancer chemotherapy via traditional Q-learning would be presented. Secondly, the study will extend towards using offline reinforcement learning in the optimal policy generation. Thus, the proposed solution follows a data-driven approach, which works on the real human colon cancer clinical data.
  The novelty of the proposed solution resides in the implementation of an offline reinforcement learning approach by means of a model-based architecture using the conservative Q-learning and the model-based offline policy optimization algorithm. As per the experimental results and the evaluations, it was revealed that the proposed Chemo RL model caters well the problem of cancer chemotherapy treatment scheduling and serves as a supportive model for the junior oncologists in deciding their treatment decisions.

papers.title: Compile-Gated Lean Proof Refactoring with Enterprise Agent Practices: A Model per Step under a US\$3 Cap, Followed by Programmatic Rewrite Rules
papers.abstract: Our closed-track entry (Arena username Vexorium-Agent) scored 86.31 points on the final board (L = 77.07, H = 81.86, Z = 100) over the 60 final problems, against 33.33 for the reference proofs, 8th at the deadline (top: 92.57), for US\$166.33 at list prices with every call counted (per problem: mean US\$2.772, at most US\$2.874; US\$3 cap). Three practices carry the entry. First, each paid stage runs the model that measured best per dollar for it among the 9 we tested in our own harness: GPT-6.1 Sol the early sessions, GPT-6.1 Terra the later ones and the tail at 70% of Sol's cost per turn, and Gemini 4 Argon the review and repair; Sol also runs the style rewrite. Second, what our development and research runs learned ships as compiler-checked programmatic rewrite rules rather than prompt text (+0.93 points from rules fixed before the release; +0.26 and +0.30, in sample, from passes built or switched on after the release). Third, every call is recorded and reviewed before each change (all 9 board scores came within -0.063 to +0.015 points of our meter's prediction). The harness, gate and many of these rules also serve our open-track entry. We report the full bill and the spread of three runs.
papers.intro:
The Lean Refactor Arena (Lu et al., 2026) asks for better proofs of theorems that already have one. Each of its 60 final problems is a theorem of a Lean 4 library (de Moura and Ullrich, 2021) with a working reference proof; an entry returns a proof per problem with the statement unchanged, and the Arena rewards fewer tokens, fewer heartbeats (Lean’s count of elaboration work) and compiling unchanged on every toolchain the problem lists (Section 2). We entered both tracks, open weights and hosted models, with one harness, built on a design principle for each technical problem: 1. A two-objective score on a noisy meter. Saving a token is worth as much as saving B/TB/T heartbeats (TT, BB: the reference proof’s tokens and heartbeats), and B/TB/T runs from 1.4 to 16,013 across the final problems (median 30); heartbeat readings vary between runs. Measure, do not guess: every candidate is read on a local copy of the Arena’s meter, back to back with the proof it would replace, and kept only by a margin above the meter’s spread (Section 3.2). 2. Every listed toolchain. 59 of the 60 problems list several toolchains (up to 4, v4.26.0 to v4.35.0-rc3), and a proof that fails on one loses points. Keep nothing whose ZZ has not been measured on all of them. 3. A hard budget: US$3 per problem at list prices, or 4 ×\times A100 80 GB for 48 h. Use the model only where rules cannot do the work: mechanical rewrites run as model-free CPU stages behind the same gate (Section 3.3). 4. Few public rows: 15 warm-up problems before a final benchmark with 47 new problems and 4 new toolchains. General mechanisms only: no stage is keyed to a problem, every final proof starts from the released reference proof, and work after the release is disclosed. Both reports share Section 2, Sections 3.2 and 3.3, Appendix H and part of Section 8; each entry’s agent stage, models, budget and results are its own.

papers.title: The Indic Token Tax in 2026: Measuring Tokenizer. Disparity and Its Cost for the Languages of India
papers.abstract: Commercial language model APIs bill per token, so a tokenizer that needs more tokens for the same content in one language makes that language more expensive, slower, and able to fit less text in a fixed context window. We measure this disparity for nine public tokenizers, including those of GPT-4, GPT-4o, Qwen2.5, DeepSeek-V3, Mistral-Nemo and four Sarvam models, on all 25 languages of India available in FLORES-200 (2,009 professionally translated sentences aligned with English) and on 13,732 human-translated Hinglish-English social media pairs from PHINC. On GPT-4o's tokenizer the same content needs between 1.57 times (Hindi) and 5.01 times (Odia) the tokens of English, and 13.7 times for Santali in Ol Chiki script; GPT-4's tokenizer needs up to 12.8 times. Sarvam-30B/105B is the only third-party tokenizer that stays below 2.6 times on every language (median 1.53). In an illustrative scenario using official list prices accessed on 5 November 2026 and stated assumptions, a support bot handling 100,000 chats a month on GPT-4o would cost about INR 56,640 in English and INR 102,829 in Marathi; these are estimates, not measured production costs. Against an openly licensed Hindi and Marathi morphological segmentation set, no tokenizer places more than 35% of its word-internal boundaries on morpheme boundaries (boundary F1 at most 0.48). In a companion paper we present a tokenizer that reduces this tax. Code, pinned artifacts and raw token counts are available at https://github.com/HavonAI/indic-token-tax.
papers.intro:
Large language model (LLM) APIs charge per input and output token, and model context windows are measured in tokens. Tokenizers are usually trained on corpora dominated by English, so text in other languages tends to be split into more, smaller pieces. Speakers of those languages then pay more for the same request, wait longer for the same answer, and fit less of their text into the same context window.

Speakers of those languages then pay more for the same request, wait longer for the same answer, and fit less of their text into the same context window.

This effect was documented in 2023 for commercial and open tokenizers across many languages [1, 2]. Since then, newer tokenizers with much larger vocabularies have been released, including OpenAI’s o200k_base (used from GPT-4o onwards) and models built specifically for Indian languages by Sarvam AI. Romanized Indian-language text, such as Hinglish (Hindi typed in Latin letters, often mixed with English), which is how a large share of Indian users actually type, is rarely measured.

This paper makes four contributions: 1. An updated, reproducible measurement of token disparity across nine public tokenizers, including four Sarvam tokenizers released in 2024 to 2026, for every language of India in FLORES-200 (25 language and script pairs). 2. Measurements on romanized text: a parallel Hinglish-English benchmark (PHINC), and romanized versus native-script token cost for 12 South Asian languages on about 10,000 human-romanized strings each (Dakshina). 3. A worked rupee cost example based on official per-token prices. 4. A morpheme boundary alignment measurement for Hindi and Marathi against an openly licensed segmentation set. A companion paper presents a tokenizer trained to reduce the tax measured here; this paper evaluates only publicly released tokenizers.

papers.title: Aster: A Flexible and Robust Collection of Numerical Tools for N-Body Problems
papers.abstract: The Aster library is an open-source collection of numerical tools designed for large-scale gravitational N-body simulations. Aster provides a flexible environment to its users, enabling it to be used in the analysis of a broad range of astrophysical problems. The library implements efficient force calculation algorithms, including a spatial tree solver optimized with coordinate-dependent identifiers, which has been fine-tuned for both CPU and GPU architectures. Despite its high degree of modularity, many parts of the library have been optimized with SIMD instructions, heavy parallelization, and support on dedicated hardware. Aster also offers a wide variety of numerical symplectic integrators, such as SABA (from first to tenth order), the classic leapfrog algorithm, and the more advanced Wisdom-Holman (WH) integrator, while also providing a vast collection of mathematical tools, e.g., post-newtonian expansions (1PN, 2PN, 2.5PN), data collection and graphing systems, a built-in renderer, and presets for faster instantiation of large amounts of bodies. In this work we will discuss in depth the details of each module as well as the results of several performance- and accuracy-related tests, probing the library's capabilities in different physical applications.
papers.intro:
Despite the recent advances in algorithms, the long-term evolution of many-body systems remains a computationally demanding problem by nature. From the evolution of planetary rings comprised of millions of particles to the dynamics of stellar clusters and galaxy formation, modern astrophysical research demands the ability to simulate complex many-body systems over large timescales while maintaining a sufficient numerical accuracy for physically meaningful results. Aster is built as a suite of numerical tools designed to address these issues and optimized for efficient execution on CPU and dedicated hardware, resulting in an ecosystem that is both capable of offering great flexibility over a broad range of physical systems and also of maintaining high numerical accuracy without sacrificing performance.

From the evolution of planetary rings comprised of millions of particles to the dynamics of stellar clusters and galaxy formation, modern astrophysical research demands the ability to simulate complex many-body systems over large timescales while maintaining a sufficient numerical accuracy for physically meaningful results. Aster is built as a suite of numerical tools designed to address these issues and optimized for efficient execution on CPU and dedicated hardware, resulting in an ecosystem that is both capable of offering great flexibility over a broad range of physical systems and also of maintaining high numerical accuracy without sacrificing performance.

The library provides two force evaluation routines: a direct 𝒪⁡(N2)\mathcal{O}(N^{2}) solver, useful when near machine precision is needed in few-body and moderate-scale systems; and an approximate Barnes-Hut algorithm (Barnes and Hut, 1986) with O(N log N) complexity. Both solvers have been implemented with extensive parallelization using TBB, SIMD vectorization, and GPU acceleration via OpenCL.

Both solvers have been implemented with extensive parallelization using TBB, SIMD vectorization, and GPU acceleration via OpenCL.

To ensure numerical stability over long timescales and high particle counts, Aster implements a suite of integration methods designed to preserve the system’s symplectic structure. These include the SABA integrator (up to tenth order), the Wisdom-Holman method for hierarchical systems, and lower-order schemes such as leapfrog and symplectic Euler. Aster also provides post-Newtonian terms (1PN, 2PN, 2.5PN) to account for high-energy regimes where General Relativity’s effects are not negligible, as well as an automated data collection system, a real-time 3D renderer equipped with an API capable of displaying custom data, and utilities for efficient instantiation of large-scale structures. In the following sections, we describe Aster’s design choices and numerical methods in detail. We present performance benchmarks demonstrating the library’s capabilities across various regimes.

papers.title: The Left Ripple of Byte-Pair Encoding: Certified Lookbehind for Every Dictionary
papers.abstract: Berglund and van der Merwe formalized byte-pair encoding and bounded how far an appended string can change a tokenization, leaving the converse open: how far can a string prepended on the left change it, which dictionaries make that ripple infinite, and can it be computed efficiently when finite? We answer all three for every dictionary. The origin radius, how far a prepend can change covering spans, is decided with radius certificates by a product of two runs of the automaton that guesses the final tokens, in time polynomial in the dictionary written out, and it is infinite exactly when one periodic word has two canonical tilings with no common boundary. Under their ordering condition it is infinite exactly when some rule (t, t) finds its two copies adjacent at its own stage, and such a rule makes any dictionary infinite. A finite radius makes every window of a width read off the radii have a cut, and the radius is finite exactly when such cuts are dense. The token machine completes for every dictionary, and the tokenization is subsequential, extending what Berglund, Martens and van der Merwe proved for proper ones under one pass per rule. A streaming tokenizer emits after every symbol exactly the tokens that no continuation changes, in polynomial time, answering a question of Dalirrooyfard and Ye. Boundedness of the label measure, the edit distance of the token sequences, is decided for every dictionary in polynomial time as well, and under the ordering condition the largest distance one edit causes over dictionaries of m rules lies asymptotically between m^2/10 and m^2/2. GPT-2's merge table carries 244 effective self-pairs, so its origin radius is infinite from the forty-second merge on, and that of cl100k, o200k and Llama 3 from their first. Every measured number is its program's output, and what is not executed is named.
papers.intro:
A byte-pair tokenizer applies a dictionary of merge rules in priority order until none applies. Its output on a string depends on the whole string. Incremental use asks how much of a tokenization survives an edit and how much must be recomputed, and both questions reduce to how far a local change can propagate. For appending, Berglund and van der Merwe [4] proved the propagation bounded by |D||D| tokens and defined a lookahead constant. For strings appended on the left they gave an example with infinite propagation. Their closing section asks whether the dictionaries exhibiting these infinite ripples do so due to some easily decidable property, and whether the lookbehind is efficiently computable when finite. They name the lookbehind in quotation marks, by analogy with their Definition 6, and leave its definition open. From random testing they recorded that the ripple seems to often be finite. An answer therefore needs three things: a definition of how far a prepend reaches, a property that decides which dictionaries make that reach infinite, and an efficient computation of it when finite.

This paper supplies all three, with two definitions for the first. For every dictionary the origin radius is decidable and exactly computable with executable certificates, in polynomial time. Under the ordering condition the dictionaries with infinite radius are exactly those with an effective self-pair rule, a property read off the rules. The constants are computed on a census of 484 small dictionaries and on GPT-2’s merge table, and the self-pair threshold on three more production tables. All costs here are in the dictionary written out, where token lengths can be exponential in the number of rules. The compact companion [23] measures costs for the same questions by the size of a straight-line program over the dictionary’s operands. Nothing here depends on it.

papers.title: Elicitation of the parameters of a multi-criteria sorting model
papers.abstract: Multiple-criteria decision aiding (MCDA) proposes models and methods for different types of decision problems such as choice, ranking or sorting. Such models involve various parameters that must be elicited. In the elicitation process, all necessary information has to be taken from the decision-maker. For this, several direct and indirect elicitation methods are suggested in the literature. In this work, we concentrate on direct elicitation: we aim at providing a rigorous elicitation procedure for the parameters of the Non-Compensatory Sorting model (NCS), which has been characterized by an axiomatic analysis. A basic version of the NCS model is considered, i.e., a model with two categories and no vetoes. The parameters are the set of sufficient coalitions of criteria and the profile separating the two categories. Regarding the sufficient coalitions, we propose several questioning algorithms that engraft questions on classical graph exploration algorithms such as depth-first search. Such algorithms are implemented and evaluated by simulation. For eliciting the limit profile, we design a questioning algorithm using dichotomy. Questioning algorithms can be optimal in the worst case or on average. An optimal algorithm in the worst case has been proposed by Hansel in the framework of monotone Boolean functions. We implement and evaluate this algorithm as a variant of the depth-first search approaches. Regarding optimal questioning strategies on average, we evaluate decision trees for up to four criteria. On the other hand, we assess how more general is NCS as compared to MR-Sort, a particular case of the NCS model in which sufficient coalitions can be represented by additive weights.

papers.title: Activation-Guided Graph Retrieval for Cognitive Memory Reconstruction in Language Model Systems
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented language model systems generally select context by query-conditioned relevance. We argue that long-lived AI systems require a second operator: activation-conditioned memory availability. We specify an architecture in which request and goal cues seed an authorized memory graph, activation and fan attenuation allocate a bounded traversal frontier, retrieved entities recursively emit cues, and a typed evidence graph is reconstructed before generation. The specification yields five architectural consequences about candidate selection, traversal control, graph regularization, evidence reconstruction, and reinforcement. We derive implementation-level cost estimates and define ablations, failure conditions, and a reproducible evaluation protocol. The central claim is narrowed or falsified if a simpler graph reranker matches full traversal on causal and temporal recovery under equal budgets. This architecture-and-analysis preprint reports no benchmark measurements. If the claim holds, retrieval returns the evidence path that makes a memory available, not only a ranked list.

papers.title: Agreeing on the Answer but Not the Reason: Measurement Limits of LLM Reasoning Failure Taxonomies
papers.abstract: Failure taxonomies for LLM reasoning are increasingly reported as measurements: papers state what fraction of a model's errors fall into named categories, then compare those fractions across models. We show that for one such category the reported fraction is largely a property of the measurement procedure. We defined Compositional Collapse (a model notices a required sub-part of a problem, then drops or misapplies it) and measured it across twelve models and eleven languages on a public multilingual math benchmark (2,316 graded records). First, 50.1% of failures carry evidence for more than one category, so the reported plurality depends on the order in which the classifier tests them: reversing two tests moves it in eleven of twelve models, and across all six orderings Collapse's share spans 26.4% to 76.4%. Second, agreement collapses for the category but not for the task. Native speakers of all eleven languages judged 179 transcripts, agreeing with our inspector at kappa = 0.932 on answer correctness but only kappa = 0.093 on Collapse. A second native speaker per language re-rated 142 items; on 121 determinate pairs the two humans agree with each other at kappa = 0.659, while each agrees with the inspector at kappa <= 0.094. Re-running the same inspector model with the human instructions verbatim raises kappa against Human 2 from 0.147 to 0.636, so the gap is largely attributable to the prompt, not the model. Third, the inspector labels Collapse 1.81 times as often as native speakers, but only 1.17 times once a defective benchmark item (a deleted clause in the Bengali and Chinese translations) is excluded. We recommend four cheap checks before comparing failure-mode rates across models: report label co-occurrence, permute the tie-break, validate on a shared independent sample, and audit systematic disagreements.

A now-common move in LLM evaluation is to go beyond accuracy and characterise how models fail. A taxonomy of failure modes is defined, a judge model applies it to transcripts, and the resulting distribution is reported per model and compared across models. The appeal is obvious: accuracy alone does not distinguish a model that misreads a problem from one that reasons correctly and then slips.

A taxonomy of failure modes is defined, a judge model applies it to transcripts, and the resulting distribution is reported per model and compared across models. The appeal is obvious: accuracy alone does not distinguish a model that misreads a problem from one that reasons correctly and then slips.

This paper began as such a study. We defined a failure mode we call Compositional Collapse: the model explicitly notices a required structural sub-part of a problem (a rate that changes partway through, a quantity that must be excluded) and then drops it or misapplies it wholesale in a later step. It is distinct from never grasping the structure, and distinct from a local arithmetic slip. We built a two-stage pipeline, applied it to twelve models across eleven languages on a public benchmark, and obtained the kind of result such papers report: Collapse appeared to be the dominant failure mode everywhere we looked.

papers.title: Multimodal Judges Flag, Humans Decide: A Review-and-Edit Framework for AI-Generated Product Video Ads
papers.abstract: Generative pipelines can now turn every product page of an e-commerce catalog into a short video ad, but deciding whether such an ad is usable is not one good-or-bad call. We describe how we operationalized the review and editing of these ads so that both can keep pace with generation: reviewers go through each ad scene by scene and answer six questions, on the product, scene quality, pronunciation, script, sound and captions; judges built from vision-language, speech and language models file each finding under the matching question, and reviewers accept or reject each finding and add what the judges missed. Each confirmed issue then opens an edit tool matched to it. The questions and the routing from a finding to its fix do not depend on the models that generate the ad. Across 120 ads from our pipeline, reviewed with judge findings on screen, reviewers marked the product wrong on 60% of scenes, and script, caption or sound problems on under 10% each. On 60 of these ads, they marked the product wrong on 58% of scenes, far more than the 26% marked by two reviewers who later saw the ads with the judges hidden; one reviewer who saw the ads both ways marked 57% with judge findings and 19% without. On 120 blind-labeled scenes, a product judge that watches the clip with the catalog photos reached AUC 0.84, while video-quality and photo-similarity scores were close to chance. We tune the judges for recall: the product judge catches nearly all defects but also flags many clean scenes, so reviewers decide; together, the judges widen what reviewers mark and reviewers add what the judges miss. Without judge findings, one reviewer's marking faded over a session. We release a review-portal template and our review data (120 ads and 562 scenes with judge findings and human marks, plus 120 blind-labeled scenes with baseline scores) at https://github.com/anoubhav/ad-review-and-edit.
papers.intro:
Short video ads are increasingly generated: models cut them from product footage, generate them from a product’s selling points and serve them in production [73, 38, 4]. E-commerce has long checked its catalog automatically, extracting and correcting product attributes [71, 11, 62] and verifying product images [36, 18, 29], and generated ad images are already scored and inspected at scale [68, 6, 12]. Video is the next step. Our pipeline turns a product’s own data (its listing, specifications and catalog photos) into a 15-second ad with a script, narration, four or five generated scenes, captions and an end card, so it can make an ad for every catalog product. This paper is about what makes such ads usable at that scale: reviewing and editing them, taking the generator as given.

That review is hard, for reviewers and models alike. Every product has its own details, and an ad is usable only if it stays true to them. Yet generative models invent plausible details, in the pictures and in the words: an extra pocket on a pair of pants, a suitcase wheel in the wrong place, a script that calls a suitcase ‘unbreakable’ when its listing does not. Reviewers can miss such a defect but agree on it once it is pointed out: on scenes more than one reviewer saw, 90% of the product problems the judge had not flagged were marked by a single reviewer, against 12% of those it had flagged. Problems are also local and of different kinds: one scene garbles the label while the next is fine, the narration mispronounces the brand, a caption covers a face. Calling the ad good or bad hides where each problem is, and discards ads that redoing a scene or a line could save.

Neither people nor judges can carry this review alone. Judges are hard to build: generic video-quality and photo-similarity scores miss product errors, many speech-to-text models write down the word the script expects and so hide the mispronunciation they should catch, and a model’s pick of caption placement changes from run to run (Sec. 6). Even the best product judge flags many clean scenes. People struggle too: they miss defects no one points out, yet with findings on screen some of their marks may only follow the judges (Sec. 4). We therefore built a single review that judges and reviewers share (Fig. 1).

The dataset holds the ads’ 562 scenes with every reviewer’s marks and the judges’ findings with the reviewers’ votes, and 120 scenes from other ads, labeled before any judge existed (blind labels), with every baseline’s score (catalog photos as hashes only). Both are at github.com/anoubhav/ad-review-and-edit. 4. We build a judge for each question that sees what a reviewer sees (Sec. 6). On these blind labels, the product judge, which watches the clip with every catalog photo, reached AUC 0.84, while generic video-quality and photo-similarity scores reached 0.48 to 0.57; Tab. 4 ties each design choice to its labels. 5. papers.title: Stinging the Swarm: Extracting Attacker Intelligence from a Twin-Controller OT Honeypot
papers.abstract: Autonomous language-model agents can drive industrial controllers over fieldbus protocols, probing a plant at machine speed and in coordinated swarms. We present Talos, an inline gate that judges every agent request to a controller in milliseconds and routes agents it flags as hostile to a device-faithful decoy -- a mirror twin of the real plant -- where their attack continues harmlessly and is read for intelligence. We evaluate the full pipeline (detect -> quarantine -> mirror -> extract) against 2,400 autonomous attacker agents, 600 in each of four tiers that escalate the attacker's effort to stay hidden, from no concealment to an explicit non-disclosure rule and a trained cover story. No write reached the real plant in any tier: the gate denies the damage path and a device-level envelope check backstops it, while unmapped registers are denied without exception and the gate still permits safe-direction stop commands. Decisions are model-driven in every tier with no inference timeouts, closing a common objection to small on-device judges. Beyond blocking, the pipeline reads the attacker. We find a behavioral structure along two axes -- how persistently an agent attacks and how much it discloses -- and show that the system has a capture channel for three of the four resulting regions: hardened, silent attackers escalate most and are read on the mirror; compliant, talkative attackers volunteer their identity to a diagnostic form before they are ever quarantined; only the paranoid, low-yield region resists both. Attacker identity fields are self-authored cover stories, but involuntary tells -- the self-reported toolchain fingerprint and the attacker's own list of targeted registers -- accumulate across the swarm into a high-confidence profile drawn from agents under explicit orders to stay silent. The gate, mirror, and harness are released under Apache 2.0 with a synthetic device family.
papers.intro:
Operational-technology (OT) networks assume the entity on the other end of a Modbus or OPC-UA connection is a human engineer or a program a human wrote. That assumption is ending. A general-purpose language model can hold a tool-use loop, read a register, reason about what it means, and write a new value, with no human in the loop and no vendor manual. One model can enumerate a controller it has never seen; a coordinated group can do it in parallel, each agent touching the device once to stay under rate limits. The dynamic that made automated traffic the dominant load on the public web is arriving at the plant floor, where the devices are far more fragile and the consequences are physical.
