The reflexive defense is to block the connection. Blocking is cheap and often correct, but against a swarm it is a losing game: each blocked identity is replaced. And blocking discards what the attacker was about to reveal. We argue for a defense that does both jobs at once — stops the damage and reads the attacker — and we show it works against autonomous agents under realistic concealment.

Talos is an inline gate on the fieldbus, in front of the real controller. It judges every agent request in milliseconds, assigns each agent identity its own reputation and quarantine state, and permits normal operation while denying the write patterns that damage equipment. When it flags an agent as hostile it does not cut the connection; it silently reroutes that agent to a mirror twin — a decoy built from the same device family and seed, whose register map and feedback physics match what the agent has already seen. On the twin the attack continues, harmlessly, and every frame is logged and read. Because the twin accepts the writes the real plant refuses, the agent believes it is succeeding, and keeps acting, and keeps revealing.

papers.title: Ostrik's Theorem for Operator Algebras in a Unitary Tensor Category
papers.abstract: We define Hilbert modules for $\mathrm{C^*}$ and $\mathrm{W^*}$ algebra objects in the ind-completion of a unitary tensor category. We then prove an operator algebraic Ostrik's theorem in an ind-category: the 2-category of $\mathrm{C^*}$ or $\mathrm{W^*}$ algebras objects, their modules, and adjointable intertwiners is $\dagger$-equivalent to the 2-categories of $\mathrm{C^*}$ or $\mathrm{W^*}$ module categories.

papers.title: Bounding the security of the Bromberg-Shpilrain-Vdovina hash function
papers.abstract: The Bromberg-Shpilrain-Vdovina hash functions are a family of Cayley hash functions indexed by an integer parameter $k\ge 2$. Hashes are matrices in $SL_2(p)$ where $p$ is a large prime. We present an attack which finds collisions of length $O(\log p)$ whose average-case time complexity is $O(p^{0.28})$ when $k=2$ and $O(p^{0.36})$ when $k=3$ under an assumption in the spirit of Zaremba's Conjecture on continued fractions. This is an improvement on the more general attacks of Mullan-Tsaban and Slaughter which have average-case time complexity $O(\sqrt{p})$. For any $k$, the average-case time complexity of our attack is $O(p^{1-\delta_k+o(1)})$ where $\delta_k$ is the Hausdorff dimension of a certain Cantor set. This tends to $O(\sqrt{p})$ as $k\to\infty$, so our attack has time complexity comparable to Mullan-Tsaban and Slaughter's attacks as $k$ grows. We give examples of collisions for large primes found by our attack when $k=2, 3$.

papers.title: Sanity Checks for Attention Surgery: Null Models and Matched Interventions for Representation-Motivated Design
papers.abstract: Transformer architectural modifications frequently measure a statistic on internal representations, observe that it is large, remove it architecturally, and report an improvement. Interpreting that sequence requires evaluating whether the statistic exceeds its noise floor, whether it survives a geometric null, and whether the training gain requires the specific direction removed. We formulate these requirements as three reusable checks and apply them to self-attention removal, which deletes the component of an attention head's output aligned with its own value vector. Across nine multi-head pretrained models (5,408 heads, 124M to 6.9B parameters), an earlier-position causal null accounts for 48% to 63% of the head-value cosine alignment, with no monotone scale trend. Under grouped-query attention, this alignment is specific to each head's own key-value group and reverses across groups (+0.24 to +0.27 within-group, -0.11 to -0.19 across-group). Split-half reliability demonstrates that the per-head intervention effect is resolvable in GPT-2 ($r_\Delta = 0.80$) but attenuated in Pythia-160M (0.42) and Pythia-410M (0.53), whereas structural self-cosine reliability is near-perfect in all three ($r_{\text{stat}} > 0.99$); which statistic predicts its own intervention is model-dependent. In a pre-registered 3-arm by 8-seed paired factorial at $4.0 \times 10^8$ tokens per run (399,900,672 tokens), a fixed arbitrary rank-one direction does not differ from baseline (+0.0011 nats, $p = 0.197$), while self-directed removal lowers validation loss (-0.0029 nats, Holm-corrected $p = 0.0023$) and outperforms the fixed arbitrary control directly (-0.0040 nats, $p = 0.0018$). At 50.9M scale the training benefit requires the own-value direction rather than a fixed arbitrary one, but a large cosine alignment alone does not establish redundancy in frozen models.

papers.title: A Threshold-Crossing Condition for the Least Colossally Abundant Counterexample to Robin's Inequality
papers.abstract: We study the constraints that a hypothetical least Colossally Abundant (CA) counterexample to Robin's Inequality would place on the non-trivial zeros of $\zeta(s)$. In the single-prime case we express the least CA counterexample $N$ as $M\cdot p$, where $M$ is its CA predecessor and $p$ is prime. Using the von Mangoldt explicit formula for $\psi(x)$, we express $\ln p$ in terms of a sum over the non-trivial zeros of $\zeta(s)$ and split that expression into its baseline contribution $\mathcal{R}_0(p)$ and its off-line distortion. When both converge, we show that the off-line distortion is negative whenever $1+1/(e^{\mathcal{R}_0(p)}+e^{2\mathcal{R}_0(p)}+\cdots+e^{(v+1)\mathcal{R}_0(p)})\le\ln(\ln M+\mathcal{R}_0(p))/\ln\ln M$, where $v$ is the $p$-adic valuation of $M$. In the case where the least CA counterexample is the product of its CA predecessor and two primes (the semiprime case), the logarithm of the product of the two primes is the sum of two von Mangoldt expansions. An analogous inequality implies that at least one of the off-line distortions of the two expansions is negative.

papers.title: Topological Dynamics Under Non-Stationary Supervision: Persistent Homology of Neural Network Weight Evolution
papers.abstract: We investigate how the persistent topology of neuron- weight point clouds evolves under stable and non-stationary supervision. An identical multilayer perceptron is trained on Fashion-MNIST with correct labels, a fixed random permutation of the training-label vector, or a fresh permutation every epoch. Five paired seeds share initialisation and minibatch order, yielding 15 models trained for 100 epochs. Raw and row-normalised incoming weight clouds are analysed with H0 and H1 Vietoris Rips persistence at 22 checkpoints. Correct-label models reach 89.39% mean true-label test accuracy; fixed-random models fit 67.94% of their assigned training targets without generalising to the original task. Correct-label models have descriptively greater time-averaged normalised fc3 H1 persistence than either random-label condition, but the configured exact comparisons do not reach conventional significance after Holm correction. Early condition classification achieves 60.0% mean balanced accuracy using topology, 66.7% using conventional diagnostics, and 60.0% using both. Thus, no incremental predictive improvement is demonstrated in this setting. The archive contains all 3,300 configured topology cases. Interpretation is limited by five seeds, a single architecture and dataset, 282 capped H1 distance comparisons, and deferred bottleneck analysis.
papers.intro:
Ordinary supervised training assumes a fixed relationship between examples and targets. Relabeling, changing teachers, and online adaptation can instead modify the objective while optimization is in progress. Understanding such dynamics requires separating target informativeness from target stability. A correct-versus-changing-label comparison alone cannot distinguish the two: random targets remove useful image–label structure, and changing them adds non-stationarity.

Random-label memorization demonstrates that neural networks can fit mappings unrelated to input semantics, although its extent depends on model, optimization, and training budget [1, 2]. Work on plasticity further establishes that networks can become less able to adapt during continued learning [3, 4]. Our changing-random condition is an extreme supervision intervention, not a standard continual-learning benchmark; we do not measure later-task plasticity or retention. A fixed-random control is essential because it retains an arbitrary but temporally stable assignment.

Loss and accuracy quantify fitting and generalization, but do not exhaustively describe internal organization. Persistent homology [5] supplies a multiscale summary of a chosen representation; persistence landscapes provide vector-valued summaries [6]. Applied to incoming-weight vectors, these tools may expose changes in neuron similarity. Equally, the summaries may recapitulate ordinary geometric or spectral changes. Demonstrating a visually different trajectory is therefore weaker than demonstrating useful information beyond a conventional baseline.

papers.title: Berry phase and Hannay angle as Taylor coefficients of the minimal action
papers.abstract: For a Hamiltonian system with one degree of freedom whose parameters are varied slowly around a closed loop, with slowness $\delta$, we study the minimal action $\beta_\delta$ of the resulting time-periodic system and its convex conjugate, Mather's $\alpha$-function $\alpha_\delta$, both normalized per unit time. The cycle map of such a system is an area-preserving map of the cylinder which in general is not integrable. We prove that $\beta_\delta(\rho)$ and $\alpha_\delta(c)$ have asymptotic expansions in $\delta$ to every finite order, locally uniformly in the rotational regime of the frozen systems, and we identify the coefficients geometrically. The zeroth coefficient of $\alpha_\delta$ is the average of the frozen effective Hamiltonians, as shown by Evans and Gomes. The first coefficient is the classical Berry phase: at fixed rotation number $\rho$, the first Taylor coefficient of $\beta_\delta(\rho)$ is, modulo periods, Weinstein's Berry phase of the loop of frozen invariant curves of the class whose averaged frozen frequency is $\rho$, each curve weighted by its Mather measure. In particular, the minimal action selects the weighting in Weinstein's construction. The Hannay angle, the derivative of the Berry phase, governs the rotation numbers of all minimizing measures, including those supported on Aubry--Mather sets of the cycle map, where no invariant curve exists; and the intervals of classes on which a rotation number is locked have length $O(\delta^\infty)$. Since the expansions concern exact convex functions, no adiabatic approximation is involved. A transformation rule under loops of point transformations explains why the Berry phase is defined only modulo $2\pi c\mathbb{Z}$. Linear oscillators, treated by the same method, recover Berry's formula for the generalized harmonic oscillator and show that the expansions are asymptotic only.

papers.title: Optimal Regulation and Information Institutions with Hidden Network Equilibria
papers.abstract: Aggregate outcomes can conceal network configurations that expose households to uninsurable risk and require different public services. We study a regulator's joint choice of a corrective activity charge and an information institution in a two-population network game. Although aggregate behavior follows an exact stable law, distinct specialization equilibria require different targeted interventions. With purchased Gaussian monitoring, primitive conditions imply a discontinuous switch between strong regulation without purchased information and informed specialization. The regulator may alternatively obtain signed certification or elicit a privately known state through a report backed by committed random audits. We characterize the three institutions' optimized values and the cost thresholds at which credible disclosure replaces government monitoring. The institutional choice also changes optimal regulation: even when certification and truthful reporting reveal the same state, costly audits favor less specialization and a higher corrective charge. This ordering and monotonicity in audit costs hold under an explicit interiority condition without global concavity of the audit problem. The institutional comparison is solved in the benchmark without feedback from anticipated policy, while the policy switch and strict institutional rankings admit local persistence under additional regularity conditions. Results depend on enforceable verification, restrictions on data access, and an explicitly limited institutional menu.
papers.intro:
Regulators often observe an aggregate outcome more precisely than the configuration of activities that produces it. A national output measure, sectoral activity index, or average adoption rate may remain stable while firms and households reorganize along different technologies or production links. Those differences matter for public policy when decentralized activity exposes third parties to uninsured risk and when public services deliver different benefits across the resulting configurations. The regulator then faces two distinct instruments: an ex ante charge that discourages risky divergence and ex post targeting informed by costly monitoring.

For example, a confidential standards assessor might verify penalties for technological incompatibilities among interconnected producers, while a separate public agency allocates adjustment capacity to the cluster that needs it most. A verified count of incompatibilities need not disclose which named cluster follows which technology. The information problem becomes consequential when producers’ choices also expose households to risks that cannot be insured through verifiable state-contingent contracts. This example motivates a feasible institutional separation; its empirical prevalence and the costs of maintaining it are outside the model.

A conventional regulatory calculation starts with the marginal external damage from an activity and asks how strongly the government should discourage it. This paper adds a policy-design margin. Regulation changes the size of the economic differences about which information might later be acquired. Better monitoring in turn increases the expected benefit of allowing those differences, since the government can better direct a subsequent intervention. When agents foresee this response, information policy also affects their earlier private activity. Consequently, the desired degree of regulation and the value of public monitoring are jointly endogenous.

We develop these effects in a network game with a fixed, two-block interaction structure. Uninsured households bear a risk externality generated by the private activity difference. The government selects a charge on connected agents’ activity differences and a precision level for a private Gaussian monitoring signal. After private choices have been made and a stable specialization configuration has emerged, the regulator observes its signal and chooses a contingent public service. The service is then sequentially optimal, and private actors rationally anticipate its expected return.

The analysis combines three results. First, the average activity obeys an exact, stable aggregate equation even when the network supports distinct specialization equilibria requiring different targeted interventions. Second, the expectation of more precisely targeted public services strengthens private specialization under a transparent feedback condition. Third, explicit inequalities in the primitives of network interaction, monitoring technology, regulatory cost, and outside risk guarantee a discontinuous switch between no monitoring with strong regulation and positive monitoring with more specialization. A comparative-static result establishes how uninsured risk, information costs, and targeting benefits shift the critical network exposure. These results establish existence and local robustness for a specified class of networks; they do not establish the same conclusions for arbitrary network topology.

The economic point is a public-finance distinction between instruments that restrain an externality before its realization and institutions that reveal its subsequent allocation-relevant configuration. An institutional-choice result places purchased governmental monitoring alongside signed certification and incentive-compatible reporting with committed random audits. The cost thresholds identify when private information displaces government monitoring. A further regulatory result shows that even equally informative institutions lead to different ex ante corrective charges: the expected audit expenditure needed to deter false reports increases with the permitted specialization amplitude. Higher unit audit costs therefore weakly raise the optimal charge within the active reporting institution. These results require robust reporting incentives and do not treat a favorable cheap-talk equilibrium as guaranteed implementation. The exact aggregate law makes the public-finance trade-off transparent: forecasting remains valid while policy-relevant information depends on institutions. We next relate the argument to the literature, present the economic environment, derive private equilibrium and welfare, and compare the available instruments. Proofs appear in the appendix.

papers.title: Deterministic, Reproducible Inference in Exact Integer Arithmetic, and Verifiable Distributed Inference as Its Consequence
papers.abstract: Optimized floating-point inference is not reproducible across environments: the same model on different hardware, compilers or thread counts can produce different bits. We present tritify, an open-source runtime that executes the forward pass of real models -- decoder-only language models, Mixture-of-Experts decoders, and the Segment Anything 2.1 image/video stack -- with the entire run-time path in exact integer arithmetic; floating point is confined to offline quantization and the float reference used for verification. We make three separate claims and verify each. (1) Cross-hardware reproducibility: the integer path produces bit-identical output run to run, across CPU instruction-set architectures, and across CPU/GPU, carried by a reproducing SHA-256 of the output. (2) Decision fidelity: the integer path reproduces the float reference's decision on the models and inputs tested, with the numeric exceptions measured; per-layer fidelity through sixteen layers of OLMoE-1B-7B and of a 106-billion-parameter MoE shows no fidelity cliff. (3) Location independence: a model's computation can be split across instruction sets, CPU and GPU, and networked machines with zero effect on the output bits. GLM-4.5-Air (106,852,251,264 parameters, 427 GB of integer codes) generated its answer across three machines, none of which can hold its integer codes in RAM, bit-identically to a single-host reference. The consequence is verifiable distributed inference: an untrusted server or a fleet of devices runs the model while an open scalar oracle re-derives the exact bytes; a guarantee against a dishonest server is future work. We do not claim a per-device speed-up, bit-equality of floating-valued intermediates, or confidentiality. Code: https://github.com/pelloran-inc/tritify
papers.intro:
Machine-learning inference is hard to reproduce bit-for-bit, because typical optimized floating-point execution is not deterministic across environments. IEEE-754 addition is not associative, so a change in reduction order — a different BLAS, a different thread count, a fused multiply-add, a different GPU — changes the result in the low bits. Transcendental functions (exp\exp, tanh\tanh, 1/1/\sqrt{\,}) are not required to be correctly rounded, so two platforms’ math libraries disagree. Reproducible floating point is achievable (for example reproducible BLAS such as ReproBLAS [8], which pins the reduction), but at a cost and not by default in standard inference stacks. tritify removes the source of that nondeterminism from the inference path. The weights are quantized to fixed-point integers once; activations are quantized dynamically, per tensor, with no calibration pass; and the entire element-wise data path — matrix-multiply accumulation, requantization, residual addition, the application of normalization and attention scales — is carried in exact integer arithmetic. Our contribution is not a new quantization algorithm — the arithmetic building blocks are standard. It is a fully specified, self-verifying inference path whose output is reproducible bit-for-bit across hardware, an empirical demonstration on real models including a frontier MoE, an engineering architecture (a frozen generic engine plus per-family plugins) that makes the property reusable, and — the step this paper adds — the consequence of bit-identity for distributed inference. Because the output does not depend on where each operation runs, a model can be split across many machines and the gather is bit-for-bit the single-machine result; and a server’s work can be checked, not merely trusted, by re-deriving its exact bytes against the open reference. The market for serving AI is otherwise binary — all-local (private but constrained by one device’s memory) or all-cloud (powerful but you must blindly trust the provider). Bit-identity opens a third position: cloud (or fleet) capacity with a reproducible, independently checkable result. Standard optimized float inference does not occupy it by default: it is not bit-identical across heterogeneous backends (CPU-float ≠\neq GPU-float ≠\neq other-CPU-float), so a split float result depends on the split and is not reproducible without special effort — a reduction-pinned BLAS [8] fixes summation order, but does not by itself make a whole heterogeneous model’s inference bit-identical.

papers.title: Camera equalisation of an 11.5x drop in environmental illuminance: four imitation-learning policies on an SO-101 arm
papers.abstract: Real-robot benchmarks of learned visuomotor policies often record room illuminance as the lighting condition. We show that, on a typical low-cost rig, room light and image light can be almost unrelated. Four imitation-learning policies (ACT, SmolVLA, Diffusion Policy and pi0.5) were trained on the same 50 demonstrations of a pick-and-place task on an SO-101 arm. Each was run for ten rollouts at about 520 lux and again at about 45 lux, an 11.5x reduction. Success was 20/40 in normal light and 19/40 in low light: a change of -2.5 percentage points (95% CI -23 to +19), with no evidence that the policies differed in sensitivity (interaction p = 0.86). The recorded video shows why: mean image brightness was only 3% lower in low light on the front camera and 19% lower on the wrist camera. Both cameras were set to automatic exposure and white balance, which most likely absorbed the difference; exposure was not locked in this experiment. An accidental repeat of one 10-rollout block reproduced its success count (7/10) but matched the first block at only 6 of 10 placements, consistent with chance. We conclude that lux alone does not describe what a policy sees. Camera settings, and image statistics compared with the training recordings, are the quantities to report and control. Data and code are public.

This note asks how much the success of four learned manipulation policies changes when the room light drops about tenfold, and why.

Visuomotor policies map camera images to robot actions. Lighting changes those images everywhere at once, and a simulated perturbation benchmark ranks lighting among the changes that hurt manipulation policies most [8]. A natural safeguard in real-robot evaluation is to fix the light and log illuminance in lux, assuming that equal lux means equal inputs.

Lighting changes those images everywhere at once, and a simulated perturbation benchmark ranks lighting among the changes that hurt manipulation policies most [8]. A natural safeguard in real-robot evaluation is to fix the light and log illuminance in lux, assuming that equal lux means equal inputs.

We tested that assumption on a common low-cost setup: an SO-101 arm [6] driven through LeRobot [5], with two off-the-shelf USB cameras. Four widely used policies were trained on identical demonstrations: ACT [1], SmolVLA [3], Diffusion Policy (DP) [2] and π0.5\pi_{0.5} [4]. We then benched them at the recording light level and at about one eleventh of it. The contributions are: 1. A paired real-robot comparison of four policies under an 11.5×\times illuminance drop: 80 rollouts, with effect estimates and intervals. 2. Measurements of what the cameras actually recorded. The images were barely darker, so the finding concerns the camera pipeline more than the policies. 3. A same-day repeat of one block, which shows how much a single 10-rollout block varies on its own. 4. Practical recommendations for reporting and controlling lighting in small real-robot benchmarks. The experiment ran as an exploratory side study during a larger, pre-registered benchmark on the same rig. It was not itself pre-registered.

papers.title: Antalia-2 Mini: A 7.6-million-parameter Turkish text-to-speech model trained entirely on synthetic speech
papers.abstract: Antalia-2 Mini is a single-voice Turkish text-to-speech model with 7,620,931 parameters. It reads characters and produces 48 kHz audio at 41 times real time on an Apple M5 laptop CPU (2 threads). Its training audio came only from VoxCPM2 (the teacher), about 300 times larger, cloning one synthetic clip; automatic checks kept about 1,790 h. Fine-tuning the vocoder on the acoustic model's own mel spectrograms cut the word error rate (WER) of Whisper's transcripts from a mean of 3.89% to 1.75% at adjacent pre-release checkpoints. The teacher corrupts the start of a clip when the first word begins with \"o, the student learned this, and a spoken prefix we cut from the output hides it. On the 495-sentence Freya-TR-Eval benchmark, where we tuned settings, version 1.0.1 has WER 1.09% and character error rate 0.22% on our public harness. A paired bootstrap cannot distinguish these from EMA Lightning, an 8.6M Turkish model, which scores higher on full-band UTMOS, an English-trained quality proxy. No human listening test exists. Weights, inference code and the benchmark harness are public under Apache-2.0; training code and data are not.

A text-to-speech (TTS) model small enough for a CPU can run on the machine that needs the speech, with no GPU server and no text leaving the device. Among the Turkish systems we ran, two small open-weights models, Piper (voice dfki) at 16M parameters and MMS-TTS at 36M, have word error rates (WER) of 3.41% and 6.38%, against 1.16% for Trendyol-TTS at about 2.38B. We get a WER by having the Whisper speech recognizer (Radford et al., 2023) transcribe a model’s audio and comparing the transcript with the input text, here on the public harness of the Freya-TR-Eval benchmark. Antalia-2 Mini (Mini below) aims for the low error rates of large systems at 7.62M, in one voice.

Mini reads characters, 47 symbols in all, with no phonemizer to turn spelling into sound symbols, and learns how letters sound from its training audio. Turkish spelling suits this choice. Öney and Durgunoğlu (1997) describe it as phonologically transparent, with regular letter-sound correspondences, and Babayiğit (2022) names Ğ as the exception. A text normalizer first turns numbers, dates, times, amounts, initialisms, web addresses and English or brand words into spoken form (Table 2), and its known defects carry into the speech.

papers.title: Swanada: Split-Encoder Capability-Routed Conformer CTC and Sub-30 MB On-Device Speech Recognition Across Twelve Scripts
papers.abstract:
Client-side automatic speech recognition (ASR) across Indic and Classical scripts eliminates cloud transcription costs, network tail latency, and server-side audio retention, yet neural exports face four systems bottlenecks in browsers and mobile runtimes: (1) monolithic per-language Conformer checkpoints require ~177 MiB per script (> 2.1 GiB across 12 scripts), exhausting CacheStorage quotas; (2) static relative positional encoding tables embed 10.2-20.5 MB of FP32 constants while 1x1 Conv1d layers trigger slow or unsupported ConvInteger kernels in WebAssembly SIMD; (3) sliding-window CTC flickers on boundary tokens; and (4) mobile WebAudio pipelines suffer 44.1/48 kHz sample-rate mismatches and silent AudioWorklet stalls under iOS WKWebView.
  We present Swanada, an open-source 16 kHz streaming ASR system spanning Classical Sanskrit, Indian English, and ten Indian languages (sa, en, hi, kn, mr, bn, ta, te, ml, gu, pa, or) across browser WebAssembly, Node.js, and Python. Swanada pairs capability-routed shared INT8 Conformer encoders (a 17-layer 177.38 MiB Studio tier at $d = 512$ for desktop/servers and a distilled 14-layer 25.35 MiB Mobile tier at $d = 256$ for phones) with twelve hot-swappable 515.0 KiB native-script linear CTC heads ($257 \times 512$), cutting 12-language storage by $11.6\times$ (183.4 MiB) and $67.8\times$ (31.39 MiB; 25.85 MiB first load). Runtime protobuf tail surgery exposes the shared representation in $< 2$ ms, while dynamic positional synthesis, MatMul pointwise convolutions, and post-quantization QInt8 head calibration preserve sub-30 MB accuracy. Across $N = 480$ held-out and $N = 1,280$ open public test clips (FLEURS, LibriSpeech, GLOBE, AMI, wild Sanskrit), Swanada achieves 5.43% held-out and 8.87% 12-language open CER on Studio (18.56% and 19.23% on Mobile) at $0.0097\times$-$0.0264\times$ RTF, with 30.6 ms median TTFT and 0.00% committed-prefix churn.
papers.intro:
Running speech-to-text directly inside a browser tab or local edge process removes per-minute API billing, round-trip network jitter, and transmission of private microphone audio to remote servers. Voice input for South Asian digital public infrastructure, Sanskrit recitation study, bilingual developer tools, and offline accessibility interfaces requires native script fidelity across Brahmic and Latin orthographies, sub-100 ms streaming partial updates, and reliable execution within smartphone browser memory budgets, complementing client-side speech synthesis [9].

Convolution-augmented Transformers (Conformers) [7] trained with Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) [6] are attractive for on-device ASR because frame-synchronous emission avoids the O⁡(U2)O(U^{2}) autoregressive decoder loop and hallucination modes of sequence-to-sequence models such as Whisper [13]. However, deploying Conformer-CTC across twelve scripts inside real desktop and mobile browsers exposes four concrete systems bottlenecks: 1. Monolithic Fleet Storage vs. Joint-Vocabulary Dilution: Shipping one quantized Conformer-Large per language requires 12×177.38=2,128.512\times 177.38=2{,}128.5 MiB, exceeding mobile browser cache budgets. Conversely, pooling twelve scripts into a single flat output softmax (>3,000>3{,}000 classes) inflates final projection compute by 12×12\times at every frame and permits cross-script token leakage during noisy frames. 2. ONNX Constant Bloat and ConvInteger Quantization Gaps: Standard Conformer exports materialize a static 2​Lmax×d2L_{\max}\times d FP32 relative positional encoding buffer (20.48 MB at d=512d=512, 10.24 MB at d=256d=256 for Lmax=5,000L_{\max}=5{,}000), consuming over a third of a 30 MB mobile budget on uncompressible constants. Simultaneously, exporting 1×11\times 1 pointwise convolutions inside Conformer macaron blocks as Conv nodes either leaves weights in FP32 or emits ConvInteger operators lacking fast WebAssembly SIMD kernels in onnxruntime-web. 3. Quantization Feature Drift Under Narrow Student Bottlenecks: Compressing a 115.2M-parameter teacher into a <30<30 MB student and applying dynamic INT8 weight/activation quantization perturbs top-layer hidden norms and directions, degrading pre-trained linear CTC decision boundaries unless explicitly recalibrated on quantized ONNX activations. 4. Streaming Prefix Flicker and Mobile WebAudio Fragility: Evaluating bounded audio windows causes trailing subwords to oscillate as right acoustic context arrives, while mobile browsers lock AudioContext to hardware rates (44.1/48 kHz) and intermittently stall AudioWorklet threads under iOS WKWebView rules.

papers.title: Oscillatory Processing Units as a computing substrate for biomimetic intelligence
papers.abstract: Biological intelligence emerges from neural activity that connects sensation, memory and action. Synaptic plasticity, neuronal assemblies and oscillations provide principles for biomimetic computing, but translating them into reusable operations requires a defined computational unit. We introduce Oscillatory Processing Units (OPUs), groups of synthetic neurons sharing a rhythm. Their directed interactions transform incoming activity and prior receiving state into an Oscillatory Occupancy Space (OOS), which becomes available to subsequent computation. We show that source--receiver conditions and oscillatory organization shape these transformations, including their geometry, persistence and historical accessibility. An Atlas of measured relationships supports prospective composition with predicted response classes. Configured circuits perform logical and numerical operations, express associative recall and generate closed-loop decisions with fixed synaptic weights. OPUs and OOS establish a computing substrate for biomimetic intelligence in which experience remains part of the state through which new input becomes action.

papers.title: Alania-2: Turkish text-to-speech with instant and fine-tuned voice cloning
papers.abstract: We present Alania-2, a Turkish text-to-speech (TTS) system with two built-in voices, voice design from text descriptions, and two kinds of voice cloning. Alania-2 is a 488M-parameter model with the VoxCPM architecture, which generates continuous audio latents with a diffusion head on top of a language-model backbone. We train it from scratch on 18,195 hours of Turkish speech, 90% of which is synthetic speech produced by a larger teacher model and filtered automatically. A text normalizer rewrites numbers, abbreviations and foreign names into the words a Turkish speaker would say; without it, none of 96 test sentences with digits kept all its critical parts, such as an amount or a date, through synthesis and speech recognition, against 86 with it. On Freya-TR-Eval, a public benchmark of 495 Turkish sentences scored with automatic speech recognition, Alania-2 reaches a word error rate of 1.44%, compared with 5.99% for our previous system. On its built-in voices, it comes within half a point of character error rate of a 2.3B-parameter model at under a quarter of the size, and a 7.6M-parameter single-voice model trained with the same recipe matches the most intelligible systems we measured, which suggests that training data matters more for intelligibility than model size. We also report practical findings on voice cloning: conditioning on the reference audio alone, rather than continuing it, cuts skipped words from 21.9% to 1.7%; 20-30 seconds of reference audio works best; and a low-rank adapter trained in about two minutes raises speaker similarity well above instant cloning. Finally, we describe inference-engine changes that bring first audio down to 32 ms for a single stream. We release our evaluation harness and three Turkish speech and text datasets.

Recent zero-shot TTS models (Chen et al., 2025a; Du et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025b; Zhou et al., 2025) were trained mainly on English and Chinese speech. Multilingual successors such as VoxCPM2 (Zhou et al., 2026) support Turkish as one of 30 languages, and open Turkish systems differ by an order of magnitude in intelligibility (Section 6).

papers.title: Are Causal Neuron Circuits Unique and Transferable?
papers.abstract: Interpretability demonstrations often show that intervening on a group of neurons changes a model's answer. A recent example removes an 18-neuron group in Qwen3-32B and the model answers "Simba" instead of "Scar" to a two-hop Lion King riddle. Such a demonstration establishes that the group matters, but not how much of it is necessary, whether other groups could do the same, or whether the effect carries over to other inputs. We ask: when intervening on a group of neurons changes a model's answer, how much of that group is actually necessary? For every selected group we measure all 4,096 subsets of 12 MLP neurons. On a two-alternative capital task (Qwen3-0.6B), zero-ablating 12 selected neurons lowers the answer margin by 27% while random neurons barely change it, yet replacing the same neurons with their values from other questions also barely changes it: their activations are nearly constant across questions, and we find no evidence that they carry question-specific content. On two-hop relation chains, patching 12 neurons with activations from the first-hop question shifts the answer to the bridge entity (from Scar to Simba): the greedy answer starts with the bridge in 9/11 chains for Qwen3-1.7B, 9/11 for Llama-3.2-1B and 8/10 for Gemma-3-1B; random neurons never do. The full group is rarely necessary: a few neurons often suffice, and in many chains disjoint subsets each flip the answer on their own, in an exploratory analysis most often when the model is less confident. Group effects transfer to rephrasings of the same chain but are much weaker on other tested chains. We study neuron-level causal interventions and alternative subsets; we do not recover the full connectivity of circuits.
papers.intro:
A common form of evidence in mechanistic interpretability is a group intervention: a set of internal components is selected, removed or overwritten, and the model’s output changes. Goodfire’s recent essay on neuron interpretability gives a vivid example [1]. Qwen3-32B answers a riddle about the Pride Lands with “Scar”; removing an 18-neuron “Lion King” group found in an attribution graph makes it answer “Simba” (P(Scar) = 0.24), whereas removing 18 random neurons from the same layers leaves P(Scar) at 0.91. The demonstration is a genuine causal experiment, and the random control is appropriate.

Goodfire’s recent essay on neuron interpretability gives a vivid example [1]. Qwen3-32B answers a riddle about the Pride Lands with “Scar”; removing an 18-neuron “Lion King” group found in an attribution graph makes it answer “Simba” (P(Scar) = 0.24), whereas removing 18 random neurons from the same layers leaves P(Scar) at 0.91. The demonstration is a genuine causal experiment, and the random control is appropriate.

What such a demonstration does not show is the internal structure of the group. Would 17 neurons have been enough? 10? 4? Could a completely different set of four neurons produce the same change? Do the neurons act independently, so that their effects add up, or only in combination? And does the group do the same thing for a rephrased question, or for a different question? Without these answers it is hard to say how much explanatory weight “these 18 neurons” can carry. The public write-up does not report how the group size was chosen, what intervention was used to remove the neurons, or how subsets of the group behave; we treat these as open questions rather than as shortcomings of that work, whose broader claims do not rest on this one example.

Uniqueness: can other, disjoint subsets produce the same change? Interaction: are the neurons’ effects additive, or do they depend on each other? Transfer: does the same frozen group have the same effect on rephrasings of the question, and on other questions?

Because a group of 12 neurons has only 4,096 subsets, these questions can be answered exhaustively rather than by sampling. We do this in two studies and three model families:

Twelve neurons selected by zero-ablation effect pass the usual random-neuron control (−-27% margin vs. ∼\sim0%), their effects are almost perfectly additive and they transfer to rephrasings and new questions. Yet replacing them with values from other questions has almost no effect. A group can look causal, additive and transferable without any evidence of question-specific content on the tested questions. • Study 2 (two-hop relation chains, Qwen3-1.7B, Llama-3.2-1B, Gemma-3-1B). Patching 12 neurons with activations from the first-hop question reproduces the Scar →\rightarrow Simba shift in most chains of all three families, random neurons never do, and the frozen group has much smaller effects on other chains. Within the group, a few neurons usually suffice, and in many chains disjoint subsets each flip the answer. • A practical point for group demonstrations. papers.title: On the strong Dixmier-Moeglin equivalence for the quantum semisimple groups
papers.abstract: The Dixmier-Moeglin equivalence, when it holds for an algebra, characterizes its primitive ideals ( that is, the annihilators of irreducible representations) both algebraically and topologically within the prime spectrum. A stronger form, known as the strong Dixmier-Moeglin equivalence, was introduced by Bell, Launois, and Nolan in their work on 'A strong Dixmier-Moeglin equivalence for quantum Schubert cells'. In this paper, we prove that the generic quantized coordinate rings of connected, simply connected semisimple complex algebraic groups satisfy the strong Dixmier-Moeglin equivalence.
papers.intro:
Throughout this paper, 𝕂\mathbb{K} denotes an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, every algebra is a unital associative 𝕂\mathbb{K}-algebra and every ideal is two-sided.

Throughout this paper, 𝕂\mathbb{K} denotes an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, every algebra is a unital associative 𝕂\mathbb{K}-algebra and every ideal is two-sided.

Classifying simple modules over an algebra is a fundamental and often difficult problem in representation theory. Simple modules play a role analogous to that of simple groups in group theory, as they are the building blocks of module categories. Their connection to ideals is captured by annihilators: the annihilator of a module consists of the elements of the algebra that act trivially on every element of that module. This naturally leads to the notion of primitive ideals, which are defined as the annihilators of simple left modules. While every primitive ideal is prime the converse is not always true: not all prime ideals are primitive.

The Dixmier–Moeglin equivalence does not hold in all cases. Lorenz [15] constructed an algebra with a primitive ideal that is not locally closed, while Irving [11] provided an example of a rational ideal that is not primitive. Conversely, the equivalence has been established for various classes of algebras endowed with a Hopf structure, such as group algebras [19] and quantized coordinate rings [8]. Motivated by these observations, Bell and Leung [3, Conjecture 1.3] conjectured that every finitely generated complex Noetherian Hopf algebra of finite Gelfand–Kirillov dimension satisfies the Dixmier–Moeglin equivalence. papers.title: The Feynman Dyson argument extended to the inhomogeneous Maxwell equations
papers.abstract: The Feynman-Dyson argument gives the homogeneous Maxwell equations but does not identify the sources in the other two equations with the charge and current carried by matter. Taking the homogeneous equations as given, we derive Gauss's law and the Ampere-Maxwell law for the sources entering the Lorentz force and the power delivered to matter. We assume, in particular, that the field densities and fluxes are at most quadratic in the fields and covariant under proper rotations. We require the same expressions for the sources to satisfy local energy and momentum conservation for every field that obeys the homogeneous equations, and to be continuous in spacetime along every smooth such field. The charge and current densities are then unique up to the values of $\varepsilon_0$ and $\mu_0$. We also discuss how these assumptions might be relaxed.
papers.intro: In his 1865 account of the electromagnetic field, Maxwell brought electrical, magnetic and optical phenomena into a common dynamical framework. His theory connected the propagation of light with electromagnetic disturbances and related the energy of the field to the mechanical forces acting on electrified bodies and currents [1]. These connections invite a further investigation of the assumptions underlying the theory, particularly the relation between the action of a field on matter and the role of matter as its source. In October 1948, Feynman showed Dyson an argument that approached electrodynamics from the motion of a single nonrelativistic particle. Starting from Newton’s equation Fj​(x,x˙,t)=m​x¨jF_{j}(x,\dot{x},t)=m\ddot{x}_{j} and the commutation relations [xi,xj]=0,m⁡[xi,x˙j]=i​ℏ​δi​j[x_{i},x_{j}]=0,\quad m[x_{i},\dot{x}_{j}]=i\hbar\delta_{ij}, he obtained the Lorentz form of the force and the two homogeneous Maxwell equations. According to Dyson, Feynman sought to explore particle dynamics without initially assuming the usual Hamiltonian or Lagrangian formulation. The argument remained unpublished until 1990, when Dyson presented a reconstruction of Feynman’s exposition together with an account of its motivation [2]. The equations containing charge and current occupy a different position in Dyson’s presentation. He remarks that they “merely define” the external charge and current densities [2]. This statement leaves a physical identification unresolved. Given electric and magnetic fields, one can introduce quantities through the differential expressions appearing in Gauss’s law and the Ampère-Maxwell law. Such definitions do not, however, establish that these quantities coincide with the charge and current carried by matter. Once ρ\rho and JJ denote the physical densities entering the force and power delivered to matter, the source equations express physical laws relating the electromagnetic field to the charge and current carried by matter. Their validity requires an argument beyond the introduction of notation. Subsequent work has examined the compatibility of Galilean mechanics with the full Maxwell equations [3] and the role of minimal coupling, where a conserved current is introduced through the divergence of the field tensor [4]. Harikumar et al. extend the minimal coupling construct to κ\kappa Minkowski spacetime to first order in the deformation, defining a deformed conserved current [5], while Kauffman develops a noncommutative generalization of the Feynman-Dyson argument [6]. Di Mauro et al. reconstruct Feynman’s later route to the source equations from electrostatics, relativistic covariance and charge conservation [7]. We take this unresolved identification as the starting point of the present work. Retaining the homogeneous equations obtained in the Feynman-Dyson argument, we investigate which additional assumptions allow the source equations to follow from local conservation of energy and momentum. The physical motivation is direct: the force exerted on matter and the work done on it must be balanced by changes and transport of field momentum and energy. The same charge and current must enter both descriptions of this exchange. We therefore introduce ρ\rho and JJ through their role in the Lorentz force and electrical power, and seek to determine their relation to the fields. The use of conservation principles in reconstructing electrodynamics has substantial antecedents. Imai developed a formulation based on energy and momentum conservation [8], while Nöckel obtained Maxwell’s equations from local energy and momentum conservation within relativistic mechanics, using independent variation of the field values at fixed derivatives [9]. Assuming the Maxwell energy and momentum tensor in a relativistic setting, Arminjon also recovered the source equations from the conservation laws and the Lorentz force where E⋅B≠0E\cdot B\neq 0 [10, 11]. Related work by Navarro and Sancho characterizes electromagnetic energy tensors through geometric and divergence conditions [12]. In macroscopic electrodynamics, Gratus, McCall and Kinsler expressed free charge and current through first order linear differential operators acting on EE and BB, eliminating the excitation fields DD and HH [13]. Complementary classifications determine local conservation laws assuming the full source free Maxwell equations [14]. Our investigation concerns the particular extension needed by the Feynman-Dyson argument: the homogeneous equations are given, while the source equations and the admissible field densities and fluxes are to be determined without postulating covariance under boosts. To make this reconstruction precise, we assume that the field energy, momentum, energy flux and stress depend algebraically on the electric and magnetic fields at the same point. Their dependence is restricted to polynomials of degree at most two, with constant coefficients and covariance under proper spatial rotations. We assume that the charge and current densities are finite functions of the field values and first derivatives at the same point. The same functions must satisfy both conservation laws for every choice of these data compatible with the homogeneous equations. This is an additional assumption i.e. the same source functions must satisfy both conservation laws for every field configuration allowed by the homogeneous equations, not just for one particular configuration. Along every smooth field satisfying those equations, the assigned sources must be continuous in spacetime. Under these assumptions, we obtain Gauss’s law and the Ampère-Maxwell law for the physical sources entering mechanical exchange. For fixed electromagnetic constants, the stated assumptions uniquely determine the charge and current densities from the fields and their first derivatives. The same analysis determines the field densities and fluxes up to two explicitly conserved additions and constant offsets. After subtracting the constant energy offset, positivity of the field energy selects positive values of the two electromagnetic constants. Neither parity, time reversal, covariance under boosts nor a field action is assumed in the reconstruction. We first state the premises and classify the permitted field quantities, then derive the source equations and examine the freedom left by conservation. Particular attention is given to configurations in which the electric and magnetic fields have vanishing scalar product, where continuity is needed to complete the source identification. Finally, a nonlinear example in the appendix shows that the other premises do not imply the quadratic restriction. The result is therefore a conditional extension of the Feynman-Dyson argument, with the assumptions responsible for recovering the physical source equations stated explicitly.

papers.title: Triviality of metric fibrations over locally finite metric graphs
papers.abstract: In this note, we give a direct proof that every metric fibration over a geodesic metric space locally modeled on finite metric stars is isometrically isomorphic, over its base, to the $\ell^1$ product of its base and a fiber. Neither compactness nor completeness of the base is assumed. We also construct a nontrivial example over a closed interval with a truncated metric, showing that the local star condition alone does not imply the conclusion.

papers.title: Equivariant Quantisation of Hypertoric Varieties via Symplectic Cuts
papers.abstract: We study the equivariant geometric quantisation of a non-compact hypertoric orbifold of complex dimension $2n$ by compact symplectic cuts. When the defining arrangement has a non-empty bounded base region and the fixed lift is integral, we prove that, at every positive regular integral level $d$, the space of sections on the cut is the sum of the fibre-rotation weight spaces of weight at most $d$ in the original quantisation. The higher cohomology of the cut pre-quantum line orbibundle vanishes, so its equivariant index is the character of its actual section space. Using the moment polyptychs introduced in a companion paper, we give an orbifold Kawasaki-Riemann-Roch localisation formula for this character. We also compute it as a weighted lattice-point sum: a residual weight $x$ occurs at level $d$ if and only if the arrangement slack function satisfies $\mathcal{S}(x) \leq d$, with multiplicity $\binom{d - \mathcal{S}(x) + n}{n}$. The examples compare these calculations in rank one, including a cut with an orbifold point, and in rank two, for smooth cuts that are not toric.

papers.title: Fine-Tuning an Order-Flow Foundation Model for Sub-Second Forecasting
papers.abstract:
Generative models have become the standard approach in language and vision. These models are typically pretrained first and then fine-tuned. Recent work demonstrates how to pretrain an autoregressive generative model on Level-3 order-flow data. However, to our knowledge, no one has fine-tuned such a model yet for downstream tasks.
  Here we first pretrain a 300M-parameter generative model on Level-3 order-flow data collected from two crypto exchanges, Bitstamp and Bitfinex. Then we fine-tune the pretrained model to predict the microprice return and its realized volatility. We show that our fine-tuned model outperforms classical baselines, such as gradient boosting on handcrafted features, in predicting microprice returns over sub-second horizons. Furthermore, the predictive ability of the model transfers zero-shot to assets it was never fine-tuned on. Due to the short-term nature of these forecasts, the predicted microprice moves are smaller than the bid-ask spread plus fees, so the natural applications are in execution and market making.
  These results indicate that a pretrained generative model can be turned into a competitive short-horizon price forecaster via fine-tuning.
papers.intro:
Level-3 market data is a sequence of orders that market participants send to the exchange. Recent work (Kawawa-Beaudan et al., 2026; Sood et al., 2026) shows that a generative model can be trained to autoregressively predict the next event in the order sequence, one event at a time. For most financial markets, including the crypto markets we model here, the orders arrive at high frequency, often hundreds of orders per second. At the same time submitting your own order to an exchange might take more than 100 ms and receiving data from the exchange takes tens of milliseconds as well (Jha et al., 2020; Albers et al., 2025; Foley et al., 2023). Hence a market participant will want to know the market prices hundreds of milliseconds in advance, which is a much longer horizon than just one order ahead. So a generative model predicting the next order by itself cannot be used directly to answer practical questions such as “is it a good idea to submit a limit order at bid right now”, as by the time the order arrives to the exchange it will be outside of the modeling horizon of the generative model.

To convert the order flow into a form a neural network can consume, we tokenize the orders (Kawawa-Beaudan et al., 2026; Sood et al., 2026). In our approach we normally convert one order into one token, so ten buy limit orders will be converted into ten tokens in the sequence. Crypto exchanges also allow their participants to modify resting orders by changing the price or size. These update orders we convert into two separate orders, a delete and an add, with the same timestamp.

The microprice prediction is done for several horizons: 200 ms, 500 ms, 1, 2, 5, 10 and 30 seconds. For each of these horizons our model predicts the change in microprice and its volatility. We then benchmark the fine-tuned model against classical benchmarks such as gradient boosting and GARCH. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the fine-tuned model can be applied zero-shot to new assets it has not been fine-tuned on and is capable of beating basic baselines there.

papers.title: Monotone Rearrangement for Flattening Weights $F_2$
papers.abstract: We consider a subclass of the Muckenhoupt $A_2$ weights with added smoothness, which we refer to as flattening weights $F_2.$ We quantify how such weights arise as exponents of VMO functions and prove that monotone rearrangement does not increase the class modulus in $F_2.$

papers.title: Verifiable Agentic Traffic Class: A Policed Quality-of-Service Mechanism for Agentic AI Traffic, Evaluated from Simulation to Real-Kernel Adversarial Testing
papers.abstract: Software agents built on large language models generate traffic unlike human web traffic, yet routers have no class for it and cannot verify a sender's claim to be an agent. This paper proposes the Verifiable Agentic Traffic Class (VATC), which combines a reserved Differentiated Services Code Point (DSCP) value declaring agent traffic, a router-side classifier that demotes flows contradicting the declaration to a class served after best-effort traffic, and a rate-limited priority queue. VATC was compared with static Differentiated Services (DiffServ), a dedicated class that trusts the marking, and fq_codel, a per-flow fair-queuing scheduler, in two simulators and on a real Linux kernel. VATC matched DiffServ under steady load. In a constructed burst it cut mean agent queuing delay by 98% relative to DiffServ in simulation (assuming an immediate verdict), at a 12% increase in human delay; most of the gain came from the separate class. Under a spoofed flood in the kernel, the rate limit held human latency 11 times below DiffServ's. Without verification, DiffServ and a tightly configured fq_codel gave legitimate agents lower latency than VATC; a live four-feature classifier then demoted all 20 bulk-shaped spoofers and gave agents 0.30 ms, but missed six spoofers that copied the agent pattern. With emulated network delay, a timing feature of the classifier stopped separating agent from human flows. In real agent harnesses on a congested link, router queueing took 13% to 63% of task time, depending on harness and assumed model latency. The traffic was synthetic or sandbox-scale.
papers.intro:
Software agents built on large language models (LLMs) plan multi-step tasks, call external tools, and exchange messages with models and with other agents. In this paper, agentic traffic means the network traffic these agents produce, in particular the chains of dependent request and response exchanges between an agent, the inference services it calls, and the tools it invokes. An artificial intelligence (AI) gateway is a middleware component, such as a proxy, service, or library, through which an organization channels and mediates such calls [1]. Cisco’s 2026 wide-area network (WAN) analysis reports that AI inference flows differ measurably from ordinary web flows in duration, rate, and direction, and projects that AI inference could account for about a quarter of network traffic by 2035 [2]. These figures come from one vendor’s measurements and model and describe inference flows rather than agent sessions as such; Section III-A gives them with their limits.

Two problems follow. First, standard router quality-of-service (QoS) mechanisms have no class for agentic traffic, so a latency-sensitive agent call shares queues with web and bulk transfers (Section II). Second, any new priority marking invites misuse: a flow can claim agent status to obtain priority, so a marking is useful only if it can be checked.

VATC has three components: an enumerated Agentic QoS Identifier (AQI) mapped to a reserved Differentiated Services Code Point (DSCP) at ingress; a router-side verification engine that compares the declared marking with observed flow behavior and demotes flows that do not match; and a dedicated agentic queue that is served first but policed to a fixed rate, so that errors in verification cannot let marked traffic take the whole link.

papers.title: Semantic Chains: From Reachable Facts to Justified Answers
papers.abstract: How can the facts that justify an answer be found from a question and presented as a sequence of connected statements? This paper models a context as a graph of logical facts and takes as given which expressions represent each fact. A parent fact can express a relation among its subfacts, and a preserving edge allows the content of a subfact to be recovered within a full representation of its parent. Suppose a root fact justifies the full answer and a path of preserving edges leads from that root to a fact that designates an object shared by the question and the answer. Under the conditions of the model, a search starting from the objects in the question reaches the root and covers every fact in the selected expansion. The root then admits a text that forms a single link connecting the question to the full answer and justifying it. For chains with several links, the paper gives a complete enumeration of candidate orders within the stated class and specifies when the link texts jointly preserve the justification and support every transition.

papers.title: Examples of homological mirror symmetry via Zariski descent
papers.abstract: This paper considers a general setting in which the Fukaya category of an exact symplectic manifold may be decomposed as a fiber product of Fukaya categories of smaller pieces. We establish a property of Fukaya categories that is mirror to Zariski descent of coherent sheaves. This fits into a natural strategy to prove homological mirror symmetry by a local-to-global analysis. The examples we consider in detail are open Riemann surfaces and exact log Calabi-Yau surfaces, and we provide proofs of homological mirror symmetry in these cases.

papers.intro:
In this paper, we present a general strategy for proving homological mirror symmetry (HMS) for a given manifold by reducing the problem to HMS for smaller manifolds. It applies to some exact symplectic manifolds, including log Calabi-Yau surfaces with exact symplectic structure, and open Riemann surfaces (that is, affine complex curves). While these results are not new, the method is interesting because it is the mirror counterpart of Zariski descent for coherent sheaves in algebraic geometry.

papers.title: Poisson boundaries of lattices in locally compact groups
papers.abstract: For a random walk on a general locally compact group we provide a discretization procedure transforming the walk to one on a lattice of the group, preserving the Poisson boundary and some finiteness of moments.
papers.intro:
The Poisson-Furstenberg boundary is a powerful measure-theoretic object associated to a general Markov chain, which keeps track of the asymptotic behaviour of the chain as well as bounded harmonic functions for that chain. If the Markov chain happens to be a right random walk on a group, say GG with law μ\mu, the Poisson boundary inherits a measure-class preserving GG-action, which is both amenable in the sense of Zimmer and ergodic. Moreover, it is μ\mu-stationary, and it is in a sense the maximal such object, all μ\mu-stationary GG-spaces being (measure-preserving extensions of) a factor of the Poisson boundary. Finally, if the step measure μ\mu is symmetric, the Poisson boundary is the prime example of a strong boundary in the sense of Bader-Furman Bader and Furman (2014), opening up the door for a number of applications to rigidity theory if its combinatorics is well understood Bader and Furman (2014); Bader et al. (2025); Guirardel et al. (2022); Derimay (2025).

(2025); Guirardel et al. (2022); Derimay (2025).

Hence the Poisson boundary is a versatile object, whose understanding can be used in a number of contexts and applications. Amenability of the GG-action in particular means that for any compact metrizable space XX on which GG acts, there is a GG-equivariant map from the Poisson boundary of GG to the set of probability measures on GG. What Furstenberg noticed in Furstenberg (1973) is that this property passes to lattices in GG: if Γ\Gamma is a lattice in GG and μ\mu is a “reasonable” measure on GG, then for any compact metrizable Γ\Gamma-space XX there is a Γ\Gamma-map from the Poisson boundary of GG to the space of probability measures on XX. This fact then turns out to be a crucial ingredient of the celebrated Margulis superrigidity and normal subgroup theorems (see Margulis (1991), the discretization procedure is Proposition VI.4.1).

The proof of Furstenberg’s result hinges on a “discretization procedure”, the idea of which has then been improved several times in the context of Brownian motion on Riemannian manifolds, first by Lyons and Sullivan in Lyons and Sullivan (1984), see also Kaimanovich (1992); Ballmann and Ledrappier (1996), where it is proven that for a big enough discrete subset of the manifold, there is a Markov chain on this subset for which the restrictions of bounded harmonic functions on the manifold are harmonic, and the datum of this restriction is enough to recover the whole function. In other words, the Poisson boundaries of the manifold and the Markov chain are naturally isomorphic.

papers.title: An Archival Search for Outer Solar System Objects in the NOIRLab Source Catalog DR2: 65 Candidates, Including Four L4 Neptune Trojans
papers.abstract: I search the single-epoch detections of the NOIRLab Source Catalog DR2 (DECam, 2012-2019) for outer Solar System objects. Single-night detections are linked with a bound orbit model, vetted against artefacts, static sources and known objects, and confirmed by forced measurements on at least two new archival nights. The linker recovers 96% of known objects present on four nights in one sky tile, but end-to-end recall is about 7%, limited by cadence, tiling and catalogue incompleteness; no selection function is provided. Of 81 catalogue objects, four are designated; of the other 77, 53 are in evidence class A (multi-opposition, at least nine nights), 12 in class B and 12 in class C (not counted). On exposures never used in a fit, forced photometry detects 41 testable objects at 99% of predicted positions, as for known TNOs, against 6% at control positions; 22 pass a post hoc rule, 19 are inconclusive, none fails. Shifted controls were never confirmed by the archival image search (0 of 11,467) but were in 2.2% of trials by the catalogue precovery behind most scripted confirmations, so its nights alone are not sufficient. For the 65 class A and B candidates, 10-Myr integrations give four candidate L4 Neptune Trojans with 13-19 yr arcs, 21 resonant, 13 detached, nine scattering, two Centaurs and 16 classical objects; a detached class-B candidate has q=48.8 au. No object beyond 80 au was confirmed, which barely constrains Planet Nine. Positions are withheld until designation or 2027 June 30; their digests are published.

papers.title: Regularity of $Q$-valued $C^1$ harmonic functions with applications to stable minimal hypersurfaces
papers.abstract:
We show that the derivative of a $Q$-valued $C^1$ function on an $n$-dimensional domain that is locally harmonic on its regular set is locally Dirichlet minimising, and that its branch set coincides with that of its derivative. As a consequence, we get that a $Q$-valued $C^1$ harmonic function is $C^{1,\alpha}$ and that its branch set is countably $(n-2)$-rectifiable when $n\geq 3$ and discrete when $n=2$.
  Our methods are directly applicable to the regularity theory of stable minimal hypersurfaces. We show that a multi-valued Lipschitz function whose graph is a two-sided, properly immersed, stable minimal $n$-dimensional hypersurface with locally $\mathcal{H}^{n-2}$-finite singular set, and whose Lipschitz constant is sufficiently small is in fact multi-valued $C^{1,\alpha}$. As a consequence, we obtain optimal regularity conclusions for a branched sheeting theorem of Bellettini for singular immersions.
  When $n=2$, we obtain stronger conclusions and show that locally about a branch point, a $Q$-valued $C^1$ harmonic function is the real part of a Dirichlet minimiser which is itself obtained from a finite number of holomorphic functions via classical branching, thus giving a full series expansion for the function near the branch point. Furthermore, we prove that the class of branched, two-sided, properly immersed, stable minimal surfaces with isolated singularities is compact under varifold convergence.

papers.title: Earlybird: Predictive Streaming Speech Recognition in 29M Parameters
papers.abstract: Streaming speech recognizers output a word only after the speaker has finished it, typically 90-400 ms later. For a voice agent every millisecond counts: the sooner the words are outputted, the sooner the agent can start a search or plan its reply. We present Earlybird, a 29M-parameter streaming recognizer (16.8 MB at 4 bits). Earlybird learns from audio cut off at random points, including partway through a word, and is asked to predict every word that is due by then in full, plus a guess of the next two words. Its raw token probabilities give a confidence for every word including the one still being spoken. On clean audiobook speech (LibriSpeech test-clean), the median word is predicted correctly 90 ms before the speaker finishes it, while released streaming models get it 90 to 400 ms after it ends. Earlybird is the earliest on all six test sets we time, covering audiobooks, TED talks, public speech, earnings calls, and synthetic speech. On the same audiobooks, 69% of words are predicted correctly before they end, against 3-25% for the other models. For words still being spoken, confidence is calibrated, with an expected calibration error (ECE) of 3.7 to 5.5. On the eight English Open ASR Leaderboard sets, it is more accurate than Moonshine Tiny on every set and roughly ties Whistle, a model of the same size.
papers.intro:
A spoken request to a voice agent reaches the agent as text. With a streaming recognizer, each word of that text arrives a few hundred milliseconds after the speaker finished saying it. For a voice agent, that delay is time it could have spent starting a search or planning a reply while the speaker is still talking.

People listening to speech do not wait for the end of a word to know what it is. Most words can be recognized from their first few phonemes in context, and the next word is often predictable. We ask whether a small on-device recognizer can do the same: predict each word from its first sounds, guess the word after it, and say how sure it is.

We ask whether a small on-device recognizer can do the same: predict each word from its first sounds, guess the word after it, and say how sure it is.

Earlybird trains on utterances cut off at random 80 ms steps, which is exactly the position a streaming model is in at each update. The target is every word that is due at that point, written in full even if its audio has only begun, followed by an end marker and the next two words of the transcript as a guess. Because the targets for successive cut points only ever extend one another, the model also learns not to output what it will later take back. Every word it outputs carries the product of its token probabilities as a confidence.

papers.title: One Policy for 100 Household Tasks: Our Solution for the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge
papers.abstract: We describe our solution for the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge: 100 long-horizon household tasks in the OmniGibson simulator. We placed 9th on the final leaderboard, the only independent team in the top 10. The core of the solution is a single vision-language-action (VLA) model, one checkpoint for all 100 tasks, built on our 1st-place 2025 solution, which is based on $\pi_{0.5}$. On the 50 tasks shared with 2025, its Q rises from 0.260 to 0.371; across all 100 tasks it scores 0.392. Our main conclusion from 2025 was that the model was undertrained, so most of the 2026 work went into training the model for longer, optimizing some training parameters, making each training step slightly faster and reducing the gradient noise: a migration from 50 to 100 tasks (semantic stages built from the demonstrations' skill annotations, task and stage embeddings of new tasks warm-started from similar old ones, and a 21-dimensional action space matching the teleoperation controls); variance-reduced multi-sample flow matching with a simple noise-vs-compute model that picks the number of action-expert samples per observation without ablations; and a 200k-step training run, about one pass over the 211M frames of the demonstrations. A cloud evaluation infrastructure keeps a shared record with provenance, episode diagnostics and restorable simulator states, and runs six simulators on one GPU together faster than real time. On top of the learned policy, 14 tasks are routed to a GPT-6 Astra coding agent that controls the robot through observation and motion tools, starting every episode from a frozen copy of its own practice session on training instances. Across these 14 tasks, Astra's mean Q is 0.639, against 0.108 for the learned policy. The public submission included only part of the Astra results and scored 0.446 Q with 27.3% full-task success.

papers.intro:
The BEHAVIOR Challenge [4, 3] evaluates robot policies on long-horizon household activities in the OmniGibson simulator, built on NVIDIA Isaac Sim. The 2026 edition doubles the 2025 task set: 100 activities, from turning on a radio to cooking a meal, each with 200 teleoperated demonstrations (20,000 episodes, 211M frames or about 1,950 hours, in the LeRobot [6] format). The robot is the same Galaxea R1Pro: a holonomic base, a 4-joint torso and two 7-DOF arms with parallel grippers, observed through a head camera and two wrist cameras plus proprioception. An episode is a full success if all goal predicates are satisfied, which scores 1. Otherwise its q-score (we also call it Q) is the fraction of satisfied predicates. Scores are averaged over instances and then over tasks. The time limit of an episode is 1.5×\times the mean duration of the human demonstrations of the task (2×\times in 2025). The 50 tasks of 2025 are included with the same demonstrations; the other 50 are new.

Vision-language-action models (VLAs) fine-tune a pretrained vision-language model to output robot actions [8]. The π0\pi_{0} family [9, 10] pairs a PaliGemma VLM [15] with a smaller “action expert” trained by flow matching [18] to generate chunks of continuous actions, optionally co-trained with discrete FAST action tokens [12]. Many alternatives have appeared since, such as GR00T [13] and, increasingly prominent, MolmoAct2 [14]. Yet more than a year after its release (paper in April 2025, code and weights in September 2025 [11]), π0.5\pi_{0.5} is still widely used as a base for fine-tuning: both top 2025 BEHAVIOR solutions were built on it [1, 7]. We built our 2026 solution on top of our 2025 one, so we kept its π0.5\pi_{0.5}-based architecture. For this reason, in parts of this report we call our learned policy simply π0.5\pi_{0.5}.

Our 2025 solution [1] won the first BEHAVIOR Challenge. It took π0.5\pi_{0.5} and changed the following: trainable task embeddings instead of text prompts, correlated noise for flow matching, a learnable mixture of all VLM layers’ keys and values for the action expert, a stage-prediction head with voting (“System 2”), a FAST auxiliary loss, several flow samples per VLM forward pass, and correlation-aware inpainting at inference. The 2025 checkpoints were clearly undertrained: the loss was still falling when the deadline came, and four checkpoints split the 50 tasks between them. The LeHome Challenge solution [2] of one of our team members was built on top of the 2025 BEHAVIOR solution and introduced several engineering fixes and improvements that we inherit here as well. The 2025 runner-up [7] also starts from π0.5\pi_{0.5} and studies the effect of image resolution, of the training data and of rejection-sampling fine-tuning.

papers.title: On the symplectic cohomology of orbifold divisor complements
papers.abstract: This article studies the symplectic cohomology of Liouville domains whose contact boundaries admit a periodic Reeb flow, with a particular focus on affine varieties which arise as orbifold divisor complements. We describe a computation of the transverse Conley-Zehnder indices which allows for a simple computation of the positive equivariant symplectic cohomology in cases when the inertia orbifold of the compactifying divisor has only even cohomology. This is then applied to the classification of orbifold compactifications of $\mathbb{C}^n$. Moreover, we study the action of multiplication by the principal orbit on V-shaped symplectic cohomology and prove that if the compactification $(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{D})$ is positively monotone, then this class induces a periodic structure on symplectic cohomology, reducing the problem of computing an infinite-dimensional group to a finite-dimensional repeating portion. We combine the index computations and this periodic structure to compute the symplectic cohomology of various Milnor fibers of surface singularities, the rational homology balls $B_{p,1}$ as well as complements of star-shaped configurations of rational curves in K3 surfaces, which includes the Milnor fibers of the exceptional unimodal singularities.

papers.title: Pterodactyl: Pushing the Limits of Efficient Automated Translation Evaluation
papers.abstract: In this paper, we present 1020 Group's submission to the WMT26 shared task on automated quality evaluation. Our system, Pterodactyl, was engineered specifically for subtasks 2 and 3, that is, segment-level quality score prediction and the detection of error-free segments. Pterodactyl is a highly customizable, ultra-low cost system optimized for binary classification in translation triage and data curation. It is based on an LLM-as-a-judge approach, with prompt engineering and model selection guided by ROC analysis. We also developed several variants of Pterodactyl that were specifically adapted for subtasks 3.
papers.intro:
In recent WMT competitions, reference-free quality estimation (QE) systems based on an LLM-as-a-judge approach have gained increasing traction for automated translation quality evaluation Lavie et al. (2025); Freitag et al. (2024); Zerva et al. (2024). However, the development and deployment of such systems can be complex and costly. Here, we develop an efficient, production-oriented strategy for pushing the cost-performance frontier of automated translation evaluation: achieving better task-specific performance with faster and cheaper models and prompt configurations.
